title: מבנה הסוגיות – Zevachim
note: חלוקה לסוגיות ולשלבי הדיון שנוצרה בבינה מלאכותית באתר talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: all offerings slaughtered not for their own name are valid but do not fulfill the owner's obligation, except for the Pesach offering in its time and the Chatat at all times. Rabbi Eliezer adds the Asham, and other opinions introduce further distinctions regarding slaughtering for the name of a higher or lower sanctity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the general rule: all offerings slaughtered not for their own name are valid but do not fulfill the owner's obligation, except for the Pesach offering in its time and the Chatat at all times.
Rabbi Eliezer adds the Asham to the list of offerings that are invalid when slaughtered not for their own name, reasoning by analogy from the Chatat.
Yosei ben Choni states that offerings slaughtered for the name of Pesach or Chatat are invalid.
Shimon Achi Azaryah introduces a distinction: slaughtering for a higher sanctity is valid, but for a lower sanctity is invalid.

The Mishnah illustrates Shimon's rule with examples: קָדְשֵׁי קָדָשִׁים (most holy offerings) slaughtered for קֳדָשִׁים קַלִּים (lesser holy offerings) are invalid, while the reverse is valid; similarly, בכור (firstborn) and מעשר (tithe) slaughtered for שלמים (peace offerings) are valid, but the reverse is invalid.

items.text: Gemara's question on Mishnah's phrasing
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Mishnah's phrasing
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah says 'אֶלָּא שֶׁלֹּא עָלוּ' (but they do not count) instead of simply 'וְלֹא עָלוּ' (and they do not count). It answers that the extra word teaches that while they do not fulfill the owner's obligation, they retain their sanctity and it is forbidden to change their designation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah uses the word 'אֶלָּא' (but) instead of 'וְ' (and) in the phrase 'אֶלָּא שֶׁלֹּא עָלוּ' (but they do not count).
The Gemara answers that the word 'אֶלָּא' teaches that while the offerings do not fulfill the owner's obligation, they retain their sanctity and it is forbidden to change their designation.

items.text: Support from Rava
items.text_en: Support from Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rava's statement that if an olah was slaughtered not for its own name, it is forbidden to sprinkle its blood not for its own name, reinforcing the principle that one may not change the offering's designation.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that if an olah was slaughtered not for its own name, it is forbidden to sprinkle its blood not for its own name, reinforcing the principle that one may not change the offering's designation.

items.text: Two alternative rationales
items.text_en: Two alternative rationales
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents two alternative explanations for the prohibition: one based on logic (since one has changed the offering, why continue to change it?) and one based on a verse (Deuteronomy 23:24), which implies that one must fulfill exactly what was vowed, not a substitute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara announces that two alternative rationales will be presented for the prohibition against changing the offering's designation: one based on logic and one based on a verse.
The Gemara presents the logical rationale: since one has already changed the offering's designation once, why continue to change it further?
The Gemara presents the verse-based rationale: citing Deuteronomy 23:24, which implies that one must fulfill exactly what was vowed, not a substitute.

items.text: Gemara's initial question on changing a vow
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question on changing a vow
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one may change a vow from a sacrifice to a freewill offering, and whether a freewill offering can be altered at all.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's implication that one can change a vow (נדר) into a freewill offering (נדבה), asking whether a freewill offering can be altered at all.
The Gemara asks whether a freewill offering (נדבה) is permitted to be changed at all.

items.text: Ravina's anecdote about Rava's teaching
items.text_en: Ravina's anecdote about Rava's teaching
items.desc_en: Ravina tells Rav Pappa that Rava resolved a contradiction between two sources regarding the validity of unspecified intent.

sub.desc_en: Ravina tells Rav Pappa that he missed Rava's resolution of a contradiction between two sources regarding the validity of unspecified intent.

items.text: Rava's resolution: sacrifices vs. gittin
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: sacrifices vs. gittin
items.desc_en: Rava contrasts the Mishnah in Zevachim, where unspecified sacrifices are valid, with gittin, where unspecified intent invalidates a get, explaining that sacrifices are inherently for their own sake while a woman is not assumed to be for divorce.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'excellent matters' Rava juxtaposed, citing the Mishnah that all sacrifices offered שלא לשמן (not for their own sake) are valid, implying that unspecified intent (סתמא) is also considered לשמן (for their own sake).
The Gemara raises a contradiction: a get written שלא לשם אשה (not for the sake of a specific woman) is invalid, and even an unspecified get is invalid, unlike sacrifices.

Rava resolves the contradiction: sacrifices are inherently designated for their own sake (לשמן), so unspecified intent is valid, but a woman is not assumed to be standing for divorce, so unspecified intent in a get is invalid.

items.text: Seeking proof for validity of unspecified sacrifices
items.text_en: Seeking proof for validity of unspecified sacrifices
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to derive the rule from various tannaitic sources, but each proof is deflected by alternative explanations, such as the principle that the act follows initial intent or that the end clarifies the beginning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that unspecified sacrifices are valid, and proposes a proof from the Mishnah that only explicitly 'not for their sake' is invalid, implying that unspecified is valid; it then deflects a counter-proof from the parallel case of a get.

The Gemara proposes a second proof from the Mishnah's case of 'for the sake of Pesach and for the sake of Shelamim', where the explicit mention of two intentions implies that a single unspecified intention is valid.
The Gemara deflects the proof by suggesting that the case is different because the person acts based on his initial intention, so the end does not clarify the beginning.
The Gemara proposes a third proof from the second clause of the Mishnah, where the explicit mention of two intentions again implies that an unspecified intention is valid.
The Gemara deflects the third proof by suggesting that the end clarifies the beginning, so the case is not a proof for unspecified sacrifices.
The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the Tanna simply paired the two cases for stylistic symmetry, not to teach a halachic principle.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Yosei's statement about the six names
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Yosei's statement about the six names
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yosei's ruling that a sacrifice offered without any specific intent is valid due to a court condition, proving that unspecified intent is valid; otherwise the court would not institute a condition that invalidates.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah listing six names for which a sacrifice is offered, including a sin-offering and guilt-offering for sin.

Rabbi Yosei rules that even one who had no specific intent for any of these names is valid, because the court instituted a condition that one should not explicitly say 'for its name' lest one come to say 'not for its name'.
The Gemara argues that if unspecified intent were invalid, the court would not institute a condition that could lead to invalidation, proving that unspecified intent is valid.

items.text: Seeking proof for invalidity of unspecified gittin
items.text_en: Seeking proof for invalidity of unspecified gittin
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to derive the rule for gittin from a baraita about a man hearing scribes practice, but Rav Pappa deflects by explaining the scribes were merely learning, not writing for divorce.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that an unspecified get (גט) is invalid?
The Gemara proposes deriving the rule from a baraita (תנן) about a man who hears scribes reciting a get formula and declares it matches his name and his wife's name — the get is invalid for divorce.
Rav Pappa deflects the proof: the scribes were merely learning (להתלמד) and the document was never written for the purpose of divorce (לשום כריתות) at all.

items.text: Transition to another source
items.text_en: Transition to another source
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite another source to prove the rule for gittin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara transitions to cite another source to prove the rule for gittin.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation: Get written for another woman
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation: Get written for another woman
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one wrote a get to divorce his wife, changed his mind, and then found a fellow townsman with matching names, the get is invalid for divorcing the second woman.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites the case of one who wrote a get for his wife, changed his mind, and then found a fellow townsman with matching names — the get is invalid for divorcing the second woman.

items.text: First rejection: Designated for the first woman
items.text_en: First rejection: Designated for the first woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof because the get was initially designated for the first woman's divorce, so it cannot be used for another.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, arguing that the case is different because the get was initially designated for the first woman's divorce.

items.text: Second Mishnah citation: Two wives with same name
items.text_en: Second Mishnah citation: Two wives with same name
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another Mishnah: if one has two wives with the same name and writes a get for the older one, he cannot use it for the younger one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah: if one has two wives with the same name and writes a get for the older one, he cannot use it for the younger one.

items.text: Second rejection: Designated for that woman
items.text_en: Second rejection: Designated for that woman
items.desc_en: Again, the Gemara rejects because the get was designated for the older woman's divorce.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes: perhaps it differs there because he explicitly designated it for that woman's divorce.

items.text: Third Mishnah citation: Blank get for any woman
items.text_en: Third Mishnah citation: Blank get for any woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a case where one tells a scribe to write a get for whichever woman he chooses, and it is invalid due to lack of retroactive clarification (ברירה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: one who writes blank get forms must leave place for the man, woman, witnesses, date, and the clause 'you are permitted to any man'. Rav Yehuda said Shmuel said: also must leave place for 'you are permitted to any man'.

items.text: Third rejection: No retroactive clarification
items.text_en: Third rejection: No retroactive clarification
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects because the invalidity stems from the principle of אין ברירה, not from lack of specific intent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: perhaps it differs there because there is no ברירה (deterministic choice).

items.text: Fourth Mishnah citation: Blank get forms
items.text_en: Fourth Mishnah citation: Blank get forms
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites that one writing blank get forms must leave spaces for names and the formula, and Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel that one must also leave space for 'הרי את מותרת לכל אדם'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: one who writes blank get forms must leave place for the man, woman, witnesses, date, and the clause 'you are permitted to any man'. Rav Yehuda said Shmuel said: also must leave place for 'you are permitted to any man'.
Rav Yehuda adds in the name of Shmuel that one must also leave space for the formula 'הרי את מותרת לכל אדם' (you are permitted to any man).

items.text: Analogy from sacrifices and resolution
items.text_en: Analogy from sacrifices and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from Rav Yehuda's ruling that a sin-offering slaughtered for the sake of a burnt-offering is invalid, but for the sake of non-sacred meat is valid, implying that only a change within its category invalidates. It then resolves by distinguishing between a get for a gentile woman (which is invalid because removing her leaves a blank, which is invalid) and sacrifices where removing non-sacred leaves a valid default.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from Rav Yehuda's ruling that a sin-offering slaughtered for the sake of a burnt-offering is invalid, but for the sake of non-sacred meat is valid, implying that only a change within its category invalidates.

The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that any get written not for a specific woman is invalid, even if written for a gentile woman, contradicting the principle that only a change within its category invalidates.

The Gemara resolves by distinguishing: in a get, removing the gentile woman leaves a blank (סתמא) which is invalid, while in sacrifices, removing non-sacred meat leaves a valid default (סתמא) of sacred intent.

items.text: Second analogy from sacrifices and resolution
items.text_en: Second analogy from sacrifices and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another contradiction from the same ruling of Rav Yehuda, comparing it to a Mishnah about an oven partitioned by boards where a dead creeping animal in one part does not affect the other. It resolves that non-sacred meat relative to sacrifices is like a partition relative to an oven—it has no effect at all, so it does not invalidate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises another contradiction: Rav Yehuda said Rav ruled that a sin-offering slaughtered for the sake of a burnt-offering is invalid, but for the sake of non-sacred meat is valid, implying that only something of its own kind invalidates, not something foreign.

The Gemara cites a baraita that teaches the principle of 'its interior' (תוכו) and not 'the interior of its interior', and even a washbasin interposed saves from impurity, contradicting the idea that a foreign substance has no effect.

The Gemara resolves: non-sacred meat relative to sacrifices is like a partition relative to an oven — just as a partition has no effect on the oven's impurity status, so non-sacred meat has no effect on the sacrifice's validity.

The Gemara cites a Mishnah about an oven partitioned by boards or curtains, where a dead creeping animal in one part makes everything impure, and Rabbi Eliezer's dissenting view that a washbasin interposed saves from impurity.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's kal vachomer and rejection
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's kal vachomer and rejection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that if a partition saves from the severe impurity of a corpse, it should certainly save from the lighter impurity of a clay vessel. The Sages reject this argument.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer opens with a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if a partition saves from the severe impurity of a corpse, it should certainly save from the lighter impurity of a clay vessel.
The Sages reject Rabbi Eliezer's argument with a simple 'no'.

items.text: Opening kal vachomer argument
items.text_en: Opening kal vachomer argument
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a kal vachomer: if a clay vessel can protect in the case of a severe impurity (corpse), it should certainly protect in the case of a light impurity (a clay vessel itself).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if a clay vessel protects in the case of severe corpse impurity, it should certainly protect in the case of light impurity from a clay vessel.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Eliezer's position
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Eliezer's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the kal vachomer for the Rabbis, but for Rabbi Eliezer, what can be said? It then notes that Rabbi Eliezer himself uses a kal vachomer, and challenges that if so, the same logic should apply elsewhere: sacred items can desecrate sacred items, so surely non-sacred items should be able to desecrate sacred items?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the kal vachomer argument works for the Rabbis, but asks what can be said for Rabbi Eliezer's position.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Eliezer himself employs a kal vachomer argument.

The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Eliezer uses a kal vachomer, the same logic should apply elsewhere: sacred items can desecrate sacred items, so surely non-sacred items should be able to desecrate sacred items.

items.text: Rav's reasoning and the need for a verse
items.text_en: Rav's reasoning and the need for a verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav's reasoning follows Rabbi Elazar, who derives from a verse that sacred items can desecrate sacred items but non-sacred items cannot. This shows that a verse overrides the kal vachomer; here too, the word 'tokho' should override the kal vachomer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav's reasoning follows Rabbi Elazar, who derives from a verse that sacred items can desecrate sacred items but non-sacred items cannot.
The Gemara asks: since a verse overrides the kal vachomer there, why should the word 'tokho' not also override the kal vachomer here?

items.text: Alternative use of 'tokho'
items.text_en: Alternative use of 'tokho'
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the word 'tokho' is needed for a different case: foods mixed with clay and placed in the airspace of an oven. The Rabbis do not need this verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the word 'תּוֹכוֹ' (its interior) is needed to teach that foods mixed with clay and placed in the airspace of an oven are susceptible to טומאה (ritual impurity) from the oven's airspace, countering a possible leniency.
The Rabbis note that they do not need this verse for that derivation, implying their own alternative understanding.

items.text: Rav Yosef bar Ami's contradiction on change of owner
items.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Ami's contradiction on change of owner
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Ami raises a contradiction between two rulings of Rav: one regarding a sin-offering slaughtered for a different type of offering (change of designation) and another regarding a sin-offering slaughtered for a different person (change of owner). He resolves it by citing verses: for change of owner, the verse 'and he shall slaughter it for a sin-offering' applies, while for change of person, the verse 'and he shall atone for him' excludes a fellow who is not similarly obligated.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Ami raises a contradiction between two rulings of Rav regarding change of designation and change of owner.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Ami's first premise
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Ami's first premise
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Ami cites Rav's ruling that a sin-offering slaughtered for a different type of offering is invalid, implying that a change within the same type does not invalidate.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Ami's second premise
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Ami's second premise
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Ami cites Rav's contradictory ruling that a sin-offering slaughtered for a person obligated for a sin-offering is invalid, while for a person obligated for a burnt-offering it is valid.
Rav Yosef bar Ami resolves the contradiction by citing the verse 'and he shall slaughter it for a sin-offering' for change of designation, which validates the same type.
Rav Yosef bar Ami cites the verse 'and he shall atone for him' for change of owner, which excludes a fellow who is not similarly obligated.

items.text: Rav Chaviva's contradiction on 'tokho'
items.text_en: Rav Chaviva's contradiction on 'tokho'
items.desc_en: Rav Chaviva raises a contradiction between Rav's ruling on change of owner and the law of 'tokho' that even a vessel that can be rinsed saves. He resolves it by noting that four instances of 'tokho' are written, each for a different derivation: one for the basic law, one for a gezerah shavah, one for 'tokho of this and not of another', and one for 'tokho and not the inside of the inside'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chaviva raises a contradiction between Rav's ruling on change of owner and the law of 'tokho' that even a vessel that can be rinsed saves.

Rav Chaviva resolves the contradiction by noting that four instances of 'tokho' are written, each for a different derivation: one for the basic law, one for a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy), one for 'tokho of this and not of another', and one for 'tokho and not the inside of the inside'.

items.text: Derivation of slaughter for the sake of the offering
items.text_en: Derivation of slaughter for the sake of the offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks where we learn that slaughter must be for the sake of the offering. It answers from the verse "וְאִם זֶבַח שְׁלָמִים קׇרְבָּנוֹ" — the extra word "זֶבַח" teaches that the slaughter must be for the sake of peace-offerings. The objection that this might just be the name of the offering is rejected by noting that elsewhere the Torah writes "הַמַּקְרִיב אֶת דַּם הַשְּׁלָמִים" without "זֶבַח", so here it is extra.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where we derive that slaughter must be performed for the sake of the offering, and answers from the verse "וְאִם זֶבַח שְׁלָמִים קׇרְבָּנוֹ" that the extra word "זֶבַח" teaches that slaughter must be for the sake of peace-offerings.
An objection is raised: perhaps the word "זֶבַח" is simply the name of the offering, not an extra teaching.

The objection is rejected by noting that elsewhere the Torah writes "הַמַּקְרִיב אֶת דַּם הַשְּׁלָמִים" without "זֶבַח", so here it is extra and teaches that slaughter must be for the sake of peace-offerings.

items.text: Attempt to derive other services from slaughter
items.text_en: Attempt to derive other services from slaughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found slaughter, but from where do we derive the other services? If you say we should learn from slaughter, it is rejected because slaughter has a unique stringency: it is invalidated if not done for the sake of the eaters in the Paschal offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found slaughter, but from where do we derive the other services?

The Gemara objects: if you say we should learn from slaughter, it is rejected because slaughter has a unique stringency — it is invalidated if not done for the sake of the eaters in the Paschal offering.

items.text: Derivation of receiving the blood for the sake of the offering
items.text_en: Derivation of receiving the blood for the sake of the offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives receiving the blood from the verse "הַמַּקְרִיב אֶת דַּם הַשְּׁלָמִים" — that receiving must be for the sake of peace-offerings. The objection that we should write this for receiving and learn slaughter from it is rejected because receiving has a unique stringency: it is invalid when performed by a non-priest or a woman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the derivation by citing the verse 'הַמַּקְרִיב אֶת דַּם הַשְּׁלָמִים' to teach that receiving the blood must be for the sake of peace-offerings.
An objection is raised: why not write the requirement for receiving and derive slaughter from it by analogy?
The objection is rejected because receiving has a unique stringency: it is invalid when performed by a non-priest or a woman, so slaughter cannot be derived from it.

items.text: Derivation of sprinkling for the sake of the offering
items.text_en: Derivation of sprinkling for the sake of the offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have slaughter and receiving, from where do we derive sprinkling? If you say learn from these, it is rejected because they require north (for certain offerings) and exist for inner sin-offerings. So the Gemara derives sprinkling from the verse "הַזּוֹרֵק אֶת דַּם הַשְּׁלָמִים" — that sprinkling must be for the sake of peace-offerings. The objection that we should write this for sprinkling and learn from it is rejected because sprinkling has a unique stringency: a non-priest is liable for death for performing it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have derived slaughter and receiving for the sake of peace-offerings, from where do we derive sprinkling?

The Gemara objects: if you say learn sprinkling from slaughter and receiving, those have unique stringencies — they require north (for certain offerings) and exist for inner sin-offerings — so the analogy fails.
The Gemara answers: rather, the verse 'הַזּוֹרֵק אֶת דַּם הַשְּׁלָמִים' (who sprinkles the blood of the peace-offerings) teaches that sprinkling must be for the sake of peace-offerings.
An objection is raised: let the Torah write the requirement for sprinkling alone and derive the other services from it.
The objection is rejected because sprinkling has a unique stringency: a non-priest (זר) is liable for death for performing it, so it cannot serve as a source for other services.

items.text: Derivation of conveying for the sake of the offering
items.text_en: Derivation of conveying for the sake of the offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have all these, from where do we derive conveying? If you say learn from all of them, it is rejected because they are services that cannot be nullified, whereas conveying can be nullified. So the Gemara derives conveying from the verse "וְהִקְרִיב אֶת הַכֹּל הַמִּזְבֵּחָה" — which the Master said refers to conveying limbs to the ramp. And it is taught that "וְהִקְרִיבוּ" refers to receiving the blood, and the Torah expressed it in the language of conveying to teach that conveying is not excluded from the category of receiving.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where we derive that the carrying of the blood to the altar must be for the sake of the offering, and considers learning from all the other services but rejects it because carrying can be omitted.

The Gemara answers that the verse "וְהִקְרִיב אֶת הַכֹּל הַמִּזְבֵּחָה" refers to carrying the limbs to the ramp, and a baraita teaches that "וְהִקְרִיבוּ" refers to receiving the blood, and the Torah used the language of carrying to indicate that carrying is not excluded from the category of receiving.

items.text: Derivation of change of owner from the verse
items.text_en: Derivation of change of owner from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found change of sanctity, from where do we derive change of owner? Rav Pinchas bar Rav Ami says the verse "וּבְשַׂר זֶבַח תּוֹדַת שְׁלָמָיו" teaches that slaughter must be for the sake of a thanksgiving-offering. If this is not needed for change of sanctity (derived elsewhere), apply it to change of owner. The Gemara objects that this verse is needed for the teaching of Abba Chanin in the name of Rabbi Eliezer about the difference between a thanksgiving-offering slaughtered for peace-offerings and vice versa. The Gemara responds that we are speaking from the word "זֶבַח". The Gemara further objects that it is needed to include sin-offering and guilt-offering. The Gemara answers that if so, the verse should have written "וּבְשַׂר תּוֹדַת שְׁלָמָיו [זֶבַח]"; the extra "זֶבַח" teaches two things.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found the source for change of sanctity (שינוי קודש), from where do we derive change of owner (שינוי בעלים)?

Rav Pinchas bar Rav Ami answers: the verse 'וּבְשַׂר זֶבַח תּוֹדַת שְׁלָמָיו' teaches that slaughter must be for the sake of a thanksgiving-offering; if this is not needed for change of sanctity (derived elsewhere), apply it to change of owner.

The Gemara objects: this verse is needed for the teaching of Abba Chanin in the name of Rabbi Eliezer, that a thanksgiving-offering slaughtered for peace-offerings is valid, but peace-offerings slaughtered for a thanksgiving-offering are invalid, because a thanksgiving-offering is called 'שלמים' (peace-offerings) but peace-offerings are not called 'תודה' (thanksgiving).
The Gemara responds: we are speaking from the word 'זֶבַח' (sacrifice), not from the entire verse.
The Gemara further objects: the word 'זֶבַח' is still needed to include sin-offering (חטאת) and guilt-offering (אשם) in the requirement of slaughter for their own sake.

The Gemara resolves: if so, the verse should have written 'וּבְשַׂר תּוֹדַת שְׁלָמָיו [זֶבַח]'; the extra 'זֶבַח' teaches two things — change of owner and inclusion of sin-offering and guilt-offering.

items.text: Extension of change of owner to all services via analogy
items.text_en: Extension of change of owner to all services via analogy
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found slaughter, from where do we derive the other services for change of owner? If you say learn from slaughter, it is rejected because slaughter has a unique stringency (invalid for not being for the sake of eaters in the Paschal offering). The Gemara then argues by analogy: slaughter is stated for change of sanctity and slaughter is stated for change of owner; just as for change of sanctity you did not distinguish between slaughter and other services, so too for change of owner you should not distinguish. This is rejected because change of sanctity has unique features: its invalidation is inherent, it applies to four services, it applies after death, and it applies to the community as to an individual.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found slaughter (as derived from the verse), but from where do we derive the other services for change of owner?

The Gemara rejects the possibility of learning other services from slaughter, because slaughter has a unique stringency: it is invalid when performed not for the sake of the eaters in the Paschal offering.

The Gemara argues by analogy: slaughter is stated for change of sanctity and for change of owner; just as for change of sanctity you did not distinguish between slaughter and other services, so too for change of owner you should not distinguish.

The Gemara rejects the analogy because change of sanctity has unique features: its invalidation is inherent, it applies to four services, it applies after death, and it applies to the community as to an individual.

items.text: Initial challenge: why is change of ownership not like change of sanctity?
items.text_en: Initial challenge: why is change of ownership not like change of sanctity?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why change of ownership is not considered a disqualification in the body of the animal, while change of sanctity is. It argues that both are merely mental intent, yet the latter disqualifies; so too should the former.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why change of ownership is not considered a disqualification in the body of the animal, given that change of sanctity is also mere mental intent yet disqualifies.
The Gemara resolves that just as change of sanctity disqualifies because the intent disqualifies it, so too change of ownership should disqualify because the intent disqualifies it.

items.text: Rav Pinchas's objection: change of ownership after death
items.text_en: Rav Pinchas's objection: change of ownership after death
items.desc_en: Rav Pinchas bar Rav Mari holds that change of ownership applies even after death, which would create a further difficulty for the previous argument.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that according to Rav Pinchas bar Rav Mari, who holds that change of ownership applies even after death, there would be two difficulties with the previous argument.

items.text: Rav Ashi's verse-based derivation from 'וְנִרְצָה לוֹ'
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's verse-based derivation from 'וְנִרְצָה לוֹ'
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi derives the disqualification for change of ownership from the verse 'וְנִרְצָה לוֹ לְכַפֵּר עָלָיו', implying atonement for him and not for another. The Gemara questions whether this verse is needed for another teaching of Rabbi Shimon regarding responsibility for the offering.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi derives the disqualification for change of ownership from the verse 'וְנִרְצָה לוֹ לְכַפֵּר עָלָיו', implying atonement for him and not for another.
The Gemara objects that this verse is already needed for Rabbi Shimon's teaching about responsibility for the offering.
Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning: saying 'עָלַי' (upon me) makes the person responsible like one carrying a burden on his shoulders.

items.text: Clarification: Rav Ashi's source is the verse itself
items.text_en: Clarification: Rav Ashi's source is the verse itself
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rav Ashi indeed derives the law from the verse 'וְנִרְצָה לוֹ לְכַפֵּר', not from the other teaching.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rav Ashi derives the law from the verse 'וְנִרְצָה לוֹ לְכַפֵּר' (and it shall be accepted for him to atone), not from the other teaching.

items.text: Deriving acceptance (קַבָּלָה) from the ram of the Nazirite
items.text_en: Deriving acceptance (קַבָּלָה) from the ram of the Nazirite
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that acceptance (קַבָּלָה) is also included in the requirement for intent. After considering a derivation from slaughter and sprinkling, Rav Ashi derives it from the ram of the Nazirite, where the verse 'יַעֲשֶׂה זֶבַח שְׁלָמִים' teaches that all actions must be for the sake of peace-offerings, and if not needed for change of sanctity, it applies to change of ownership.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found slaughter and sprinkling (derived from the ram of the Nazirite), but from where do we derive acceptance (קַבָּלָה)?
The Gemara objects: if you try to derive acceptance from slaughter and sprinkling via a common feature, those two are services for which one is liable outside the Temple, unlike acceptance.

Rav Ashi derives acceptance from the ram of the Nazirite, where the verse 'יַעֲשֶׂה זֶבַח שְׁלָמִים' teaches that all actions must be for the sake of peace-offerings, and if not needed for change of sanctity, it applies to change of ownership.

items.text: Hermeneutical debate: כלל ופרט vs. כלל שאינו מלא
items.text_en: Hermeneutical debate: כלל ופרט vs. כלל שאינו מלא
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Abba challenges Rav Ashi's derivation using a כלל ופרט argument, limiting it to slaughter. Rava responds that the verse is a כלל שאינו מלא, not subject to that rule. Ravina suggests that 'לַה׳' serves as a second general term, creating a כלל ופרט וכלל. Rav Acha from Difti objects that the two general terms are not equivalent, and the school of Rabbi Yishmael would interpret it as a כלל ופרט וכלל, leading to multiple possible interpretations, which are left unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Abba challenges Rava by applying a כלל ופרט (general followed by specific) hermeneutic to the verse 'יַעֲשֶׂה זֶבַח', arguing that only slaughter is included.
Rava rejects the objection, arguing that the verse is a כלל שאינו מלא (an incomplete general term), which is not subject to the rule of כלל ופרט.
Ravina asserts that the verse can still be interpreted via כלל ופרט, because 'לַה׳' serves as a second general term, creating a כלל ופרט וכלל (general-particular-general) structure.

Rav Acha from Difti objects that the two general terms are not equivalent, as the first general term includes only 'עשיות' (actions of making) while the second includes all acts done 'לַה׳' (for God), even pouring remnants and burning fats.
The gemara cites the school of Rabbi Yishmael's rule for כלל ופרט וכלל: one may only include items similar to the פרט (particular), which here would be any service requiring intent for its name.
An alternative interpretation suggests the פרט is a service that incurs liability outside the Temple, limiting inclusion to slaughter and sprinkling, excluding receiving and carrying.

sub.text: Another alternative interpretation of the פרט
sub.text_en: Another alternative interpretation of the פרט
sub.desc_en: Another alternative suggests the פרט is a service requiring northward placement and applicable to inner sin-offerings, limiting inclusion to slaughter and receiving, excluding sprinkling.
The gemara concludes that the interpretations are equally balanced (שקולין) and the matter remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Alternative: sprinkling derived from Rav Ashi's earlier verse
items.text_en: Alternative: sprinkling derived from Rav Ashi's earlier verse
items.desc_en: An alternative resolution: sprinkling (זְרִיקָה) is already derived from Rav Ashi's earlier verse, so the derivation from the ram of the Nazirite is only needed for acceptance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the requirement for sprinkling (זְרִיקָה) to be performed לשמה (for its own sake) is already derived from Rav Ashi's earlier verse, so the derivation from the ram of the Nazirite is only needed for acceptance (ריצוי).

items.text: Extending to all peace-offerings and all sacrifices
items.text_en: Extending to all peace-offerings and all sacrifices
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know the law applies to other peace-offerings and then to all sacrifices. It rejects a simple analogy due to unique features of the ram of the Nazirite and peace-offerings. Finally, it cites the verse 'זֹאת הַתּוֹרָה' which equates all sacrifices to peace-offerings, requiring intent for both change of sanctity and change of ownership.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found the law for the ram of the Nazirite; from where do we derive it for other peace-offerings?
The Gemara objects: if you try to learn from the ram of the Nazirite, that ram is unique because it has other accompanying blood-offerings.
The Gemara answers: if the law were limited to the Nazirite's ram, the verse would have said 'שְׁלָמָיו' (his peace-offerings); the plural 'שְׁלָמִים' (peace-offerings) includes all peace-offerings.
The Gemara asks: we have found the law for peace-offerings; from where do we derive it for all other sacrifices?
The Gemara objects: if you try to learn from peace-offerings, they are unique because they require laying of hands, libations, and waving of the breast and thigh.
The Gemara resolves: the verse 'זֹאת הַתּוֹרָה' (This is the law) equates all sacrifices to peace-offerings, requiring intent for both change of sanctity and change of ownership.

items.text: The consequence: disqualification for improper intent and the verse 'מוֹצָא שְׂפָתֶיךָ'
items.text_en: The consequence: disqualification for improper intent and the verse 'מוֹצָא שְׂפָתֶיךָ'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether slaughtering not for its sake disqualifies the offering. It answers with the verse 'מוֹצָא שְׂפָתֶיךָ', which teaches that if one fulfills his vow as promised, it is a vow; otherwise, it becomes a free-will offering. Both verses are necessary: 'מוֹצָא' alone would imply that only a change from vow to free-will is permitted, but not other changes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if one slaughters the offerings not for their sake, should they be disqualified?
The Gemara answers with the verse 'מוֹצָא שְׂפָתֶיךָ' (the utterance of your lips), which teaches that if one fulfills his vow as promised it remains a vow, otherwise it becomes a free-will offering.
The Gemara explains that both verses 'מוֹצָא שְׂפָתֶיךָ' and 'זֹאת הַתּוֹרָה' are necessary: 'מוֹצָא' alone would imply that only a change from vow to free-will is permitted, but not other changes.

items.text: Gemara's initial question about the need for both verses
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question about the need for both verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah wrote both 'zot haTorah' and 'motza sefatecha' regarding offerings that are valid but do not achieve atonement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah wrote both 'זאת התורה' and 'מוצא שפתיך' regarding offerings that are valid but do not achieve atonement.

items.text: Reish Lakish's difficulty
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's difficulty
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish raises a contradiction: if offerings are valid, they should achieve atonement; if not, why bring them?

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish raises a contradiction: if offerings are valid, they should achieve atonement; if not, why bring them?

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's answer from offerings after death
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's answer from offerings after death
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar answers that offerings brought after the owner's death are valid but do not achieve atonement, citing a mishnah about a woman who died.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar answers that offerings brought after the owner's death are valid but do not achieve atonement, citing a mishnah about a woman who died.

items.text: Reish Lakish's objection regarding asham
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's objection regarding asham
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish concedes the point for olah but asks how we know this for asham, which is not brought after death.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish concedes the point for עולה (burnt offering), which comes after death, but asks how we know this for אשם (guilt offering), which does not come after death.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's citation of Rabbi Eliezer and Reish Lakish's rejection
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's citation of Rabbi Eliezer and Reish Lakish's rejection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar cites Rabbi Eliezer's opinion that asham also applies, but Reish Lakish dismisses this as merely a single authority, not a mishnah.

items.text: Reish Lakish's own opening from 'motza sefatecha'
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's own opening from 'motza sefatecha'
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish proposes his own derivation from the verse 'motza sefatecha', arguing it refers to nedavah, not neder, as explained earlier.

items.text: Abaye and colleagues' difficulty with Reish Lakish's approach
items.text_en: Abaye and colleagues' difficulty with Reish Lakish's approach
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira, Rabbi Yitzchak bar Abba, and Abaye question why Reish Lakish uses 'motza sefatecha' for asham, which does not come after death; they suggest that only nedavah and neder should be valid but not achieve atonement, while asham should not be brought at all.

items.text: Abaye's alternative derivation and the ensuing kal vachomer and tzad hashaveh
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative derivation and the ensuing kal vachomer and tzad hashaveh
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that Reish Lakish actually derived from 've'shachat otah le'chatat' that other offerings slaughtered not for their name are valid, and 'motza sefatecha' teaches they do not achieve atonement. The Gemara then questions why asham should not achieve atonement, leading to a kal vachomer from olah, a rebuttal from shelamim, and a tzad hashaveh that is challenged by public offerings and resolved with todah.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that Reish Lakish derived from the verse 'וְשָׁחַט אוֹתָהּ לְחַטָּאת' that other offerings slaughtered not for their name are valid, and 'מוֹצָא שְׂפָתֶיךָ' teaches they do not achieve atonement.
The Gemara questions why asham should not achieve atonement, suggesting that offerings brought by vow or donation should not achieve atonement, but asham should.

Abaye argues that asham cannot achieve atonement, using a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from olah: just as olah, which does not atone, does not achieve atonement, so asham, which does atone, certainly does not achieve atonement.
The Gemara objects that olah is unique because it is entirely burnt (כָּלִיל), so the קל וחומר is not valid.
The Gemara counters that shelamim (peace offerings) can prove the point, as they are not entirely burnt.
The Gemara objects that shelamim require libations and breast-and-thigh waving, making them different from asham.

The Gemara concludes with a צד השווה (common element argument) from olah and shelamim: both are sacred offerings, slaughtered not for their name they are valid but do not achieve atonement, so asham is likewise.
The Gemara objects that the common element (צד השווה) of olah and shelamim includes public offerings, which asham does not.
The Gemara resolves that todah (thanksgiving offering) proves the point, as it is a private offering like asham and does not achieve atonement when slaughtered not for its name.

items.text: Partners cannot effect temurah
items.text_en: Partners cannot effect temurah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that partners cannot effect temurah because the verse 'if he shall substitute' includes an heir but excludes multiple people from substituting together.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that partners cannot effect temurah, and questions: if they do not acquire ownership, why can't they merely declare substitution verbally?
The Gemara answers that the verse 'אִם הָמֵר יָמִיר' includes an heir but excludes multiple people from substituting together.

items.text: Rav Yaakov's objection from ma'aser
items.text_en: Rav Yaakov's objection from ma'aser
items.desc_en: Rav Yaakov from Nehar Pekod objects: if the same logic applies to ma'aser, would it mean only one person can redeem it? The Gemara answers that ma'aser is different because it can be owned in partnership even by its owner.

sub.text: Rav Yaakov from Nehar Pekod's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Yaakov from Nehar Pekod's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Yaakov from Nehar Pekod objects: if the same logic applies to ma'aser, would it mean only one person can redeem it?
The Gemara answers that ma'aser is different because it can be owned in partnership even by its owner.

items.text: Rav Asi's question to Rav Ashi
items.text_en: Rav Asi's question to Rav Ashi
items.desc_en: Rav Asi asks Rav Ashi: if partners do not acquire the animal, how can even one of them effect temurah?

sub.text: Rav Asi's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Asi's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Asi asks Rav Ashi: if partners do not acquire the animal, how can even one of them effect temurah?

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's statement about one who consecrates
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's statement about one who consecrates
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu quotes Rabbi Yochanan: one who consecrates adds a fifth, one who achieves atonement effects temurah, and one who separates terumah from his own for another's produce gets the benefit. The Gemara clarifies that the temurah does not atone for the original, but for the substituted animal.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu quotes Rabbi Yochanan's rule: one who consecrates adds a fifth, one who achieves atonement effects temurah, and one who separates terumah from his own for another's produce gets the benefit.
The Gemara clarifies that the temurah does not atone for the original animal (קיבוע), but for the substituted animal (קופיא).

items.text: Did the first animal atone?
items.text_en: Did the first animal atone?
items.desc_en: A dilemma: did the first animal brought for a sin atone, so that the second is unnecessary? Rav Sheishet bar Rav Idi argues it did not atone, because otherwise why bring a second? Rav Ashi explains the logic: if it did not atone, the second comes to atone; if it did atone, the second is superfluous.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: did the first animal brought for a sin atone, or did it not atone?
Rav Sheshet bar Rav Idi argues that it stands to reason the first did not atone, because if it did, why would a second be brought?
The Gemara objects: if the first did not atone, why is it sacrificed at all?

Rav Ashi explains Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's reasoning: if the first did not atone, it is brought on the strength of its prior consecration, and the second comes to atone; but if it did atone, the second is superfluous.

items.text: Does the offering atone for a positive commandment after separation?
items.text_en: Does the offering atone for a positive commandment after separation?
items.desc_en: A dilemma: does the sin-offering atone for a positive commandment performed after the animal was separated? The Gemara compares it to a chatat, which only atones for sins before separation. A brayta suggests that if one performed the mitzva of semikha improperly, it is as if he did not atone for the positive commandment of semikha. Rava distinguishes: semikha is a positive commandment that can only be performed after slaughter, so it is not relevant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: does a burnt offering atone for a positive commandment violated after the animal was designated, or not?
The Gemara suggests that just as a חטאת (sin offering) atones only for sins before designation, so too a burnt offering atones only for violations before designation.
The Gemara offers an alternative: a burnt offering is unlike a חטאת (sin offering), because it atones for multiple positive commandments, so it might also atone for violations after designation.

The Gemara cites a ברייתא (baraita) that derives from the verse 'וְסָמַךְ... וְנִרְצָה' (and he shall lay his hand… and it shall be accepted) that if one treats סמיכה (laying of hands) as a non-essential מצוה (commandment), the verse considers him as if he did not atone, yet he did atone.

The Gemara infers from the ברייתא (baraita) that the offering atoned for positive commandments before designation but not for the positive commandment of סמיכה (laying of hands), which is a positive commandment after designation, implying that a burnt offering does not atone for violations after designation.

Rava rejects the proof: the positive commandment of סמיכה (laying of hands) is different because it can only be violated after שחיטה (slaughter), and the dilemma about violations after designation does not apply to violations after slaughter.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Yehuda's question to Rava
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda's question to Rava
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda asks Rava to explain the brayta: 'atones' refers to the person, implying the positive commandment of semikha is atoned for.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Yehuda's question to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda's question to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda asks Rava to explain the brayta: 'atones' refers to the person, implying the positive commandment of semikha is atoned for.

items.text: Opening statement: 'If it did not atone – before Heaven!'
items.text_en: Opening statement: 'If it did not atone – before Heaven!'
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a principle: if a sacrifice did not atone, it is as if it did not atone before Heaven, implying that atonement is not achieved in the eyes of God.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a principle: if a sacrifice did not atone, it is as if it did not atone before Heaven.

items.text: Mishnah citation and analysis of Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri
items.text_en: Mishnah citation and analysis of Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about the oil of the leper's offering: Rabbi Akiva says if the oil was not placed on the thumb, it does not atone; Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri says it atones either way, but it is considered as if it did not atone. The Gemara explains that 'as if it did not atone' means it atones for the person but not before Heaven, and applies this to the case of the oil.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah: Rabbi Akiva rules that if the oil of the leper's offering was not placed on the thumb, it does not atone.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri states that the leftover oil is a residual commandment; whether placed or not, it atones, but it is considered as if it did not atone.
The Gemara asks what 'as if it did not atone' means, rejecting the possibility that it requires a new sacrifice since it already atoned.
The Gemara explains: it atones for the person but not before Heaven, and applies this principle to the case of the oil.
The Gemara resolves: similarly, the oil atones for the thumb placements but not for the head placements.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's statement about the goats of Shavuot
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's statement about the goats of Shavuot
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a statement from Rabbi Shimon about the goats of Shavuot, which come for the purification of the Temple and its holy things from impurity. He explains that if the blood of the first goat was sprinkled, the second goat atones for impurity that occurred between them, implying that a sacrifice can atone even after its designated purpose.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a statement from Rabbi Shimon about the goats of Shavuot, asking why they are brought.
The Gemara clarifies that the lambs of Shavuot are peace-offerings, so the question is about the goats of Shavuot.
Rabbi Shimon answers that the goats come for the purification of the Temple and its holy things from impurity.

Rabbi Shimon explains that if the first goat's blood was sprinkled, the second goat atones for impurity that occurred between them, implying that a sacrifice can atone even after its designated purpose, and that Israel could have offered sacrifices at any time but the Torah limited them.

items.text: Challenge and resolution: Atonement after separation
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution: Atonement after separation
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: Here, the second goat atones even though it was separated after the first, showing that a sacrifice can atone after its designation. The resolution is that this applies only if the goats were separated at once; if separated one after another, the second does not atone.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: Here, the second goat atones even though its atonement occurs after its separation, contradicting the principle that a sacrifice cannot atone after designation.
The Gemara resolves: If the goats were separated at once, the second does atone; but here we deal with a case where they were separated one after another, so the second does not atone.

items.text: Objection and Rav Pappa's answer: Communal offerings and the court's intention
items.text_en: Objection and Rav Pappa's answer: Communal offerings and the court's intention
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Why not say that the verse itself speaks of separation one after another? Rav Pappa answers: This is about communal offerings, where the court's intention (לב בית דין מתנה) overrides, as per Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that a knife draws communal offerings to whatever they are.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Why not simply say that the verse itself speaks of sequential separation, so the atonement applies even after the fact?

Rav Pappa answers: This case involves communal offerings (קרבנות ציבור), where the court's intention (לב בית דין מתנה) overrides, as per Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that a knife draws communal offerings to whatever they are.

items.text: Rav Yosef's challenge: Does Rabbi Shimon accept the court's intention?
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's challenge: Does Rabbi Shimon accept the court's intention?
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef the son of Rav Shmuel challenges Rav Pappa: Does Rabbi Shimon accept the principle of the court's intention? He cites Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rav Amram citing Rabbi Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan that daily offerings that were not needed for the community are not brought, implying that the court's intention does not apply to Rabbi Shimon.

sub.text: Rav Yosef the son of Rav Shmuel's question to Rav Pappa
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef the son of Rav Shmuel's question to Rav Pappa
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef challenges Rav Pappa: Does Rabbi Shimon accept the principle that the court's intention (לב בית דין מתנה עליהם) applies to communal offerings?

sub.text: Rav Yosef's citation of a tradition from Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's citation of a tradition from Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites a tradition from Rabbi Yochanan that daily offerings (תמידין) that were not needed for the community are not brought, implying that Rabbi Shimon does not accept the court's intention.

items.text: Opening dispute on redeeming firstborn animals
items.text_en: Opening dispute on redeeming firstborn animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages regarding whether firstborn animals can be redeemed when they are unblemished.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states the dispute: according to Rabbi Shimon, unblemished firstborn animals are not redeemable; according to the Sages, they are redeemable.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about the second cup of blood
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about the second cup of blood
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira about the purpose of a second cup of blood for the Se'irei Atzeret when the first was already sprinkled, and the Gemara clarifies the scope of the question.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira: for the Se'irei Atzeret (festival goats), if the blood was collected in two cups and the first was already sprinkled, what purpose does the second cup serve?
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yirmeya's question only concerns a case of טומאה (impurity) occurring after slaughter but before the second sprinkling, not after the initial designation of the goats.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yirmeya's question was posed in the form of 'אם תימצי לומר' (if you should say), meaning it was a hypothetical inquiry rather than a practical one.

items.text: Dispute on Todah slaughtered for a friend's Todah
items.text_en: Dispute on Todah slaughtered for a friend's Todah
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Chisda argue whether a Todah slaughtered for the sake of a friend's Todah is valid; Rabbah deems it kosher, Rav Chisda deems it invalid.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbah and Rav Chisda regarding a Todah slaughtered for the sake of a friend's Todah.
Rabbah explains his ruling: the animal was slaughtered for the sake of a Todah, which is valid.
Rav Chisda explains his ruling: we require the animal to be slaughtered for the sake of its own owner's Shelamim, not a friend's Todah.

items.text: Rabbah's proof from a baraita and the Gemara's analysis
items.text_en: Rabbah's proof from a baraita and the Gemara's analysis
items.desc_en: Rabbah cites a baraita from Abba Chanin in the name of Rabbi Eliezer that a Todah slaughtered for Shelamim is valid, but Shelamim for Todah is invalid. The Gemara questions whether this applies to a friend's Todah and concludes the baraita refers to one's own Todah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah introduces his proof by citing a baraita about a Todah slaughtered for Shelamim.

sub.text: Baraita of Abba Chanin in the name of Rabbi Eliezer
sub.text_en: Baraita of Abba Chanin in the name of Rabbi Eliezer
sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that a Todah slaughtered for Shelamim is valid, but Shelamim for Todah is invalid, because Todah is called Shelamim but not vice versa.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita's case of Todah for Todah refers to a friend's Todah, implying that one's own Todah would be invalid.
The Gemara answers that the baraita refers to one's own Todah, not a friend's.
The Gemara objects that if the baraita only teaches about one's own Todah, it should have stated 'Todah for Todah' and then all the more so 'Shelamim for Todah'.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita needed to teach about Shelamim for Todah of one's own, because one might have thought that since Todah is called Shelamim, Shelamim is also called Todah and would be valid; the baraita teaches otherwise.

items.text: Rava's ruling on Chatas slaughtered for Chatas or Olah
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on Chatas slaughtered for Chatas or Olah
items.desc_en: Rava rules that a Chatas slaughtered for the sake of a Chatas is valid, but for the sake of an Olah is invalid, based on the verse 'and he shall slaughter it for a Chatas'.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that a חטאת (sin offering) slaughtered for the sake of a חטאת is valid, but for the sake of an עולה (burnt offering) is invalid.
Rava explains the reason: the Torah says 'and he shall slaughter it for a חטאת', so slaughtering for a חטאת is valid, but for an עולה is invalid.

items.text: Rava on Chatas slaughtered for a different owner
items.text_en: Rava on Chatas slaughtered for a different owner
items.desc_en: Rava rules that a Chatas slaughtered for someone liable for a Chatas is invalid, but for someone liable for an Olah is valid, based on the verse 'and he shall atone for him'.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a sin offering slaughtered for someone liable for a sin offering is unfit, but for someone liable for a burnt offering is fit.

Rava explains the reason: the verse 'and he shall be forgiven' indicates atonement for the owner and not for another, and the other person must be similar to the owner in being obligated for atonement.

items.text: Rava on Chatas for someone with no liability
items.text_en: Rava on Chatas for someone with no liability
items.desc_en: Rava rules that a Chatas slaughtered for someone with no liability is invalid, as every Jew is liable for a positive commandment.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a Chatas slaughtered for someone with no liability is invalid, because every Jew is liable for a positive commandment (עשה).

items.text: Rava's kal vachomer and the Gemara's objection
items.text_en: Rava's kal vachomer and the Gemara's objection
items.desc_en: Rava argues that a Chatas atones for those liable for positive commandments a fortiori from those liable for kareis, but the Gemara objects based on Rava's earlier ruling.

sub.desc_en: Rava argues that a Chatas atones for those liable for positive commandments a fortiori from those liable for kareis.

The Gemara objects: does this imply that a Chatas is of the same category as a Chatas for kareis? But Rava himself ruled that a Chatas slaughtered for someone liable for a Chatas is invalid, while for someone liable for an olah it is valid.

items.text: Rava's ruling on an olah slaughtered not for its sake
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on an olah slaughtered not for its sake
items.desc_en: Rava states that if an olah is slaughtered not for its sake, it is forbidden to sprinkle its blood not for its sake. The Gemara offers two explanations: a biblical verse and a logical reason.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a principle: an offering does not atone through its fixed status but through its application.
Rava rules that if an עולה (burnt offering) is slaughtered not for its sake, it is forbidden to sprinkle its blood not for its sake.
The Gemara offers two explanations for Rava's ruling: a biblical verse and a logical reason.

items.text: Olah brought after the owner's death
items.text_en: Olah brought after the owner's death
items.desc_en: Rava rules that an olah brought after the owner's death is invalid if slaughtered with a change of sanctity but valid if slaughtered with a change of owner, since there are no owners after death. Rav Pinchas bar Rav Ami disagrees, and Rav Ashi clarifies his position.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that an olah brought after the owner's death is invalid if slaughtered with a change of sanctity but valid if slaughtered with a change of owner, since there are no owners after death.

sub.text: Rav Pinchas bar Rav Ami's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Pinchas bar Rav Ami's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Pinchas bar Rav Ami disagrees, asserting that there are owners after death.
Rav Ashi asks Rav Pinchas bar Rav Ami whether he means that the owner's existence is precise, requiring a replacement olah, or that the olah can atone for multiple positive commandments.

sub.text: Rav Pinchas bar Rav Ami's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Pinchas bar Rav Ami's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Pinchas bar Rav Ami answers that he means the precise sense: there are owners after death, requiring a replacement olah.

items.text: Olah as a gift and the order of sacrifices
items.text_en: Olah as a gift and the order of sacrifices
items.desc_en: Rava explains that an olah is a gift (doron). The Gemara questions how it can atone if there is no repentance, and concludes it is a gift. A beraita from Rabbi Shimon illustrates that the chatat comes before the olah, like an advocate entering before a gift.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that an olah (עולה) is a gift (דורון).
The Gemara asks: In what scenario does this apply?
The Gemara objects: If there is no repentance, the verse says 'the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination' (משלי כא, כז).
The Gemara objects further: If there is repentance, a baraita teaches that one who violates a positive commandment and repents is immediately forgiven, so why would an olah be needed?
The Gemara concludes: Rather, the olah is a gift (דורון) that brings favor even without specific atonement.
A mnemonic is given: 'Chatat atones for whom, olah after a gift – a sign.'
A baraita supports this: Rabbi Shimon explains that the chatat comes before the olah, like an advocate (פרקליט) who enters first to appease, followed by a gift.

items.text: Deriving the laws of pesach from verses
items.text_en: Deriving the laws of pesach from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that the pesach must be performed for its own sake from verses. It finds sources for change of sanctity and change of owner, first for the mitzvah and then for invalidation. Rav Safra challenges the derivation and reinterprets the verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive the law that the pesach offering must be performed for its own sake?
The Gemara cites the verse 'שָׁמוֹר אֶת חֹדֶשׁ הָאָבִיב וְעָשִׂיתָ פֶּסַח' to teach that all actions of the pesach must be for the sake of pesach.
The Gemara asks: we have found the source for change of sanctity (שִׁינּוּי קוֹדֶשׁ), but from where do we derive the law for change of owner (שִׁינּוּי בְּעָלִים)?
The Gemara cites the verse 'וַאֲמַרְתֶּם זֶבַח פֶּסַח הוּא' and explains that if it is not needed for change of sanctity, apply it to change of owner.
The Gemara asks: we have found the source for the mitzvah (ideal standard), but from where do we derive that it is indispensable (מְעַכֵּב)?
The Gemara cites the verse 'וְזָבַחְתָּ פֶּסַח לַה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ' as the source for invalidation.
Rav Safra objects: does this verse 'וְזָבַחְתָּ' come for this purpose?

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Safra cites Rav Nachman's teaching that the verse 'וְזָבַחְתָּ פֶּסַח לַה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ צֹאן וּבָקָר' teaches that leftover pesach offerings are brought as shelamim.

Rav Safra reinterprets the verses: 'וְזָבַחְתָּ פֶּסַח' is for Rav Nachman's teaching, 'שָׁמוֹר' is for the mitzvah of change of sanctity, 'וַאֲמַרְתֶּם זֶבַח פֶּסַח' is for change of owner as a mitzvah, and 'הוּא' is for invalidation in both cases.
The Gemara asks: we have found the source for slaughter (זְבִיחָה), but from where do we derive the other services?

items.text: Deriving other services for pesach
items.text_en: Deriving other services for pesach
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi rejects the argument from analogy and derives other services from a verse. A beraita teaches that all sacrifices are compared to shelamim, so all services require proper intent for the mitzvah, and for pesach, all services are invalidating.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi rejects the previous argument that since the matter is revealed, it is revealed, asserting that this reasoning is not accepted.
The Gemara asks from where we derive the requirement of proper intent for other services of the pesach offering.
The Gemara cites a verse to derive the requirement for other services.
A baraita is cited that identifies the verse as referring to bekhor, maaser, and pesach offerings.
The Gemara concludes that the verse compares these offerings to shelamim, so all require proper intent for the mitzvah regarding both change of sanctity and change of owner.
The Gemara further resolves that just as for shelamim, all services are treated equally for the mitzvah, so for pesach, all services are treated equally for invalidation.
The Gemara notes that the word 'הוּא' (it) in the context of slaughter is only for invalidation.
The Gemara asks what the word 'הוּא' (it) in the verse is needed for.

items.text: The word 'hu' in pesach and chatat
items.text_en: The word 'hu' in pesach and chatat
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the word 'hu' in pesach teaches invalidation, unlike the asham. It then seeks the source for chatat, finding it in the verse 'and he shall slaughter it as a chatat', and begins to derive other services.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the purpose of the word 'הוּא' (it) in the context of pesach, given that other derivations have already been made.

A baraita explains that the word 'הוּא' in pesach teaches invalidation for shechita, whereas in asham it applies only after the burning of the sacrificial portions and does not invalidate the sacrifice if the portions were not yet burned.
The Gemara asks what the source is for the requirement that the chatat be slaughtered for its own sake.
The Gemara derives the requirement from the verse 'וְשָׁחַט אֹתָהּ לְחַטָּאת' (and he shall slaughter it as a chatat).
The Gemara asks what the source is for the requirement that the receiving of the blood also be performed for the sake of chatat.

items.text: Initial derivation from the sin-offering verses
items.text_en: Initial derivation from the sin-offering verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'And the priest shall take from the blood of the sin-offering' that collection must be for the sake of sin-offering. From 'and the priest shall make atonement for him from his sin-offering' it derives sprinkling for the sake of sin-offering. From 'for him' it derives that a change of owner is invalid. Finally, Rav Huna bar Yehoshua uses the repetition 'chatat' and 'chatato' to show that these requirements are indispensable (akeiv).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'And the priest shall take from the blood of the sin-offering' that collection must be for the sake of sin-offering.
The Gemara derives from 'and the priest shall make atonement for him from his sin-offering' that sprinkling must be for the sake of sin-offering.
The Gemara derives from 'עָלָיו' (for him) that a change of owner invalidates the offering.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua uses the repetition 'חַטָּאת'–'חַטָּאתוֹ' (sin-offering–his sin-offering) to show that these requirements are indispensable (עַכֵּב).

items.text: Question on the source for other services and combinations
items.text_en: Question on the source for other services and combinations
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found the requirement for mitzvah in change of sanctity and for sprinkling in change of owner (both for mitzvah and akeiv), but for akeiv in all services for change of sanctity, and for other services in change of owner (both for mitzvah and akeiv) – what is the source?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found the source for mitzvah in change of sanctity and for sprinkling in change of owner, but for akeiv in all services for change of sanctity and for other services in change of owner – what is the source?

items.text: Derivation from the Nazirite's sin-offering
items.text_en: Derivation from the Nazirite's sin-offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yona derives from the verse regarding the Nazirite's sin-offering that all its actions must be for the sake of sin-offering. The Gemara then asks about change of owner and akeiv, and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua again uses the 'chatat–chatato' derivation.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yona derives from the Nazirite's sin-offering verse that all its actions must be performed for the sake of sin-offering.
The Gemara asks: from this derivation we have change of sanctity, but change of owner and the requirement for withholding (עכוב) — from where?
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua answers by applying the verbal analogy of 'חטאת–חטאתו' (sin-offering – his sin-offering) to derive the requirement for withholding.

items.text: Ravina's objection and the rejection of the Nazirite derivation
items.text_en: Ravina's objection and the rejection of the Nazirite derivation
items.desc_en: Ravina objects: if we use 'chatat–chatato', what would we derive from 'olah–olato'? The Gemara explains that those verses are needed for other laws. Moreover, the two sin-offerings (of fat and Nazirite) cannot be compared to each other due to differing characteristics (presence of other blood vs. karet).

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects: if we derive from 'chatat–chatato', what would we derive from 'olah–olato'?
Ravina extends the objection: similarly, what would be derived from 'minchat–minchato' and 'nesech–nischo'?
The Gemara answers that the verses for minchah and nesachim are needed for other laws (night and next day), but the question about 'olah–olato' remains.
The Gemara rejects the Nazirite derivation entirely: the two sin-offerings (fat and Nazirite) cannot be compared due to differing characteristics (presence of other blood vs. karet).

items.text: Derivation from the leper's sin-offering and its rejection
items.text_en: Derivation from the leper's sin-offering and its rejection
items.desc_en: Rava derives from the leper's sin-offering that all its actions must be for the sake of sin-offering, and from the verse 'and he shall make atonement for the one being purified' that change of owner is excluded. However, the Gemara again notes that the two sin-offerings (of fat and leper) cannot be compared due to the same differences (other blood vs. karet).

sub.desc_en: Rava proposes deriving the requirement for all actions to be for the sake of sin-offering from the leper's sin-offering (חטאת מצורע).
Rava derives the exclusion of change of owner from the verse 'וְכִפֶּר עַל הַמִּטַּהֵר' (and he shall make atonement for the one being purified).
The Gemara objects that the two sin-offerings (of fat and leper) cannot be compared due to the same differences (other blood vs. karet).

items.text: Attempt to derive from two sources and the rejection of each possibility
items.text_en: Attempt to derive from two sources and the rejection of each possibility
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that since one source alone is insufficient, we might derive from two. It considers omitting the verse from the sin-offering of fat, from the Nazirite's, or from the leper's, but each is rejected because the remaining two share a common feature not present in the omitted one (other blood, no hatarah, no poverty).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that since a single source is insufficient, we should derive the law from two sources together.
The Gemara considers omitting the verse from the sin-offering of fat, but rejects it because the other two share the feature of having other blood accompanying them.
The Gemara considers omitting the verse from the Nazirite's sin-offering, but rejects it because the other two share the feature of having no hatarah (nullification by a sage).
The Gemara considers omitting the verse from the leper's sin-offering, but rejects it because the other two share the feature of not being brought in poverty.

items.text: Final derivation from the analogy to peace-offerings
items.text_en: Final derivation from the analogy to peace-offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes by citing the verse 'This is the law for the burnt-offering, the meal-offering, etc.' which likens all offerings to peace-offerings. Just as peace-offerings require intent for both change of sanctity and change of owner as a mitzvah, so too the sin-offering. Therefore, the mitzvah requirement comes from peace-offerings, and the earlier verses are for akeiv. This is found in the sin-offering of fat where 'lachatat' is written.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the derivation by citing the verse 'זאת התורה לעולה ולמנחה' (This is the law for the burnt-offering and the meal-offering), which likens all offerings to peace-offerings, establishing that both change of sanctity and change of owner require intent for their name as a mitzvah.
The Gemara concludes that the mitzvah requirement comes from peace-offerings, while the earlier verses (from sin-offerings) are for akeiv (to disqualify if omitted).
The Gemara notes that this derivation is found specifically in the sin-offering of fat, where the word 'לחטאת' (for a sin-offering) is written.

items.text: Introduction: deriving the law for other sin-offerings
items.text_en: Introduction: deriving the law for other sin-offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that the sin-offering for idolatry, the oath of testimony, the oath of utterance, and impurity of the Temple and its holy things require a sacrifice even though the Torah does not explicitly mention a sin-offering for them. It answers that the sin-offering for idolatry is derived from the sin-offering for forbidden fat via the common feature of karet, and the others are derived via a binyan av.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we derive the sin-offering for idolatry, oath of testimony, oath of utterance, and impurity of the Temple and its holy things, which are not explicitly mentioned in the Torah.

The Gemara answers that the sin-offering for idolatry is derived from the sin-offering for forbidden fat via the common feature of karet, and the others are derived via a binyan av (a common feature analogy).

items.text: Tannaic statement about Passover
items.text_en: Tannaic statement about Passover
items.desc_en: The Tanna teaches: A Passover offering brought in its proper time (the 14th of Nisan) is valid if offered for its own sake, but invalid if offered not for its own sake; during the rest of the year, it is invalid if offered for its own sake and valid if offered not for its own sake.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna teaches the rule for a Passover offering: in its proper time it is valid for its own sake and invalid not for its own sake; during the rest of the year the opposite applies.

items.text: Siman (mnemonic)
items.text_en: Siman (mnemonic)
items.desc_en: A mnemonic is provided for the following discussion.

sub.desc_en: A mnemonic (סימן) is provided to organize the following discussion.

items.text: First derivation: Avuh deShmuel's verse
items.text_en: First derivation: Avuh deShmuel's verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for this law. Avuh deShmuel cites the verse 'And if his offering is from the flock, a sacrifice of peace-offerings to the Lord' – implying that an item that comes from the flock should be treated as a peace-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the rule that a sacrifice brought from the flock is treated as a peace-offering.
Avuh deShmuel cites the verse 'וְאִם מִן הַצֹּאן קׇרְבָּנוֹ לְזֶבַח שְׁלָמִים לַה׳' to derive that an item from the flock should be treated as a peace-offering.

items.text: Objection and Rabbi Ila's expansion
items.text_en: Objection and Rabbi Ila's expansion
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: this would only include peace-offerings, not other sacrifices. Rabbi Ila in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers that the word 'sacrifice' (לְזֶבַח) serves to include all sacrifices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse would only include peace-offerings (שְׁלָמִים), not other sacrifices.

sub.text: Rabbi Ila in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ila in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila citing Rabbi Yochanan answers that the word 'לְזֶבַח' (for a sacrifice) serves to include all sacrifices.

items.text: Further objection and resolution
items.text_en: Further objection and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: then any animal slaughtered should be like the peace-offering itself.
