The Gemara answers: if the verse were written 'for peace-offerings and a sacrifice' it would be as you say; but now that it is written 'for a sacrifice of peace-offerings', it means that whatever one slaughters should be considered a peace-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the verse includes all sacrifices, then any animal slaughtered should be like the peace-offering itself.

The Gemara answers that the verse's phrasing 'for a sacrifice of peace-offerings' means whatever one slaughters should be considered a peace-offering, not that it becomes like the peace-offering itself.

items.text: Klal u'prat argument and Rav Yaakov's challenge
items.text_en: Klal u'prat argument and Rav Yaakov's challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a klal u'prat argument: 'sacrifice' is a general term, 'peace-offerings' is a specific term, so only peace-offerings are included. The verse adds 'to the Lord' as a second general term, but Rav Yaakov from Nehar Pekod challenges that the second general term is not similar to the first: the first includes only sacrifices, while 'to the Lord' includes even bird-offerings and meal-offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a klal u'prat (general and specific) argument: 'sacrifice' is a general term, 'peace-offerings' is a specific term, so only peace-offerings are included, excluding all other offerings.
The Gemara answers that the verse adds 'to the Lord' as a second general term, creating a klal u'prat u'chlal (general, specific, and general) pattern.

Rav Yaakov from Nehar Pekod challenges that the second general term 'to the Lord' is not similar to the first: the first includes only sacrifices, while 'to the Lord' includes even bird-offerings and meal-offerings.

items.text: Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael's method
items.text_en: Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael's method
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael who interprets such cases with the rule of klal u'prat u'chlal: you may only include items similar to the specific case. The specific case (peace-offerings) is offered not for its own sake and is valid, so all items offered not for their own sake are valid. But then it would only include items brought as vows and free-will offerings (burnt-offerings and peace-offerings), excluding sin-offerings and guilt-offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael who interprets using the rule of כלל ופרט וכלל (general, specific, general).

The Tanna states the rule: from a general-specific-general pattern, you may only include items similar to the specific case; the specific case (peace-offerings) is offered not for its own sake and is valid, so all such items are valid.

The Gemara objects that the specific case (peace-offerings) is a vow or free-will offering, so the rule would only include burnt-offerings and peace-offerings, excluding sin-offerings and guilt-offerings.

items.text: Conclusion: 'sacrifice' is a ribbui
items.text_en: Conclusion: 'sacrifice' is a ribbui
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that 'sacrifice' (לְזֶבַח) is a ribbui (amplification). The Gemara then raises the objection that it would mean any animal slaughtered should be like the peace-offering itself. Rabbi Avin begins to answer, but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the word 'לְזֶבַח' (for a sacrifice) is a ribbui (amplification), meaning it includes all sacrifices.
The Gemara objects that if 'לְזֶבַח' is an amplification, then any animal one slaughters should be like the peace-offering itself, which is absurd.
Rabbi Avin begins to answer the objection, but the text cuts off before his full response.

items.text: Opening statement: distinction between edible and non-edible offerings
items.text_en: Opening statement: distinction between edible and non-edible offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a principle: edible offerings may be substituted for other edible offerings, but not for non-edible ones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a principle: edible offerings may be substituted for other edible offerings, but not for non-edible ones.

items.text: Refinement of the principle: all people vs. not all people
items.text_en: Refinement of the principle: all people vs. not all people
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that sin-offerings and guilt-offerings are also edible, so the principle is refined: offerings edible by all people may be substituted for those edible by all people, but not for those not edible by all people.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that sin-offerings (חטאת) and guilt-offerings (אשם) are also edible, contradicting the earlier principle that only non-edible offerings are excluded.
The Gemara refines the principle: offerings edible by all people may be substituted for those edible by all people, but not for those not edible by all people.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin's alternative: light vs. most holy
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin's alternative: light vs. most holy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin offers a different distinction: light offerings may be substituted for light offerings, but not for most holy offerings.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin proposes that light offerings (קָדָשִׁים קַלִּים) may be substituted for light offerings, but not for most holy offerings (קׇדְשֵׁי קָדָשִׁים).

items.text: First objection: could leftover be sacrificed as tithe?
items.text_en: First objection: could leftover be sacrificed as tithe?
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Savrin objects: why not sacrifice the leftover as a tithe offering? The Gemara answers that the verse 'the tenth shall be holy' excludes any other from becoming tithe.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Savrin objects: why not slaughter the leftover as a tithe offering (מעשר), which would exempt it from libations and make it subject to the prohibition of redemption?
The Gemara answers that the verse 'the tenth shall be holy' teaches that only a designated tenth becomes tithe, and no other animal can become tithe.

items.text: Second objection: could leftover be sacrificed as firstborn?
items.text_en: Second objection: could leftover be sacrificed as firstborn?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why not sacrifice it as a firstborn? The answer is derived from a verbal analogy (גזירה שוה) of 'עברה' from tithe.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why not sacrifice the leftover as a firstborn (בכור), so it would not require libations or be given to priests?
The Gemara answers: a firstborn (בכור) is also excluded by the verbal analogy (גזירה שוה) of 'עברה' from tithe (מעשר).

items.text: Third objection: could leftover be sacrificed as a substitute (תמורה)?
items.text_en: Third objection: could leftover be sacrificed as a substitute (תמורה)?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why not sacrifice it as a substitute? Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman answers that the verse 'it and its substitute' excludes any other from being a substitute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes sacrificing the leftover as a substitute (תמורה) to incur the prohibitions of not being sold or redeemed.
Mar Zutra bar Rav Nachman answers that the verse 'הוּא וּתְמוּרָתוֹ' (it and its substitute) teaches that only that specific animal becomes a substitute, not another.

items.text: Fourth objection: could leftover be sacrificed as a thanks-offering?
items.text_en: Fourth objection: could leftover be sacrificed as a thanks-offering?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why not sacrifice it as a thanks-offering, requiring bread? The Gemara rejects this: the leftover of a thanks-offering itself does not require bread, so how could a leftover from elsewhere require bread?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the leftover could be sacrificed as a thanks-offering (תודה), which requires accompanying bread.
The Gemara objects: since the paschal offering itself does not require bread, how could its leftover require bread?
The Gemara rejects this, arguing that the same logic would undermine the previous ruling that leftover requires libations, since the paschal offering itself does not require libations.
The Gemara clarifies: the point is that even the leftover of a thanks-offering itself does not require bread, so how could leftover from elsewhere require bread?

items.text: Objection: perhaps the verse refers to leftover of guilt-offering
items.text_en: Objection: perhaps the verse refers to leftover of guilt-offering
items.desc_en: Rav Yemar bar Rav Hillel objects: perhaps the verse about 'if from the flock' refers to the leftover of a guilt-offering, not a Passover-offering.

sub.text: Rav Yemar bar Rav Hillel's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Yemar bar Rav Hillel's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Yemar bar Rav Hillel objects that the verse 'if from the flock' might refer to the leftover of a guilt-offering, not a Passover-offering.

items.text: Rava's answer: the verse refers to something common to all flock
items.text_en: Rava's answer: the verse refers to something common to all flock
items.desc_en: Rava answers that the verse 'if from the flock his offering for a peace-offering' refers to something common to all flock, i.e., the leftover of Passover which can become a peace-offering.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that the verse 'if from the flock his offering for a peace-offering' refers to something common to all flock, i.e., the leftover of Passover which can become a peace-offering.

items.text: Objection: 'from' usually excludes, here it includes?
items.text_en: Objection: 'from' usually excludes, here it includes?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin bar Chiyya objects: everywhere 'from' excludes, but here it is used to include? Rabbi Mani answers that here too 'from' excludes: a two-year-old and a female.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avin bar Chiyya objects that everywhere the word 'מִן' (from) excludes, but here it is used to include.
Rabbi Mani answers that here too 'מִן' excludes: a two-year-old animal and a female.

items.text: Objection: the verse cannot be about leftover of Passover
items.text_en: Objection: the verse cannot be about leftover of Passover
items.desc_en: Rav Chana Bagdata'ah objects: the verse mentions 'if a lamb' and 'if a goat', implying it is not about leftover of Passover. The Gemara resolves that the verse is needed for other teachings, and the source for leftover of Passover as peace-offering is from elsewhere.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chana Bagdata'ah objects that the verse with 'if a lamb' and 'if a goat' cannot be about leftover of Passover, since it distinguishes between species.
The Gemara answers that the verse is needed for other teachings about the Passover offering and the fat tail (אליה).
The Gemara objects that the source for leftover Passover as peace-offering should come from Avuh deShmuel's verse, not from the current one.
The Gemara objects further that the source is actually from Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha, who derives leftover Passover as peace-offering from a different verse.
The Gemara resolves that three verses are written, each serving a different purpose regarding the leftover of Passover.

items.text: Conclusion: three verses are written
items.text_en: Conclusion: three verses are written
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that there are three verses supporting the law of leftover of Passover becoming peace-offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that three verses are written to support the law of leftover of Passover becoming peace-offerings.

items.text: Three cases of intercalation
items.text_en: Three cases of intercalation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the necessity of three verses regarding intercalation: one for when both the year and the time are intercalated, one for when only the time is intercalated, and one for when neither is intercalated. Each case is needed to avoid a mistaken leniency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara lists three cases of intercalation requiring separate verses: both year and time intercalated, only time intercalated, and neither intercalated.
The Gemara explains why each case is needed: without the verse for time-only intercalation, one might mistakenly think it is exempt from the second Passover.
The Gemara concludes that all three verses are necessary to prevent mistaken leniency in each scenario.

items.text: Rav's first ruling: sin-offering for Nachshon's sin-offering is valid
items.text_en: Rav's first ruling: sin-offering for Nachshon's sin-offering is valid
items.desc_en: Rav, citing the Sage of Mavog, rules that a sin-offering slaughtered for the sake of Nachshon's sin-offering is valid, based on the verse "This is the Torah of the sin-offering" indicating one law for all sin-offerings.

sub.text: Rav citing the Sage of Mavog
sub.text_en: Rav citing the Sage of Mavog
sub.desc_en: Rav, citing the Sage of Mavog, rules that a sin-offering slaughtered for the sake of Nachshon's sin-offering is valid, based on the verse 'זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַחַטָּאת' (This is the Torah of the sin-offering) indicating one law for all sin-offerings.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Shimon's ruling on meal-offerings
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Shimon's ruling on meal-offerings
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya objects to Rava's teaching of Rav's ruling, citing Rabbi Shimon who says meal-offerings are valid when offered not for their own name because their actions prove their identity, implying that without such proof they would be invalid. This challenges Rav's use of the verse "one Torah" for sin-offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara sets the scene: Rava was teaching a certain tradition, and Rav Mesharshiya raised an objection against him.
Rav Mesharshiya cites Rabbi Shimon's ruling that all meal-offerings are valid when their kemitzah (handful removal) was performed not for their own name, because their actions prove their identity.
Rabbi Shimon contrasts meal-offerings with animal sacrifices, where all have the same slaughter, receipt, and sprinkling, so actions do not prove identity.

The Gemara infers that without actions proving identity, the meal-offering would be invalid, and questions why the verse 'זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַמִּנְחָה' (this is the Torah of the meal-offering) would not teach a single law for all meal-offerings.

The Gemara asks why the verse 'זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַמִּנְחָה' (this is the Torah of the meal-offering) should not teach a single law for all meal-offerings, challenging Rav's use of the analogous verse for sin-offerings.

items.text: Revised version of Rav's ruling: for atonement of a dead person
items.text_en: Revised version of Rav's ruling: for atonement of a dead person
items.desc_en: The Gemara revises Rav's statement: a sin-offering slaughtered with the intent that Nachshon (a dead person) be atoned through it is valid, because there is no atonement for the dead. This implies that if the person were alive and similar to Nachshon, it would be invalid, referring to the sin-offerings of a nazirite and a leper.

sub.text: Gemara's revised version of Rav's statement
sub.text_en: Gemara's revised version of Rav's statement
sub.desc_en: The Gemara revises Rav's statement: a sin-offering slaughtered with the intent that Nachshon (a dead person) be atoned through it is valid, because there is no atonement for the dead.
The Gemara asks: why not simply say 'a dead person' in general, rather than specifying Nachshon?

The Gemara answers: the specification of Nachshon teaches that only because he is dead is it valid, but if the intended recipient were a living person similar to Nachshon (i.e., a nazirite or leper who brings a sin-offering that is actually an עולה (burnt-offering)), it would be invalid.

items.text: Further revisions: for one obligated like Nachshon, and alternative versions
items.text_en: Further revisions: for one obligated like Nachshon, and alternative versions
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two more versions of Rav's statement: one where the sin-offering is valid if slaughtered for one obligated like Nachshon, and another where it is invalid because Nachshon's sin-offering was actually a burnt-offering. The Gemara explains why the latter does not mention the nazirite's or leper's sin-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the sin-offerings of a nazirite and a leper are actually burnt-offerings, not sin-offerings.
The Gemara offers a revised version of Rav's statement: a sin-offering slaughtered for one obligated like Nachshon is valid, because Nachshon's sin-offering was actually a burnt-offering.
An alternative version states that a sin-offering slaughtered for Nachshon's sin-offering is invalid, because Nachshon's sin-offering was a burnt-offering.
The Gemara asks why the alternative version mentions only Nachshon's sin-offering and not the nazirite's or leper's sin-offering.
The Gemara answers that the version cites only the primary sin-offering (Nachshon's), not the secondary ones.

items.text: Rav's ruling on different types of sin-offerings and Rava's query
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on different types of sin-offerings and Rava's query
items.desc_en: Rav rules that a sin-offering for fat slaughtered for the sake of a sin-offering for blood or idolatry is valid, but for a nazirite's or leper's sin-offering it is invalid (as they are burnt-offerings). Rava then queries about a sin-offering for fat slaughtered for a sin-offering for impurity of the Temple, questioning whether the common element of karet makes it valid.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that a sin-offering for fat slaughtered for the sake of a sin-offering for blood or idolatry is valid, but for a nazirite's or leper's sin-offering it is invalid because those are burnt-offerings.

Rava queries whether a sin-offering for fat slaughtered for a sin-offering for impurity of the Temple is valid, questioning if the common element of karet makes it like the original or if the lack of a fixed time makes it different.

items.text: Rav Acha's tradition and resolution of Rava's query
items.text_en: Rav Acha's tradition and resolution of Rava's query
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava teaches all such cases as invalid, citing the verse "and he shall slaughter it for a sin-offering" meaning for that specific sin-offering. Rav Ashi asks how they teach Rava's query, and Rav Acha explains they teach it regarding a change of owners. The query remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava teaches that all such cases are invalid, citing the verse "and he shall slaughter it for a sin-offering" meaning for that specific sin-offering.
Rav Ashi asks Rav Acha bar Rava how they teach Rava's query.

Rav Acha bar Rava explains that they teach the query regarding a change of owners, presenting Rava's ruling that a חטאת חלב (fat sin-offering) slaughtered for someone liable for a blood or idolatry sin-offering is invalid, but for a nazirite or leper sin-offering it is valid.

Rava's query is presented: whether a חטאת חלב (fat sin-offering) slaughtered for someone liable for a sin-offering for טומאת מקדש וקדשיו (Temple impurity) is invalid because both involve כרת (extirpation), or valid because the latter is not a fixed sin-offering.
The query remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on intent across different services
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on intent across different services
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute: if one slaughtered a sin-offering for its own name but intends to sprinkle its blood not for its own name, Rabbi Yochanan rules it invalid, deriving from the laws of piggul that intent can transfer between services, while Reish Lakish rules it valid, holding that intent does not transfer between services.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute: if one slaughtered a sin-offering for its own name but intends to sprinkle its blood not for its own name, Rabbi Yochanan rules it invalid (פסולה) and Reish Lakish rules it valid (כשרה).
The gemara explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: one can transfer intent from one service to another, and this is derived from the laws of piggul (פגול).
The gemara explains Reish Lakish's reasoning: one cannot transfer intent between services, and the laws of piggul do not serve as a source for such transfer.
The gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish follow their previously established positions, and transitions to the next discussion.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish on transferring intent between acts
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish on transferring intent between acts
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan holds that if one slaughters a beast intending to sprinkle its blood for idolatry, the animal is forbidden, because we derive intent from one act to another (outside from inside). Resh Lakish permits it, arguing no such derivation is made. The Gemara notes that both cases are necessary to avoid assuming each would concede in the other case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the case: one slaughters a beast intending to sprinkle its blood for idolatry; Rabbi Yochanan rules it forbidden, deriving intent from one act to another (outside from inside).
Resh Lakish rules the animal permitted, arguing that no such derivation of intent from one act to another is made.
The Gemara explains that both cases (outside-from-inside and inside-from-inside) are necessary to avoid assuming each sage would concede in the other case.

items.text: Introduction of supporting arguments from Rav Dimi
items.text_en: Introduction of supporting arguments from Rav Dimi
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Rav Yirmeyah attempts to support Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Ila attempts to support Resh Lakish.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Rav Yirmeyah attempted to support Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Ila attempted to support Resh Lakish.

items.text: Rav Yirmeyah's a fortiori argument for Rabbi Yochanan and its refutations
items.text_en: Rav Yirmeyah's a fortiori argument for Rabbi Yochanan and its refutations
items.desc_en: Rav Yirmeyah argues that if slaughter for improper time (outside its time) is valid but intending to sprinkle outside its time invalidates, then slaughter not for its name (which invalidates) should certainly invalidate when intending to sprinkle not for its name. Rava bar Ahilai and Rav Ashi refute the analogy by noting unique stringencies of the compared cases, and Rav Ashi offers a corrected version comparing slaughter for a person's name (valid) with sprinkling for that name (invalid).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yirmeyah (רב ירמיה) proposes an a fortiori argument: if slaughter with intent for outside its time (valid) yet intent to sprinkle outside its time invalidates, then slaughter not for its name (which already invalidates) should certainly invalidate when intending to sprinkle not for its name.
Rava bar Ahilai (רבא בר אחילאי) objects that the analogy fails because intent beyond its time carries the unique stringency of כרת (karet), which intent not for its name lacks.
Rava bar Ahilai (רבא בר אחילאי) reformulates the argument using intent outside its designated area (which lacks כרת) as the basis for the a fortiori inference.
Rav Ashi (רב אשי) objects that intent outside its area applies to all offerings, whereas intent not for its name applies only to the Paschal offering and sin offering, breaking the analogy.

Rav Ashi (רב אשי) reformulates the argument using intent for a person's name (valid in slaughter but invalid in sprinkling) as the basis for the a fortiori inference, supporting Rabbi Yochanan (רבי יוחנן).

items.text: Rabbi Ila's support for Resh Lakish and subsequent debate
items.text_en: Rabbi Ila's support for Resh Lakish and subsequent debate
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ila argues that the Torah wrote the law of slaughter not for its name to teach that intent is not transferred between acts; otherwise, a kal vachomer would have sufficed. Rav Pappa objects that perhaps the Torah does transfer intent. The Gemara explains that if so, the verse would be superfluous. The other side (the refuter) counters that the compared cases (slaughter and receiving) require north and are used for inner sin-offerings, but the current case is peace-offerings.

sub.text: Rabbi Ila's support for Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ila's support for Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila argues that the Torah wrote the requirement for sprinkling not for its sake to teach that intent is not transferred between acts; otherwise, a kal vachomer from slaughter and collection would have sufficed.
Rav Pappa objects that perhaps the Torah wrote the requirement to teach that intent is transferred between acts, expanding disqualification.
The Gemara answers that if intent were transferred, the verse would be superfluous, as Rav Ashi's kal vachomer would have derived it; therefore the verse teaches that intent is not transferred.
Rabbi Yochanan refutes that slaughter and collection cannot serve as sources because they require north and apply to inner sin-offerings, unlike sprinkling.
Reish Lakish responds that the discussion concerns peace-offerings, which do not require north and are not inner sin-offerings, so the refutation is irrelevant.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Nachman and Rabbah on slaughter for its name with intent to sprinkle not for its name
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Nachman and Rabbah on slaughter for its name with intent to sprinkle not for its name
items.desc_en: It was stated: If one slaughtered an offering for its name but intended to sprinkle its blood not for its name, Rav Nachman says it is invalid, Rabbah says it is valid. Rabbah later retracted due to Rav Ashi's kal vachomer.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states a dispute: if one slaughtered an offering for its name but intended to sprinkle its blood not for its name, Rav Nachman rules it invalid, Rabbah rules it valid.
The gemara reports that Rabbah retracted his position in favor of Rav Nachman, based on Rav Ashi's kal vachomer (a fortiori argument).

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding the guilt-offering
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding the guilt-offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that the guilt-offering, like the sin-offering, is invalid if slaughtered not for its name, since both come for sin. Rabbi Yehoshua counters that the sin-offering's blood is applied above (on the altar horns), unlike the guilt-offering. Rabbi Eliezer cites Passover, whose blood is below yet is invalid when not for its name. Rabbi Yehoshua responds that Passover has a fixed time. Rabbi Eliezer then cites the sin-offering itself, but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer's position that the guilt-offering, like the sin-offering, is invalid if slaughtered not for its name, based on a verbal analogy from sin.
Rabbi Yehoshua objects that the sin-offering's blood is applied above the red line, unlike the guilt-offering, so the analogy fails.
Rabbi Eliezer counters that the Passover offering, whose blood is applied below, is also invalid when not for its name, proving the location is not decisive.
Rabbi Yehoshua objects that the Passover offering has a fixed time, a unique stringency not shared by the guilt-offering.
Rabbi Eliezer responds that the sin-offering itself, which has no fixed time, proves the point, as it is invalid when not for its name.
Rabbi Yehoshua begins to respond, but the text cuts off, leaving the argument incomplete.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's second argument from 'hu'
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's second argument from 'hu'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer returns to argue that just as a chatat is valid only when slaughtered for its own name, and a pesach is valid only when slaughtered for its own name, so too an asham, which also has the word 'hu' written regarding it, is valid only when offered for its own name.

sub.desc_en: רבי אליעזר (Rabbi Eliezer) opens a new argument: just as a חטאת (sin offering) is valid only when slaughtered for its own name, and a פסח (Paschal offering) is valid only when slaughtered for its own name, so too an אשם (guilt offering) should be valid only when offered for its own name.

רבי אליעזר (Rabbi Eliezer) concludes that since the word 'הוּא' (it) is stated regarding an אשם (guilt offering), it too is valid only when offered for its own name, and invalid when offered not for its own name.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's rebuttal
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's rebuttal
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua counters that the word 'hu' for asham is written only after the burning of the sacrificial portions, and the asham itself is valid even if the portions have not been burned, so the analogy fails.

sub.desc_en: רבי יהושע (Rabbi Yehoshua) objects that the word 'הוּא' (it) for an אשם (guilt offering) is written only after the burning of the sacrificial portions, and the אשם itself is valid even if those portions have not been burned, so the analogy to חטאת (sin offering) and פסח (Paschal offering) fails.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's citation of 'kachatas ka'asham'
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's citation of 'kachatas ka'asham'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer responds by citing the verse 'kakhatas ka'asham' (like the chatat, like the asham), arguing that just as a chatat is invalid when not offered for its own name, so too an asham is invalid.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer cites the verse 'כַּחַטָּאת כָּאָשָׁם' (like the chatat, like the asham) to argue that just as a chatat offered not for its own name is invalid, so too an asham offered not for its own name is invalid.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the debate and attempted analogies
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the debate and attempted analogies
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yehoshua initially said 'chozrani chalila' instead of using a binyan av. It then explores various attempted analogies and refutations, including distinctions based on karet, blood placement, inner sanctum entry, atonement, number of applications, and corners, concluding that Rabbi Eliezer holds multiple reasons.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yehoshua initially said 'חוֹזְרַנִי חֲלִילָה' instead of using a binyan av (analogy from common features).
The Gemara objects that a binyan av is refutable because both offerings share the aspect of karet (divine excision).
Rabbi Yehoshua attempts to distinguish the chatat by its blood being placed above the red line and entering the inner sanctum.
The Gemara rejects the distinction, noting that the discussion concerns outer chatat offerings, not inner ones.
The Gemara objects that if the blood of an outer chatat enters the inner sanctum, it becomes invalid, so the distinction fails.
Rabbi Eliezer holds that the asham also has the aspect of 'even the asham' from the verse 'כַּחַטָּאת כָּאָשָׁם'.
The Gemara objects that the chatat atones for those liable to karet, which the asham does not.
The Gemara rejects the objection, noting that the chatat of hearing the voice does not atone for karet.
The Gemara objects that the chatat requires four blood applications, unlike the asham.
The Gemara rejects the objection by citing Rabbi Yishmael, who holds that all bloods require four applications.
The Gemara objects that the chatat requires application on four corners of the altar, unlike the asham.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Eliezer holds multiple reasons (one of two or three) for his position, as the distinctions are not absolute.

items.text: Abaye's objection and resolution regarding blood placement
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and resolution regarding blood placement
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that one cannot say the asham's blood is placed above, using a kal vachomer from olah. The Gemara then constructs a binyan av from chatat ha'of and olah, concluding that the common denominator is that they are kodshei kodashim with blood placed below, so asham is similar.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that one cannot claim the asham's blood is placed above, using a kal vachomer from olah: since olah is entirely burnt yet its blood is below, the asham which is not entirely burnt should certainly have its blood below.

sub.text: Gemara's objection to the kal vachomer
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to the kal vachomer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the kal vachomer is flawed because olah does not provide atonement (כפרה), unlike asham.
The Gemara proposes chatat ha'of (חטאת העוף) as a counter-example to refute the objection.
The Gemara objects that chatat ha'of is not a type of animal sacrifice (זבח), unlike asham.
The Gemara counters with olah again to balance the argument.

The Gemara resolves by constructing a binyan av (בנין אב) from chatat ha'of and olah, concluding that the common denominator is that they are קדשי קדשים (most holy) with blood placed below, so asham is similar.

items.text: Rava's objection and the true reason from the verse
items.text_en: Rava's objection and the true reason from the verse
items.desc_en: Rava from Parzikya objects that the binyan av fails because chatat and olah have no fixed value, unlike asham. The Gemara then states the true reason of Rabbi Eliezer: the verse 'hakohen hamechatei otah' teaches that only the chatat's blood is placed above, not another's.

sub.desc_en: Rava from Parzikya objects to Rabbi Eliezer's binyan av (analogical construction) by noting that chatat and olah have no fixed value, unlike asham which has a fixed value.
The Gemara states the true reason of Rabbi Eliezer: the verse 'הַכֹּהֵן הַמְחַטֵּא אוֹתָהּ' teaches that only the chatat's blood is placed above, not another's.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding the verse
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that the verse 'otah' would imply that only chatat is invalid when not for its own name, but other sacrifices are valid. It resolves that the verse is not exclusive, as it excludes pesach and olat ha'of, and then suggests the mishna follows Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's view on blood placement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that if the verse 'אותה' (her) excludes other sacrifices from the rule of invalidating when not for their own name, then even a chatat would be valid when not for its own name, which is absurd.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'אותה' is not exclusive, as it excludes the pesach sacrifice from the rule.
The Gemara similarly explains that the verse here is not exclusive, as it also excludes the olat ha'of (bird burnt offering).
The Gemara objects that regarding slaughter (זביחה), the verse excludes nothing, so the challenge remains.
The Gemara alternatively resolves that the mishna follows Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who holds that the blood of a chatat behemah is placed on the body of the horn itself, not below the red line.

items.text: Mishnah citation and debate on blood entering the Heichal
items.text_en: Mishnah citation and debate on blood entering the Heichal
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah where Rabbi Akiva says all blood that enters the Heichal is invalid, while the Sages say only chatat, and Rabbi Eliezer includes asham based on 'kakhatas ka'asham'. The Gemara questions the Sages' reasoning, and Rava begins a kal vachomer from olah to argue that asham's blood entering the Heichal is not invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, presenting three positions: Rabbi Akiva invalidates all blood entering the Heichal, the Sages limit invalidation to chatat, and Rabbi Eliezer includes asham based on the verse 'כַּחַטָּאת כָּאָשָׁם'.
The Gemara asks: Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is clear from the verse, but what is the Sages' reasoning for excluding asham?
Rava answers that one cannot say asham's blood entering the Heichal is invalid, because a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from olah would prove otherwise.

items.text: Initial argument: Is an asham whose blood entered the inner sanctuary valid?
items.text_en: Initial argument: Is an asham whose blood entered the inner sanctuary valid?
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with a kal vachomer: if an olah, which is entirely burnt, is valid when its blood enters the inner sanctuary, then an asham, which is not entirely burnt, should certainly be valid. The Gemara then refutes this with a series of comparisons and counterexamples, ultimately concluding with a common element (tzad hashaveh) that both olah and minchat choteit are kodshei kodashim, so asham should also be valid.

items.text: Rava mibarnish's objection to the common element
items.text_en: Rava mibarnish's objection to the common element
items.desc_en: Rava mibarnish asks Rav Ashi: can we not refute the common element by noting that olah and minchat choteit have no fixed measure, whereas asham does have a fixed measure?

items.text: The Rabbis' scriptural derivation and the dispute over the verse
items.text_en: The Rabbis' scriptural derivation and the dispute over the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Rabbis derive from the verse 'damah' that only the blood of that specific offering (olah) is valid when brought inside, not another's. The other opinion (Rabbi Eliezer) interprets 'damah' to exclude the meat, and another opinion derives from 'dam' and 'damah'. The final opinion does not expound 'dam' and 'damah'.

items.text: The analogy of minchah to chatat and asham according to the Rabbis
items.text_en: The analogy of minchah to chatat and asham according to the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to the Rabbis, who hold that an asham slaughtered not for its name is valid, the verse equates minchah to chatat and asham. A baraita from Rabbi Shimon states that a minchat choteit is like a chatat, so if its kemitzah is not for its name it is invalid, while a minchat nedavah is like an asham, so it is valid.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's interpretation of the analogy and Rabbi Shimon's other teaching
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's interpretation of the analogy and Rabbi Shimon's other teaching
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for Rabbi Eliezer, what halacha is derived from the analogy of minchah to chatat and asham? It answers that it is for another teaching of Rabbi Shimon, regarding service without sacred vessels. Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiya explains that the verse teaches that if one performs the service by hand, it must be with the right hand like a chatat; if with a vessel, with the left hand like an asham. The Gemara questions how Rabbi Shimon can use the same verse for both teachings, and explains that the primary derivation is for Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiya's teaching, while the invalidity of minchat choteit not for its name comes from the word 'hi'.

items.text: The Rabbis' derivation of semichah for asham from chatat
items.text_en: The Rabbis' derivation of semichah for asham from chatat
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the Rabbis, what halacha is derived from the analogy of asham to chatat? It answers: to teach that just as a chatat requires semichah, so too an asham requires semichah.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding offerings slaughtered for another's name
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding offerings slaughtered for another's name
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Yosef ben Choni and Rabbi Eliezer said the same thing. Rabba explains that they dispute regarding 'acherim' (other offerings) slaughtered for the sake of a chatat. A baraita details the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer invalidates a pesach that was slaughtered for its own name after its year, and similarly other offerings slaughtered for the sake of a pesach in its time, while Rabbi Yehoshua validates. They engage in a kal vachomer argument, and Rabbi Eliezer presents another kal vachomer based on the principle that the surplus of a pesach becomes shelamim, but the surplus of shelamim does not become a pesach.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's argument from the surplus of a sin-offering
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's argument from the surplus of a sin-offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua argues that since the surplus of a sin-offering becomes a burnt-offering, and a sin-offering slaughtered for the sake of a burnt-offering is invalid, then a burnt-offering slaughtered for the sake of a sin-offering should also be invalid.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's rebuttal regarding the Passover
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's rebuttal regarding the Passover
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer rejects the analogy, arguing that the sin-offering is valid for its own name all year, whereas the Passover is only valid for its own name at its appointed time; therefore, since the Passover is invalid for its own name, it is fitting that other offerings slaughtered for its name should also be invalid.

items.text: Shimon brother of Azaryah's opinion and its scriptural basis
items.text_en: Shimon brother of Azaryah's opinion and its scriptural basis
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Shimon brother of Azaryah's opinion and explains it via a verse: offerings are not desecrated by a higher sanctity but are desecrated by a lower one. Rav Ashi and Rav Acha bar Rava attribute this to Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yannai. The Gemara questions whether the verse is needed for Shmuel's teaching about eating untithed produce, and concludes that the verse teaches both.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry about the dispute's scope
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry about the dispute's scope
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks whether the dispute between the Sages and Shimon brother of Azaryah is only about validity or also about acceptance. Abaye (or Rabbi Zerika) brings a baraita about firstborn and tithe offerings to show that they are valid but not accepted, and the Gemara clarifies that the dispute is about high and low sanctity, not just between קדשי קדשים and קדשים קלים.

items.text: Mishnah: The Passover slaughtered in the morning on the fourteenth
items.text_en: Mishnah: The Passover slaughtered in the morning on the fourteenth
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Yehoshua validates a Passover slaughtered in the morning of the fourteenth not for its own name, comparing it to one slaughtered on the thirteenth; Ben Beteira invalidates it, comparing it to one slaughtered in the afternoon. Ben Azzai adds that all edible offerings not for their own name are valid but do not fulfill the owner's obligation, except for the Passover and sin-offering, and he adds the burnt-offering, but the Sages disagree.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying Ben Beteira's position and the meaning of 'between the evenings'
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying Ben Beteira's position and the meaning of 'between the evenings'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Oshaya explains that Ben Beteira would validate a Passover slaughtered in the morning for its own name, as the entire day is its time. The Gemara questions why the Mishnah uses 'as if' and explains that Rabbi Yehoshua's use of 'as if' led Ben Beteira to use it too. The Gemara then discusses the meaning of 'between the evenings' for the Passover, with Ulla bar Rav Illai explaining it as between the two evenings.

items.text: Distinguishing the Passover from the daily offering, lamps, and incense
items.text_en: Distinguishing the Passover from the daily offering, lamps, and incense
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Ulla's interpretation by asking about the daily offering, lamps, and incense, which also have the phrase 'between the evenings'. It explains that for the daily offering, the verse 'one lamb in the morning' implies that 'between the evenings' is literal; for the lamps, the verse 'from evening until morning' limits the time; and for the incense, it is different due to its unique nature.

items.text: Gemara's question on the verse for Pesach
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the verse for Pesach
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse for Pesach specifies 'in the evening' if it is already linked to the lamps. It answers that this is a case of 'delaying a matter' – the verse with 'in the evening' and 'between the evenings' takes precedence over one with only 'between the evenings'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse for Pesach specifies 'in the evening' if it is already linked to the lamps.
The Gemara answers that this is a case of 'delaying a matter' – the verse with 'in the evening' and 'between the evenings' takes precedence over one with only 'between the evenings'.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding delaying
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding delaying
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if slaughtering in the morning is within its time, how can delaying apply? It resolves with Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that one prays the Minchah prayer before Musaf, showing that a later time can be primary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if slaughtering in the morning is within its time, how can the rule of 'delaying' apply to the evening?
The Gemara resolves: yes, as Rabbi Yochanan rules that one prays the Minchah prayer before Musaf, showing that a later time can be primary.

items.text: Question on 'between the evenings' for incense and lamps
items.text_en: Question on 'between the evenings' for incense and lamps
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah writes 'between the evenings' for incense and lamps. It then cites Rabbi's response to Ben Beteira's view: if on the 13th, when none of the day is fit, you say it's invalid, how can you say on the 14th, when part of the day is fit, it's invalid? The Gemara counters that if so, the entire day is fit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah writes 'between the evenings' (בין הערבים) for the incense and lamps.

sub.text: Rabbi's response to Ben Beteira's view
sub.text_en: Rabbi's response to Ben Beteira's view
sub.desc_en: Rabbi responds on behalf of Ben Beteira to Rabbi Yehoshua: if on the 13th, when none of the day is fit, you say it's invalid, how can you say on the 14th, when part of the day is fit, it's invalid?
The Gemara counters that if so, the entire day is fit, undermining the distinction.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on Ben Beteira's view
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on Ben Beteira's view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Ben Beteira would invalidate a Pesach slaughtered on the morning of the 14th, whether for its own sake or not, because part of the day is fit for the Pesach.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan resolves the dispute by stating that Ben Beteira would invalidate a Pesach slaughtered on the morning of the 14th, whether for its own sake or not, because part of the day is fit for the Pesach.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu challenges: if so, how can a valid Pesach exist for Ben Beteira? If set aside now, it is rejected from the start; if set aside yesterday, it is 'seen and rejected'. He resolves that it must be after midday.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu challenges: if so, how can a valid Pesach exist for Ben Beteira? If set aside now, it is rejected from the start; if set aside yesterday, it is 'seen and rejected'.
Rabbi Avahu resolves that the valid Pesach must be set aside after midday (after חצות), avoiding both problems.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's alternative views on time
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's alternative views on time
items.desc_en: Abaye says even in the morning, there is no lack of time within the day. Rava says even at night, night is not considered lacking time, citing the teaching that the eighth night enters the pen for tithing. Rabbi Aftoriki resolves a contradiction: night is for sanctity, day for acceptance.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that even if the sacrifice is offered in the morning, there is no lack of time within the day.

sub.text: Rav Pappa citing Rabbi Ishmael's school
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa citing Rabbi Ishmael's school
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa argues that even at night, night is not considered lacking time, citing the teaching that the eighth night enters the pen for tithing.
Rabbi Aftoriki resolves a contradiction between verses by assigning night for sanctity and day for acceptance.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's question and Rabbi Yochanan's proof on rejection
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's question and Rabbi Yochanan's proof on rejection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks if Rabbi Yochanan holds that living animals can be rejected. Rabbi Avahu confirms, citing Rabbi Yochanan's case of a jointly owned animal where half is consecrated, then the other half is bought and consecrated – it is holy but not offered, and its substitute is like it. Three principles are derived: living animals can be rejected, initial rejection is permanent, and the substitute is like the original.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rabbi Avahu
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rabbi Avahu
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Avahu whether Rabbi Yochanan holds that living animals can be rejected (נדחין).

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu's affirmative answer with proof
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's affirmative answer with proof
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu confirms, citing Rabbi Yochanan's case of a jointly owned animal where half is consecrated, then the other half is bought and consecrated – it is holy but not offered.

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu's additional ruling on substitute
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's additional ruling on substitute
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu adds that the animal can be exchanged (תמורה) and its substitute is like it, reinforcing the rejection status.
The Gemara states that three principles are derived from this case: living animals can be rejected, initial rejection is permanent, and the substitute is like the original.

items.text: Opening principle: rejection applies to blood
items.text_en: Opening principle: rejection applies to blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with the general principle that the concept of rejection (דיחוי) applies to the blood of sacrifices, meaning that once a sacrifice is rejected, it cannot be offered later.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the general principle that the concept of rejection (דיחוי) applies to the blood of sacrifices.

items.text: Ulla and Rabbi Yochanan's case of apostasy and rejection
items.text_en: Ulla and Rabbi Yochanan's case of apostasy and rejection
items.desc_en: Ulla quotes Rabbi Yochanan: if someone ate forbidden fat, set aside a sin-offering, then apostatized, and later repented, the offering is rejected. Rabbi Yirmeya adds a similar case of insanity. The Gemara explains why both cases are necessary: one involves active rejection, the other passive, and the latter might be considered like sleep, while the former involves ability to return.

sub.desc_en: Ulla reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: one who ate forbidden fat, set aside a sin-offering, then apostatized, and later repented — the offering is rejected (since it was already pushed aside).

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya citing Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya citing Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya adds a parallel case: one who ate forbidden fat, set aside a sin-offering, then became insane, and later recovered — the offering is also rejected.
The Gemara explains why the first case (apostasy) was necessary: it involves active self-rejection, whereas the second (insanity) is passive and might have been considered like sleep.
The Gemara explains why the second case (insanity) was necessary: it involves inability to return, whereas the first (apostasy) involves ability to return, so both are needed.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about a court ruling
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about a court ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks: if someone set aside a sin-offering, then a court ruled that fat is permitted, and later the court retracted, is the offering rejected? An elder answers that Rabbi Yochanan began his discussion of rejection with this case, because here both the person and the offering are rejected, unlike the previous cases where only the person was rejected.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether a sin-offering set aside for eating forbidden fat becomes rejected if a court first ruled fat is permitted and then retracted.

An elder answers that Rabbi Yochanan began his discussion of rejection with this case, because here both the person and the offering are rejected, unlike previous cases where only the person was rejected.

items.text: Ben Azzai's tradition from seventy-two elders
items.text_en: Ben Azzai's tradition from seventy-two elders
items.desc_en: Shimon ben Azzai states that he received a tradition from seventy-two elders that certain offerings are invalid if slaughtered not for their sake. The Gemara questions why he specifies seventy-two elders, and explains that they all held the same view.

sub.desc_en: Shimon ben Azzai states that he received a tradition from seventy-two elders that certain offerings are invalid if slaughtered not for their sake.
The Gemara asks why Ben Azzai specifies the number seventy-two elders.
The Gemara explains that the number indicates that all seventy-two elders held the same view.

items.text: Ben Azzai's addition: the עולה
items.text_en: Ben Azzai's addition: the עולה
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Ben Azzai added only the עולה (burnt offering) to the list of offerings that are invalid if slaughtered not for their sake.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Ben Azzai added only the עולה (burnt offering) to the list of offerings invalid if slaughtered not for their sake.

items.text: Rav Huna's explanation and the debate over the verse
items.text_en: Rav Huna's explanation and the debate over the verse
items.desc_en: Rav Huna explains Ben Azzai's reasoning: the verse says 'עולה הוא' – it is an עולה, implying that only when offered for its sake is it valid. The Gemara objects that an אשם also has the word 'הוא', but that verse is after the burning of the limbs. The Gemara counters that the same applies to עולה, but there are two instances of 'הוא' in the עולה passage. The Gemara then notes that the אשם also has two instances of 'הוא', leading to a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna explains Ben Azzai's reasoning: the verse 'עולה הוא אשה ריח ניחח לה׳' teaches that an עולה (burnt offering) is valid only when offered for its sake, and invalid when offered not for its sake.
The Gemara objects that an אשם (guilt offering) also has the word 'הוא' written in its verse, yet it is not disqualified when offered not for its sake.
The Gemara answers that the verse regarding the אשם (guilt offering) is written after the burning of the sacrificial portions, so it does not apply to the main sacrificial rites.
The Gemara counters that the verse regarding the עולה (burnt offering) is also written after the burning of the sacrificial portions.
The Gemara answers that regarding the עולה (burnt offering), the word 'הוא' is written twice, so one instance is superfluous and is interpreted in reference to the main sacrificial rites.
The Gemara objects that regarding the אשם (guilt offering) as well, the word 'הוא' is written twice, which would similarly imply disqualification, leading to a difficulty.

items.text: Ben Azzai's kal vachomer argument
items.text_en: Ben Azzai's kal vachomer argument
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Ben Azzai actually derives his ruling through a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if a חטאת, which is not entirely burnt, is invalid when slaughtered not for its sake, then an עולה, which is entirely burnt, should certainly be invalid. The Gemara raises objections: a חטאת atones, but a פסח proves otherwise; the פסח has a fixed time, but the חטאת proves otherwise. The common element is that both are sacred and invalid if not for their sake, so the עולה follows. The Gemara then objects that both have an element of כרת, but the text breaks off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Ben Azzai derives his ruling through a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument: if a חטאת (sin offering), which is not entirely consumed, is invalid when slaughtered not for its sake, then an עולה (burnt offering), which is entirely consumed, should certainly be invalid.
The Gemara objects that the חטאת (sin offering) is unique because it atones, unlike the עולה (burnt offering).
The Gemara answers that the פסח (Paschal offering) can prove the point, as it does not atone yet is invalid when slaughtered not for its sake.
The Gemara objects that the פסח (Paschal offering) is unique because its time is fixed, unlike the עולה (burnt offering).

The Gemara answers that the חטאת (sin offering) can prove the point, as it has no fixed time, and the common element of both is that they are sacred and invalid if not for their sake, so the עולה (burnt offering) follows.
The Gemara objects that the common element of both offerings involves an element of כרת (karet), which the עולה (burnt offering) lacks.
The text breaks off mid-sentence, indicating that the discussion is incomplete.

items.text: Resolution of Ben Azzai's kal vachomer
items.text_en: Resolution of Ben Azzai's kal vachomer
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the earlier argument that a sin-offering cannot be brought for a doubtful case because it has a side of karet, and questions why an asham cannot be brought. It answers that an asham is invalid because it shares a common side with communal offerings. Alternatively, Ben Azzai had a tradition that a sin-offering is also invalid, and Rav Huna's kal vachomer was only to sharpen students.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the earlier argument that a sin-offering cannot be brought for a doubtful case because it has a side of karet.
The Gemara asks why an asham (guilt-offering) cannot be brought for a doubtful case.
The Gemara answers that an asham is invalid because it shares a common side with communal offerings.
The Gemara offers an alternative: Ben Azzai had a tradition that a sin-offering is also invalid, and Rav Huna's kal vachomer was only to sharpen students.

items.text: Mishnah: Invalidating intentions for Pesach and Chatat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Invalidating intentions for Pesach and Chatat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a Pesach or Chatat slaughtered not for its name, or with mixed intentions (lishmah and shelo lishmah), is invalid. It lists four services that can invalidate: slaughter, collection, walking, and sprinkling. Rabbi Shimon validates walking if unnecessary, and Rabbi Eliezer distinguishes between necessary and unnecessary walking.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a Pesach or Chatat slaughtered not for its name, or with mixed intentions (lishmah and shelo lishmah), is invalid.
The Mishnah clarifies the two cases of mixed intentions: first for Pesach then for shelamim, or first for shelamim then for Pesach.

sub.text: Mishnah's list of four invalidating services
sub.text_en: Mishnah's list of four invalidating services
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the four services that can invalidate the sacrifice: slaughter, collection, walking, and sprinkling.
Rabbi Shimon validates walking, arguing that it is possible to slaughter and sprinkle without walking.
Rabbi Eliezer distinguishes between necessary walking, where intention invalidates, and unnecessary walking, where it does not.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: Does collection invalidate?
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Does collection invalidate?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether collection of blood can invalidate, citing a baraita that derives collection from the verse 'vehikrivu' and requires a fit priest and vessel. Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Tarfon debate the distinction between collection and sprinkling regarding intention and liability. Rabbi Tarfon praises Rabbi Akiva's explanation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's inclusion of collection (קבלה) among the four actions that can invalidate a sacrifice, questioning whether collection indeed has the power to invalidate.
The Gemara cites a baraita that derives collection (קבלה) from the verse 'וְהִקְרִיבוּ' and requires a fit priest and service vessel, establishing collection as a valid service.
Rabbi Akiva derives from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between 'בְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן' here and the anointed priests that collection must be performed by a fit priest with a service vessel.
Rabbi Tarfon swears he heard a tradition distinguishing between collection and sprinkling but cannot explain it himself.

Rabbi Akiva explains the distinction: collection does not treat improper intention (מחשבה) as equivalent to the action itself, while sprinkling does, and collection outside the Temple does not incur כרת (excision) while sprinkling outside does.
Rabbi Tarfon praises Rabbi Akiva, declaring that his explanation aligns with the received tradition and that anyone who separates from Rabbi Akiva is like one separating from life itself.

items.text: Rava's resolution: Pigul vs. shelo lishmah
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: Pigul vs. shelo lishmah
items.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between pigul intention and shelo lishmah intention: the Mishnah's ruling that collection invalidates refers to shelo lishmah, not pigul. The Gemara supports this from the Mishnah's wording 'nifsal' rather than 'mitpallel'.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between pigul intention and shelo lishmah intention: the Mishnah's ruling that collection invalidates refers to shelo lishmah, not pigul.

The Gemara supports Rava's distinction by noting that the Mishnah uses the term 'נִפְסָל' (invalidated) rather than 'מִתְפַּגֵּל' (rendered pigul), confirming that the ruling applies to shelo lishmah, not pigul.

items.text: Challenge: Does pigul not invalidate collection?
items.text_en: Challenge: Does pigul not invalidate collection?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's distinction, citing a baraita that includes slaughter and collection in pigul through a gezerah shavah. The baraita excludes pouring remnants and burning fats because they do not effect atonement. This shows pigul does apply to collection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's distinction by asking whether pigul does not invalidate collection.
The Gemara cites a baraita that includes slaughter and collection in pigul through a verbal analogy, showing pigul applies to collection.
The baraita excludes pouring remnants and burning fats from pigul because they do not effect atonement, reinforcing that collection is included.

items.text: Resolution of contradiction regarding intent for pouring remnants
items.text_en: Resolution of contradiction regarding intent for pouring remnants
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves an apparent contradiction: one who says 'I am slaughtering on condition to receive its blood tomorrow' is invalid, but one who says 'I am receiving its blood on condition to pour the remnants tomorrow' is not, because pouring remnants is not a sacrificial act that can be invalidated by intent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between intent during slaughter (which invalidates) and intent during blood reception for pouring remnants (which does not, since pouring remnants is not a sacrificial act that can be invalidated by intent).

items.text: Question about pouring remnants and burning portions being subject to pigul
items.text_en: Question about pouring remnants and burning portions being subject to pigul
items.desc_en: A rabbi challenges Rava: does not a baraita teach that pouring remnants and burning portions are included in pigul through the verse 'if eaten, eaten'? The Gemara cites the baraita that includes these acts.

sub.text: A certain rabbi's objection to Rava
sub.text_en: A certain rabbi's objection to Rava
sub.desc_en: A certain rabbi objects to Rava: pouring remnants and burning sacrificial parts are indeed invalidated by improper intent, as a baraita teaches that the verse 'וְאִם הֵאָכֹל יֵאָכֵל' (if it be eaten at all) includes both human consumption and altar consumption.

The Gemara cites a baraita that includes pouring remnants and burning portions in pigul through the verse 'וְאִם הֵאָכֹל יֵאָכֵל' (if eaten, eaten), teaching two eatings: human eating and altar eating.

items.text: Second resolution distinguishing between intent for pouring and burning
items.text_en: Second resolution distinguishing between intent for pouring and burning
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one who says 'I am throwing the blood on condition to pour the remnants tomorrow' is invalid, but one who says 'I am pouring the remnants on condition to burn the portions tomorrow' is not, because burning portions is a separate act that does not retroactively invalidate the pouring.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing: intent during sprinkling for pouring remnants is invalid, but intent during pouring remnants for burning sacrificial parts is not invalid.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya's tradition about finger-dipping in inner sin-offering
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya's tradition about finger-dipping in inner sin-offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya states a tradition: finger-dipping (for sprinkling) in the inner sin-offering causes pigul.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya's tradition
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya's tradition
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya states a tradition: dipping the finger (to apply blood) causes פיגול (invalidating intent) in an inner sin-offering.

items.text: Ilfa's challenge and the Gemara's response via scriptural derivation
items.text_en: Ilfa's challenge and the Gemara's response via scriptural derivation
items.desc_en: Ilfa reports the tradition to Rav Peda, who objects: pigul is learned from peace-offerings, where finger-dipping does not cause pigul. The Gemara counters that not everything is learned from peace-offerings, and the inner sin-offering's pigul comes from a scriptural derivation.

sub.desc_en: Ilfa heard the tradition and reported it before Rav Peda.
Rav Peda objects: pigul is learned only from peace-offerings, where finger-dipping does not cause pigul, so the same should apply to the sin-offering.
The Gemara rejects the analogy: not everything is learned from peace-offerings, as shown by the fact that performing a sin-offering not for its sake does not remove pigul, unlike peace-offerings.

The Gemara resolves: just as the rule for sin-offering not for its sake comes from a scriptural derivation, so too the pigul of finger-dipping in the inner sin-offering comes from a scriptural derivation.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's tradition and Resh Lakish's challenge
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's tradition and Resh Lakish's challenge
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states he heard in the upper chamber that finger-dipping causes pigul. Resh Lakish objects using the same logic from peace-offerings, and the Gemara again counters that not everything is learned from peace-offerings.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reports a tradition heard in the upper chamber that finger-dipping causes pigul in the inner sin-offering.
Resh Lakish objects, arguing that since pigul is learned from peace-offerings, and finger-dipping does not cause pigul there, it should not cause pigul in the sin-offering either.

The Gemara rejects the analogy, noting that not all laws are derived from peace-offerings, as demonstrated by the fact that improper intent (שלא לשמה) does not remove pigul from peace-offerings but does from sin-offerings.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's analogy and Rabbi Yirmeya's counter, with final principle
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's analogy and Rabbi Yirmeya's counter, with final principle
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina argues that all pigul is learned from peace-offerings, drawing an analogy between 'outside its place' in peace-offerings and 'not for its sake' in sin-offerings. Rabbi Yirmeya objects that the analogy fails because 'outside its place' applies to all sacrifices, while 'not for its sake' applies only to Pesach and sin-offering. The Gemara concludes with a general principle: a disqualifying factor removes pigul, while an essential factor brings pigul.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina asserts that all pigul is learned from peace-offerings, drawing an analogy between 'outside its place' in peace-offerings and 'not for its sake' in sin-offerings.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects that the analogy fails because 'outside its place' applies to all sacrifices, while 'not for its sake' applies only to Pesach and sin-offering.
The Gemara concludes with a general principle: a disqualifying factor removes pigul, while an essential factor brings pigul.

items.text: Rav Mari's support from the general rule of meal-offerings
items.text_en: Rav Mari's support from the general rule of meal-offerings
items.desc_en: Rav Mari cites a Mishnaic rule about meal-offerings: the one who scoops, places in a vessel, conveys, and burns. The Gemara analyzes the parallel to sacrificial services, debating whether 'placing in a vessel' is analogous to receiving blood or to conveying, concluding it is a significant act.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mari cites a Mishnaic rule about meal-offerings listing the acts of scooping, placing in a vessel, conveying, and burning.
The Gemara asks which sacrificial act 'placing in a vessel' corresponds to, since scooping parallels slaughtering, conveying parallels conveying, and burning parallels sprinkling.
The Gemara objects that placing in a vessel cannot be analogous to receiving blood, because receiving blood happens automatically while placing in a vessel is an active act of taking and putting.
The Gemara answers that since placing in a vessel is indispensable, it is a significant act, and in the sacrificial context it corresponds to conveying (הולכה).
The Gemara resolves that placing in a vessel is indeed analogous to receiving blood, because both involve placing into a vessel, and the difference between automatic and active is irrelevant.

items.text: Attempt to resolve the dispute as a Tannaic disagreement
items.text_en: Attempt to resolve the dispute as a Tannaic disagreement
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute about finger-dipping is between Tannaim: one baraita says it causes pigul, another says it does not. It then rejects this, attributing the lenient view to Rabbi Shimon, who holds that no action that is not essential causes pigul.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute about finger-dipping causing pigul is a Tannaic disagreement between two baraitot.
The Gemara rejects the suggestion, attributing the lenient baraita to Rabbi Shimon, who holds that non-essential actions do not cause pigul.
The Gemara objects that if the lenient view is Rabbi Shimon's, why single out finger-dipping, since he holds that no non-essential action causes pigul at all.

items.text: Opening statement: Pigul only for outer altar offerings like shelamim
items.text_en: Opening statement: Pigul only for outer altar offerings like shelamim
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a principle: anything not offered on the outer altar like shelamim is not subject to pigul. This sets up the discussion about inner sin-offerings.

items.text: Reconciling the principle with inner sin-offerings
items.text_en: Reconciling the principle with inner sin-offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves an apparent contradiction: the principle applies to outer sin-offerings, but inner sin-offerings are different. It explains why the Torah did not write 'and dipped' for outer sin-offerings, countering a potential inference from the word 'and took'.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon validates walking for pigul; Resh Lakish's qualification
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon validates walking for pigul; Resh Lakish's qualification
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon validates walking (holakhah) as a service for pigul. Resh Lakish says Rabbi Shimon agrees that for inner sin-offerings, improper thought disqualifies during walking because it is an indispensable service.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Shimon's principle and Rabbi Yosei's resolution
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Shimon's principle and Rabbi Yosei's resolution
items.desc_en: An objection is raised: Rabbi Shimon said pigul does not apply to offerings not like shelamim on the outer altar. Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina answers that Rabbi Shimon would concede pigul disqualifies via a kal vachomer: if not-for-its-sake (valid for shelamim) disqualifies in sin-offering, then pigul (which disqualifies shelamim) certainly should.

items.text: Deriving 'outside its place' from 'outside its time'
items.text_en: Deriving 'outside its place' from 'outside its time'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know 'outside its place' (pigul) from 'outside its time'. It considers analogies from 'outside its time' (which carries karet) and from 'not-for-its-sake' (which applies to bamot), but rejects them. It then offers an alternative: a hekesh linking 'third' (outside its time) and 'pigul' (outside its place).

items.text: Rava's multiple scenarios for Rabbi Shimon's view on walking
items.text_en: Rava's multiple scenarios for Rabbi Shimon's view on walking
items.desc_en: Rava presents several conditional scenarios: if Rabbi Shimon follows his son (that between the Ulam and the altar is north), thought only works from the Ulam entrance inward; if he follows Rabbi Yehuda (that the courtyard sanctifies), thought only works from the Heichal entrance outward; if he holds the Heichal and Ulam are one sanctity, thought works from the Ulam entrance outward; if he holds the threshold is like inside, thought works only within hand's reach; if he holds walking without feet is not walking, thought does not work at all.

items.text: Abaye's question about walking by a non-priest
items.text_en: Abaye's question about walking by a non-priest
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Chisda's spokesman whether walking by a non-priest (zar) is valid for pigul. The answer is yes, supported by a verse about the Passover where Levites skinned while priests sprinkled. Rav Sheishet objects with a baraita about a zar or onen.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation and challenge
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation and challenge
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a drunkard, a blemished priest, a sitting priest, or using the left hand invalidates the services of receiving, carrying, and sprinkling. The Gemara initially challenges this as a contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists invalidating conditions for receiving, carrying, and sprinkling, and the Gemara initially declares this a contradiction.

items.text: Rav Chisda's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that the Mishnah refers to a case where the priest performed the service while sitting on a platform (istava), not to a zar. This resolves the apparent contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: But Rav Chisda cited a verse to support his position, implying a contradiction with the Mishnah's ruling.
Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah refers to a case where the priest performed the service while sitting on a platform (איצטבה), not to a non-priest (זר).

items.text: Rabbah and Rav Yosef's dispute
items.text_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef's dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef state that carrying by a zar is a dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis: Rabbi Shimon holds that a service which can be omitted is not a service and is valid by a zar, while the Rabbis invalidate it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef state that carrying by a zar is a dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis: Rabbi Shimon holds that a service which can be omitted is not a service and is valid by a zar, while the Rabbis invalidate it.

items.text: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that slaughter, which cannot be omitted, is valid by a zar, contradicting the principle. The Gemara responds that slaughter is not a service. Further objections about the red heifer and the analogy to leprosy signs are addressed, concluding that the red heifer is Temple treasury property, not an altar sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that slaughter, which cannot be omitted, is valid when performed by a zar (non-priest), contradicting the principle that only services that can be omitted are valid by a zar.
The Gemara responds that slaughter is not considered a service (עבודה) in this context.
The Gemara objects further, citing Rabbi Zeira quoting Rav that slaughter of the red heifer (פרה) by a zar is invalid, as the Torah writes 'Eleazar' and 'חוקה' (a statute) regarding it.
The Gemara answers that the red heifer is different because it is consecrated for Temple treasury (קדשי בדק הבית), not for the altar.
The Gemara objects: if Temple treasury property requires a priestly service, then altar sacrifices (קדשי מזבח) should certainly require it as well.

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's resolution
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi resolves the objection by comparing the red heifer to the inspection of leprosy signs (מראות נגעים), which is not a service but still requires a priest.

items.text: Objection from carrying limbs and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from carrying limbs and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that carrying limbs to the ramp, which can be omitted, is invalid by a zar, contradicting Rabbi Shimon. The Gemara distinguishes that where the Torah explicitly requires a priest, it is required; where not, it is not. A further a fortiori argument is rejected.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that carrying limbs to the ramp, which can be omitted, is invalid by a zar, contradicting Rabbi Shimon's principle.
The Gemara answers that where the Torah explicitly requires a priest, it is required; where not, it is not.
The Gemara raises a further a fortiori argument: if carrying limbs, which does not impede atonement, requires a priest, then carrying blood, which does impede atonement, certainly should.
The Gemara rejects the a fortiori argument by citing Ulla in the name of Rabbi Elazar that carrying by a zar is invalid even for Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Ulla's ruling in Rabbi Elazar's name
items.text_en: Ulla's ruling in Rabbi Elazar's name
items.desc_en: Ulla states in the name of Rabbi Elazar that carrying by a zar is invalid even according to Rabbi Shimon, settling the dispute.

sub.text: Talmudic phrase 'אִיתְּמַר נָמֵי' (this too was stated) introducing supporting tradition
sub.text_en: Talmudic phrase 'אִיתְּמַר נָמֵי' (this too was stated) introducing supporting tradition
sub.desc_en: A parallel tradition is cited: Ulla says in Rabbi Elazar's name that carrying by a zar is invalid, even according to Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Inquiry about carrying without walking
items.text_en: Inquiry about carrying without walking
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether carrying without walking (e.g., sitting) is considered valid carrying. Attempts to prove from the Mishnah and other sources are refuted, until Ulla in Rabbi Yochanan's name rules that carrying without walking is not called carrying.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether carrying without walking (e.g., sitting) is considered valid carrying (הוֹלָכָה) or not.
The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that a sitting person's carrying is invalid, implying that standing without walking is valid.
The Gemara rejects the proof: the sitting case involves no movement at all, while the standing case involves slight movement, so the comparison is invalid.
