The Gemara attempts to prove from a baraita about passing the blood from one priest to another, implying that carrying without walking is valid.
The Gemara rejects the proof: there too the priests moved slightly, and the baraita merely teaches the principle of 'in a multitude of people is the king's glory' (משלי יד:כח).
The Gemara attempts to prove from a baraita that if a valid priest gave the blood to an invalid one, the invalid one must return it, implying that carrying without walking is valid.
The Gemara rejects the proof: the baraita means the valid priest should take it back, not that the invalid one's carrying is valid.
Ulla rules in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that carrying without walking is not called carrying (הוֹלָכָה).

items.text: Can a flawed procedure be rectified?
items.text_en: Can a flawed procedure be rectified?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a flawed sacrificial act can be repaired. It cites a baraita where a valid priest received blood and gave it to an invalid one, and the blood is returned to the valid priest, implying repair is possible. The Gemara objects that if repair were impossible, the blood would be invalidated, but it resolves that the invalid priest was outside the courtyard, not inside.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a flawed sacrificial procedure can be rectified (אפשר לתקנה) or not.
The Gemara cites a baraita: if a valid priest received blood and gave it to an invalid one, the blood is returned to the valid priest, implying repair is possible.
The Gemara objects: if repair were impossible, the blood would be invalidated upon being given to the invalid priest.
The Gemara resolves that the invalid priest was standing outside the courtyard (בָּרַאי), not inside, so the blood was not invalidated.

items.text: Ulla's ruling on walking without foot motion
items.text_en: Ulla's ruling on walking without foot motion
items.desc_en: Ulla states in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that walking (holakhah) without proper foot motion is invalid, implying that such a flaw cannot be rectified.

sub.text: Stam's citation of Ulla in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Stam's citation of Ulla in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Ulla reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that walking (הוֹלָכָה) performed without proper foot motion (שֶׁלֹּא בָּרֶגֶל) is invalid (פְּסוּלָה), implying that such a flaw cannot be rectified (לָא אֶפְשָׁר לְתַקּוֹנַהּ).

items.text: Rav Nachman's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects to Ulla from a baraita about blood spilled on the floor and gathered, which is valid. The Gemara resolves that the case is when the blood went outside. It then questions why the Tanna didn't simply distinguish within the same case, and concludes that the objection stands as a refutation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects to Ulla by citing a baraita where blood spilled on the floor and gathered is valid, contradicting Ulla's ruling.
The Gemara resolves the objection by explaining that the baraita deals with a case where the blood went outside the Temple courtyard.
The Gemara questions how blood can go outside but not enter inside, and offers alternative explanations involving a sloped area, a pit, or a wall.

The Gemara rejects the resolution, arguing that the Tanna would not need to teach all these cases and could have distinguished within the same case, concluding that the objection stands as a refutation.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the dispute about walking without foot motion is between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages. In the case of major walking (holakhah rabbati), all agree it is invalid; the dispute is only about minor walking (holakhah zutarti).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the dispute about walking without foot motion is between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages, and clarifies that all agree major walking (holakhah rabbati) is invalid, while the dispute is only about minor walking (holakhah zutarti).

items.text: Challenge from bird sin-offering
items.text_en: Challenge from bird sin-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara in the West raises a difficulty: for a bird sin-offering, where improper intent invalidates, how can Rabbi Shimon's view apply? If the intent occurred before the blood left, it is meaningless; if after, the mitzvah is already performed. The Gemara suggests the case is from the separation until reaching the altar, citing Rabbi Yirmeya's question about a severed hand during sprinkling, which is invalid because we require 'and he shall sprinkle... and he shall give'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara in the West raises a difficulty: for a bird sin-offering, where improper intent invalidates, how can Rabbi Shimon's view apply? If the intent occurred before the blood left, it is meaningless; if after, the mitzvah is already performed.
The Gemara resolves: the case is from the separation until reaching the altar, where intent can still be relevant.

sub.text: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Zeira
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Zeira
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asked Rabbi Zeira about a severed hand during sprinkling, and Rabbi Zeira ruled it invalid because we require 'and he shall sprinkle... and he shall give'.

items.text: Correction of the dispute's scope
items.text_en: Correction of the dispute's scope
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua report from the school of Rav that the earlier statement is a joke: the dispute is actually about major walking, not minor walking. All agree that minor walking does not invalidate.

sub.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua report from the school of Rav that the earlier statement is a joke, questioning whether the dispute is really about major walking.

sub.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: They resolve the confusion: all agree that minor walking does not invalidate, and the dispute is actually about major walking.

items.text: Dispute about repair with a non-priest
items.text_en: Dispute about repair with a non-priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses cases where a non-priest walked the blood and a priest returned it, or vice versa. The sons of Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Yannai dispute whether repair is possible. Rav Shimi bar Ashi and Rava further analyze the positions, with Rava ruling that even according to the one who invalidates, if a priest walked and then a non-priest walked, it is invalid because the blood requires proper walking.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute between the sons of Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Yannai regarding a case where a non-priest walked the blood, a priest returned it, and then a non-priest walked it again.
The Gemara explains that one sage holds it is possible to repair the walking (אפשר לתקונה), while the other holds it is not possible to repair it (לא אפשר לתקונה).

sub.text: Gemara's introduction of a new case
sub.text_en: Gemara's introduction of a new case
sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a second case: a priest walked the blood, returned it, and then a non-priest walked it; Rav Shimi bar Ashi rules that according to the one who validates the first case, this is invalid, and according to the one who invalidates the first case, this is valid.
Rava rules that even according to the one who invalidates the first case, the second case is invalid because the blood requires proper walking (צריך).

items.text: The dispute about carrying blood back into the courtyard
items.text_en: The dispute about carrying blood back into the courtyard
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya tells Rav Ashi that the phrase 'it needs to be carried' is the point of dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis. Rava clarifies that all agree on the basic cases of walking in and out, but they disagree when one brings the blood in and then takes it out again: one holds it needs to be carried back in, the other holds it is not like a walk necessary for the service.

items.text: Abaye's objection and the response
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and the response
items.desc_en: Abaye raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer states that if one received the blood outside and brought it in, that is a necessary walk, and if one received it inside and took it out, that is an unnecessary walk. Abaye argues that if one then brings it back in, that should be a necessary walk, contradicting the earlier dispute. Rav Ashi responds that if it is taught that way, it is taught that way, implying acceptance of the baraita.

items.text: The Mishnah listing invalid priests
items.text_en: The Mishnah listing invalid priests
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all sacrifices whose blood was received by a non-priest, an onen, a tevul yom, one lacking atonement, one lacking garments, one who did not wash hands and feet, an uncircumcised person, a tamei person, one sitting, one standing on vessels, on an animal, or on a friend's feet, are invalid. Receiving with the left hand is invalid, but Rabbi Shimon validates it.

items.text: Gemara: Deriving the disqualification of a non-priest
items.text_en: Gemara: Deriving the disqualification of a non-priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the disqualification of a non-priest (zar). It cites a baraita of Levi that interprets the verse 'And they shall separate from the holy things of the children of Israel' – 'children of Israel' excludes women? That can't be because a woman's offering can be brought in impurity. It then considers excluding gentiles, but that is also problematic because the tzitz does not appease for gentiles. Rather, the verse means: 'And they shall separate from the holy things – children of Israel – and they shall not profane them.' The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives it via a kal vachomer from a ba'al mum: just as a ba'al mum, who may eat, if he serves he profanes, so too a non-priest.

items.text: First kal vachomer from blemished priest
items.text_en: First kal vachomer from blemished priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer: if a blemished priest, who may eat sacrifices, desecrates service, then a zar, who may not eat, certainly desecrates. The argument is challenged and refined through a tzad hashaveh comparing blemished and impure priests.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if a blemished priest, who may eat sacrifices, desecrates service, then a zar (non-priest), who may not eat, certainly desecrates.
The objection is raised: the blemished priest is unique because the Torah equates the offering (קָרֵב) with the offerer (מַקְרִיב), a quality not shared by a zar.
The Gemara counters by citing the impure priest (טָמֵא) as a parallel: though he also desecrates service, he has his own unique quality (he transmits impurity), so the comparison is reframed.
The Gemara constructs a tzad hashaveh (common element): both the blemished and impure priests are warned (מוּזְהָרִין) and desecrate if they serve, so the zar, who is also warned, is included.

items.text: Source for zar's warning and refutation
items.text_en: Source for zar's warning and refutation
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source that a zar is warned (muzhar) and finds it in the verse 'v'zar lo yikrav'. However, a refutation is raised: the tzad hashaveh is flawed because both blemished and impure priests were never permitted at a bamah (private altar).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that a zar is warned (muzhar), and rejects the verse 'וְיִנָּזְרוּ' because it already discusses desecration (חילול) in its own context.
The Gemara proposes that the source is the verse 'וְזָר לֹא יִקְרַב אֲלֵיכֶם' (a stranger shall not approach you).
An objection is raised: the common element (צד השוה) of the previous argument is flawed because both blemished and impure priests were never permitted at a private altar (במה).

items.text: Revised kal vachomer with onen
items.text_en: Revised kal vachomer with onen
items.desc_en: The Gemara replaces the impure priest with an onen (mourner) to avoid the refutation. Rav Sama bar Rava challenges this, questioning whether an onen is indeed permitted at a bamah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara replaces the impure priest with an onen (mourner) in the kal vachomer to avoid the earlier refutation.

sub.text: Gemara's continuation of the kal vachomer
sub.text_en: Gemara's continuation of the kal vachomer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara completes the revised kal vachomer, concluding that the common factor is that all are warned and if they serve they invalidate.
Rav Sama bar Rava challenges the revised kal vachomer by questioning whether an onen is indeed forbidden at a bamah (private altar), potentially undermining the common factor.

items.text: Kal vachomer from seated priest
items.text_en: Kal vachomer from seated priest
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya proposes a kal vachomer from a seated priest (yoshev): if a seated priest, who may eat, desecrates, then a zar certainly does. The Gemara refines this by considering a Torah scholar seated priest and notes that the seated priest is valid at a bamah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from a seated priest (יושב): if a seated priest, who may eat, desecrates when he serves, then a zar (non-priest), who may not eat, certainly desecrates if he serves.
The Gemara objects that a seated priest is disqualified from testimony, which is a unique stringency not shared by a zar, undermining the kal vachomer.
The Gemara refines the argument by specifying a Torah scholar (תלמיד חכם) who is seated, who is not disqualified from testimony, thus removing the objection.
The Gemara raises a further objection: even a Torah scholar who sits is called 'seated' (שם יושב), and the term 'seated' itself implies disqualification from testimony.
The Gemara rejects this objection, stating that the mere name 'seated' does not create a valid refutation (פירכא).

The Gemara concludes that even if one considers the objection valid, the kal vachomer can be derived from the seated priest combined with one of the other disqualifications (e.g., בעל מום or אונן) to establish the common element.

items.text: Sources for yoshev and onen at bamah
items.text_en: Sources for yoshev and onen at bamah
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides scriptural sources: a seated priest is invalid for the Mishkan but valid at a bamah, and an onen who does not leave the Temple desecrates service.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that a seated priest is valid at a bamah, and answers with the verse 'לעמוד לפני ה׳ לשרתו' (to stand before the Lord to serve Him), implying that standing is required only before the Lord in the Mishkan, not before a bamah.

The Gemara asks for the source regarding an onen, and answers with the verse 'ומן המקדש לא יצא ולא יחלל' (and from the sanctuary he shall not go out, nor profane), implying that any other who does not leave profanes the service.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's alternative derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's alternative derivation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar derives the desecration of a zar from the verse 'hen hikrivu', implying that if others (non-priests) had offered, they would have been consumed. The Gemara explains why Rabbi Elazar rejects the previous source and why the other sages reject his.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar derives the desecration of a zar from the verse 'הן הקריבו' (they offered), implying that if others had offered they would have been consumed.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Elazar does not derive the desecration from the verse 'ומן המקדש לא יצא' (and from the sanctuary he shall not go out).
Rabbi Elazar rejects the verse because it does not explicitly state that another who did not go out desecrated.
The Gemara asks why the other sages do not derive the desecration from the verse 'הן הקריבו'.
The other sages hold that the offering was burned because of טומאה (ritual impurity), not because of the zar's desecration.

items.text: Beit Rabbi Yishmael's kal vachomer
items.text_en: Beit Rabbi Yishmael's kal vachomer
items.desc_en: The daf begins a tannaitic tradition from Beit Rabbi Yishmael, deriving the desecration of a zar via a kal vachomer from a blemished priest, but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: Beit Rabbi Yishmael teaches a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) deriving the desecration of a zar (non-priest) from a blemished priest, but the text cuts off.

items.text: First a fortiori argument: from a blemished priest to an onen
items.text_en: First a fortiori argument: from a blemished priest to an onen
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that if a blemished priest, who may eat holy things, invalidates service when he performs it, then an onen, who may not eat, should certainly invalidate service. The argument is challenged by noting that a blemished priest is unique because he is disqualified for both offering and eating. The Gemara responds with a tzad ha-shaveh (common element) argument comparing a blemished priest and a non-priest (zar), concluding that any warned priest who serves invalidates, including an onen.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a first a fortiori argument: if a blemished priest, who may eat holy things, invalidates service when he performs it, then an onen, who may not eat, should certainly invalidate service.
The objection argues that a blemished priest is unique because the law treats offerings brought by him as equivalent to those he offers himself, a quality not shared by an onen.
The Gemara responds by introducing a non-priest (zar) as a counterexample, noting that a zar has no remedy for his disqualification.

The Gemara completes the tzad ha-shaveh (common element) argument: both a blemished priest and a zar are warned, and if they serve they invalidate; therefore an onen, who is also warned, should invalidate service.

items.text: Source of the warning for an onen
items.text_en: Source of the warning for an onen
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions where the onen is warned against serving. It rejects the possibility that the warning comes from the verse 'and from the sanctuary he shall not go out' because that verse itself mentions the invalidation. Instead, it suggests the warning comes from the incident of Nadav and Avihu, who were punished for offering while in a state of aninut.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the onen is warned, and answers that it is derived from the verse 'הֵן הִקְרִיבוּ' (they offered), implying that the warning comes from the incident where Nadav and Avihu died due to their aninut.
The Gemara answers that the warning comes from the incident of Nadav and Avihu (הֵן הִקְרִיבוּ), who were punished for offering while in a state of aninut.

items.text: Refutation of the tzad ha-shaveh and a new argument from a tamei priest
items.text_en: Refutation of the tzad ha-shaveh and a new argument from a tamei priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to refute the tzad ha-shaveh by noting that both a blemished priest and a non-priest are never permitted in any context (their disqualification is absolute). The Gemara responds by introducing a tamei (impure) priest as a third case, and then constructs a new tzad ha-shaveh from all three cases, concluding that any warned priest who serves invalidates.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection against the tzad ha-shaveh (common element) argument: the two cases (blemished priest and non-priest) share the trait that they were never permitted in any context, unlike the onen.
The Gemara responds by introducing a tamei (impure) priest as a third case that breaks the objection.
The Gemara constructs a new tzad ha-shaveh from all three cases (blemished priest, non-priest, and tamei priest), concluding that any warned priest who serves invalidates the service.

items.text: Further refutation: leniency for the High Priest in individual offerings
items.text_en: Further refutation: leniency for the High Priest in individual offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a further objection: the tzad ha-shaveh is flawed because all three cases (blemished, non-priest, tamei) are never permitted even for the High Priest in his individual offering, whereas an onen is permitted for the High Priest. The Gemara notes that impurity (tum'ah) was at least permitted in some contexts.

sub.desc_en: A further objection is raised: the common element of blemished priest, zar, and tamei is that none were permitted even for a High Priest in a personal offering, but the Gemara notes that impurity was permitted in some contexts.

items.text: Alternative a fortiori argument: from a seated priest
items.text_en: Alternative a fortiori argument: from a seated priest
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya proposes a different a fortiori argument: if a seated priest, who may eat, invalidates service, then an onen, who may not eat, should certainly invalidate. The objection that a seated priest is disqualified for testimony is countered by positing a Torah scholar who is fit for testimony. The Gemara concludes that even if the objection stands, the argument can be made from a seated priest combined with one of the previous cases.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya proposes an a fortiori argument: if a seated priest, who may eat, invalidates service, then an onen, who may not eat, should certainly invalidate.
An objection is raised: a seated priest is disqualified for testimony, but the Gemara counters by positing a Torah scholar who is fit for testimony.
The Gemara concludes that even if the objection stands, the argument can be made from a seated priest combined with one of the previous cases.

items.text: Rava's distinction: an onen is invalid only for individual offerings
items.text_en: Rava's distinction: an onen is invalid only for individual offerings
items.desc_en: Rava states that an onen is invalid only for individual offerings, but for communal offerings he is acceptable. He supports this with a fortiori argument from impurity: just as impurity, which is never permitted for the High Priest in his individual offering, is permitted for a common priest in communal offerings, so too aninut, which is permitted for the High Priest in his individual offering, should certainly be permitted for a common priest in communal offerings.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that the rule of an onen being invalid applies only to individual offerings, but for communal offerings he is acceptable.

Rava supports his distinction with a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from impurity: just as impurity, which is never permitted for the High Priest in his individual offering, is permitted for a common priest in communal offerings, so too aninut, which is permitted for the High Priest in his individual offering, should certainly be permitted for a common priest in communal offerings.

items.text: Rava bar Ahilai's counter-argument and the resulting symmetrical kal va-chomer
items.text_en: Rava bar Ahilai's counter-argument and the resulting symmetrical kal va-chomer
items.desc_en: Rava bar Ahilai challenges Rava's conclusion with a counter a fortiori argument: if impurity, permitted for a common priest in communal offerings, is not permitted for the High Priest in his individual offering, then aninut, not permitted for a common priest in communal offerings, should certainly not be permitted for the High Priest in his individual offering. The Gemara then presents a series of symmetrical arguments showing that the same logic could be used to permit impurity for the High Priest or forbid it for the common priest, demonstrating the circularity of the reasoning.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Ahilai challenges Rava's conclusion with a counter a fortiori argument: if impurity, permitted for a common priest in communal offerings, is not permitted for the High Priest in his individual offering, then aninut, not permitted for a common priest in communal offerings, should certainly not be permitted for the High Priest in his individual offering.
The Gemara presents a symmetrical a fortiori argument that would permit impurity for the High Priest in his individual offering, using the same logic as Rava bar Ahilai.
The Gemara presents another symmetrical a fortiori argument that would forbid impurity for the common priest in communal offerings, using the same logic.
The Gemara provides a mnemonic (סִימָן) summarizing the four symmetrical arguments: 'and not permitted, and not permitted, aninut, and impurity, impurity, individual, and individual, communal'.

items.text: Gemara's observation on multiple possible objections
items.text_en: Gemara's observation on multiple possible objections
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that there are multiple possible objections to the previous argument, each left unresolved in its place.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that there are multiple possible objections to the previous argument, each left unresolved in its place.

items.text: Source for tevul yom disqualifying service
items.text_en: Source for tevul yom disqualifying service
items.desc_en: Rabbi Simai derives a hint that a tevul yom who serves desecrates the service from the verse 'Kedoshim yihyu ve-lo yechalelu', applying it to tevul yom since the case of a tamei person is already derived from 've-yinazeru'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that a tevul yom (one who immersed but awaits sunset) who serves desecrates the service?

A baraita is cited: Rabbi Simai derives a hint for tevul yom from the verse 'קְדֹשִׁים יִהְיוּ וְלֹא יְחַלְּלוּ' (they shall be holy and not desecrate), applying it to tevul yom since the case of a tamei person is already derived from 'וְיִנָּזְרוּ'.

items.text: Objection: apply to other cases instead
items.text_en: Objection: apply to other cases instead
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why apply the verse to tevul yom rather than to one who makes a bald spot or mars the corner of the beard?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why apply the verse to tevul yom rather than to one who makes a bald spot or mars the corner of the beard?

items.text: Source for tevul yom's death penalty
items.text_en: Source for tevul yom's death penalty
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that a tevul yom who serves is liable to death via a gezeirah shavah of 'chillul' from terumah: just as he disqualifies terumah, he desecrates service.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives that a tevul yom who serves is liable to death via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'חילול' from תרומה (priestly portion): just as he disqualifies תרומה, he desecrates service.

items.text: Why the Torah lists all three: tamei, tevul yom, mechusar kippurim
items.text_en: Why the Torah lists all three: tamei, tevul yom, mechusar kippurim
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains that each category is necessary because none can be derived from the others: tamei is unique in defiling a tevul yom, mechusar kippurim is unique in being invalid for terumah, and tevul yom is unique in lacking an act. The Gemara then questions why not omit one and derive it from the other two, but concludes that each has a unique leniency preventing derivation.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah asks why the Torah needs to list all three categories — טמא (impure), טבול יום (one who immersed that day), and מחוסר כפורים (one lacking atonement) — separately.

Rabbah explains that each category is necessary because none can be derived from the others: טמא (impure) is unique in defiling a טבול יום (one who immersed that day), מחוסר כפורים (one lacking atonement) is unique in being invalid for תרומה (priestly portion), and טבול יום (one who immersed that day) is unique in lacking an act.
The Gemara objects that while one category cannot be derived from a single other, it could be derived from the combination of the other two.
The Gemara rejects omitting מחוסר כפורים (one lacking atonement) because the other two share the common leniency of being invalid for תרומה (priestly portion), which מחוסר כפורים lacks.
The Gemara rejects omitting טבול יום (one who immersed that day) because the other two share the common leniency of lacking an act, while טבול יום's impurity is ultimately weaker.

items.text: Gemara's initial claim
items.text_en: Gemara's initial claim
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Yosei holds that a mechusar kippurim who is a zav is considered like a zav himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asserts that Rabbi Yosei considers a mechusar kippurim who is a zav (one with a seminal emission) to be like a zav himself.

items.text: Debate about mechusar kippurim of a zav
items.text_en: Debate about mechusar kippurim of a zav
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the status of a mechusar kippurim of a zav is a dispute among Tannaim. It then reinterprets the dispute as being about the source of impurity for a tevul yom in the context of the red heifer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the status of a mechusar kippurim of a zav (one lacking atonement after a zav's discharge) being like a zav is a dispute among Tannaim.

The Gemara cites a baraita where the first Tanna rules that both an onen (mourner before burial) and a mechusar kippurim may burn the red heifer, while Yosef HaBavli rules that an onen is valid but a mechusar kippurim is invalid.
The Gemara asks whether the dispute is about whether a mechusar kippurim of a zav is like a zav, with one opinion holding it is and the other holding it is not.

The Gemara rejects this, stating that all agree a mechusar kippurim of a zav is like a zav, and the dispute is about the source of impurity for a tevul yom (one who immersed that day) in the context of the red heifer, based on the verse 'וְהִזָּה הַטָּהֹר' (the pure one shall sprinkle) implying he was impure.

The Gemara resolves that one opinion holds the impurity is like all other Torah impurities (where a tevul yom is impure), and the other holds it is only the impurity specific to this parashah (the red heifer, where a tevul yom is pure).

items.text: Conclusion about mechusar kippurim of a zav
items.text_en: Conclusion about mechusar kippurim of a zav
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that an onen and a tevul yom from a light impurity (like a sheretz) can be derived via a kal vachomer from a tevul yom from a corpse, but a mechusar kippurim of a zav, whose impurity is severe, cannot be derived.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that an onen and a tevul yom from a light impurity (like a sheretz) can be derived via a kal vachomer from a tevul yom from a corpse, but a mechusar kippurim of a zav, whose impurity is severe, cannot be derived.

items.text: Source for mechusar begadim
items.text_en: Source for mechusar begadim
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avuh quoting Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon derives that a priest lacking vestments is disqualified from service, based on the verse that equates their priesthood with their garments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that a priest lacking vestments (מחוסר בגדים) is disqualified from service?

sub.text: Rabbi Avuh citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avuh citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avuh, citing Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, derives from the verse 'וְחָגַרְתָּ אוֹתָם...' that when the priests' garments are upon them, their priesthood is upon them; when their garments are not upon them, their priesthood is not upon them.

items.text: Alternative source for mechusar begadim
items.text_en: Alternative source for mechusar begadim
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the derivation is necessary, as another source (from a baraita) already derives the disqualification of a priest lacking vestments from the juxtaposition of the prohibition of wine to the service.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the derivation from the verse is necessary, since another source already provides it.
The Gemara cites a baraita that derives the disqualification of a priest lacking vestments from the juxtaposition of the prohibition of wine to the service.

items.text: Gezeirah shava for drunk priest
items.text_en: Gezeirah shava for drunk priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a gezeirah shava from the word "חוקה" to derive that a drunk priest is disqualified from service, just as a priest lacking garments is. Without this derivation, one might have thought the death penalty for a non-priest only applies to services that a non-priest is liable for, but not to a drunk priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'חוקה' to disqualify a drunk priest from service.

The Gemara explains that without this derivation, one might have thought the death penalty for a non-priest only applies to services a non-priest is liable for, but not to a drunk priest; the גזירה שווה teaches otherwise.

items.text: Source for drunk priest from lacking garments
items.text_en: Source for drunk priest from lacking garments
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found the source for a priest lacking garments, but from where do we derive the disqualification of a drunk priest? It answers: it comes via a gezeirah shava from the word "חוקה" used in the context of a priest lacking garments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found the source for a priest lacking garments, but from where do we derive the disqualification of a drunk priest?
The Gemara answers: it comes via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'חוקה' used in the context of a priest lacking garments.

items.text: Reconciling the baraita with the gezeirah shava
items.text_en: Reconciling the baraita with the gezeirah shava
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a difficulty: the baraita cites the verse "וּלְהַבְדִּיל" as the source, not the gezeirah shava. It explains that the baraita was stated before the gezeirah shava was established. The Gemara then clarifies that the baraita actually means: from where do we know that there is no distinction between a priest lacking garments and a drunk priest or one who has not washed hands and feet? The answer is the gezeirah shava.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita cites the verse "וּלְהַבְדִּיל" as the source, not the gezeirah shava.
The Gemara answers that the baraita was stated before the gezeirah shava was established.
The Gemara objects that the baraita seems to derive the law of a priest lacking garments from the drunk priest, not the other way around.

The Gemara clarifies that the baraita actually asks: from where do we know that there is no distinction between a priest lacking garments and a drunk priest or one who has not washed hands and feet? The answer is the gezeirah shava.

items.text: Purpose of the verse "לְהַבְדִּיל"
items.text_en: Purpose of the verse "לְהַבְדִּיל"
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if so, what is the purpose of the verse "לְהַבְדִּיל"? It answers: it is in accordance with the practice of Rav, who would not appoint an interpreter for his colleague on a festival due to intoxication.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the gezeira shava already teaches the disqualification of a priest who is a shatuyei yayin (intoxicated), what is the purpose of the verse 'לְהַבְדִּיל' (to separate)?
The Gemara answers: the verse is in accordance with the practice of Rav, who would not appoint an interpreter for his colleague on a festival due to intoxication (שכרות).

items.text: Source for high priest wearing common priest's garments
items.text_en: Source for high priest wearing common priest's garments
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the disqualification of a drunk priest is derived from here; perhaps it is derived from the verse "וְנָתְנוּ בְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֵן" which teaches that a high priest who wore the garments of a common priest and served, his service is invalid. Without this, one might have thought this only applies to services that effect atonement, but not to other services.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the disqualification of a drunk priest might already be derived from the verse "וְנָתְנוּ בְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֵן" which teaches that a high priest who wore common priest's garments and served, his service is invalid.

The Gemara answers that without the derivation from here, one might have thought the disqualification only applies to services that effect atonement (עֲבוֹדָה דִּמְעַכְּבָא כַּפָּרָה), but not to other services.

items.text: Source for common priest wearing high priest's garments
items.text_en: Source for common priest wearing high priest's garments
items.desc_en: The Gemara further questions: perhaps the disqualification is derived from the verse "וְעָרְכוּ בְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֲנִים" which teaches that a common priest who wore the garments of a high priest and served, his service is invalid. Without this, one might have thought this applies only to a deficiency (lacking garments), but not to an excess (wearing extra garments); the verse teaches us that it applies to excess as well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the source for disqualifying a common priest wearing high priest's garments is actually from the verse "וְעָרְכוּ בְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֲנִים" or from a different verse.

The Gemara answers that the verse "וְעָרְכוּ בְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֲנִים" teaches that a common priest wearing high priest's garments is disqualified, and without this, one might have thought the disqualification applies only to a deficiency (lacking garments) but not to an excess (wearing extra garments); the verse teaches that it applies to excess as well.

items.text: Baraita on various garment defects
items.text_en: Baraita on various garment defects
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that lists cases where the service is valid: if the priestly garments were torn, folded, or worn out; but if he wore two pairs of trousers, two belts, was missing one garment, had an extra one, or had a bandage under his garment, the service is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists cases where the service is valid (torn, folded, or worn-out garments) and cases where it is invalid (two pairs of trousers, two belts, missing a garment, an extra garment, or a bandage under the garment).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if priestly garments are wrinkled or torn and the service was performed, the service is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if priestly garments are wrinkled or torn and the service was performed, the service is invalid.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rami bar Chama's resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rami bar Chama's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel distinguishing between wrinkled (valid) and removed (invalid) garments, but a baraita says removed garments are valid. Rami bar Chama resolves the contradiction: one case refers to removal via the belt, the other to garments never having the belt at all.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel distinguishes: garments that are 'raised' (מְרוּשָּׁלִין) are valid, but 'folded up' (מְסוּלָּקִין) are invalid.
The Gemara objects: a baraita explicitly states that 'folded up' garments are valid, contradicting Shmuel.
Rami bar Chama resolves the contradiction: the baraita refers to garments folded up by the belt (אַבְנֵט), while Shmuel refers to garments that were never properly set at all.

items.text: Rav's opposing view
items.text_en: Rav's opposing view
items.desc_en: Rav states that both wrinkled and removed garments are invalid, contradicting Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that both 'raised' and 'folded up' garments are invalid.

items.text: Challenge to Shmuel and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge to Shmuel and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Huna is challenged by his host: Shmuel says removed garments are invalid, but a baraita says they are valid. Rav Huna responds that the baraita is the one Rami bar Chama distinguished.

sub.desc_en: A story: Rav Huna was challenged by his host about Shmuel's ruling, and he replied that Rami bar Chama's resolution distinguishes the cases.
Rav Huna responds that the baraita is the one Rami bar Chama distinguished, so it does not contradict Shmuel.

items.text: Challenge to Rav
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav's position: if wrinkled means removed via the belt, then the belt cuts the garment, so removed garments are problematic, but the baraita says removed garments are valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rav's position is difficult, because even if 'raised' means 'folded up by the belt', the baraita still contradicts Rav regarding 'folded up' garments.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira states that one Tanna teaches: wrinkled garments that were removed via the belt are valid.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav clarifies: 'raised' garments that were folded up by the belt are valid, resolving the difficulty.

items.text: Digression on tzitzit and the number of corners
items.text_en: Digression on tzitzit and the number of corners
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmiya from Difti connects the dispute about wrinkled garments to a Tannaitic dispute about the number of corners for tzitzit: whether a garment with five corners is included or excluded, based on the verse 'asher techaseh bah'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmiya from Difti introduces a Tannaitic dispute about whether a garment with five corners is included in the obligation of tzitzit, based on the verse 'asher techaseh bah'.
A second baraita is cited, which excludes a five-cornered garment, and the Gemara suggests the dispute is about whether an extra corner is considered present or absent.
The Gemara rejects the proposed explanation, stating that all agree an extra corner is considered present, and the dispute is about the exegetical force of the verse 'asher techaseh bah'.
The Gemara asks what the second Tanna does with the verse 'asher techaseh bah', and answers that it is used to exclude a night garment from the obligation of tzitzit.
The Gemara explains the reasoning: a blind person's garment is included because others can see it, while a night garment is excluded because it is not seen by others.
The Gemara notes that the first Tanna derives the inclusion of a five-cornered garment from the word 'asher', while the second Tanna does not expound the word 'asher' at all.

items.text: Derivation of laws of priestly garments from 'bad'
items.text_en: Derivation of laws of priestly garments from 'bad'
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that 'bad' implies linen, new, twisted, with six-fold thread, and not worn with ordinary garments. Abaye questions the necessity of 'new', citing a baraita that worn garments are valid. Rav Yosef explains that 'bad' is a general requirement, some for mitzvah and some for validity. The Gemara then derives that 'bad' means linen from various verses, including Ezekiel.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists five requirements derived from the word 'בד' (bad) for priestly garments: they must be of linen, new, twisted, with six-fold thread, and not worn with ordinary garments.
Abaye questions Rav Yosef: the requirement that garments be new seems contradicted by a baraita that worn-out garments are valid.
Rav Yosef responds that the word 'בד' does not imply all requirements are absolute; some are for the ideal standard (מצוה) and some for validity (עיכוב).
The Gemara asks how we know 'בד' means linen, and Rabbi Yosef bar Chanina answers: it is something that grows from the ground 'בד בבד' (stalk by stalk).
The Gemara objects that wool also grows stalk-like, but the reply is that wool splits, while flax splits only when damaged.
Ravina cites Ezekiel 44:18, which explicitly mentions 'פשתים' (flax/linen) for priestly garments, as proof that 'בד' means linen.
Rav Ashi questions how the law was known before Ezekiel; the resolution is that it was a received tradition (גמרא), and Ezekiel merely provided a scriptural support.

items.text: Explanation of 'lo yachgeru baya'za'
items.text_en: Explanation of 'lo yachgeru baya'za'
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the verse means they should not gird themselves in a place that sweats, and a baraita specifies the proper place for the belt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of 'לֹא יַחְגְּרוּ בַּיָּזַע' (they shall not gird themselves with sweat), and Abaye explains: they should not gird in a place that causes sweating.
A baraita supports this: when girding, they should not gird below the loins or above the elbows, but rather at the proper place.
A baraita supports Abaye's interpretation, specifying that when girding, they should not gird below their loins or above their elbows, but rather at the proper place.

items.text: Story of Rav Ashi and the king
items.text_en: Story of Rav Ashi and the king
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi recounts an incident where he stood before King Izgaddar, and his belt slipped. The king handed it back to him, citing the verse 'a kingdom of priests and a holy nation'. When Rav Ashi came before Amemar, Amemar said the verse 'and kings shall be your nursemaids' was fulfilled in him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the story of Rav Ashi and the king, citing the verse about the priests' elbows.
Rav Ashi recounts how King Izgaddar returned his belt and cited the verse 'a kingdom of priests', and Amemar said the verse 'kings shall be your nursemaids' was fulfilled in him.

items.text: Mishnah: Priest with a wounded finger
items.text_en: Mishnah: Priest with a wounded finger
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that a priest with a wounded finger may wrap a reed around it in the Temple, but not in the provinces. If the purpose is to draw blood, it is forbidden both here and there.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a priest with a wounded finger may wrap a reed around it in the Temple but not in the provinces, and if the purpose is to draw blood it is forbidden everywhere.

items.text: Dispute about a small bell as an interposition
items.text_en: Dispute about a small bell as an interposition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya says the Mishnah only permits a reed, but a small bell is considered an excess of garments. Rabbi Yochanan says excess garments only apply where garments are worn, but not where garments are not worn, so it is not an excess.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya states that the Mishnah only permits a reed, but a small bell is considered an excess of garments (יתור בגדים).
Rabbi Yochanan responds that the rule of excess garments (יתור בגדים) applies only where garments are worn, but not where garments are not worn, so a small bell is not an excess.

items.text: Objection from interposition and Rava's ruling
items.text_en: Objection from interposition and Rava's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why not consider the reed an interposition? It answers: it is on the left hand, or not in the place of service. This disagrees with Rava, who said in the name of Rav Chisda: in the place of garments, even a single hair interposes; not in the place of garments, three by three fingerbreadths interpose, less than that does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why not consider the reed an interposition (חציצה) for the priest's service?
The Gemara answers: the reed is on the left hand, which is not the place of service.
Alternatively, the reed is not in the place of service (where the priest's garments must be worn).

sub.text: Rava's ruling in the name of Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rava's ruling in the name of Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this answer disagrees with Rava's ruling in the name of Rav Chisda: in the place of garments, even a single hair interposes; not in the place of garments, three by three fingerbreadths interpose, less than that does not.

items.text: Clarification: Does Rava disagree with Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya?
items.text_en: Clarification: Does Rava disagree with Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Rava certainly disagrees with Rabbi Yochanan, but does he also disagree with Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya? It answers: a small bell is different because it is significant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rava's ruling disagrees only with Rabbi Yochanan or also with Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya.
The Gemara answers that a small bell is different because it is significant (חשיב), so Rava does not disagree with Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya.

items.text: Alternative version of the dispute
items.text_en: Alternative version of the dispute
items.desc_en: An alternative version: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya says a small bell interposes. Rabbi Yochanan says interposition with less than three by three only applies where garments are worn, but not in other places. This is the same as Rava's ruling. The Gemara asks if this disagrees with Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya, and answers: a small bell is different because it is significant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents an alternative version of the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya says a small bell interposes, and Rabbi Yochanan says interposition with less than three by three only applies where garments are worn, and this is the same as Rava's ruling.
The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yochanan's position disagrees with Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya.
The Gemara answers that a small bell is different because it is significant.

items.text: Why the Mishnah mentions a reed specifically
items.text_en: Why the Mishnah mentions a reed specifically
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Yochanan, why mention a reed? Let it teach about a small bell. It answers: the Mishnah incidentally teaches that a reed heals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Yochanan, why does the Mishnah specifically mention a reed (גמי) rather than a small bell (צילצול קטן), which would also not constitute an interposition?
The Gemara answers: the Mishnah incidentally teaches along the way that a reed (גמי) heals, which is why it specifically mentions a reed rather than a small bell.

items.text: Series of inquiries about interpositions
items.text_en: Series of inquiries about interpositions
items.desc_en: Rava asks about wind entering his garment, a louse (alive or dead), dust, the armpit, inserting a hand into the bosom, loose hair, and hair protruding from the garment. Rabbi Zeira asks about phylacteries. The matter reaches Rabbi Ami, who says it is an established tradition that phylacteries interpose.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether wind entering his garment constitutes an interposition (חציצה) during priestly service, since the garment is not directly on his skin.
Rava asks whether a louse interposes, distinguishing between a dead louse (certainly interposes) and a live one (which moves and may not be considered an interposition).
Rava asks whether dust interposes, clarifying that coarse dust certainly does, but fine dust (אבק עפר) is questionable.
Rava asks whether the armpit area interposes, since the garment does not directly touch the skin there.

sub.text: Rava's question about inserting a hand
sub.text_en: Rava's question about inserting a hand
sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether inserting one's hand into one's own bosom creates an interposition, i.e., whether one's own body can interpose.
Rava asks whether a single hair interposes, clarifying that a normal hair certainly does, but a loose hair (נימא מדולדלת) is questionable.
Mar bar Rav Ashi asks whether hair protruding from one's garment is considered like one's body (and thus not an interposition) or not.

Rabbi Zeira asks whether phylacteries (תפילין) interpose, distinguishing between the opinion that night is not a time for phylacteries (they certainly interpose) and the opinion that night is a time for phylacteries (the question is whether a מצוה (commandment) of the body interposes).
The matter reaches Rabbi Ami, who states that it is an established tradition (תלמוד ערוך) that phylacteries interpose.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah about priests and phylacteries
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah about priests and phylacteries
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: a Mishnah says priests in their service, Levites on the platform, and Israelites at the watch are exempt from prayer and phylacteries. Does this mean if they put them on, they do not interpose? It answers: no, if they put them on, they do interpose. The Gemara objects: if so, why say 'exempt'? It should say 'forbidden'! It answers: since Levites and Israelites are not commanded about 'forbidden', it says 'exempt'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges with a Mishnah stating that priests in their service, Levites on the platform, and Israelites at the watch are exempt from prayer and phylacteries.
The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that if they did put on phylacteries, they do not interpose.
The Gemara answers that if they put them on, they do interpose.
The Gemara objects: if so, the Mishnah should have said 'forbidden' rather than 'exempt'.
The Gemara resolves: since Levites and Israelites are not subject to the prohibition of interposition, the Mishnah uses the term 'exempt'.

items.text: Resolution: Distinction between hand and head phylacteries
items.text_en: Resolution: Distinction between hand and head phylacteries
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that says if they put them on, they do not interpose. It resolves: this is not difficult; one refers to hand phylacteries, the other to head phylacteries. The Gemara asks: what is the difference? For the hand, it is written 'he shall wear on his flesh' – nothing should interpose between him and his flesh. For the head, it is also written 'you shall place the turban on his head'!

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that states if priests put on phylacteries, they do not interpose between the priestly garments and the body.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between hand phylacteries (which interpose) and head phylacteries (which do not).
The Gemara asks what is the difference between hand and head phylacteries, explaining that for the hand the verse 'he shall wear on his flesh' implies nothing should interpose.
The Gemara objects that for the head as well, the verse 'you shall place the turban on his head' similarly implies nothing should interpose.

items.text: Baraita about hair between the frontplate and turban
items.text_en: Baraita about hair between the frontplate and turban
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: his hair was visible between the frontplate and the turban.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the high priest's hair was visible between the frontplate (ציץ) and the turban (מצנפת), implying no interposition.

items.text: Opening context: where tefillin are placed
items.text_en: Opening context: where tefillin are placed
items.desc_en: The Gemara briefly notes that tefillin are placed at a specific location, serving as a transition to the main discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that tefillin are placed at a specific location, serving as a transition to the main discussion.

items.text: Deriving the law for a מחוסר כיפורים and unwashed hands/feet
items.text_en: Deriving the law for a מחוסר כיפורים and unwashed hands/feet
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for a מחוסר כיפורים (one lacking atonement) and for one who did not wash hands and feet. Rav Huna derives the former from a verse, and the latter is derived via a גזירה שווה of 'חוקה' from מחוסר בגדים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the disqualification of a מחוסר כיפורים (one lacking atonement).
Rav Huna derives the law from the verse 'וכפר עליה הכהן וטהרה', implying she was impure before atonement.

sub.text: Gemara's derivation for unwashed hands and feet
sub.text_en: Gemara's derivation for unwashed hands and feet
sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives the disqualification for unwashed hands and feet via a גזירה שווה of 'חוקה' from the case of a מחוסר בגדים (one lacking priestly garments).

items.text: Baraita: High priest's lack of immersion vs. morning sanctification
items.text_en: Baraita: High priest's lack of immersion vs. morning sanctification
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a High Priest who did not immerse or sanctify between garments or services performs valid service, but any priest who did not sanctify hands and feet in the morning performs invalid service.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches: a High Priest who did not immerse or sanctify between garments or between services — his service is valid; but any priest who did not sanctify hands and feet in the morning — his service is invalid.

items.text: Rav Assi's question and Rabbi Yochanan's answer
items.text_en: Rav Assi's question and Rabbi Yochanan's answer
items.desc_en: Rav Assi asks Rabbi Yochanan: since the five immersions and ten sanctifications are from the Torah and 'חוקה' is written about them, they should be indispensable. Rabbi Yochanan answers that the verse 'ולבשם' teaches that only wearing the garments is indispensable, not other things.

sub.desc_en: Rav Assi asks Rabbi Yochanan: since the five immersions and ten sanctifications are from the Torah and 'חוקה' is written about them, they should be indispensable.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the verse 'ולבשם' teaches that only wearing the garments is indispensable, not other things.

items.text: Objection: the morning sanctification
items.text_en: Objection: the morning sanctification
items.desc_en: Rav Assi's face lit up, but Rabbi Yochanan rebukes him, saying a 'vav' was written for you as an addition—if so, the morning sanctification should also be indispensable. This challenges the previous answer.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi's face lit up (in approval), but then he objects: if so, the same should apply to the morning sanctification as well.

items.text: Hezekiah and Rabbi Yonatan's derivations, and their debate
items.text_en: Hezekiah and Rabbi Yonatan's derivations, and their debate
items.desc_en: Hezekiah derives from the verse 'והיתה להם חק עולם' that only what is indispensable for his descendants is indispensable for him. Rabbi Yonatan derives from 'ורחצו ממנו משה ואהרן ובניו' that only what is indispensable for his sons is indispensable for him. The Gemara explains why each rejects the other's derivation: Hezekiah's verse is written for generations, and Rabbi Yonatan's verse is needed for Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's law about the laver's capacity.

sub.desc_en: Hezekiah derives from the verse 'והיתה להם חק עולם' that only what is indispensable for his descendants is indispensable for the High Priest.
Rabbi Yonatan derives from the verse 'ורחצו ממנו משה ואהרן ובניו' that only what is indispensable for his sons is indispensable for the High Priest.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yonatan does not use Hezekiah's derivation, and answers that Hezekiah's verse is written for generations and thus not applicable to the High Priest himself.
The Gemara asks why Hezekiah does not use Rabbi Yonatan's derivation, and answers that the verse is needed for Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's law about the laver's capacity to sanctify four priests.

items.text: The method of sanctification and the requirement of standing
items.text_en: The method of sanctification and the requirement of standing
items.desc_en: A baraita describes how to sanctify: placing right hand on right foot, left on left. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda says to place hands on top of each other and feet on top of each other, but the Sages say this is impossible. Rav Yosef says a friend helps. Abaye explains the difference is standing sideways. Rav Sama bar Rav Ashi asks why not sit, and the Gemara answers that 'לשרת' implies service while standing.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by describing the standard method of sanctification: placing the right hand on the right foot and the left hand on the left foot.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda proposes an alternative: placing both hands on top of each other and both feet on top of each other.
The Sages object that Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's method is impossible to perform.
Rav Yosef affirms the objection and explains that a friend assists the priest in performing the alternative method.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two positions.
Abaye answers that the difference lies in standing sideways to allow the friend to assist.
Rav Sama bar Rav Ashi asks why the priest cannot simply sit while sanctifying, avoiding the difficulty entirely.
The Gemara resolves that the verse 'לְשָׁרֵת' (to serve) implies service must be performed while standing.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon about overnight effect
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon about overnight effect
items.desc_en: A baraita states: if one sanctified by day, he need not sanctify at night; if at night, he must sanctify by day—Rabbi's view, as he holds that overnight invalidates. Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon holds that overnight does not invalidate. Another baraita adds: if one serves all night until dawn, Rabbi says he needs sanctification, Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon says once at the start suffices even for ten days. The Gemara explains why both cases are necessary.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states Rabbi's view: if one sanctified by day, he need not sanctify at night; if at night, he must sanctify by day, because overnight invalidates sanctification.
Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon disputes, holding that overnight does not invalidate sanctification.
A second baraita adds: if one serves all night until dawn, Rabbi says he needs sanctification again.
Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon holds that once sanctified at the start, no further sanctification is needed even for ten days.
The Gemara explains why both baraitot are necessary: each case teaches a nuance where one might think the other rabbi would concede, so both are needed to show the full dispute.

items.text: Scriptural bases for the dispute and additional derivations
items.text_en: Scriptural bases for the dispute and additional derivations
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi's reason from 'בגשתם' and Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon's from 'בבאם'. It then clarifies why both verses are needed: without 'בבאם' one might think every approach requires sanctification; without 'בגשתם' one might think even an empty approach. The Gemara then uses 'בגשתם' for Rav Acha bar Yaakov's point about the second sanctification, and questions the purpose of 'להקטיר אשה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what scriptural basis underlies Rabbi's position.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi derives his view from the verse 'בגשתם' (when they approach).
The Gemara asks what scriptural basis underlies Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon's position.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon derives his view from the verse 'בבאם' (when they enter).
The Gemara objects that Rabbi also has the verse 'בבאם', and explains that without it one might have required sanctification for every approach, so the verse limits it.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon also has the verse 'בגשתם', and explains that without it one might have thought even an empty approach requires sanctification.

The Gemara objects that an empty approach is already excluded by 'לשרת', and resolves that 'בגשתם' is needed for Rav Acha bar Yaakov's point about the second sanctification requiring only approach, not dressing.
The Gemara asks what purpose the phrase 'להקטיר אשה' (to burn a fire-offering) serves.

items.text: Gemara's conclusion on the previous Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's conclusion on the previous Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier statement applies even to non-atonement services, lest one think otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a potential misunderstanding: the previous ruling applies even to non-atonement services, lest one think it only applies to atonement services.

items.text: Ilfa's question about water of the laver
items.text_en: Ilfa's question about water of the laver
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan reports Ilfa's question: according to the one who says לינה does not invalidate sanctification of hands and feet, does לינה invalidate the water of the laver?

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's question via Rav Dimi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's question via Rav Dimi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan, via Rav Dimi, reports Ilfa's question: according to the view that לינה (overnight stay) does not invalidate the sanctification of hands and feet, does the water of the laver itself become invalid due to לינה?

items.text: Ravin's report: Ilfa resolved the question
items.text_en: Ravin's report: Ilfa resolved the question
items.desc_en: Ravin reports in the name of Rabbi Yirmeya, Rabbi Ami, and Rabbi Yochanan that Ilfa resolved the question: the dispute about water of the laver parallels the dispute about sanctification itself.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan, via Ravin, reports that Ilfa resolved the question: the dispute about לינה in the laver's water parallels the dispute about לינה in the sanctification itself.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Bisna's correction and the unresolved question
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Bisna's correction and the unresolved question
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Bisna challenges the report, citing Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that Ilfa actually said: a laver not sunk from the evening sanctifies for night service but not for the next day. The Gemara then debates whether this is because it is unnecessary or because it was invalidated by לינה, and notes that Mar (Ilfa) resolved it definitively.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Bisna objects to the previous report, citing Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that Ilfa actually said: a laver not sunk from the evening sanctifies for night service but not for the next day.
The Gemara raises an unresolved question: whether the laver's disqualification for the next day is because it is unnecessary or because it was invalidated by לינה (overnight stay).
The Gemara notes that the question remains unresolved for us, but Mar (Ilfa) had resolved it definitively.

items.text: Proof from Ben Katin's laver
items.text_en: Proof from Ben Katin's laver
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof: Ben Katin made twelve spouts for the laver and a mechanism to prevent its water from being invalidated by לינה. It asks whether this follows Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, and answers that it is Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a supporting baraita: Ben Katin made twelve spigots for the laver and a mechanism so its water would not be invalidated by לינה.
The Gemara asks: is this baraita according to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon? It answers: no, it is according to Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi).
The Gemara answers that it is Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi), not Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Analysis of the Mishnah's location and the dispute about צפון
items.text_en: Analysis of the Mishnah's location and the dispute about צפון
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that since the first clause of the Mishnah follows Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon (who includes between the Ulam and the altar as צפון), the latter clause must also be his. It then examines the Tosefta's definitions of צפון, showing that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon adds the area between the Ulam and altar, while Rabbi adds the place of the priests' and Israelites' footsteps. The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by invoking the weakness of the High Priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that since the first clause of the Mishnah follows Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, the latter clause must also be his.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of the Mishnah's first clause
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of the Mishnah's first clause
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's first clause showing the bull stands between the Ulam and the altar, which only Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon considers צפון (north).

The Tosefta defines צפון (north) with three positions: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's basic definition, Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon adding the area between the Ulam and altar, and Rabbi adding the place of the priests' and Israelites' footsteps.
The Gemara objects: if the baraita is Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's view, why does Rabbi add to it but not to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's view?
The Gemara suggests that if the Mishnah followed Rabbi, it could have placed the bull in the area of the priests' and Israelites' footsteps.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by invoking the weakness of the High Priest, explaining that the bull was placed between the Ulam and the altar to minimize the distance the weak High Priest had to walk.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and the dispute between Abaye and Rava
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and the dispute between Abaye and Rava
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who sanctified for the removal of ashes does not need to sanctify again the next day. The Gemara questions this: according to Rabbi, לינה invalidates; according to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, no sanctification is needed even for ten days. Abaye answers that Rabbi holds לינה is only rabbinic and does not apply from cockcrow until morning. Rava answers that Rabbi Yochanan refers to the beginning of the service, not the end.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who sanctified for the removal of ashes does not need to sanctify again the next day, since he already sanctified at the beginning of the service.

The Gemara questions to whom Rabbi Yochanan's ruling applies: according to Rabbi, לינה (overnight stay) invalidates, and according to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, no sanctification is needed even for ten days.
Abaye answers that Rabbi Yochanan's ruling is according to Rabbi, and that לינה (overnight invalidation) is only rabbinic and does not apply from cockcrow until morning.
Rava answers that Rabbi Yochanan's ruling is according to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, and that Rabbi Yochanan refers to the beginning of the service, not the end.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah about the priests' haste
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah about the priests' haste
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a Mishnah describing the priests running and sanctifying from the laver after the High Priest descended, implying that sanctification is needed even after the initial service.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: when the High Priest descended, the other priests ran and hurried to sanctify their hands and feet from the laver, implying that sanctification is needed even after the beginning of the service.

items.text: Reconciling the Mishnah with Abaye and Rava's views
items.text_en: Reconciling the Mishnah with Abaye and Rava's views
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah's ruling fits with Abaye's and Rava's interpretations of Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon regarding whether 'from cockcrow until dawn' invalidates overnight stay. It concludes that the Mishnah deals with new priests.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to Abaye, who interprets the Mishnah as Rabbi's view, the Mishnah is consistent because Rabbi agrees that from cockcrow until dawn does not invalidate overnight stay.

The Gemara raises a difficulty according to Rava, who interprets the Mishnah as Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's view, because Rabbi holds that from cockcrow until dawn does invalidate overnight stay, and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon says even ten days does not require sanctification.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah always follows Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, but it deals with new priests who have not yet performed service, so the concern of overnight stay does not apply.

items.text: Question: Does exiting invalidate sanctification?
items.text_en: Question: Does exiting invalidate sanctification?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: does exiting the Temple invalidate the sanctification of hands and feet, since it involves a departure, or not, because the priest can return?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about whether exiting the Temple invalidates the sanctification of hands and feet, considering the possibility of distraction versus the ability to return.

items.text: First attempted proof from a baraita
items.text_en: First attempted proof from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: if hands and feet became impure after sanctification, immersion suffices; if they exited, they remain in their sanctity. The Gemara clarifies that the question is about the entire body exiting, not just hands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: if hands and feet became impure after sanctification, immersion suffices; if they exited, they remain in their sanctity.
The Gemara clarifies that the question is about the entire body exiting, not just hands, and asks what the ruling is in that case.

items.text: Second attempted proof from a baraita on sanctification outside
items.text_en: Second attempted proof from a baraita on sanctification outside
items.desc_en: A baraita states that sanctifying with service vessels outside invalidates, implying that sanctifying inside and then exiting is valid. The Gemara limits this to exiting hands only, not the whole body.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: one who sanctifies hands and feet with service vessels outside invalidates the service, implying that sanctifying inside and then exiting is valid.
The Gemara rejects the proof: the baraita only addresses exiting hands, not the whole body, so the question of exiting the entire body remains unresolved.

items.text: Third attempted proof from a baraita on exiting the courtyard
items.text_en: Third attempted proof from a baraita on exiting the courtyard
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid cites a baraita: exiting the courtyard for a prolonged stay requires immersion; for a short time, only sanctification. Rav Pappa explains it refers to relieving oneself or urinating, but the Gemara notes the baraita already states that explicitly.

sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid cites a baraita to Rav Pappa: one who exits the courtyard wall needs immersion if staying long, but only sanctification if brief.
Rav Pappa explains the baraita deals with a case of exiting to relieve oneself or urinate.
The Gemara objects that the baraita already explicitly states the rule for relieving oneself and urinating.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita first states the general rule and then explains it.

items.text: Proof from the Red Heifer
items.text_en: Proof from the Red Heifer
items.desc_en: A dispute between Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef and Rabbi Yochanan about the Red Heifer's sanctification is cited. Rav Pappa distinguishes the Red Heifer because all its acts are outside, so exiting does not invalidate; sanctification is only to mimic inner service.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef requires sanctification inside with sacred vessels, while Rabbi Yochanan permits even outside with a clay pot.
Rav Pappa distinguishes the Red Heifer: since all its acts are outside, exiting does not invalidate, and sanctification is only to mimic inner service.

items.text: Question: Does impurity invalidate sanctification?
items.text_en: Question: Does impurity invalidate sanctification?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether impurity invalidates sanctification, since the priest becomes unfit. It attempts to prove from the baraita that if hands become impure, immersion suffices, but the question is about the whole body becoming impure close to sunset, so immersion and waiting for sunset are needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether impurity (טומאה) invalidates the sanctification of hands and feet, considering that the priest becomes unfit, and presents two possibilities: either he removes his attention (since he is unfit) or he does not (since he will become fit again).

The Gemara attempts to prove from a baraita that if hands become impure after sanctification, immersion suffices without re-sanctification, implying impurity does not invalidate the original sanctification.

The Gemara objects that the baraita only addresses impurity of the hands, but the question is about impurity of the entire body, where the priest must wait for sunset and thus might remove his attention.

The Gemara resolves the objection by specifying that the case is where the priest became impure close to sunset, so immersion and waiting for sunset are needed, and the question remains whether he removes his attention.

items.text: Unresolved proof from the Red Heifer
items.text_en: Unresolved proof from the Red Heifer
items.desc_en: The Gemara again cites the dispute about the Red Heifer, but the issue remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the dispute between Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef and Rabbi Yochanan regarding the Red Heifer's sanctification, but the issue remains unresolved.

items.text: Gemara's question about impurity in the red heifer
items.text_en: Gemara's question about impurity in the red heifer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the red heifer, which is deliberately made impure, disproves the notion that impurity disqualifies the heifer. It answers that the red heifer is different because a טבול יום does not disqualify it, and sanctification must be similar to the service.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the red heifer, which is deliberately made impure (טמא), disproves the notion that impurity disqualifies the heifer, citing the Mishnah that the priest is made impure and then immersed to counter the Sadducees.
The Gemara answers that the red heifer is different because a טבול יום (one who immersed that day) does not disqualify it, and sanctification must be similar to the service (כעין עבודה).

items.text: Inquiry about sanctifying hands and feet inside the laver
items.text_en: Inquiry about sanctifying hands and feet inside the laver
items.desc_en: A question is raised: may one sanctify hands and feet by immersing them inside the laver? The verse says 'from it' (ממנו), implying not inside it, or perhaps even inside it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: may one sanctify hands and feet by immersing them inside the laver, given the verse says 'from it' (ממנו) implying not inside it, or perhaps even inside it is permitted.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's proof from cave water
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's proof from cave water
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak brings a proof: if one immersed in cave water and performed service, it is invalid, implying that laver water, which is similar to cave water, would render the service valid. The Gemara rejects this, saying cave water was needed to counter a possible argument that if one can immerse his whole body, certainly hands and feet are valid.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak brings a baraita: one who immersed in cave water and performed service—his service is invalid, implying that laver water, which is similar to cave water, would render the service valid.

The Gemara rejects the proof: the cave water case was needed to counter a possible argument that if one can immerse his whole body in them, certainly hands and feet are valid, so it does not prove anything about laver water.

items.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef's ruling on laver water
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef's ruling on laver water
