items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef states that laver water is disqualified for permittees like permittees, and for limbs like limbs.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef rules that laver water is disqualified for permittees like permittees, and for limbs like limbs.

items.text: Rav Chisda and Rabbi Yochanan's opinions
items.text_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbi Yochanan's opinions
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda adds that laver water is disqualified for permittees only at dawn, like limbs. Rabbi Yochanan says that once one sinks the laver, he may not raise it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that laver water is disqualified for permittees only at dawn, like limbs.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that once one sinks the laver, he may not raise it.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Yochanan's statement
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Yochanan's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan means the laver is unfit for night service, but cites Rabbi Asi quoting Rabbi Yochanan that if the laver was not sunk at evening, one may sanctify from it for night service but not for the next day. It concludes that Rabbi Yochanan's 'may not raise it' refers only to day service, and this is the same as Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef's ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan's statement that one may not raise the laver after sinking it implies it is unfit even for night service.

sub.text: Rabbi Asi quoting Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Ilfa
sub.text_en: Rabbi Asi quoting Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Ilfa
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Asi's tradition that Rabbi Yochanan ruled: if the laver was not sunk at evening, one may sanctify from it for night service but not for the next day.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan's 'may not raise it' refers only to day service, but for night service the laver remains fit.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yochanan's ruling is identical to that of Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef.

items.text: The difference between Abaye and Rava: גזירת שיקוע
items.text_en: The difference between Abaye and Rava: גזירת שיקוע
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the practical difference between Abaye and Rava is the decree of immersion (גזירת שיקוע) of the laver.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the practical difference between Abaye and Rava is the decree of immersion (גזירת שיקוע) of the laver.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and the contradiction to Abaye
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and the contradiction to Abaye
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that one who sanctified his hands for the removal of ashes does not need to sanctify again the next day. This creates a difficulty for Abaye, who holds like Rabbi, because Rabbi requires immersion of the laver, yet Rabbi Yochanan's case seems to involve only draining, not immersion. The Gemara answers that the laver was drained and then re-immersed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that one who sanctified his hands for the removal of ashes does not need to sanctify again the next day.
The Gemara explains that Rava's position is consistent because he interprets the earlier case according to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, while Rabbi Yochanan's case follows Rabbi.
The Gemara raises a contradiction for Abaye, who holds like Rabbi, asking why Rabbi requires immersion of the laver in one case but not in Rabbi Yochanan's case.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the laver was drained and then re-immersed.

items.text: Objection: If drained and re-immersed, why no need to sanctify?
items.text_en: Objection: If drained and re-immersed, why no need to sanctify?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the laver was drained and re-immersed, why does Rabbi Yochanan say that one does not need to sanctify again? This implies that the water is still fit for sanctification, which is the same point as Rav Chisda's. The difference between them is the mitzvah of immersion (מצות שיקוע).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the laver was drained and re-immersed, why does Rabbi Yochanan say that one does not need to sanctify again tomorrow? This implies the water is still fit for sanctification.
The Gemara questions: does this mean the water is still fit for the permissive act (sanctification)? That is exactly Rav Chisda's position.
The Gemara resolves: the difference between Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Chisda is the mitzvah of immersion (מצות שיקוע).

items.text: Baraita about the sound of the laver's wheel
items.text_en: Baraita about the sound of the laver's wheel
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that describes the sound of the wooden wheel made by Ben Katin for the laver, which signaled the time for sanctification. The Gemara initially assumes this proves the laver was drained, but then concludes it was immersed using a wheel (גילגלא) or by its weight (חומרתיה). Two announcements were made: one for those who heard from one side, and one for the other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about the sound of Ben Katin's wooden wheel for the laver, and challenges that it proves the laver was drained (מסלק) and not immersed (משקע).
The Gemara rejects the challenge and answers that the laver was indeed immersed (משקע), but using a wheel (גילגלא) so that its sound was heard.
An alternative version states that the laver was immersed by its own weight (חומרתיה) so that its sound would be heard and the priests would come.
The Gemara resolves that there were two announcements: one for those who heard from one side and one for the other, reconciling the baraita with the existence of Gevini the herald.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's ruling and a challenge
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's ruling and a challenge
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina states that a laver without enough water to sanctify four priests is invalid, based on the verse about Moses, Aaron, and his sons. The Gemara challenges this with a baraita that says all vessels sanctify, even if they contain only a quarter-log.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina rules that a laver (כיור) lacking enough water to sanctify four priests is invalid, citing the verse about Moses, Aaron, and his sons.
The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's ruling by citing a baraita that states all vessels sanctify, even if they contain only a quarter-log (רביעית).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the laver requires a quarter-log of water, even if the vessels are service vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that the laver requires a quarter-log of water, even if the vessels are service vessels.
Rav Adda bar Acha explains that the Mishnah refers to a case where one drills a hole in the laver to draw water.
The Gemara objects that the verse says 'from it' (ממנו), implying the water must come from the laver itself, and 'they shall wash' (ירחצו) includes service vessels.
The Gemara asks why non-sacred vessels are not also included, and Abaye answers with a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from the laver's base.
A baraita with Rabbi Yehuda proves that the base (כנו) does not sanctify, based on a scriptural comparison.
Mar Zutra objects that the base is not made to hold water, unlike a non-sacred vessel, so the verse 'ממנו' excludes non-sacred vessels.
The Gemara asks why service vessels are not also excluded, and answers that the verse 'ירחצו' includes them.
The Gemara resolves the distinction: service vessels require anointing like the laver, while non-sacred vessels do not.
Reish Lakish states that anything which completes a mikveh also completes the laver's water, but not for the quarter-log requirement.
The Gemara asks what is excluded, and rejects the possibility of thick mud because it either qualifies for both or neither.
The Gemara answers that it excludes red insects, citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi about immersion in a fish's eye.
Rav Pappa says it excludes the case of adding and removing a se'ah from a mikveh, citing a Mishnah and Rabbi Yochanan's limit of up to its majority.
Rav Pappa rules that if one drills a quarter-log hole, one may immerse needles and hooks in it, since it comes from the fitness of a mikveh.
Rabbi Yirmeya quotes Reish Lakish that mikveh water is valid for the laver.
The Gemara questions whether this implies that living water is not required, citing a baraita that includes other waters and a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) for the laver.
The Gemara answers that the קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) refers to the sanctity of the water, not living water, and cites the school of Shmuel that water without a specific name is valid.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on service vessels and ordinary vessels
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on service vessels and ordinary vessels
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Acha explains that the laver's water must be drawn from within it. The Gemara questions whether ordinary vessels can also sanctify, and Abaye argues from a kal vachomer from the base of the laver. Mar Zutra objects, and the Gemara concludes that the verse excludes ordinary vessels, while service vessels are included via the word 'ירחצו'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Acha explains that the laver's water must be drawn from within it by boring a hole.
The Gemara questions why the verse 'ממנו' (from it) is needed, and answers that 'ירחצו' (they shall wash) includes service vessels.
The Gemara objects that if service vessels are included, ordinary vessels might also be included, and Abaye rejects this via a kal vachomer from the base of the laver.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda derives from the verse that the base of the laver is not sanctified like the laver itself.
Mar Zutra objects to Abaye's kal vachomer, arguing that the base is not made to contain water while ordinary vessels are, so the verse 'ממנו' excludes ordinary vessels.
The Gemara questions why service vessels would be included if ordinary vessels are excluded, and answers that the verse 'ירחצו' includes them.
The Gemara resolves the distinction: service vessels require anointing like the laver, while ordinary vessels do not.

items.text: Reish Lakish's principle and its application
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's principle and its application
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that anything that completes a mikveh also completes the laver, but not for a quarter-log. The Gemara considers what this excludes: first, thick mud (טיט הנידוק) is rejected; then, red gnats (יבחושין אדומין) are rejected because they are valid in their own right; finally, Rav Pappa says it excludes the case of adding and removing a se'ah, citing a Mishnah and Rabbi Yochanan's limit.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that anything that completes a mikveh also completes the laver, but not for a quarter-log.
The Gemara asks what case Reish Lakish's principle excludes.

The Gemara considers and rejects the possibility that the exclusion refers to thick mud (טיט הנידוק), arguing that if a cow can drink from it, it is valid even for a quarter-log, and if not, it does not complete a mikveh either.

The Gemara considers and rejects red gnats (יבחושין אדומין), citing a baraita that such creatures are valid for immersion in their own right, as per Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi.

Rav Pappa resolves that the exclusion refers to the case of adding a se'ah and removing a se'ah, citing a Mishnah and Rabbi Yochanan's limit that this is valid only until the majority (רובו) of the water is removed.

items.text: Rav Pappa's ruling on a hole in the laver
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's ruling on a hole in the laver
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that if one drilled a quarter-log hole in the laver, one can immerse needles and hooks in it, because it comes from the fitness of a mikveh.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that if one drilled a quarter-log hole in the laver, one can immerse needles and hooks in it, because it comes from the fitness of a mikveh.

items.text: The status of mikveh water for the laver
items.text_en: The status of mikveh water for the laver
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya quotes Reish Lakish that mikveh water is valid for the laver. The Gemara questions whether this implies that the laver does not require living water, citing a baraita that includes other waters. It concludes that the laver's water is sanctified and of superior sanctity, and cites the school of Shmuel that water without a specific name is valid.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya states in the name of Reish Lakish that mikveh water is valid for the laver's water.
The Gemara questions whether this implies that the laver does not require living water (מים חיים).
The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'במים' (in water) that other waters are included for the laver, implying that the laver requires living water.
The Gemara resolves that the laver's water is sanctified and of superior sanctity (קדישי מעליותא), not that it requires living water.
The school of Shmuel teaches that the term 'מים' (water) refers to water that has no specific name (i.e., not wine or mixed liquids), supporting the validity of mikveh water.

items.text: The laver's water: living water or not?
items.text_en: The laver's water: living water or not?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the water of the laver must be living water, based on a previous statement. Rabbi Yochanan resolves this as a dispute between Rabbi Yishmael, who says it must be spring water, and the Sages, who say any water is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the laver's water, which has a distinct name, must be living water (spring water), implying it is indeed living water.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves that the matter is a dispute between Tannaim: Rabbi Yishmael holds the laver's water must be spring water, while the Sages hold any water is valid.

items.text: Source for disqualification of an uncircumcised priest
items.text_en: Source for disqualification of an uncircumcised priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for disqualifying an uncircumcised priest from service. Rav Chisda states it is learned from Ezekiel. A baraita explains that 'ben nechar' refers to one whose deeds are alienated from God, and both 'uncircumcised of heart' and 'uncircumcised of flesh' are needed, as each alone might be insufficient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that an uncircumcised priest is disqualified from service?

Rav Chisda answers that this law was not learned from the Torah of Moses but from the words of Ezekiel ben Buzi, citing the verse: 'Any alien, uncircumcised of heart and uncircumcised of flesh, shall not enter My sanctuary to minister to Me.'

The Gemara provides additional support that an uncircumcised priest invalidates service, citing the verse: 'When you bring aliens, uncircumcised of heart and uncircumcised of flesh, into My sanctuary to profane My house.'

A baraita teaches that 'ben nechar' cannot mean a literal foreigner, because the verse says 'uncircumcised of heart'; rather it refers to one whose deeds are alienated from God, and both 'uncircumcised of heart' and 'uncircumcised of flesh' are needed, each derived from the verse.

The Gemara explains why both terms are necessary: if only 'uncircumcised of flesh' were written, one might think it is only because it is repulsive, but 'uncircumcised of heart' would not disqualify; conversely, if only 'uncircumcised of heart' were written, one might think it is only because his heart is not directed to Heaven, but 'uncircumcised of flesh' would not disqualify; therefore both are needed.

items.text: Elders of the South: impure from corpse vs. impure from creeping thing
items.text_en: Elders of the South: impure from corpse vs. impure from creeping thing
items.desc_en: The Elders of the South distinguish between a priest impure from a creeping thing, who cannot perform service, and one impure from a corpse, who can, because the latter is accepted in communal offerings. The Gemara challenges this with a kal vachomer, but the Elders hold that the power of the one being atoned for is greater, and just as a corpse-impure person can send his offering, so too the priest can serve.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an impure priest disqualifies the service.

The Elders of the South distinguish between a priest impure from a creeping thing (טומאת שרץ), who disqualifies service, and a priest impure from a corpse (טומאת מת), who does not, because a corpse-impure priest is accepted via the power of communal offerings (מרצה בציבור) and thus also serves for individuals.

The Gemara objects with a kal vachomer (קל וחומר): if a corpse-impure priest, who requires the more severe third- and seventh-day sprinkling, is accepted, then a creeping-thing impure priest, who requires no such sprinkling, should certainly be accepted — so why do the Elders reject him?

sub.text: Elders of the South's reasoning (reported by Gemara)
sub.text_en: Elders of the South's reasoning (reported by Gemara)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Elders hold a principle: the atoning power of the person being atoned for (מתכפרין) is greater than the power of the one atoning (מכפרין). Thus, just as a corpse-impure person can send his offering to the Temple while a creeping-thing impure person cannot, so too the priest serving for them follows the same rule.

items.text: Clarifying the Elders' position on slaughtering for an impure person
items.text_en: Clarifying the Elders' position on slaughtering for an impure person
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Elders' underlying assumption: if they hold that we do not slaughter and sprinkle for a person impure from a creeping thing, why not perform the offering in impurity for the community? It concludes that they hold we do slaughter and sprinkle for such a person.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Elders of the South hold: if they hold that one does not slaughter and sprinkle for a person impure from a creeping thing, why not perform the offering in impurity for the community, given the principle that what is deferred for an individual is performed in impurity for the community?
The Gemara concludes that the Elders of the South hold that one does slaughter and sprinkle for a person impure from a creeping thing.

items.text: Resh Lakish's refutation and the Elders' counter-argument
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's refutation and the Elders' counter-argument
items.desc_en: Ulla reports that Resh Lakish strongly refuted the Elders of the South, arguing that the power of the one being atoned for is greater, so if a corpse-impure person cannot send his offering, a corpse-impure priest should not serve. The Elders, however, hold that a corpse-impure person can send his offering.

sub.desc_en: Ulla reports that Resh Lakish shouted to the Elders of the South, asking which power is greater — that of the one who effects atonement or that of the one who achieves atonement, concluding that the power of the one who achieves atonement is greater.

Resh Lakish argues by a fortiori inference: if an owner impure from a creeping animal may send his offering yet a priest impure from a creeping animal does not effect acceptance, then an owner impure from a corpse, who may not send his offering, certainly a priest impure from a corpse should not effect acceptance.
The Elders of the South respond that they hold that an owner impure from a corpse may also send his offerings, thus the a fortiori inference does not apply.

items.text: Scriptural challenge to the Elders' position
items.text_en: Scriptural challenge to the Elders' position
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Elders' claim that a corpse-impure person can send his offering, citing the verse about the second Passover. It suggests this is only a mitzvah, not a full permission, and the verse continues, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing the verse about the second Passover (איש איש כי יהיה טמא), arguing that it only establishes a mitzvah (מצוה) for a corpse-impure person to send his offering, not a full permission.
The Gemara begins to cite the continuation of the verse (והא כתיב: 'איש'), but the text is cut off, leaving the argument incomplete.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: Is eating by registrants essential?
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Is eating by registrants essential?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the requirement that the Paschal lamb be eaten only by those registered is merely a mitzvah or essential (me'akev). It cites a baraita that derives from the verse "תָּכֹסּוּ" that slaughtering not for its registrants is invalid, and notes that eaters are linked to registrants.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the requirement that the Paschal lamb be eaten only by those registered is merely a mitzvah (commandment) or essential (me'akev).

The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'בְּמִכְסַת נְפָשׁוֹת' (by the count of persons) that the Paschal lamb is slaughtered only for its registrants, and that slaughtering not for its registrants is invalid (me'akev), linking eaters to registrants.

items.text: Elders of the South's objection
items.text_en: Elders of the South's objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Elders of the South do not make the a fortiori argument (kal vachomer) from impurity of owners to impurity of priests. Even if they don't, they have a different objection: if a priest impure from a creeping thing cannot serve, then a priest impure from a corpse certainly cannot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Elders of the South do not make the a fortiori argument (קל וחומר) from impurity of owners to impurity of priests.
The Elders of the South present an alternative objection: if a priest impure from a creeping thing (שרץ) cannot serve, then a priest impure from a corpse (מת) certainly cannot serve.

items.text: Objection from the tzitz ruling
items.text_en: Objection from the tzitz ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a teaching that the tzitz atones for blood impurity but not for body impurity. If this refers to corpse impurity, it implies that owners impure from a corpse cannot send their offerings, contradicting the earlier claim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita stating that the tzitz (frontlet) atones for blood impurity but not for body impurity, implying that owners impure from a corpse cannot send their offerings.
The Gemara asks: what impurity does this refer to? If it is sheratzim (creeping animal) impurity, that is already permitted; it must be corpse impurity.
The Gemara concludes that since the tzitz does not atone for corpse impurity, it proves that owners impure from a corpse cannot send their offerings.

items.text: Answer: The case is priest impure from a creeping thing
items.text_en: Answer: The case is priest impure from a creeping thing
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the teaching refers to a case where the priest, not the owners, became impure from a creeping thing. In that case, the tzitz does not atone, but for owners impure from a corpse, the tzitz would atone.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the teaching refers to a case where the priest, not the owners, became impure from a creeping thing (שרץ), so the ציץ (frontlet) does not atone, but for owners impure from a corpse it would.

items.text: Further challenge from tum'at hatehom
items.text_en: Further challenge from tum'at hatehom
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if so, the teaching says that tum'at hatehom (undetermined impurity) is atoned for by the tzitz. Rabbi Chiya taught that this applies only to corpse impurity, excluding creeping thing impurity. This supports the distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if so, the end of the baraita says that tum'at hatehom (undetermined impurity) is atoned for by the tzitz; Rabbi Chiya taught that this applies only to corpse impurity, excluding creeping thing impurity — does this not support the distinction?
The Gemara answers: no, Rabbi Chiya's exclusion refers to tum'at hatehom of a zav (a person with a discharge), not of a creeping thing.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's dilemma and resolution
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's dilemma and resolution
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether a priest who serves for others is permitted to have tum'at hatehom. The Gemara suggests resolving from the previous discussion, but concludes that Rami bar Chama's case is different and disputed.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether a priest who serves as a representative (מרוצה) for others is permitted to have טומאת התהום (undetermined impurity of the depths) or not.
The Gemara suggests resolving from the previous discussion that טומאת התהום (undetermined impurity of the depths) is permitted for the priest, since the context there involves a priest.
The Gemara rejects the resolution, concluding that Rami bar Chama's case is different and the authorities dispute it.

items.text: New inquiry: What sin does the tzitz bear?
items.text_en: New inquiry: What sin does the tzitz bear?
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new discussion, citing the verse "וְנָשָׂא אַהֲרֹן אֶת עֲוֹן הַקֳּדָשִׁים" and asking what specific sin the tzitz atones for.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens a new inquiry, citing the verse "וְנָשָׂא אַהֲרֹן אֶת עֲוֹן הַקֳּדָשִׁים" and asking what specific sin the tzitz atones for.

items.text: Identifying the sin of tumah
items.text_en: Identifying the sin of tumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the verse already addresses piggul and notar, so the remaining sin must be tumah, which was permitted in the case of communal sacrifices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that since the verse already addresses piggul and notar, the remaining sin must be tumah, which was permitted in the case of communal sacrifices.

items.text: Clarifying which tumah is permitted
items.text_en: Clarifying which tumah is permitted
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the tumah referred to is from a sheretz or a corpse, and concludes it must be corpse-tumah, which is permitted for those offering the Paschal lamb.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which type of טומאה (ritual impurity) is meant, suggesting it cannot be from a שרץ (creeping thing) since that was never permitted in the community.
The Gemara concludes it must be טומאת מת (corpse-impurity), which is permitted specifically for those offering the Paschal lamb.

items.text: Alternative interpretation: sheretz tumah
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation: sheretz tumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative reading: the tumah is always from a sheretz, and the phrase 'tumah' is used in a general sense.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by asserting that the tumah is always from a sheretz, and the term 'tumah' is used in a general sense.

items.text: Another derivation: sin of the offerings, not the owners
items.text_en: Another derivation: sin of the offerings, not the owners
items.desc_en: A different version deduces that the verse only addresses the sin of the offerings, not the owners, and again questions whether the tumah is from a sheretz or a corpse.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version deduces that the verse only addresses the sin of the offerings, not the sin of the owners, and questions whether the impurity is from a sheretz or a corpse.
The gemara resolves that the impurity is always from a sheretz, and the term 'tumah' is used in a general sense.

items.text: Source for prohibition of sitting in the Temple service
items.text_en: Source for prohibition of sitting in the Temple service
items.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman derives from the verse 'la'amod leshareit' that standing is required, not sitting. A baraisa adds that 'ha'omdim' indicates a necessary condition.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: from where do we derive that a priest must stand (not sit) during the Temple service?

sub.text: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rava citing Rav Nachman derives from the verse 'לַעֲמֹד לְשָׁרֵת' (to stand to serve) that standing is required, not sitting.
A baraisa adds that the verse 'לַעֲמֹד לְשָׁרֵת' indicates a מצוה (commandment), and the additional phrase 'הָעֹמְדִים' (those who stand) teaches that standing is an absolute requirement (לעכב).

items.text: Why a seated priest is not liable to death
items.text_en: Why a seated priest is not liable to death
items.desc_en: Rava questions Rav Nachman why a seated priest is not liable to death like a zar, and the answer is that it is derived from two verses together with other disqualifications (lack of garments, unwashed hands and feet).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman: since a seated priest is like a zar (non-priest) and disqualifies the service, why is he not liable to death like a zar, as the baraita states that an uncircumcised priest, an onen, and a seated priest are only warned but not executed?

The gemara answers that the seated priest is not liable to death because his disqualification is derived together with the disqualifications of lacking garments and unwashed hands and feet, which are two verses that come as one (שני כתובים הבאים כאחד) and thus do not establish a general rule for capital punishment.

items.text: Introduction: Two verses that come as one do not teach
items.text_en: Introduction: Two verses that come as one do not teach
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a general principle that two verses that come together do not teach a common lesson. For one who holds they do teach, the case of a drunk Kohen would be a third instance, and three instances do not teach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the general principle that two verses that come as one do not teach a common lesson.
The Gemara notes that for one who holds they do teach, the case of a drunk Kohen would be a third instance, and three instances do not teach.

items.text: Source for no interposition between Kohen and floor
items.text_en: Source for no interposition between Kohen and floor
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from a baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael that just as there must be no interposition between the Kohen and the service vessels, so too there must be no interposition between him and the floor. It then explains why all three cases (vessels, animal, friend's feet) are necessary to teach.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a Kohen standing on vessels, an animal, or a friend's foot is invalid for service.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of this law.

sub.text: Baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from a verbal analogy between the floor (רצפה) and service vessels (כלי שרת) that nothing may interpose between the Kohen and the floor.
The Gemara explains why all three cases (vessels, animal, friend's feet) are necessary to teach, as each might otherwise be permitted by a different reasoning.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling on partial standing
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's ruling on partial standing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer rules that if the Kohen stands with one foot on a vessel or stone and one foot on the floor, we evaluate whether he could stand on one foot if the vessel were removed; if so, the service is valid, otherwise invalid.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer rules that if the Kohen stands with one foot on a vessel or stone and one foot on the floor, we evaluate whether he could stand on one foot if the vessel were removed; if so, the service is valid, otherwise invalid.

items.text: Rabbi Ammi's query about a loosened stone
items.text_en: Rabbi Ammi's query about a loosened stone
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi asks whether a stone that has become loosened but is intended to be reattached constitutes an interposition. Rabba Zuti rephrases the query: if the stone was uprooted and the Kohen stood in its place, does the sanctity extend only to the upper surface or to the depths? The Gemara concludes that the sanctity extends to the depths, but the question remains whether this is a proper mode of service; it is left unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi asks whether a loosened stone that is intended to be reattached constitutes an interposition (חוצץ) for the Kohen standing on it.
Rabba Zuti rephrases Rabbi Ammi's query: if the stone was uprooted and the Kohen stood in its place, what is the law?
The Gemara clarifies the query: does the sanctity of the Temple floor extend only to the upper surface or to the depths of the earth?
The Gemara concludes that the sanctity extends to the depths, but the question of whether standing in the cavity is a proper mode of service remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Dispute: Receiving blood with the left hand
items.text_en: Dispute: Receiving blood with the left hand
items.desc_en: The Sages derive from the verses that both receiving and placing the blood must be done with the right hand. Rabbi Shimon argues that since the verse says 'with his finger' for receiving, not 'hand', receiving with the left is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the dispute: the Sages rule that receiving blood with the left hand disqualifies the service, while Rabbi Shimon validates it; a baraita derives from the verses that both receiving and placing must be done with the right hand.
Rabbi Shimon objects that the word 'hand' was not stated regarding receiving, only 'finger', so receiving with the left is valid, while placing must be with the right.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and Rav Yehuda's explanation
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and Rav Yehuda's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Shimon's logic: if he accepts the gezerah shavah, why does the absence of 'hand' matter? If he does not, why does its presence matter? Rav Yehuda explains that Rabbi Shimon indeed rejects the gezerah shavah, and his point is that the verse never specifies the right hand for receiving.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Shimon's position by posing a dilemma: if he accepts the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy), why does the absence of the word 'hand' in receiving matter? If he does not accept it, why does its presence matter?

Rav Yehuda explains that Rabbi Shimon indeed rejects the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy), and his point is that the verse never specifies the right hand for receiving, so receiving with the left is valid.

items.text: Rabba's objection and Rava's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rabba's objection and Rava's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rabba objects that if so, even placing could be done with the left, and notes that Rabbi Shimon does accept the gezerah shavah. Rava explains that Rabbi Shimon's point is that since the verse says 'finger' for receiving, and one cannot receive with a finger, the absence of 'hand' allows the left hand.

sub.desc_en: Rabba objects that if Rava's explanation were correct, even placing (נתינה) could be done with the left, and notes that Rabbi Shimon does accept the גזירה שוה (verbal analogy).
Rava explains that Rabbi Shimon's point is that since the verse says 'אצבע' (finger) for receiving, and one cannot receive with a finger, the absence of 'יד' (hand) allows the left hand.

items.text: Rav Sama's objection and Abaye's response
items.text_en: Rav Sama's objection and Abaye's response
items.desc_en: Rav Sama objects that one could make a rim on the bowl and receive with the finger. The Gemara notes that Abaye then offers an alternative explanation, but the text cuts off.

sub.text: Rav Sama bar Rav Ashi to Ravina
sub.text_en: Rav Sama bar Rav Ashi to Ravina
sub.desc_en: Rav Sama objects to Ravina that one could make a rim (אוזן) on the lip of the bowl and receive the blood with it, thereby avoiding the need for a finger.
The Gemara notes that Abaye then offered an alternative explanation, but the text cuts off without recording it.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon's principle and the dispute over 'מִקְרָא נִדְרָשׁ לְפָנָיו וּלְאַחֲרָיו'
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon's principle and the dispute over 'מִקְרָא נִדְרָשׁ לְפָנָיו וּלְאַחֲרָיו'
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute about whether a verse is interpreted by its immediate context or by both preceding and following context. Abaye explains that Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon's ruling—that changing the hand in receiving (kabbalah) disqualifies but in giving (netinah) is valid, and vice versa—derives from both his father's view and the Rabbis' view. The verse 'וְנָתַתָּ עַל קַרְנֹת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ בְּאֶצְבָּעֶךָ' is cited, and Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon holds that the verse is interpreted only by what precedes it, not by what follows.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states that the dispute between Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon and the Rabbis is about whether a verse is interpreted by its immediate context (לפניו) or by both preceding and following context (לפניו ולאחריו).

Abaye explains that Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon's ruling—that changing the hand in receiving (kabbalah) disqualifies but in giving (netinah) is valid, and vice versa—derives from both his father's view and the Rabbis' view, citing the baraita that states this principle.

Abaye identifies the verse where 'finger' is stated in the context of giving (netinah)—'וְנָתַתָּ עַל קַרְנֹת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ בְּאֶצְבָּעֶךָ'—and explains that Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon holds that the verse is interpreted only by what precedes it (לפניו), not by what follows (לפני פניו ולאחריו).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's statement and the initial assumption requiring both 'etzba' and 'kehuna'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statement and the initial assumption requiring both 'etzba' and 'kehuna'
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quotes Rabbi Yochanan: wherever 'etzba' and 'kehuna' are mentioned, it indicates the right hand. The Gemara initially assumes that both terms are required, deriving from the metzora (leper) that 'etzba' implies right, and from kemitzah (handful) that 'kehuna' alone also implies right, as the Mishnah rules that kemitzah with the left is invalid.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quotes Rabbi Yochanan's principle: wherever 'etzba' (finger) and 'kehuna' (priesthood) are mentioned together, it indicates the right hand.

The Gemara initially assumes that both 'etzba' and 'kehuna' are required, deriving from the metzora (leper) that 'etzba' implies right, and from kemitzah (handful) that 'kehuna' alone also implies right, as the Mishnah rules that kemitzah with the left is invalid.

items.text: Rava's alternative: either 'etzba' or 'kehuna' suffices
items.text_en: Rava's alternative: either 'etzba' or 'kehuna' suffices
items.desc_en: Rava argues that only one of the two terms—either 'etzba' or 'kehuna'—is needed to require the right hand, not both.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the difficulty by asserting that only one of the two terms—either 'אצבע' (finger) or 'כהונה' (priesthood)—is needed to require the right hand, not both.

items.text: Abaye's objection from the carrying of limbs and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's objection from the carrying of limbs and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye objects: the carrying of limbs to the ramp (holakhat evarim lakavesh) is written with 'kehuna' but the Mishnah rules that the right leg is placed in the left hand, implying no right-hand requirement. Rava resolves that the principle 'either etzba or kehuna' applies only to matters that effect atonement (me'akev kapara), like the metzora.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the carrying of limbs to the ramp (הולכת איברים לכבש) is written with 'kehuna' yet the Mishnah rules the right leg is placed in the left hand, contradicting the principle that 'etzba or kehuna' requires right-hand use.
Rava resolves that the principle 'either אצבע or כהונה' applies only to matters that effect atonement (מעכב כפרה), like the metzora, not to the carrying of limbs.

items.text: Objection from kabbalah (receiving) and Rabbi Shimon's position
items.text_en: Objection from kabbalah (receiving) and Rabbi Shimon's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: kabbalah (receiving the blood) has 'kehuna' and is a matter that effects atonement, yet the Mishnah states that receiving with the left is invalid, but Rabbi Shimon validates it. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon requires both 'etzba' and 'kehuna'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: kabbalah (receiving the blood) has 'kehuna' and is a matter that effects atonement, yet the Mishnah states that receiving with the left is invalid, but Rabbi Shimon validates it.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon requires both 'etzba' and 'kehuna' to invalidate left-handed performance.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Shimon's requirement and clarification
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Shimon's requirement and clarification
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: does Rabbi Shimon really require both? A baraita states that Rabbi Shimon says wherever 'yad' is mentioned it means right, and 'etzba' means right. The Gemara clarifies: 'etzba' does not require 'kehuna', but 'kehuna' requires 'etzba'. The word 'kohen' in the verse is interpreted as referring to his priesthood (bikhunno).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Shimon's requirement of both 'etzba' and 'kehuna' by citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon says 'yad' and 'etzba' each alone indicate the right hand.
The Gemara clarifies: 'etzba' does not require 'kehuna', but 'kehuna' requires 'etzba'.
The Gemara resolves that the word 'kohen' in the verse is interpreted as referring to his priesthood (bikhunno).

items.text: Objection from zerikah (sprinkling) and Abaye's resolution with a baraita
items.text_en: Objection from zerikah (sprinkling) and Abaye's resolution with a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: zerikah (sprinkling) has only 'kehuna', yet the Mishnah rules that sprinkling with the left is invalid, and Rabbi Shimon does not dispute this. Abaye responds that Rabbi Shimon does dispute it in a baraita, where he validates both kabbalah and zerikah with the left.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that zerikah (sprinkling) has only 'kehuna' (priesthood) written, yet the Mishnah rules that sprinkling with the left is invalid, and Rabbi Shimon does not dispute this.
Abaye responds that Rabbi Shimon does dispute it in a baraita, where he validates both kabbalah (receiving) and zerikah (sprinkling) with the left.

items.text: Rava's derivations from 'yad', 'regel', 'ozen' and their necessity
items.text_en: Rava's derivations from 'yad', 'regel', 'ozen' and their necessity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rava derives right-hand requirements from 'yad' for kemitzah, 'regel' for chalitzah, and 'ozen' for retzi'ah, since these could be derived from Rabba bar bar Chana's principle. The answer: one derivation is for the handful itself (kometz), and another for the sanctification of the handful (kiddush kometz).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rava's derivations from 'yad' for kemitzah, 'regel' for chalitzah, and 'ozen' for retzi'ah are necessary, since they could be derived from Rabba bar bar Chana's principle.
The Gemara answers that one derivation is for the handful itself (kometz), and another for the sanctification of the handful (kiddush kometz).

items.text: The need for the right hand in kemitzah according to Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: The need for the right hand in kemitzah according to Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse 'yad' is needed for Rabbi Shimon, who does not require sanctification of the handful. It explains that the verse teaches that if one performs kemitzah with the left hand, it is invalid, and this is necessary for the case of a sinner's meal offering, where one might think it could be done with the left hand to avoid a handsome offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse 'yad' is needed for Rabbi Shimon, who does not require sanctification of the handful, and for those who say he does, why the left hand would disqualify.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning: the verse 'קֹדֶשׁ קָדָשִׁים הִיא כַּחַטָּאת וְכָאָשָׁם' teaches that if one performs the service with the hand, it must be the right hand like a חטאת (sin-offering), but if with a vessel, the left hand is allowed like an אשם (guilt-offering).

The Gemara resolves that the verse is necessary for the case of a sinner's meal offering, where one might think Rabbi Shimon would permit the left hand to avoid a handsome offering, but the verse teaches that even so, the left hand disqualifies.

items.text: Mishnah: Blood spilled on the floor and gathered is invalid
items.text_en: Mishnah: Blood spilled on the floor and gathered is invalid
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if blood was spilled on the floor and then gathered, it is invalid for use on the altar.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that blood spilled on the floor and then gathered is invalid for use on the altar.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation that blood must be received directly from the animal
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation that blood must be received directly from the animal
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'midam hapar' that the blood must be from the lifeblood, not from the skin or the residue. It further explains that the phrase 'midam hapar' means the blood from the bull, not just any blood, and that one must receive all the blood, as per Rav's statement.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from the verse that the blood must be from the lifeblood (דם הנפש), not from the skin or the residue.
The Gemara questions the baraita's interpretation, arguing that if 'midam hapar' were taken literally it would imply only part of the blood, contradicting Rav's requirement to receive all the blood.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita interprets 'midam hapar' as 'blood from the bull' (requiring direct reception from the animal), and holds the principle of subtracting and adding letters to derive meaning.

items.text: Rav's statement on receiving all the blood and its derivation
items.text_en: Rav's statement on receiving all the blood and its derivation
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav that the slaughterer must receive all the blood of the bull, as it says 've'et kol dam hapar yishpoch'. The Gemara questions that this verse is about the remnants, but explains that if it cannot apply to the remnants (since not all blood remains), apply it to the reception.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav that the slaughterer must receive all the blood of the bull, citing the verse 'וְאֵת כׇּל דַּם הַפָּר יִשְׁפֹּךְ' (and all the blood of the bull he shall pour out).
The Gemara objects that the verse cited by Rav is written about the remnants (שִׁירַיִים) of the blood, not about the initial reception.
The Gemara resolves that since the verse cannot apply to the remnants (שִׁירַיִים) because not all the blood remains, apply it instead to the reception (קַבָּלָה) of the blood.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on lifting the knife and cleaning it
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on lifting the knife and cleaning it
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that the slaughterer must lift the knife upward to avoid mixing blood from the knife with the bull's blood, as derived from 'velakach midam hapar'. Abaye then explains that the knife is cleaned on the rim of the receiving vessel, as it says 'keforei zahav'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that the slaughterer must lift the knife upward to avoid mixing blood from the knife with the bull's blood, as derived from 'וְלָקַח מִדַּם הַפָּר' (and he shall take from the blood of the bull).
Abaye answers that the knife is cleaned on the rim of the receiving vessel, as it says 'כְּפוֹרֵי זָהָב' (bowls of gold).

items.text: Rav Chisda's statement on giving (incomplete)
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's statement on giving (incomplete)
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda quotes Rav Yirmeya bar Abba that the slaughterer must give... (the text cuts off).

sub.text: Rav Chisda quoting Rav Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda quoting Rav Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda begins a statement in the name of Rav Yirmeya bar Abba that the slaughterer must give something, but the text cuts off.

items.text: Opening statement: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on veins and vessel airspace
items.text_en: Opening statement: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on veins and vessel airspace
items.desc_en: Rav Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the veins must see the airspace of the vessel for valid reception.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the veins must see the airspace of the vessel for valid reception.

items.text: Rabbi Asi's question and Rabbi Yochanan's answer about airspace without rest
items.text_en: Rabbi Asi's question and Rabbi Yochanan's answer about airspace without rest
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi asks about a vessel whose bottom was broken before blood reached its airspace—whether air that will not rest is considered as resting. Rabbi Yochanan answers with a Mishna about a barrel under a spout, but the Gemara notes the answer addresses air that will rest, not the question asked. The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Asi asked two questions.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi asks Rabbi Yochanan whether air that will not rest (אוויר שאין סופו לנוח) in a broken vessel is considered like resting (כמונח דמי) for the purpose of receiving blood.
Rabbi Yochanan cites a Mishna about a barrel under a spout, where water inside and outside is invalid unless the barrel's mouth is attached to the spout, implying a distinction about airspace.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Asi asked about air that will not rest, but Rabbi Yochanan answered about air that will rest (אוויר שסופו לנוח), showing a mismatch.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Asi actually asked two questions: first about air that will not rest, and then, assuming that is not considered resting, about air that will rest.

items.text: Different versions of the tradition: Rav Yosef, Rav Kahana, and Rabbah
items.text_en: Different versions of the tradition: Rav Yosef, Rav Kahana, and Rabbah
items.desc_en: Three Amoraic versions of the exchange are presented: Rav Yosef says the question and answer were both about a barrel; Rav Kahana says the question was about a barrel and the answer about a barrel; Rabbah says the question was about a barrel and the answer about a sprinkler, arguing that a sprinkler inevitably involves a spout.

sub.text: Stam's introduction of Rav Yosef's version
sub.text_en: Stam's introduction of Rav Yosef's version
sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces Rav Yosef's version of the tradition, where both the question and answer concern a barrel (חָבִית).

sub.text: Stam's introduction of Rav Kahana's version
sub.text_en: Stam's introduction of Rav Kahana's version
sub.desc_en: The gemara presents Rav Kahana's version, where the question was about a barrel and the answer also about a barrel.
The gemara presents Rabbah's version, where the question was about a barrel and the answer about a sprinkler (מִזְרָק), arguing that a sprinkler inevitably involves a spout (זִינּוּק).

items.text: Mishna about passing water through hands or leaves, and its scriptural source
items.text_en: Mishna about passing water through hands or leaves, and its scriptural source
items.desc_en: A Mishna teaches that if one places his hand or leaves to let water pass into a barrel, the water is invalid if the object can contract impurity, but valid if not. Rabbi Yochanan cites a verse to derive that the water's formation must be through purity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishna rules that if one places his hand, foot, or leaves to let water pass into a barrel, the water is invalid if the object can contract impurity, but valid if not.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yosei bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yosei bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Abba derives from the verse 'אך מעין ובור מקוה מים יהיה טהור' that the formation of the water must be through purity.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's principle: airspace of a vessel is like the vessel itself
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's principle: airspace of a vessel is like the vessel itself
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the Mishna implies the airspace of a vessel is considered like the vessel. Rabbi Zeira objects that perhaps it refers to a case where the water flows directly (שותת), but Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba rejects this, citing the Mishna's phrase 'so that water passes to the barrel'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya reports Rabbi Yochanan's principle that the Mishna implies the airspace of a vessel is considered like the vessel itself.
Rabbi Zeira objects to Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba that perhaps the Mishna refers to a case where the water flows directly (שותת) rather than through the airspace.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba rejects the objection, calling it foolish, and cites the Mishna's phrase 'so that water passes to the barrel' to prove the water goes through the airspace.

items.text: Testimony of Rabbi Tzadok about flowing water through nut leaves
items.text_en: Testimony of Rabbi Tzadok about flowing water through nut leaves
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports that the Mishna was taught based on Rabbi Tzadok's testimony that flowing water channeled through nut leaves is valid, a case that occurred in Ohalya and was approved by the Sages in the Chamber of Hewn Stone.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the Mishna was taught based on the testimony of Rabbi Tzadok.
The Mishna is cited: Rabbi Tzadok testified that flowing water channeled through nut leaves is valid.
The case occurred in Ohalya, was brought before the Sages in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, and they approved it.

items.text: Blemish and age requirements for all stages of sacrifice
items.text_en: Blemish and age requirements for all stages of sacrifice
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira quotes Rabbi that cutting the ear of the bull before receiving its blood invalidates it, based on the verse 'and he shall take from the blood of the bull'—a bull that already was. Rava cites a baraita that the requirement of being unblemished and a year old applies at the time of slaughter, and extends to reception, carrying, and sprinkling via the word 'יִהְיֶה'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira quotes Rabbi that cutting the ear of the bull before receiving its blood invalidates it, based on the verse 'and he shall take from the blood of the bull'—a bull that already was.
The gemara asks: we have found this rule for most holy sacrifices; from where do we derive it for lesser holy sacrifices?
Rava cites a baraita that the requirement of being unblemished and a year old applies at the time of slaughter, and extends to reception, carrying, and sprinkling via the word 'יִהְיֶה'.

items.text: Abaye's objection and Rava's resolution: hours invalidate in sacrifices
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and Rava's resolution: hours invalidate in sacrifices
items.desc_en: Abaye objects from Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling that if a leftover olive's bulk of meat or fat remains, one may still sprinkle the blood—implying the animal need not be a year old at sprinkling. The Gemara explains that the ruling applies only to a year-old animal. Rava concludes that this shows hours invalidate in sacrifices, meaning the age requirement applies at each stage.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects by citing Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling that if an olive's bulk of meat or fat remains from any sacrifice, one may still sprinkle the blood, implying the animal need not be a year old at sprinkling.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling applies only to a בן שנה (year-old animal).
Abaye objects: is there anything that is a year old at slaughter but two years old at the time of walking and sprinkling?
Rava resolves that this shows hours invalidate in sacrifices, meaning the age requirement applies at each stage.

items.text: Rabbi Ami's ruling: animal with head inside and legs outside
items.text_en: Rabbi Ami's ruling: animal with head inside and legs outside
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami quotes Rabbi Elazar that if an animal's head is inside the Temple courtyard and its legs outside, and one cuts and then slaughters, it is valid.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami reports Rabbi Elazar's ruling that if an animal's head is inside the Temple courtyard and its legs outside, cutting the head off first and then slaughtering is valid.

items.text: Opening question on cutting after slaughter
items.text_en: Opening question on cutting after slaughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions a baraita that states if one slaughtered and then cut the animal it is invalid, but if one cut and then slaughtered it is valid. It objects that cutting before slaughter would be like offering a blemished animal, so it reinterprets the case as cutting before blood reception.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that slaughtering and then cutting invalidates, but cutting and then slaughtering is valid.
The Gemara objects that cutting before slaughter would be like offering a blemished animal, which is invalid.
The Gemara reinterprets the baraita as referring to cutting before or after blood reception, not slaughter.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Zeira's ruling
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Zeira's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that cutting before reception should still be invalid, citing Rabbi Zeira's ruling that cutting the ear of a firstborn after slaughter but before blood reception invalidates it, based on a verse requiring the bull to be intact. Rav Chisda in the name of Avimi answers that the cutting is only until reaching the bone, not severing the limb.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that cutting before reception should be invalid, citing Rabbi Zeira's ruling that cutting the ear of a firstborn after slaughter but before blood reception invalidates it based on the verse requiring the bull to be intact.

sub.text: Rav Chisda in the name of Avimi
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda in the name of Avimi
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda in the name of Avimi answers that the cutting is only until reaching the bone, not severing the limb, so it does not invalidate the offering.

items.text: Inferences from the baraita
items.text_en: Inferences from the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to infer from the baraita that blood absorbed in limbs is considered blood, and that meat of קדשים קלים that left before sprinkling is invalid. Both inferences are rejected: the first may be due to fat, the second may refer only to קדשי קדשים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita that blood absorbed in limbs is considered blood, since the limb was cut after receiving the blood and the offering was invalidated.
The Gemara rejects the inference, suggesting the invalidation might be due to the fat (שומן) that was cut, not the blood.
The Gemara infers from the baraita that meat of קדשים קלים (offerings of lesser sanctity) that left the Temple courtyard before the sprinkling of blood is invalid.
The Gemara rejects the inference, noting the baraita might refer only to קדשי קדשים (offerings of the highest sanctity), not to קדשים קלים.

items.text: Baraita on location for slaughter and reception
items.text_en: Baraita on location for slaughter and reception
items.desc_en: A baraita details the laws for קדשי קדשים and קדשים קלים regarding slaughter and blood reception in the north or inside. It rules that if the animal's head and most of its body entered, it is considered fully inside. The Gemara tries to infer that meat of קדשים קלים that left before sprinkling is invalid, but rejects this, suggesting it refers to specific parts like the tail and liver.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the laws for קדשי קדשים (most holy sacrifices) regarding slaughter and blood reception in the north, including the rule that if the animal's head and most of its body entered, it is considered fully inside.

The baraita continues with the laws for קדשים קלים (lesser holy sacrifices), and the Gemara attempts to infer from the rule about an animal that left and returned that meat of קדשים קלים that left before sprinkling is invalid.

The Gemara rejects the inference, suggesting that the baraita's ruling about the animal that left and returned refers only to specific parts like the tail, liver lobe, and two kidneys, not to the general meat.

items.text: Questions on animal's position and hanging
items.text_en: Questions on animal's position and hanging
items.desc_en: Avuha d'Shmuel asks Shmuel about an animal with its body inside and legs outside, and about hanging slaughter and reception. Shmuel gives answers, but Avuha d'Shmuel corrects him each time, citing the need for slaughter on the thigh and proper service posture.

sub.desc_en: Avuha d'Shmuel asks Shmuel about the validity of slaughter when the animal's body is inside the Temple courtyard but its legs are outside.
Shmuel answers that it is invalid, citing the verse 'וֶהֱבִיאוּם לַה׳' (they shall bring them to the Lord) requiring the entire animal to be inside.
Avuha d'Shmuel asks about the validity of slaughtering an animal that is hanging (suspended) rather than resting on the ground.
Shmuel answers that hanging slaughter is valid.
Avuha d'Shmuel corrects Shmuel, stating that slaughter must be performed on the thigh (i.e., the animal must be resting on its side), and hanging lacks that condition.
Avuha d'Shmuel asks about the validity of slaughtering an animal that was already hanging (i.e., it was hung and then slaughtered).
Shmuel answers that slaughtering a hanging animal is invalid.
Avuha d'Shmuel corrects Shmuel, explaining that the requirement is for the animal to be on its thigh (resting), not for the slaughterer to be on the thigh.
Avuha d'Shmuel asks about the validity of receiving the blood from an animal that was already hanging.
Shmuel answers that receiving blood from a hanging animal is valid.
Avuha d'Shmuel corrects Shmuel, stating that this is not the proper manner of service (דרך שירות) for receiving blood.
Avuha d'Shmuel asks about the validity of receiving blood while the animal is being hung (i.e., the slaughterer hangs the animal and then receives the blood).
Shmuel answers that receiving blood while hanging is invalid.
Avuha d'Shmuel corrects Shmuel, clarifying that the requirement for slaughter on the thigh does not apply to receiving blood.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's rulings on hanging
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's rulings on hanging
items.desc_en: Abaye rules that for קדשי קדשים all hanging cases are invalid except hanging and slaughter, while for קדשים קלים all are valid except hanging and reception. Rava initially questions this, then revises to say all are valid except hanging and slaughter in קדשי קדשים, and hanging and reception in both categories.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that for קדשי קדשים all hanging cases are invalid except hanging and slaughter, while for קדשים קלים all are valid except hanging and reception.
Rava questions why Abaye distinguishes between קדשי קדשים and קדשים קלים regarding hanging and reception, arguing that the principle of airspace should apply equally.
Rava revises the ruling: all hanging cases are valid except hanging and slaughter in קדשי קדשים, and hanging and reception in both categories.

items.text: Question on tzitzit outside
items.text_en: Question on tzitzit outside
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira about an animal whose tzitzit (wool) is outside while the body is inside. Rabbi Zeira answers by analogy to the verse requiring the entire animal to be brought inside, and applies a similar verse for the priest's entry into the Tent of Meeting.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira about an animal whose body is inside the courtyard but its tzitzit (wool) protrudes outside.

Rabbi Zeira answers by analogy: just as the verse 'וֶהֱבִיאוּם לַה׳' requires the entire animal to be brought inside, so too the verse 'בְּבוֹאָם אֶל אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד' requires the priest's entire body to enter the Tent of Meeting.

items.text: Mishnah on improper placement of blood
items.text_en: Mishnah on improper placement of blood
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where placing blood on the altar ramp, not opposite the base, or in the wrong location (upper/lower, inside/outside) invalidates the offering but does not incur karet.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases of improper blood placement that invalidate the offering but do not incur karet.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on atonement despite invalid flesh
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on atonement despite invalid flesh
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that if the flesh becomes invalid, the owners still achieve atonement because the verse says 'I have given it to you upon the altar to atone'—once the blood reaches the altar, atonement is achieved. The Gemara asks why the flesh is not also permitted, and answers that the verse specifies 'to atone' and not for any other purpose.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that if the flesh becomes invalid, the owners still achieve atonement, citing the verse 'I have given it to you upon the altar to atone'—once the blood reaches the altar, atonement is achieved.
The Gemara asks why the flesh is not also permitted for consumption if the blood has already achieved atonement.
The Gemara answers that the verse specifies 'to atone'—the blood is given for atonement only, not for any other purpose like permitting the flesh.

items.text: Objection from the baraita on improper placement
items.text_en: Objection from the baraita on improper placement
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that Shmuel holds that improper placement is like proper placement. It then cites a baraita from another chapter stating that if blood was placed on the ramp not opposite the base, or if upper blood was placed below or vice versa, etc., a valid priest must collect the blood again. The Gemara objects: if improper placement is like proper placement, why is a second collection needed? And if one suggests it is to permit the flesh for eating, the Gemara retorts: is there any sprinkling that does not effect atonement yet permits the flesh?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if Shmuel holds that improper placement is like proper placement, why does the baraita require a second collection of blood, and if the purpose is to permit the flesh for eating, is there any sprinkling that does not effect atonement yet permits the flesh?

items.text: Resolution: the case involves an invalid priest
items.text_en: Resolution: the case involves an invalid priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that if a valid priest had performed the placement, indeed it would be effective; but here the case involves an invalid priest who performed the placement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that if a valid priest had performed the placement, indeed it would be effective; but here the case involves an invalid priest who performed the placement.

items.text: Further objection: the law of rejection (dachui)
items.text_en: Further objection: the law of rejection (dachui)
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: even if an invalid priest performed the placement, the blood should be considered rejected (dachui), as taught in a baraita: if invalid priests received the blood outside the proper time or place, a valid priest must collect again—but only if they received, not if they sprinkled. The Gemara suggests this is because the blood is rejected. It then answers: no, it is because the invalid priest's improper intention (machshavah) disqualifies the blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the blood should be considered rejected (דָּחוּי), citing a baraita where invalid priests who received blood outside the proper time or place require a valid priest to collect again, but not if they sprinkled, implying rejection.
The Gemara answers that the reason is not rejection but because the invalid priest's improper intention (מַחְשָׁבָה) disqualifies the blood.

items.text: Challenge and correction regarding machshavah
items.text_en: Challenge and correction regarding machshavah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if machshavah disqualifies, why is reception not also disqualified? Moreover, does machshavah even apply here? Rava said machshavah only applies to one fit for service, with a fit item, in a fit place. The Gemara then corrects the baraita's wording: instead of 'if they sprinkled, no', it should say 'if they slaughtered, no'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if disqualifying machshavah (improper intent) is the reason, why is reception (קַבָּלָה) not also disqualified? Moreover, does machshavah even apply here?

The Gemara cites Rava's principle: machshavah (improper intent) only disqualifies when performed by one fit for service (רָאוּי לַעֲבוֹדָה), with a fit item (דָּבָר הָרָאוּי), in a fit place (מָקוֹם הָרָאוּי).
The Gemara corrects the baraita's wording: instead of 'if they sprinkled (זָרְקוּ), no', it should read 'if they slaughtered (שָׁחֲטוּ), no'.

items.text: Clarification of the baraita's novel teaching
items.text_en: Clarification of the baraita's novel teaching
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what does the baraita teach—that machshavah disqualifies? That is already known. It answers: it teaches that machshavah does not disqualify from the point of reception onward, for the reason given by Rava.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what novel teaching the baraita intends to convey, since it is already known that improper intent (מחשבה) disqualifies a sacrifice.
The Gemara answers that the baraita teaches that improper intent (מחשבה) does not disqualify from the point of reception onward, based on Rava's principle.

items.text: New objection from a baraita on piggul
items.text_en: New objection from a baraita on piggul
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: if one intended to place upper blood below or lower blood above, it is valid immediately but becomes piggul the next day. If one intended again... (the text is cut off).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: if one intended to place blood designated for above below, or below above, it is valid immediately but becomes piggul the next day; if one intended again...

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Distinction between chutz li'zmano and chutz li'mkomo
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Distinction between chutz li'zmano and chutz li'mkomo
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that improper time (chutz li'zmano) makes a sacrifice piggul with karet, while improper place (chutz li'mkomo) makes it merely pasul without karet. If one then thinks about improper time or place after the fact, it remains pasul without karet.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the basic rule: intent outside the proper place disqualifies without karet, while intent outside the proper time renders piggul with karet.
The Mishnah adds that if one had intent for the next day (improper time) together with improper place, the offering is merely disqualified without karet.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why is chutz li'mkomo not piggul?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why is chutz li'mkomo not piggul?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if improper place is considered like improper time (kimkomo dami), why is it only pasul and not piggul?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if improper place is considered like improper time (kimkomo dami), why is it only pasul and not piggul?

items.text: Mar Zutra's answer: Only blood that permits flesh brings piggul
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's answer: Only blood that permits flesh brings piggul
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra explains that only a sprinkling that permits the flesh for consumption can bring piggul; a sprinkling that does not permit the flesh (like chutz li'mkomo) cannot. Rav Ashi supports this with a verse from Leviticus 7:18, showing that piggul applies only when the piggul itself causes the prohibition, not when another prohibition (like improper place) does.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra answers that only a sprinkling which permits the flesh for consumption can bring piggul; a sprinkling that does not permit the flesh cannot.
Rav Ashi supports Mar Zutra's answer by citing Leviticus 7:18, showing that piggul applies only when the piggul itself causes the prohibition, not when another prohibition (like improper place) does.

items.text: Objection and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution
items.text_en: Objection and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if so, why does chutz li'mkomo even invalidate (pasul)? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that the Mishnah's case is about a thought of 'rest' (hinuch) according to Rabbi Yehuda, which invalidates but does not make piggul.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the thought of 'outside its place' does not make piggul, then it should not even invalidate (pasul).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves: the Mishnah's case involves a thought of 'rest' (hinuch) according to Rabbi Yehuda, which invalidates but does not make piggul.

items.text: Resh Lakish's answer: Distinction between silent and verbalized intent
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's answer: Distinction between silent and verbalized intent
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish argues that chutz li'mkomo is indeed pasul mamash, and it is considered like chutz li'zmano. The Mishnah's distinction is between a case where the blood was given in silence (pasul) and where it was given with verbalized intent (piggul).

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that the offering is completely disqualified (pasul mamash), and blood not in its proper place is considered like in its proper place; the distinction is between giving the blood in silence (disqualified) and with verbalized intent (piggul).
A baraita is cited that discusses intent to place blood designated for below above, etc., up to the point of the concept of 'intent of rest' according to Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's answer: Distinction between blood of the soul and other blood
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's answer: Distinction between blood of the soul and other blood
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says both cases are in silence, and chutz li'mkomo is not like chutz li'zmano. The difference is between blood that permits the flesh (dam ha'nefesh) and blood that does not (e.g., blood of a bird or other offerings).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan answers that both cases (the mishna here and the mishna in the next chapter) involve placing the blood in silence, and blood placed not in its proper place is not considered as if placed in its proper place; the distinction between the two mishnayot is whether there is דם הנפש (blood of the soul) remaining to be sprinkled again or not.

items.text: Analysis of the Mishnah's wording and Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.text_en: Analysis of the Mishnah's wording and Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the Mishnah's phrase 'pasul ve'ein bo karet' from the perspectives of Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan. For Resh Lakish, it fits naturally. For Rabbi Yochanan, it is problematic, leading to a discussion with Shmuel. The Gemara then addresses an objection to Rabbi Yochanan: if chutz li'mkomo is not like chutz li'zmano, why not collect the spilled blood? Rabbi Yochanan holds like the opinion that one may not collect it, citing a dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's phrase 'pasul ve'ein bo karet' as the starting point for analysis.
The Gemara notes that for Resh Lakish the Mishnah's wording fits, but for Rabbi Yochanan it is problematic.
Shmuel explains that the Mishnah means: if one placed the blood with intent, it is invalid but without karet.
The Gemara objects: if chutz li'mkomo is not like chutz li'zmano, why not collect the spilled blood?

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's position via Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's position via Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan holds like the opinion that one may not collect the blood, citing the dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Rav Chisda's ruling on misplaced blood applications
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's ruling on misplaced blood applications
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that all agree that if blood meant for below was placed above, it must not be gathered (i.e., the offering is invalid and must be removed). The dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon is only about blood meant for inside placed outside or vice versa.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that the mishnah aligns with the view that misplaced blood is not gathered, and explains the unanimous and disputed cases.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on the verse 'This is the law of the burnt-offering'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on the verse 'This is the law of the burnt-offering'
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda limits the cases where an offering that ascended must descend, while Rabbi Shimon expands the list to include many disqualifications, deriving from 'תורת העולה' that once an offering ascends it does not descend, except for those disqualified before sanctity.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak introduces a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda limits the cases where an offering that ascended must descend, deriving from the verse 'זֹאת הִיא הָעוֹלָה' (this is the law of the burnt-offering) that only offerings disqualified before sanctity descend.

Rabbi Shimon expands the list of disqualifications that do not cause descent, including many cases like slaughter at night, blood spilled, and improper placement, deriving from 'תּוֹרַת הָעוֹלָה' (the law of the burnt-offering) that all offerings that ascend do not descend.

The baraita resolves the scope by excluding disqualifications that originated outside sanctity (like a tereifah or animal used for bestiality), limiting the rule to disqualifications that occurred within the sacred context.

items.text: Proof from the baraita that Rabbi Yehuda agrees with 'lo ya'asfenu'
items.text_en: Proof from the baraita that Rabbi Yehuda agrees with 'lo ya'asfenu'
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita includes cases of blood placed above or below without Rabbi Yehuda disputing, implying he agrees that such offerings are not gathered, supporting Rav Chisda's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita that Rabbi Yehuda does not dispute the cases of blood placed above or below, implying he agrees that such offerings are not gathered, supporting Rav Chisda's position.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's statement about the inner altar sanctifying unfit items
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's statement about the inner altar sanctifying unfit items
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer teaches that the inner altar sanctifies unfit offerings. The Gemara questions why this is necessary, since a Mishnah already states that offerings placed inside or outside are not gathered. The answer is that the Mishnah only applies to blood, but Rabbi Eliezer extends it to the handful (קומץ) which is not suitable for the inner altar.

sub.desc_en: רבי אליעזר (Rabbi Eliezer) states that the inner altar sanctifies unfit offerings, meaning they do not descend if they ascend.
The Gemara asks why this teaching is necessary, since a Mishnah already states that offerings placed inside or outside are not gathered.
