The Gemara answers that the Mishnah only applies to blood, which is suitable for the inner altar in some contexts, but Rabbi Eliezer extends the rule to the handful (קומץ) which is not suitable for the inner altar, teaching that even it does not descend.

items.text: Objection from the baraita on foreign incense and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the baraita on foreign incense and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita states that foreign incense that ascended the outer altar must descend, implying only the outer altar sanctifies fit items, not the inner. The Gemara resolves by reinterpreting: the baraita refers to the outer altar, but the inner altar sanctifies both fit and unfit items because it is like a service vessel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: foreign incense that ascended the altar must descend, implying only the outer altar sanctifies fit items, not the inner altar.
The Gemara resolves by reinterpreting: the baraita refers to the outer altar, but the inner altar sanctifies both fit and unfit items because it is like a service vessel.

items.text: Mishnah on improper intent for slaughter and the Gemara's question on tail skin
items.text_en: Mishnah on improper intent for slaughter and the Gemara's question on tail skin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where improper intent (e.g., to sprinkle blood outside or eat meat outside) renders the offering invalid (פסול) or piggul. The Gemara begins to discuss the status of the tail skin (עור האליה) in these laws.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases of improper intent for slaughter outside the Temple, including intent to eat a כזית (olive's bulk) from the tail skin (עור האליה) outside, which renders the offering פסול (invalid) but not subject to כרת (extirpation).
The Mishnah continues with cases of intent for the next day (pigul), including intent to eat a כזית from the tail skin tomorrow, which renders the offering פיגול (pigul) and liable for כרת.
The Gemara begins to question the status of the tail skin (עור האליה) in the Mishnah's laws of improper intent.

items.text: Shmuel's resolution of the contradiction in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Shmuel's resolution of the contradiction in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one can have intent from eating of the altar to eating of man regarding the tail. Shmuel answers that the Mishnah is Rabbi Eliezer's view, who holds that such intent is valid. The Gemara then challenges this by noting the contradiction between the first clause (Rabbi Eliezer) and the later clause (Rabbis), and accepts that the Mishnah is a composite.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah can consider the tail like the fat tail, since one would be intending from eating of the altar to eating of man.
Shmuel answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that one can have intent from eating of the altar to eating of man and vice versa.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer invalidates a sacrifice for intent to eat something not normally eaten, supporting his position.
The Gemara objects that the later clause of the Mishnah (the general rule) implies only things normally eaten are considered, which follows the Rabbis, creating a contradiction.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is a composite: the first clause follows Rabbi Eliezer and the later clause follows the Rabbis.

items.text: Rav Huna's alternative: the skin of the tail is not like the tail
items.text_en: Rav Huna's alternative: the skin of the tail is not like the tail
items.desc_en: Rav Huna argues that the skin of the tail is not considered like the tail itself. Rava explains his reasoning: the verse says 'its fat, the tail' (חֶלְבּוֹ הָאַלְיָה), excluding the skin of the tail.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna asserts that the skin of the tail is not considered like the tail itself.
Rava explains Rav Huna's reasoning: the verse 'חֶלְבּוֹ הָאַלְיָה' (its fat, the tail) excludes the skin of the tail.

items.text: Rav Chisda's alternative: the skin is like the tail, but this is a kid's tail
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's alternative: the skin is like the tail, but this is a kid's tail
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda maintains that the skin of the tail is indeed like the tail, but the case here involves the tail of a kid, which is not offered on the altar.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asserts that the skin of the tail is indeed like the tail, but the case here involves the tail of a kid, which is not offered on the altar.

items.text: Analysis of the three positions
items.text_en: Analysis of the three positions
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why each Amora rejects the others' views. Shmuel's position is rejected because it forces a split Mishnah. Rav Huna's is rejected because it implies the skin is not like the tail, contradicting a known teaching. Rav Chisda's is defended: his teaching is necessary because one might think that for the altar, kings do not eat the skin, so it is not considered part of the tail.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that all other Amoraim reject Shmuel's view because they do not want to split the Mishnah between Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis, and they reject Rav Huna's view because they hold that the skin of the tail is considered like the tail itself.
The Gemara asks why Shmuel and Rav Huna reject Rav Chisda's view, noting that the teaching about the skin of the tail being like the tail itself is already known from a Mishnah in tractate Hullin.

The Gemara defends Rav Chisda's position, explaining that his teaching is necessary because one might think that for the altar, kings do not eat the skin, so it is not considered part of the tail; the Mishnah teaches otherwise.

items.text: Challenge from a Baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from a Baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: A Baraita is brought that discusses intent to burn the skin under the tail of an olah, which implies that the skin is considered like the tail. This challenges Rav Chisda. The Gemara notes that the Baraita specifically says 'olah', not 'zebach', which supports Rav Huna. Rav Chisda responds that it deals with a kid's tail, or alternatively, one should read 'zebach' in the Baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a Baraita that discusses intent to burn the skin under the tail of an עולה (burnt offering), implying the skin is considered like the tail, which challenges Rav Chisda's position.

The Baraita continues with a statement from אליעזר בן יהודה (Elazar ben Yehuda) and רבי שמעון בן יהודה (Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda) listing skins that are like meat, including the skin under the tail, and reiterating the same ruling about piggul and karet.

The Gemara notes that the Baraita specifically says 'עולה' (burnt offering) and not 'זבח' (any offering), which supports Rav Huna's view that the skin is not like the tail for other offerings, but challenges Rav Chisda's view that it is always like the tail.
Rav Chisda responds with two possible resolutions: either the Baraita deals with a kid's tail (which is not burned except in an עולה), or one should emend the text to read 'זבח' (any offering).

items.text: Source for the distinction between piggul and disqualification without karet
items.text_en: Source for the distinction between piggul and disqualification without karet
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that improper place (chuts li'mkomo) renders the offering disqualified but without karet, while improper time (chuts li'zmano) is piggul with karet. Shmuel says two verses are written. Abaye explains the derivation from the superfluous 'third' in the Kedoshim section.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source that improper place (חוץ למקומו) renders the offering disqualified but without karet, while improper time (חוץ לזמנו) is piggul with karet.
Shmuel states that two verses are written to establish the distinction.

Rabbah explains that the word 'שלישי' (third) refers to improper time, and the word 'פיגול' refers to improper place, while the phrase 'והנפש האוכלת ממנו' (and the soul that eats from it) limits liability to one who eats it, excluding improper place from karet.
The Gemara objects that the verse could be interpreted in the opposite way, and debates which interpretation is more plausible based on proximity.

sub.text: Abaye's resolution via Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi
sub.text_en: Abaye's resolution via Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi
sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the issue by citing Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi, who reports that the Tanna relies on the superfluous 'third' in the Kedoshim section, since the same law was already stated in the Emor section.

items.text: Initial proposal: apply 've'ochlav' to exclude outer place from karet
items.text_en: Initial proposal: apply 've'ochlav' to exclude outer place from karet
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that since the verse 've'ochlav avono yisa' is not needed for notar (already punished by karet), it should be applied to exclude outer place from karet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that since the verse 'וְאֹכְלָיו עֲוֹנוֹ יִשָּׂא' is not needed for notar (already punished by karet), it should be applied to exclude outer place from karet.

items.text: Counterproposal: apply 've'ochlav' to outer place, exclude notar from karet
items.text_en: Counterproposal: apply 've'ochlav' to outer place, exclude notar from karet
items.desc_en: An alternative suggestion: the verse 've'ochlav avono yisa' refers to outer place, and notar is excluded from karet.

sub.desc_en: The gemara objects that the verse 'וְאֹכְלָיו עֲוֹנוֹ יִשָּׂא' could refer to eating outside the proper place (חוץ למקומו), thereby excluding notar (leftover) from the punishment of karet.

items.text: First reasoning: notar is more fitting for karet via gezerah shavah
items.text_en: First reasoning: notar is more fitting for karet via gezerah shavah
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that notar should be punished by karet because it shares a gezerah shavah of 'avon' with outer time (piggul), which is similar in being a matter of eating. The counterargument claims outer place is more similar to outer time due to sanctity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that notar should be punished by karet because it shares a gezerah shavah of 'avon' with outer time (piggul), which is similar in being a matter of eating.
The counterargument claims outer place is more similar to outer time due to sanctity, so it should be punished by karet instead.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's resolution via gezerah shavah of 'kodesh'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's resolution via gezerah shavah of 'kodesh'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites a tradition from Zavdi bar Levi: a gezerah shavah of 'kodesh' teaches that the karet verse refers to notar, and 've'ochlav' excludes outer place from karet.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Zavdi bar Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Zavdi bar Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan introduces a tradition from Zavdi bar Levi: a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'קדש' (holy) teaches that the verse about karet refers to נותר (leftover), not outer place.

sub.text: Gemara's conclusion from Rabbi Yochanan's tradition
sub.text_en: Gemara's conclusion from Rabbi Yochanan's tradition
sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the verse 'וְאֹכְלָיו עֲוֹנוֹ יִשָּׂא' (and its eaters shall bear their iniquity) in the context of נותר (leftover) excludes eating outside the place from karet.

items.text: Challenge and counter-challenge on which verse applies to which
items.text_en: Challenge and counter-challenge on which verse applies to which
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the long verse (Arikha) is assigned to outer time and the 'shlishi' of Kedoshim to outer place, and proposes the opposite. Both sides argue based on similarity and context.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assignment of the long verse (Arikha) to outer time and the 'shlishi' of Kedoshim to outer place, proposing the opposite assignment.
The Gemara argues that the long verse fits outer time because it learns a verbal analogy of 'עון' (sin) from leftover (נותר), which is similar in being a piggul (זבח) issue.
The Gemara counters that the long verse should apply to outer place, and the 'shlishi' of Kedoshim to outer time, because the verse's context (the Mikdash) is similar to outer place.

items.text: Rava's comprehensive derivation from the long verse
items.text_en: Rava's comprehensive derivation from the long verse
items.desc_en: Rava explains that all laws come from the long verse: 'he'achol ye'achel' indicates two eatings (human and altar), 'mibesar zevach shelamav' teaches that all sacrifices are subject to piggul, 'shlishi' refers to outer time, 'lo yeratzeh' equates acceptance of valid and invalid, 'hamakriv' and 'oto' limit the disqualification to the offering and not the priest.

sub.desc_en: Rava declares that all the laws of piggul come from the long verse, beginning with 'הֵאָכֹל יֵאָכֵל' which teaches two eatings: human and altar.
Rava derives from 'מִבְּשַׂר זֶבַח שְׁלָמָיו' that just as peace-offerings (שלמים) can become piggul and cause piggul, so too all sacrifices are subject to piggul.
Rava explains that the word 'שְׁלִישִׁי' (third) in the verse refers to חוּץ לִזְמַנּוֹ (outside its proper time), i.e., piggul.
Rava derives from 'לֹא יֵרָצֶה' that the acceptance of a disqualified offering parallels the acceptance of a valid one, requiring all permitting factors to be offered.
Rava explains that 'הַמַּקְרִיב' teaches disqualification occurs only at the act of offering, not on the third day, and 'אוֹתוֹ' limits the disqualification to the offering itself, not the priest.
The gemara begins citing the final word 'לֹא יֵחָשֵׁב' from the verse, but the move is cut off, likely continuing the derivation.

items.text: Opening derivation of piggul and its components
items.text_en: Opening derivation of piggul and its components
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the biblical derivation of piggul: the word "פיגול" refers to intent outside the proper place, "יהיה" teaches that multiple improper intentions combine, and "והנפש האוכלת ממנו" limits liability to one who eats, not two, drawing an analogy to notar via "עון".

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the biblical derivation of piggul: the word 'פיגול' refers to intent outside the proper place, 'יהיה' teaches that multiple improper intentions combine, and 'והנפש האוכלת ממנו' limits liability to one who eats, not two, drawing an analogy to notar via 'עון'.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question and Rav Ashi's resolution about 'שלישי'
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question and Rav Ashi's resolution about 'שלישי'
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Rava about the word "שלישי" in the Kedoshim section; Rava says it teaches that the sacrifice must be tripled in blood, flesh, and fats. Rav Pappa objects that this could be derived from the first verse. Rav Ashi reports that Rav Mattanah explained: without "שלישי", one might think it is a particular case, and "פיגול" a general rule, expanding to other places; thus the verse teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Rava what he derives from the word "שלישי" in the Kedoshim section.
Rava answers that the word teaches that the sacrifice must be tripled in blood, flesh, and fats.
Rav Pappa objects that this could be derived from the first verse, which uses the language "שלישי".

sub.text: Rav Ashi's report of Rav Mattanah's explanation
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's report of Rav Mattanah's explanation
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that Rav Mattanah explained: without "שלישי", one might think it is a particular case and "פיגול" a general rule, expanding to other places; thus the verse teaches otherwise.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva debate third-day disqualification
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva debate third-day disqualification
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that the verse "ואם האכל יאכל מבשר זבח שלמיו" speaks of one who intends to eat on the third day, not one who actually eats. Rabbi Eliezer argues that a valid sacrifice cannot become invalid on the third day. Rabbi Akiva counters with examples of zav, zavah, and shomeret yom kineged yom who are presumed pure but become impure upon seeing. Rabbi Eliezer then cites "המקריב" to show disqualification occurs only at the time of offering, not on the third day, and clarifies that "אותו" refers to the sacrifice, not the priest.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that the verse 'ואם האכל יאכל מבשר זבח שלמיו' speaks of one who intends to eat on the third day, not one who actually eats.
Rabbi Eliezer questions whether the verse could refer to actual eating on the third day, arguing that a valid sacrifice cannot become invalid on the third day.
Rabbi Akiva counters with examples of zav, zavah, and shomeret yom kineged yom who are presumed pure but become impure upon seeing, showing that something valid can later become invalid.
Rabbi Eliezer cites the word 'המקריב' to show that disqualification occurs only at the time of offering, not on the third day.
Rabbi Eliezer clarifies that 'אותו' refers to the sacrifice, not the priest, confirming that disqualification applies only to the offering itself.

items.text: Ben Azzai and Acherim on 'אותו' and 'לא יחשב'
items.text_en: Ben Azzai and Acherim on 'אותו' and 'לא יחשב'
items.desc_en: Ben Azzai derives from "אותו" that only the sacrifice itself is subject to "לא ירצה" for piggul, not one who delays his vow. Acherim derive from "לא יחשב" that disqualification is by intent, not by the third day itself.

sub.desc_en: Ben Azzai derives from the word 'אותו' that only the sacrifice itself is subject to 'לא ירצה' for piggul, not one who delays his vow.
Acherim derive from 'לא יחשב' that disqualification is by intent, not by the third day itself.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Ben Azzai's sources
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Ben Azzai's sources
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Ben Azzai knows that the verse speaks of the sacrifice, not the priest, and offers two answers: from Acherim's teaching or from the dual phrasing "לא ירצו" and "לא ירצה". It then asks how Ben Azzai derives that a delay of a vow does not incur "לא ירצה", and suggests it comes from Acherim's baraita about a firstborn that passed its year.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Ben Azzai knows that the verse speaks of the sacrifice and not the priest.
The Gemara offers a first answer: Ben Azzai derives it from Acherim's teaching.
The Gemara offers a second answer: from the dual phrasing 'לֹא יֵרָצוּ' and 'לֹא יֵרָצֶה', indicating the subject is the sacrifice.
The Gemara questions how Ben Azzai derives that a delay of a vow does not incur 'לֹא יֵרָצֶה' from this verse.
The Gemara answers that Ben Azzai derives it from Acherim's baraita.
The Gemara cites Acherim's baraita about a firstborn that passed its year, which serves as the source for Ben Azzai's ruling.

items.text: Derivation that a firstborn is not disqualified by passage of a year
items.text_en: Derivation that a firstborn is not disqualified by passage of a year
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a firstborn animal, like other consecrated animals that become disqualified, can be disqualified by the passage of a year. It derives from a verse that a firstborn is compared to tithe, which is not disqualified from year to year, so a firstborn is also not disqualified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a firstborn animal, like other consecrated animals that become disqualified, can be disqualified by the passage of a year.
The Gemara derives from a verse that a firstborn is compared to tithe, which is not disqualified from year to year, so a firstborn is also not disqualified.

items.text: Need for the derivation regarding other sacrifices
items.text_en: Need for the derivation regarding other sacrifices
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the derivation was necessary: one might have thought that only a firstborn, which cannot effect atonement, is not disqualified by time, but other sacrifices that do effect atonement might be disqualified. The verse teaches that they are not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the derivation was necessary because one might have thought that only a firstborn, which cannot effect atonement (הרצאה), is not disqualified by time, but other sacrifices that do effect atonement might be disqualified; the verse teaches that they are not.

items.text: Alternative derivation and Ben Azzai's interpretation
items.text_en: Alternative derivation and Ben Azzai's interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the derivation from the verse, citing another verse that implies the sin is in the person, not the offering. Ben Azzai uses that verse to teach that a man's wife does not die for his sin of delaying vows unless he lacks money to pay, countering a possible inference from Rabbi Elazar or Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the derivation from the verse is unnecessary, citing another verse that implies the sin is in the person, not the offering.

Ben Azzai explains that the verse teaches that a man's wife does not die for his sin of delaying vows unless he lacks money to pay, countering a possible inference from Rabbi Elazar or Rabbi Yochanan.

items.text: Acherim's opinion and Rabbi Eliezer's use of the verse
items.text_en: Acherim's opinion and Rabbi Eliezer's use of the verse
items.desc_en: Acherim state that an offering is disqualified by improper intent (machshavah) but not by being left until the third day. The Gemara asks what Rabbi Eliezer does with the verse 'lo yeichashev' (it shall not be reckoned).

sub.desc_en: Acherim state that an offering is disqualified by improper intent (מחשבה) but not by being left until the third day.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Eliezer does with the verse 'לֹא יֵחָשֵׁב' (it shall not be reckoned), since Acherim's position seems to leave it unused.

items.text: Rabbi Yannai's two teachings on 'lo yeichashev'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yannai's two teachings on 'lo yeichashev'
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents two versions of Rabbi Yannai's teaching: one that improper thoughts can cancel each other out, and another that one who has improper intent is liable to lashes. Rav Ashi questions the latter because it is a prohibition without action, and Rav Mari answers that it follows Rabbi Yehuda's view that such prohibitions incur lashes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Yannai's first teaching: that the verse 'לֹא יֵחָשֵׁב' teaches that improper thoughts about a sacrifice can cancel each other out.

sub.text: Rav Mari's version of Rabbi Yannai's teaching
sub.text_en: Rav Mari's version of Rabbi Yannai's teaching
sub.desc_en: Rav Mari presents a second version of Rabbi Yannai's teaching: that one who has improper intent regarding sacrifices is liable to lashes, derived from the same verse.
Rav Ashi objects that improper intent is a prohibition without action (לאו שאין בו מעשה), and generally such prohibitions do not incur lashes.
Rav Mari answers that the teaching follows Rabbi Yehuda's view, who holds that even a prohibition without action (לאו שאין בו מעשה) incurs lashes.

items.text: Mishnah: The rule of piggul and pasul
items.text_en: Mishnah: The rule of piggul and pasul
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: if one slaughters, receives, carries, or sprinkles with intent to eat or burn an olive's bulk outside its proper place, it is pasul (invalid) without karet; if with intent outside its proper time, it is piggul with karet, provided the permitting act is done properly. It gives examples of proper and improper permitting acts, and discusses cases of mixed intentions. Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages dispute whether time-based intent overriding place-based intent renders piggul or pasul.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: intent outside the proper place renders the offering pasul (invalid) without karet, while intent outside the proper time renders it piggul with karet, provided the permitting act is performed properly.

The Mishnah gives examples of how the permitting act is performed properly: slaughter in silence with later intent outside the proper time, or slaughter with time-intent followed by silent receiving, carrying, and sprinkling.
The Mishnah gives examples of when the permitting act is not performed properly: mixing place-intent and time-intent in the same or different services.
The Mishnah adds that for a Paschal offering or sin-offering slaughtered not for its own name, combined with time-intent, the permitting act is not performed properly.
The Mishnah rules that mixed intentions of half an olive's bulk outside the place and half outside the time render the offering pasul without karet.
Rabbi Yehuda states his rule: if time-intent precedes place-intent, the offering is piggul with karet; if place-intent precedes time-intent, it is pasul without karet.

The Sages disagree with Rabbi Yehuda, ruling that both cases (time-intent first or place-intent first) are pasul without karet, and add that eating and burning half-olive bulks do not combine to form a full measure.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Ilfa and Rabbi Yochanan on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Ilfa and Rabbi Yochanan on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Ilfa says the dispute in the Mishnah (between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages) applies only when the improper intentions are in two different services, but in one service all agree it is a mixed intention (invalid). Rabbi Yochanan says the dispute applies even in one service. The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yochanan explains the structure of the Mishnah's examples.

sub.desc_en: Ilfa asserts that the Mishnah's dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages applies only when the improper intentions occur in two different services, but in a single service all agree it is a mixed intention (invalid).
Rabbi Yochanan counters that the dispute applies even when the improper intentions are in a single service.
The Gemara notes that according to Ilfa, the Mishnah's first clause (reisha) and last clause (seifa) both involve two services, which is consistent.

The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yochanan explains the Mishnah's structure, since the first clause involves two services but the last clause would then involve only one service, creating an inconsistency.

items.text: Challenge to Ilfa from Rabbi Yehuda's rule
items.text_en: Challenge to Ilfa from Rabbi Yehuda's rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Yochanan, the phrase 'this is the rule' in the Mishnah is consistent, but for Ilfa, who holds that the rule applies only to two services, the phrase is problematic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the beginning of the Mishnah deals with two services, while the end deals with both one and two services.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda states 'this is the rule' and challenges Ilfa: for Rabbi Yochanan the phrase fits, but for Ilfa it is problematic.

items.text: Mishnah on temurah with two designations
items.text_en: Mishnah on temurah with two designations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where one says 'this is a substitute for an olah, a substitute for a shelamim,' and Rabbi Meir rules it is a substitute for an olah. Rabbi Yosei distinguishes between intending both simultaneously (valid) and changing his mind (only olah).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites the case of one who says 'this is a substitute for an olah, a substitute for a shelamim,' and Rabbi Meir rules it is a substitute for an olah.
Rabbi Yosei distinguishes: if he intended both simultaneously, his words stand; if he changed his mind after saying 'olah,' it is only an olah.

items.text: Abaye and Rava dispute the scope of Rabbi Meir's concession
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava dispute the scope of Rabbi Meir's concession
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised about a case where one says 'this is a substitute for an olah and shelamim' or 'half and half.' Abaye asserts that Rabbi Meir would concede in this case, while Rava maintains the dispute remains.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma about a case where one says 'this is a substitute for an olah and shelamim' or 'half and half' — what is the law?
Abaye asserts that in this case Rabbi Meir would certainly concede that the animal is a substitute for an olah.
Rava maintains that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei remains in this case.

items.text: Rava's challenge from slaughter and Abaye's response
items.text_en: Rava's challenge from slaughter and Abaye's response
items.desc_en: Rava challenges Abaye by citing the case of slaughter, which is like 'half and half,' yet Rabbi Meir disputes it. Abaye responds that slaughter exists from beginning to end, and the Mishnah involves one sign outside its time and another outside its place.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges Abaye by citing the case of slaughter, which is like 'half and half,' yet Rabbi Meir disputes it.
Abaye responds that slaughter exists from beginning to end, and the Mishnah involves one sign outside its time and another outside its place.

items.text: Challenge from kemitzah and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from kemitzah and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava challenges further from the case of kemitzah (taking a handful), which is like 'half and half,' yet Rabbi Meir disputes. Abaye responds that there too, one kemitzah is offered outside its time and the other outside its place.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges Abaye by pointing out that kemitzah (taking a handful) is analogous to 'half and half' (two intentions in one act), yet Rabbi Meir disputes there too.
Abaye responds that there too, one kemitzah was offered outside its time and the other outside its place, so the two intentions are not simultaneous.

items.text: Challenge from the minchat chotei and final resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from the minchat chotei and final resolution
items.desc_en: Rava challenges from the case of the minchat chotei (sin-offering meal offering) which has no frankincense, yet Rabbi Meir disputes. Abaye says they do not dispute there. Rav Ashi adds that if you say they dispute, it is about the steps.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges from the case of the minchat chotei (sin-offering meal offering) which has no frankincense, yet Rabbi Meir disputes.
Abaye responds that they do not dispute in that case.
Rav Ashi adds that if you say they dispute, it is about the steps (פסיעות).

items.text: Different traditions and Rav Dimi's explanation linking Rabbi Meir to Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Different traditions and Rav Dimi's explanation linking Rabbi Meir to Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi teaches like Abaye, Rav Huna bar Natan like Rava. Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Meir stated his view following Rabbi Yehuda's principle of 'grasp the first expression,' citing the Mishnah with Rabbi Yehuda's rule.

sub.desc_en: Reports that Rav Shimi bar Ashi teaches the tradition like Abaye, and Rav Huna bar Natan teaches like Rava.
Rav Dimi explains that Rabbi Meir stated his view following Rabbi Yehuda's principle of 'grasp the first expression' (תפוס לשון ראשון).
Cites the Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda states the rule: if the thought of time precedes the thought of place, the offering is פיגול (invalid) and one is liable for כרת (extirpation).

items.text: Abaye challenges the claim that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosi do not disagree
items.text_en: Abaye challenges the claim that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosi do not disagree
items.desc_en: Abaye objects to the assertion that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosi do not disagree, citing a statement by Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan. The response clarifies that they disagree only on certain points, not on others.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges the claim that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosi do not disagree, citing Rabbah bar bar Chanah's statement in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that they do not disagree, and then pointing out that they actually do disagree.
The response clarifies that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosi disagree only on certain points, not on others.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef clarifies the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosi
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef clarifies the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosi
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef in the name of Rabbi Yochanan explains that everyone agrees about certain formulations of conditional statements. The dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosi is specifically about the case where one says 'temurat olah temurat shelamim', with each rabbi interpreting the redundancy differently.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef reports Rabbi Yochanan's statement that all agree on two conditional formulations: 'תָּחוּל זוֹ וְאַחַר כָּךְ תָּחוּל זוֹ' (let this take effect and afterward let this take effect) does not take effect, while 'לֹא תָּחוּל זוֹ אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן חָלָה זוֹ' (this shall not take effect unless that takes effect) does take effect.

The Gemara states that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosi is specifically when one says 'תְּמוּרַת עוֹלָה תְּמוּרַת שְׁלָמִים' (a substitute for a burnt-offering, a substitute for a peace-offering), and presents Rabbi Meir's position: since he could have said 'תְּמוּרַת עוֹלָה וּשְׁלָמִים' (a substitute for a burnt-offering and a peace-offering) but instead repeated 'תְּמוּרַת', he retracted the first statement.

Rabbi Yosi explains that if he had said 'תְּמוּרַת עוֹלָה וּשְׁלָמִים', one might think it is half a substitute for a burnt-offering and half for a peace-offering; therefore he said 'תְּמוּרַת עוֹלָה תְּמוּרַת שְׁלָמִים' to indicate that the entire animal is a substitute for both a burnt-offering and a peace-offering.

items.text: Conclusion of the dispute: one says they disagree, the other says they do not
items.text_en: Conclusion of the dispute: one says they disagree, the other says they do not
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that one authority claims they do not disagree, while another claims they do disagree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the dispute: one authority claims they do not disagree, while the other claims they do disagree.

items.text: Ulla or Rav Oshaya raises a question about the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Ulla or Rav Oshaya raises a question about the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: Ulla (or Rav Oshaya) asks whether the Mishnah teaches 'kezayit kezayit' or 'kezayit u'khezayit', and explains the implications for whether mixed intentions are considered an 'eruv machshavot' or a detail according to Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: Ulla (or Rav Oshaya) asks whether the Mishnah teaches 'kezayit kezayit' (two separate olive-sized intentions) or 'kezayit u'khezayit' (one olive-sized intention and another), and explains the implications: if it is 'kezayit kezayit', then 'kezayit u'khezayit' is certainly an 'eruv machshavot' (mixed intentions); if it is 'kezayit u'khezayit', then according to Rabbi Yehuda it is a 'perata' (detail), and 'kezayit kezayit' is all the more so.

items.text: Levi's question to Rabbi and Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi's response
items.text_en: Levi's question to Rabbi and Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi's response
items.desc_en: Levi asks Rabbi about a case of intending to eat an olive's worth tomorrow outside the proper place. Rabbi calls it an 'eruv machshavot'. Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi objects, citing a Mishnah that seems to rule similarly, but Rabbi distinguishes between the cases.

sub.desc_en: Levi asks Rabbi whether intending to eat an olive's worth tomorrow outside the proper place constitutes an עירוב מחשבות (combination of intentions).
Rabbi responds that this is a wise question and rules that it is an עירוב מחשבות (combination of intentions).
Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi objects, citing the Mishnah that already rules similarly, implying the question is already answered.

items.text: Rabbi explains the background of Levi's question
items.text_en: Rabbi explains the background of Levi's question
items.desc_en: Rabbi explains that Levi asked a wise question because he had only learned one version of the Mishnah, while others had learned two versions, leading to confusion about which is the primary ruling and which is an 'eruv machshavot'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi (Rabbi) tells his son Rabbi Shimon that Levi asked a wise question, whereas Rabbi Shimon merely cited the Mishnah, because Rabbi Shimon was taught two versions of the Mishnah and thus had no difficulty.

Rabbi explains that Levi, who was taught only one version and heard the Rabbis reciting two, was uncertain whether his own version was exact and theirs was a combination of intentions, or theirs was exact and his version omitted a case, and if so, perhaps their version also omitted another case.

items.text: Analysis of which version Levi learned and the resulting dilemma
items.text_en: Analysis of which version Levi learned and the resulting dilemma
items.desc_en: The Gemara deduces that Levi was taught 'kezayit kezayit' (not 'kezayit u'khezayit'), and explores why he did not ask about the other version. It considers whether he assumed the other version was a general rule or a detail, and concludes that if he had asked the other version, he might have become angry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara deduces that Levi was taught only the version 'kezayit kezayit' (not 'kezayit u'khezayit'), because the latter would not constitute a 'shiur' (omission) in his learning.
The Gemara asks: why did Levi not also ask about the version 'kezayit u'khezayit'?

The Gemara answers: Levi reasoned that by asking one case (kezayit le'machar ba'chutz), he would learn both versions; if the answer was a general rule (כללא), it would cover the other version, and if it was a detail (פרטא), his original question would still be answered.
The Gemara objects: if the answer was a detail (פרטא), the other version would be covered, but if it was a general rule (כללא), Levi would still need to ask about 'kezayit u'khezayit'.
The Gemara resolves: if Levi had asked about the other version, Rabbi would have become angry at him for not understanding the implication.

items.text: Gemara's initial question on combining intentions
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question on combining intentions
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's phrasing 'kezayit u'khezayit' (general) or 'kezayit le'machar ba'chutz' (specific) implies a need to consider combined intentions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's phrasing 'kezayit u'khezayit' (general) or 'kezayit le'machar ba'chutz' (specific) implies a need to consider combined intentions.

items.text: Rava and Rav Hamnuna debate piggul from combined half-intentions
items.text_en: Rava and Rav Hamnuna debate piggul from combined half-intentions
items.desc_en: Rava argues that half an olive for time and half for place combine to make piggul, citing a mishnah about food impurity. Rav Hamnuna disagrees, calling it a mixture of thoughts.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a debate between Rava and Rav Hamnuna about whether half an olive's worth of piggul intent for time and half for place combine to make piggul.
Rava supports his position by citing a mishnah about food impurity where combining half-measures of different impurity levels creates a unified first-degree impurity.
Rava further proves his point from the continuation of the mishnah, showing that when two half-measures fall together they create a second-degree impurity.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's counter-argument and proof
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's counter-argument and proof
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna distinguishes the impurity case (where there is a minimum measure) from the piggul case (where there is none), and brings a baraita about food impurity to support his view.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna counters Rava's proof by distinguishing the food impurity case, which has a minimal measure (שיעור), from the piggul case, which has no such measure.

Rav Hamnuna cites a baraita about food impurity where two types of contaminated foods join together to impurify according to the lighter level, supporting his position that joining requires a measure.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the baraita only applies when one did not supplement the smaller pieces to reach the full measure, suggesting the inference is not valid for the piggul case.

items.text: Bar Kappara's ruling and alternative versions
items.text_en: Bar Kappara's ruling and alternative versions
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi and Ravin report Bar Kappara's ruling that half an olive for time and half for place do not combine to make piggul. Rav Ashi presents a different version of the case.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Bar Kappara rules: if one intends half an olive-bulk outside the area, then half beyond the time, then another half beyond the time, the offering is piggul, because the half-olive for area does not interfere where the time-intent totals a full olive-bulk.

Ravin reports a different order: half beyond the time, then another half beyond the time, then half outside the area; Bar Kappara still rules piggul, because the half-olive for area does not interfere where the time-intent totals a full olive-bulk.

Rav Ashi presents a third version: half beyond the time, then a whole olive-bulk half of which is intended for outside the area and half beyond the time; Bar Kappara rules piggul, because the half-olive does not interfere where the time-intent concerns a whole olive-bulk.

items.text: Rabbi Yannai on eating by dogs and Rabbi Ammi's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Yannai on eating by dogs and Rabbi Ammi's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai rules that intending for dogs to eat the sacrifice makes piggul, citing a verse. Rabbi Ammi objects, arguing that fire would then also make piggul, which contradicts a mishnah.

sub.desc_en: רבי ינאי (Rabbi Yannai) rules that if one intended for dogs to eat the offering the next day, it is פיגול (piggul), citing the verse about Jezebel being eaten by dogs.
רבי אמי (Rabbi Ammi) objects: if so, intending for fire to consume it should also be פיגול (piggul), but a mishnah states that eating and burning do not join together, contradicting that possibility.

הגמרא (the Gemara) resolves: if the intention was expressed in terms of eating, it would indeed be פיגול (piggul); but here the mishnah deals with a case expressed in terms of burning, which is a separate category.

items.text: Rav Ashi's query on eating by two people
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's query on eating by two people
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether intending for two people to eat a kezayit total is piggul, focusing on the thought versus the eaters. Abaye cites a mishnah that eating and burning half-olives do not combine.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether intending for two people to eat a kezayit total constitutes piggul, questioning whether we follow the thought (which has the requisite measure) or the eaters (each lacking a full kezayit).
Abaye cites a mishnah that eating and burning half-olives do not combine, implying that the thought is not followed when the eaters lack a full kezayit each.

items.text: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that intent to eat and to eat combine, just as intent to eat and to burn combine, but only when two people are involved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that intent to eat and to eat combine, just as intent to eat and to burn combine, but only when two people are involved.

items.text: Rava's question about eating in more than the time of a half-loaf
items.text_en: Rava's question about eating in more than the time of a half-loaf
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether intent to eat an olive's bulk in more than the time it takes to eat a half-loaf is considered like eating for the altar or like eating for a common person.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether one who intended to eat an olive's bulk in more than the time of eating a half-loaf is judged by the standard of divine consumption or human consumption.

items.text: Abaye's attempted proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Abaye's attempted proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Abaye brings a Mishnah that half an olive to eat and half to burn do not combine, implying that two half-olives to eat do combine, even though burning is done in more than the time of a half-loaf. The Gemara deflects that burning might be with a large fire.

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a Mishnah that half an olive to eat and half to burn do not combine, inferring that two half-olives to eat would combine, even though burning takes more than the time of eating a half-loaf.
The Gemara deflects that the burning might be done with a large fire, which could complete the burning within the time of eating a half-loaf.

items.text: Another attempted proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Another attempted proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove from the Mishnah that two half-olives of something not normally eaten combine, but notes that the first clause already says that only something normally eaten combines.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that two half-olives of something not normally eaten combine, since the Mishnah says that eating and burning do not combine, implying that eating two halves of something not normally eaten would combine.
The Gemara objects that the first clause already teaches that only something normally eaten combines, so the inference from the latter clause is unnecessary and the attempted proof fails.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's resolution: the Mishnah follows Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's resolution: the Mishnah follows Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya explains that the Mishnah's ruling that something not normally eaten does not combine follows Rabbi Eliezer, who considers intent for eating and burning interchangeable.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya identifies the Mishnah's ruling as following Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that one can transfer intent from human consumption to altar consumption.
Rabbi Yirmeya cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer invalidates an offering slaughtered with intent to eat or burn something not normally consumed or burned, supporting his identification.

items.text: Abaye's alternative explanation: the Mishnah follows the Rabbis
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative explanation: the Mishnah follows the Rabbis
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that even according to the Rabbis, the Mishnah can be explained as referring to something normally eaten, and the Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah teaches that intent to eat and to burn does not combine, even though one might think it should.

sub.desc_en: Abaye proposes that even according to the Rabbis, the Mishnah's inference should be reinterpreted as referring to two halves of an item normally eaten, not to an item not normally eaten.
The Gemara questions what the Mishnah teaches, noting that the first clause already implies that two halves of an item normally eaten combine to disqualify.
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah's inference is about eating and burning, the first clause already teaches that intent to eat something not normally eaten does not combine.
The Gemara argues that if intent to eat two items, one not normally eaten, does not combine, then certainly intent to eat and to burn should not combine, making the Mishnah's teaching redundant.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's teaching about eating and burning was necessary, because one might have thought that since each half is used in its typical manner, they should combine; the Mishnah teaches that they do not.
The Gemara marks the end of the previous chapter and transitions to the next Mishnah.

items.text: Mishnah: All disqualified persons may slaughter
items.text_en: Mishnah: All disqualified persons may slaughter
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all disqualified persons (non-priests, women, slaves, and those impure) may slaughter, even for most holy offerings, as long as they do not touch the meat. However, they can invalidate through improper intent.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that all disqualified persons may slaughter offerings validly, even most holy ones, provided they do not touch the meat, and they can invalidate through improper intent.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Receiving blood by invalid priests
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Receiving blood by invalid priests
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where blood was received by invalid priests (e.g., outside proper time or place, by a disqualified priest, with the left hand, or in a non-sacred vessel) and rules that if there is still lifeblood, a valid priest may collect it again. It also addresses blood spilled on the floor and then gathered, which is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that if invalid priests collected blood outside the proper time or place, a valid priest may collect it again if lifeblood remains.
The Mishnah lists additional cases: blood given to an unfit priest, moved to the left hand, placed in a non-sacred vessel, or spilled and gathered—all are valid or require return to a valid priest.
The Mishnah rules that if blood was placed on the ramp, not opposite the base, or in the wrong location (above/below, inside/outside), a valid priest may collect it again if lifeblood remains.

items.text: Gemara's inference: Slaughter by non-priests is only post-facto
items.text_en: Gemara's inference: Slaughter by non-priests is only post-facto
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah uses the past tense 'שָׁחֲטוּ' (they slaughtered), implying that slaughter by non-priests is valid only after the fact (דִּיעֲבַד), but not initially (לְכַתְּחִלָּה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's past-tense 'שָׁחֲטוּ' (they slaughtered) that slaughter by non-priests is valid only after the fact (דִּיעֲבַד), but not initially (לְכַתְּחִלָּה).

items.text: Challenge from the baraita: Slaughter is valid even initially
items.text_en: Challenge from the baraita: Slaughter is valid even initially
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that derives from the verse 'וְשָׁחַט' that slaughter is valid even by non-priests, including women, slaves, and impure individuals, even for most holy offerings. The baraita concludes that from the verse 'וְשָׁחַט אֶת בֶּן הַבָּקָר' we learn that slaughter is valid by any person, implying it is permitted initially.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that derives from the verse 'וְשָׁחַט' that slaughter is valid even by non-priests, including women, slaves, and impure individuals, even for most holy offerings, and asks whether it might be limited to priests.
The baraita answers that from the verse 'וְשָׁחַט אֶת בֶּן הַבָּקָר' we learn that slaughter is valid by any person, implying it is permitted initially.

items.text: Answer: The Mishnah teaches about impure individuals
items.text_en: Answer: The Mishnah teaches about impure individuals
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's use of 'שָׁחֲטוּ' is not to limit slaughter to post-facto; rather, it is because the Mishnah also discusses impure individuals, for whom slaughter is initially prohibited due to a decree lest they touch the meat. Therefore, the Mishnah teaches the case of 'they slaughtered' (post-facto) to include impure individuals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that even לכתחילה (the ideal standard) slaughter by a non-priest is valid, but the Mishnah used the past tense 'שָׁחֲטוּ' because it wanted to include the case of טמאים (impure priests), which is only valid בדיעבד (after the fact) due to a decree lest they touch the meat.

items.text: Challenge: Impure slaughter is valid post-facto?
items.text_en: Challenge: Impure slaughter is valid post-facto?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether slaughter by an impure person is even valid post-facto, citing a baraita that derives from 'וְסָמַךְ... וְשָׁחַט' that just as semikhah requires purity, so does slaughter. The Gemara explains that this is a rabbinic decree, and addresses the difficulty by noting that one can use a long knife to avoid entering the courtyard, and that partial entry is considered entry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that slaughter by an impure person is valid post-facto, citing a baraita that derives from the juxtaposition of 'וְסָמַךְ' and 'וְשָׁחַט' that slaughter requires purity just like semikhah.

The Gemara objects that both semikhah and slaughter are associated with 'לִפְנֵי ה׳', so the derivation seems equally strong, but answers that one can use a long knife to slaughter from outside the courtyard, avoiding impurity.

The Gemara resolves that for semikhah, partial entry (inserting only the hand) is considered entry, so the impurity concern remains, distinguishing it from slaughter where a long knife avoids entry entirely.

items.text: Rav Chisda's alternative version
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's alternative version
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda teaches the baraita in reverse: just as slaughter requires purity, so does semikhah. He explains that slaughter requires purity because the verse says 'לִפְנֵי ה׳'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda teaches the baraita in reverse: just as slaughter requires purity, so does leaning, because the verse 'לִפְנֵי ה׳' (before the Lord) is written for slaughter.

items.text: Gemara's objection to partial entry
items.text_en: Gemara's objection to partial entry
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a kohen can perform semikhah or shechitah if partial entry is considered entry, suggesting he can insert his hand or use a long knife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that semikhah and shechitah also require being 'before the Lord,' yet a kohen can perform them by inserting his hand or using a long knife, implying partial entry is not considered entry.

items.text: Attribution to Shimon HaTimni
items.text_en: Attribution to Shimon HaTimni
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the source as Shimon HaTimni, who derives from a verse that the slaughterer must be before the Lord, i.e., inside the courtyard.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the anonymous view as Shimon HaTimni, who derives from the verse that the slaughterer must be before the Lord, i.e., inside the courtyard.

items.text: Ulla's statement in the name of Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Ulla's statement in the name of Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: Ulla says that a tamei person who inserts his hand into the Temple is liable, because the verse equates entry with touch, and partial touch is called touch.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states in the name of Reish Lakish that a tamei person who inserts only his hand into the Temple is liable, because the verse equates entry with touch, and partial touch is called touch.

items.text: Rav Hoshaiah's objection from a metzora
items.text_en: Rav Hoshaiah's objection from a metzora
items.desc_en: Rav Hoshaiah cites a case where a metzora whose eighth day falls on Passover eve and who had a seminal emission is allowed to enter, despite being a tevul yom, because the positive commandment with karet overrides one without karet. Rabbi Yochanan adds that even without a positive commandment, tevul yom is forbidden by Torah law based on a new enactment.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hoshaiah objects to Ulla by citing a case of a metzora (leper) whose eighth day falls on Passover eve, who had a seminal emission and immersed.
The Sages rule that although no other tevul yom (one who immersed that day) may enter, this metzora may enter, because a positive commandment with karet (excision) overrides one without karet.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that by Torah law, even a positive commandment is not involved; rather, tevul yom is forbidden based on a new enactment in the 'new courtyard' (חצר החדשה).

items.text: Gemara's challenge to Ulla
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Ulla
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if partial entry is considered entry, how could the metzora insert his hand? Both the metzora's entry and the partial entry involve a positive commandment with karet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Ulla: if partial entry is considered entry (ביאה במקצת), how can the metzora insert his hand into the Temple, since both the metzora's entry and the partial entry involve a positive commandment with karet (עשה שיש בו כרת)?

items.text: Ulla's answer: metzora is different
items.text_en: Ulla's answer: metzora is different
items.desc_en: Ulla answers that the metzora is different because once he was permitted for his leprosy, he is also permitted for his seminal emission.

sub.desc_en: Ulla answers that the metzora is different because once he was permitted for his leprosy, he is also permitted for his seminal emission.

items.text: Debate about the principle of extension
items.text_en: Debate about the principle of extension
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains Ulla's reasoning: most zavim are also tamei meitim, so once permitted for their impurity, they are permitted for their zivah. Abaye objects that impurity is permitted but zivah is not. Rava argues the opposite: for a metzora, permission is specific, while for impurity, since it is pushed aside, one push is like two.

sub.text: Rav Yosef's explanation of Ulla's reasoning
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's explanation of Ulla's reasoning
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that Ulla holds that most zavim become tamei meitim, so once they are permitted for their impurity, they are also permitted for their zivah.
Abaye objects that the cases are not comparable: impurity was permitted, but zivah was not.
Rav Yosef clarifies that the master (Ulla) meant that most tamei meitim become zavim, and Abaye confirms this interpretation.
Abaye objects again: a metzora is a case of היתירא (permission) where once permitted, all is permitted, but impurity is a case of דחויה (pushed aside), so one push does not extend to another.
Rava argues the opposite: for a metzora, permission is specific, so one permission does not extend to another; but for impurity, since it is pushed aside, one push is like two.

items.text: Gemara's inference from the previous discussion
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the previous discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that both sides of a prior dispute agree that impurity is pushed aside for communal offerings.

items.text: Supporting baraita about semikhah at Nikanor's Gate
items.text_en: Supporting baraita about semikhah at Nikanor's Gate
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that lists all semikhah sites except the one at Nikanor's Gate, because a leper cannot enter until sprinkled with blood. This challenges the view that partial entry is not considered entry.

items.text: Rav Yosef's first answer: the baraita follows Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's first answer: the baraita follows Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef deflects the challenge by identifying the baraita as the opinion of Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda, who holds that the north side of the altar was distanced, so the leper could not approach anyway.

items.text: Objection and Abaye and Rava's response
items.text_en: Objection and Abaye and Rava's response
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: let him make a hole (פִּישְׁפֵּשׁ) to insert his hand? Abaye and Rava answer that the verse 'all in writing from the hand of God' teaches that the Temple structure was fixed and cannot be altered.

items.text: Alternative version: Rav Yosef's reason is that the leper must insert his head and most of his body
items.text_en: Alternative version: Rav Yosef's reason is that the leper must insert his head and most of his body
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav Yosef said any one who performs semikhah must insert his head and most of his body, which is impossible for a leper.

items.text: Gemara's question on the alternative version
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the alternative version
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if both semikhah and 'immediately after semikhah slaughter' are biblical, why not let him enter and perform semikhah?

items.text: Rav Adda bar Matna's two answers
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Matna's two answers
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Matna gives two answers: either a decree lest he take many steps, or that semikhah is biblical but 'immediately after semikhah slaughter' is not biblical.

items.text: Refutation and reversal of the positions
items.text_en: Refutation and reversal of the positions
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought that links semikhah and slaughter to purity, implying that 'immediately after semikhah slaughter' is biblical. The Gemara therefore reverses the positions: semikhah of the leper's asham is not biblical, but 'immediately after semikhah slaughter' is biblical.

items.text: Ravina's statement: the dispute is about lashes
items.text_en: Ravina's statement: the dispute is about lashes
items.desc_en: Ravina says that the dispute between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan regarding touching sacred food while impure was stated in the context of lashes (i.e., whether one is liable to lashes for such contact).

sub.desc_en: Ravina states that the dispute between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan was stated in the context of lashes (מלקות).

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's version: the dispute is about an impure person touching sacred food
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's version: the dispute is about an impure person touching sacred food
items.desc_en: When Ravin came, he reported Rabbi Avahu's statement that the dispute was stated regarding an impure person who touched sacred food. The Gemara then cites the dispute: Resh Lakish says he is lashed, citing the verse "בכל קדש לא תגע"; Rabbi Yochanan says he is not lashed, arguing that verse is written about terumah.

sub.text: Gemara's report of Rabbi Avahu's statement
sub.text_en: Gemara's report of Rabbi Avahu's statement
sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that when Ravin came, he cited Rabbi Avahu's statement that the dispute was stated regarding an impure person who touched sacred food.
The Gemara cites the dispute: Resh Lakish says the impure person who touched sacred food is lashed, while Rabbi Yochanan says he is not lashed.
Resh Lakish argues that the verse 'בכל קדש לא תגע' (Do not touch any sacred food) serves as a negative commandment that warrants lashes for touching sacred food while impure.
Rabbi Yochanan counters that the verse 'בכל קדש לא תגע' is written about תרומה (the priestly portion), not about sacred food in general, so it does not apply here.

items.text: Gemara's question: the verse is needed for the eater
items.text_en: Gemara's question: the verse is needed for the eater
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Resh Lakish's position: the verse "בכל קדש לא תגע" is needed to derive a warning for one who eats sacred meat while impure, as stated in a separate dispute between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Resh Lakish: the verse 'בכל קדש לא תגע' is needed to derive a warning for one who eats sacred meat while impure, so how can he use it for the case of touching?
Resh Lakish responds that the same verse indeed serves as the warning for the eater, citing the established dispute where he derives the warning for the eater from this verse.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's alternative derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's alternative derivation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites a baraita of Bardela that derives the warning for the eater via a verbal analogy (גזירה שוה) of "טומאתו" from entry into the Temple, and explains that the verse's language of "touching" is used for the impure person who touches sacred food, while the warning for the eater comes from the juxtaposition of קדש to מקדש.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites a baraita of Bardela that derives the warning for the eater via a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) of 'טומאתו' from entry into the Temple, establishing that just as there is punishment and warning there, so too here.

Rabbi Yochanan explains that the verse's language of 'touching' is used for the impure person who touches sacred food, while the warning for the eater comes from the juxtaposition (היקש) of קדש (sacred food) to מקדש (the Temple).

items.text: Baraita supporting Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Resh Lakish: it states that the verse "בכל קדש לא תגע" is a warning for the eater, and then questions whether it might be for the toucher. It concludes by juxtaposing קדש to מקדש, showing that just as entry into the Temple involves something that has... (the text is cut off).

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited supporting Resh Lakish: it states that the verse 'בכל קדש לא תגע' is a warning for the eater, and then questions whether it might be for the toucher.
The baraita resolves the question by juxtaposing קדש (sacred food) to מקדש (the Temple), showing that just as entry into the Temple involves something that has... (the text is cut off).

items.text: Gemara's initial analysis of the verse
items.text_en: Gemara's initial analysis of the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse 'al kol kodesh lo tigga' refers to eating, not touching, because touching does not involve 'taking of life' (netilat neshamah). It then raises the question of a tamei person eating kodashim before zerikah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the verse 'al kol kodesh lo tigga' must refer to eating, not touching, because touching does not involve נטילת נשמה (taking of life).

items.text: Dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on tamei eating before zerikah
items.text_en: Dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on tamei eating before zerikah
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish holds that a tamei who eats kodashim before zerikah is liable to lashes, deriving from 'bechol kodesh lo tigga'. Rabbi Yochanan disagrees, citing a gezeirah shavah from 'tum'ato' that the prohibition applies only after zerikah. The Gemara notes that the extra word 'bechol' teaches two things.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the verse 'bechol kodesh lo tigga' applies to a tamei who eats kodashim before zerikah.
The Gemara introduces the dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan regarding a tamei who eats kodashim before zerikah.
Reish Lakish holds that the prohibition applies both before and after zerikah, so the tamei is liable to lashes.
Rabbi Yochanan holds that the prohibition applies only after zerikah, based on a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from 'tum'ato' as taught by Bardela.
The Gemara resolves that the extra word 'בכל' in the verse teaches two things: the prohibition for a tamei before zerikah and the general prohibition.

items.text: Abaye's distinction: tum'at haguf vs. tum'at basar
items.text_en: Abaye's distinction: tum'at haguf vs. tum'at basar
items.desc_en: Abaye states that the dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan applies only to tum'at haguf (impurity of the person). Regarding tum'at basar (impurity of the meat), all agree that one is liable to lashes.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan by distinguishing between טומאת הגוף (impurity of the person) and טומאת בשר (impurity of the meat), ruling that all agree one is liable to lashes for the latter.

items.text: Proof from the verse 'vehabasar'
items.text_en: Proof from the verse 'vehabasar'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'vehabasar' which includes even non-edible items like wood and frankincense, supporting that tum'at basar is punishable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'וְהַבָּשָׂר' (and the flesh) to include non-edible items like wood and frankincense, proving that tum'at basar (impurity of the flesh) is punishable even for inedible items.

items.text: Rava's opposing view and resolution
items.text_en: Rava's opposing view and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava argues that in tum'at basar, all agree one is not lashed because the verse 'vetum'ato alav venichretah' does not apply. The Gemara objects citing the inclusion of wood and frankincense, and resolves that the case is where items were sanctified in a vessel, which is like their matirim have been offered.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that the dispute between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan is only regarding tum'at ha-guf (impurity of the body), but regarding tum'at basar (impurity of the meat), all agree one is not lashed, because the verse 'vetum'ato alav venichretah' does not apply.
The Gemara objects: but the Master (the Tanna of the Mishnah) said that the verse 'והבשר' (and the meat) includes wood and frankincense, implying that tum'at basar does carry liability.
The Gemara resolves: here we are dealing with a case where the wood and frankincense were sanctified in a vessel, which is like their matirim (permitters) have been offered, so the verse applies.

items.text: New dispute: offering limbs of a non-kosher animal on the altar
items.text_en: New dispute: offering limbs of a non-kosher animal on the altar
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan dispute whether one who offers limbs of a non-kosher animal (behemah teme'ah) on the altar is liable to lashes. Reish Lakish says yes, deriving from a lav haba miklal aseh; Rabbi Yochanan says no.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan regarding one who offers limbs of a non-kosher animal (בהמה טמאה) on the altar: Reish Lakish holds he is liable to lashes, Rabbi Yochanan holds he is not.

Reish Lakish derives the prohibition from the positive command 'a clean animal you may offer' (טהורה אין, טמאה לא), making it a לאו הבא מכלל עשה (a prohibition derived from a positive command), for which one is liable to lashes.
Rabbi Yochanan argues that a לאו הבא מכלל עשה (prohibition derived from a positive command) does not carry lashes.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeyah's objection from the verse 'otah tochelu'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeyah's objection from the verse 'otah tochelu'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeyah objects that the verse 'otah tochelu' excludes non-kosher animals, and a lav haba miklal aseh is a positive command, not a prohibition.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeyah objects that the verse 'אֹתָהּ תֹּאכֵלוּ' (it you shall eat) excludes non-kosher animals, and a לאו הבא מכלל עשה (a prohibition derived from a positive command) is a positive command, not a prohibition.

items.text: Rabbi Yaakov's clarification: dispute is about chayah, not behemah teme'ah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov's clarification: dispute is about chayah, not behemah teme'ah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov explains that the dispute is actually about offering limbs of a chayah (non-domesticated kosher animal), not a behemah teme'ah. Rabbi Yochanan says one violates a positive command; Reish Lakish says one violates nothing at all.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov to Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Tachlifa
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov to Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Tachlifa
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov tells Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Tachlifa that the dispute is not about limbs of a behemah teme'ah (non-kosher domestic animal), but about a chayah (non-domesticated kosher animal).
The gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan says one violates a positive command (עשה), while Reish Lakish says one violates nothing at all.

The gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan derives the positive command from the exclusion of chayah from the verse about behemah, while Reish Lakish holds that the verse about chayah is merely a mitzvah (advisory command) with no punitive consequence.

items.text: Rava's objection and the baraita excluding chayah from sacrifice
items.text_en: Rava's objection and the baraita excluding chayah from sacrifice
items.desc_en: Rava objects that the verse 'bakar vatzon' excludes chayah from being offered. The baraita explains that if one brings chayah, it is invalid, and the verse teaches that only bakar vatzon are acceptable, not chayah.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that if the verse had said 'קרבן לה׳ בהמה', one might think chayah is included, but the verse 'בקר וצאן' excludes chayah.
The baraita raises the possibility that if one brings chayah, it might be valid, comparing it to a student who adds to his master's request.
The baraita concludes that the verse 'בקר וצאן' explicitly excludes chayah, comparing it to a student who violates his master's instruction by adding forbidden items.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous refutation
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous refutation
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the refutation of Reish Lakish's earlier position stands, as it is a conclusive refutation.

items.text: Reish Lakish's question about a disqualified person making shirayim
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's question about a disqualified person making shirayim
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan whether a disqualified person who received blood can make the remaining blood into shirayim. Rabbi Yochanan answers that only one who is piggul (outside its time) or outside its place can make shirayim, because they effect acceptance for piggul.

items.text: Rav Zevid's version: Question about a disqualified cup
items.text_en: Rav Zevid's version: Question about a disqualified cup
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid teaches that Reish Lakish asked Rabbi Yochanan about a disqualified cup of blood: can it make its fellow cup shirayim? Rabbi Yochanan responds that the status of the cup depends on whether a disqualified person can make shirayim.

items.text: Rav Yirmiyah from Difti's version: Question about a cup making its fellow dachui or shirayim
items.text_en: Rav Yirmiyah from Difti's version: Question about a cup making its fellow dachui or shirayim
items.desc_en: Rav Yirmiyah from Difti teaches that Abaye asked Rabbah whether a cup of blood can make its fellow cup dachui or shirayim. Rabbah explains that this is a dispute between Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon and the Rabbis, based on a baraita about the verses for the blood of a sin-offering. Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon holds that all blood from multiple cups is poured onto the foundation, while the Rabbis distinguish between the cup from which the sprinkling was done and the others. Rav Ashi clarifies that the verse 've'et damo' excludes the shirayim in the animal's neck.

items.text: The necessity of listing all disqualifications
items.text_en: The necessity of listing all disqualifications
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah needed to list all three cases (disqualified person, left hand, ordinary vessels) separately, as each teaches a unique point that would not be derived from the others.

items.text: The principle that what is in one's hand is not dachui
items.text_en: The principle that what is in one's hand is not dachui
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the disqualified cup does not become dachui. Ravina quotes Rav Yirmiyah from Difti in the name of Rava that the Mishnah follows Chanan the Egyptian, who holds that there is no concept of dachui. Rav Ashi states a general principle: anything still in one's hand is not considered dachui. Rav Shayya supports Rav Ashi, citing Rabbi Yehuda who holds that dachui exists but agrees that what is in one's hand is not dachui, as shown by a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda allows mixing blood from multiple cups.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda on the cup of mixture
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda on the cup of mixture
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita itself: Rabbi Yehuda says one cup is filled from the mixture of bloods, so that if one cup is spilled, the mixture renders it fit. The Rabbis object that they don't know which cup was not received in a vessel, but Rabbi Yehuda responds.

items.text: Gemara's response to previous objection about blood of tamtzit
items.text_en: Gemara's response to previous objection about blood of tamtzit
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier statement about priests knowing when blood is fully received applies only when it was received in a vessel, and priests are diligent to do it properly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the earlier statement about priests knowing when blood is fully received applies only when it was received in a vessel, and priests are diligent to do it properly.

items.text: Objection: blood of tamtzit is mixed in
items.text_en: Objection: blood of tamtzit is mixed in
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the blood of tamtzit (residual blood) is mixed with the sacrificial blood, and explains that Rabbi Yehuda follows his own reasoning that tamtzit blood is called blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the blood of tamtzit (residual blood) is mixed in, and explains that Rabbi Yehuda follows his own reasoning that tamtzit blood is called blood.

items.text: Baraita on tamtzit blood and Rabbi Elazar's qualification
items.text_en: Baraita on tamtzit blood and Rabbi Elazar's qualification
items.desc_en: A baraita states that tamtzit blood is subject to a prohibition, with Rabbi Yehuda adding it is subject to karet. Rabbi Elazar notes that Rabbi Yehuda agrees tamtzit blood does not effect atonement, as only blood that carries the soul is called blood.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that tamtzit blood is subject to a prohibition (אזהרה), and Rabbi Yehuda adds it is subject to karet (כרת).
The Gemara objects by citing Rabbi Elazar's statement that Rabbi Yehuda concedes tamtzit blood does not effect atonement (כפרה), since only blood that carries the soul is called blood.

items.text: Alternative explanation: blood does not nullify blood
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: blood does not nullify blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another explanation: Rabbi Yehuda holds that blood does not nullify blood, so the tamtzit blood does not affect the sacrificial blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by stating that Rabbi Yehuda holds the principle that blood does not nullify blood, so the tamtzit blood does not affect the sacrificial blood.

items.text: Dispute about priests walking in blood and the issue of interposition
items.text_en: Dispute about priests walking in blood and the issue of interposition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda asks why the courtyard is dammed if blood is not a problem; the Sages say it is praiseworthy for priests to walk in blood up to their knees. The Gemara questions whether blood constitutes an interposition (chatzitzah), and answers that moist blood does not interpose, citing a baraita.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda's question to the Sages
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's question to the Sages
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda asks the Sages: according to your view, why is the courtyard dammed up (to prevent blood from flowing out)?
The Sages answer that it is praiseworthy for the priests to walk in blood up to their knees.
The Gemara objects: blood on the priests' legs constitutes an interposition (חציצה) that would invalidate their service.
The Gemara answers that moist blood does not interpose, citing a baraita that dry liquids interpose but moist ones do not.

items.text: Issue of garments becoming soiled and the solution of carrying on beams
items.text_en: Issue of garments becoming soiled and the solution of carrying on beams
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises that garments become soiled, which would invalidate service, and considers whether they lift them; but the Torah requires the measure not to be lacking or excessive. The Gemara resolves that this applies to carrying limbs to the ramp, which is not a service, or carrying wood to the pyre; for actual service they walk on beams.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the priests' garments become soiled with blood, which would invalidate the service according to the Mishnah.
