The Gemara rejects the possible solution of lifting the garments, citing the requirement that the priestly garments must fit exactly without excess or deficiency.
The Gemara answers that the concern applies only to carrying limbs to the ramp, which is not a service requiring priestly garments.
The Gemara objects that a baraita explicitly calls carrying limbs to the ramp a service.
The Gemara revises its answer, saying the concern applies to carrying wood to the pyre, which is not a service.
The Gemara resolves that for actual service, the priests walk on beams to avoid soiling their garments.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of piggul regarding unusual items and parts
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of piggul regarding unusual items and parts
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one slaughters a sacrifice intending to eat or burn something not normally eaten or burned, it is valid, but Rabbi Eliezer invalidates. It details cases of less than an olive's bulk, combining half-olives, and eating parts like skin, bones, etc., which do not incur piggul. It also covers slaughtering for a fetus or placenta outside, and molesting birds for eggs.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule: one who slaughters a sacrifice intending to eat or burn something not normally eaten or burned — the offering is valid, but Rabbi Eliezer invalidates it.
The Mishnah continues: if one intends to eat or burn a normal item but less than an olive-bulk, it is valid; half an olive for eating and half for burning do not combine.

The Mishnah rules: one who slaughters intending to eat an olive-bulk from hide, gravy, spices, tendons, bones, horns, or hooves outside the proper time or place — the offering is valid, and no liability for piggul, notar, or tum'ah applies.
The Mishnah states: one who slaughters consecrated animals to eat the fetus or placenta outside, or who pinches doves to eat their eggs outside, has not rendered the offering piggul.
The Mishnah concludes: milk of consecrated animals and eggs of doves incur no liability for piggul, notar, or tum'ah.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Elazar's distinctions on piggul and supporting baraita
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Elazar's distinctions on piggul and supporting baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that piggul in the sacrifice affects the fetus, but not vice versa; similarly for the maw and crop, and for the sacrificial portions and the bulls. The Gemara attempts to support this from a baraita about bulls, but concludes the baraita does not necessarily support him.

sub.desc_en: רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar) states that piggul in the sacrifice renders the fetus piggul, but not vice versa; similarly for the maw and the crop.
רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar) adds that piggul in the sacrificial portions renders the bulls piggul, but not vice versa.
The Gemara suggests that a baraita supports Rabbi Elazar, as it states that if one intended to eat or burn the bulls, it is ineffective.
The Gemara infers that the baraita implies that if one intended regarding the sacrificial portions, the bulls are rendered piggul.
The Gemara rejects the inference, concluding that the baraita does not necessarily support Rabbi Elazar.

items.text: Initial question on piggul in eimurim
items.text_en: Initial question on piggul in eimurim
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether improper intent (chishshev) regarding eimurim causes piggul only in the eimurim themselves, not the entire offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether improper intent (חישב) regarding the eimurim causes piggul only in the eimurim themselves, not the entire offering.

items.text: Proof from parim hanisrafim and distinction between meat and eimurim
items.text_en: Proof from parim hanisrafim and distinction between meat and eimurim
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about parim hanisrafim to argue that disqualification by linah applies to meat, implying machshavah also applies. It then distinguishes between linat basar and linat eimurim, showing the baraita's first clause refers to eimurim and the latter to meat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about parim hanisrafim (burned bulls) and se'irim hanisrafim (burned goats) that become subject to disqualification by טבול יום (one who immersed that day), מחוסר כיפורים (one lacking atonement), and לינה (overnight stay) after slaughter.

The Gemara asks whether the baraita refers to לינת בשר (overnight stay of the meat), and if so, can we infer that since לינה disqualifies, so too מחשבה (improper intention) disqualifies these offerings.

The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that the baraita's first clause refers to לינת אימורים (overnight stay of the sacrificial parts), not meat; the later clause about the ash-pit deals with meat, so the two clauses are distinct.

items.text: Baraita on items that do not cause or become piggul
items.text_en: Baraita on items that do not cause or become piggul
items.desc_en: Rabbah cites a baraita listing items like wool, hair, skin, and fetal parts that neither cause piggul nor become piggul. The Gemara debates whether this means they do not affect the sacrifice or themselves, and explains the redundancy in the baraita as due to the need to list related laws.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah cites a baraita listing items that neither cause piggul nor become piggul.
The baraita states that these items are not subject to piggul, leftover, or impurity laws, and one who offers them outside is exempt.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita means these items do not cause piggul in the sacrifice and do not become piggul from the sacrifice.
The Gemara answers that the baraita means these items do not cause piggul in the sacrifice and do not become piggul on their own account.
The Gemara objects that if so, the baraita's repetition of 'all do not cause piggul and do not become piggul' is redundant.

The Gemara rejects the objection by noting that the same redundancy exists for the phrase 'no liability for piggul,' which is included only because the baraita needed to list leftover and impurity laws.
The Gemara resolves that here too, the phrase 'all do not cause piggul and do not become piggul' is included because the baraita needed to list the law of one who offers them outside.

items.text: Proof from mishnah on shochet for shalil and shilya
items.text_en: Proof from mishnah on shochet for shalil and shilya
items.desc_en: Rava brings a mishnah where slaughtering for fetal parts outside does not cause piggul, but the baraita implies liability for shalil and shilya. This proves the distinction: one clause refers to piggul from the sacrifice, the other from the items themselves.

sub.desc_en: Rava introduces a mishnah about slaughtering consecrated animals to eat the fetal parts (שליל or שיליא) outside, which does not cause piggul.

sub.text: Rava's citation of the mishnah's continuation
sub.text_en: Rava's citation of the mishnah's continuation
sub.desc_en: Rava notes that the mishnah then states that for חלב (sacred fat) and bird eggs one is exempt from piggul, implying that for שליל and שיליא one is liable.
The Gemara concludes that the distinction is proven: one clause deals with piggul from the sacrifice, the other from the items themselves.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva on blemished offerings and the case of a female olah
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva on blemished offerings and the case of a female olah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports Rabbi Yochanan's teaching that Rabbi Akiva permits only certain eye blemishes in offerings if the blemish preceded sanctification. Rabbi Zeira challenges this with a baraita about liability for offering such items outside, and the Gemara resolves it by distinguishing between the items themselves and their eimurim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah that discusses blemished offerings, where Rabbi Akiva permits them.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports that Rabbi Yochanan limited Rabbi Akiva's permission to eye blemishes that are valid in birds, and only when consecration preceded the blemish.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba adds that Rabbi Akiva concedes regarding a female burnt offering, treating it as if the blemish preceded consecration.
Rabbi Zeira objects by citing a baraita that exempts one who offers such items outside, implying liability for the mother's flesh, which he identifies as a female burnt offering.
Rabbi Zeira argues that the baraita only aligns with Rabbi Akiva if he holds that a female burnt offering does not descend from the altar; otherwise, it is unattributed.
The Gemara suggests that the baraita refers to sacrificial portions of the mother, not the flesh itself.

The Gemara rejects the first answer because the baraita says 'from them,' implying the flesh; it then revises to say the baraita exempts one who offers their sacrificial portions outside, but one who offers the mother's sacrificial portions is liable.

items.text: Mishnah on intent to leave blood or eimurim for tomorrow
items.text_en: Mishnah on intent to leave blood or eimurim for tomorrow
items.desc_en: The mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages regarding slaughter with intent to leave blood or eimurim for the next day or take them outside, and lists other invalid intentions.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages regarding slaughter with intent to leave blood or eimurim for the next day or take them outside, and lists other invalid intentions.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that such intent renders the offering unfit.
The Sages rule that such intent does not disqualify the offering.

The Mishnah lists additional intentions that render the offering unfit, such as placing blood on the ramp or not opposite the base, or placing blood designated for above the red line below it, and vice versa.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists several cases where improper intent does not disqualify a sacrifice, concluding that only intent regarding time (chutz lizmano) or place (chutz limkomo) or improper designation (shelo lishman) for Pesach and Chatat disqualifies.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rabbi Elazar's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rabbi Elazar's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning? Rabbi Elazar answers that two verses about notar (leftover) imply that intent to leave over (machshevet hinuch) disqualifies, as one verse is superfluous for the prohibition of leaving and is applied to disqualifying intent.

items.text: Objection and defense of Rabbi Yehuda's derivation
items.text_en: Objection and defense of Rabbi Yehuda's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the second verse is needed to teach the time limit for eating various sacrifices (todah, etc.). It then shows that the verse is still superfluous for that purpose, so it can be used for machshevet hinuch.

items.text: Challenge: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning is actually a sevara
items.text_en: Challenge: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning is actually a sevara
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning is not from a verse but from a logical argument (sevara): just as actually leaving the meat until the next day disqualifies, so too intent to leave disqualifies. The Gemara then asks why he doesn't apply this to all cases in the Mishnah.

items.text: Answer: Distinction between cases
items.text_en: Answer: Distinction between cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehuda does not dispute the cases of breaking bones or eating raw because those do not disqualify the sacrifice itself. Similarly, intent that impure or uncircumcised people eat does not disqualify the sacrifice. An alternative version says all such cases are within his dispute.

items.text: Explanation of other Mishnah cases
items.text_en: Explanation of other Mishnah cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda's positions on mixing blood with invalid blood and on giving blood in the wrong place follow his own established views: blood does not nullify blood, and 'not in its place' is still considered 'its place' for disqualification.

items.text: Discussion of Rabbi Yehuda's requirement for a 'triangular' place
items.text_en: Discussion of Rabbi Yehuda's requirement for a 'triangular' place
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehuda doesn't dispute the cases of giving inner blood outside or outer blood inside. It answers that he requires a place that is 'triangular' (involving blood, meat, and fats). A challenge from a baraita about a Chatat slaughtered in the south or its blood brought inside is resolved by positing two Tannaitic versions of Rabbi Yehuda's view.

items.text: Incomplete continuation
items.text_en: Incomplete continuation
items.desc_en: The daf ends mid-sentence with the beginning of a statement about Rabbi Yehuda's view on a Chatat slaughtered in the south.

items.text: Derivation that all blood requires יסוד
items.text_en: Derivation that all blood requires יסוד
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that all sacrificial blood requires application to the altar's base. It cites Rabbi's teaching that the extra word 'בדם' in the verse 'והנשאר בדם ימצה' teaches that all blood, not just those with four applications, requires יסוד.

items.text: Objection: verse needed for pouring instead of sprinkling
items.text_en: Objection: verse needed for pouring instead of sprinkling
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse 'ודם זבחיך ישפך' is needed for a different teaching: that blood which should be sprinkled is valid if poured, following Rabbi Akiva's view that pouring and sprinkling are distinct categories.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Akiva's view from Mishnah
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Akiva's view from Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Akiva rules that the blessing for the Passover sacrifice does not exempt the blessing for other sacrifices, and vice versa, demonstrating that pouring and sprinkling are not interchangeable.

items.text: Alternative derivation for bechor, maaser, and pesach
items.text_en: Alternative derivation for bechor, maaser, and pesach
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another objection: the verse is needed to teach that bechor, maaser, and pesach require blood and limbs on the altar, following Rabbi Yose HaGlili's derivation from the plural forms 'דמם' and 'חלבם'.

items.text: Reconciliation of conflicting tannaitic views
items.text_en: Reconciliation of conflicting tannaitic views
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that there are two tannaim who interpret the verse according to Rabbi Yishmael's method. It then questions how Rabbi Yose HaGlili explains the phrase 'ובשרם יהיה לך' if maaser and pesach are eaten by owners, and answers that it refers to both unblemished and blemished animals.

items.text: Distinction between the two verses regarding the Sukkah
items.text_en: Distinction between the two verses regarding the Sukkah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that in the case of the Sukkah, one verse is for the requirement itself and another for the requirement of shade, and the halakhah came and reduced the requirement to a tefach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that regarding the Sukkah, one verse is for the requirement itself and another for shade, and the halakhah (הלכה) reduced the requirement to a tefach (טפח).

items.text: Challenge from the verse "ve'tame'ah shvu'ayim"
items.text_en: Challenge from the verse "ve'tame'ah shvu'ayim"
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if we apply the same logic to the verse "ve'tame'ah shvu'ayim" which is read as "shiv'im" (seventy), then a woman would have to sit forty-two days! The Gemara deflects by noting that there it is written "keniddatah".

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if the same logic of reading the written form (כתיב) against the oral tradition (מסורת) applies to the verse 'וְטָמְאָה שְׁבֻעַיִם' (she shall be impure two weeks), which is read as 'שִׁבְעִים' (seventy), then a woman would have to sit forty-two days of impurity.
The Gemara deflects the challenge by noting that there it is different, because the verse writes 'כְּנִדָּתָהּ' (like her menstrual impurity), which limits the duration.

items.text: Derivation from "vechipper" three times
items.text_en: Derivation from "vechipper" three times
items.desc_en: The Tanna cites the verse "vechipper" repeated three times to teach that even one application of blood on the outer altar atones, countering a logical argument that would require four applications like the inner altar or like the outer sin-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna cites the threefold repetition of 'וְכִפֶּר' (and he shall atone) to counter a logical argument.
The Gemara proposes a logical analogy: just as one application of blood below (on the outer altar) atones, so too one application above (on the inner altar) should atone.
The Gemara raises a counter-analogy: just as missing one application of blood inside (the inner altar) invalidates the atonement, so too missing one application outside should invalidate it.
The Gemara resolves the conflict by preferring the analogy of outer to outer (outer sin-offering with four horns) over outer to inner, and then cites the verse to override even that analogy.
The Tanna concludes from the threefold 'וְכִפֶּר' that even one application of blood on the outer altar atones, overriding both logical arguments.

items.text: Rava's explanation: "vechipper" is needed for its own meaning
items.text_en: Rava's explanation: "vechipper" is needed for its own meaning
items.desc_en: Rava, citing Bar Adda Mari, explains that the verse "vechipper... venislach" teaches that atonement and forgiveness are the same, so the threefold repetition is not superfluous for the derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the threefold 'vechipper' is needed for its own meaning, not for the derivation.
Rava, citing Bar Adda Mari, explains that the verse 'vechipper... venislach' teaches that atonement and forgiveness are identical, so the threefold repetition is not superfluous for the derivation.

items.text: Challenge: possible distributions of blood between upper and lower
items.text_en: Challenge: possible distributions of blood between upper and lower
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that "vechipper" might allow various distributions of blood between upper and lower parts of the altar. Rav Adda bar Yitzchak objects that this would nullify the law of four corners, but the Gemara retorts that if God says so, let them be nullified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the threefold 'וְכִפֶּר' (and he shall atone) might allow distributing the blood applications between the upper and lower parts of the altar in various combinations, even all below.
Rav Adda bar Yitzchak objects that this would nullify the law requiring four corners (קרנות) of the altar.
The Gemara retorts that if the Merciful One says to nullify the law of four corners, then let them be nullified.

items.text: Rava's clarification and further challenge
items.text_en: Rava's clarification and further challenge
items.desc_en: Rava clarifies that the three applications refer specifically to the corners. The Gemara then challenges that perhaps one application above and three below suffice, but the Gemara responds that we never find blood half above and half below. The Gemara counters with the case of the Yom Kippur service where one sprinkling is above and seven below, and explains that it is like a whip.

sub.desc_en: Rava clarifies that the three applications of blood required by the Torah refer specifically to the four corners of the outer altar.
The Gemara challenges that perhaps the three applications could be distributed as one above and three below on the altar.
The Gemara rejects the challenge by stating that we never find a case where blood is applied half above and half below on the same altar.
The Gemara counters by citing the Yom Kippur service where one sprinkling is above and seven below on the inner altar.

The Gemara resolves that the Yom Kippur sprinkling is like a whip (מצליף), where the single upward stroke is part of the same motion as the seven downward strokes, not a separate distribution of blood.

items.text: Mishnah citation: sprinkling on the pure part of the altar
items.text_en: Mishnah citation: sprinkling on the pure part of the altar
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that one sprinkles on the pure part of the altar seven times, which serves as a proof or illustration.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited as a proof that one sprinkles seven times on the pure part of the altar.

items.text: Interpretation of 'clear' and the issue of remaining blood
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'clear' and the issue of remaining blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether 'clear' refers to the middle of the altar, as people say 'the clear of the day'. Rava bar Sheila answers that it refers to the sky, as in the verse 'like the clear sky'. The Gemara then raises the issue of the remaining blood (שִׁירַיִם), but concludes that the remaining blood does not impede, and the internal remaining blood is discussed in one place.

items.text: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on placements
items.text_en: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on placements
items.desc_en: A Tannaic source states that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says Beit Shammai holds that two placements in the sin-offering and one in all other offerings permit and disqualify, while Beit Hillel holds that one in the sin-offering and one in all other offerings permit and disqualify. Rav Oshaya objects that this should be listed among the leniencies of Beit Shammai and stringencies of Beit Hillel. Rava answers that the question was asked regarding permission, and Beit Shammai were stringent.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on three placements of sin-offerings
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on three placements of sin-offerings
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the three placements of sin-offerings are not brought at night, are brought after the death of the owner, and one who offers them outside is liable. Rav Pappa then elaborates that some aspects are like their beginning and some like their end: outside, night, foreign worship, service vessels, horn, finger, laundering, and remaining blood are like their beginning; while brought after death does not permit, does not disqualify, and does not enter inside – these are like their end.

items.text: Rav Pappa's proof and discussion of laundering
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's proof and discussion of laundering
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa brings a proof from a Mishnah: blood that splattered from the neck onto a garment does not require laundering, but blood from the horn or foundation does not require laundering, implying that blood fit for the horn does require laundering. The Gemara objects that the same logic would apply to the foundation, but the verse 'which shall be sprinkled' excludes that which has already been sprinkled. The Gemara identifies this as the view of Rabbi Nechemya, who holds that one who offers the remaining blood outside is liable. The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Nechemya's view extends to laundering, and concludes that it does.

items.text: Baraita on blood requiring base vs. poured into channel
items.text_en: Baraita on blood requiring base vs. poured into channel
items.desc_en: A baraita distinguishes between blood that requires a base (יסוד) and blood poured into the channel (אמה). The former requires laundering, is affected by improper intent, and one who offers it outside is liable; the latter does not require laundering, is not affected by improper intent, and one who offers it outside is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The baraita distinguishes between blood requiring a base (יסוד) and blood poured into the channel (אמה), listing their differing halachic consequences.

items.text: Identifying the authority as Rabbi Nehemya
items.text_en: Identifying the authority as Rabbi Nehemya
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies that the one who holds that offering such blood outside is liable is Rabbi Nehemya, and he also holds that it requires laundering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies that the authority who holds that offering such blood outside is liable is Rabbi Nehemya, and he also holds that it requires laundering.

items.text: Contradiction regarding improper intent
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding improper intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the baraita says improper intent is effective for these bloods, but another baraita excludes remnants and burning of sacrificial portions from the effect of improper intent. The resolution is that the latter baraita refers to the three blood applications of a sin-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the baraita says improper intent (מחשבה) is effective for these bloods, but another baraita excludes remnants (שיריים) and burning of sacrificial portions (הקטרת אימורין) from the effect of improper intent.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the latter baraita refers specifically to the three blood applications of a sin-offering (שלוש מתנות שבחטאת).

items.text: Objection and reinterpretation of 'require base'
items.text_en: Objection and reinterpretation of 'require base'
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if it refers to the three applications, they go to the horn, not the base. It reinterprets 'require base' as 'require a base' (i.e., they are poured at the base). Regarding improper intent, the Gemara notes that these bloods are not fit for piggul or entering the inner sanctuary, so intent is ineffective as in their final state.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the baraita refers to the three applications of the חטאת (sin-offering), they require the horn, not the base, so how can it say they require a base?
The Gemara reinterprets the baraita: it does not mean the blood is placed on the base, but that it requires a base (i.e., the leftover blood is poured at the base).
The Gemara objects: how can improper intent (מחשבה) be effective for these bloods, given the baraita that says intent is ineffective for leftover bloods and burning of fats?
The Gemara resolves: these bloods are not fit for piggul (פגול) or entering the inner sanctuary, so intent is ineffective, just as in their final state (after the blood is poured at the base).

items.text: Alternative resolution: referring to inner bloods
items.text_en: Alternative resolution: referring to inner bloods
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: the baraita about improper intent refers to inner bloods (those brought inside the Sanctuary).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by asserting that the baraita about improper intent refers specifically to inner bloods (those brought inside the Sanctuary), not to outer bloods.

items.text: Challenge and identification of the baraita's author
items.text_en: Challenge and identification of the baraita's author
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if so, for outer bloods one would be exempt, but the baraita should have distinguished within its own case. It answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Nehemya, who holds that offering leftover blood outside is liable, and the baraita did not want to list three exemptions alongside three liabilities.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if the baraita refers to inner bloods, then for outer bloods one would be exempt, so why didn't the baraita distinguish within its own case?
The Gemara answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Nehemya, who holds that offering leftover blood outside is liable, and the baraita did not want to list three exemptions alongside three liabilities.

items.text: Ravina's distinction and Rav Tachlifa's objection
items.text_en: Ravina's distinction and Rav Tachlifa's objection
items.desc_en: Ravina explains: 'from the horn' means literally from the horn, 'from the base' means from what is fit for the base. Rav Tachlifa bar Gaza objects: if 'from the horn' excludes what is fit for the horn, then 'from the base' should also exclude what is fit for the base. Ravina revises: 'from the horn' means literally from the horn, 'from the base' means from what is fit for the base.

sub.desc_en: Ravina explains that 'from the horn' means literally from the horn, while 'from the base' means from what is fit for the base.
Rav Tachlifa bar Gaza objects: if 'from the horn' excludes what is fit for the horn, then 'from the base' should also exclude what is fit for the base.
Ravina revises: 'from the horn' means literally from the horn, 'from the base' means from what is fit for the base.

items.text: Derivation regarding inner altar blood applications
items.text_en: Derivation regarding inner altar blood applications
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: from the verse 'and he shall do as he did' we learn to repeat the sprinkling, and that if any application is missing the atonement is invalid. This applies to seven applications; four applications are derived from 'thus he shall do'. The baraita continues with 'for the bull' referring to the Yom Kippur bull.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'וְעָשָׂה כַּאֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה' (and he shall do as he did) and asks what it comes to teach.
The baraita answers that the verse comes to repeat the sprinkling, teaching that if any application is missing, the priest has done nothing.
The baraita asks: from where do we derive that the four applications on the inner altar are also indispensable?
The baraita answers that the verse 'כֵּן יַעֲשֶׂה' (so shall he do) teaches that the four applications are also indispensable.
The baraita concludes by interpreting 'לַפָּר' (for the bull) as referring to the bull of Yom Kippur.

items.text: Derivation of included sin-offerings
items.text_en: Derivation of included sin-offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'as he did for the bull' to refer to the bull of the anointed priest, and 'the sin-offering' to include the goats for idolatry. It then questions whether this also includes the goats of festivals and new moons, and concludes with 'lo' to exclude them, based on the principle that these latter goats do not atone for a known transgression of a commandment.

items.text: Dispensation for lack of laying of hands and remainder of blood
items.text_en: Dispensation for lack of laying of hands and remainder of blood
items.desc_en: The verse 'and he shall atone' teaches that atonement is achieved even if the owner did not lay hands on the offering. Similarly, 'and it shall be forgiven' teaches that forgiveness is granted even if the priest did not pour out the remainder of the blood at the base of the altar.

items.text: Distinction between sprinkling and other rites
items.text_en: Distinction between sprinkling and other rites
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why sprinkling is indispensable while laying of hands and the remainder of the blood are not. It answers that sprinkling is required everywhere (in all sin-offerings), whereas laying of hands and the remainder of the blood are not required everywhere.

items.text: Opening question about the source of four applications
items.text_en: Opening question about the source of four applications
items.desc_en: Mar states that only the seven applications are indispensable everywhere, and Rav Pappa specifies that this refers to the red heifer and leprosy. The Gemara then asks: from where do we derive the four applications?

sub.desc_en: Mar states that only the seven applications are indispensable everywhere.
The Gemara asks: to which contexts does this apply?
Rav Pappa answers that it refers to the red heifer and leprosy.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: why not derive four from the same verse?
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: why not derive four from the same verse?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: just as the seven applications are written and repeated, so too are the four applications written and repeated, so why is a separate verse needed?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: since the four applications are also written and repeated in the verse, why is a separate verse 'כֵּן יַעֲשֶׂה' needed to teach them?

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's answer: needed for Rabbi Shimon's view
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's answer: needed for Rabbi Shimon's view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya explains that the verse is only necessary according to Rabbi Shimon, who derives four applications from the word 'keren' and 'karnot' below. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees, deriving from 'Ohel Mo'ed' that all applications are included. The Gemara then asks what Rabbi Yehuda does with the verse 'ken ye'aseh', and answers that it is needed for the bull of Yom Kippur for semikha and the remaining blood.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya explains that the verse 'כֵּן יַעֲשֶׂה' is only necessary according to Rabbi Shimon, who derives four applications from the words 'קֶרֶן' and 'קַרְנוֹת' above and below.
Rabbi Yehuda states that the verse is unnecessary, because the phrase 'בְּאֹהֶל מוֹעֵד' includes all applications mentioned in the Tent of Meeting.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yehuda does with the verse 'כֵּן יֵעָשֶׂה' if he does not need it for the four applications.
The Gemara answers that the verse is needed for the bull of Yom Kippur for semikha (סמיכה) and the remaining blood (שיירי הדם), as taught in a baraita.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the bull of Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the bull of Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: we already learned that 'la-par' refers to the bull of Yom Kippur, so why is a separate verse needed? It answers that it is necessary because one might think that only services that atone are indispensable, but services that do not atone are not; the verse teaches that they are.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that we already learned that the verse 'la-par' refers to the bull of Yom Kippur, so why is a separate verse needed for its application?
The Gemara answers that the verse is necessary because one might think that only services that atone are indispensable, but services that do not atone are not; the verse teaches that they are.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's use of 'Ohel Mo'ed' and the other opinion
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's use of 'Ohel Mo'ed' and the other opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Shimon does with the verse 'Ohel Mo'ed'. It answers that he uses it to teach that if the ceiling of the Sanctuary was lowered, he would not sprinkle. The other opinion (Rabbi Yehuda) derives this from 'asher', but Rabbi Shimon does not expound 'asher'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Shimon does with the verse 'באהל מועד' (in the Tent of Meeting) since he does not derive the requirement for all sanctuary-related sprinklings from it.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Shimon uses the verse to teach that if the ceiling of the Sanctuary was lowered, he would not sprinkle the blood.
The Gemara states that the other opinion (Rabbi Yehuda) derives this halacha from the word 'אשר' (which).
The Gemara concludes that the other opinion (Rabbi Shimon) does not expound the word 'אשר' (which) as a source for halacha.

items.text: Abaye's alternative: the verse is also needed for Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative: the verse is also needed for Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Abaye says that even according to Rabbi Yehuda the verse is necessary, because one might think that since semikha and remaining blood are written and repeated but do not impede, the four applications also should not impede; the verse teaches that they do.

sub.desc_en: Abaye argues that even for Rabbi Yehuda the verse is necessary, because one might think that since semikha and remaining blood are written and repeated but do not impede, the four applications also should not impede; the verse teaches that they do.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explanation for the bull of Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explanation for the bull of Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the halakha of 'la-par' referring to the bull of Yom Kippur? If it is for impediment, it is obvious because 'chok' is written. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that it is necessary for Rabbi Yehuda, who says that 'chok' applies only to inner services in white garments, but outer services in white garments do not impede if the order is changed; one might think that the sprinklings also do not impede, so the verse teaches that they do.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the halakhic purpose of the phrase 'la-par' referring to the bull of Yom Kippur? If it is to teach that the sprinklings impede (מעכב), that is obvious because the verse writes 'חוקה' (a fixed statute) regarding it.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that the verse is necessary for Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that 'חוקה' (the fixed statute) applies only to inner services performed in white garments.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak concludes: for Rabbi Yehuda, outer services in white garments do not impede if the order is changed, so one might think the sprinklings also do not impede; therefore the verse teaches that they do impede.

items.text: Rav Pappa's objection and final resolution
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's objection and final resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects: how can you say that? There is a baraita where Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda debate the order of Yom Kippur services. Rav Pappa then explains that the verse is only needed for the blood and the immersion, and Rav Acha bar Yaakov says it is to validate them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects to the previous statement by citing a baraita where Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda debate the order of Yom Kippur services, implying the verse is needed for the order.
The baraita presents Rabbi Akiva's position that completion of atonement depends on performing the service, and Rabbi Yehuda's counter-position that completion of the service depends on atonement.
Rav Pappa resolves the objection by explaining the verse is only needed for the blood and the immersion, and Rav Acha bar Yaakov adds it is to validate them.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the verses regarding the blood
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the verses regarding the blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the necessity of both the phrase 'in the blood' and 'and dip' in the verse. 'In the blood' teaches that there must be a sufficient quantity of blood for dipping from the outset, and 'and dip' teaches that one must dip and not merely wipe the blood from the vessel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the two halakhot derived from the verses: 'in the blood' teaches that there must be a sufficient quantity of blood for dipping from the outset, and 'and dip' teaches that one must dip and not merely wipe the blood from the vessel.
The Gemara explains that the phrase 'in the blood' was necessary because if only 'and dip' were written, one might think the dipping is valid even without sufficient blood from the outset.
The Gemara explains that the phrase 'and dip' was necessary because if only 'in the blood' were written, one might think that wiping the blood from the vessel is sufficient.

items.text: The verse 'altar of incense of spices'
items.text_en: The verse 'altar of incense of spices'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse specifies 'the altar of incense of spices' and answers that if the altar had not been inaugurated with the incense of spices, the priest would not sprinkle the blood upon it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse specifies 'the altar of incense of spices'.
The Gemara answers that if the altar had not been inaugurated with the incense of spices, the priest would not sprinkle the blood upon it.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi and Rabbi Yishmael on the inclusion of the Yom Kippur bull
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi and Rabbi Yishmael on the inclusion of the Yom Kippur bull
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Pappa. Rabbi expounds the verse 'and he shall do... as he did for the bull' to include the bull of Yom Kippur in all the details stated in the pericope. Rabbi Yishmael argues using a kal vachomer and explains that the verse 'for the bull' actually refers to the bull of communal unwitting sin and the bull of the anointed priest.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited supporting Rav Pappa: Rabbi expounds the verse 'וְעָשָׂה... כַּאֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה' to include the bull of Yom Kippur in all the details stated in the pericope.

Rabbi Yishmael argues using a kal vachomer (a fortiori) that since in a case where the offerings are not equated the acts are equated, certainly where the offerings are equated the acts should be equated.
Rabbi Yishmael explains that the verse 'לַפָּר' refers to the bull of communal unwitting sin, and 'לְפַר' refers to the bull of the anointed priest.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yishmael's kal vachomer
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yishmael's kal vachomer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yishmael's kal vachomer by asking which two offerings are being compared. It first suggests the bull and goat of Yom Kippur, but rejects it because their blood enters the innermost sanctum. It then suggests the bull of communal unwitting sin and the goats of idolatry, but rejects it because they atone for a known sin. Finally, it concludes that the comparison is between the bull of communal unwitting sin and the goat of Yom Kippur, where the kal vachomer is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which two offerings are being compared in Rabbi Yishmael's kal vachomer (a fortiori argument).
The Gemara suggests the comparison is between the bull of Yom Kippur and the goat of Yom Kippur.
The Gemara rejects this suggestion because both offerings have blood that enters the innermost sanctum (לפני ולפנים), making the kal vachomer invalid.
The Gemara suggests the comparison is between the bull of communal unwitting sin and the goats of idolatry.
The Gemara rejects this suggestion because both offerings atone for a known sin (עבירת מצוה ידועה), which would undermine the kal vachomer.

The Gemara concludes that the comparison is between the bull of communal unwitting sin and the goat of Yom Kippur, where the kal vachomer is valid because the offerings are dissimilar in type but the rites are equated.

items.text: Gemara's question and initial derivation
items.text_en: Gemara's question and initial derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the derivation that equates the acts of the Yom Kippur bull and goat with those of the anointed priest's bull, and then proposes that the goat of Yom Kippur is derived from the goats for idolatry through a fortiori argument.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the derivation that equates the acts of the Yom Kippur bull and goat with those of the anointed priest's bull, and then proposes that the goat of Yom Kippur is derived from the goats for idolatry through a fortiori argument.

items.text: Objection and Rav Pappa's answer
items.text_en: Objection and Rav Pappa's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a matter learned through a verbal analogy cannot teach through a fortiori argument. Rav Pappa answers that the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael holds that it can.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a matter learned through a verbal analogy (היקש) cannot in turn teach through a fortiori argument (קל וחומר).
Rav Pappa answers that the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael holds that a matter learned through a verbal analogy (היקש) can indeed teach through a fortiori argument (קל וחומר).

items.text: Interpretation of 'for the bull' and Rav Pappa's explanation
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'for the bull' and Rav Pappa's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the phrase 'for the bull' refers to the communal bull of an unwitting sin, and Rav Pappa clarifies that this is needed to teach that the communal bull, which is derived through a verbal analogy, should be considered as if written explicitly, so that a matter learned through a verbal analogy does not teach through another verbal analogy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies that the phrase 'for the bull' in the verse refers to the communal bull of an unwitting sin.
The Gemara objects: the communal bull is already written explicitly in the Torah, so why is a separate verse needed?

Rav Pappa answers: the verse is needed to teach that the communal bull, which is derived through a verbal analogy, should be considered as if written explicitly, so that a matter learned through a verbal analogy does not teach through another verbal analogy.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rav Pappa
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav Pappa
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Pappa, explaining the verse 'and he shall do as he did for the bull' to teach that the communal bull and the anointed priest's bull are derived through a verbal analogy, and that the phrase 'for the bull' prevents a matter learned through a verbal analogy from teaching through another verbal analogy.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a baraita that supports Rav Pappa, citing the verse 'and he shall do as he did' and asking why the extra word 'for the bull' is needed.

The baraita explains that the verse 'they brought their offering' teaches that the sin-offering (שעירי עבודה זרה) is like the unintentional sin (פר העלם דבר של ציבור), which itself was learned through a verbal analogy (היקש).
The baraita objects: can a matter learned through a verbal analogy (היקש) then teach another matter through a verbal analogy?

The baraita resolves the objection by citing the verse 'for the bull' (לפר), teaching that the communal bull (פר העלם דבר של ציבור) and the anointed priest's bull (פר כהן משיח) are both written explicitly, preventing the verbal analogy from being used to teach another verbal analogy.

items.text: Question on the baraita and Rav Pappa's answer
items.text_en: Question on the baraita and Rav Pappa's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita needs to derive the goats for idolatry from the phrase 'their sin-offering' when it was already derived from an earlier verse. Rav Pappa answers that it was necessary, as one might have thought that earlier derivation only applied to the sprinklings, which are written explicitly in the context of the bull.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita needs to derive the goats for idolatry from the phrase 'their sin-offering' when it was already derived from an earlier verse.
Rav Pappa answers that the derivation was necessary, as one might have thought that the earlier derivation only applied to the sprinklings, which are written explicitly in the context of the bull.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous sugya: the extra portions are included
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous sugya: the extra portions are included
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that even though the yoteret and two kidneys are not explicitly written in the body of the bull of Yom Kippur, the verse teaches that they are included.

items.text: Rav Huna's objection and resolution: Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Rav Huna's objection and resolution: Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Natan objects to Rav Pappa that the tanna is speaking about the bull of Yom Kippur in the same context. The Gemara resolves that it is a dispute between the Tanna of the school of Rav and the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael.

items.text: Two parables from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Two parables from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael explains why the yoteret and two kidneys are mentioned in the bull of the anointed priest but not in the bull of the community's unwitting sin, using a parable of a king and his friend. A second parable explains why the phrase 'parochet hakodesh' is mentioned in the former but not the latter, comparing to a province that sinned against a king.

items.text: Mishnah: Piggul in half of the permitting factor
items.text_en: Mishnah: Piggul in half of the permitting factor
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah: If one had the intent of piggul for the handful (kometz) but not for the frankincense, or vice versa, Rabbi Meir says it is piggul and one is liable for karet, while the Sages say there is no karet until one has piggul in the entire permitting factor.

items.text: Resh Lakish's explanation: the case is one of silence
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's explanation: the case is one of silence
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish says that Rabbi Meir's reasoning is not that one can have piggul in half a permitting factor; rather, the case is where one performed the kometz with improper intent and the frankincense in silence, and Rabbi Meir holds that one who acts later does so based on the initial intent.

items.text: Proof from the mishnah's continuation
items.text_en: Proof from the mishnah's continuation
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from the mishnah's statement: 'Therefore, if he placed all of them properly and one improperly, it is invalid and there is no karet.' This implies that if one was improper and the rest proper, it is piggul. The Gemara analyzes that this must be according to Rabbi Meir, and if his reasoning were half a permitting factor, even the case stated would be piggul; rather, it must be because he holds that one acts based on initial intent.

items.text: Alternative explanations: Rava and Rav Ashi
items.text_en: Alternative explanations: Rava and Rav Ashi
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak suggests the mishnah can be explained according to the Sages, interpreting 'properly' as proper for piggul. Rava explains 'improperly' as outside its place, and Rav Ashi as not for its sake. The Gemara concludes that the mishnah's structure is due to the contrast between the first clause (piggul with karet) and the last clause (invalid without karet).

items.text: Introduction of a new beraita
items.text_en: Introduction of a new beraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite a beraita that limits the previous discussion to blood placed on the outer altar.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of blood offerings on the inner altar (e.g., Yom Kippur, anointed priest, communal sin-offering). Rabbi Meir holds that piggul in any of the three applications (first, second, or third) renders the offering piggul and liable to karet, while the Sages require piggul in all the permitting acts.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding piggul in inner altar blood offerings: Rabbi Meir holds that piggul in any application renders the offering piggul and liable to karet, while the Sages require piggul in all the permitting acts.

items.text: Gemara's initial observation
items.text_en: Gemara's initial observation
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah explicitly states piggul in the first, second, or third application, and the Sages dispute this, implying a disagreement even when piggul occurs in only one act.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah explicitly states 'piggul in the first, second, or third' and then records a dispute, implying that the Sages disagree with Rabbi Meir's lenient position.

items.text: First answer: Rav Yitzchak bar Avin
items.text_en: First answer: Rav Yitzchak bar Avin
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Avin suggests the case is where piggul occurred in the slaughter, which is a single permitting act. The Gemara then questions why the Sages would disagree if only one act is involved.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avin explains that the case involves piggul in the shechita (slaughter), which is a single permitting act, so the Sages' requirement for piggul in all permitting acts is not triggered.
The Gemara objects: if the case is piggul in shechita alone, why do the Sages still require piggul in all the permitting acts, since shechita is only one act?

items.text: Rava's identification of the Sages as Rabbi Elazar
items.text_en: Rava's identification of the Sages as Rabbi Elazar
items.desc_en: Rava identifies the Sages as Rabbi Elazar, citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Elazar exempts from liability for offering a handful outside unless the entire offering is brought, showing he requires completion of all parts.

sub.desc_en: Rava identifies the anonymous 'Sages' as Rabbi Elazar, who holds that for offerings brought outside the Temple, one is liable only if all parts are offered, paralleling the requirement for piggul in all permitting acts.

items.text: Objection: Rava's own statement about Rabbi Elazar and blood
items.text_en: Objection: Rava's own statement about Rabbi Elazar and blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rava himself said Rabbi Elazar concedes regarding blood, citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon say one begins from where one stopped, implying piggul can apply to a single act.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rava himself stated that Rabbi Elazar concedes regarding blood offerings, citing a baraita where Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon say that one continues from where one stopped, implying a different rule for blood.

items.text: Rava's revised answer and Rav Ashi's challenge
items.text_en: Rava's revised answer and Rav Ashi's challenge
items.desc_en: Rava revises the case to where piggul occurred in the first application, silence in the second, and piggul again in the third, to show that piggul in the third is not redundant. Rav Ashi challenges that the Mishnah does not mention silence.

sub.desc_en: Rava revises the case to one where piggul occurred in the first application, silence in the second, and piggul again in the third, to show that piggul in the third is not redundant.
Rav Ashi challenges that the Mishnah does not mention silence, so Rava's revised case is unsupported.

items.text: Rav Ashi's final answer
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's final answer
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the case is where piggul occurred in all three applications, and the Mishnah teaches that even so, each act is considered independently, not as a continuation of the first intention.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi offers a final explanation: the case is where one intended piggul in all three applications, and the Mishnah teaches that each application is independent, so piggul in any one suffices for Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says 'whether inside or outside' (בֵּין בֵּין), implying that both cases are treated equally, which creates a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's wording 'whether inside or outside' (בֵּין בֵּין), which implies equal treatment, creating a difficulty.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's position and the problem of incomplete matirim
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's position and the problem of incomplete matirim
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Meir's view that piggul incurs karet only when all matirim have been offered, but here the blood was invalidated inside, so subsequent sprinkling in the Heikhal is like sprinkling mere water.

sub.desc_en: Mar cites Rabbi Meir's position that piggul (improper intention) incurs karet (divine excision) only when all matirim (permissive acts) have been offered, based on the principle that the acceptance of a disqualified offering parallels the acceptance of a valid one.

The Gemara objects that since the blood was invalidated by improper intention inside (the Kodesh Kodashim), the subsequent sprinkling in the Heikhal (Sanctuary) is like sprinkling mere water, so no matirim remain.

items.text: Rabbah and Rava's resolutions
items.text_en: Rabbah and Rava's resolutions
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains that the Mishnah refers to four bulls and four goats, while Rava argues that even with one bull and one goat, the blood can still effect piggul.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah resolves the difficulty by explaining that the Mishnah's case involves four bulls and four goats, each with its own separate blood application.
Rava argues that even with one bull and one goat, the blood of the second application can still effect piggul (פגול) for the offering.

items.text: Contradictions between baraitot on the number of matirim
items.text_en: Contradictions between baraitot on the number of matirim
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves contradictions between baraitot that state 43, 47, or 48 matirim, attributing them to disputes about whether blood from different horns is combined and whether the remnants are indispensable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: one baraita states 43 matirim, but another baraita states 47 matirim.

The Gemara resolves: the baraita of 43 follows the opinion that blood from different horns is not combined (אֵין מְעָרְבִין לַקְּרָנוֹת), while the baraita of 47 follows the opinion that it is combined (מְעָרְבִין לַקְּרָנוֹת).
The Gemara raises another contradiction: yet another baraita states 48 matirim.

The Gemara resolves: the baraita of 48 follows the opinion that the remnants (שִׁירַיִים) are indispensable (מְעַכְּבִין), while the baraita of 47 follows the opinion that they are not indispensable (אֵין מְעַכְּבִין).

items.text: Baraita on piggul in the meal-offering
items.text_en: Baraita on piggul in the meal-offering
items.desc_en: A baraita states that piggul applies only to kemitzah, putting it in a vessel, and walking; but for the actual burning, if one puts the kemitzah with intent and the frankincense silently, or vice versa, Rabbi Meir says it is piggul with karet, while the Sages say no karet unless all matirim are invalidated.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the rule that piggul applies only to kemitzah, putting in a vessel, and walking, and then presents the case of mixed intent and silence for the kemitzah and frankincense.
Rabbi Meir rules that the offering is piggul and one is liable to karet even if only one of the matirim was invalidated by intent.
The Sages rule that there is no karet unless one invalidates all the matirim with intent.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's case of putting the kemitzah silently and the frankincense with intent, noting that the Sages dispute it. It suggests that the frankincense was already placed, but then notes a contradiction with another baraita that says 'afterwards'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's case of putting the kemitzah silently and the frankincense with intent, noting that the Sages dispute it.
The Gemara suggests that the frankincense was already placed with intent before the kemitzah was placed silently.
The Gemara objects that this answer is identical to the first case in the baraita, and a second baraita explicitly says 'afterwards', creating a contradiction.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: items not subject to piggul
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: items not subject to piggul
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that do not incur piggul liability: the kemitzah, the frankincense, and the levonah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing items that do not incur piggul liability: the kemitzah (handful), the ketoret (frankincense), and the levonah (frankincense).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Items not subject to piggul and dispute about the log of oil of a metzora
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Items not subject to piggul and dispute about the log of oil of a metzora
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that are not subject to piggul, including the handful, frankincense, and blood. It then records a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon regarding the log of oil of a metzora, and concludes with Rabbi Shimon's general principle that only items offered on the outer altar like peace-offerings are subject to piggul.

items.text: Gemara: Ulla's statement about a piggul kemitzah that ascended the altar
items.text_en: Gemara: Ulla's statement about a piggul kemitzah that ascended the altar
items.desc_en: Ulla states that if a kemitzah that was piggul was offered on the altar, its piggul status is nullified. The Gemara questions what Ulla is teaching, since it is already known that a kemitzah is not subject to piggul.

items.text: Gemara: First objection – the Mishnah already lists the kemitzah as not subject to piggul
items.text_en: Gemara: First objection – the Mishnah already lists the kemitzah as not subject to piggul
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah already explicitly states that the kemitzah is not subject to piggul, so Ulla's statement seems redundant.

items.text: Gemara: Second objection – the rule of 'if they ascended they do not descend' is already taught
items.text_en: Gemara: Second objection – the rule of 'if they ascended they do not descend' is already taught
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the rule that items that ascended the altar do not descend is already taught in a baraita, so Ulla's statement is again redundant.

items.text: Gemara: Third objection – the rule of 'if they descended they do not ascend' is also taught
items.text_en: Gemara: Third objection – the rule of 'if they descended they do not ascend' is also taught
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even the rule that if they descended they do not ascend is already taught in the same baraita, so Ulla's statement seems entirely redundant.

items.text: Gemara: Ulla's statement is needed for the case where fire had taken hold
items.text_en: Gemara: Ulla's statement is needed for the case where fire had taken hold
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Ulla's statement is necessary for the case where fire had already taken hold of the kemitzah on the altar, in which case it does not descend even if it was piggul.

items.text: Gemara's clarification about the kometz
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification about the kometz
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the previous ruling about an organ applies when it is attached, but for a handful (kometz) which is separate, one might think it is not included; the text teaches that it is.

items.text: Rav Achai's practical ruling
items.text_en: Rav Achai's practical ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Achai rules that if a kometz of piggul was divided, half placed on the ground and half on the altar, and fire caught it, we bring up the entire kometz to the altar ab initio.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's principle and the objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's principle and the objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that piggul, notar, and tamei items that are brought up to the altar lose their prohibition. Rav Chisda objects, questioning if the altar is a mikveh of purity. Rabbi Zeira explains that the fire consumes them.

items.text: Objection from the baraita of Acheirim and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the baraita of Acheirim and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Bisna raises an objection from a baraita where Acheirim say that the verse 'v'tum'ato alav' refers to one from whom tum'ah can depart, excluding meat which cannot. If the altar removes tum'ah, then meat should also be excluded. Rava and Rav Pappa resolve the objection: Rava says we are speaking of a mikveh, but the verse doesn't mention a mikveh; Rav Pappa says we are dealing with meat of shelamim which is not fit for offering.

items.text: Ravina's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Ravina's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that the verse 'v'tum'ato alav' refers to one from whom tum'ah can depart when he is whole, excluding meat, which cannot have tum'ah depart when whole, only when lacking.

items.text: The baraita on tum'at haguf vs. tum'at basar
items.text_en: The baraita on tum'at haguf vs. tum'at basar
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita that interprets 'v'tum'ato alav' as referring to tum'at haguf (bodily impurity). Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi, and Acheirim each offer different derivations: Rabbi Yosei from the singular language of tum'ah, Rabbi from the word 'v'achal', and Acheirim from the phrase 'v'tum'ato alav' itself.

items.text: Explanation of Rabbi's derivation
items.text_en: Explanation of Rabbi's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi derives from 'v'achal' that it refers to tum'at haguf. Rava says that any verse not explained by Rav Yitzchak bar Avudimi and any mishnah not explained by Rav Ze'iri is not explained. Rav Yitzchak bar Avudimi explains: since the verse opens and closes in feminine language, with masculine in the middle, it refers to tum'at haguf.

items.text: Discussion of the baraita about leniencies and stringencies
items.text_en: Discussion of the baraita about leniencies and stringencies
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a baraita that asks why both lenient and stringent punishments were stated. It clarifies that the leniencies refer to tum'at sheretz and the stringencies to tum'at met, and the discussion involves whether the punishments apply to terumah or ma'aser, with objections about the logic of the derivations.

items.text: Ze'iri's explanation of the kalot and chamurot
items.text_en: Ze'iri's explanation of the kalot and chamurot
items.desc_en: Ze'iri explains the earlier argument: the 'light' (kalot) refer to impurity of a carcass, and the 'severe' (chamurot) refer to impurity of a corpse. He clarifies that if only impurity of a carcass had been stated, one might have thought that eating light items in a state of severe impurity incurs death, so the Torah stated the severe ones to teach otherwise.

items.text: Mishnah: Principle of matirin for piggul
items.text_en: Mishnah: Principle of matirin for piggul
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any offering which has 'matirin' (permitters) – whether for human consumption or for the altar – one is liable for piggul.

items.text: Baraitha: Derivation of piggul from shelamim
items.text_en: Baraitha: Derivation of piggul from shelamim
items.desc_en: A baraitha derives that piggul applies to all offerings that have matirin, using a series of scriptural expansions. It begins by comparing to shelamim (eaten for two days), then includes offerings eaten for one day via 'mib'sar', the olah via 'zevach', and birds and meal-offerings via 'asher hem makdishim li'. It then uses a gezeirah shavah to include notar and piggul, and concludes that the purpose of mentioning shelamim is to teach the principle of matirin.

items.text: List of offerings with matirin and exceptions
items.text_en: List of offerings with matirin and exceptions
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists various offerings and their matirin: the olah's blood permits its flesh for the altar and its hide for priests; the bird olah's blood permits its flesh for the altar; the bird chatat's blood permits its flesh for priests; the burnt bulls and goats' blood permits their fats for the altar. It then excludes the kemitzah, levonah, ketoret, meal-offerings of priests, the anointed priest, libations, and blood.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's alternative principle
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's alternative principle
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon offers a different principle: just as shelamim are offered on the outer altar and are subject to piggul, so too any offering that is on the outer altar is subject to piggul, excluding the burnt bulls and goats which are not on the outer altar.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the baraitha's derivation
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the baraitha's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraitha's method: what is the 'ke'yotzei b'shlamim'? It suggests the bekhor, which is eaten for two days. But then it asks how it is derived – if by a 'mah matzinu', there are refutations (shemalim require semichah, nesachim, and tenufah). Instead, it is derived from 'im he'achol ye'achel'. Rava then explains the rule of two adjacent general principles with a specific between them.

items.text: Debate about the log of oil of a metzora and libations
items.text_en: Debate about the log of oil of a metzora and libations
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraitha's inclusion of the log of oil of a metzora follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that piggul applies to it. But the end of the baraitha excludes libations and blood, which follows the Rabbis. A baraitha is cited where Rabbi Meir says libations of an animal are subject to piggul because the blood permits them, but the Rabbis object that one can bring the animal today and libations up to ten days later; Rabbi Meir clarifies he only meant when they come with the animal.

items.text: Rav Yosef's attribution to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's attribution to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef says the baraitha follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who holds that the log of oil's 'matanot' (applications) permit it, and thus its matanot can also cause piggul. A baraitha is cited: all agree that the log of oil is subject to me'ilah until the blood is sprinkled; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says me'ilah applies until its applications are given; they agree it is forbidden to eat until the seven applications and the thumb application are given. Rabbi Yirmeya marvels that Rav Yosef would say such a thing.

items.text: The log of oil for a metzora and piggul
items.text_en: The log of oil for a metzora and piggul
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines Rabbi Meir's view that the log of oil brought with the asham is subject to piggul because the blood permits it for the fingers. The Sages object that one can bring the asham now and the log up to ten days later, implying the log is independent. Rabbi Meir clarifies he only spoke when the log comes with the asham. Rabbi Yirmeya suggests the source is about libations, but Abaye rejects this, explaining the tannaitic teaching covers both cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the log of oil brought alone, noting that for all opinions its blood permits it and piggul does not apply.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Meir rules that the log of oil for a metzora is subject to piggul because the blood permits it for the fingers.
The Sages object to Rabbi Meir: one can bring the asham now and the log up to ten days later, implying the log is independent.
Rabbi Meir clarifies that he only spoke when the log comes with the asham.
Rabbi Yirmeya suggests that the source is about libations, implying a different derivation.

Abaye rejects Rabbi Yirmeya's suggestion, explaining that the tannaitic teaching covers both cases: the log with the asham and libations with the sacrifice, and then separately libations alone and the log alone.

items.text: Bird sin-offering: blood permits its flesh
items.text_en: Bird sin-offering: blood permits its flesh
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the blood of a bird sin-offering permits its flesh for the priests, and asks for the scriptural source.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the blood of a bird sin-offering permits its flesh for the priests.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of this rule.
The Gemara introduces a baraita of Levi that will provide the scriptural derivation.

items.text: Levi's baraita: Scriptural inclusions for various offerings
items.text_en: Levi's baraita: Scriptural inclusions for various offerings
items.desc_en: Levi's baraita derives from the verse 'all their offerings' that the log of oil of a metzora is included, despite not being from the fire. From 'all their meal-offerings' it includes the omer and the meal-offering of jealousy. From 'all their sin-offerings' it includes the bird sin-offering, despite being like a carcass. From 'all their guilt-offerings' it includes the guilt-offering of a nazirite and a metzora, though they come to permit. The Gemara clarifies that the guilt-offering of a metzora is explicit, so it includes the nazirite's. The verse 'which they return' refers to the theft of a convert, and 'to you it shall be' allows using it to betroth a woman.

sub.desc_en: Levi's baraita derives from 'all their offerings' that the log of oil of a metzora is included, despite not being from the fire.
From 'all their meal-offerings' it includes the omer and the meal-offering of jealousy, despite their atypical purposes.
From 'all their sin-offerings' it includes the bird sin-offering, despite being like a carcass.
From 'all their guilt-offerings' it includes the guilt-offering of a nazirite and a metzora, though they come to permit.
The Gemara clarifies that the guilt-offering of a metzora is explicit, so the verse includes the nazirite's guilt-offering by analogy.
The verse 'which they return' refers to the theft of a convert, and 'to you it shall be' allows using it to betroth a woman.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's ruling on piggul: inside vs. outside
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's ruling on piggul: inside vs. outside
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says in the name of Rabbi Yossi HaGelili that if one had improper intent for an action done outside while standing outside, it disqualifies; but if the intent was for an action done inside while standing outside, it does not. Similarly, intent inside for an outside action does not disqualify. Examples are given: slaughtering outside to sprinkle inside does not disqualify; sprinkling inside to burn fats or pour remnants outside does not disqualify; but slaughtering outside to pour remnants or burn fats outside does disqualify.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Yossi HaGelili
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Yossi HaGelili
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states the general principle in the name of Rabbi Yossi HaGelili: improper intent (פיגול) for an action done outside disqualifies, but for an action done inside does not.
The Gemara provides examples: standing outside and intending to sprinkle inside does not disqualify; standing inside and intending to burn fats or pour remnants outside does not disqualify.
The Gemara concludes: standing outside and intending to pour remnants or burn fats outside does disqualify, because the intent matches the location of the action.

items.text: Scriptural source for Rabbi Elazar's ruling
items.text_en: Scriptural source for Rabbi Elazar's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi derives the principle from the verse 'as is taken from the ox of the peace-offering', comparing the anointed priest's bull to the peace-offering: just as the peace-offering requires all actions and intentions on the outer altar, so too the bull requires intentions and actions on the outer altar.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi asks what scriptural verse supports Rabbi Elazar's ruling about piggul (פיגול) in the outer altar.
He derives the principle by comparing the anointed priest's bull (פר כהן משיח) to the peace-offering (שור זבח השלמים), requiring that all actions and intentions be on the outer altar.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling and Rava's statement
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling and Rava's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman quotes Rav that the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar's ruling in the name of Rabbi Yossi. Then Rava begins a statement, but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman transmits in the name of Rav that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabbi Elazar's ruling in the name of Rabbi Yossi regarding piggul in external vs. internal actions.
Rava begins a statement, but the text cuts off immediately, leaving his intended teaching incomplete.

items.text: Abaye's response to the question about halakha for the messianic era
items.text_en: Abaye's response to the question about halakha for the messianic era
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges the premise that discussing the halakha of non-Jewish offerings is irrelevant for the present, arguing that one should study and receive reward. He clarifies that his question was about the practical halakha.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges the premise that discussing the halakha of non-Jewish offerings is irrelevant for the present, arguing that one should study and receive reward, and clarifies that his question was about the practical halakha.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Non-Jewish offerings exempt from piggul, notar, tum'ah, and slaughter outside
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Non-Jewish offerings exempt from piggul, notar, tum'ah, and slaughter outside
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that offerings of non-Jews are not subject to piggul, notar, or tum'ah, and one who slaughters them outside the Temple is exempt. Rabbi Shimon holds this view, while Rabbi Yosei imposes liability.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that non-Jewish offerings are exempt from piggul, notar, and tum'ah, and slaughtering them outside is exempt, according to Rabbi Shimon.
The Mishnah concludes by recording Rabbi Yosei's dissenting opinion that one is liable for slaughtering non-Jewish offerings outside.

items.text: Baraita elaborating on the laws of non-Jewish offerings
items.text_en: Baraita elaborating on the laws of non-Jewish offerings
items.desc_en: A baraita details that non-Jewish offerings are not subject to benefit, me'ilah, piggul, notar, tum'ah, temurah, and libations, but their offerings require libations. Rabbi Yosei disagrees, applying stringency to all, except for consecrated property for Temple maintenance where me'ilah applies.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by listing leniencies for non-Jewish offerings: no benefit, no me'ilah, no liability for piggul, notar, tum'ah, temurah, and they do not bring libations.
Rabbi Shimon adds that although non-Jews do not bring libations, their offerings require libations.
Rabbi Yosei objects, stating he sees all these cases as stringent because the verse says 'to the Lord' regarding them.
Rabbi Yosei qualifies that his stringency applies only to offerings consecrated for the altar, but for consecrated property for Temple maintenance, me'ilah applies.

items.text: Gemara's explanation: No benefit is rabbinic, no me'ilah is biblical
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation: No benefit is rabbinic, no me'ilah is biblical
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the prohibition of benefit from non-Jewish offerings is rabbinic, while the exemption from me'ilah is derived from a verbal analogy with terumah, which applies only to Israelites.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the prohibition of benefit from non-Jewish offerings is rabbinic (מדרבנן).

The Gemara explains that the exemption from me'ilah (מעילה) is derived from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of 'חטא-חטא' from תרומה (terumah), where the verse specifies 'בני ישראל' (Israelites) and not gentiles.

items.text: Gemara's explanation: Exemption from piggul, notar, and tum'ah
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation: Exemption from piggul, notar, and tum'ah
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the exemption from piggul, notar, and tum'ah through verbal analogies, ultimately linking to the verse that mentions 'children of Israel' and excludes non-Jews.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason that offerings of non-Jews are exempt from piggul, notar, and tum'ah.
The Gemara derives the exemption through a chain of verbal analogies: piggul from notar, notar from tum'ah, and tum'ah from the verse 'בני ישראל' (children of Israel), excluding non-Jews.

items.text: Gemara's discussion: Exemption from temurah and the hekesh debate
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion: Exemption from temurah and the hekesh debate
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that temurah is exempt because it is linked to animal tithe, which is linked to grain tithe, which applies only to Israelites.
