It then addresses a challenge about the validity of a hekesh teaching another hekesh, and offers an alternative explanation based on the nature of animal tithe as an obligation without a fixed time.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why gentile offerings are exempt from temurah, and answers via a chain of hekesh: temurah is linked to animal tithe, animal tithe to grain tithe, and grain tithe excludes gentiles.
The Gemara objects that a concept derived through a hekesh cannot itself teach another hekesh, but resolves that grain tithe is חוּלִּין (non-sacred), so the hekesh chain is valid.
The Gemara raises a further objection: even if the hekesh chain works for one opinion, what can be said for the opinion that follows the לָמֵד (the derived term)?
The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: animal tithe is a חוֹבָה (obligation) without a fixed time, and such obligations are brought only by Israelites, not gentiles.

items.text: Gemara's explanation: Non-Jews do not bring libations, but their offerings require them
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation: Non-Jews do not bring libations, but their offerings require them
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a non-Jew does not bring libations, but his burnt offering requires libations, as derived from the verse 'kakah'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that a non-Jew does not bring libations, but his burnt offering requires them, as derived from the verse 'כָּכָה' (thus).

items.text: Gemara's explanation: Rabbi Yosei's distinction between consecrated property for the altar and for Temple maintenance
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation: Rabbi Yosei's distinction between consecrated property for the altar and for Temple maintenance
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Yosei's reasoning: the verbal analogy for me'ilah applies only to items with inherent sanctity, not to those sanctified for Temple maintenance, which have monetary sanctity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reason for Rabbi Yosei's distinction between consecrated property for the altar and for Temple maintenance.

The Gemara explains that the verbal analogy for me'ilah (מעילה) applies only to items with inherent sanctity (קדושת הגוף), not to those sanctified for Temple maintenance (קדושת בדק הבית), which have monetary sanctity (קדושת דמים).

items.text: Baraita: Blood that became impure and was sprinkled
items.text_en: Baraita: Blood that became impure and was sprinkled
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses the case of blood that became impure and was sprinkled, stating that if done unintentionally, it effects acceptance.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that blood which became impure and was sprinkled, if done unintentionally (בשוגג), effects acceptance (הורצה).

items.text: Baraita on acceptance of offerings and the Gemara's discussion
items.text_en: Baraita on acceptance of offerings and the Gemara's discussion
items.desc_en: The baraita states that for an individual, an offering is not accepted if done intentionally, but for the community it is accepted regardless; for Gentiles it is never accepted. The Gemara questions whether this aligns with Rabbi Yosi, who is stringent in all cases. Rav Pappa defends the baraita by citing the verse 'lahem' to exclude Gentiles, and Rav Ashi offers an alternative derivation from 'l'ratzon lahem'.

items.text: Mishnah: Items liable for notar and tum'ah but not piggul
items.text_en: Mishnah: Items liable for notar and tum'ah but not piggul
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists that items without 'mattirin' (permitters) are not subject to piggul but are subject to notar and tum'ah, except for blood. Rabbi Shimon adds that items normally eaten are liable for tum'ah, but wood, frankincense, and incense are not.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of tum'ah liability from the verse
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of tum'ah liability from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a logical comparison (kal vachomer) from piggul to tum'ah, but rejects it, deriving instead from the verse 'asher hem makdishim li' that tum'ah applies only to items with 'mattirin'. It then interprets 'yikrav' to mean when the item is ready to be offered, either after the permitter is offered or after sanctification in a vessel.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of notar liability via gezerah shavah and baraita of Levi
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of notar liability via gezerah shavah and baraita of Levi
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for notar liability, proposing a gezerah shavah from 'chillul' to 'chillul' from tum'ah. It considers learning from piggul via 'avon' but rejects it based on a siman. Ultimately, it cites a baraita of Levi that derives notar from the verse 'v'lo yechallelu et kodshei b'nei Yisrael'.

items.text: Opening statement: two types of disqualification
items.text_en: Opening statement: two types of disqualification
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the verse speaks of two types of disqualification: leftover (notar) and impurity (tum'ah).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the verse speaks of two types of disqualification: leftover (notar) and impurity (tum'ah).

items.text: Derivations for blood's exemption from me'ilah
items.text_en: Derivations for blood's exemption from me'ilah
items.desc_en: Three amoraim derive that blood is exempt from me'ilah: Ulla from 'I have given it to you' (it is yours), the school of Rabbi Yishmael from 'to atone' (given for atonement, not misuse), and Rabbi Yochanan from 'it' (comparing before and after atonement).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where are these matters (that blood is exempt from me'ilah) derived?
Ulla derives the exemption from the verse 'וַאֲנִי נְתַתִּיו לָכֶם' (I have given it to you), implying it is yours and not subject to me'ilah.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives the exemption from the word 'לְכַפֵּר' (to atone), indicating the blood is given for atonement, not for misuse (me'ilah).

Rabbi Yochanan derives the exemption from the word 'הוּא' (it), comparing the blood before atonement to after atonement: just as after atonement there is no me'ilah, so too before atonement there is no me'ilah.

items.text: Objection to Rabbi Yochanan's derivation
items.text_en: Objection to Rabbi Yochanan's derivation
items.desc_en: An objection is raised: perhaps the comparison should be reversed, implying me'ilah after atonement? The Gemara answers that once a mitzvah is performed, there is no me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: An objection is raised: perhaps the analogy should be reversed, so that after atonement (לאחר כפרה) is like before atonement (לפני כפרה), implying me'ilah (מעילה) applies after atonement as well.
The Gemara answers that once a mitzvah (מצוה) has been performed, there is no me'ilah (מעילה) in that item.

items.text: Challenge from terumat hadeshen
items.text_en: Challenge from terumat hadeshen
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle that no me'ilah applies after a mitzvah is performed, citing terumat hadeshen (removal of ashes) where me'ilah applies. It answers that terumat hadeshen and priestly garments are two verses that come as one, and thus do not teach a general rule.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle that no me'ilah applies after a mitzvah is performed, citing terumat hadeshen (removal of ashes) where me'ilah applies.
The Gemara answers that terumat hadeshen and priestly garments are two verses that come as one, and thus do not teach a general rule.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Dosa's view
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Dosa's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the previous answer works for the Rabbis who require burial, but for Rabbi Dosa who permits use of the garments, a different answer is needed. It answers that terumat hadeshen and eglah arufah are two verses that come as one, so they do not teach a general rule.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the previous answer works for the Rabbis who require burial of the garments, but not for Rabbi Dosa.
The Gemara asks what answer can be given for Rabbi Dosa, who permits use of the garments by an ordinary priest.
The Gemara answers that תרומת הדשן (the removal of ash) and עגלה ערופה (the heifer whose neck is broken) are two verses that come as one, so they do not teach a general rule.

items.text: Challenge for those who say two verses do teach
items.text_en: Challenge for those who say two verses do teach
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what to say for those who hold that two verses that come as one do teach a general rule. It answers that there are two exclusions: 'the beheaded' (eglah arufah) and 'and he shall place it' (terumat hadeshen).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what to say for those who hold that two verses that come as one do teach a general rule.
The Gemara answers that there are two exclusions: 'הָעֲרוּפָה' (the beheaded) and 'וְשָׂמוֹ' (and he shall place it).

items.text: Purpose of three verses regarding blood
items.text_en: Purpose of three verses regarding blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that three verses about blood are needed to exclude me'ilah, notar, and tum'ah. Pigul does not require a verse because blood itself is a 'permitter' (matir), and the Mishnah states that anything with permiters is liable for pigul.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why three separate verses are needed regarding the blood of offerings.
The Gemara answers that the three verses exclude blood from the laws of me'ilah (misuse of sacred property), notar (leftover sacrifice), and tum'ah (ritual impurity).
The Gemara explains that pigul (improper intention) does not require a verse because blood itself is a 'permitter' (מתן), and the Mishnah rules that anything with permiters is liable for pigul.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's question on three kareits in shelamim
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's question on three kareits in shelamim
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks why there are three kareits (excision) penalties in the context of shelamim offerings.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks why the Torah includes three separate kareit (excision) penalties in the context of shelamim offerings.

items.text: Clarifying the third exclusion for Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Clarifying the third exclusion for Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the third exclusion in the Mishnah (for items not eaten) is needed for Rabbi Shimon, who holds that items not eaten are not subject to tum'ah liability. Without this exclusion, one might think that since Rabbi Shimon exempts from piggul anything not offered on the outer altar like a peace-offering, he would also exempt from tum'ah; the Mishnah therefore teaches that he does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the third exclusion (for items not eaten) comes to include according to Rabbi Shimon, who holds that items not eaten are not subject to liability for טומאה (ritual impurity), and answers that it includes inner sin-offerings.

The Gemara explains that without the exclusion, one might have thought that since Rabbi Shimon exempts from פיגול (piggul) anything not offered on the outer altar like a peace-offering, he would also exempt from טומאה (impurity); the Mishnah therefore teaches that he does not.

items.text: Dispute over the scope of Rabbi Shimon's liability
items.text_en: Dispute over the scope of Rabbi Shimon's liability
items.desc_en: A dispute is recorded between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish (or Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina) regarding whether the disagreement between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages applies only to tum'ah of the meat or also to tum'ah of the person. One opinion holds the dispute is only about meat tum'ah, while the other holds it applies to both, arguing that since the verse 'and the meat that touches any unclean' is read, the verse 'and his uncleanness is upon him' is also read.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish (or Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina) regarding the scope of Rabbi Shimon's liability.

One opinion holds that the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages applies only to טומאת בשר (impurity of the meat), but regarding טומאת הגוף (impurity of the person), all agree that one is not flogged.

The other opinion holds that the dispute applies to both cases, arguing that since the verse 'וְהַבָּשָׂר אֲשֶׁר יִגַּע בְּכׇל טָמֵא' (and the meat that touches any unclean) is read, the verse 'וְטֻמְאָתוֹ עָלָיו' (and his uncleanness is upon him) is also read.

items.text: Alternative version and Rava's ruling
items.text_en: Alternative version and Rava's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Tavyomei and Rav Kahana present a different version of the dispute, placing it on the concluding clause of the Mishnah. Rava rules in favor of the opinion that the dispute applies to both meat and person tum'ah, reasoning that since the verse 'and his uncleanness is upon him and he shall be cut off' is not read, the verse 'and the meat that touches any unclean shall not be eaten' is also not read. An objection is raised from the earlier teaching that 'and the meat' includes wood and frankincense, but that is dismissed as merely for disqualification.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces an alternative version of the dispute transmitted by Rav Tavyomei and Rav Kahana.

Rava rules in favor of the opinion that the dispute applies to both meat and person tum'ah, reasoning that since the verse 'and his uncleanness is upon him and he shall be cut off' is not read, the verse 'and the meat that touches any unclean shall not be eaten' is also not read.
An objection is raised from the earlier teaching that 'and the meat' includes wood and frankincense, but that is dismissed as merely for disqualification.

items.text: Mishnah: Intentions for slaughter
items.text_en: Mishnah: Intentions for slaughter
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists six intentions for which a sacrifice may be slaughtered: for the sacrifice, for the offerer, for the Name, for the fire-offering, for the scent, and for the pleasing aroma. For a sin-offering or guilt-offering, also for the sin. Rabbi Yosei adds that if one had no specific intention at all, it is valid, as it is a condition of the court that intention follows the officiating priest.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the six intentions for which a sacrifice may be slaughtered: for the sacrifice, for the offerer, for the Name, for the fire-offering, for the scent, and for the pleasing aroma.

sub.text: Mishnah's addition for sin-offering and guilt-offering
sub.text_en: Mishnah's addition for sin-offering and guilt-offering
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah adds that for a sin-offering or guilt-offering, one must also intend for the sin.
Rabbi Yosei rules that if one had no specific intention at all, the sacrifice is valid, because it is a condition of the court that intention follows the officiating priest.

items.text: Gemara: Explicating each term
items.text_en: Gemara: Explicating each term
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains each term: 'olah' excludes peace-offering, 'ishim' excludes coals, 'rei'ach' excludes limbs that were roasted and then offered (which have no scent), and 'nicho'ach' means appeasement. 'LaHashem' refers to the One who spoke and the world came into being.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that 'עולה' (olah) excludes peace-offering, and 'אישים' (fires) excludes coals.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that 'ריח' (scent) excludes limbs that were roasted and then offered, citing Rav's statement that such limbs have no scent.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that 'ניחוח' (appeasement) means satisfaction, and 'לה׳' (to the Lord) refers to the One who spoke and the world came into being.

items.text: Sin-offering slaughtered for non-sacred purposes
items.text_en: Sin-offering slaughtered for non-sacred purposes
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that a sin-offering slaughtered for the sake of a burnt-offering is invalid, but for non-sacred purposes it is valid. Rabbi Elazar explains the reasoning: sacred items can invalidate sacred items, but non-sacred items cannot. Rabba raises an objection from Rabbi Yosei's statement that if one had no intention at all it is valid, implying that if he intended for non-sacred purposes it is invalid. Abaye deflects by distinguishing between validity and acceptance. Rabbi Elazar then states that a sin-offering slaughtered for non-sacred purposes is valid, but if slaughtered because it is non-sacred (i.e., treating it as non-sacred) it is invalid, as Samuel asked Rav Huna.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that a sin-offering slaughtered for the sake of a burnt-offering is invalid, but for non-sacred purposes it is valid.
Rabbi Elazar explains Rav's reasoning: sacred items can invalidate sacred items, but non-sacred items cannot.
Rabba objects from Rabbi Yosei's statement that if one had no intention at all it is valid, implying that if he intended for non-sacred purposes it is invalid.
Abaye deflects by distinguishing between validity (כשר) and acceptance (מרצה).

Rabbi Elazar states that a sin-offering slaughtered for non-sacred purposes is valid, but if slaughtered because it is non-sacred (i.e., treating it as non-sacred) it is invalid, as Samuel asked Rav Huna.

items.text: Source for disqualification of preoccupied acts and requirement of intent
items.text_en: Source for disqualification of preoccupied acts and requirement of intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source that a preoccupied act (מתעסק) in sacrifices is invalid. It cites the verse 'and he shall slaughter the bull before the Lord' to require slaughter for the sake of the bull. Then it asks for the source that this is indispensable (לעכב), and answers with the verse 'for your acceptance you shall sacrifice it' – meaning with your intent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source that a preoccupied act (מתעסק) in sacrifices is invalid, and cites the verse 'וְשָׁחַט אֶת בֶּן הַבָּקָר לִפְנֵי ה׳' to require slaughter for the sake of the bull.
The Gemara asks for the source that this requirement is indispensable (לעכב), and answers with the verse 'לִרְצֹנְכֶם תִּזְבָּחֻהוּ' – meaning with your intent.

items.text: Introduction of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi's view on owners' intent
items.text_en: Introduction of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi's view on owners' intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling that intent follows the one performing the act (העובד) contradicts Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi, who heard that owners can also invalidate (מפגלין). Rava explains his reasoning from the verse 'and the one who offers shall offer it'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes the Mishnah's rule that intention follows only the one performing the act (העובד).
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah does not accord with Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi, who heard that owners can render an offering piggul (מפגלין).
Rava explains the reasoning of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi: the verse 'והקריב המקריב' (and the one who offers shall offer it) indicates that the owner (who brings the offering) can also cause piggul.

items.text: Abaye's grouping of three Tannaim who hold that one's intent can affect another's act
items.text_en: Abaye's grouping of three Tannaim who hold that one's intent can affect another's act
items.desc_en: Abaye states that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi, Rabbi Eliezer, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar all hold that if one person has intent and another performs the act, the intent is effective. He cites examples: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi's view on owners, Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that slaughtering for a gentile is invalid, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's principle regarding one who hides an item and another retrieves it.

sub.desc_en: Abaye opens by asserting that three Tannaim — Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi, Rabbi Eliezer, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar — share the principle that one person's intent can affect another's action (זה מחשב וזה עובד).

sub.text: Example of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi
sub.text_en: Example of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi
sub.desc_en: Abaye identifies the first example: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi's already-cited opinion that owners can piggul (מפגלין) the offering.

Abaye gives the second example: Rabbi Eliezer rules that slaughtering a sacrifice for a gentile (שוחט לגוי) renders it invalid, showing that the gentile's intent (idolatrous purpose) affects the Jew's act.

sub.text: Example of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Example of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: Abaye gives the third example: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's principle that if a person hides an item in a manner that makes him liable for carrying on Shabbat (שבת), and another retrieves it, the second person is liable because of the first's intent (מחשבה).

items.text: Analysis of logical relationships among the three Tannaim
items.text_en: Analysis of logical relationships among the three Tannaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines whether each Tanna would accept the others' rulings. It argues that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi's view (inside the Temple) would logically extend to outside, so the other two should accept it. Conversely, Rabbi Eliezer's view on Shabbat might not apply to idolatry, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view on idolatry might not apply to Shabbat, leading to distinctions.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: Since Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar both presumably accept Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi's principle that intent works even for an act done by another (in 'within' cases), then a fortiori (קל וחומר) should they not agree to it in 'outside' cases as well?

The gemara answers: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar do NOT accept Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosi's principle in full; they might limit it to 'within' cases (פנים) but not to 'outside' cases (חוץ).
The gemara asks: Since Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar presumably accepts Rabbi Eliezer's ruling about intent for idolatry (עבודה זרה), should he not certainly accept it for Shabbat (שבת)?

The gemara answers: Rabbi Eliezer does NOT accept Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's principle, because Shabbat (שבת) has a special rule that 'forbidden labor requires intent' (מלאכת מחשבת אסרה תורה), which may not apply to idolatry.

items.text: Transition phrase to new Mishnah
items.text_en: Transition phrase to new Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous discussion with the standard phrase 'We have returned to you, Beit Shammai' (הדרן עלך בית שמאי), marking the end of a chapter and the beginning of a new Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the chapter with the standard phrase 'We have returned to you, Beit Shammai', and then transitions to the new Mishnah.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Locations of sacrifices
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Locations of sacrifices
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins by asking 'What are the places of the sacrifices?' It states that the most holy offerings are slaughtered in the north. It details the procedures for the bull and goat of Yom Kippur, and for bulls and goats that are burned, all slaughtered in the north with blood applications on the curtain and golden altar.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by asking 'What is the place of the sacrifices?' and states that offerings of the most sacred order are slaughtered in the north.

sub.text: Mishnah's detailed rule for Yom Kippur
sub.text_en: Mishnah's detailed rule for Yom Kippur
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah details the procedure for the bull and goat of Yom Kippur: slaughter in the north, blood collection in the north, sprinkling on the curtain and golden altar, and pouring the remainder on the western base of the external altar.

sub.text: Mishnah's rule for burned bulls and goats
sub.text_en: Mishnah's rule for burned bulls and goats
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that bulls and goats that are burned are slaughtered in the north, their blood collected in the north, and their blood requires sprinkling on the curtain and golden altar.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the ashamot whose blood requires four placements, and notes that the leftover blood is poured on the western foundation of the outer altar, but if not done it does not invalidate. All these ashamot are burned in the ash-pit.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the ashamot whose blood requires four placements, notes that the leftover blood is poured on the western foundation of the outer altar, and states that all these ashamot are burned in the ash-pit.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why not teach that blood reception is in the north?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why not teach that blood reception is in the north?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah did not also teach that the blood of these ashamot must be received in a sacred vessel in the north. It answers that the asham metzora, whose blood is received by hand, was left out of the list.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah did not also teach that the blood of these ashamot must be received in a sacred vessel in the north.
The Gemara answers that the asham metzora, whose blood is received by hand, was left out of the list.

items.text: Objection: A later Mishnah says asham nazir and asham metzora require north and vessel
items.text_en: Objection: A later Mishnah says asham nazir and asham metzora require north and vessel
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: a later Mishnah explicitly states that the asham nazir and asham metzora are slaughtered in the north and their blood is received in a sacred vessel in the north, contradicting the claim that the asham metzora's reception is by hand.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a later Mishnah explicitly states the asham nazir and asham metzora require slaughter in the north and blood reception in a sacred vessel in the north, contradicting the earlier claim that the asham metzora's reception is by hand.

items.text: Resolution: The Tanna initially thought hand-reception, then taught vessel-reception
items.text_en: Resolution: The Tanna initially thought hand-reception, then taught vessel-reception
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that initially the Tanna thought the asham metzora's blood is received by hand, so he omitted it from the list; but since it cannot be done without a vessel, he later taught that it requires a vessel.

items.text: Baraita: Derivation that asham metzora requires both hand and vessel reception
items.text_en: Baraita: Derivation that asham metzora requires both hand and vessel reception
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from verses that the asham metzora's blood must be taken by the priest's hand (from 'v'lakach' and 'v'natan'), but also requires a vessel because it is compared to a chatat. Therefore two priests receive its blood: one by hand and one in a vessel.

sub.desc_en: The baraita begins by deriving from the verse 'וְלָקַח' (and he shall take) that one might think the blood is received in a vessel, but the verse 'וְנָתַן' (and he shall give) teaches that just as the giving is by the priest's own hand, so too the taking is by the priest's own hand.

The baraita then raises the possibility that this hand-reception applies even for the altar, but the verse 'כִּי כַּחַטָּאת הָאָשָׁם הוּא' (for like the chatat is the asham) teaches that just as a chatat requires a vessel, so too the asham requires a vessel.
The baraita concludes that the asham metzora requires two priests to receive its blood: one by hand (for application to the metzora) and one in a vessel (for the altar).

items.text: Question on Mishnah's order
items.text_en: Question on Mishnah's order
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah lists the bull and goat of Yom Kippur before the burnt offering, given that the requirement for northward slaughter is written in the context of the burnt offering.

items.text: Answers regarding order
items.text_en: Answers regarding order
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the sin offering is dearer because it is derived from a scriptural exposition, and the outer sin offerings are dearer because their blood enters the inner sanctum.

items.text: Derivation of northward slaughter for burnt offering
items.text_en: Derivation of northward slaughter for burnt offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse for northward slaughter of the burnt offering and derives the requirement for cattle from the sheep using the addition of the vav.

items.text: Debate on whether we learn from lower to upper
items.text_en: Debate on whether we learn from lower to upper
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the derivation for those who hold that we do not learn from lower to upper, citing a dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Sages regarding a suspended guilt offering.

items.text: Rav Pappa's resolution of the dispute
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's resolution of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that all agree we learn from lower to upper; the dispute is about a different gezeirah shavah, with Rabbi Akiva limiting it to fixed sin offerings.

items.text: Further analysis of the dispute
items.text_en: Further analysis of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the dispute is about the superiority of a hekesh or a gezeirah shavah, but concludes that all agree a hekesh is superior.

items.text: Explanation of the Sages' position and derivation for guilt offering
items.text_en: Explanation of the Sages' position and derivation for guilt offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Sages use the hekesh to derive the guilt offering in silver shekels, and then discusses various derivations for the value of the guilt offering.

items.text: Derivation of northward slaughter for sin offering
items.text_en: Derivation of northward slaughter for sin offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the requirement for northward slaughter for the sin offering from the verse, and then derives the requirements for receiving the blood and for the kohen himself, concluding with the requirement for the sacrifice to be invalid if not done in the north.

items.text: Derivation of north requirement for all sin-offerings
items.text_en: Derivation of north requirement for all sin-offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the source for the north requirement, citing a verse that establishes a paradigm for all sin-offerings. It clarifies that the verse comes to establish the requirement as essential, not merely to teach that this offering requires north.

items.text: Source for essential requirement in other sin-offerings
items.text_en: Source for essential requirement in other sin-offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for the nasi's goat, both the mitzvah and essential requirement are found, but for other sin-offerings only the mitzvah is found. It then cites verses to derive the essential requirement.

items.text: Exclusion of Nachshon's goat from north
items.text_en: Exclusion of Nachshon's goat from north
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the word 'אותו' is needed, and answers that it excludes the goat of Nachshon from the north requirement. A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon debate which goats are included for semikhah, and the Gemara explains that without the exclusion, one might have thought the goat of Nachshon requires north due to its inclusion for semikhah.

items.text: Ravina's challenge and Mar Zutra's response
items.text_en: Ravina's challenge and Mar Zutra's response
items.desc_en: Ravina challenges the explanation, questioning how it works for Rabbi Shimon. Mar Zutra counters that even for Rabbi Yehuda it is problematic, since the exclusion only applies to what was included. The Gemara then discusses the possibility of a בנין אב and concludes that generations cannot learn from each other.

items.text: Exclusion of the slaughterer from north
items.text_en: Exclusion of the slaughterer from north
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that 'אותו בצפון' excludes the slaughterer from being in the north. However, it notes that this is already derived from Rabbi Achiya's baraita, which teaches that the slaughterer need not be in the north, only the receiver of the blood.

items.text: Exclusion of bird-offering and Passover from north
items.text_en: Exclusion of bird-offering and Passover from north
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that 'אותו' excludes bird-offerings and the Passover offering from the north requirement, citing baraitot with logical arguments. It then refutes these arguments by comparing to other offerings, showing that each has unique features that justify the north requirement.

items.text: Resolution: exclusion of slaughterer from north, but receiver included
items.text_en: Resolution: exclusion of slaughterer from north, but receiver included
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the original explanation that 'אותו' excludes the slaughterer from the north, but clarifies that it means the slaughterer need not be in the north, while the receiver must be. It then questions whether the receiver's requirement is derived from 'לקח' and concludes that 'לקח' does not imply this.

items.text: Derivation of essential requirement for slaughter and reception in olah
items.text_en: Derivation of essential requirement for slaughter and reception in olah
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the essential requirement of slaughter and reception in the olah. Rav Ada bar Ahava proposes a kal vachomer from the sin-offering, but it is refuted because the sin-offering atones for severe sins. Ravina then challenges the logic, and Mar Zutra defends it.

items.text: Challenge from Ma'aser and its purchase
items.text_en: Challenge from Ma'aser and its purchase
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle that a sacrifice's sanctity affects its redemption, citing Ma'aser (tithe) which is redeemable, but its purchase with Ma'aser money is not redeemable unless impure. The response explains that Ma'aser's sanctity is not strong enough to affect its redemption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle by citing Ma'aser (tithe), which is itself redeemable, but its purchase with Ma'aser money is not redeemable unless impure, citing a Mishnah.
The Gemara answers that Ma'aser's sanctity is not strong enough to affect its redemption.

items.text: Challenge from Temurah
items.text_en: Challenge from Temurah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges with Temurah (substitution), which takes effect even on a blemished animal, unlike other sacrifices. The answer explains that Temurah derives its power from sacrifices, which themselves derive from non-sacred animals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: Temurah (substitution) takes effect even on a blemished animal, whereas sacrifices themselves do not take effect on such an animal.
The Gemara answers: Temurah derives its power from sacrifices, which themselves derive from non-sacred animals, so the anomaly is resolved.

items.text: Challenge from the Paschal offering's surplus
items.text_en: Challenge from the Paschal offering's surplus
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges with the Paschal offering (פסח), which itself does not require semikhah, libations, or breast-and-thigh waving, but its surplus (offered later in the year) does. The answer explains that the Paschal offering becomes a peace-offering (שלמים) during the rest of the year.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: the Paschal offering (פסח) itself does not require semikhah, libations, or breast-and-thigh waving, yet its surplus does require these.
The Gemara answers: the Paschal offering during the rest of the year is treated as a peace-offering (שלמים), which requires those rites.

items.text: Alternative answer: Scriptural derivation for the burnt-offering
items.text_en: Alternative answer: Scriptural derivation for the burnt-offering
items.desc_en: An alternative answer is given: the verse 'the burnt-offering' (העולה) teaches that it remains in its place (i.e., the north).

sub.desc_en: An alternative answer is given: the verse 'the burnt-offering' (העולה) teaches that it remains in its place (i.e., the north).

items.text: Derivation of the north for the guilt-offering
items.text_en: Derivation of the north for the guilt-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that the guilt-offering (אשם) requires slaughter in the north from the verse 'in the place where they slaughter the burnt-offering, they shall slaughter the guilt-offering'. It then extends this to the reception of blood and the person receiving it, using the words 'its blood' and 'and its blood'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that the guilt-offering (אשם) requires slaughter in the north? It cites the verse 'in the place where they slaughter the burnt-offering, they shall slaughter the guilt-offering'.

The Gemara finds the derivation for slaughter, then asks: from where do we derive that the reception of blood (קבלה) must also be in the north? It answers from the verse 'and its blood he shall sprinkle' — implying the blood reception is also in the north.

The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that the person receiving the blood (המקבל) must also be in the north? It answers from the words 'its blood' (דמו) and 'and its blood' (ואת דמו) — a verbal analogy extending the requirement to the receiver.

items.text: Derivation that the north is indispensable
items.text_en: Derivation that the north is indispensable
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for a source that the north is indispensable (מעכב), citing another verse 'and he shall slaughter the lamb'. It then explains that this verse is needed for the principle of a matter that was included in a general rule and then singled out for a new ruling, using the example of the guilt-offering of a leper (אשם מצורע) which requires blood and sacrificial portions on the altar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for a source that the north is indispensable (מעכב), citing another verse 'and he shall slaughter the lamb'.
The Gemara objects that this verse is needed for a different teaching, not for the indispensability of the north.
The Gemara cites the principle that a matter included in a general rule and singled out for a new ruling cannot be returned to its general rule unless the verse explicitly returns it.

The Tanna provides an example: the guilt-offering of a leper (אשם מצורע) was singled out for a new ruling, and the verse 'as the sin-offering, the guilt-offering is' teaches that it requires blood and sacrificial portions on the altar.

The Tanna explains that the guilt-offering of a leper was singled out for a new ruling regarding the thumb, toe, and ear, raising the possibility that it might not require blood and sacrificial portions on the altar.

The Tanna resolves that the verse 'as the sin-offering, the guilt-offering is' teaches that just as a sin-offering requires blood and sacrificial portions on the altar, so too the guilt-offering of a leper requires them.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the two verses
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the two verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if so, let the verse be written in this case and not in that case. It then notes that this works if we accept the principle of 'singled out for a new ruling', but if not, the derivation from the general rule fails.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if so, let the verse be written in this case and not in that case, implying redundancy.
The Gemara resolves: this works if we accept the principle of 'singled out for a new ruling', but if not, the derivation from the general rule fails.

items.text: Initial objection: the verse for tzafon in asham is needed for itself
items.text_en: Initial objection: the verse for tzafon in asham is needed for itself
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers the possibility that the verse teaching tzafon (north) for the asham is not derived from the chatat but is needed for its own sake. If so, the earlier argument that the asham learns tzafon from the chatat collapses.

items.text: Mar Zutra's challenge: tzafon only for blood and limbs, not slaughter
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's challenge: tzafon only for blood and limbs, not slaughter
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra suggests that the verse returning tzafon to the asham applies only to the blood presentation and the limbs (which require priesthood), but not to slaughter, which does not require priesthood.

items.text: Gemara's response: the double hekesh teaches otherwise
items.text_en: Gemara's response: the double hekesh teaches otherwise
items.desc_en: The Gemara counters that if Mar Zutra were correct, the verse would have said 'for it is like a chatat'; instead it says 'like a chatat the asham', implying it is like other ashamot. The double hekesh (to chatat and to olah) is needed to teach a principle.

items.text: Ravina's explanation: preventing a thing learned by hekesh from teaching by hekesh
items.text_en: Ravina's explanation: preventing a thing learned by hekesh from teaching by hekesh
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that both hekdeshim are necessary: if only to chatat, one might think a thing learned by hekesh can teach by hekesh; if only to olah, the same. The double hekesh teaches that a thing learned by hekesh cannot teach by hekesh.

items.text: Rava's proof from the verse 'asher yurum mishor zevach hashelamim'
items.text_en: Rava's proof from the verse 'asher yurum mishor zevach hashelamim'
items.desc_en: Rava derives the same principle from the verse about the heave offering of the bull of the peace offering. The verse is needed to teach that the law of the diaphragm and kidneys, learned by hekesh from the anointed priest's bull, is considered as if written in its own context, so it cannot teach by hekesh.

items.text: Transition: can a thing learned by hekesh teach by gezeirah shavah?
items.text_en: Transition: can a thing learned by hekesh teach by gezeirah shavah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new question: can a law derived through hekesh teach another law through gezeirah shavah? It notes that the principle 'a thing learned by hekesh cannot teach by hekesh' is established either from Rava or Ravina.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Natan ben Avtulmos and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Natan ben Avtulmos and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from Rabbi Natan ben Avtulmos regarding the law of 'parchah' (spreading) in garments, which is learned by gezeirah shavah from a law itself learned by hekesh. Rabbi Yochanan's statement that in all the Torah one may learn a learned thing from a learned thing except in kodashim supports that a thing learned by hekesh cannot teach by gezeirah shavah.

items.text: Final question: can a thing learned by hekesh teach by kal vachomer?
items.text_en: Final question: can a thing learned by hekesh teach by kal vachomer?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises the question of whether a law derived through hekesh can teach another law through kal vachomer (a fortiori argument), leaving it unresolved.

items.text: Question: Can a law derived through hekesh teach through binyan av?
items.text_en: Question: Can a law derived through hekesh teach through binyan av?
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael's principle. Rabbi Yirmeyah asks: If the Torah wrote 'tzafonah' (north) for the asham (guilt-offering) when it could have been derived from the chatat (sin-offering) via binyan av, does this imply that a law derived through hekesh cannot teach through binyan av?

items.text: Refutation and alternative derivations
items.text_en: Refutation and alternative derivations
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yirmeyah's proof: one could also derive tzafonah from the olah (burnt-offering) via binyan av, but that is refuted because olah is entirely burnt. Similarly, deriving from chatat is refuted because it atones for karet-offenses. The Gemara then considers deriving from two sources, but each potential source (olah, chatat, asham) has a unique characteristic that prevents a binyan av from the other two.

items.text: Question: Can a law derived through gezeirah shavah teach through hekesh?
items.text_en: Question: Can a law derived through gezeirah shavah teach through hekesh?
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa raises the question using the example of the todah (thanksgiving-offering) which is derived from shelamim (peace-offerings) via hekesh, but the shelamim itself is derived from another source via gezeirah shavah. Mar Zutra objects that ma'aser dagan (tithe of grain) is non-sacred, and Ravina clarifies that the principle is that a sacred matter derived through gezeirah shavah can teach another sacred matter via hekesh.

items.text: Question: Can a law derived through gezeirah shavah teach through another gezeirah shavah?
items.text_en: Question: Can a law derived through gezeirah shavah teach through another gezeirah shavah?
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama cites a baraisa about the revuchah (boiled offering) where the requirement for challot (loaves) and rekikin (wafers) is derived through gezeirah shavah from the word 'challot' and 'matzot'. Ravina challenges that the derivation of matzot might be from the general law of ma'afeh tanur (oven-baked) rather than from challot, questioning the validity of the gezeirah shavah chain.

items.text: Alternative example: The law of removing the innards of the bull
items.text_en: Alternative example: The law of removing the innards of the bull
items.desc_en: Rava cites a baraisa about the bull brought for the anointed priest, where the verse teaches that the innards are removed whole. A gezeirah shavah from the olah teaches that it must be cut into pieces, but the verse 'kirbo ufirsho' limits this to not requiring flaying. Rabbi adds that the skin and flesh are removed together with the innards.

items.text: Initial gezeirah shavah application
items.text_en: Initial gezeirah shavah application
items.desc_en: The Gemara applies a gezeirah shavah to teach that the burning of the red heifer must be done through dissection without flaying, just as with the daily offering.

items.text: Question: Can a gezeirah shavah teach a kal vachomer?
items.text_en: Question: Can a gezeirah shavah teach a kal vachomer?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a principle derived from a gezeirah shavah can be used to teach a kal vachomer. It proposes a kal vachomer: if a hekesh, which does not teach via hekesh, can teach a kal vachomer (per the school of Rabbi Yishmael), then a gezeirah shavah, which does teach via hekesh (per Rav Pappa), should certainly teach a kal vachomer.

items.text: Objection: What about those who reject Rav Pappa?
items.text_en: Objection: What about those who reject Rav Pappa?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that this kal vachomer only works for those who accept Rav Pappa's principle. For those who do not, the argument fails, and the question remains unanswered.

items.text: Alternative kal vachomer using Rami bar Chama
items.text_en: Alternative kal vachomer using Rami bar Chama
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative kal vachomer: if a hekesh, which does not teach via hekesh, can teach a kal vachomer, then a gezeirah shavah, which teaches another gezeirah shavah (per Rami bar Chama), should certainly teach a kal vachomer.

items.text: Question: Can a gezeirah shavah teach a binyan av?
items.text_en: Question: Can a gezeirah shavah teach a binyan av?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a principle derived from a gezeirah shavah can teach a binyan av, and concludes with teiku (let it stand unresolved).

items.text: Question: Can a kal vachomer teach a hekesh?
items.text_en: Question: Can a kal vachomer teach a hekesh?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a principle derived from a kal vachomer can teach a hekesh. It proposes a kal vachomer: if a gezeirah shavah, which does not teach via hekesh (per Rabbi Yochanan), can teach a hekesh (per Rav Pappa), then a kal vachomer, which learns from hekesh (per the school of Rabbi Yishmael), should certainly teach a hekesh. The Gemara objects that this depends on accepting Rav Pappa, and for those who do not, it concludes with teiku.

items.text: Question: Can a kal vachomer teach a gezeirah shavah?
items.text_en: Question: Can a kal vachomer teach a gezeirah shavah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a principle derived from a kal vachomer can teach a gezeirah shavah. It proposes a kal vachomer: if a gezeirah shavah, which does not teach via hekesh (per Rabbi Yochanan), can teach a gezeirah shavah (per Rami bar Chama), then a kal vachomer, which learns from hekesh (per the school of Rabbi Yishmael), should certainly teach a gezeirah shavah.

items.text: Question: Can a kal vachomer teach a kal vachomer?
items.text_en: Question: Can a kal vachomer teach a kal vachomer?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a principle derived from a kal vachomer can teach another kal vachomer. It proposes a kal vachomer: if a gezeirah shavah, which does not teach via hekesh (per Rabbi Yochanan), can teach a kal vachomer (as previously stated), then a kal vachomer, which learns from hekesh (per the school of Rabbi Yishmael), should certainly teach a kal vachomer. The Gemara notes that this would be a kal vachomer ben kal vachomer, but corrects that it is actually a 'ben beno' (grandchild) of a kal vachomer. It then offers a revised kal vachomer using the school of Rabbi Yishmael for both premises, concluding that this is indeed a kal vachomer ben kal vachomer.

items.text: Question: Can a kal vachomer teach a binyan av?
items.text_en: Question: Can a kal vachomer teach a binyan av?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a principle derived from a kal vachomer can teach a binyan av. Rabbi Yirmeyah brings a proof from a Mishnah: if one performs melikah on a bird and it is found to be a tereifah, Rabbi Meir says it does not convey impurity in the gullet, while Rabbi Yehudah says it does. Rabbi Meir argues via a kal vachomer: if an animal carcass, which conveys impurity through touch and carrying, has its slaughter purify its tereifah from impurity, then a bird carcass, which does not convey impurity through touch and carrying, should certainly have its slaughter purify its tereifah from impurity. The Gemara begins to analyze the kal vachomer.

items.text: Dispute about melikah purifying a tereifah
items.text_en: Dispute about melikah purifying a tereifah
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a tannaitic dispute: the first opinion holds that melikah purifies a tereifah bird from its impurity, just as slaughter purifies a tereifah animal. Rabbi Yosei argues that melikah is only comparable to the carcass of a clean animal, where slaughter purifies but melikah does not.

items.text: Clarification of the dispute
items.text_en: Clarification of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute is not about the principle itself but about the source: the first opinion derives from slaughter of hullin, while Rabbi Yosei does not accept that derivation.

items.text: Question about hermeneutical principles
items.text_en: Question about hermeneutical principles
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a principle learned through a בנין אב can teach through other hermeneutical methods like היקש, גזירה שוה, קל וחומר, or another בנין אב.

items.text: Derivation of disqualifications from the principle
items.text_en: Derivation of disqualifications from the principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to derive various disqualifications (such as לָן, יוֹצֵא, טָמֵא, חוּץ לִזְמַנּוֹ, חוּץ לִמְקוֹמוֹ, and acceptance by invalid priests) from the principle, but then objects that one cannot derive a case that is not in its proper context from one that is.

items.text: Answer to the objection
items.text_en: Answer to the objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Tanna relies on the verse "זֹאת תּוֹרַת הָעוֹלָה" which includes all these cases.

items.text: Reason for remaining blood going to the yesod
items.text_en: Reason for remaining blood going to the yesod
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the remaining blood of the olah is poured at the yesod of the outer altar: the verse "אֶל יְסוֹד מִזְבַּח הָעֹלָה אֲשֶׁר פֶּתַח אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד" indicates that it goes to the first yesod encountered.

items.text: Derivations from the verse about the yesod
items.text_en: Derivations from the verse about the yesod
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a baraisa that derives multiple laws from the phrase "אֶל יְסוֹד מִזְבַּח הָעֹלָה": that the inner altar has no yesod, that the outer altar requires a yesod, and a debate between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva about whether the initial blood of the olah requires the yesod. The Gemara then clarifies that the exclusion of the inner altar is derived from "אֲשֶׁר פֶּתַח אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד" rather than from the word "הָעֹלָה" itself.

items.text: Opening statement
items.text_en: Opening statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the requirement to place the base of the altar for the burnt offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the requirement to place the base of the altar for the burnt offering.

items.text: Gemara's question on the need for a verse
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the need for a verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a verse is needed for the remnants of the blood, arguing that if one thought the verse was written as is, the remnants are already dealt with externally.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a verse is needed for the remnants of the blood, arguing that if one thought the verse was written as is, the remnants are already dealt with externally.

items.text: Consideration of reversal
items.text_en: Consideration of reversal
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers the possibility that the application might be reversed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the possibility that the application of the verses might be reversed, suggesting an alternative interpretation.

items.text: Gemara's initial question on the verse
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question on the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the verse 'to the foundation of the altar of the burnt-offering' teaches that the blood is poured on the side of the foundation or on its top. It concludes that since it says 'foundation of the altar of the burnt-offering' (not just 'foundation of the burnt-offering'), it means on the top (gag) of the foundation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the verse teaches that the blood is poured on the side of the foundation or on its top.
The Gemara concludes that since the verse says 'to the foundation of the altar of the burnt-offering' (not just 'foundation of the burnt-offering'), it means on the top (gag) of the foundation.

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva's kal vachomer
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva's kal vachomer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael argues that the beginning of the olah, which atones, should certainly require gag yesod, as the remnants of the chatat, which do not atone, require it. Rabbi Akiva adds that the beginning of the olah, which atones and comes to atone, certainly requires it; he then asks why the verse is needed, concluding it teaches to give a foundation to the altar of the olah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael argues that the requirement of pouring on the top of the foundation (גג יסוד) is derived by a kal vachomer (a fortiori) from the leftover blood of the sin-offering.
Rabbi Akiva adds a kal vachomer and then explains that the verse 'אֶל יְסוֹד מִזְבַּח הָעוֹלָה' teaches that the foundation is given to the altar of the burnt-offering.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Adda bar Ahava and Rav Pappa
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Adda bar Ahava and Rav Pappa
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava says the difference between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva is whether shrayim (remnants) are indispensable (me'akev). Rav Pappa says all agree shrayim are not indispensable; rather, they dispute whether mitzui (squeezing) of a bird chatat is indispensable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between the explanations of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva.
Rav Adda bar Ahava answers that the difference is whether failure to pour the remainder of the blood (שיריים) disqualifies the offering: one Sage holds it disqualifies, the other holds it does not.
Rav Pappa answers that all agree שיריים (remnants) are not indispensable; rather, they dispute whether מיצוי (squeezing) of a bird sin offering is indispensable.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rav Pappa on the bull of Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav Pappa on the bull of Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Pappa: it teaches that the bull of Yom Kippur requires blood application to the foundation. Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva argue via kal vachomer that it requires the foundation, but the verse 'and he shall finish atoning' teaches that the remnants do not impede. The Gemara concludes that the verse 'and all the blood of the bull he shall pour' makes it a remaining mitzvah, showing shrayim are not indispensable.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Pappa: it teaches that the bull of Yom Kippur requires blood application to the foundation.
Rabbi Yishmael argues via a kal vachomer that the bull of Yom Kippur requires the foundation.
Rabbi Akiva argues via a kal vachomer that the bull of Yom Kippur requires the foundation.
Rabbi Yishmael cites the verse 'and he shall finish atoning' to teach that the remnants do not impede.
The Gemara derives a kal vachomer for the bull of the anointed priest from the goat of the king.
The Gemara concludes that the verse 'and all the blood of the bull he shall pour' makes it a remaining mitzvah, showing shrayim are not indispensable.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yishmael's view on mitzui
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yishmael's view on mitzui
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges whether Rabbi Yishmael really holds that mitzui of a bird chatat is indispensable, citing a baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael that interprets 'and the remainder of the blood shall be squeezed out' to imply that the remainder is squeezed, suggesting it is not indispensable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yishmael holds that the squeezing of the bird sin-offering (מיצוי חטאת העוף) is indispensable.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing the school of Rabbi Yishmael, which teaches that the verse 'וְהַנִּשְׁאָר בַּדָּם יִמָּצֵה' implies that the remaining blood is squeezed, indicating it is not indispensable.

items.text: Introduction of the dispute about שיריים
items.text_en: Introduction of the dispute about שיריים
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the earlier statement about leftover blood not being presented reflects a dispute between two Tannaim according to Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute about whether leftover blood (שיריים) that won't remain should not be presented, stating it reflects two Tannaitic views according to Rabbi Yishmael.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's explanation and the baraita
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's explanation and the baraita
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama explains that the Tanna holds that שיריים are essential. He cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'הכהן המחטא אותה' that only blood placed above is valid, not below. The baraita includes a logical argument (kal vachomer) and concludes with a scriptural decree.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama states that this Tanna holds that the remaining blood (שיריים) is essential (מעכב).
A baraita is cited, deriving from the verse 'הכהן המחטא אותה' that only a sin-offering whose blood is placed above (on the horns) is valid, not one placed below.
The baraita asks: from where do we derive this? It notes that from the verse 'ודם זבחיך ישפך' we learn that for offerings requiring four placements, if one gives a single placement, it atones.
The baraita raises the possibility that offerings whose blood is placed above, if placed below, might also atone.
The baraita presents a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: just as blood placed below, if placed above, does not atone, so too blood placed above, if placed below, does not atone.
The baraita objects: the kal vachomer is refuted because lower blood has no part that is offered above, whereas upper blood has some that is offered below (the remnants).
The baraita counters: the inner blood (שיריים) proves the point, for some of it is offered outside, yet if placed outside initially it does not atone.
The baraita objects again: the inner blood lacks a purging altar, whereas the upper blood has the horns that purge it, so if placed below it might be valid.
The baraita concludes with a scriptural decree: the verse 'אותה' teaches that only the offering whose blood is placed above is valid, not one placed below.

items.text: Gemara's question on the baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's statement that the inner altar does not finish the blood, asking if this refers to the leftover blood (שיריים).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's statement that the inner altar does not finish the blood, asking if this refers to the leftover blood (שיריים).

items.text: Rava's kal vachomer and resolution
items.text_en: Rava's kal vachomer and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava argues that if the inner leftover blood, which eventually becomes an obligation outside, is invalid when done outside initially, then upper blood that never becomes an obligation below should certainly be invalid. The Gemara then clarifies that not only the altar but also the curtain finishes the blood.

sub.desc_en: Rava presents a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if inner leftover blood (שייריים פנימיים), which ultimately becomes an obligation outside, invalidates when offered outside initially, then upper blood (עליונים), which never becomes an obligation below, should certainly invalidate when offered below.
The Gemara clarifies that the inner altar is not the sole finisher of the blood; rather, the curtain (פרכת) also finishes the blood, implying a distinction that saves the earlier reasoning.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi Akiva says that if atonement is completed, the service is finished; Rabbi Yehuda says that if the service is finished, atonement is achieved, implying that missing any presentation invalidates the service.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Akiva expounds the verse 'וְכִלָּה מִכַּפֵּר' (and he shall finish from atoning) meaning if atonement is completed, then the service is finished; Rabbi Yehuda counters that the phrase means if the service is completed (with all required presentations), then atonement is achieved, and missing any presentation invalidates the entire service.

items.text: The difference between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.text_en: The difference between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the difference between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda is whether they interpret the verse's meaning or whether שיריים are essential. Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi disagree on this. The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds that שיריים are essential, and that Rabbi Yochanan also holds that view but attributes it to a different Tanna.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda, and reports that Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi disagree: one says the difference is in interpreting the verse's meaning, the other says it is whether שיריים (the remaining blood) are essential.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds that שיריים (the remaining blood) are essential, citing his statement that according to that view one brings one bull and begins again inside.
The Gemara objects: does Rabbi Yochanan not hold this view? He himself said that the Tanna Rabbi Nechemya follows the opinion that שיריים are essential.

The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Yochanan's statement is 'according to the one who says' but not to these specific Tannaim; similarly here, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's statement is 'according to the one who says' but not to these specific Tannaim.

items.text: Mishnah: Communal and individual sin-offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: Communal and individual sin-offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins listing the communal sin-offerings: the goats of New Moons and festivals. Their slaughter is in the north, their blood is received in a service vessel in the north, and the blood requires four presentations on the four corners.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing the communal sin-offerings (goats of New Moons and festivals) and states that their slaughter and blood reception are in the north, and the blood requires four presentations on the four corners.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for applying blood to the four horns of the altar and pouring the remaining blood on the southern base. It also states that the offerings are eaten within the curtains by male priests for one day and night until midnight.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for applying blood to the four horns of the altar and pouring the remaining blood on the southern base, and states that the offerings are eaten within the curtains by male priests for one day and night until midnight.

items.text: Gemara's dispute on blood application method
items.text_en: Gemara's dispute on blood application method
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar: one says the priest places blood one cubit this way and one cubit that way along the horn, the other says he purifies downward opposite the horn's tip. The Gemara clarifies that the dispute is according to Rabbi's view, not Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon's.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the priest applies the blood to the horn, and presents two opinions: Rabbi Yochanan says he places one cubit this way and one cubit that way, and Rabbi Elazar says he purifies downward opposite the tip of the horn.
The Gemara clarifies that the dispute is only according to Rabbi's view, not Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon's, and explains each opinion's reasoning.

items.text: Objection from a baraita
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that describes the sin-offering blood application as purifying downward opposite the horn's tip until all blood is consumed. The Gemara resolves that the baraita describes the ideal method (mitzvah), but if one did it one cubit this way and that, it is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that describes the sin-offering blood application as purifying downward opposite the horn's tip until all blood is consumed, implying the method is fixed, not flexible.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita describes the ideal method (מצוה) of applying at the horn's tip, but if one did it one cubit this way and that, it is valid בדיעבד (after the fact).

items.text: Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon's dispute on blood placement
items.text_en: Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon's dispute on blood placement
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the positions of Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon: Rabbi says upper blood is given above the red line and lower blood below it, while Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon says for a bird offering that applies, but for a animal sin-offering the blood is placed on the horn itself. Rabbi Avahu explains Rabbi's scriptural basis from the 'har'el' (altar top).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon is, and cites a baraita where Rabbi states that upper blood is given above the red line and lower blood below it.

Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon responds that Rabbi's rule applies only to a bird burnt-offering (עולת העוף), but for a animal sin-offering (חטאת בהמה) the blood is placed directly on the body of the horn.
Rabbi Avahu explains Rabbi's scriptural basis from the verse 'וההריאל ארבע אמות' (the altar top was four cubits), indicating the area above the red line.
The Gemara objects that the verse says four cubits, but the altar top was only one cubit; Rav Adda bar Ahava answers that it refers to the place of the four horns.
The Gemara objects that the place of the horns is not four cubits either; the text is emended to say 'רשות קרנות ארבע' (the area of the horns is four [handbreadths]).

items.text: Source for the red line
items.text_en: Source for the red line
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a red line encircling the altar's midpoint to separate upper and lower blood, and Rav Acha bar Rav Katina derives this from the verse 'the netting was up to half the altar' – the Torah created a partition to separate the bloods.

sub.desc_en: A Mishnah is cited stating that a red line encircles the altar at its midpoint to separate upper and lower blood.
The Gemara asks the scriptural source for this red line.
Rav Acha bar Rav Katina derives the source from the verse 'and the netting shall be until half the altar,' indicating the Torah created a partition to separate upper and lower blood.

items.text: Dispute on the location for pouring remaining blood
items.text_en: Dispute on the location for pouring remaining blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the Mishnah's statement that the remaining blood is poured on the southern base. A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi Yishmael says it is the western base, Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says the southern base. The Gemara explains the reasoning: one learns from the explicit verse about the altar's base, and the other holds the entire altar stands in the north or the entire entrance is in the south.

sub.desc_en: A baraita opens by stating that the verse 'אל יסוד המזבח' refers to the southern base, and then raises the possibility that it might instead refer to the western base.
The Gemara asks: should we not learn the unspecified base from the explicit one (the southern base mentioned elsewhere)?
The Gemara answers by drawing an analogy: just as the exit from the Heikhal is adjacent to it, so too the descent from the ramp is adjacent to it (the southern side).
A baraita records the dispute: Rabbi Yishmael says both bases are western, while Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says both are southern.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yishmael's position is based on learning the unspecified base from the explicit one (the western base).
The Gemara asks: what is the reasoning of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai, who holds the base is southern?
Rabbi Assi explains that this Tanna holds either that the entire altar stands in the north or that the entire entrance is in the south.

items.text: Baraita on the western foundation
items.text_en: Baraita on the western foundation
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael, aligning with Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, states that the western foundation (יסוד מערבי) is the one used for both the olah and the chatat. A mnemonic is given: 'משכו גברי לגברא'.

sub.text: Baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael, aligning with Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, states that both the olah and the chatat use the western foundation (יסוד מערבי), with a mnemonic 'משכו גברי לגברא'.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of the olah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of the olah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that the olah, classified as most holy (קדשי קדשים), must be slaughtered in the north, its blood received in a sacred vessel in the north, requires two placements that are four, and entails flaying, cutting into pieces, and being entirely consumed by fire.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the olah is classified as קדשי קדשים (most holy), its slaughter is in the north, its blood is received in sacred vessels in the north, its blood requires two placements that are four, and it requires flaying and cutting into pieces, and it is entirely consumed by fire.

items.text: Gemara's question on 'most holy'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on 'most holy'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies that the olah is 'most holy', noting that unlike other offerings, the Torah does not explicitly call the olah 'most holy'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah teaches that the olah is קדשי קדשים (most holy), and answers that it is because the verse does not explicitly write 'קדשי קדשים היא' (it is most holy) regarding the olah.

items.text: Debate between Rav and Shmuel on blood application
items.text_en: Debate between Rav and Shmuel on blood application
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the blood of the olah is applied. Rav says he gives and returns and gives (two separate applications). Shmuel says he gives one application like a Greek letter gamma (one stroke covering two corners).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the two placements of blood are performed, and Rav answers that the priest gives and then gives again (two separate placements).
Shmuel answers that the priest gives one placement in the shape of a Greek gamma (two opposite corners simultaneously).
Shmuel says the priest gives one application shaped like a Greek letter gamma (a single stroke covering two corners).

items.text: Tannaic support for Shmuel
items.text_en: Tannaic support for Shmuel
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Shmuel: one might think to sprinkle once, but the verse says 'around'; one might think to encircle like a thread, but the verse says 'and they shall sprinkle'. Therefore how? Like a gamma – two placements that are four.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one might think the blood can be thrown in one throw, but the verse says 'סָבִיב' (around), implying multiple placements.

The baraita objects: if 'סָבִיב' (around) is taken literally, one might think the priest encircles the altar like a thread, but the verse says 'וְזָרְקוּ' (and they shall throw), indicating a throwing motion.
The baraita resolves: how then? In the shape of a gamma (two opposite corners), and thus the blood requires two placements that are four.

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael's gezerah shavah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's gezerah shavah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael derives from a gezerah shavah of 'around' that the olah requires the same four separate placements as the chatat. The Gemara objects that perhaps it requires four corners of the altar, but the answer is that the olah requires the foundation, and the southeastern corner lacked a foundation.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael derives from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'סָבִיב' (around) that the olah requires the same four separate placements (פיסוק) as the chatat.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the analogy implies the olah requires four placements on the four corners of the altar, like the chatat.
The Gemara answers that the olah requires the foundation (יסוד), and the southeastern corner lacked a foundation, so the analogy cannot mean the four corners.

items.text: Reason for missing foundation on southeastern corner
items.text_en: Reason for missing foundation on southeastern corner
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains: because that corner was not in the portion of the one who tears (the tribe of Benjamin?). Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak adds that the altar consumed a cubit from Judah's portion. Rabbi Levi bar Chama in the name of Rabbi Chama bar Chanina describes a strip of land from Judah's portion entering Benjamin's portion, and the righteous Benjamin was distressed daily wanting to take it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the southeastern corner of the altar lacked a foundation (יסוד).
Rabbi Elazar explains that the southeastern corner was not in the portion of the one who tears (the tribe of Benjamin, who was destined to build the altar).

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's supporting statement
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's supporting statement
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak adds that the altar itself consumed a cubit from Judah's portion, further explaining the missing foundation.

sub.text: Rabbi Levi bar Chama in the name of Rabbi Chama bar Chanina's explanation
sub.text_en: Rabbi Levi bar Chama in the name of Rabbi Chama bar Chanina's explanation
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi bar Chama in the name of Rabbi Chama bar Chanina describes a strip of land from Judah's portion entering Benjamin's portion, and that the righteous Benjamin was distressed daily wanting to take it.

items.text: Opening statement: Benjamin's merit
items.text_en: Opening statement: Benjamin's merit
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse about Benjamin being a host for the Divine Presence, linking it to the altar's location in his territory.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing a verse about Benjamin's merit as host for the Divine Presence, linking it to the altar's location in his territory.

items.text: Challenge from bird-offering procedure
items.text_en: Challenge from bird-offering procedure
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the idea that the altar had no foundation (יסוד) in Benjamin's territory, citing the bird-offering procedure where blood is pressed on the wall of the altar. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the airspace was Benjamin's but the ground was Judah's.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the idea that the altar had no foundation (יסוד) in Benjamin's territory by citing the bird-offering procedure where blood is pressed on the wall of the altar, implying a physical wall existed.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the airspace (אוירא) was Benjamin's but the ground (קרקע) was Judah's, so the blood was pressed on the wall in Judah's territory.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Levi on 'foundation'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Levi on 'foundation'
items.desc_en: Rav and Levi argue whether 'foundation' (יסוד) refers to the physical building or to the blood (i.e., the place where blood is applied). Rav translates a verse as 'in his inheritance the altar will be built,' while Levi translates it as 'in his inheritance the sanctuary will be built' – a place sanctified for blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'it had no foundation' (יסוד) means in the context of Benjamin's territory.
Rav explains that 'foundation' refers to the physical building, translating the verse as 'in his inheritance the altar will be built.'
Levi explains that 'foundation' refers to the blood (the place where blood is applied), translating the verse as 'in his inheritance the sanctuary will be built' – a place sanctified for blood.

items.text: Support from the foundation's dimensions
items.text_en: Support from the foundation's dimensions
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita describing the foundation as extending along the north and west, and 'eating' one cubit on the south and east. It explains that 'eating' refers to blood (i.e., the foundation's function for blood application).
