sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita describing the foundation's dimensions along the north, west, and its 'eating' one cubit on the south and east.
The Gemara resolves that 'eating' in the baraita refers to blood, not physical consumption of the foundation.

items.text: Challenge from the altar's dimensions
items.text_en: Challenge from the altar's dimensions
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites that the altar was 32 by 32 cubits, and explains that this measurement is from the side (i.e., including the foundation's projection).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous position by citing a baraita that the altar was 32 by 32 cubits, implying a contradiction.
The Gemara resolves the challenge by explaining that the measurement is from the side, including the foundation's projection.

items.text: Challenge from the 'flying' cubit
items.text_en: Challenge from the 'flying' cubit
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites that the altar 'flies' one cubit over the foundation and one cubit over the surrounding ledge (סובב). It reinterprets this as 'opposite' the foundation and ledge, not literally flying.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous interpretation by citing a baraita that states the altar 'flies' one cubit over the foundation and one cubit over the surrounding ledge (סובב).
The Gemara reinterprets 'flying' as 'opposite' the foundation and ledge, not literally flying, resolving the challenge.

items.text: Levi's baraita on building the altar
items.text_en: Levi's baraita on building the altar
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings Levi's teaching detailing the construction of the altar: a 32-cubit base for the foundation, then a 30-cubit layer for the surrounding ledge (סובב), then a 28-cubit layer for the woodpile (מערכה), and finally one-cubit horns at each corner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Levi's baraita on how to build the altar, describing the first 32-cubit square layer as the foundation (יסוד).
Levi describes the second 30-cubit layer, five cubits high, which forms the surrounding ledge (סובב), and the third 28-cubit layer, three cubits high, which is the place for the woodpile (מערכה).
Levi concludes by describing the one-cubit square horns (קרנות) at each corner of the altar.

items.text: Gemara's resolution regarding 'whole stones'
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution regarding 'whole stones'
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction about the requirement for whole stones on the altar by explaining that the stones are cut from a larger block, not that they are naturally whole. This is supported by a parallel from Rav Kahana's teaching about hollow corner stones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the verse says 'whole stones' (אבנים שלמות), implying they must be naturally whole, not cut.
The Gemara answers: the stones are cut from a larger block (דמיחת מידי מתותיה ושקיל ליה), so they are whole in the sense of being hewn from a single piece.

The Gemara supports this by citing Rav Kahana's teaching that the corner stones of the altar were hollow (אבנים של קרנות חלולות), derived from the verse, and similarly the 'whole stones' requirement is fulfilled by cutting from a larger block.

items.text: Rava's homily on the location of the Temple
items.text_en: Rava's homily on the location of the Temple
items.desc_en: Rava interprets a verse about David and Samuel sitting in 'Noyot' in Ramah as referring to them engaging in the 'beauty of the world' (the Torah), hinting at the Temple's location.

sub.desc_en: Rava interprets the verse about David and Samuel sitting in 'Noyot' in Ramah as referring to them engaging in the beauty of the world (the Torah), hinting at the Temple's location.

items.text: Determining the Temple's location from the book of Joshua
items.text_en: Determining the Temple's location from the book of Joshua
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Temple Mount is the highest point in Israel, and they deduced its location from the book of Joshua: only the territory of Benjamin has the boundary described as 'ascending' without 'descending', indicating the Temple's site.

sub.desc_en: The Sages state that the verse 'וקםת ועלית אל המקום' teaches that the Temple Mount is the highest point in Israel, but they did not know its exact location.

The Gemara concludes that they brought the book of Joshua and found that only in the territory of Benjamin is the boundary described as 'ascending' without 'descending', indicating that the Temple's location is there.

items.text: Debate on building the Temple in Ein Eitam or lowering it
items.text_en: Debate on building the Temple in Ein Eitam or lowering it
items.desc_en: They considered building the Temple in Ein Eitam, which is higher, but decided to lower it slightly, as it is written 'between his shoulders he dwells'. Alternatively, a tradition that the Sanhedrin is in Judah's portion and the Divine Presence in Benjamin's portion led them to lower it to avoid excessive division.

sub.desc_en: The Sages initially thought to build the Temple at עין עיטם (Ein Eitam), which is higher than other places.
They decided to lower it a bit, citing the verse 'וּבֵין כְּתֵפָיו שָׁכֵן' (between his shoulders he dwells).
Alternatively, a tradition holds that the סנהדרין (Sanhedrin) is in Judah's portion and the שכינה (Divine Presence) in Benjamin's portion.
They reasoned that raising it would cause excessive division, so it is better to lower it a bit, as the verse says 'וּבֵין כְּתֵפָיו שָׁכֵן' (between his shoulders he dwells).

items.text: Doeg's jealousy and David's efforts to find the Temple site
items.text_en: Doeg's jealousy and David's efforts to find the Temple site
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Doeg the Edomite was jealous of David over this matter, and David swore not to enter his home until he found the place for the Temple. The verse 'Behold we heard of it in Ephratah' refers to Joshua (from Ephraim) and 'found it in the field of the forest' refers to Benjamin (the wolf).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Doeg the Edomite was jealous of David over the discovery of the Temple site, and cites verses describing David's oath not to enter his home until he found a place for the Lord.
Rava explains the verse: 'In Ephrath' refers to Joshua from Ephraim, and 'in the field of the forest' refers to Benjamin, as it is written 'Benjamin is a wolf that tears apart.'

items.text: Mishnah: Communal peace offerings and guilt offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: Communal peace offerings and guilt offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the guilt offerings (theft, me'ilah, designated maidservant, nazirite, leper, and suspensive guilt offering) and states their laws: slaughter in the north, blood collection in sacred vessels in the north, two applications that are four, and they are eaten within the curtains by male priests, any food, for a day and night until midnight.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing the categories of communal peace offerings and guilt offerings, enumerating the six types of guilt offerings.

The Mishnah states the halachic requirements for these offerings: slaughter in the north, blood collection in sacred vessels in the north, two applications that are four, and they are eaten within the curtains by male priests, any food, for a day and night until midnight.

items.text: Source for tzafon in communal peace-offerings
items.text_en: Source for tzafon in communal peace-offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that communal peace-offerings require slaughter in the north. It cites a baraita of Rabbah bar Rav Chanan that derives this from a hekesh to the chatat. Rava objects that the chatat itself learned from the olah, so a hekesh cannot teach another hekesh. Rav Mari's baraita then derives it directly from the olah via a different hekesh. The first hekesh is repurposed to teach that these offerings are eaten only by male priests.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that communal peace-offerings require slaughter in the north, and Rabbah bar Rav Chanan cites a baraita deriving this from a hekesh (analogy) to the chatat (sin-offering).
Rava objects that the chatat itself learned from the olah (burnt-offering), so a thing learned through a hekesh cannot teach another hekesh.

sub.text: Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana's baraita
sub.text_en: Rav Mari bar Rav Kahana's baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Mari's baraita derives the requirement of tzafon (north) for communal peace-offerings directly from the olah via a different hekesh.
The Gemara repurposes the first hekesh to teach that communal peace-offerings are eaten only by male priests, like the chatat.

items.text: Challenge from the nazirite's ram and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from the nazirite's ram and resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges the repurposed hekesh: if the hekesh to chatat teaches that communal peace-offerings are eaten only by male priests, then the nazirite's ram, which is also juxtaposed to a chatat, should likewise be restricted to male priests. The Gemara initially objects because the ram is eaten by the owners, as shown by the priest taking only the foreleg. The difficulty remains, but an alternative answer is given: the nazirite's ram is called 'kodashim' but not 'kodashei kodashim', and the hekesh is needed to teach that if the nazirite shaved on any of the three offerings, he fulfills his obligation.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges that if the hekesh teaches that communal peace-offerings are eaten only by male priests, then the nazirite's ram, also juxtaposed to a chatat, should likewise be restricted to male priests.
The Gemara objects that the nazirite's ram is eaten by the owners, as shown by the priest taking only the foreleg.
The Gemara notes that the difficulty remains, since the foreleg itself should be restricted to male priests.

The Gemara offers an alternative answer: the nazirite's ram is called 'קדשים' (holy offerings) but not 'קדשי קדשים' (most holy offerings), and Rava explains that the hekesh teaches that if the nazirite shaved on any of the three offerings, he fulfills his obligation.

items.text: Mishnah: Todah and nazirite's ram
items.text_en: Mishnah: Todah and nazirite's ram
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the todah and the nazirite's ram are lesser holy things (kodashim kalim), slaughtered anywhere in the courtyard, their blood requires two placements that are four, and they are eaten anywhere in the city, by anyone, with any food, for one day and night until midnight. The portion lifted up (the breast and thigh) is similar but eaten only by priests and their families.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the laws of the todah and nazirite's ram: they are lesser holy things (קדשים קלים), slaughtered anywhere in the courtyard, their blood requires two placements that are four, and they are eaten anywhere in the city, by anyone, with any food, for one day and night until midnight; the portion lifted up is similar but eaten only by priests and their families.

items.text: Gemara: Location for eating the breast and thigh
items.text_en: Gemara: Location for eating the breast and thigh
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Nechemiah interprets the verse 'in a pure place' for eating the breast and thigh. He deduces that 'pure' implies it is impure in another sense, referring to the Israelite camp (Machaneh Yisrael), excluding the Levite camp. Abaye and Rava debate the derivation from the verses, with Abaye concluding that the place is Machaneh Yisrael, and Rava initially suggests a different reading but ultimately agrees with Abaye.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Nechemiah's interpretation of the verse 'in a pure place' for the breast and thigh, deducing that 'pure' implies impurity elsewhere, referring to the Israelite camp (מחנה ישראל).
The Gemara objects that the verse could be interpreted as 'pure from the impurity of a zav and impure from the impurity of a corpse,' which would refer to the Levite camp (מחנה לויה) instead.

Abaye explains that the verse 'וַאֲכַלְתֶּם אֹתָהּ בְּמָקוֹם קָדוֹשׁ' (and you shall eat it in a holy place) excludes the Levite camp, and the subsequent phrase 'בְּמָקוֹם טָהוֹר' (in a pure place) excludes the Israelite camp, establishing the location as the Israelite camp.

Rava initially suggests that 'אוֹתָהּ בְּמָקוֹם קָדוֹשׁ' excludes the entire holy area, and 'תֹּאכְלוּ בִּמְקוֹם טָהוֹר' includes the Israelite camp, but the Gemara objects that it could include the Levite camp, and Rava responds that we include only one camp, not two.

The Gemara rejects Rava's logic, arguing that if exclusion works only for one camp, then inclusion should also work for only one, and cites the verse 'לֹא תוּכַל לֶאֱכוֹל בִּשְׁעָרֶיךָ' (you may not eat within your gates) to conclude that the correct interpretation follows Abaye.

items.text: Mishnah: Shelamim
items.text_en: Mishnah: Shelamim
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that shelamim are lesser holy things, slaughtered anywhere in the courtyard, their blood requires two placements that are four, and they are eaten anywhere in the city, by anyone, with any food, for two days and one night. The portion lifted up is similar but eaten only by priests and their families.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the laws of shelamim (שלמים) as lesser holy things, including their slaughter, blood application, and eating restrictions.

items.text: Gemara: Source for slaughter in any direction for kodashim kalim and tzafon
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for slaughter in any direction for kodashim kalim and tzafon
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from three verses that kodashim kalim may be slaughtered in any direction (all winds) of the courtyard. It then applies a kal vachomer to argue that if kodashei kodashim, which are not permitted in all directions, are permitted in the north, then kodashim kalim, which are permitted in all directions, should certainly be permitted in the north. Rabbi Eliezer argues that the verse is only needed to permit the north, because a kal vachomer might have excluded it; the verse 'Ohel Moed' teaches that it is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites three verses (וְשָׁחַטוֹ פֶּתַח אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד, וְשָׁחַט אֹתוֹ לִפְנֵי אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד, וְשָׁחַט אוֹתוֹ לִפְנֵי אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד) as the source for permitting slaughter of קָדָשִׁים קַלִּים (lesser sanctities) in any direction (all winds) of the courtyard.

The Tanna Kamma applies a קַל וָחוֹמֶר (a fortiori argument): if קָדְשֵׁי קֳדָשִׁים (most holy offerings), which are not permitted in all directions, are permitted in the north, then קָדָשִׁים קַלִּים (lesser sanctities), which are permitted in all directions, should certainly be permitted in the north.
Rabbi Eliezer argues that the verse is only needed to permit the north, because a קַל וָחוֹמֶר might have excluded it; the verse 'אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד' teaches that it is permitted.

items.text: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Eliezer on the verses
items.text_en: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Eliezer on the verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the disagreement: the Tanna Kamma holds that three verses are written—one for the requirement of the Tent of Meeting opening, one to validate the sides, and one to disqualify the sides of the sides; no verse is needed for the north. Rabbi Eliezer holds that one verse is for the opening, one to validate the north, and one to validate the sides; no verse is needed for the sides of the sides.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: On what basis do the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Eliezer disagree?

The Gemara explains that the Tanna Kamma holds three verses are written: one for the requirement of the Tent of Meeting opening, one to validate the sides, and one to disqualify the sides of the sides; no verse is needed for the north.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer holds one verse is for the opening, one to validate the north, and one to validate the sides; no verse is needed for the sides of the sides.

items.text: Derivation that slaughter requires open doors
items.text_en: Derivation that slaughter requires open doors
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse says 'opening of the Tent of Meeting' in one place and 'before the Tent of Meeting' in another. It teaches as Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: peace-offerings slaughtered before the doors of the Heikhal were opened are invalid, as the verse implies when it is open, not when it is locked. Mar Ukva bar Chama and Rav Yosef bar Chanina concur, and in the West they add that in the Tabernacle, slaughter before the Levites erected it or after they dismantled it is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse uses 'פתח אהל מועד' (opening of the Tent of Meeting) in one place and 'לפני אהל מועד' (before the Tent of Meeting) in another.

The Gemara answers that this teaches as Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: peace-offerings slaughtered before the doors of the Heikhal were opened are invalid, because the verse implies when it is open, not when it is locked.

sub.text: Mar Ukva bar Chama said Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Mar Ukva bar Chama said Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Mar Ukva bar Chama in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina similarly rules that peace-offerings slaughtered before the doors open are invalid, citing the same verse.

sub.text: Rav Yaakov bar Acha said Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Yaakov bar Acha said Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: In the West they teach in the name of Rav Yaakov bar Acha citing Rav Ashi that the same invalidity applies in the Tabernacle: slaughter before the Levites erected it or after they dismantled it is invalid.

items.text: Status of a closed curtain and a Vilun
items.text_en: Status of a closed curtain and a Vilun
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that a closed door is like a locked one, but asks about a Vilun (curtain). Rabbi Zeira states that the Vilun itself is considered like an open door.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a closed door is obviously like a locked one, then asks about the status of a Vilun (curtain).
Rabbi Zeira answers that the Vilun itself is considered like an open door, not a closed one.

items.text: Height of gates and the Pishpeshin
items.text_en: Height of gates and the Pishpeshin
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the height (gavha) of gates. A baraita states that there were two Pishpeshin (small gates) in Beit HaChalifot, eight cubits high, to validate the entire courtyard for eating most holy sacrifices and slaughtering lesser holy sacrifices. The Gemara clarifies that the Pishpeshin themselves were eight cubits high, not that there were eight cubits before them. An objection is raised that all gates were twenty cubits high, but the Pishpeshin are different. The sides are brought in at a corner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the height (גובה) of the gates and proposes to bring a baraita to answer.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda
sub.desc_en: The baraita states that there were two Pishpeshin (small gates) in Beit HaChalifot, eight cubits high, to validate the entire courtyard for eating most holy sacrifices and slaughtering lesser holy sacrifices.
The Gemara initially understands that there were eight cubits of space before the Pishpeshin.
The Gemara rejects this and clarifies that the Pishpeshin themselves were eight cubits high.
An objection is raised from a baraita that all gates were twenty cubits high and ten cubits wide, contradicting the eight-cubit height of the Pishpeshin.
The Gemara answers that the Pishpeshin are different from the regular gates.
The Gemara resolves that the sides (צדדין) are brought in at a corner, explaining how the Pishpeshin function despite their lower height.

items.text: Area behind the Holy of Holies
items.text_en: Area behind the Holy of Holies
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the area behind the Holy of Holies. Rami bar Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: there was a small window (lul) behind the Holy of Holies, eight cubits high, to validate the courtyard for eating most holy sacrifices and slaughtering lesser holy sacrifices. This is the meaning of the verse 'two for the Parbar'—Rabbah bar Rav Sheila explains it means 'towards the outside'.

items.text: Beginning of a new topic: liability for impurity
items.text_en: Beginning of a new topic: liability for impurity
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: one is only liable for impurity... (the text is cut off, but this begins a new discussion).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that liability for impurity applies only under certain conditions, introducing a new topic.

items.text: Opening statement and Tanna's teaching
items.text_en: Opening statement and Tanna's teaching
items.desc_en: The mishnah states the dimensions of the courtyard. A Tanna teaches before Rav Nachman that the entire courtyard was 187 by 135 cubits, and Rav Nachman reports his father's tradition that this area is where priests enter to eat most holy offerings, slaughter lesser holy offerings, and are liable for impurity.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states the dimensions of the courtyard as 187 by 135 cubits.

A Tanna teaches before Rav Nachman that the entire courtyard was 187 by 135 cubits, and Rav Nachman reports his father's tradition that this area is where priests enter to eat most holy offerings, slaughter lesser holy offerings, and are liable for impurity.

items.text: Gemara's question: What does the measurement exclude?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: What does the measurement exclude?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the measurement excludes. It first suggests windows, doors, and wall thickness, but a baraita states these are considered inside. Then it suggests chambers, but a baraita says chambers built outside and opening to the courtyard are considered holy by rabbinic law. The Gemara questions whether they are not holy by Torah law, citing a verse that includes many courtyards for eating.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the measurement of the courtyard (מאה שמונים ושבע על מאה שלשים וחמש) excludes.
The Gemara suggests the measurement excludes windows, doors, and wall thickness, but a baraita states these are considered inside (כליפנים).
The Gemara suggests the measurement excludes chambers (לשכות), but a baraita states that chambers built outside and opening to the courtyard are holy by rabbinic law (מדרבנן).
The Gemara objects that the chambers are not holy by Torah law, citing a baraita that derives from the verse 'בחצר אהל מועד יאכלוה' that the Torah includes many courtyards for eating קדשי קדשים.

items.text: Rava's distinction: Eating is different
items.text_en: Rava's distinction: Eating is different
items.desc_en: Rava states that the Torah's inclusion of many courtyards applies only to eating, not to other matters.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the difficulty by asserting that the Torah's inclusion of many courtyards applies specifically to eating, not to other matters like slaughter or impurity.

items.text: Challenge: Liability for impurity in chambers
items.text_en: Challenge: Liability for impurity in chambers
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava, citing a baraita that states chambers built outside and opening to the courtyard are liable for impurity. The Gemara suggests reading 'not liable' instead of 'liable' to align with Rava's distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava by citing a baraita that states chambers built outside and opening to the courtyard are חייבין (liable) for impurity, contradicting Rava's distinction.
The Gemara suggests reading the baraita as 'אֵין חַיָּיבִין' (not liable) instead of 'חַיָּיבִין' (liable), to align with Rava's position.

items.text: Analysis of the baraita's wording
items.text_en: Analysis of the baraita's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes why the baraita says 'they do not slaughter' and 'they are not liable'. It explains that slaughter requires being opposite the entrance, which is lacking, but liability for impurity is independent of that requirement. The Gemara concludes that even if slaughter is opposite the entrance, the chambers are not sanctified for slaughter, so they are also not liable for impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Granted that the baraita says 'they do not slaughter' because slaughter requires being opposite the entrance, which is lacking; but why does it say 'they are not liable' for impurity?

The Gemara answers: According to your reasoning, even 'they do not slaughter' is said despite slaughter being opposite the entrance, because the chambers are not sanctified for slaughter; similarly, 'they are not liable' for impurity is said because the chambers are not sanctified for impurity liability.

items.text: Challenge regarding eating and the entrance requirement
items.text_en: Challenge regarding eating and the entrance requirement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether eating requires being opposite the entrance, citing Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's teaching about two wickets that enable the courtyard for eating most holy offerings and slaughtering lesser holy offerings. Ravina suggests that eating is derived from this source. The Gemara counters with a verse requiring eating at the entrance, but distinguishes that this applies only to the temporary offerings of the dedication period.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges whether eating requires being opposite the entrance, citing Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's teaching about two wickets that enable the courtyard for eating most holy offerings and slaughtering lesser holy offerings.
Ravina suggests that eating is derived from this source, implying that eating does not require being opposite the entrance.
The Gemara objects with a verse requiring eating at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting.
The Gemara resolves that the verse applies only to the temporary offerings of the dedication period (קדשי שעה), not to permanent offerings.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avudimi's teaching on blood
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avudimi's teaching on blood
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avudimi derives from a verse that blood is invalidated at sunset, because the verse says 'on the day of his offering' – on the day you slaughter you may offer, but on a day you do not slaughter you may not offer. The Gemara begins to question this derivation.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avudimi derives from the verse 'ביום הקריבו את זבחו יאכל' that blood is invalidated at sunset, because the verse implies that only on the day of slaughter may one offer the blood.
The Gemara objects that the verse is needed for another purpose, questioning the validity of the derivation.

items.text: Gemara's derivation that sacrifice must be on the day of slaughter
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation that sacrifice must be on the day of slaughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the verse 'on the day of his offering' teaches that one may only sacrifice on the day of slaughter, not later. It rejects an alternative interpretation that the verse refers to the time of eating, by noting that the word 'his sacrifice' would then be superfluous.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse needs the word 'הקריבו' (his offering) if it already says 'on the day of his sacrifice it shall be eaten', and answers that it teaches the sacrifice must be on the day of slaughter, not later.

The Gemara objects that perhaps the verse means the time of eating follows the time of offering, and then answers that the word 'זבחו' (his sacrifice) would be superfluous, proving the intended derivation.

items.text: Dispute about the third night: Chizkiyah vs. Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Dispute about the third night: Chizkiyah vs. Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: A dispute is reported: regarding one who intends to eat sacrificial meat on the third night (אור שלישי), Chizkiyah rules it valid, while Rabbi Yochanan rules it invalid. Similarly, for one who actually eats on the third night, Chizkiyah exempts him from punishment, while Rabbi Yochanan holds him liable.

sub.desc_en: Reports a dispute: regarding one who intends to eat sacrificial meat on the third night (אור שלישי), Chizkiyah rules it valid, while Rabbi Yochanan rules it invalid.
Chizkiyah explains his ruling: the meat is valid because it has not yet been designated for burning (לא אינתיק לשריפה).
Rabbi Yochanan explains his ruling: the meat is invalid because it has already been excluded from eating (אידחי ליה מאכילה).
Reports a parallel dispute: regarding one who actually eats on the third night, Chizkiyah exempts him from punishment, while Rabbi Yochanan holds him liable.
Chizkiyah explains his exemption: the meat has not been designated for burning, so eating it does not violate the prohibition of נותר (leftover).
Rabbi Yochanan explains his liability: the meat has already been excluded from eating, so eating it constitutes a violation.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Yochanan's position. It states that for offerings eaten for one day, one may begin to think about their blood from sunset, and for their meat and fats from dawn; for offerings eaten for two days and one night, the same applies, with the meat's time beginning from sunset of the second day.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan: for sacrifices eaten for one day, intent regarding the blood is counted from sunset, and for the meat from dawn; for two-day sacrifices, intent regarding the blood is from sunset, and for the meat from sunset of the second day.

items.text: Derivation that meat is not eaten on the third night
items.text_en: Derivation that meat is not eaten on the third night
items.desc_en: A baraitha teaches that one might think offerings eaten for two days could also be eaten on the third night, but the verse 'and that which remains until the day' teaches that it is eaten only during the day, not on the third night.

sub.desc_en: The Sages taught: One might think that sacrifices eaten for two days may also be eaten on the night after the second day, by a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument from one-day sacrifices.
The verse 'והנותר עד יום' (and that which remains until the day) teaches that it is eaten only during the day, not on the night after the second day.

items.text: Derivation that burning is not on the third night
items.text_en: Derivation that burning is not on the third night
items.desc_en: The baraitha continues: one might think that burning should immediately follow eating, but the verse 'on the third day it shall be burned with fire' teaches that burning is done during the day, not at night.

sub.desc_en: One might think that leftover meat should be burned immediately after the eating period, by a kal vachomer from one-day sacrifices.
The verse 'ביום השלישי באש ישרף' (on the third day it shall be burned with fire) teaches that burning is done on the day, not at night.

items.text: Mishnah: Rules for firstborn, tithe, and Passover
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rules for firstborn, tithe, and Passover
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the firstborn, tithe, and Passover offerings are קדשים קלים, slaughtered anywhere in the courtyard, and their blood requires one application opposite the foundation. It then details their differences in consumption: the firstborn is eaten by priests, the tithe by anyone, both in any city, with any food, for two days and one night; the Passover is eaten only at night, until midnight, by its registered group, and roasted.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: The bekhor (firstborn), maaser (tithe), and pesach (Passover) — lesser holy offerings — their slaughter is anywhere in the courtyard, and their blood requires one application, provided it is given opposite the foundation (יסוד).

The Mishnah details the differences in their eating: the bekhor is eaten by priests, the maaser by anyone; they are eaten anywhere in the city, with any food, for two days and one night; the pesach is eaten only at night, only until midnight, only by its registered group, and only roasted.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna and source for foundation
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna and source for foundation
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda identifies the Mishnah's Tanna as Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who derives from the plural forms 'their fat' and 'their blood' that the firstborn, tithe, and Passover require blood and fat offerings on the altar. Rabbi Eliezer then derives that the blood must be given opposite the foundation via a verbal analogy of 'sprinkling' from the burnt offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the Mishnah regarding the firstborn, tithe, and Passover offerings.
Rav Chisda identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
A baraita cites Rabbi Yosei HaGelili who derives from the plural forms 'their fat' and 'their blood' that the firstborn, tithe, and Passover require blood and fat offerings on the altar.
The Gemara asks from where is it derived that the blood must be given opposite the foundation.
Rabbi Eliezer derives that the blood must be given opposite the foundation via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'sprinkling' from the burnt offering.

items.text: Derivation of the burnt-offering's requirement for a foundation and the debate about learning from multiple verses
items.text_en: Derivation of the burnt-offering's requirement for a foundation and the debate about learning from multiple verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that a burnt-offering requires a foundation, citing a verse. It then questions whether the law of two placements that are four (as with a sin-offering) applies here. Abaye answers that the word 'around' is written for both the burnt-offering and the sin-offering, making them two verses that come as one, which cannot teach by analogy. The Gemara then notes that this works for one opinion, but for those who say such verses do teach, there is a third offering (the guilt-offering) making three, and three certainly do not teach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that a burnt-offering requires a foundation, citing the verse 'אֶל יְסוֹד מִזְבַּח הָעוֹלָה' (to the foundation of the altar of the burnt-offering).
The Gemara objects: just as with the sin-offering there are two placements that are four, should the burnt-offering also require two placements that are four?
Abaye answers that the word 'סָבִיב' (around) is written for both the burnt-offering and the sin-offering, making them two verses that come as one, which cannot teach by analogy.
The Gemara objects that this works only for the opinion that two verses coming as one do not teach; for those who say they do teach, the guilt-offering makes three, and three certainly do not teach.

items.text: Tannaic source: The firstborn is eaten for two days and one night
items.text_en: Tannaic source: The firstborn is eaten for two days and one night
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the firstborn is eaten for two days and one night, based on a verse that likens it to the breast and thigh of a peace-offering, which are eaten for two days and one night.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the firstborn is eaten for two days and one night, based on a verse that likens it to the breast and thigh of a peace-offering.

items.text: The question in Yavne and Rabbi Tarfon's answer
items.text_en: The question in Yavne and Rabbi Tarfon's answer
items.desc_en: A question was asked before the sages in the vineyard in Yavne: For how long is a firstborn eaten? Rabbi Tarfon answered: For two days and one night.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that a question was asked in the vineyard at Yavne about how long a firstborn is eaten, and Rabbi Tarfon answered: for two days and one night.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's challenge and the debate with Rabbi Tarfon
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's challenge and the debate with Rabbi Tarfon
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, a student, asked Rabbi Tarfon for his source. Rabbi Tarfon argued from peace-offerings, which are light sacrifices like the firstborn. Rabbi Yosei countered by comparing the firstborn to a sin-offering and guilt-offering, which are also gifts to the priest but are eaten for only one day. Rabbi Tarfon then refined his argument, noting that peace-offerings do not come for sin, unlike sin-offerings. Rabbi Yosei responded that sin-offerings and guilt-offerings do not come as voluntary offerings, unlike the firstborn, so the analogy to them is stronger.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili asks Rabbi Tarfon for the source of his ruling that a firstborn is eaten for two days and one night.
Rabbi Tarfon argues from peace-offerings (שלמים), which are light sacrifices like the firstborn, that the firstborn is eaten for two days and one night.
Rabbi Yosei objects by comparing the firstborn to a sin-offering (חטאת) and guilt-offering (אשם), which are also gifts to the priest but eaten for only one day.
Rabbi Tarfon refines his argument by noting that peace-offerings do not come for sin, unlike sin-offerings, so the analogy to peace-offerings is stronger.
Rabbi Yosei responds that sin-offerings and guilt-offerings do not come as voluntary offerings (בנדר ונדבה), unlike the firstborn, so the analogy to them is stronger.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's intervention and the resolution via a verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's intervention and the resolution via a verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva jumped in and Rabbi Tarfon stepped aside. Rabbi Akiva cited the verse that likens the firstborn to the breast and thigh of peace-offerings, concluding it is eaten for two days and one night. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili countered that one could liken it to the breast and thigh of a thanks-offering, which is eaten for one day. Rabbi Akiva then explained that the extra phrase 'to you it shall be' in the verse adds another existence for the firstborn, implying a longer period.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva jumps in and Rabbi Tarfon steps aside, setting the stage for Rabbi Akiva's argument.

Rabbi Akiva cites the verse 'וּבְשָׂרָם יִהְיֶה לָּךְ' (and their flesh shall be yours) to liken the firstborn to the breast and thigh of peace-offerings, concluding it is eaten for two days and one night.
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili objects that one could instead liken the firstborn to the breast and thigh of a thanks-offering (תודה), which is eaten for only one day and night.

Rabbi Akiva resolves the dispute by noting the extra phrase 'לְךָ יִהְיֶה' (to you it shall be) in the verse, which adds another existence (הֲוָיָה) for the firstborn, implying a longer eating period.

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael's critique and the underlying dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's critique and the underlying dispute
items.desc_en: When these words were said before Rabbi Yishmael, he told them to tell Rabbi Akiva he was mistaken: the thanks-offering itself learned from peace-offerings via a hekesh, and something learned via a hekesh cannot teach via a hekesh. The Gemara then explains what Rabbi Yishmael does with the extra phrase 'to you it shall be'—it teaches that a blemished firstborn is a gift to the priest, which is not found elsewhere in the Torah. Rabbi Akiva learns this from the word 'their flesh' (one for a perfect animal, one for a blemished one). The dispute is whether 'from it and something else' constitutes a hekesh.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that when Rabbi Yishmael heard the exchange, he declared that Rabbi Akiva had erred.

Rabbi Yishmael argues that the thanks-offering itself learned from peace-offerings via a היקש (analogy), and something learned via a היקש cannot in turn teach via a היקש, so the correct derivation is the first one (peace-offerings).

The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yishmael does with the extra phrase 'לְךָ יִהְיֶה' (to you it shall be), and answers that it teaches that a blemished firstborn is a gift to the priest, a concept not found elsewhere in the Torah.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva derives the law for a blemished firstborn from the word 'בְּשָׂרָם' (their flesh) — one for a perfect animal and one for a blemished one — while Rabbi Yishmael interprets 'בְּשָׂרָם' as referring to those firstborns (the perfect ones).
The Gemara concludes that the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva is whether a derivation 'from it and something else' (הֵימֶנּוּ וְדָבָר אַחֵר) constitutes a valid היקש (analogy) or not.

items.text: Application of the dispute to the Yom Kippur service
items.text_en: Application of the dispute to the Yom Kippur service
items.desc_en: The Gemara applies the dispute about whether 'from it and something else' constitutes a hekesh to the verse 'And so shall he do for the Tent of Meeting'—just as he sprinkles in the Holy of Holies, so he sprinkles in the Sanctuary. For the opinion that it is not a hekesh, the verse is needed; for the opinion that it is a hekesh, the verse is explained as teaching that the places learn from each other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the application of the dispute about 'from it and something else' to the Yom Kippur service, noting that for the opinion that it is not a hekesh, the verse 'And so shall he do for the Tent of Meeting' is needed.
The Gemara explains that the verse teaches that just as the High Priest sprinkles the blood of the bull and the goat in the Holy of Holies, so he sprinkles in the Sanctuary.
The Gemara asks what the verse teaches for the opinion that 'from it and something else' constitutes a hekesh.
The Gemara resolves that for that opinion, the verse teaches that the places (Holy of Holies and Sanctuary) learn from each other through a hekesh.

items.text: Alternative explanation of the hekesh and derivation of the tenth for matzah
items.text_en: Alternative explanation of the hekesh and derivation of the tenth for matzah
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation is offered: the hekesh between the two breads was taught in one instance. For the one who says there is no hekesh, the extra word "tavi'u" teaches that any bread brought from another place is like this one, and the word "tihyena" limits the number of tenths. The tenth for matzah is derived from the juxtaposition of "chametz" and "matzah" in the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative explanation: the hekesh (verbal analogy) between the two breads was taught in one instance.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation for the one who says no hekesh
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation for the one who says no hekesh
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that for the one who says there is no hekesh, the extra word 'תָּבִיאוּ' (you shall bring) teaches that any bread brought from another place is like this one, requiring a tenth for the loaf.
The Gemara raises an objection: perhaps just as there are two tenths there, so too here there should be two tenths, but the word 'תִּהְיֶינָה' (they shall be) limits the number.
The Gemara derives the tenth for matzah from the juxtaposition of 'חָמֵץ' (leaven) and 'מַצָּה' (unleavened bread) in the verse.
The Gemara asks: for the one who says there is no hekesh, what can be said? The answer is that the word 'תָּבִיאוּ' is extra.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah's statement about the pesach
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah's statement about the pesach
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna who holds that the pesach is not eaten after midnight. Rav Yosef says it is Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, based on a baraisa where he derives from a gezeirah shavah between "balaylah hazeh" here and in Egypt that the pesach is eaten only until midnight.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna behind the Mishnah's ruling that the pesach is not eaten after midnight.
Rav Yosef identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya derives from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between 'בַּלַּיְלָה הַזֶּה' here and in Egypt that the pesach is eaten only until midnight.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's objection and alternative interpretation
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's objection and alternative interpretation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva objects to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's derivation, arguing that the verse "va'achaltem oto bechipazon" already indicates the time of haste, which is until midnight. He then explains that the phrase "balaylah hazeh" teaches that the pesach is eaten at night and not during the day, unlike other sacrifices.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva objects to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's derivation, arguing that the verse 'וַאֲכַלְתֶּם אוֹתוֹ בְּחִפָּזוֹן' already indicates the time of haste until midnight.
Rabbi Akiva explains that the phrase 'בַּלַּיְלָה הַזֶּה' teaches that the pesach is eaten at night and not during the day, unlike other sacrifices.

items.text: Abaye's challenge: Is the midnight rule biblical or rabbinic?
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge: Is the midnight rule biblical or rabbinic?
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Yosef's identification, arguing that perhaps the Mishnah follows the Rabbis who rule until midnight as a rabbinic safeguard to distance from sin, not as a biblical law. He concludes that the Mishnah's phrase "ela ad chatzot" (but only until midnight) indicates it is biblical, just as the gezeirah shavah is biblical.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Yosef's identification, arguing that the Mishnah might follow the Rabbis who rule until midnight as a rabbinic safeguard (להרחיק מן העבירה) rather than as a biblical law.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's phrase 'אלא עד חצות' (but only until midnight) indicates a biblical law, just as the gezeirah shavah (גזירה שווה) is biblical.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Yosei says that kodshei kodashim slaughtered on top of the altar are as if slaughtered in the north. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda distinguishes between the southern and northern halves of the altar.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Yosei says that kodshei kodashim slaughtered on top of the altar are as if slaughtered in the north; Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda distinguishes between the southern and northern halves of the altar.

items.text: Gemara's first explanation of Rabbi Yosei's view
items.text_en: Gemara's first explanation of Rabbi Yosei's view
items.desc_en: Rav Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan: Rabbi Yosei holds that the entire altar is in the north. The phrase 'as if' teaches that even though the requirement of 'on the thigh' (i.e., the north side) is not met, it is still valid.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan explaining that Rabbi Yosei holds the entire altar is in the north, and the phrase 'כאילו' (as if) teaches that even without the requirement of 'על ירך' (on the thigh) it is still valid.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's challenge regarding Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's challenge regarding Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rav Asi: According to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, does it follow that half the altar is in the north and half in the south? Rav Asi responds with a statement from Rabbi Yochanan that Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda concedes that if one slaughtered opposite them on the ground, it is invalid.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rav Asi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rav Asi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira challenges Rav Asi: according to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, does it follow that half the altar is in the north and half in the south?

sub.text: Rav Asi's objection citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Asi's objection citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Asi objects: you yourself said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda concedes that if one slaughtered opposite them on the ground, it is invalid.

items.text: Scriptural derivation of the dispute
items.text_en: Scriptural derivation of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Asi explains that both Tannaim derive their views from the same verse: 'And you shall slaughter on it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings.' Rabbi Yosei holds the entire altar is for both, while Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda holds half for each. The Gemara then clarifies the necessity of the verse for each opinion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi states that both Tannaim derive their positions from the same verse: 'And you shall slaughter on it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings.'

sub.text: Rav Asi's explanation of Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Rav Asi's explanation of Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei holds that the entire altar is designated for both burnt offerings and peace offerings.

sub.text: Rav Asi's explanation of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rav Asi's explanation of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda holds that half the altar is for burnt offerings and half for peace offerings.
The Gemara objects: if one assumes the entire altar is valid for burnt offerings, then surely it is also valid for peace offerings, so why would the verse be needed for Rabbi Yosei?

The Gemara resolves that the verse is necessary for Rabbi Yosei, because one might have thought that only burnt offerings, which require a large space, are permitted on the altar, but peace offerings, which require less space, might be excluded; the verse teaches that they are also permitted.

items.text: Clarification of 'opposite them on the ground'
items.text_en: Clarification of 'opposite them on the ground'
items.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti asks Ravina what 'opposite them on the ground' means. After rejecting possibilities like the foundation or the surrounding ledge, and the idea of digging cavities, he concludes it refers to reducing the height of the altar by cutting it down.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha mi'Difti asks Ravina what 'opposite them on the ground' means, rejecting the possibility that it refers to the foundation or the surrounding ledge (אמה יסוד אמה סובב) because those are part of the altar itself.

Rav Acha mi'Difti objects that if one were to dig cavities in the ground to slaughter there, the altar would not be made of earth (מזבח אדמה) as required, citing a baraita that prohibits building the altar over cavities or arches.
Ravina resolves that 'opposite them on the ground' means reducing the height of the altar by cutting it down (בצריה בצורי), so the slaughter is performed at ground level opposite the altar's top.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's search for a Mishnaic source
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's search for a Mishnaic source
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira wonders if Rabbi Yochanan's statement is not taught in a Mishnah. He finds support from a Mishnah about the arrangement of wood for the incense, which he identifies as following Rabbi Yosei's view.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira questions whether Rabbi Yochanan's statement is not taught in a Mishnah.
Rabbi Zeira finds support from a Mishnah about arranging wood for the incense, which he identifies as following Rabbi Yosei's view.
Rabbi Zeira identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Yosei's view, citing a supporting baraita.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's rule
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's rule
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei states a general principle: anything taken inside to be given outside must be given near the inside, and anything taken outside to be given inside must be taken near the inside.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei states a general principle: anything taken inside to be given outside must be given near the inside, and anything taken outside to be given inside must be taken near the inside.

items.text: Gemara identifies the cases
items.text_en: Gemara identifies the cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what cases Rabbi Yosei's rule applies to, rejecting the obvious examples of remnants and Yom Kippur coals, and instead identifies the two bowls of frankincense and the daily coals as the intended cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what cases Rabbi Yosei's rule applies to, and rejects the obvious examples of remnants (שיריים) and Yom Kippur coals because their placement is explicitly written in the Torah.

The Gemara identifies the two bowls of frankincense (שני בזיכי לבונה) of the showbread and the daily coals (גחלים דכל יומא) as the intended cases, derived by analogy from remnants and Yom Kippur coals respectively.

items.text: Calculating the altar's dimensions
items.text_en: Calculating the altar's dimensions
items.desc_en: The Gemara calculates how many cubits are needed from the altar to the entrance based on different assumptions about the altar's placement, concluding that Rabbi Yosei must hold that the entire altar is in the north.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yosei assumes about the altar's placement, and calculates that if the entire altar is in the south, one would need 27 cubits.
The Gemara calculates that if the sanctity of the Sanctuary and the Entrance Hall are considered one, one would need 22 cubits.
The Gemara calculates that if half the altar is in the north and half in the south, one would need 11 cubits.
The Gemara calculates that if the sanctity of the Sanctuary and Entrance Hall are one and the altar is half in the north, one would need 6 cubits.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yosei must hold that the entire altar is in the north, as only that assumption yields the required 4 cubits.

items.text: Explanation of the four cubits
items.text_en: Explanation of the four cubits
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the four cubits mentioned consist of one cubit for the base, one for the surrounding ledge, one for the horns, and one for the priests' feet, leaving no space for the entrance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the four cubits of the altar's base consist of one cubit for the base, one for the surrounding ledge, one for the horns, and one for the priests' feet, leaving no space for the entrance.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava identifies the mishnah as Rabbi Yehuda's, who holds the altar is centered, but the Gemara questions the calculation, and resolves that the four cubits exclude the base and surrounding ledge.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava identifies the mishnah as Rabbi Yehuda's, who holds the altar is centered in the courtyard.
The Gemara questions the calculation: according to Rabbi Yehuda's position, the altar should require eleven or six cubits, not four.
The Gemara resolves that the four cubits exclude the base (אמה יסוד) and the surrounding ledge (אמה סובב), so the calculation fits.

items.text: Alternative attribution to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
items.text_en: Alternative attribution to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers attributing the mishnah to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who holds a different view about the altar's placement, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests attributing the mishnah to Rabbi Yosei, who holds the altar is centered, but the text is cut off.
The Gemara rejects this because Rabbi Yehuda explicitly states the altar is centered, making Rabbi Yosei's position unnecessary.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and initial placement of the laver
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and initial placement of the laver
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the laver is placed between the Entrance Hall and the altar, slightly to the south. The Gemara begins by questioning the reasoning behind this placement.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the laver is placed between the Entrance Hall and the altar, slightly to the south.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the laver's position
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the laver's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers various possibilities for the altar's location (entirely in the south, or half north and half south) and the sanctity of the Entrance Hall and Sanctuary, concluding that the laver's placement implies the entire altar is in the north.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by asking what assumption underlies the laver's placement, and considers the first possibility: if the entire altar stood in the south, the laver could be placed from the Sanctuary wall southward, still between the Entrance Hall and the altar.

The Gemara raises a second possibility: if the sanctity of the Sanctuary and Entrance Hall is one, the laver could be placed from the Entrance Hall wall southward, still between the Entrance Hall and the altar.

The Gemara considers a third possibility: if half the altar was in the north and half in the south, the laver could be placed from the Sanctuary wall southward, between the Entrance Hall and the altar.

The Gemara raises a fourth possibility: if the sanctity of the Entrance Hall and Sanctuary is one, the laver could be placed from the Entrance Hall wall southward, between the Entrance Hall and the altar.
The Gemara concludes that the only way to explain the laver's placement is that the Tanna holds the entire altar stood in the north.

items.text: Alternative placement and resolution
items.text_en: Alternative placement and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests an alternative placement for the laver if the altar were entirely in the north, but then resolves the issue by citing a verse requiring the north to be free of vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative placement for the laver: if the altar were entirely in the north, one could place the laver from the wall of the Sanctuary northward, between the Entrance Hall and the altar.
The Gemara further suggests placing the laver from the wall of the Entrance Hall northward, still between the Entrance Hall and the altar.
The Gemara resolves the issue by citing the verse 'צָפוֹנָה' (northward), which requires the north to be free of vessels, thus preventing the laver from being placed there.

items.text: Scriptural support and the dispute with Rabbi Yose HaGelili
items.text_en: Scriptural support and the dispute with Rabbi Yose HaGelili
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse requiring the north to be free of vessels, and identifies the Tanna who disagrees with Rabbi Yose HaGelili as Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who holds the north must be free of everything, even the altar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'צָפוֹנָה' (northward) to require that the north side of the courtyard be free of vessels.
The Gemara identifies the Tanna who disputes Rabbi Yose HaGelili as Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who holds that the north must be free of everything, even the altar.

items.text: Rav's ruling on a damaged altar and its source
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on a damaged altar and its source
items.desc_en: Rav states that all sacrifices slaughtered at a damaged altar are invalid, though he forgot the scriptural source. Rav Kahana later finds the source from Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi Yose: the verse 'and you shall slaughter on it' implies when it is whole, not when it is lacking.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that all sacrifices slaughtered at a damaged altar are invalid, though he forgot the scriptural source.
Rav Kahana finds the source from Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi Yose citing Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yose: the verse 'and you shall slaughter on it' implies when the altar is whole, not when it is lacking.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that both a damaged altar and a damaged Sanctuary invalidate sacrifices. The Gemara explains their dispute: Rav holds that living animals are not rejected (from the altar), while Rabbi Yochanan holds they are rejected.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that both a damaged altar and a damaged Sanctuary invalidate sacrifices.
The Gemara asks: On what principle do Rav and Rabbi Yochanan disagree?
The Gemara explains that Rav holds living animals are not rejected (from the altar), while Rabbi Yochanan holds they are rejected.

items.text: Challenges and resolution regarding Rav's ruling
items.text_en: Challenges and resolution regarding Rav's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's ruling with a baraita about sacrifices before the altar was built or after it was damaged, and with Rav Giddel's statement that incense may be offered at a displaced altar. Rava resolves the contradiction by noting that Rav concedes regarding blood (which is not a living animal).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about sacrifices before the altar was built or after it was damaged, initially questioning the wording.
The Gemara corrects the baraita's wording to 'before the altar was damaged' and rejects the previous formulation.
The Gemara settles on the baraita's correct reading: sacrifices before the altar was damaged are valid, but after it was damaged they are invalid, and the text should read 'that were slaughtered'.
The Gemara objects further by citing Rav Giddel's statement in Rav's name that incense may be offered at a displaced altar, contradicting Rav's ruling about invalid sacrifices.

Rava resolves the contradiction by noting that Rav concedes regarding blood (דמים), meaning that blood offerings are treated differently from living animals, just as Rabbi Yehuda conceded regarding blood in a different context.

items.text: Support from Rabbi Yehuda's opinion
items.text_en: Support from Rabbi Yehuda's opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the source of Rabbi Yehuda's view that a smaller altar is acceptable, citing a verse about King Solomon sanctifying the courtyard because the bronze altar was too small.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the source of Rabbi Yehuda's opinion, citing a baraita that interprets the verse about King Solomon sanctifying the courtyard because the bronze altar was too small, and presents Rabbi Yehuda's position that the verse is understood literally.
Rabbi Yose objects to Rabbi Yehuda's interpretation, beginning his response.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute on altar measurement
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute on altar measurement
items.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda on whether the altar's dimensions (5x5 amot) are measured from the center (Rabbi Yosei) or from the edges (Rabbi Yehuda). The Gemara begins by citing a contradiction from Solomon's offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: Solomon offered 1,000 burnt offerings on the small altar, but in the permanent Temple he offered 22,000 cattle, implying the altar was larger.
The Gemara resolves: 'too small to contain' means the altar was like a dwarf — small in stature but not in capacity, and a dwarf is invalid for service.
The Gemara objects: Rabbi Yehuda should accept Rabbi Yosei's position, but he follows his own reasoning that Moses' altar was large.
A baraita cites Rabbi Yosei's view that the dimensions 'five cubits by five cubits' are literal.
Rabbi Yehuda argues via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'רָבוּעַ' (square) that the altar's dimensions are measured from the center.
The Gemara asks how we know the later altar was measured from the center, and answers from the verse 'twelve cubits to each side' and 'to its four corners'.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei applies the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) only to the height, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda takes the height literally.
Rabbi Yosei argues via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) that the height is twice the length, as in the later altar.
Rabbi Yehuda objects: if the altar were 10 cubits high, a priest on it would be visible from outside the 5-cubit courtyard wall, contradicting the verse.

Rabbi Yosei responds by citing a verse linking the altar to the Mishkan, arguing that just as the Mishkan was 10 cubits high, so too the altar, and the courtyard curtains were 15 cubits, allowing visibility.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Contradiction in Solomon's offerings
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Contradiction in Solomon's offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Solomon offered 1000 burnt offerings on the altar, but also 22,000 peace offerings. The discrepancy suggests the altar was larger than 5x5, prompting the need to reconcile the verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: when calculating burnt offerings and cubit measurements, Solomon's altar in the Temple was larger than Moses' altar, yet the verse says it was too small.
Rabbi Yosei explains that 'too small to receive' is a euphemism meaning the copper altar was disqualified from service, like calling someone a dwarf to indicate disqualification.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda should accept Rabbi Yosei's claim, but notes that Rabbi Yehuda follows his own reasoning that Moses' altar was large.
Rabbi Yehuda uses a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between 'square' here and in Ezekiel to argue that Moses' altar was measured from its center, making it 10x10 cubits.
The Gemara supports Rabbi Yehuda by citing Ezekiel 43:16, which shows that the altar was measured from its center, as indicated by 'to its four sides'.

items.text: First answer: Rabbi Yosei's center-based measurement
items.text_en: First answer: Rabbi Yosei's center-based measurement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei argues the altar is measured from the center, making it 10x10 amot (since 5 from center = 10 total). This resolves the contradiction by showing the altar could accommodate both offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei learns the verbal analogy only with regard to the altar's height.
A baraita is cited stating that Rabbi Yehuda interprets the verse 'and its height three cubits' literally.
Rabbi Yosei argues via a verbal analogy that the altar's height is twice its length, i.e., ten cubits.

items.text: Objection: Rabbi Yehuda's edge-based measurement
items.text_en: Objection: Rabbi Yehuda's edge-based measurement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda counters that the altar is measured from the edges, making it only 5x5. He cites the verse about the courtyard's height to argue that the priest standing on the altar would be visible to all, contradicting the notion of a 10-amot altar.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda objects that the altar cannot be 10 amot tall because the courtyard wall is only 5 amot high, and a priest standing on a 10-amah altar would be visible to all outside, contradicting the verse's implication of privacy.

items.text: Rebuttal: Rabbi Yosei's response with courtyard verse
items.text_en: Rebuttal: Rabbi Yosei's response with courtyard verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei responds by citing the verse about the courtyard's curtains, arguing that the Mishkan's dimensions (10 amot) imply the altar also is 10 amot, and the priest's visibility is not an issue.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei rebuts Rabbi Yehuda's objection by citing the verse about the courtyard curtains, arguing that just as the Mishkan is 10 amot high, so too the altar is 10 amot, and the priest's visibility is not an issue.

items.text: Gemara's question on the dimensions of the altar
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the dimensions of the altar
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah specifies 'five cubits' and 'three cubits its height' in the description of the altar, explaining that these measurements are from the lip of the altar and from the lip of the surrounding ledge respectively.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah specifies 'five cubits' for the altar, and answers that this measurement is from the lip of the altar upward.
The Gemara further asks why the Torah specifies 'three cubits its height', and answers that this measurement is from the surrounding ledge upward.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's application of the gezeirah shavah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's application of the gezeirah shavah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda, when he learns from a gezeirah shavah, learns specifically about the width of the altar. It then addresses the objection that the priest would be visible, answering that although the priest is visible, the work performed by his hand is not visible.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that when Rabbi Yehuda learns from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy), he learns specifically about the width of the altar.
The Gemara objects that according to Rabbi Yehuda, the priest would be visible above the altar.
The Gemara resolves that although the priest is visible, the work performed by his hand is not visible.

items.text: Interpretation of 'Kiddesh' and 'Katan'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'Kiddesh' and 'Katan'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verses 'Kiddesh' and 'Katan' according to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei. For Rabbi Yehuda, 'Kiddesh' refers to the sanctification of the altar, while for Rabbi Yosei it means to establish the altar. 'Katan' for Rabbi Yosei refers to the small altar, while for Rabbi Yehuda it means the stone altar that Solomon made was small.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Yehuda, the verse 'קידש' (sanctified) is understood, but according to Rabbi Yosei, what does 'קידש' mean?
The Gemara answers: for Rabbi Yosei, 'קידש' means to establish the altar there.
The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Yosei, the verse 'קטן' (small) is understood, but according to Rabbi Yehuda, what does 'קטן' mean?
The Gemara answers: for Rabbi Yehuda, 'קטן' means that the stone altar Solomon made under the copper altar was small.

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the basis of the dispute: one Sage (Rabbi Yosei) holds that we derive outside from outside, and not outside from inside; the other Sage (Rabbi Yehuda) holds that we derive a vessel from a vessel, and not a vessel from a building.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: On what basis do they disagree?
One Sage (Rabbi Yosei) holds: we derive outside from outside, and not outside from inside.
The other Sage (Rabbi Yehuda) holds: we derive a vessel from a vessel, and not a vessel from a building.

items.text: Rava's statement about Rabbi Yehuda's view on blood
items.text_en: Rava's statement about Rabbi Yehuda's view on blood
items.desc_en: Rava says that Rabbi Yehuda concedes regarding blood, as taught in a baraita: Rabbi Yehuda says one cup fills from the mixed blood and pours it on the altar, so that if the blood of one of them is spilled, this one renders it fit. The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Yehuda held the entire courtyard sanctifies, then his mitzvah would already be fulfilled. It then considers alternative reasons: perhaps he requires pouring from the force of a person, or perhaps he requires the choicest mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that Rabbi Yehuda concedes regarding blood, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says one cup fills from the mixed blood and pours it on the altar to render fit if one animal's blood is spilled.
The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Yehuda held the entire courtyard sanctifies, then his mitzvah would already be fulfilled.
The Gemara considers an alternative reason: perhaps Rabbi Yehuda requires pouring from the force of a person, but then rejects it by asking why not just take the blood and pour it in its place.
The Gemara offers a second alternative: perhaps Rabbi Yehuda requires the choicest mitzvah (מצוה מן המובחר).

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's teaching on a damaged altar
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's teaching on a damaged altar
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says that if the altar is damaged, one may not eat the remnants of the meal offering in its merit, as derived from the verse 'and they shall eat it as matzot near the altar' – when it is whole, not when it is lacking. The Gemara then extends this to other sacrifices: for most holy sacrifices from the verse 'Kodesh Kodashim', and for lesser holy sacrifices from Rabbi Yosei's exposition.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that if the altar is damaged, one may not eat the remnants of the meal offering in its merit, deriving this from the verse 'וְאִכְלוּהָ מַצּוֹת אֵצֶל הַמִּזְבֵּחַ' — when the altar is whole, not when it is lacking.
The Gemara asks: we have found the source for meal offerings; from where do we derive the same rule for most holy sacrifices and lesser holy sacrifices?
The Gemara answers that for most holy sacrifices, the verse 'קֹדֶשׁ קָדָשִׁים' (holy of holies) teaches the rule.
Abaye answers that for lesser holy sacrifices, the rule is derived from the exposition of Rabbi Yosei, who stated three matters in the name of tradition.

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael's initial argument and conclusion
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's initial argument and conclusion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael proposes that ma'aser sheni might be brought to Jerusalem now, using a kal vachomer from bekhor. After an objection from bikurim, a hekesh from the verse establishes that ma'aser sheni is limited to the time of the Temple like bekhor.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael opens with a kal vachomer: just as bekhor requires the Temple, so too ma'aser sheni may only be brought in the Temple's presence.
The Gemara objects that bekhor requires blood and portions on the altar, unlike ma'aser sheni.
Rabbi Yishmael answers that bikurim prove the point, as they require placement but no blood, yet are limited to the Temple's presence.
Rabbi Yishmael resolves with a hekesh from the verse, juxtaposing ma'aser to bekhor, establishing that ma'aser sheni is limited to the Temple's presence.

items.text: Attempt to revive the kal vachomer and its refutation
items.text_en: Attempt to revive the kal vachomer and its refutation
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests returning to a kal vachomer via a 'tzad hashaveh' argument, but it is rejected because both bekhor and bikurim have a 'tzad mizbe'ach' (aspect of the altar) that ma'aser sheni lacks.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes reviving the logical derivation by using a 'מה הצד' (common element) argument from bekhor and bikurim to ma'aser sheni.
The Gemara rejects the proposal because both bekhor and bikurim share an aspect of the altar (צד מזבח) that ma'aser sheni lacks, making the derivation invalid.

items.text: Question about the underlying assumption
items.text_en: Question about the underlying assumption
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yishmael's assumption: if he believes the original sanctity of the land remains, then bekhor itself should be permitted now; if not, then bekhor should also be questionable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yishmael's underlying assumption: if he holds that the original sanctity sanctified both for its time and for the future, then bekhor itself should be permitted now; if he holds it did not sanctify for the future, then bekhor should also be questionable.

items.text: Ravina's resolution: a specific case of bekhor
items.text_en: Ravina's resolution: a specific case of bekhor
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that Rabbi Yishmael holds that the original sanctity did not endure, and the case involves a bekhor whose blood was sprinkled before the Temple's destruction, and its meat remains. The meat is linked to the blood via hekesh, and ma'aser sheni learns from bekhor.

sub.desc_en: Ravina resolves the contradiction by asserting that Rabbi Yishmael holds the original sanctity did not endure for the future, and the case involves a bekhor whose blood was sprinkled before the Temple's destruction and whose meat still remains.
Ravina explains that the meat of the bekhor is linked to its blood via a hekesh (verbal analogy), and ma'aser sheni learns from bekhor through the same hekesh.

items.text: Objection: can a hekesh teach another hekesh?
items.text_en: Objection: can a hekesh teach another hekesh?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a matter learned through hekesh cannot teach another hekesh. Ravina responds that ma'aser dagan is chullin, and for those who follow the 'lammed' (the derived item), it is fine; for those who follow the 'melammed' (the source), blood and meat are considered one matter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a matter learned through a hekesh (verbal analogy) cannot itself teach another hekesh.
Ravina answers that the ma'aser dagan (tithe of grain) is chullin (non-sacred), so the hekesh is not from a sacred source.
The Gemara questions that this answer works for those who follow the lammed (derived item), but what about those who follow the melammed (source)?
The Gemara resolves that blood and meat are considered one matter, so the hekesh is not teaching another hekesh.

items.text: Ravin's report and Rabbi Yirmeya's critique
items.text_en: Ravin's report and Rabbi Yirmeya's critique
items.desc_en: When Ravin ascended to Eretz Yisrael, he presented this teaching before Rabbi Yirmeya, who criticized the Babylonians for their 'dark' reasoning. He cites two baraitot about the time of the removal of the camps and the two places where kodashim are eaten, implying a different understanding.

sub.desc_en: Ravin ascends to Eretz Yisrael and presents the teaching before Rabbi Yirmeya, who criticizes the Babylonians for their 'dark' reasoning.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's citation of first baraita
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's citation of first baraita
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya cites a baraita about the time of the removal of the camps, when קָדָשִׁים (sacred offerings) become invalid and זָבִים וּמְצוֹרָעִים (those with discharges and lepers) are sent outside the partition.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's citation of second baraita
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's citation of second baraita
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya cites another baraita about two places where קָדָשִׁים (sacred offerings) are eaten, and asks whether the first baraita refers to קָדְשֵׁי קָדָשִׁים (most holy offerings) and the second to קָדָשִׁים קַלִּים (lesser holy offerings).
Ravina resolves the difficulty by stating that both baraitot refer to קָדָשִׁים קַלִּים (lesser holy offerings), and there is no contradiction.

items.text: Distinction between Rabbi Yishmael and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Distinction between Rabbi Yishmael and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that one view follows Rabbi Yishmael and the other follows the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the dispute by attributing one view to Rabbi Yishmael and the other to the Rabbis.

items.text: Alternative explanation
items.text_en: Alternative explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: both views refer to offerings of the highest sanctity, and the phrase 'two places' refers to before the Levites erected the Tabernacle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: both views refer to offerings of the highest sanctity (קׇדְשֵׁי קָדָשִׁים), and the phrase 'two places' refers to the period before the Levites erected the Tabernacle.

items.text: Status of the altar after dismantling the Tabernacle
items.text_en: Status of the altar after dismantling the Tabernacle
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the altar becomes invalid due to being outside (יוצא) after the Levites dismantle the Tabernacle. It concludes that even when the Tabernacle travels, it retains its sanctity, as derived from the verse 'וְנָסַע אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern: after the Levites dismantle the Tabernacle, might the altar become invalid due to being outside (יוצא) its proper place?
The Gemara objects: one might think the altar indeed becomes invalid, so why not say so?
The Gemara resolves: the verse 'וְנָסַע אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד' teaches that even when the Tabernacle travels, it remains an אוהל מועד (Tent of Meeting) and retains its sanctity.

items.text: The Shiloh altar was made of stones
items.text_en: The Shiloh altar was made of stones
