items.desc_en: Rav Huna citing Rav states that the altar at Shiloh was made of stones, based on a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov derives from three mentions of 'אֲבָנִים' that there were three stone altars: Shiloh, Nov, Gibeon, and the eternal Temple.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states in the name of Rav that the altar at Shiloh was made of stones.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov derives from three occurrences of 'אֲבָנִים' that there were three stone altars: Shiloh, Nov and Gibeon, and the eternal Temple.

items.text: Objection from the heavenly fire
items.text_en: Objection from the heavenly fire
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Ami objects: the heavenly fire that descended in Moses' time remained on the copper altar until Solomon's time, and the fire that descended in Solomon's time remained until Menashe removed it. If the Shiloh altar were stone, the fire would have been removed earlier. The Gemara answers that Rav Huna follows Rabbi Nathan, who says the Shiloh altar was copper but hollow and filled with stones.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Ami objects: if the Shiloh altar were stone, the heavenly fire would have left it immediately, contradicting the tradition that it remained until Menashe.
The Gemara answers that Rav Huna follows Rabbi Nathan, who says the Shiloh altar was copper but hollow and filled with stones, so the fire remained on the copper surface.

items.text: Alternative resolution: the fire was not nullified
items.text_en: Alternative resolution: the fire was not nullified
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that 'not removed' means it was not nullified; rather, a spark (שְׁבִיבָא) was sent forth, or it held a crucible (אוּשְׁפִּיזָא) sometimes here and sometimes there.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak reinterprets 'not removed' to mean the fire was not nullified, not that it remained continuously.
The Rabbis explain that the fire sent forth a spark (שְׁבִיבָא) rather than being fully present.
Rav Pappa explains that the fire held a crucible (אוּשְׁפִּיזָא), sometimes here and sometimes there.

items.text: Expansion of the altar in the Second Temple
items.text_en: Expansion of the altar in the Second Temple
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when the exiles returned, they added four cubits to the south and west of the altar, making it like a gamma. Rav Yosef says this was because the space was insufficient. Abaye objects: the First Temple had many people, yet it sufficed; the Second Temple had only 40,000, so why was it insufficient? Rav Yosef answers that in the First Temple, heavenly fire assisted them, but in the Second Temple, there was no heavenly fire.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when the exiles returned, they added four cubits to the south and west of the altar, making it like a gamma.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind this expansion.
Rav Yosef answers that the expansion was because the space was insufficient.
Abaye objects: the First Temple had many people yet sufficed; the Second Temple had only 40,000, so why was it insufficient?
Rav Yosef resolves that in the First Temple, heavenly fire assisted them, but in the Second Temple, there was no heavenly fire.

items.text: Alternative explanation: sixty cubits added
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: sixty cubits added
items.desc_en: When Ravin came, he reported Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi in the name of Bar Kappara that they added sixty cubits. Initially they thought 'מִזְבַּח אֲדָמָה' means it is sealed with earth, but later they thought that drinking is like eating, and 'מִזְבַּח אֲדָמָה' means it is connected to the ground, not built on arches.

sub.desc_en: Ravin reports in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi citing Bar Kappara that they added sixty cubits, initially interpreting 'מִזְבַּח אֲדָמָה' (an earthen altar) as sealed with earth.
Bar Kappara concludes that drinking is like eating, and 'מִזְבַּח אֲדָמָה' means the altar is connected to the ground, not built on arches.

items.text: Opening statement: The altar was not built on cavities
items.text_en: Opening statement: The altar was not built on cavities
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with a brief statement that the altar was not built on cavities, setting the stage for the discussion about its construction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a statement that the altar was not built on cavities.

items.text: Rav Yosef's resolution: The altar's dimensions derived from the Temple
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's resolution: The altar's dimensions derived from the Temple
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef initially questions how the exiles knew the altar's dimensions, citing a verse about the altar being set on its base. He then resolves that David found a verse equating the altar's height to the Temple's height of sixty cubits.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef questions how the exiles knew the altar's dimensions, citing a baraita about the altar being set on its base and a verse that all was given by divine inspiration.
Rav Yosef resolves that David found a verse equating the altar's height to the Temple's height of sixty cubits.

items.text: How they knew the altar's location: Three opinions
items.text_en: How they knew the altar's location: Three opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how they knew the altar's location, since the Temple was not yet built. Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha, and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani offer different answers: they saw the altar built with Michael sacrificing, Isaac's ashes, or smelled the aroma of limbs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how they knew the altar's location, since the Temple's form was recognizable but the altar was not.
Rabbi Elazar answers that they saw the altar already built, with the archangel Michael standing and offering on it.
Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha answers that they saw Isaac's ashes lying in that place.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani answers that from the entire Temple they smelled the incense aroma, but from that spot they smelled the aroma of limbs.

items.text: Three prophets who testified: Two versions
items.text_en: Three prophets who testified: Two versions
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that three prophets ascended with the exiles: one testified about the altar, one about its place, and one that sacrifices may be offered even without the Temple. A baraita adds that a third prophet testified about the Torah being written in Assyrian script.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that three prophets ascended with the exiles: one testified about the altar, one about its place, and one that sacrifices may be offered even without the Temple.

sub.text: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: A baraita adds that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov gives a different version: one prophet testified about the altar and its place, one about sacrifices without the Temple, and a third about the Torah being written in Assyrian script.

items.text: Essential parts of the altar: Horn, ramp, base, and square
items.text_en: Essential parts of the altar: Horn, ramp, base, and square
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that the horn, ramp, base, and square are indispensable, while length, width, and height are not. Rav Huna derives this from the word 'the altar' implying indispensability. The Gemara questions whether this applies to other parts like the laver or surrounding ledge, and cites a baraita that a missing horn was plugged with salt, proving these parts are essential.

sub.desc_en: The Sages taught in a baraita that the horn, ramp, base, and square of the altar are indispensable, but its length, width, and height are not.
The Gemara asks: From where are these matters derived?
Rav Huna answers that the verse uses the definite form 'the altar' (המזבח) wherever these parts are mentioned, implying they are indispensable.

The Gemara objects: If so, would the laver (כיור) according to Rabbi, or the surrounding ledge (סובב) according to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, also be indispensable, since the verse 'תַּחַת כַּרְכֹּב הַמִּזְבֵּחַ' uses 'the altar'?

The Gemara cites a baraita that when the altar's horn was damaged, they plugged it with salt, not because it was fit for service but to avoid a defective appearance, and it rules that any altar lacking horn, ramp, base, or square is invalid; Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda adds the surrounding ledge.

items.text: Definition of the כרכוב (surrounding ledge)
items.text_en: Definition of the כרכוב (surrounding ledge)
items.desc_en: The Sages define the כרכוב as a one-amah walking space for priests between the horns. The Gemara clarifies that priests did not walk between the horns, so it is a walking space of one amah. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves a contradiction by stating there were two ledges: one for decoration and one to prevent priests from slipping.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines the כרכוב (surrounding ledge) as a one-amah walking space for priests between the horns.
The Gemara objects: Do priests actually walk between the horns?
The Gemara emends the baraita: the ledge is a one-amah walking space for priests (not necessarily between the horns).
The Gemara objects from the verse that mentions the כרכוב (ledge) under the altar, implying a different location.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by stating there were two ledges: one for decoration and one to prevent priests from slipping.

items.text: Minimum dimensions: Not less than Moses' altar
items.text_en: Minimum dimensions: Not less than Moses' altar
items.desc_en: Rabbi Mani states that the altar's length, width, and height, though not indispensable, must not be less than the altar Moses made. Rav Yosef says that was one amah. Abaye questions this, citing a verse that the altar was five cubits. Rav Yosef responds that he meant the place of the arrangement, and the verse refers to the entire altar.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that the altar's length, width, and height are not indispensable (אֵין מְעַכְּבִין).
Rabbi Mani qualifies that the dimensions must not be less than the altar Moses made.
The gemara asks how large that minimum is, and Rav Yosef answers: one amah.
The gemara objects by citing the verse that the altar was five cubits, not one.

sub.text: Abaye's clarification and Rav Yosef's response
sub.text_en: Abaye's clarification and Rav Yosef's response
sub.desc_en: Abaye suggests that Rav Yosef meant the place of the arrangement (מְקוֹם מַעֲרָכָה), not the entire altar, and Rav Yosef confirms this.

items.text: Opening anecdote about the sons of Keturah
items.text_en: Opening anecdote about the sons of Keturah
items.desc_en: The sons of Rabbi Tarfon's sister were sitting before him, and he opened with a verse misreading 'Keturah' as 'Yochani', prompting them to correct him.

sub.desc_en: The narrator recounts that the sons of Rabbi Tarfon's sister were sitting before him, and he opened with a verse misreading 'Keturah' as 'Yochani', prompting them to correct him.

items.text: Dimensions of the boards made by Moses
items.text_en: Dimensions of the boards made by Moses
items.desc_en: Abaye bar Huna citing Rav Chama bar Guria states the boards were one cubit long, one cubit wide, and as thick as the rim of a se'ah measure. Rabbi Yirmeya specifies this was a truncated cubit, and Rav Yosef connects this to a baraita about wood not protruding from the altar.

sub.text: Abaye bar Huna citing Rav Chama bar Guria
sub.text_en: Abaye bar Huna citing Rav Chama bar Guria
sub.desc_en: Abaye bar Huna citing Rav Chama bar Guria states that the boards made by Moses were one cubit long, one cubit wide, and as thick as the rim of a se'ah measure.
Rabbi Yirmeya specifies that the cubit mentioned was a truncated cubit (אמה גדומה), smaller than the standard cubit.
Rav Yosef connects this to a baraita that interprets the verse 'על העצים אשר על האש אשר על המזבח' to mean that no wood should protrude from the altar at all.

items.text: Derivation of the ramp's orientation
items.text_en: Derivation of the ramp's orientation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the ramp was on the south, 32 cubits long and 16 wide. Rav Huna derives from the verse that the 'thigh' (ramp) must be in the north and the altar's face in the south. A challenge is raised that both could be in the north, but Rava and Abaye debate the meaning of 'square' (רָבוּעַ) to resolve it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the ramp was on the south of the altar, 32 cubits long and 16 wide.
The Gemara asks: from where are these dimensions derived?
Rav Huna derives from the verse 'וְשָׁחַט אוֹתוֹ עַל יֶרֶךְ הַמִּזְבֵּחַ צָפוֹנָה' that the 'thigh' (ramp) must be in the north and the altar's face in the south.
The Gemara objects: perhaps both the thigh and the face are in the north.
Rava answers: the verse implies the ramp is placed like a man facing his own face — the ramp's face (the side where the priest ascends) faces the altar's face (the south).
Abaye objects: on the contrary, the verse means the ramp is placed like a man sitting with his face to the north.
Rava resolves: the word 'רָבוּעַ' (square) is written, which can be read as 'רָבוּץ' (crouching) or 'רָבוּעַ' (square), implying the ramp is both square and crouching — thus the face is in the south.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Yehuda and the sea of Solomon
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Yehuda and the sea of Solomon
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda that all turns should be to the right toward the east. A challenge that it could be left is rejected by Rami bar Yechezkel's teaching about Solomon's sea, which shows all turns are to the right. The Gemara counters that this teaching is needed for its own context, but the repetition of 'facing' proves the principle.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is brought citing Rabbi Yehuda who derives from the verse 'וּמַעֲלֹתֵהוּ פְּנוֹת קָדִים' that all turns must be to the right toward the east.
The Gemara objects that one could interpret the turn as left toward the east, but immediately rejects this possibility.
Rami bar Yechezkel's teaching about Solomon's sea (ים שעשה שלמה) is cited, showing that all turns are to the right toward the east.
The Gemara objects that the teaching about Solomon's sea is needed for its own context and cannot be used as a general proof.
The Gemara resolves that the repetition of the word 'פֹּנִים' (facing) in the verse proves the general principle, as otherwise the repetition would be superfluous.

items.text: Airspace between the ramp and the altar
items.text_en: Airspace between the ramp and the altar
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei ben Lakonya asks Rabbi Yosi whether there is airspace between the ramp and the altar. Rabbi Yosi argues from the verse that flesh is thrown like blood, implying airspace. Rabbi Shimon suggests standing by the arrangement and throwing, but Rabbi Yosi counters that one throws to the burning arrangement. Rav Pappa concludes that just as blood requires airspace of the ground, so does flesh.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei ben Lakonya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei ben Lakonya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei ben Lakonya asks Rabbi Yosi whether Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai held that there is airspace between the ramp and the altar.
Rabbi Yosi affirms the airspace, citing the verse 'וְעָשִׂיתָ עֹלֹתֶיךָ הַבָּשָׂר וְהַדָּם' to argue that flesh is thrown like blood, implying airspace.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei ben Lakonya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei ben Lakonya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon objects, suggesting one could stand by the arrangement and throw without needing airspace.
Rabbi Yosi counters that one throws to the burning arrangement, which is impossible without airspace because the arrangement is on the altar.
Rav Pappa concludes that just as blood requires airspace of the ground to be thrown, so does flesh, resolving the question.

items.text: Two small ramps for the foundation and the surround
items.text_en: Two small ramps for the foundation and the surround
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that two small ramps emerge from the main ramp for the foundation and the surround, separated by a hair's breadth, based on the verse 'around'. Rabbi Avahu adds the verse 'square'. The Gemara explains both verses are needed: 'around' alone would imply circular, and 'square' alone would imply elongated.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that two small ramps emerge from the main ramp for the foundation and the surround, separated by a hair's breadth, based on the verse 'סָבִיב' (around).
Rabbi Avahu adds that the verse 'רָבוּעַ' (square) also supports the design.

The Gemara explains that both verses are necessary: 'סָבִיב' alone would imply a circular shape, and 'רָבוּעַ' alone would imply an elongated rectangle, so both are written to teach the correct square form.

items.text: Calculation of the ramp and altar dimensions
items.text_en: Calculation of the ramp and altar dimensions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the ramp and altar together are 62 cubits, but the calculation yields 64. The Gemara resolves that one cubit of the ramp flies over the foundation and one over the surround.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the Mishnah that the ramp and the altar together total 62 cubits.
The gemara objects: they should be 64 cubits (32 for the ramp + 32 for the altar).
The gemara answers: it turns out that one cubit of the ramp overhangs the base (יסוד) and one cubit overhangs the surrounding ledge (סובב), reducing the total to 62.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's statement on ramp measurements
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's statement on ramp measurements
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama states that all ramps are three cubits per cubit, except the altar's ramp which is three and a half cubits plus a finger and a third of a finger in its masculinity.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama states that all ramps are three cubits per cubit, except the altar's ramp which is three and a half cubits plus a finger and a third of a finger in its masculinity.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Meal offerings
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Meal offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that meal offerings are pinched (kemitzah) anywhere in the courtyard and eaten within the curtains by male priests, in any food, for a day and a night until midnight.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule for meal offerings: they are pinched anywhere in the courtyard, eaten within the curtains by male priests, in any food, for a day and a night until midnight.

items.text: Gemara: Validity of kemitzah in the Heichal
items.text_en: Gemara: Validity of kemitzah in the Heichal
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that a meal offering pinched in the Heichal is valid, citing the precedent of the removal of the bowls of frankincense. Rabbi Yirmiyah objects with a verse requiring the kemitzah from where the feet of a non-priest stand. Ben Beteira offers a different derivation. The Gemara resolves the objection by explaining that the verse is needed to permit the entire courtyard.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that a meal offering pinched in the Heichal is valid, citing the precedent of the removal of the bowls of frankincense.
Rabbi Yirmiyah objects with a verse requiring the kemitzah from where the feet of a non-priest stand, implying the courtyard, not the Heichal.
Ben Beteira offers a different derivation from the same verse, teaching that if one pinched with the left hand he must return and pinch with the right.

sub.text: Stam (or Rabbi Akiva to Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Tachlifa)
sub.text_en: Stam (or Rabbi Akiva to Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Tachlifa)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by explaining that the verse is needed to permit the entire courtyard, not to restrict the Heichal.

items.text: Gemara: Why the verse is needed for the entire courtyard
items.text_en: Gemara: Why the verse is needed for the entire courtyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that without the verse, one might have thought that a meal offering requires the north side like an olah, or other sacrifices. The verse teaches that kemitzah is done at the southwest corner, following the placement of the meal offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the possibility that a meal offering, like an olah, might require the north side of the altar.
The Gemara rejects the analogy to an olah because an olah is entirely burnt (כליל), unlike a meal offering.
The Gemara rejects the analogy to a chatat because a chatat atones for sins punishable by karet, unlike a meal offering.
The Gemara rejects the analogy to an asham because an asham involves blood rites, unlike a meal offering.
The Gemara rejects the collective analogy to all blood-offerings because they all involve blood, unlike a meal offering.
The Gemara concludes that the verse is necessary to teach that kemitzah is performed at the southwest corner, following the placement of the meal offering, not the north side.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan: Shelamim slaughtered in the Heichal
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan: Shelamim slaughtered in the Heichal
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that shelamim slaughtered in the Heichal are valid, based on the principle that the secondary (the Heichal) cannot be stricter than the primary (the entrance of the Tent of Meeting). An objection from Rabbi Yochanan ben Beteira about eating in the courtyard is resolved by distinguishing between service and eating.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that shelamim (peace-offerings) slaughtered in the Heichal (Sanctuary) are valid, citing the principle that the secondary (the Heichal) cannot be stricter than the primary (the entrance of the Tent of Meeting).

sub.text: Gemara's objection from Rabbi Yochanan ben Beteira
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from Rabbi Yochanan ben Beteira
sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from Rabbi Yochanan ben Beteira, who derives from a verse that קדשי קדשים (most holy offerings) may be eaten in the Heichal when the courtyard is surrounded by gentiles, seemingly contradicting the principle that the secondary cannot be stricter than the primary.

The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing between service (עבודה) and eating (אכילה): regarding service, one may serve in the master's place, so the secondary is not stricter; but regarding eating, one does not eat in the master's place, so the principle does not apply.

items.text: Mishnah: Bird sin-offering and the southwest corner
items.text_en: Mishnah: Bird sin-offering and the southwest corner
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes that the bird sin-offering is performed at the southwest corner of the altar, though valid anywhere. That corner serves three functions below (bird sin-offering, presentations, leftover blood) and three above (wine libation, water libation, bird olah when abundant in the east). All who ascend the altar ascend on the right.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the bird sin-offering is performed at the southwest corner, though valid anywhere, and that this is its designated place.
The Mishnah lists the three functions served by that corner below: bird sin-offering, presentations, and leftover blood.
The Mishnah lists the three functions served by that corner above: wine libation, water libation, and bird olah when abundant in the east.
The Mishnah concludes with the general rule that all who ascend the altar ascend on the right side.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all offerings ascend and descend via the right side, except for the three that ascend and descend via the heel (the ramp).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all offerings ascend and descend via the right side, except for the three that ascend and descend via the heel (the ramp).

items.text: Gemara's derivation of the southwestern corner
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation of the southwestern corner
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the Mishnah's rule. Rabbi Yehoshua derives from a verse that a sin-offering requires the north, and a meal-offering requires the southwestern corner; through a reciprocal analogy, both are required for each other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the Mishnah's rule that the meal-offering is presented at the southwestern corner.
Rabbi Yehoshua cites a verse that calls the meal-offering 'חטאת (sin-offering)' and the sin-offering 'מנחה (meal-offering)', establishing a reciprocal analogy.

Rabbi Yehoshua derives that just as a sin-offering requires the north, so too a meal-offering requires the north; and just as a meal-offering requires the southwestern corner, so too a sin-offering requires the southwestern corner.

items.text: Source for the meal-offering's location
items.text_en: Source for the meal-offering's location
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives the meal-offering's placement at the southwestern corner from the verses 'before the Lord' and 'toward the front of the altar', concluding it is presented at the southwestern corner opposite the horn's tip.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive the meal-offering's own placement, and cites the beginning of a baraita that juxtaposes the verses 'before the Lord' and 'toward the front of the altar'.

The baraita concludes: If one says 'toward the front of the altar' alone, it could be in the south; therefore both verses together teach that the meal-offering is presented at the southwestern corner opposite the tip of the horn.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's alternative approach and Rav Ashi's resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's alternative approach and Rav Ashi's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer proposes a different hermeneutic principle: when two verses conflict, one that fulfills both is preferred. He argues that placing the offering in the west fulfills 'before the Lord' but not 'toward the front of the altar', while the south fulfills both. Rav Ashi explains that this Tanna holds the entire altar stands in the north.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer proposes a hermeneutic principle: when two verses conflict, prefer the one that fulfills both itself and its counterpart, rather than the one that fulfills itself but nullifies its counterpart.
The gemara applies Rabbi Eliezer's principle: placing the offering in the west fulfills 'before the Lord' but not 'toward the front of the altar', while placing it in the south fulfills both.
Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty by explaining that this Tanna holds the entire altar stands in the north, so the south side of the altar is still considered 'before the Lord'.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's statement
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'in any place it was valid'. Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah refers to melikah being valid anywhere, but the specified place is for the blood application.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'in any place it was valid'.
Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah refers to melikah being valid anywhere, but the specified place is for the blood application.

items.text: Baraita on melikah and blood application
items.text_en: Baraita on melikah and blood application
items.desc_en: A baraita taught by the Rabbis states that melikah anywhere on the altar is valid, and blood application anywhere is valid, even without squeezing, provided it is below the red line and from the lifeblood.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that melikah anywhere on the altar is valid, blood application anywhere is valid even without squeezing, provided it is below the red line and from the lifeblood.
The gemara asks: what is the baraita saying?
Rav Ashi clarifies: the baraita means that melikah anywhere on the altar is valid, and squeezing the blood anywhere on the altar is valid.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Bird offering validity and placement
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Bird offering validity and placement
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one performed the sprinkling but not the squeezing, the offering is valid, provided it is done from the red line downward, from the blood of the life.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one performed the sprinkling but not the squeezing, the offering is valid, provided it is done from the red line downward, from the blood of the life.

items.text: Gemara: Scriptural sources for the three items
items.text_en: Gemara: Scriptural sources for the three items
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the three items mentioned in the Mishnah: the bird sin-offering (from the verse 'and he shall bring it near'), the pressing (from the verse 'and all the blood of the bull he shall pour'), and the remaining blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the three items from the Mishnah, beginning with the bird sin-offering, which was already discussed.

The Gemara cites the scriptural source for the pressing (הגשות) from the verse 'and he shall bring it near' and for the remaining blood (שיירי הדם) from the verse 'and all the blood of the bull he shall pour'.

items.text: Gemara: Items performed on the upper half of the altar
items.text_en: Gemara: Items performed on the upper half of the altar
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists items done on the upper half: water libation, wine libation, and the bird burnt-offering when it is large, in the east. Rabbi Yochanan explains the reason: because it is near the ash pit.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items performed on the upper half of the altar: water libation, wine libation, and the large bird burnt-offering in the east.
The Gemara asks for the reason why these items are performed on the upper half.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that it is because the upper half is near the ash pit (בית הדשן), where the ashes are deposited.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan: The great strength of the priests
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan: The great strength of the priests
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan praises the priests' strength, noting that even the lightest bird parts (crop and feathers) are sometimes thrown over thirty cubits. He cites a Mishnah describing the priest's actions on the ramp, and the Gemara calculates the distance, concluding that the place of the men is not counted.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan opens by praising the priests' great strength, noting that even the lightest bird parts (crop and feathers) are sometimes thrown over thirty cubits.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah describing the priest's actions on the ramp, including the placement of the crop and feathers, to support Rabbi Yochanan's claim.
The Gemara questions the calculation, noting that the distances add up to more than thirty cubits, and resolves that the place of the men is not counted.

items.text: Gemara: Reason for all items that ascend the altar
items.text_en: Gemara: Reason for all items that ascend the altar
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why all items that ascend the altar do so, and Rabbi Yochanan answers: for libations, lest they become smoky; for the bird burnt-offering, lest it die from smoke. A contradiction is raised from a Mishnah about the priest's circuit, and Rabbi Yochanan responds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why all items that ascend the altar do so via the right side and circle around, except for the exceptions listed in the mishna.
Rabbi Yochanan answers: for libations, lest they absorb smoke; for the bird burnt-offering, lest it die from smoke.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a mishna (Tamid 33b) where the High Priest circles the altar while holding wine for the libation, implying no concern about smoke.
Rabbi Yochanan begins his response to the objection (the continuation is cut off in the source).

items.text: Rava's proof regarding the libation
items.text_en: Rava's proof regarding the libation
items.desc_en: Rava deduces from the Mishnah's phrasing that the wine for the libation is given to the priest without verbal instruction, as the Mishnah says 'they give him wine to pour' rather than 'they tell him to pour'.

sub.desc_en: Rava deduces from the Mishnah's phrasing that the wine for the libation is given to the priest without verbal instruction, as the Mishnah says 'they give him wine to pour' rather than 'they tell him to pour'.

items.text: The rule of ascent and descent on the altar
items.text_en: The rule of ascent and descent on the altar
items.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that all who ascend the altar go up on the right and descend on the left, except for three items where they go up and down on the west side. The Gemara questions the terminology 'right' and 'left', with Ravina and Rava offering explanations, and concludes with a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: A baraisa states the general rule that all who ascend the altar go up on the right and descend on the left, except for three items that go up and down on the west side.
The Gemara objects: the baraisa says 'right' but the direction described is actually left.
Ravina answers: read the text as 'left' instead of 'right'.
Rava explains: 'right' means the right side of the altar, and 'left' means the left side of the person.
The Gemara objects: the baraisa should have used consistent terminology, either both relative to the altar or both relative to the person; the difficulty remains unresolved.

items.text: Mishnah: Procedure for chatas ha'of
items.text_en: Mishnah: Procedure for chatas ha'of
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes how the bird chatas is performed: the priest ascends the ramp, turns to the surrounding ledge, goes to the southeastern corner, performs melikah from the nape without separating, and sprinkles the blood on the lower wall of the altar.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for the sin-offering of a bird, including the ascent, pinching, and blood application.

items.text: Gemara: Source for sprinkling on the lower wall
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for sprinkling on the lower wall
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraisa that derives from the verse that the sprinkling is from the body of the chatas onto the lower wall of the altar. A logical argument suggesting the upper wall is rejected by a verse about the remnants going to the base. Rava explains that the verse says 'yimatzeh' implying automatic flow.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'וְהִזָּה מִדַּם הַחַטָּאת' (and he shall sprinkle from the blood of the chatas) to teach that the sprinkling is from the body of the bird onto the lower wall of the altar, not the upper wall.

The Gemara raises a logical objection: since a chatas of a large animal is offered on the upper part of the altar, and an olah of a bird is offered on the upper part, a chatas of a bird should also be offered on the upper part.

The Gemara resolves the objection by citing the verse 'וְהַנִּשְׁאָר בַּדָּם יִמָּצֵה אֶל יְסוֹד הַמִּזְבֵּחַ' (and the remainder of the blood shall be pressed out onto the base of the altar), teaching that the sprinkling is on the wall whose remnants flow to the base, which is the lower wall.
The Gemara asks: why not perform the sprinkling on the upper wall first and then on the lower wall?
Rava answers that the verse uses the passive form 'יִמָּצֵה' (shall be pressed out), implying automatic flow, not an active pressing that could be done in stages.

items.text: How to perform melikah for chatas ha'of
items.text_en: How to perform melikah for chatas ha'of
items.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah quotes Rav describing the melikah procedure: holding the wings and legs with fingers, stretching the neck over the thumb. A baraisa adds that the bird is held from outside and the neck is stretched over two fingers, calling it the most difficult service. The Gemara notes that kemitzah and chafinah are also difficult, so it is rephrased as 'one of the most difficult'.

sub.text: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah quotes Rav describing the melikah procedure for a chatas ha'of: holding the wings with two fingers and the legs with two fingers, stretching the neck over the thumb, and performing melikah.
A baraita adds that the bird is held from outside, the neck is stretched over two fingers, and calls this the most difficult service in the Temple.
The Gemara objects that kemitzah and chafinah are also difficult, so this cannot be the only difficult service.
The Gemara resolves by rephrasing: it is one of the most difficult services in the Temple.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Procedure for olah ha'of and laws of intent
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Procedure for olah ha'of and laws of intent
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details the olah ha'of procedure: melikah from the nape with separation, pressing the blood, removing the crop and feathers, and the laws of intent regarding piggul and disqualification. The Gemara clarifies the conditions for piggul and the distinction between proper and improper offering of the matir.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the procedure for the olah ha'of (bird burnt-offering), describing the ascent, melikah from the nape with separation, pressing the blood, and placing the head on the altar.
The Mishnah continues with the removal of the crop, feathers, and entrails, tearing the body without separating, salting, and throwing it on the fire.
The Mishnah states that omissions or changes after pressing the blood do not invalidate, and specifies cases of separation in the chatat versus olah, and pressing blood from head versus body.
The Mishnah rules on improper intent (שלא לשמה) for chatat ha'of versus olah ha'of, stating that chatat is invalid while olah is valid but does not fulfill the owner's obligation.

The Mishnah introduces the laws of piggul (פגול) and disqualification for both chatat and olah ha'of, distinguishing between intent to eat outside the proper place (פסול) and outside the proper time (פגול with כרת), provided the matir (מתן דם) is offered properly.
The Mishnah defines how the matir is offered properly: melikah performed לכתחילה (the ideal standard) with pressing the blood outside the proper time, or vice versa, or both outside the proper time.
The Mishnah defines how the matir is not offered properly: melikah outside the proper place combined with pressing the blood outside the proper time, or vice versa, or both outside the proper place.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Laws of improper intent for bird chatat
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Laws of improper intent for bird chatat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where the bird chatat is invalid due to improper intent (not for its sake, outside its time, or both), and defines the rule for combining half-olive portions. Rabbi Yehudah and the Sages dispute whether pigul (with karet) or pasul (without karet) applies when time and place intentions conflict.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing cases where a bird chatat is invalid due to improper intent (not for its sake, outside its time, or both), defining the common principle that the permitting act was not performed properly.
The Mishnah states that combining half-olive portions of improper intent (outside the place and outside the time) renders the offering pasul (invalid) without karet.
Rabbi Yehudah states his rule: if time-intent precedes place-intent, it is pigul (with karet); if place-intent precedes time-intent, it is pasul (without karet).
The Sages disagree, ruling that in both cases the offering is pasul without karet.
The Mishnah concludes that half-olive portions for eating and for burning do not combine, so the offering remains valid.

items.text: Gemara: Deriving the minimum bird offering and the requirement of a kohen for melikah
items.text_en: Gemara: Deriving the minimum bird offering and the requirement of a kohen for melikah
items.desc_en: The Gemara expounds verses to teach that even one bird may be offered, that a kohen must perform the melikah, and that melikah must be done with the kohen's own hand (not a knife), as per Rabbi Akiva's deduction.

sub.desc_en: The baraita asks why the verse says 'וְהִקְרִיבוֹ' (and he shall offer it), suggesting one might think a bird offering requires at least two birds.
The baraita answers that the word 'וְהִקְרִיבוֹ' teaches that even a single bird may be brought to the altar.

The baraita asks why the verse mentions 'הַכֹּהֵן' (the priest), given a logical inference that since a sheep offering requires the north side but not a priest, a bird offering which does not require the north side should not require a priest either.
The baraita answers that the word 'הַכֹּהֵן' comes to establish that a kohen must perform the melikah.
The baraita asks whether one might think melikah can be performed with a knife, based on a logical inference from slaughter which requires a vessel.
The baraita answers that the juxtaposition of 'כֹּהֵן' and 'וּמָלַק' teaches that melikah must be done with the kohen's own hand, not a knife, as Rabbi Akiva explains.

items.text: Gemara: Location of melikah and the requirement to separate the head
items.text_en: Gemara: Location of melikah and the requirement to separate the head
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that melikah must be performed at the top of the altar (like haqtarah), from the nape of the neck (mimul oreph), and that the head must be separated from the body, as learned from the juxtaposition of melikah and haqtarah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether melikah may be performed anywhere on the altar, either above or below.

The Gemara answers with a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'וְהִקְטִיר' (and he shall burn), teaching that just as haqtarah is performed at the top of the altar, so too melikah must be at the top.

The Gemara derives from the word 'וּמָלַק' (and he shall pinch) that melikah is performed from the nape (ממול עורף), using a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the other occurrence of 'וּמָלַק' in the context of the bird chatat.
The Gemara objects: if the analogy is complete, then just as in the chatat case the kohen pinches without separating the head, so too here he should not separate the head.

The Gemara answers with a second גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from 'וּמָלַק וְהִקְטִיר' (and he shall pinch and burn), teaching that just as haqtarah separates the head from the body, so too melikah requires separation.

The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'וְהִקְטִיר אוֹתוֹ' (and he shall burn it) that the head is burned separately from the body, and the phrase 'וְהִקְטִיר הַמִּזְבֵּחָה' (and he shall burn on the altar) refers specifically to the burning of the head.

items.text: Gemara: The mitsuy (squeezing) of blood and its location
items.text_en: Gemara: The mitsuy (squeezing) of blood and its location
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the blood must be entirely squeezed ("וְנִמְצָה דָּמוֹ – כּוּלּוֹ") onto the upper wall of the altar, not the lower wall or the ramp. It uses a kal vachomer to reject the lower wall and a gezerah shavah to place the mitsuy at the top of the altar, describing the procedure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by interpreting the verse 'וְנִמְצָה דָּמוֹ' to mean the blood must be entirely squeezed onto the upper wall of the altar, not the lower wall or the ramp.
The Gemara raises a possible alternative that the blood might be squeezed on the lower wall, and proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from animal offerings to support this.

The Gemara rejects the lower wall possibility by citing a gezerah shavah (verbal analogy) from the word 'וְהִקְטִיר' to place the mitsuy (squeezing) at the top of the altar, and describes the procedure of ascending the ramp and squeezing the blood on the upper wall.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Nehemyah and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov regarding the location of the entire procedure
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Nehemyah and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov regarding the location of the entire procedure
items.desc_en: Rabbi Nehemyah and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov argue that the entire bird offering must be performed at the top of the altar. Abaye and Rava explain that the dispute is about whether one may arrange a pile of wood on the surrounding ledge (sovev) to perform the melikah there.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Nehemyah and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov assert that the entire bird offering is performed only at the top of the altar.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two rabbis' positions.
Abaye and Rava explain that the dispute concerns whether one may arrange a woodpile on the surrounding ledge (סוֹבֵב) to perform the melikah there.

items.text: Gemara: Removal of the crop with the feathers
items.text_en: Gemara: Removal of the crop with the feathers
items.desc_en: The Gemara expounds the verse "וְהֵסִיר אֶת מֻרְאָתוֹ בְּנֹצָתָהּ" to teach that the crop (zefek) must be removed with its feathers, not cut with a knife. Abba Yosei ben Chanan adds that the gizzard is taken as well, and the school of Rabbi Yishmael describes cutting it like an arched opening.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'וְהֵסִיר אֶת מֻרְאָתוֹ בְּנֹצָתָהּ' and identifies the 'crop' (מֻרְאָה) as the זֶפֶק (the bird's crop).
The Gemara raises a possible alternative: perhaps one may cut the crop out with a knife.
The baraita resolves that the verse 'בְּנֹצָתָהּ' teaches that one must take the feathers along with the crop, not cut it out.
Abba Yosei ben Chanan adds that one takes the crop and also takes the gizzard (קוּרְקְבָן) along with it.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that 'בְּנֹצָתָהּ' means with its own feather, and describes cutting it with a knife like an arched opening (אֲרוּבָּה).

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Baraita on tearing
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Baraita on tearing
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one tore but did not separate, it is invalid. A baraita teaches that 'tearing' must be done by hand, as in the verse about Samson.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one tore but did not separate, the offering is invalid.
A baraita teaches that 'tearing' (שיסוע) must be done by hand, citing the verse about Samson tearing the lion.

items.text: Introduction of the dispute
items.text_en: Introduction of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling that one must not remove the crop contradicts Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who heard a tradition that one does separate in a bird chatat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling that one must not remove the crop contradicts Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who heard a tradition that one does separate in a bird chatat.

items.text: Rav Chisda's explanation: מיצוי
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's explanation: מיצוי
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that the difference between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon is whether the squeezing of blood in a bird chatat is indispensable. The Tanna Kamma holds it is indispensable, so separating would be performing an olah act on a chatat; Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon holds it is not indispensable, so separating is merely cutting flesh.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon.
Rav Chisda answers that the difference is whether מיצוי (squeezing of blood) in a bird chatat is indispensable (מעכב).

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Tanna Kamma's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Tanna Kamma's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Tanna Kamma holds מיצוי is indispensable, so separating would be performing an olah act on a chatat.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon holds מיצוי is not indispensable, so separating is merely cutting flesh.

items.text: Rava's explanation: שהייה in the second siman
items.text_en: Rava's explanation: שהייה in the second siman
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the difference is whether a pause in cutting the second siman in a bird olah is indispensable. The Tanna Kamma holds it is not indispensable, so even with a pause, one is performing an olah act on a chatat; Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon holds it is indispensable, so a pause makes it mere cutting of flesh.

sub.desc_en: Rava proposes that the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon concerns whether a pause (שהייה) in cutting the second siman of a bird olah is indispensable.

Rava explains that the Tanna Kamma holds a pause is not indispensable, so one still performs an olah act on a chatat, while Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon holds it is indispensable, making the pause mere cutting of flesh.

items.text: Abaye's explanation and the dispute between Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak
items.text_en: Abaye's explanation and the dispute between Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak
items.desc_en: Abaye says the difference is whether most of the flesh is indispensable. The Gemara notes that this is the same as the dispute between Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak: one says the difference is a pause in the second siman, the other says it is most of the flesh.

sub.desc_en: Abaye proposes that the dispute between the first tanna and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon concerns whether cutting the majority of the flesh of the nape of a bird sin offering is indispensable.

The Gemara notes that Abaye's explanation aligns with the dispute between Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak: one says the difference is a pause in the second siman, the other says it is the majority of the flesh.

items.text: Proof that most flesh is required initially
items.text_en: Proof that most flesh is required initially
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the dispute that most flesh is required at the outset, and cites a baraita describing the proper procedure for melikah in a bird chatat, which requires cutting the spine and neck without most flesh until reaching the gullet or windpipe, then cutting one siman or most of it with most of the flesh.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute implies that cutting רוב בשר (the majority of surrounding flesh) is required לכתחילה (the ideal standard).
The Gemara answers affirmatively and introduces a supporting baraita.

The baraita describes the proper procedure for melikah in a bird chatat, requiring cutting the spine and neck without most flesh until reaching the gullet or windpipe, then cutting one siman or most of it with most of the flesh, and for a bird olah, cutting two simanim or most of two.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya objects that the disputants have not heard the tradition of Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim citing Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat citing Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua, who said that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon explicitly stated he heard that one separates in a bird chatat. The Gemara then asks what the Mishnah means by 'he shall not separate'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya objects that the disputants have not heard the tradition of Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim citing Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat citing Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua, who said that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon explicitly stated he heard that one separates in a bird chatat.
The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'he shall not separate'.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution on the need to separate
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution on the need to separate
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava challenges Rav Ashi: if the verse 'and he shall not separate' implies no need to separate, then by analogy, regarding a pit where it says 'and he shall not cover it,' would it also mean no need to cover? The Gemara rejects this analogy, explaining that in the pit case the owner is liable to pay, so the responsibility to cover falls on him, but here the verse 'and he shall bring it' distinguishes between the bird sin-offering and burnt-offering, so the phrase 'he shall not separate' teaches that separation is indeed not required.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava challenges Rav Ashi: if the verse 'and he shall not separate' implies no need to separate, then by analogy, regarding a pit where it says 'and he shall not cover it,' would it also mean no need to cover?

The Gemara rejects the analogy, explaining that in the pit case the owner is liable to pay, so the responsibility to cover falls on him, but here the verse 'and he shall bring it' distinguishes between the bird sin-offering and burnt-offering.
The Gemara concludes that the phrase 'he shall not separate' teaches that separation is indeed not required.

items.text: The requirement to squeeze blood from the body
items.text_en: The requirement to squeeze blood from the body
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that for a burnt-offering, even if one squeezed the blood of the body but not the head, it is valid, but if one squeezed the blood of the head and not the body, it is invalid, as derived from the word 'it' (הוּא). Ravina explains the logic: most blood is found in the body.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that for a burnt-offering (עולה), squeezing blood from the body without the head is valid, but squeezing from the head without the body is invalid, derived from the word 'הוּא' (it).
Ravina explains the logic: most blood is found in the body, so the word 'הוּא' teaches that the body's blood is essential for validity.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The standard closing formula 'Hadran alach Kodshei Kodashim' marks the end of the previous chapter.

sub.desc_en: The standard closing formula 'Hadran alach Kodshei Kodashim' marks the end of the previous chapter.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of bird sin-offering and burnt-offering performed in the wrong place or with wrong intent
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of bird sin-offering and burnt-offering performed in the wrong place or with wrong intent
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: A bird sin-offering performed below the red line (as a sin-offering) with the intent of a sin-offering is valid. If performed with the intent of a burnt-offering, or a burnt-offering performed with the intent of a sin-offering, or a burnt-offering performed with the intent of a burnt-offering, it is invalid. If performed above the red line with any of these intents, it is invalid. For a bird burnt-offering performed above the red line with the intent of a burnt-offering, it is valid; with the intent of a sin-offering, it is valid but does not count for the owner. If performed with the intent of a sin-offering below, or with the intent of a sin-offering below, it is invalid. If performed below with any intent, it is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the law of a bird sin-offering performed below the red line with the correct intent.
The Mishnah lists cases where a bird sin-offering performed below with wrong intent or above with any intent is invalid.
The Mishnah states that a bird burnt-offering performed above with correct intent is valid, and with sin-offering intent is valid but does not count for the owner.
The Mishnah concludes with cases where a bird burnt-offering performed below with any intent is invalid.

items.text: First question: Is the distinction in melikah?
items.text_en: First question: Is the distinction in melikah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: In what aspect does the Mishnah's first case differ? If it is in melikah, then the Mishnah would not align with Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who holds that one separates the head in a bird chatat. But wasn't that already established?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: In what aspect does the Mishnah's first case differ? If it is in melikah, then the Mishnah would not align with Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara objects: But wasn't that already established that the Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon?

items.text: Answer: The distinction is in hata'ah
items.text_en: Answer: The distinction is in hata'ah
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers: No, the distinction is in the sprinkling (hata'ah). This is supported by the Mishnah's latter clause, which implies the difference is in hata'ah, as melikah is valid anywhere on the altar. Thus both the first and latter clauses refer to hata'ah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the distinction between the first and latter clauses of the Mishnah is in the sprinkling (הזאה), not in the melikah.
The Gemara supports this answer by citing the latter clause of the Mishnah, which implies the distinction is in the sprinkling, since melikah is valid anywhere on the altar.

items.text: Objection: The cases are different
items.text_en: Objection: The cases are different
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Are they comparable? Each case is as it is! The first clause and latter clause may differ in their distinctions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Are they comparable? Each case stands on its own.

items.text: Second question: Distinction in the bird olah case
items.text_en: Second question: Distinction in the bird olah case
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the bird olah case: In what does it differ? If in melikah, then the Mishnah's latter clause (about me'ilah) would not align with Rabbi Yehoshua, who holds there is no me'ilah. But the Mishnah states there is me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: In what does the bird olah case differ from the bird chatat case?
The Gemara objects: If the difference is in melikah, then the Mishnah's latter clause about me'ilah would not align with Rabbi Yehoshua, who holds there is no me'ilah.

items.text: Attempt to distinguish by mitsuy and resolution
items.text_en: Attempt to distinguish by mitsuy and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the distinction is in mitsuy (squeezing). But then the latter clause (Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua's dispute) would be problematic: if the distinction is in mitsuy, Rabbi Yehoshua would not argue, as he only disputes regarding melikah. So it must be in melikah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the distinction between the first and middle clauses of the Mishnah is in מיצוי (squeezing the blood from the bird's neck).
The Gemara objects by citing the latter clause of the Mishnah (Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua's dispute) and asks what the distinction is there.

The Gemara rejects the suggestion: if the latter clause's distinction were in מיצוי (squeezing), Rabbi Yehoshua would not have argued, since he only disputes regarding מליקה (pinching the neck), not squeezing.

items.text: Resolution: The Mishnah varies by clause
items.text_en: Resolution: The Mishnah varies by clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: The first and latter clauses refer to melikah, while the middle clause refers to mitsuy. This explains the differing rulings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's varying rulings can be explained by assigning the first and latter clauses to melikah and the middle clause to mitsuy.
The Gemara affirms the resolution: the first and latter clauses refer to melikah, and the middle clause refers to mitsuy.

items.text: Mishnah and dispute on me'ilah
items.text_en: Mishnah and dispute on me'ilah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all bird offerings do not cause impurity in the gullet and have me'ilah, except a chatat done below as a chatat. For a bird olah done below as a chatat, Rabbi Eliezer holds there is me'ilah, Rabbi Yehoshua holds there is not. Rabbi Eliezer argues a fortiori: if a chatat, which has no me'ilah when done for its own name, gains me'ilah when its name is changed, then an olah, which has me'ilah for its own name, should certainly have me'ilah when its name is changed. Rabbi Yehoshua responds: No, a chatat changed to an olah is changed to something with me'ilah, but an olah changed to a chatat is changed to something without me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: all bird offerings do not cause impurity in the gullet and have me'ilah, except a chatat done below as a chatat.
The Mishnah presents the dispute: for a bird olah done below as a chatat, Rabbi Eliezer holds there is me'ilah, Rabbi Yehoshua holds there is not.

Rabbi Eliezer argues a fortiori: if a chatat, which has no me'ilah when done for its own name, gains me'ilah when its name is changed, then an olah, which has me'ilah for its own name, should certainly have me'ilah when its name is changed.
Rabbi Yehoshua responds: No, a chatat changed to an olah is changed to something with me'ilah, but an olah changed to a chatat is changed to something without me'ilah.

items.text: First round of the debate: Rabbi Eliezer's kodshei kodashim argument and Rabbi Yehoshua's rebuttal
items.text_en: First round of the debate: Rabbi Eliezer's kodshei kodashim argument and Rabbi Yehoshua's rebuttal
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that kodshei kodashim slaughtered in the south for the sake of kodashim kalim prove that me'ilah applies despite changing the name to something without me'ilah. Rabbi Yehoshua counters that kodshei kodashim have both issur and heter, unlike olah which is entirely heter.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that kodshei kodashim slaughtered in the south for the sake of kodashim kalim prove that me'ilah applies despite changing the name to something without me'ilah, so olah should also incur me'ilah.
Rabbi Yehoshua rebuts that kodshei kodashim have both issur and heter, unlike olah which is entirely heter, so the analogy fails.

items.text: Second and third rounds: asham arguments and rebuttals
items.text_en: Second and third rounds: asham arguments and rebuttals
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer brings an asham slaughtered in the north for shelamim, then an asham slaughtered in the south for shelamim, each time arguing that me'ilah applies despite changes. Rabbi Yehoshua rebuts each: first that asham didn't change place, then that asham didn't change its actions, unlike olah which changed both place and actions.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces Rabbi Eliezer's first argument: an asham slaughtered in the north for shelamim proves that me'ilah applies despite changing the name, so the same should hold for olah.
Rabbi Yehoshua rejects the proof: in the asham case, the location (north) was unchanged, but in the olah case both name and location changed.
Rabbi Eliezer counters with a second case: an asham slaughtered in the south for shelamim, where both name and location changed, yet me'ilah still applies.
Rabbi Yehoshua rejects again: the asham did not change its procedure, but the olah changed its name, location, and procedure.

items.text: Rava's observation: Rabbi Eliezer could have cited an asham with change of owners
items.text_en: Rava's observation: Rabbi Eliezer could have cited an asham with change of owners
items.desc_en: Rava notes that Rabbi Eliezer could have argued using an asham slaughtered in the south for shelamim with a change of owners, which would have changed name, place, and actions, but he did not.

sub.desc_en: Rava questions why Rabbi Eliezer did not argue using an asham slaughtered in the south for shelamim with a change of owners, which would have changed name, place, and actions.

items.text: Gemara's inference: Rabbi Eliezer conceded to Rabbi Yehoshua's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's inference: Rabbi Eliezer conceded to Rabbi Yehoshua's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Rava's observation that Rabbi Eliezer descended to Rabbi Yehoshua's reasoning, citing Rav Adda bar Ahava's statement that Rabbi Yehoshua held: a bird olah done below as a chatat becomes a chatat after one siman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Rava's observation that Rabbi Eliezer conceded to Rabbi Yehoshua's reasoning, citing Rav Adda bar Ahava's statement that Rabbi Yehoshua held: a bird olah done below as a chatat becomes a chatat after one siman.

items.text: Objection and resolution: why the same logic doesn't apply to chatat done above
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: why the same logic doesn't apply to chatat done above
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if so, a bird chatat done above as an olah should also become an olah after one siman. It cites Rabbi Yochanan's statement that 'this is the layout of the entire Mishnah,' and resolves that the phrase means the entire Mishnah is laid out that way.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Yehoshua's logic applies, a bird chatat performed above as an olah should also become an olah after one siman.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan's statement 'this is the layout of the entire Mishnah' means the entire Mishnah is laid out that way, not that the case is limited.

items.text: Rav Ashi's explanation: the difference between bird olah and chatat
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's explanation: the difference between bird olah and chatat
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that for a bird olah done below as a chatat, since its proper place is above and it is valid with one siman, after one siman it becomes a chatat. But for a bird chatat, since melikah is valid anywhere, after one siman it becomes invalid, so it cannot become an olah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that for a bird olah performed below as a chatat, since its proper place is above and it is valid with one siman, after one siman it becomes a chatat.
Rav Ashi explains that for a bird chatat, since melikah is valid anywhere, after one siman it becomes invalid, so it cannot become an olah.

items.text: Repetition of Rav Adda bar Ahava's statement
items.text_en: Repetition of Rav Adda bar Ahava's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara repeats Rav Adda bar Ahava's statement about Rabbi Yehoshua's view that a bird olah done below as a chatat becomes a chatat after one siman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara repeats Rav Adda bar Ahava's statement that Rabbi Yehoshua holds a bird olah performed below as a chatat becomes a chatat after one siman.

items.text: First baraita: chatat for this one and olah for that one
items.text_en: First baraita: chatat for this one and olah for that one
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a case where one designated a bird as a chatat and another as an olah. If both were offered above or both below, half are valid and half invalid; if one above and one below, both are invalid because chatat must be above and olah below.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that rules: if one designated a bird as a chatat and another as an olah, offering both above or both below yields half valid and half invalid, but offering one above and one below invalidates both, because a chatat must be offered above and an olah below.

items.text: Gemara's objection: let the olah be drawn down
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: let the olah be drawn down
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: even if the olah is offered below, let it be drawn down and become a bird chatat? This challenges the baraita's ruling that both are invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: even if the olah is offered below, let it be drawn down and become a bird chatat, challenging the baraita's ruling that both are invalid.

items.text: Defense: Rabbi Yehoshua only said this for one person
items.text_en: Defense: Rabbi Yehoshua only said this for one person
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehoshua's principle only applies when one person designates both birds; here there are two people, so his principle does not apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehoshua's principle only applies when one person designates both birds; here there are two people, so his principle does not apply.

items.text: Second baraita: chatat, olah, unspecified, and specified
items.text_en: Second baraita: chatat, olah, unspecified, and specified
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites another baraita about a case with chatat, olah, unspecified, and specified birds. If all are offered above or below, half are valid; if half above and half below, only the unspecified bird is valid and divided between them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a case with chatat, olah, unspecified, and specified birds, where if all are offered above or below, half are valid, and if half above and half below, only the unspecified bird is valid and divided between them.

items.text: Gemara's objection: why not draw down the specified ones?
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: why not draw down the specified ones?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the baraita says specified birds are not valid, but why? Even if the olah is offered below, let it be drawn down and become a bird chatat!

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the baraita says specified birds are not valid, but why? Even if the olah is offered below, let it be drawn down and become a bird chatat!

items.text: Challenge: is this not according to Rabbi Yehoshua?
items.text_en: Challenge: is this not according to Rabbi Yehoshua?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if you say this baraita is not according to Rabbi Yehoshua, can you really say that? It implies the baraita must align with Rabbi Yehoshua's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that the baraita is not according to Rabbi Yehoshua, arguing that one cannot say this.

items.text: Third baraita: the woman who vowed a bird nest
items.text_en: Third baraita: the woman who vowed a bird nest
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a woman who vowed a bird nest if she gives birth to a male. The baraita details how the priest must offer the birds, and what happens if he does not follow the proper procedure, including cases where she specified or fixed her vow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita about a woman who vowed a bird nest if she gives birth to a male, describing her obligation to bring two bird nests (קינין) — one for her vow (נדרה) and one for her mandated postpartum offering (חובתה).

The baraita explains that when the woman gives the birds to the priest, the priest must arrange and offer them so that three are offered above (the חַטָּאת placements) and one below (the עוֹלָה placement).

The baraita introduces a case where the priest deviated from the proper procedure, offering two above and two below without consulting the woman, and the ruling is that she must bring one additional bird (פרידה) and offer it above.

sub.text: Baraita's ruling — supply from one type
sub.text_en: Baraita's ruling — supply from one type
sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that if all the birds were from one type (מין אחד), the woman brings one additional bird, but if from two types (שני מינים), she brings two additional birds.
The baraita teaches that if the woman specified her vow (פֵּרְשָׁה נִדְרָהּ), she must bring three more birds from one type, or four from two types.
The baraita begins a ruling for the case where the woman fixed her vow (קבעה נדרה), but the text is cut off at this point in the daf excerpt.

items.text: Mishnah: Bird offerings for a woman with uncertain obligations
items.text_en: Mishnah: Bird offerings for a woman with uncertain obligations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a woman is obligated to bring bird offerings and is uncertain whether she brought one or two types, she must bring additional birds. If she gave the birds to the priest but does not know what she gave, and the priest performed the service without knowing what he did, she needs four birds for her vow, two for her obligation, and one sin-offering. Ben Azzai says she needs two sin-offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a woman with uncertain bird offerings must bring five additional birds if from one species, or six if from two species.
The Mishnah adds that if she gave birds to the priest and neither knows what was given or done, she needs four birds for her vow, two for her obligation, and one sin-offering.
Ben Azzai says she needs two sin-offerings instead of one.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's statement about the living and dead
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's statement about the living and dead
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua comments that this case exemplifies the saying: when he is alive his voice is one, but when he is dead his voice is seven, referring to the multiple uncertainties.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua states that this case exemplifies the proverb: when a person is alive his voice is one, but when dead his voice is seven, referring to the multiple uncertainties.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Yehoshua's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Yehoshua's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehoshua's statement was only to exempt from me'ilah (misuse of sacred property), but not to allow the birds to count toward her obligation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehoshua's statement was only to exempt from me'ilah (misuse of sacred property), but not to allow the birds to count toward her obligation.

items.text: Mishnah: Invalid melikah and tum'ah in the gullet
items.text_en: Mishnah: Invalid melikah and tum'ah in the gullet
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all disqualified persons who perform melikah (pinching of the bird's neck) render the melikah invalid, and the bird does not convey tum'ah through the gullet. Similarly, if one performed melikah with the left hand or at night, or slaughtered non-sacred animals inside the Temple or sacred animals outside, they do not convey tum'ah through the gullet. The Mishnah continues with additional cases.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that all disqualified persons who perform melikah render the melikah invalid, and the bird does not convey טומאה (ritual impurity) through the gullet; similarly, melikah with the left hand, at night, slaughter of non-sacred animals inside the Temple, or sacred animals outside do not convey טומאה (ritual impurity) through the gullet.
The Mishnah adds additional cases: melikah with a knife, slaughter of non-sacred animals inside the Temple, and sacred animals outside.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rule of impurity in the gullet
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rule of impurity in the gullet
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists disqualified bird offerings that do not convey impurity when swallowed (e.g., underdeveloped turtledoves, overdeveloped pigeons, a dried wing, blind or lame birds). It then states the general rule: any disqualification that occurred in sanctity does not convey impurity in the gullet; otherwise it does.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists disqualified bird offerings that convey impurity when swallowed.
The Mishnah states the general principle: disqualification in sanctity does not convey impurity in the gullet; otherwise it does.

items.text: Rav's ruling: Left hand, night, zar, and knife
items.text_en: Rav's ruling: Left hand, night, zar, and knife
items.desc_en: Rav states that offering with the left hand or at night does not convey impurity in the gullet, but a non-priest (zar) or a knife does convey impurity.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that pinching with the left hand or at night does not render the bird a carcass causing impurity in the throat, but pinching by a non-priest or with a knife does render it a carcass.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: Why is zar different?
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Why is zar different?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav's distinction: left hand and night have alternative valid contexts (Yom Kippur, limbs/fat), but zar also has a valid context (slaughter). The Gemara objects that slaughter is considered a service, citing Rabbi Zeira that a zar's slaughter of the red heifer is invalid. Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi resolves that slaughter is not a service, but the red heifer is a special case of Temple funds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why zar is distinguished from left hand and night, noting that zar also has a valid context in slaughter, but the Gemara answers that slaughter is not a service.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Zeira ruled a zar's slaughter of the red heifer invalid, implying slaughter is a service.
The Gemara answers that the red heifer is different because it is Temple funds (קדשי בדק הבית).
The Gemara objects that if Temple funds require priesthood, then altar sanctities should certainly require it.

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's resolution
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi resolves that slaughter is not a service, but the red heifer is a special case analogous to the inspection of leprous signs (נגעים), which is not a service yet requires priesthood.

items.text: Attempted proof from a private altar (bamah)
items.text_en: Attempted proof from a private altar (bamah)
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests learning from a bamah that a zar's slaughter is valid, but rejects this because a bamah is not a valid source for Temple law. A baraita is cited that an animal that left the Temple courtyard is valid on a bamah, but the Gemara deflects by noting the verse 'This is the law of the burnt-offering' is adjacent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes learning from a private altar (בָּמָה) that a zar's slaughter is valid, but immediately rejects this because a bamah is not a valid source for Temple law.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that an animal that left the Temple courtyard is valid on a bamah, implying a bamah could be a source.
The Tanna resolves the objection by noting that the baraita is adjacent to the verse 'This is the law of the burnt-offering,' limiting its applicability.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: Zar does not convey impurity
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: Zar does not convey impurity
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan disagrees with Rav, ruling that a zar does not convey impurity in the gullet, but a knife does.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that a non-priest (זר) does not convey impurity in the gullet, but a knife does.

items.text: Supporting evidence from the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Supporting evidence from the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings the Mishnah's phrase 'all who are disqualified' to support Rabbi Yochanan (including zar) and challenges Rav to explain what 'all' includes. Rav could say it includes left hand and night, but those are already explicit. The Gemara then cites the general rule again, similarly favoring Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah: all disqualified persons who pinch produce invalid pinching.
The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Yochanan, 'all' includes a non-priest; according to Rav, what does 'all' include?
The Gemara answers that 'all' includes left hand and night, and explains that the Mishnah states the general rule and then specifies.
The Gemara brings the Mishnah's general rule again, showing it supports Rabbi Yochanan and challenges Rav to explain what 'all' adds.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's extra phrase
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's extra phrase
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the mishnah's phrase 'whose disqualification was not in the sanctuary' comes to include. It answers that the first clause includes slaughter of sacrifices inside, and the latter clause includes melikah of unconsecrated birds outside.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the mishnah's phrase 'שלא היה פסולו בקדש' (whose disqualification was not in the sanctuary) comes to include.
The Gemara answers that the first clause includes slaughter of sacrifices inside, and the latter clause includes melikah of unconsecrated birds outside.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan
