items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's question on limbs of קדשים קלים
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's question on limbs of קדשים קלים
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks whether limbs of קדשים קלים that were brought up before the blood was sprinkled must be taken down. Rabbi Ammi suggests the question is about me'ilah, but Rabbi Yochanan clarifies his question is about descent, and resolves that they do not descend and have no me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks whether limbs of קדשים קלים (lesser holy offerings) that were taken up before sprinkling the blood must be brought down or not.
Rabbi Ami objects that the issue of מעילה (misappropriation) should be the question, to which Rabbi Yochanan replies that מעילה is not his concern since sprinkling determines מעילה.
Rabbi Yochanan clarifies his question is about descent, and resolves that the limbs do not descend and there is no מעילה.
The Gemara resolves that the limbs do not descend and there is no me'ilah.

items.text: Alternate version of the question by Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
items.text_en: Alternate version of the question by Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak presents a different version: Rabbi Yochanan asked about me'ilah, and Rabbi Ammi suggested the question was about descent. The resolution is the same: they do not descend and have no me'ilah.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternate version
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternate version
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak presents an alternate version of the inquiry, where Rabbi Yochanan's question is about מעילה rather than descent.
Rabbi Ami objects that the question should be about descent, to which Rabbi Yochanan responds that descent is not his concern since the limbs have become 'bread of the altar'.
The resolution is the same: the limbs do not descend and there is no מעילה.

items.text: Mishnah citation: 'These were not invalid...'
items.text_en: Mishnah citation: 'These were not invalid...'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that were not invalid for the altar, including blemished animals. This serves as a transition to the Gemara's discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited listing items whose disqualification was in the sanctuary.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's limitation on Rabbi Akiva's ruling
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's limitation on Rabbi Akiva's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabbi Akiva only permitted blemishes that are like a speck in the eye, since such blemishes are valid in birds, and only if the blemish preceded the consecration. He adds that Rabbi Akiva agrees that a female burnt-offering is like a blemish that preceded consecration.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's qualification of Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's qualification of Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan qualifies that Rabbi Akiva only permitted blemishes in the eye, and only when their consecration preceded their blemish.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that Rabbi Akiva concedes regarding a female burnt-offering, which is analogous to when its blemish preceded its consecration.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question: Is there נִרְבָּע in birds?
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question: Is there נִרְבָּע in birds?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether a bird that was the object of bestiality (נִרְבָּע) is disqualified from the altar. He considers whether the exclusion of רוֹבֵעַ and נִרְבָּע from the verse applies only where both exist, or whether the bird is disqualified because a transgression was committed with it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether the category of an animal that was used for bestiality applies to birds.
The Gemara analyzes the two sides: from the verse we might exclude the animal used for bestiality, but perhaps the fact that a transgression was performed with it still disqualifies it.
Rabbi Yirmeya alternatively considers that the bird is disqualified because a transgression was committed with it, regardless of the exclusion's scope.

items.text: Rabbah's proof from Rabbi Akiva's ruling
items.text_en: Rabbah's proof from Rabbi Akiva's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbah brings a proof: Rabbi Akiva permits blemished animals, but if a נִרְבָּע bird were valid, he would have permitted it too. Since he did not, it must be invalid. The Gemara concludes that this is conclusive.

sub.desc_en: Rabba brings a proof from Rabbi Akiva's ruling permitting blemished animals, implying that there is no נרבע in birds.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's additional proof from a Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's additional proof from a Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a Mishnah listing נִרְבָּע among items that are disqualified and convey impurity to garments, proving that a נִרְבָּע bird is indeed invalid.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's citation of a Mishnah
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's citation of a Mishnah
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a Mishnah listing animals that disqualify from the altar, which does not include a bird used for bestiality, supporting that no such category exists for birds.

items.text: Explanation of Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim's statement
items.text_en: Explanation of Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains what Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim teaches: either it is a historical account, or the word 'דּוֹחֶה' means indirectly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what novel point Rabbi Chanina, the deputy High Priest, is teaching us.
The Gemara suggests that either he teaches us the incident itself, or he teaches that the term 'pushing' here means indirect action.

items.text: Ulla's distinction regarding fire on the altar
items.text_en: Ulla's distinction regarding fire on the altar
items.desc_en: Ulla says that the Mishnah's rule that if something ascended it should descend applies only if the fire had not taken hold, but if the fire had taken hold, it remains.

sub.desc_en: Ulla rules that if a limb was taken up and the fire had taken hold, it may remain on the altar, unlike when the fire has not taken hold.

items.text: Two versions of Ulla's statement and their implications
items.text_en: Two versions of Ulla's statement and their implications
items.desc_en: Rav Mari teaches Ulla's statement on the first clause (bones etc. when attached), and Rav Chanina from Sura teaches it on the latter clause (when detached). The Gemara explains that the one who teaches it on the latter clause applies it all the more to the first, but the one who teaches it on the first clause holds that the latter items are not fit for burning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rav Mari taught Ulla's statement on the first clause of the Mishnah (bones etc. when attached), while Rav Chanina from Sura taught it on the latter clause (when detached).

The Gemara explains the logic: the one who teaches it on the latter clause applies it all the more to the first, but the one who teaches it on the first clause holds that the latter items are not fit for burning.

items.text: Mishnah: Items that descend if they ascended
items.text_en: Mishnah: Items that descend if they ascended
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that, if they ascended the altar, must be taken down, including flesh of קדשי קדשים and קדשים קלים, the omer, two loaves, showbread, remnants of meal-offerings, and incense. It also discusses wool, hair, bones, etc., which ascend when attached but not when detached.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that if taken up must be brought down, and cites the verses regarding what ascends and what does not.
The Mishnah adds that wool, hair, bones, sinews, horns, and hooves ascend when attached but not when detached, citing verses for each rule.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of the law from verses
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of the law from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'וְהִקְטִיר הַכֹּהֵן אֶת הַכֹּל' that bones, sinews, horns, and hooves are included when attached, but from 'וְעָשִׂיתָ עֹלֹתֶיךָ הַבָּשָׂר וְהַדָּם' that when detached they are excluded. It then begins to analyze the verse further.

sub.desc_en: A baraita expounds the verse 'and the priest shall burn everything on the altar' to include bones and sinews, but if detached they are excluded by the verse 'you shall make your burnt offerings, the flesh and the blood'.
The baraita raises the possibility that the verse might include even detached bones and sinews.
The baraita answers that the verse 'וְעָשִׂיתָ עֹלֹתֶיךָ הַבָּשָׂר וְהַדָּם' excludes detached parts.
The Gemara begins to analyze the verse further, starting with the phrase 'אִי בָּשָׂר וָדָם' (if only flesh and blood).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rule on separated limbs
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rule on separated limbs
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if limbs are attached they may be brought up, but if they have separated, even if they are on top of the altar, they must be taken down.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: attached limbs may be brought up, but separated limbs must be taken down even if already on the altar.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna and the source of the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the Tanna and the source of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Tanna who holds that separated limbs descend as Rabbi, citing a baraita where Rabbi derives from verses that bones and sinews are included in the burning, but a separate verse limits it to flesh and blood when separated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna who holds that separated limbs descend from the altar.
The Gemara answers that it is Rabbi, citing a baraita where Rabbi includes bones and sinews in the burning even if separated.
The Tanna Kamma explains that the verse 'flesh and blood' teaches that only the consumable parts of the burnt-offering are returned, not bones and sinews.
Rabbi resolves the two verses: one includes all parts, the other limits to flesh and blood; when attached they ascend, when separated they descend.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's distinction: direction of separation
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's distinction: direction of separation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira limits the Mishnah's rule to when limbs separate downward, but if they separate upward, they are considered as having been offered for burning.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira proposes a distinction: the Mishnah's rule applies only when limbs separated downward, but if they separated upward they are considered already offered; the Gemara objects that even if separated upward, they are still separated.
The Gemara objects: even if they separated upward, the Mishnah explicitly says they descend — how can Rabbi Zeira claim otherwise?

items.text: Rabbah's distinction: before or after sprinkling
items.text_en: Rabbah's distinction: before or after sprinkling
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains that the Mishnah refers to separation after sprinkling, but if separation occurred before sprinkling, the sprinkling permits them even for making knife handles.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah reinterprets Rabbi Zeira's statement: the distinction is about timing — if limbs separated before the blood sprinkling, the sprinkling permits them even for mundane use like knife handles.

items.text: Support from Rabbi Yochanan's analogy to the guilt-offering
items.text_en: Support from Rabbi Yochanan's analogy to the guilt-offering
items.desc_en: Rabbah's view aligns with Rabbi Yochanan's teaching that a verbal analogy between the burnt-offering and the guilt-offering permits the bones of the burnt-offering after sprinkling, and the analogy is free from refutation.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states that Rabbah holds like Rabbi Yochanan's teaching in the name of Rabbi Yishmael, who derives a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the phrase 'לוֹ יִהְיֶה' in the burnt-offering and guilt-offering, permitting the bones of the burnt-offering after sprinkling.

The gemara objects that the analogy must be free (מופני) from refutation, otherwise one could challenge that the guilt-offering's flesh is permitted, but the burnt-offering's flesh is not; the gemara resolves that the extra 'לוֹ יִהְיֶה' is written, making the analogy immune.

items.text: Objection from Rav Adda bar Ahava and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from Rav Adda bar Ahava and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava objects with a baraita that bones of a burnt-offering always have me'ilah, but the Gemara emends it to distinguish before and after sprinkling, and notes that this disagrees with Rabbi Elazar's view.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava objects by citing a baraita that bones of קדשים (sacred offerings) have מעילה (misappropriation) before sprinkling but not after, yet bones of a burnt-offering always have מעילה.
The Gemara emends the baraita to distinguish: bones of a burnt-offering that separated before sprinkling have no מעילה, but after sprinkling they have מעילה forever.
The Gemara notes that this emended baraita disagrees with Rabbi Elazar's view that bones separated before sprinkling have מעילה, and after sprinkling are neither benefited from nor subject to מעילה.

items.text: Mishnah: Limbs that fall from the altar
items.text_en: Mishnah: Limbs that fall from the altar
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that limbs that fall from the altar before midnight may be returned and have me'ilah, but after midnight they may not be returned and have no me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states rules for limbs and coals that fell from the altar: before midnight they are returned and have מעילה, after midnight they are not returned and have no מעילה.

items.text: Mishnah: The altar, ramp, and vessels sanctify
items.text_en: Mishnah: The altar, ramp, and vessels sanctify
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that just as the altar sanctifies what is fit for it, so too the ramp and the vessels sanctify what is fit for them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states a general principle: just as the altar sanctifies what is fit for it, so does the ramp, and just as the altar and ramp sanctify, so do the vessels.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's distinction between before and after midnight, and resolves that the case involves limbs that have substance but are not substantial enough to remain on the altar after midnight.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what are the circumstances? If the limbs have substance, they should be returned even after midnight; if they have no substance, they should not be returned even before midnight.
The Gemara begins to answer that the case is necessary (to explain the distinction), but the text cuts off; the continuation is implied.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the rule that the removal of ashes (תרומת הדשן) is done at midnight. Rav answers by citing two verses that use the phrase 'all night' – one for burning and one for removal – implying that the night is divided between the two.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source of the rule that the removal of ashes (תרומת הדשן) is performed at midnight.

Rav answers by citing two verses that both use the phrase 'all night' (כל הלילה) — one for burning the fats and one for removing the ashes — implying that the night is divided between the two services.

items.text: Objection from Rav Kahana
items.text_en: Objection from Rav Kahana
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana objects based on a Mishnah that states the removal of ashes is done at different times on different days: daily at cockcrow, on Yom Kippur at midnight, and on festivals at the first watch. If midnight were biblically mandated, how could the Mishnah allow earlier or later times?

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana objects from a Mishnah that specifies different times for the removal of ashes on different days, arguing that if midnight were biblically mandated, the Mishnah could not allow earlier or later times.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the verse 'until morning' teaches that the night is divided into two parts for burning and removal, but the exact time is not fixed. Therefore, on ordinary days cockcrow suffices; on Yom Kippur, due to the High Priest's weakness, it is done at midnight; on festivals, because many Israelites come early, it is done at the first watch.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that the verse 'עד בוקר' (until morning) is superfluous and teaches that the night is divided into two parts for burning and removal, with the exact time not fixed by Torah.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that on ordinary days cockcrow suffices; on Yom Kippur, due to the High Priest's weakness, it is done at midnight; on festivals, because many Israelites come early, it is done at the first watch, as the baraita's end describes the courtyard filling with Israelites before cockcrow.

items.text: Dispute about limbs offered before midnight
items.text_en: Dispute about limbs offered before midnight
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbah and others regarding limbs that were separated before midnight and then returned to the altar after midnight, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute about limbs that were separated before midnight and returned after midnight, but the text is cut off, leaving Rabbah's position unstated.

items.text: Opening dispute about the power of dawn
items.text_en: Opening dispute about the power of dawn
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that the second midnight (dawn) invalidates limbs, and the school of Rav explains his reasoning: if midnight, which does not cause overnight invalidation, causes invalidation via ikkul, then dawn, which does cause overnight invalidation, should certainly cause ikkul.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that dawn (עמוד השחר) causes invalidation (עיכול) of limbs on the altar.

The school of Rav asks for the reasoning behind Rav Chisda's statement, proposing a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument: if midnight (חצות), which does not cause overnight invalidation (לינה), causes invalidation via עיכול, then dawn, which does cause overnight invalidation, should certainly cause invalidation.

items.text: Dispute about limbs returned after dawn
items.text_en: Dispute about limbs returned after dawn
items.desc_en: For limbs that left the altar before midnight and were returned after dawn, Rabbah says the second midnight invalidates them, while Rav Chisda says they can never be invalidated. Rav Yosef objects, questioning whether midnight at the top of the altar is what causes invalidation, and a ruling is sent from the academy in accordance with Rav Yosef.

sub.desc_en: Rabba rules that limbs removed before midnight and returned after dawn are invalidated by the second midnight (חצות שני).
Rav Chisda disagrees, stating that such limbs never undergo invalidation (עיכול).
Rav Yosef objects: who says that midnight causes invalidation only when the limbs are on the altar? Perhaps it causes invalidation wherever they are found.
The sages in the West (Eretz Yisrael) send a ruling that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rav Yosef.

items.text: Supporting baraitot about limbs returned before midnight
items.text_en: Supporting baraitot about limbs returned before midnight
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba and bar Kappara state that limbs which left before midnight and were returned after midnight are not subject to benefit or misuse (me'ilah) — they have been removed from sanctity.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba states that limbs that left before midnight and were returned after midnight are not subject to benefit or misuse (מעילה).
Bar Kappara similarly teaches that such limbs are removed from the prohibition of מעילה (misuse of sanctified property).

items.text: Rav Pappa's question about the remaining dispute
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question about the remaining dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: since the ruling follows Rav Yosef, and Rabbi Chiya bar Abba and bar Kappara support him, what do Rabbah and Rav Chisda disagree about? Abaye answers: they disagree about the fatty parts (shumanim).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: since the ruling follows Rav Yosef, and Rabbi Chiya bar Abba and bar Kappara support him, what do Rabbah and Rav Chisda disagree about?
Abaye answers: they disagree about the fatty parts (שומנים).

items.text: Does overnight stay on the altar sanctify?
items.text_en: Does overnight stay on the altar sanctify?
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah whether linah (overnight stay) is effective on the top of the altar. He clarifies that if the limbs never descended, it is obvious they may not descend; the question is whether limbs that descended are treated like those on the table (where nothing is lost) or like the ground. Rabbah answers that there is no linah on the altar's top. Rava then tests whether Rabbah accepted this, and through a baraita about limbs that stayed overnight in the courtyard versus on the altar, it is deduced that Rabbah did not accept it.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah whether linah (overnight stay) is effective on the top of the altar, clarifying the scenario: if limbs never descended, it is obvious they may not descend; the question is whether limbs that descended are treated like those on the table (where nothing is lost) or like the ground.
Rabbah answers that there is no linah (overnight stay) on the top of the altar.
The Gemara asks whether Rava accepted Rabbah's answer, and cites a baraita about limbs that stayed overnight in the courtyard versus on the altar.
The Gemara infers from the dispute about limbs that descended that Rabbah did not accept Rava's position, concluding that Rabbah did not accept Rava's question's premise.

items.text: The sanctifying power of the altar and vessels
items.text_en: The sanctifying power of the altar and vessels
items.desc_en: A braita expounds 'whoever touches the altar shall be sanctified' to include the ramp and service vessels. Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan whether service vessels sanctify invalid offerings; Rabbi Yochanan says they do, citing the mishnah. Reish Lakish then clarifies that his question was about using them initially, to which Rabbi Yochanan again cites a supporting source.

sub.desc_en: A baraita expounds the verse 'whoever touches the altar shall be sanctified' to include the ramp and service vessels.
Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan whether service vessels sanctify invalid offerings.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that they do, citing the mishnah that compares vessels to the altar and ramp.
Reish Lakish clarifies that his question was about using the vessels לכתחילה (the ideal standard) to offer invalid sacrifices.
Rabbi Yochanan responds that even for לכתחילה (the ideal standard), the mishnah already teaches that vessels sanctify.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's phrase
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's phrase
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's phrase 'invalid people received and threw the blood' means both receiving and throwing were done by invalid people, or only one of them. It concludes that it could mean either receiving by invalid people or throwing by invalid people.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's phrase 'invalid people received and threw the blood' means both receiving and throwing were done by invalid people.
The Gemara answers that the phrase could mean either receiving by invalid people or throwing by invalid people, not necessarily both.

items.text: Is the airspace of the altar like the altar?
items.text_en: Is the airspace of the altar like the altar?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises the question whether the airspace of the altar is considered like the altar. It brings a proof from the ramp: just as the ramp sanctifies, so too the airspace of the ramp must sanctify, otherwise one could not lift an offering from the ramp to the altar through the airspace. The resolution is that the majority of the offering's location determines its status.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the question whether the airspace of the altar is considered like the altar itself.

The Gemara brings a proof from the ramp: just as the altar sanctifies, so too the ramp sanctifies; if the airspace of the altar were not like the altar, then the airspace of the ramp would not be like the ramp, and one could not lift an offering from the ramp to the altar through the airspace without it being considered a descent (ירוד).

The Gemara resolves that the offering is pulled along, and the majority of its location determines its status: if most of the offering is over the ramp, it is considered on the ramp; if most is over the altar, it is considered on the altar.

items.text: Resolving Rami bar Hama's question about connection
items.text_en: Resolving Rami bar Hama's question about connection
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that from the previous discussion one can resolve Rami bar Hama's question about whether there is connection for limbs of burnt offerings. It asserts that the answer is yes, there is connection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves Rami bar Hama's question about whether there is connection for limbs of burnt offerings, concluding that there is connection.

items.text: Rava bar Rav Chanan's objection regarding bird offerings
items.text_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan's objection regarding bird offerings
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan objects: if the airspace of the altar is like the altar, how can a bird burnt offering be disqualified by intent? The altar would immediately capture it, preventing any disqualifying thought.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan objects: if the airspace of the altar is like the altar, how can a bird burnt offering be disqualified by intent, since the altar would immediately capture it?
The gemara rhetorically concludes that the altar would indeed capture the bird, making disqualifying intent impossible.

items.text: Rav Shimi bar Ashi's answer to the objection
items.text_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi's answer to the objection
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi answers that one can find a case where intent disqualifies: if the priest says he intends to bring the bird down tomorrow and then offer it, the intent takes effect before the altar captures it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi answers that one can find a case where intent disqualifies: if the priest says he intends to bring the bird down tomorrow and then offer it, the intent takes effect before the altar captures it.

items.text: Debate between Rava and Rabbah about overnight stay
items.text_en: Debate between Rava and Rabbah about overnight stay
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Shimi's answer works for Rava, who holds that overnight stay is effective on the altar top, but not for Rabbah, who holds it is not. It then provides an alternative case for Rabbah: intending to bring it down before dawn and offer it after dawn.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Shimi's answer works for Rava, who holds that לינה (overnight stay) is effective on the altar top, but not for Rabbah, who holds it is not, so the case of intending to bring it down tomorrow is irrelevant for Rabbah.
The Gemara provides an alternative case for Rabbah: intending to bring the bird down before dawn and offer it after dawn, so the overnight stay is not on the altar top.

items.text: Conclusion: airspace of the altar is like the altar
items.text_en: Conclusion: airspace of the altar is like the altar
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that from the discussion one can resolve that the airspace of the altar is indeed like the altar, because otherwise the objection of Rava bar Rav Chanan would not arise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that from the objection of Rava bar Rav Chanan one can resolve that the airspace of the altar is like the altar, because otherwise the objection would not arise.

items.text: Question about sprinkling blood from invalid offerings
items.text_en: Question about sprinkling blood from invalid offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one sprinkles blood from a disqualified bird sin-offering, as the blood would drip down. It also asks how other invalid offerings are sprinkled. The Gemara suggests that the blood is touched to the altar, but this is rejected as it is actually a squeezing action, not sprinkling. Rav Ashi answers that if the offering is held at the top of the altar, it works, but if hung on a rod, it is a problem; the issue remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how one sprinkles the blood of a disqualified bird sin-offering, since the blood would drip down, and similarly how other invalid offerings are sprinkled.
The Gemara objects that touching the blood to the altar is not sprinkling but squeezing, and pouring is not sprinkling.
The Gemara adds that this method is not the proper way of sprinkling or throwing blood.
Rav Ashi answers that if the offering is held at the top of the altar it works, but if hung on a rod it is problematic, and the issue remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Mishnah: Rules for sanctification by vessels
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rules for sanctification by vessels
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that liquid vessels sanctify liquids, and dry measures sanctify dry items. A liquid vessel does not sanctify dry items, nor does a dry vessel sanctify liquids. Vessels that are punctured sanctify only if they can still perform their original function when whole. All vessels sanctify only within the Temple.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that vessels for liquids sanctify liquids, dry measures sanctify dry items, and they only sanctify within the Temple.

items.text: Shmuel's distinction between measures and basins
items.text_en: Shmuel's distinction between measures and basins
items.desc_en: Shmuel says that the Mishnah's rule applies only to dry measures, but basins (mizrakot) sanctify even dry items, as derived from the verse 'both full of fine flour'. Rav Acha from Difti questions this, noting that a meal-offering is wet. Ravina answers that the verse refers to the dry part of the meal-offering, or alternatively, the meal-offering is considered dry relative to blood.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel distinguishes that the Mishnah's rule about dry measures applies only to dry measures, but basins (מזרקות) sanctify even dry items, citing the verse 'both full of fine flour'.
Rav Acha from Difti questions Ravina, noting that a meal-offering (מנחה) is wet, so how can it serve as a proof for dry items?
Ravina answers that the verse refers only to the dry part of the meal-offering.
Alternatively, the meal-offering is considered dry relative to blood.

items.text: Shmuel's three conditions for sanctification
items.text_en: Shmuel's three conditions for sanctification
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that service vessels sanctify only when whole, full, and from within. An alternative version adds 'from inside'. The difference between the versions is the case of smoothing out measures. A baraita teaches that vessels sanctify only when whole, full, from within, and inside.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that service vessels (כלי שרת) sanctify only when whole (שלמין), full (מלאין), and from within (מתוכן).
An alternative version of Shmuel's statement replaces 'from within' (מתוכן) with 'from inside' (מבפנים).
The gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two versions of Shmuel's statement.
The gemara answers that the difference lies in the case of smoothing out measures (בירוצי מדות) — whether the vessel's interior is considered sanctified even after the measure is leveled off.
A baraita (תנא) teaches that vessels sanctify only when whole, full, from within (מתוכן), and inside (בפנים), combining both versions.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's distinction about intention to add
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's distinction about intention to add
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi quoting Rabbi Yochanan says that the rule that vessels must be full applies only when one does not intend to add more, but if one intends to add, each initial portion is sanctified. A baraita supports this, with Rabbi Yosei stating the same distinction.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan distinguishes: the rule that vessels must be full applies only when one does not intend to add more, but if one intends to add, each initial portion is sanctified.
A baraita supports this, with Rabbi Yosei stating the same distinction: full measures are required only when there is no intention to add, but if one intends to add, each initial amount is sacred.

items.text: Rav's distinction: sanctification for offering vs. disqualification
items.text_en: Rav's distinction: sanctification for offering vs. disqualification
items.desc_en: Rav (or Rav Asi) says that vessels do not sanctify items to be offered, but they do sanctify them to become disqualified. Some teach this regarding the Mishnah's rule, while others teach it regarding a baraita about bringing offerings from untithed produce.

sub.desc_en: Rav (or Rav Asi) states that vessels used for liquids do not sanctify dry items for sacrifice, but they do sanctify them to become disqualified.

An alternative version teaches that Rav's distinction applies to a baraita about bringing offerings from untithed produce, orla, and diverse kinds: they are not sanctified for sacrifice but are sanctified for disqualification.

items.text: Baraita: Rules for damaged vessels and knives
items.text_en: Baraita: Rules for damaged vessels and knives
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that punctured sacred vessels may not be melted down or have lead poured into them. If they are chipped, they may not be repaired. A chipped knife may not be sharpened, and if the blade is dislodged, it may not be reattached. Abba Shaul recounts that there was a knife for mixing (matrefet) in the Temple, and the priests took a vote and hid it.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that perforated sacred vessels may not be melted down or have lead poured into them; Abba Shaul adds that a certain knife was hidden away by the priests.
Abba Shaul adds a tradition that there was a mixing knife (מטרפת) in the Temple, and the priests voted to hide it away.

items.text: Baraita: Rules for priestly garments and laundering
items.text_en: Baraita: Rules for priestly garments and laundering
items.desc_en: A baraita states that priestly garments must be woven, not sewn with a needle. If they become soiled, they may not be laundered with natron or alkali. Abaye explains that the baraita means that if they are soaked in water, they may be laundered with natron and alkali.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that priestly garments must be woven (not sewn) and, if soiled, may not be laundered with natron or alkali.
The gemara infers from the baraita's restriction that laundering with water alone is permitted, and questions this implication.
Abaye explains that the baraita means: if the garments were first soaked in water, then they may be laundered with natron and alkali.

items.text: Opening baraita about laundering the me'il
items.text_en: Opening baraita about laundering the me'il
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses whether the me'il can be laundered with natron and aloe, and a dissenting opinion says it should not be laundered at all because there is no poverty in a place of wealth.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that the me'il, once stained, is laundered with natron and aloe, and even with water it is not washed.
The dissenting opinion (יש אומרים) holds that the me'il should not be laundered at all, because there is no poverty in a place of wealth.

items.text: Description of the me'il and dispute about bells
items.text_en: Description of the me'il and dispute about bells
items.desc_en: The me'il was entirely of techelet. Its hem had pomegranate-shaped ornaments and bells. Rabbi Dosa in the name of Rabbi Yehuda disputes the number of bells, saying there were 36, not 72.

sub.desc_en: The baraita describes the me'il (robe) as entirely of techelet, with pomegranate-shaped ornaments at its hem.
The baraita states that 72 bells and 72 pomegranates were attached, 36 on each side.
Rabbi Dosa in the name of Rabbi Yehuda disputes the number, saying there were only 36 bells, 18 on each side.

items.text: Parallel dispute in negaim
items.text_en: Parallel dispute in negaim
items.desc_en: Rabbi Inyoni bar Sason notes that the same dispute (36 vs. 72) appears in the laws of negaim, between Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas and Akavya ben Mahalalel.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Inyoni bar Sason notes that the same dispute (36 vs. 72) appears in the laws of negaim, between Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas and Akavya ben Mahalalel.

items.text: Why the parasha of korbanot is adjacent to priestly garments
items.text_en: Why the parasha of korbanot is adjacent to priestly garments
items.desc_en: Rabbi Inyoni bar Sason explains that just as korbanot atone, so do the priestly garments atone.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Inyoni bar Sason explains that the juxtaposition of the parasha of korbanot to the priestly garments teaches that just as korbanot atone, so do the priestly garments atone.

items.text: Each garment's specific atonement
items.text_en: Each garment's specific atonement
items.desc_en: Each priestly garment atones for a specific sin: the ketonet for bloodshed, the michnasayim for sexual immorality, the mitznefet for haughtiness, the avnet for heart-thoughts, the choshen for perversion of justice, the ephod for idolatry, the me'il for evil speech, and the tzitz for brazenness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by listing the atonement of the ketonet (for bloodshed) and the michnasayim (for sexual immorality), and cites Rabbi Chanina's derivation for the mitznefet atoning for haughtiness.
The Gemara continues listing the atonement of the avnet (for heart-thoughts), the choshen (for perversion of justice), and the ephod (for idolatry), each with a supporting verse.
The Gemara concludes the list with the me'il atoning for evil speech (citing Rabbi Chanina's principle) and the tzitz atoning for brazenness, supported by a verse.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that bloodshed and evil speech have no atonement through korbanot, but do through other means: eglah arufah for bloodshed and ketoret for evil speech. A beraita from Rabbi Yishmael's school explains that ketoret atones for evil speech because it is offered in secret.

sub.desc_en: The gemara challenges the previous claim that the priestly garments atone for bloodshed and evil speech, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi who states that these two sins have no atonement through korbanot (sacrifices).

The gemara resolves that bloodshed is atoned through עגלה ערופה (the broken-necked heifer) and evil speech through קטורת (the incense), citing a beraita of Rabbi Chananya that the incense atones based on the verse 'וַיִּתֵּן אֶת הַקְּטֹרֶת וַיְכַפֵּר עַל הָעָם'.
A beraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael explains that the incense atones specifically for evil speech because it is offered in secret (בחשאי), matching the secretive nature of evil speech.

items.text: Resolution of contradictions
items.text_en: Resolution of contradictions
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes apparent contradictions regarding atonement for bloodshed and evil speech. It resolves: for bloodshed, if the murderer is known (and it was intentional without warning), the ketonet does not atone; if unknown, the eglah arufah atones. For evil speech, if done in private, the ketoret atones; if in public, the me'il atones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the me'il atones for evil speech (seg 7) but the ketoret also atones for evil speech (seg 9-10); similarly, the ketonet atones for bloodshed (seg 5) but the eglah arufah atones for bloodshed (seg 9).
The Gemara resolves the bloodshed contradiction: if the murderer is known (and it was intentional without warning), the ketonet does not atone; if unknown, the eglah arufah atones.
The Gemara resolves the evil speech contradiction: if done in private (בצינעא), the ketoret atones; if in public (בפרהסיא), the me'il atones.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: precedence by frequency
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: precedence by frequency
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any offering that is more frequent (תָּדִיר) takes precedence over its counterpart. It lists examples: the daily tamid offerings precede the additional musaf offerings; musaf of Shabbat precedes musaf of Rosh Chodesh; musaf of Rosh Chodesh precedes musaf of Rosh Hashanah, citing the verse 'besides the morning burnt-offering which is for the continual burnt-offering, you shall make these.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the principle that a more frequent offering (תָּדִיר) precedes its counterpart, listing examples from tamid to musaf offerings and citing a verse.

items.text: Gemara's question: source for the rule
items.text_en: Gemara's question: source for the rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the source for this rule? It notes that the Mishnah itself gave a verse for tamid preceding musaf, but how do we know that one musaf precedes another musaf?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the source for the Mishnah's rule that the more frequent offering precedes the less frequent one, specifically regarding one musaf (additional offering) preceding another musaf?

items.text: Rabbi Ila'a's derivation from 'ka'eleh ta'asu'
items.text_en: Rabbi Ila'a's derivation from 'ka'eleh ta'asu'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a answers that the verse 'ka'eleh ta'asu la-yom shiv'at yamim' teaches that all musaf offerings are equal in precedence. The Gemara objects that this verse is needed for its own context, but it is explained that the extra word 'la-yom' indicates that the comparison applies to each day, and 'ta'asu' implies all actions are equal.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a cites the verse 'כָּאֵלֶּה תַּעֲשׂוּ לַיּוֹם שִׁבְעַת יָמִים' (like these you shall do for the day for seven days) to derive that all musaf offerings are equal in precedence.
The Gemara objects that this verse is needed for its own context (to teach the number of offerings for the festival).
The Gemara answers that if the verse were only for its own context, it would have written 'אֵלֶּה תַּעֲשׂוּ לַיּוֹם' (these you shall do for the day) without the word 'כָּאֵלֶּה' (like these).

The Gemara questions that if the verse had written 'אֵלֶּה תַּעֲשׂוּ לַיּוֹם שִׁבְעַת הַיָּמִים' (these you shall do for the day of the seven days), one might think only these offerings apply to the seven days, but the word 'לַיּוֹם' (for the day) indicates each day individually.
The Gemara resolves that the word 'תַּעֲשׂוּ' (you shall do) teaches that all the actions (offerings) are equal in precedence across the days.

items.text: Abaye's alternative derivation
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative derivation
items.desc_en: Abaye derives the rule from the verse itself: the extra phrase 'asher le'olat hatamid' teaches that the more frequent (תְּדִירָא) takes precedence.

sub.desc_en: Abaye derives the rule from the verse itself: the extra phrase 'אשר לעולת התמיד' teaches that the more frequent (תְּדִירָא) takes precedence.

items.text: Second Mishnah: precedence by sanctity
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: precedence by sanctity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists a hierarchy of sacrifices based on their degree of sanctity and other factors: blood of a sin-offering precedes that of a burnt-offering; limbs of a burnt-offering precede sacrificial parts of a sin-offering; sin-offering precedes guilt-offering; guilt-offering precedes todah and nazirite's ram; todah and nazirite's ram precede peace-offerings; peace-offerings precede firstborn; firstborn precedes tithe; tithe precedes bird-offerings; bird-offerings precede meal-offerings; a sinner's meal-offering precedes a voluntary one; a bird sin-offering precedes a bird burnt-offering, and similarly in their consecration.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the principle that a more sanctified offering (מְקוּדָּשׁ) precedes its counterpart, giving examples: blood of a sin-offering precedes a burnt-offering, and limbs of a burnt-offering precede sacrificial parts of a sin-offering.
The Mishnah lists further precedence: sin-offering before guilt-offering, guilt-offering before thanksgiving-offering and Nazirite's ram, and these before peace-offerings.
The Mishnah states that peace-offerings precede the firstborn, and the firstborn precedes the tithe, each with its reason.

The Mishnah concludes with precedence: tithe before bird-offerings, bird-offerings before meal-offerings, a sinner's meal-offering before a voluntary one, and a bird sin-offering before a bird burnt-offering.
The Mishnah states that peace-offerings precede the firstborn because they require four applications of blood, semikhah (laying of hands), libations, and breast-and-thigh wave-offerings.
The Mishnah states that the firstborn precedes the tithe because its sanctity is from the womb and it is eaten only by priests.
The Mishnah states that the tithe precedes bird-offerings because it is a זבח (sacrificial animal) and has קדש קדשים (most holy status) in its blood and sacrificial parts.
The Mishnah states that bird-offerings precede meal-offerings because they involve blood.
The Mishnah states that a sinner's meal-offering precedes a voluntary one because it comes for sin.
The Mishnah states that a bird sin-offering precedes a bird burnt-offering, and similarly in their consecration.

items.text: Derivation of the order of blood and limbs from the verse
items.text_en: Derivation of the order of blood and limbs from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the Mishnah's rule that the blood of the sin-offering precedes the blood of the burnt-offering, and the limbs of the burnt-offering precede the sacrificial portions of the sin-offering. It cites a baraita that derives this from the verse "and the second bull you shall take for a sin-offering" (Numbers 8:8), which teaches that the sin-offering's blood precedes all acts of the burnt-offering, while the verse "make the one a sin-offering and the one a burnt-offering" (Leviticus 16:5) teaches that the burnt-offering's limbs precede the sin-offering's portions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the Mishnah's rule about the order of blood and limbs.

The baraita derives from the verse 'וּפַר שֵׁנִי' that the sin-offering's blood precedes all acts of the burnt-offering, and from 'וַעֲשֵׂה אֶת הָאֶחָד' that the burnt-offering's limbs precede the sin-offering's portions.

items.text: Question and answers on why the first blood application is not enough
items.text_en: Question and answers on why the first blood application is not enough
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the sin-offering's blood must precede all acts of the burnt-offering, since only the first application of blood atones. Ravina answers that the verse deals with the sin-offering of the Levites, which is like a burnt-offering, yet the Torah says it precedes. In the West they say: since he began with the blood applications, he completes them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why should the sin-offering's blood precede all acts of the burnt-offering? Only the first atoning application should precede, not the rest.

Ravina answers that the baraita deals with the sin-offering of the Levites, which is like a burnt-offering, yet the Torah said it should precede; in the West they say: since he began with the applications, he finishes.
The Sages of the West answer that since he began with the blood applications, he completes them.

items.text: First inquiry: blood of sin-offering vs. limbs of burnt-offering
items.text_en: First inquiry: blood of sin-offering vs. limbs of burnt-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: which comes first, the blood of the sin-offering or the limbs of the burnt-offering? It attempts to resolve this from the Mishnah, which states that the blood of the sin-offering precedes the blood of the burnt-offering, but this does not address limbs. From the Mishnah's statement that the limbs of the burnt-offering precede the portions of the sin-offering, one might infer that they do not precede the blood. The Gemara concludes that no inference can be drawn.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara inquires: between the sin-offering's blood and the burnt-offering's limbs, which precedes — the blood because it atones, or the limbs because they are entirely consumed by fire?
The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that the sin-offering's blood precedes only the burnt-offering's blood, not its limbs.
The Gemara counters from the end of the Mishnah: the burnt-offering's limbs precede only the sin-offering's portions, not its blood.
The Gemara concludes that no proof can be derived from this Mishnah.

items.text: Second inquiry: blood of burnt-offering vs. portions of sin-offering
items.text_en: Second inquiry: blood of burnt-offering vs. portions of sin-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another inquiry: which comes first, the blood of the burnt-offering or the portions of the sin-offering? It attempts to resolve this from the Mishnah, but the Mishnah only states that the blood of the sin-offering precedes the blood of the burnt-offering, and that the limbs of the burnt-offering precede the portions of the sin-offering. No inference can be drawn for the blood of the burnt-offering versus the portions of the sin-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara inquires: between the burnt-offering's blood and the sin-offering's portions, which precedes — the blood because it comes from the power of being entirely consumed, or the portions because they come from the power of atonement?
The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that the sin-offering's blood precedes the burnt-offering's blood, but the sin-offering's portions do not.
The Gemara counters from the end: the burnt-offering's limbs precede the sin-offering's portions, but the burnt-offering's blood does not.
The Gemara concludes that no proof can be derived from this Mishnah.

items.text: Third inquiry: blood of burnt-offering vs. blood of guilt-offering
items.text_en: Third inquiry: blood of burnt-offering vs. blood of guilt-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires which comes first, the blood of the burnt-offering or the blood of the guilt-offering. It attempts to resolve from the Mishnah, which states that the blood of the sin-offering precedes the blood of the burnt-offering, but does not mention the guilt-offering. The Gemara explains that the Mishnah deliberately taught about the sin-offering rather than the guilt-offering to avoid a mistaken inference. A later baraita states that the sin-offering precedes the guilt-offering, but this refers to the portions, not the blood. The Gemara confirms this from the baraita's wording.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara inquires which comes first, the blood of the burnt-offering or the blood of the guilt-offering, presenting two possible rationales.
The Gemara attempts to resolve the inquiry from the Mishnah, which states that the blood of the sin-offering precedes the blood of the burnt-offering but does not mention the guilt-offering.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah deliberately taught about the sin-offering rather than the guilt-offering to avoid a mistaken inference about the limbs of the burnt-offering.
The Gemara cites a baraita stating that the sin-offering precedes the guilt-offering, and suggests this refers to the blood.
The Gemara rejects the inference and confirms that the baraita refers to the portions (אימורים), not the blood, as indicated by its wording.

items.text: Series of priority comparisons from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Series of priority comparisons from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines each pair in the Mishnah's list of priorities, raising a counter-argument for each and then providing the reason why the Mishnah's order stands. For example, the sin-offering precedes the guilt-offering because it has more applications of blood; the guilt-offering precedes the thanksgiving-offering because it is most holy; the thanksgiving-offering precedes the peace-offering because it is eaten for one day; the peace-offering precedes the firstborn because it has additional mitzvot; the firstborn precedes the tithe because its sanctity is from the womb; and the tithe precedes the birds because it is a type of animal sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's priority of sin-offering over guilt-offering, arguing that the guilt-offering should come first because it has a fixed value.
The Gemara resolves that despite the guilt-offering's fixed value, the sin-offering's multiple blood applications on the altar take precedence.
The Gemara challenges the priority of guilt-offering over thanksgiving-offering, arguing that the thanksgiving and Nazirite ram should come first because they require bread.
The Gemara resolves that the guilt-offering, being קדשי קדשים (most holy), takes precedence over the thanksgiving-offering despite the latter's bread requirement.

The Gemara challenges the priority of thanksgiving-offering over peace-offering, arguing that the peace-offering should come first because it can be brought by the community as well as by an individual.
The Gemara resolves that the thanksgiving-offering, being eaten for only one day, takes precedence over the peace-offering which may be eaten for two days.

The Gemara raises an inquiry about which takes precedence between the thanksgiving-offering and the Nazirite ram, weighing the thanksgiving's four types of bread against the Nazirite ram's accompanying other blood offerings.
The Gemara cites a baraita that resolves the inquiry: the thanksgiving-offering precedes the Nazirite ram because it requires four types of bread while the Nazirite ram requires only two.
The Gemara challenges the priority of peace-offering over firstborn, arguing that the firstborn should come first because its sanctity is from the womb and it is eaten only by priests.
The Gemara resolves that the peace-offering, having additional mitzvot (commandments) such as the breast and thigh portions, takes precedence over the firstborn.
The Gemara challenges the priority of firstborn over tithe, arguing that the tithe should come first because it sanctifies animals before and after it.
The Gemara resolves that the firstborn, whose sanctity is from the womb, takes precedence over the tithe.
The Gemara challenges the priority of tithe over bird offerings, arguing that birds should come first because they are קדשי קדשים (most holy).
The Gemara resolves that the tithe, being a type of animal sacrifice (זבח), takes precedence over bird offerings.

items.text: Ravina bar Sheila's statement on portions that left before sprinkling
items.text_en: Ravina bar Sheila's statement on portions that left before sprinkling
items.desc_en: Ravina bar Sheila states that the sacrificial portions of lesser sanctities that left the Temple courtyard before the blood was sprinkled are invalid. A Tanna taught that this is because it is a sacrifice and it is most holy, referring to its blood and portions. The Gemara explains that just as blood is invalid if taken out before sprinkling, so too the portions are invalid if taken out before sprinkling, and they are called most holy.

sub.desc_en: Ravina bar Sheila states that the portions of lesser sacred offerings that left the courtyard before the blood was thrown are invalid, and a Tanna taught that this is because it is a sacrifice and has קָדְשֵׁי קָדָשִׁים status for its blood and portions.
The Gemara questions: bird-offerings have no portions, but they have blood — so the Tanna must be teaching that portions are like blood.
The Gemara explains: just as blood before sprinkling is invalid if it leaves, so too portions before sprinkling are invalid if they leave.
The Gemara resolves that just as blood before sprinkling is called most holy and is invalid if taken out, so too the portions before sprinkling are invalid if taken out.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on meat that left
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on meat that left
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan says that the meat of lesser sanctities that left before sprinkling is valid, because it is destined to leave eventually; Reish Lakish says it is invalid, because its time to leave has not yet arrived. The Gemara clarifies that they only dispute about meat, not portions. However, it is possible that they also dispute about portions, and the case of meat was taught to show the extent of Reish Lakish's opinion. The Gemara then cites a Tannaic dispute about portions that left before sprinkling, where Rabbi Eliezer says there is no misuse of sacred property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that a baraita supports Reish Lakish: meat of lesser sanctities that left before sprinkling is disputed — Rabbi Yochanan says it is valid, Reish Lakish says it is invalid.

The Gemara explains the reasoning: Rabbi Yochanan validates because the meat is destined to leave eventually; Reish Lakish invalidates because its time to leave has not yet arrived; they only dispute about meat, not about portions (אימורין).
The Gemara suggests that the same dispute may apply to portions (אימורין), and the case of meat was taught to show the extent of Reish Lakish's stringency.
The Gemara cites a Tannaic dispute about portions of lesser sanctities that left before sprinkling, where Rabbi Eliezer rules there is no misuse of sacred property (מעילה).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that limbs that left the courtyard are not subject to piggul, notar, or tum'ah penalties, but Rabbi Akiva says they are subject to me'ilah and those penalties.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that limbs that left the courtyard are not subject to piggul, notar, or tum'ah penalties, but Rabbi Akiva says they are subject to me'ilah and those penalties.

items.text: Gemara's initial assumption
items.text_en: Gemara's initial assumption
items.desc_en: The Gemara assumes the dispute is about limbs that were taken out and then brought back in, disagreeing whether they are invalidated by having left.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute is about limbs that were brought back in, disagreeing on whether they are invalidated by having left.

items.text: Rav Pappa's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa clarifies that all agree about limbs brought back in; the dispute is about limbs still outside, regarding whether sprinkling effects me'ilah for limbs that left. He then distinguishes between the case of the two loaves and the limbs of the offering itself.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves the dispute: all agree about limbs brought back in; the disagreement is about limbs outside, regarding whether sprinkling effects me'ilah for limbs that left.
The Gemara objects that Rav Pappa previously said the opposite regarding the two loaves: all agree about loaves outside, and the dispute is about loaves brought back in.

Rav Pappa distinguishes: the previous statement applies only to the two loaves, which are not part of the offering itself; but for the limbs, which are part of the offering, the dispute is about limbs outside.

items.text: Order of bird offerings and meal offerings
items.text_en: Order of bird offerings and meal offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses why bird offerings precede meal offerings despite meal offerings being brought in public, and why the sin meal offering precedes the free-will meal offering because it atones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why bird offerings precede meal offerings, arguing that meal offerings should come first since they are brought both as communal and individual offerings.
The Gemara answers that even so, bird offerings are types whose blood is presented, which is of greater importance.
The Gemara questions why the sin meal offering precedes the free-will meal offering, arguing that the free-will offering should come first since it requires oil and frankincense.
The Gemara answers that even so, the sin meal offering, which comes due to a sin, is of greater importance because it effects atonement.

items.text: Inquiry about sotah meal offering vs. free-will meal offering
items.text_en: Inquiry about sotah meal offering vs. free-will meal offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires which takes precedence: the sotah meal offering or the free-will meal offering. It attempts to resolve from a mishna, concluding that the sotah offering is like the sin offering because it comes for sin, and the free-will offering has two reasons for precedence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara inquires which takes precedence: the sotah meal offering (מנחת סוטה) or the free-will meal offering (מנחת נדבה), presenting two possible reasons for priority.
The Gemara attempts to resolve from a mishna that the sin meal offering (מנחת חוטא) precedes the free-will offering, and since the sotah offering also comes for sin, it should likewise precede.

The Gemara brings another baraita stating that one offering precedes another based on grain type, and initially assumes it refers to free-will over sotah, but is rejected as referring to sin offering over sotah.

The Gemara objects that the distinction between sin offering and sotah offering is clear (one atones, the other does not), and similarly between free-will and sotah (one has oil and frankincense, the other does not), so the baraita must be teaching something else.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita holds one of two possible reasons (either atonement or coming for sin) but does not specify which, leaving the original question unresolved.

items.text: Source for bird sin offering preceding burnt offering
items.text_en: Source for bird sin offering preceding burnt offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from a verse that the sin offering always precedes the burnt offering that accompanies it, establishing a precedent for all sin offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source that a bird sin offering precedes the accompanying burnt offering.
The baraita cites the verse 'וְהִקְרִיב אֶת אֲשֶׁר לַחַטָּאת רִאשׁוֹנָה' to establish that the sin offering is brought first, as the burnt offering is explicitly called 'the second'.
The Gemara explains that this verse establishes a precedent (בנין אב) that all sin offerings precede the burnt offerings that accompany them, whether bird or animal.

The Gemara concludes that the bird sin offering preceding a bird burnt offering is derived from the verse, an animal sin offering preceding an animal burnt offering is derived from the general rule, and a bird sin offering preceding an animal burnt offering is derived from this precedent.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's rule and further precedences
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's rule and further precedences
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer states that wherever a sin offering is substituted, the sin offering precedes, except for a yoledet where the burnt offering precedes. Rava explains this is because the verse mentions the burnt offering first. The Gemara then lists the order of animal offerings: bulls before rams, rams before lambs, lambs before goats.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer rules that a sin offering (חטאת) generally precedes a burnt offering (עולה), except for a yoledet where the burnt offering comes first.
Rava explains that the burnt offering precedes only because the verse mentions it first (למקראה הקדימה הכתוב).
The Gemara cites another baraita listing the precedence of animal offerings: bulls before rams, rams before lambs, lambs before goats.

items.text: Clarification of the previous ruling
items.text_en: Clarification of the previous ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier statement about bulls preceding rams refers to bulls of a freewill offering, not of Sukkot, and explains the reasoning for the order of precedence among animal offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the earlier statement about bulls preceding rams refers to the bulls of Sukkot, and answers that it refers to freewill offerings.
The Gemara explains the order of precedence: bulls precede rams because they have more libations, rams precede lambs, and lambs precede goats because they have a fat tail.

items.text: Proof from the order of communal offerings
items.text_en: Proof from the order of communal offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita listing the order of precedence for communal offerings, showing that a burnt-offering (the bull for idolatry) precedes a sin-offering (the goats for idolatry), contradicting the general rule. The Gemara resolves that the rule applies only within the same species, not across different species.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing the order of communal offerings, showing that the bull for idolatry (a burnt-offering) precedes the goats for idolatry (sin-offerings), contradicting the general rule that a sin-offering takes precedence.

The Gemara objects that earlier in the baraita, the bull for communal error (a sin-offering) precedes the bull for idolatry (a burnt-offering), which actually supports the rule that a sin-offering takes precedence.
The Gemara resolves that the rule that a sin-offering precedes a burnt-offering applies only within the same species, but across different species a burnt-offering can take precedence.

items.text: Alternative explanations for the exception
items.text_en: Alternative explanations for the exception
items.desc_en: Rava bar Mari and Ravina offer alternative explanations for why the sin-offering of idolatry is written defectively, indicating it is not a full sin-offering, or that the verse says 'according to the ordinance' implying it follows the burnt-offering. The Gemara then applies this reasoning to the bulls of Sukkot.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Mari explains that the sin-offering of idolatry is written defectively (חסר א׳, 'לחטאת' instead of 'לחטאת'), indicating it is not a full sin-offering, so the burnt-offering of idolatry can precede it.

Ravina offers an alternative explanation: the verse says 'כמשפט' (according to the ordinance) regarding the burnt-offering of idolatry, implying it follows the standard order of the burnt-offering, which precedes the sin-offering.

The Gemara concludes that now that this reasoning is established, even the bulls of Sukkot (פרים דחג) are written with 'כמשפטם' (according to their ordinance), so they too follow the standard order where the burnt-offering precedes the sin-offering.

items.text: Precedence among bird sin-offering, animal burnt-offering, and tithe
items.text_en: Precedence among bird sin-offering, animal burnt-offering, and tithe
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised about the order of precedence among a bird sin-offering, an animal burnt-offering, and animal tithe. Two resolutions are offered: in the West they say that the animal burnt-offering enters into the bird sin-offering and lifts it above the tithe.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma about the order of precedence among a bird sin-offering (חטאת העוף), an animal burnt-offering (עולת בהמה), and animal tithe (מעשר), noting that each one has a reason to precede the other.

The Babylonian tradition (הכא תרגימו) answers that the type of sacrifice (זבח) is superior, implying that the animal burnt-offering (which is a זבח) takes precedence over the bird sin-offering (which is not a זבח).

The Western tradition (במערבא אמרי) answers that the animal burnt-offering enters into the bird sin-offering and lifts it above the tithe, meaning the bird sin-offering gains precedence over the tithe by association with the animal burnt-offering.

items.text: Mishnah: Precedence of sin-offerings over guilt-offerings and other rules
items.text_en: Mishnah: Precedence of sin-offerings over guilt-offerings and other rules
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all sin-offerings precede guilt-offerings except the guilt-offering of a leper, and lists other rules about the age and value of guilt-offerings, the order of eating, and the permissibility for priests to vary the preparation of offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that all sin-offerings (חטאות) precede guilt-offerings (אשמות), except the guilt-offering of a leper, because it comes for atonement (הכשר).

The Mishnah adds that all guilt-offerings come as two-year-old animals and with silver shekels, except the guilt-offerings of a nazirite and a leper, which come as one-year-old animals and without silver shekels.

The Mishnah states that offerings precede in eating as they do in sacrifice, and then presents a dispute: Rabbi Meir says yesterday's peace-offerings precede today's sin-offering and guilt-offering, while the Sages say the sin-offering precedes because it is most holy (קדשי קדשים).

The Mishnah concludes that priests may vary the preparation of all these offerings, and records a dispute: Rabbi Shimon permits adding non-sacred and terumah spices, while Rabbi Meir forbids adding terumah spices lest it cause the terumah to become invalid.

items.text: Gemara: Dilemma about frequency vs. sanctity
items.text_en: Gemara: Dilemma about frequency vs. sanctity
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: does a frequent offering (tadir) take precedence over a more sanctified one (mekudash), or vice versa? It brings a proof from the rule that the daily tamid offerings precede the additional musaf offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: does a frequent offering (תָּדִיר) take precedence over a more sanctified one (מְקוּדָּשׁ), or vice versa?
The Gemara brings a proof from the rule that the daily tamid offerings precede the additional musaf offerings, suggesting that frequency (תָּדִיר) is the deciding factor.

items.text: Challenges to the principle that תדיר precedes מקודש
items.text_en: Challenges to the principle that תדיר precedes מקודש
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings four attempts (תא שמע) to prove that the more frequent offering takes precedence over the more sacred, but each is rejected with the same counter-argument: the more sacred day also benefits the more frequent offering, so the proof fails.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle that the more frequent (תדיר) offering takes precedence over the more sacred (מקודש), arguing that the more sacred day also benefits the more frequent offering.
The Gemara brings a baraita that Shabbat additional offerings precede Rosh Chodesh additional offerings, but rejects it because Rosh Chodesh also benefits Shabbat's offerings.
The Gemara brings a baraita that Rosh Chodesh additional offerings precede Rosh Hashanah additional offerings, but rejects it because Rosh Hashanah also benefits Rosh Chodesh's offerings.
The Gemara brings a baraita that the frequent wine blessing precedes the less frequent day blessing, but rejects it because Shabbat also benefits the wine blessing.

sub.text: Fourth attempt (תא שמע from Rabbi Yochanan)
sub.text_en: Fourth attempt (תא שמע from Rabbi Yochanan)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that one prays the afternoon prayer before the additional prayer, but rejects it because Shabbat also benefits the afternoon prayer.

items.text: A proof from the Mishnah about שלמים of yesterday and חטאת/אשם of today
items.text_en: A proof from the Mishnah about שלמים of yesterday and חטאת/אשם of today
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a fifth proof: if both offerings are from the same day, the less frequent חטאת/אשם precedes the more frequent שלמים, even though שלמים is more frequent. This seems to show that frequency does not always win.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a fifth proof from the Mishnah: if both offerings are from the same day, the less frequent חטאת/אשם precedes the more frequent שלמים, even though שלמים is more frequent, showing that frequency does not always win.

items.text: Rava's distinction between תדיר (frequent) and מצוי (common)
items.text_en: Rava's distinction between תדיר (frequent) and מצוי (common)
items.desc_en: Rava argues that the principle of תדיר applies only to the most frequent (תדיר), not merely to the common (מצוי). Rav Huna bar Yehuda objects, citing a baraita that uses תדיר for circumcision, which is common but not the most frequent. The Gemara resolves that תדיר there means frequent in commandments, or that circumcision is considered like תדיר relative to Passover.

sub.desc_en: Rava distinguishes between תדיר (frequent) and מצוי (common), asserting that the principle of תדיר applies only to the most frequent, not merely to the common.
Rav Huna bar Yehuda objects, citing a baraita that uses תדיר for circumcision, which is common but not the most frequent, challenging Rava's distinction.
The Gemara resolves that תדיר in the baraita means frequent in commandments, or alternatively, that circumcision is considered like תדיר relative to Passover.

items.text: New inquiry: what if one slaughtered the non-frequent offering first?
items.text_en: New inquiry: what if one slaughtered the non-frequent offering first?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a new question: if one slaughtered the non-frequent offering first, does it get offered first, or must one wait until the frequent offering is offered? Rav Huna Misura attempts to prove from the earlier Mishnah that if both were slaughtered, the less frequent takes precedence, but the Gemara deflects, saying the case is where both were slaughtered; if only the non-frequent was slaughtered, the question remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a new inquiry: if one slaughtered the non-frequent offering first, does one offer it immediately or wait until the frequent offering is offered?
Rav Huna Misura attempts to prove from the Mishnah that if the non-frequent (yesterday's peace-offering) was slaughtered first, it takes precedence over the frequent (today's sin-offering).
The Gemara deflects: the Mishnah's case is where both were slaughtered; if only the non-frequent was slaughtered, the question remains unresolved.

items.text: Attempts to resolve the inquiry from earlier sources
items.text_en: Attempts to resolve the inquiry from earlier sources
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to resolve the question from the earlier proof about ברכת היין and from Rabbi Yochanan's ruling about prayers, but each is rejected because in those cases both items are already present or their time has arrived, so they are considered as if both were slaughtered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a second proof from the rule about blessings, but explains that in that case, the wine is already present, analogous to both being slaughtered.

The Gemara rejects the proof because in the case of wine, the wine is already present, so both items are considered as if they were already slaughtered, unlike the case where the less frequent offering was slaughtered first.

items.text: Proof from the law of the daily offering (תמיד)
items.text_en: Proof from the law of the daily offering (תמיד)
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ashi cites a baraita: if one slaughtered the daily offering before noon it is invalid, but if before the daily offering it is valid, and one must stir its blood until the blood of the daily offering is sprinkled. This shows that if the non-frequent offering was slaughtered first, it is offered after the frequent one. Rav Acha Saba confirms this from the Mishnah's wording.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ashi's citation
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ashi's citation
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ashi cites a baraita to Ravina: if one slaughtered the daily offering before noon it is invalid, but if before the daily offering it is valid, and one must stir its blood until the blood of the daily offering is sprinkled.
The gemara clarifies that the baraita deals with a case where one slaughtered the non-frequent offering before the daily offering.
Rav Acha Saba confirms to Rav Ashi that the Mishnah's wording supports this interpretation, since it says 'until the blood is sprinkled' and not 'until one slaughters and sprinkles the blood'.

items.text: Mishnah: Priests may eat the remainder of offerings in any manner
items.text_en: Mishnah: Priests may eat the remainder of offerings in any manner
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that priests may eat the remainder of meal offerings in any manner, and Rabbi Shimon explains that oil that is distributed in the Temple is from the remainder of Israel's meal offerings or the log of oil of a metzora, while oil placed on the fire is from the remainder of the priests' meal offerings. Rabbi Tarfon adds that one may donate oil.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that priests may eat the remainder of offerings in any manner, and the Gemara explains the reason from the verse 'למשחה' (for greatness), like kings eat.
Rabbi Shimon explains that oil distributed in the Temple is from the remainder of Israel's meal offerings or the log of oil of a metzora.
Rabbi Shimon adds that oil placed on the fire is from the remainder of the priests' meal offerings, since they do not donate oil.
Rabbi Tarfon states that one may donate oil.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on donated oil according to Rabbi Tarfon
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on donated oil according to Rabbi Tarfon
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that according to Rabbi Tarfon, one who donates oil has its handful (קומץ) and remainder eaten, derived from the verse 'קרבן מנחה' which teaches that oil can be donated like a meal-offering.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that according to Rabbi Tarfon, one who donates oil has its handful (קומץ) and remainder eaten, derived from the verse 'קרבן מנחה' which teaches that oil can be donated like a meal-offering.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's support and Abaye's challenge from a baraita
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's support and Abaye's challenge from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira cites a baraita of Rabbi Shimon implying that donated oil is divided (for eating), but Abaye objects that the baraita's end implies all oil goes to the fire. The Gemara resolves that the beginning refers to remnants and the end to the handful, and explains why the baraita juxtaposes them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira cites a baraita of Rabbi Shimon to support that donated oil is divided (for eating), implying that one who permits donating oil permits its division.
Abaye objects by citing the end of the same baraita, which implies that for one who permits donating oil, all of it goes to the fire, contradicting Rabbi Zeira's inference.
The Gemara resolves that the beginning of the baraita refers to the remnants (שיריים) and the end to the handful (קומץ), but this does not resolve Abaye's difficulty.
The Gemara explains that the baraita's beginning is stated because of its end, as the Western sages say, resolving the contradiction by showing the baraita's structure is for rhetorical emphasis.

items.text: Proof from a tannaitic source about wine and oil
items.text_en: Proof from a tannaitic source about wine and oil
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a source stating that wine according to Rabbi Akiva goes to the basins, and oil according to Rabbi Tarfon goes to the fire. It questions whether this means all oil goes to the fire, but deflects that each is according to its own rule.
