sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a tannaitic source that wine goes to the basins and oil to the fire, and asks whether this implies all oil goes to the fire.
The Gemara deflects the inference, explaining that each substance follows its own rule: wine all to basins, oil all to fire, but not by analogy from one to the other.

items.text: Dispute between Sages and Rabbi on minimum oil quantity
items.text_en: Dispute between Sages and Rabbi on minimum oil quantity
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa presents a dispute: the Sages require at least one log of oil, while Rabbi says three logs. The Gemara explains their reasoning: the Sages derive from a meal-offering (one log, remnants eaten), while Rabbi derives from libations (three logs, all to the fire).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa introduces a dispute between the Sages (minimum one log) and Rabbi (minimum three logs) regarding the quantity of oil one may donate.
The Gemara asks what principle underlies the disagreement between the Sages and Rabbi.
The Sages derive from a meal-offering that oil is donated, requires one log, and its handful is burned while the remainder is eaten.
Rabbi derives the donation of oil from a meal-offering but then interprets it like libations: three logs, all burned on the altar.

items.text: Rav Pappa's objection and resolution about Rabbi's source
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's objection and resolution about Rabbi's source
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa questions why Rabbi would derive from libations if both sides derive from meal-offering; he suggests Rabbi derives from the word 'אזרח'. Rav Huna bar Rav Natan counters with a baraita that derives three logs from 'קרבן מנחה', and Rav Pappa concedes.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: if Rabbi derived the gift of oil from the meal-offering, everyone would use the principle 'דון מינה ומינה' (infer from it and from it); therefore Rabbi must derive it from the word 'אזרח' (homeborn) in the context of libations.

Rav Huna bar Rav Natan objects to Rav Pappa: how can you say that? A baraita explicitly derives the gift of oil from the word 'קרבן מנחה' (korban minḥa) and states the amount is three לוגים (log), and that is Rabbi's opinion, showing he derives it from 'קרבן' (korban).
Rav Pappa concedes: if the baraita is taught (that Rabbi derives from 'קרבן'), then it is taught, and he cannot dispute it.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on donated wine and the issue of extinguishing
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on donated wine and the issue of extinguishing
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that donated wine is poured onto the fire, deriving from a verse. The Gemara raises the problem of extinguishing the fire, and resolves that partial extinguishing is not considered extinguishing, or that extinguishing for a mitzvah is different. It distinguishes between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon's views, noting Shmuel's consistency with Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that one who donates wine brings it and sprinkles it on the fire, deriving this from a verse.
The Gemara objects that pouring wine on the fire would extinguish it, and initially resolves that partial extinguishing is not considered extinguishing.

The Gemara counters with Rav Nachman's ruling that one who removes a coal from the altar and extinguishes it is liable, and then offers an alternative resolution: extinguishing for a mitzvah (מצוה) is different.

sub.text: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov that one may not extinguish the fire to take terumah (תרומה), and distinguishes that there one could wait, but here it is different.
The Gemara brings another baraita that wine goes to the bowls and oil to the fire, and a further baraita explicitly stating that wine is not poured on the fire because one must not extinguish.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the views to Rabbi Yehuda (who forbids extinguishing) and Rabbi Shimon (who permits), and notes that Shmuel's position aligns with Rabbi Shimon, citing Shmuel's own ruling about extinguishing a metal coal in the public domain to prevent harm.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Shimon's view on coal
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Shimon's view on coal
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the previous Mishnah permits a coal of metal but not a coal of wood, suggesting that if the Tanna follows Rabbi Shimon's lenient view on unintended consequences, even a wood coal should be permitted. It resolves that the Tanna adopts Rabbi Shimon's view on 'davar she'eino mitkavein' but Rabbi Yehuda's view on 'melacha she'eina tzricha legufah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah permits only a metal coal but not a wood coal, arguing that if the Tanna follows Rabbi Shimon's lenient view on unintended consequences (דבר שאין מתכוין), even a wood coal should be permitted.

The Gemara resolves that the Tanna holds like Rabbi Shimon regarding the leniency of unintentional action (דבר שאין מתכוין) but holds like Rabbi Yehuda regarding the stricter view on unnecessary labor (מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה), thus ruling out the wood coal.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on disqualified libations
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on disqualified libations
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that libations that became impure are burned on a separate pyre, based on the verse 'bakodesh ba'eish tisaref'. A baraita supports this, and Samuel instructs Rav Chana Bagdata'ah to gather ten people to hear this ruling.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that libations that became impure are burned on a separate pyre, citing the verse 'בקדש באש תשרף' (in the sanctuary it shall be burned in fire).
A baraita supports Rav Huna's ruling, listing the various items (blood, oil, grain-offerings, libations) that are burned on a separate pyre when impure.
Samuel instructs Rav Chana Bagdata'ah to gather ten people to publicly hear the halacha that impure libations are burned on a separate pyre.

items.text: Transition phrase
items.text_en: Transition phrase
items.desc_en: A standard formula marking the end of a chapter and the beginning of the next.

sub.desc_en: The standard concluding formula for a chapter: 'הדרן עלך כל התדיר' (we return to you, chapter 'All that is frequent').

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Blood of sin-offering requiring laundering
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Blood of sin-offering requiring laundering
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that blood of a sin-offering that splashes on a garment requires laundering, even though the verse speaks only of sin-offerings that are eaten, as derived from 'Torat hachatat'. Both external and internal sin-offerings require laundering. A disqualified sin-offering does not require laundering, whether it had a period of fitness or not, with examples given.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens: blood of a sin-offering (חטאת) that spurts onto a garment requires laundering, even though Scripture only explicitly speaks about eaten sin-offerings, as it says 'במקום קדוש תאכל' (in a holy place it shall be eaten).

The Mishnah extends the rule: both eaten (exterior) sin-offerings and interior sin-offerings require laundering, based on the derivation from 'תורת החטאת' (the law of the sin-offering) — one law for all sin-offerings.
The Mishnah rules that an invalid sin-offering (חטאת פסולה) does not require laundering for its blood, whether it had a time of fitness or not, giving examples of each category.

items.text: Gemara's derivation and exclusion of bird sin-offerings
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation and exclusion of bird sin-offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why bird sin-offerings are excluded from laundering, citing a baraita that derives from 'zot' that only animal sin-offerings require laundering. Reish Lakish in the name of Bar Kappara explains that the verse 'tishachet' speaks of slaughtered offerings. The Gemara then considers whether only eaten sin-offerings are included, but derives from 'Torat' that internal ones are also included. It then explains why bird sin-offerings are excluded, reasoning that animal sin-offerings have more stringencies (animal, northern slaughter, vessel reception).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why bird sin-offerings are excluded from laundering, given the inclusive principle 'Torat' (one law for all sin-offerings).

Reish Lakish in the name of Bar Kappara explains that the verse 'tishachet' (you shall slaughter) speaks only of slaughtered offerings, excluding bird sin-offerings which are killed by pinching the nape.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the verse speaks only of eaten sin-offerings, not internal ones.
The Gemara resolves that the inclusive term 'Torat' (Torah of the sin-offering) teaches that internal sin-offerings are also included.
The Gemara asks why bird sin-offerings are not also included by the same logic.
The Gemara resolves that the restrictive term 'zot' (this) excludes bird sin-offerings.

The Gemara provides supporting reasoning that animal sin-offerings are more stringent, having animal status, northern slaughter, and reception in a vessel, justifying their inclusion over bird sin-offerings.

items.text: Comparison of bird and animal sin-offerings
items.text_en: Comparison of bird and animal sin-offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah includes horn, finger, tip, and fire for animal sin-offerings but not for bird sin-offerings, arguing that bird sin-offerings should be included due to their similar external application and consumption.

items.text: Rav Yosef's derivation from 'yochlenah'
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's derivation from 'yochlenah'
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef argues that the verse 'yochlenah' excludes bird sin-offerings from the laws of consumed offerings, and 'zot' teaches that the exclusion applies only to consumed offerings.

items.text: Rabbah's derivation from 'asher yizeh'
items.text_en: Rabbah's derivation from 'asher yizeh'
items.desc_en: Rabbah argues that the verse 'asher yizeh' speaks of sprinklings, but a baraita clarifies that this applies only to rinsing and scrubbing, not to laundering, which is derived from 'asher yizeh'.

items.text: Textual correction and exclusion of bird sin-offering
items.text_en: Textual correction and exclusion of bird sin-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara corrects the Mishnah's wording to 'one of the inner and one of the consumed', then questions why bird sin-offering is excluded, answering that 'zot' excludes it, and why outer sin-offering is not excluded, answering that 'torat' includes it.

items.text: Reconsideration of the comparison
items.text_en: Reconsideration of the comparison
items.desc_en: The Gemara reconsiders which sin-offering should be included, arguing that animal sin-offering has more commonalities, but bird sin-offering has the commonality of sprinkling, and the list of commonalities is more numerous for animal.

items.text: Rabbi Avin's query on bird sin-offering blood in the neck
items.text_en: Rabbi Avin's query on bird sin-offering blood in the neck
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin asks whether bringing a bird sin-offering's blood inside via its neck is valid, comparing the neck to a service vessel or to an animal's neck. The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between the bird entering and the blood being brought in a vessel.

items.text: Rabbi Avin's query on blood spilled on the floor
items.text_en: Rabbi Avin's query on blood spilled on the floor
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin asks whether blood spilled on the floor and then collected is valid, questioning if the Torah required a service vessel or merely disqualified blood not in one. Rava cites a verse to show that if the Torah disqualified blood not in a vessel, then the blood would be invalid due to the air of the vessel. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua explains the case involves attaching a vessel to the bird's neck.

items.text: Levi's query on blood splattering from garment to garment
items.text_en: Levi's query on blood splattering from garment to garment
items.desc_en: Levi asks whether blood that splatters from one garment to another requires laundering. The answer is yes, either because the blood is still valid or because Rabbi Akiva holds that blood that had a moment of fitness and then became invalid still requires laundering.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's inquiry about blood spattering on a impure garment
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's inquiry about blood spattering on a impure garment
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rav Chisda whether blood that spattered onto an impure garment requires laundering. Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua infers from the question that if the offering had a time of fitness and then became disqualified, its blood does not require laundering.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rav Chisda whether blood that spattered onto an impure garment requires laundering.

sub.text: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua's inference
sub.text_en: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua's inference
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua infers from the question that if the offering had a time of fitness and then became disqualified, its blood does not require laundering.

items.text: Clarifying the scope of the principle
items.text_en: Clarifying the scope of the principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies whether the principle applies only when the blood spattered sequentially (one after another) but not simultaneously, or whether there is no difference. Rav Chisda responds that this is a dispute between Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis according to Rabbah, as Abaye resolves.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the principle applies only when blood spatters sequentially (בזה אחר זה) but not simultaneously (בבת אחת), or whether there is no difference.
Rav Chisda responds that this is a dispute between Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis according to Rabbah, as Abaye resolves.

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis regarding purification water
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis regarding purification water
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Elazar says that purification water that became impure can still purify, because a menstruant can be sprinkled with it. Rabbah explains that Rabbi Elazar follows the view of Rabbi Akiva, who holds that passing a vessel over an impure place is considered as if it were placed there. This is illustrated by a mishnah about a person standing outside an oven with a reptile inside, where Rabbi Akiva deems the vessel impure and the Sages deem it pure.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Elazar rules that purification water (מי חטאת) that became impure can still purify, because a menstruant (נדה) may be sprinkled with it.
Rabbah explains that Rabbi Elazar follows the view of his teacher Rabbi Akiva, who holds that passing a vessel over an impure place is considered as if it were placed there (כמונח דמי).

A mishnah is cited about a person standing outside an oven with a reptile inside, where Rabbi Akiva deems the vessel impure and the Sages deem it pure, illustrating the dispute over the principle of 'as if placed' (כמונח דמי).

items.text: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that Rabbi Akiva admits that passing purification water over impure earthenware vessels above a impure bed or seat is pure, because nothing imparts impurity above except an olive's bulk of a corpse and other items that provide shade. Abaye then offers an alternative explanation: everyone agrees that passing is not considered as placed; rather, the dispute is whether we decree due to concern that it might rest. Rabbi Akiva decrees, while the Rabbis do not, and Rabbi Akiva admits in the case of purification water because once it has left, it has left.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that Rabbi Akiva admits that passing purification water over impure earthenware vessels above an impure bed or seat is pure, because nothing imparts impurity above except an olive's bulk of a corpse and other items that provide shade, and he adds the case of a leprous stone.

Abaye resolves the objection by explaining that everyone agrees passing is not considered as placed; rather, the dispute is whether we decree due to concern that it might rest, and Rabbi Akiva admits in the case of purification water because once it has left, it has left.

items.text: Abaye's explanation of the dispute between Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Abaye's explanation of the dispute between Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis disagree about whether we derive a prior impurity from an impurity that occurs at the same time. One opinion holds that we do derive, and the other holds that we do not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Over what principle do Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis disagree?
Abaye explains that the dispute is whether we derive a prior impurity from an impurity that occurs at the same time: one opinion holds that we do derive, and the other holds that we do not.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rava says that everyone agrees that we do not derive a prior impurity from a simultaneous impurity. Rather, the dispute is about whether purification water requires a minimum measure and whether multiple sprinklings combine. Rabbi Elazar holds that it requires a measure and they combine, while the Rabbis hold that it does not require a measure.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that everyone agrees we do not derive a prior impurity from a simultaneous impurity.
Rava explains that the dispute between Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis is about whether purification water requires a minimum measure and whether multiple sprinklings combine.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about a disqualified sin-offering
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about a disqualified sin-offering
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a disqualified sin-offering's blood does not require laundering. The Gemara cites a baraita: Rabbi Akiva says that if it had a time of fitness and then became disqualified, its blood requires laundering; if it never had a time of fitness, it does not. Rabbi Shimon says that in either case it does not require laundering, deriving from the verses 'it' and 'from its blood'. Rabbi Akiva uses 'it' to exclude terumah. Rabbi Shimon follows his own view that offerings of lesser sanctity do not require pouring and rinsing, and certainly terumah does not.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'from its blood' to exclude the blood of a disqualified sin-offering from the requirement of laundering.
Rabbi Akiva distinguishes: if the sin-offering had a time of fitness before disqualification, its blood requires laundering; if it never had a time of fitness, it does not.
Rabbi Shimon holds that in either case the blood does not require laundering.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Shimon's reasoning: the verses 'it' and 'from its blood' are used to exclude a case that had a time of fitness and a case that did not.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Akiva's use of the verse
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Akiva's use of the verse
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva uses the word 'it' to exclude terumah (the priestly portion) from the laundering requirement.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Shimon follows his own view that offerings of lesser sanctity (קדשים קלים) do not require pouring and rinsing, and certainly terumah does not.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on blood that spattered from the neck, horn, or foundation
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on blood that spattered from the neck, horn, or foundation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that blood that spattered from the neck onto a garment does not require laundering, nor from the horn or foundation. If it spilled on the floor and was gathered, it does not require laundering. Only blood received in a vessel and fit for sprinkling requires laundering. The Gemara cites baraitot that derive these laws from the verse 'which shall be sprinkled', limiting the requirement to blood fit for sprinkling, and excluding blood that has already been sprinkled.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that blood spattered from the neck, horn, or foundation, or spilled on the floor and gathered, does not require laundering; only blood received in a vessel and fit for sprinkling requires laundering.

The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'אֲשֶׁר יִזֶּה' (which shall be sprinkled) that blood spattered from the neck is excluded, and another baraita that excludes blood from the horn or foundation as already sprinkled.
The Gemara cites the continuation of the Mishnah regarding blood spilled on the floor.

items.text: Clarifying the reason for the exemption of blood spilled on the floor
items.text_en: Clarifying the reason for the exemption of blood spilled on the floor
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah exempts blood spilled on the floor from laundering, and explains that only blood received in a vessel and fit for sprinkling requires laundering. This excludes blood collected in multiple vessels each with less than the minimum for sprinkling, as taught in a baraita of Rabbi Chalafta bar Shaul.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah exempts blood spilled on the floor from laundering, and answers that only blood received in a vessel and fit for sprinkling requires laundering.
The Gemara asks what the phrase 'fit for sprinkling' excludes, and answers that it excludes blood collected in multiple vessels each with less than the minimum for sprinkling.

sub.text: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Chalafta bar Shaul
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Chalafta bar Shaul
sub.desc_en: A baraita of Rabbi Chalafta bar Shaul teaches that if one sanctified less than the minimum for sprinkling in each vessel, the sanctification is invalid.

items.text: Inquiry about the law of dipping in blood
items.text_en: Inquiry about the law of dipping in blood
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: does the halakha that one must dip the finger in blood (for sprinkling) follow the same rule as dipping in water (for the Red Heifer), or is it derived from a similar verse? Rabbi Zerika quotes Rabbi Elazar that even for blood, if there is less than the minimum, one has not sanctified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: does the law of dipping in blood follow the same rule as dipping in water for the Red Heifer, or is it derived from a similar verse?
The Gemara presents the alternative: perhaps the law is derived from the verse 'וְטָבַל בַּדָּם' (and dip in the blood), analogous to the verse about water.
Rabbi Zerika quotes Rabbi Elazar that even for blood, if there is less than the minimum, one has not sanctified, resolving the dilemma.

items.text: Derivation from the verse about dipping in blood
items.text_en: Derivation from the verse about dipping in blood
items.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'and he shall dip... in the blood' that the dipping must be with the full finger (not just wiping), that there must be a minimum amount of blood from the start, and that the blood must be from the relevant blood (not remnants). This supports Rabbi Elazar's ruling that remnants on the finger are invalid.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita that derives three halachic principles from the verse about dipping in blood: the dipping must be with the full finger (not wiping), there must be a minimum amount of blood from the start, and the blood must be from the relevant blood (not remnants).

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the necessity of both terms
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the necessity of both terms
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both terms 'וְטָבַל' (and he shall dip) and 'בַּדָּם' (in the blood) are necessary: 'בַּדָּם' teaches that there must be a minimum amount of blood from the start, and 'וְטָבַל' teaches that wiping is invalid.
Rava explains that the phrase 'מִן הַדָּם' (from the blood) excludes remnants on the finger, supporting Rabbi Elazar's ruling that remnants on the finger are invalid.

items.text: Discussion about the timing of laundering for sprinkling
items.text_en: Discussion about the timing of laundering for sprinkling
items.desc_en: Ravin bar Rav Adda reports a teaching from Rav Amram about a baraita: if a sprinkling was interrupted, the blood that splashed before the sprinkling requires laundering, but after the sprinkling it does not. Abaye challenges this with a baraita about wiping the hand on the cow, and the Gemara resolves that the distinction is between before and after the sprinkling leaves the hand.

sub.text: Ravin bar Rav Adda to Rav
sub.text_en: Ravin bar Rav Adda to Rav
sub.desc_en: Ravin bar Rav Adda reports to Rav a baraita taught by Rav Amram: if a sprinkling splashed from the hand, blood that splashed before the sprinkling requires laundering, but after the sprinkling it does not.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita means 'until he finished sprinkling' requires laundering, and 'after he finished' does not.
The Gemara rejects that interpretation and clarifies: the distinction is between before the sprinkling leaves the hand and after it leaves the hand.
Abaye objects with a baraita: when the priest finishes sprinkling he wipes his hand on the cow's body, implying that only after finishing does he wipe, not before.
Abaye resolves: after finishing, the priest wipes his hand on the cow's body as per the verse; before finishing, he wipes his finger on the lip of the bowl, as per the verse 'like golden bowls'.

items.text: Mishnah: Laundering for leather and other materials
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laundering for leather and other materials
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if blood splashed on leather before it was flayed, it does not require laundering; after flaying, it does (Rabbi Yehuda). Rabbi Elazar says even after flaying it does not require laundering unless it is a place fit for impurity and laundering. The Mishnah then lists that a garment, sack, and leather all require laundering, and details the procedures for vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Yehuda's ruling: blood that splashed on leather before flaying does not require laundering, but after flaying it does.
Rabbi Elazar adds that even after flaying, laundering is only required if the blood is on a place fit for impurity and laundering.

The Mishnah concludes by listing that garments, sacks, and leather all require laundering, and details the procedures for vessels, noting this is a stringency of the sin-offering over other most holy offerings.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of leather and sack from the verse
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of leather and sack from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of these laws. A baraita derives from the verse 'which shall be sprinkled upon it shall be washed' that leather after flaying is included, but not before flaying, since it is not yet fit to receive impurity. Rabbi Elazar adds that sack is also included via a separate derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the Mishnah's ruling that leather after flaying requires washing.
A baraita derives from the verse 'אשר יזֶּה עליה תכבֵּס' that leather after flaying is included, but before flaying it is excluded because it is not yet fit to receive impurity.
Rabbi Elazar adds that sack is also included via a separate derivation from the verse.

items.text: Opening derivation: what garments require laundering
items.text_en: Opening derivation: what garments require laundering
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse that only items that can become impure (like a garment) require laundering for blood of a sin-offering, excluding items like untanned hide.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma derives from the verse that only items capable of receiving ritual impurity (טומאה) require laundering for blood of a sin-offering, excluding untanned hide.

items.text: Dispute between Abaye and Rava on the criterion
items.text_en: Dispute between Abaye and Rava on the criterion
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava debate the practical difference between the criteria 'fit to receive impurity' and 'fit for laundering'. Abaye cites a patch less than three handbreadths; Rava cites a garment designated as a pattern or a piece designated for cutting, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two criteria 'fit to receive impurity' and 'fit for laundering'.
Abaye answers that a patch less than three handbreadths is the difference: it is fit for laundering if one intends to use it, but it cannot receive impurity.
Rava answers that a garment designated as a pattern is the difference: it is fit for laundering if one nullifies his intention, but currently it cannot receive impurity.

sub.text: Rava's second answer with supporting baraita
sub.text_en: Rava's second answer with supporting baraita
sub.desc_en: Rava answers that a piece designated for cutting is the difference: it is fit for laundering but cannot receive impurity until cut, and cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya rules that such a piece remains pure until cut.

items.text: Source that only the blood spot requires laundering
items.text_en: Source that only the blood spot requires laundering
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse that only the place where the blood spatters requires laundering, not the entire garment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (that only the blood spot requires laundering) derived?
The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'אֲשֶׁר יִזֶּה' (which it sprinkles) that only the place of the blood requires laundering, not the entire garment.

items.text: Identifying the anonymous mishnah and excluding vessels
items.text_en: Identifying the anonymous mishnah and excluding vessels
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the anonymous mishnah aligns with Rabbi Yehuda, and that the phrase 'fit for laundering' excludes vessels, which are scraped.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the anonymous mishnah's phrase 'a thing fit to receive impurity' aligns with Rabbi Yehuda's position.
The Gemara explains that the phrase 'fit for laundering' excludes vessels, which are only scraped.

items.text: Contradiction regarding leather and resolution via Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding leather and resolution via Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The mishnah includes leather as requiring laundering, but a baraita says leather is only rinsed. Abaye resolves this as a dispute between the Rabbis and Acheirim, and Rav Chiya bar Ashi's practice supports the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The gemara questions whether the mishnah's inclusion of leather implies it requires laundering (כיבוס), citing a contradictory baraita that says leather is only rinsed.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by attributing the mishnah to Acheirim (who include leather for laundering) and the baraita to the Rabbis (who exclude it).
The gemara notes that Rav Chiya bar Ashi's practice of washing Rav's shoes with water supports the Rabbis' position that leather only requires rinsing.

items.text: Rava's initial resolution: soft vs. hard leather
items.text_en: Rava's initial resolution: soft vs. hard leather
items.desc_en: Rava argues that the verse and mishnah refer to soft leather, while the dispute is about hard leather, and Rav Chiya's practice with shoes was with hard leather, aligning with the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges the premise that anyone denies leather requires laundering, citing the verse that explicitly includes leather.
Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between soft leather (which the verse and mishnah address) and hard leather (where the Tannaitic dispute applies).
The Gemara objects that Rav Chiya's practice of washing shoes with water contradicts Rava's distinction, since shoes are typically hard leather.
Rava answers that Rav Chiya's shoes were made of hard leather, and his practice aligns with the Rabbis who permit washing hard leather.

items.text: Rava retracts and offers a new explanation: leprosy softens leather
items.text_en: Rava retracts and offers a new explanation: leprosy softens leather
items.desc_en: Rava retracts his previous distinction, noting that the verse discusses imported hard leather, and instead explains that leprosy itself softens the leather, making it fit for laundering.

sub.desc_en: Rava retracts his previous distinction between soft and hard leather, questioning whether the verse about laundering applies only to soft leather.
Rava points out that the verse discusses imported hard leather (כלי אכסלגיא) which is hard, yet the Torah requires laundering, undermining his earlier distinction.
Rava explains that leprosy itself softens the leather, making it fit for laundering, regardless of its original hardness.
Rava signals that he still has a remaining difficulty, setting up a further question.

items.text: Rava's principle on laundering without scrubbing
items.text_en: Rava's principle on laundering without scrubbing
items.desc_en: Rava establishes that any laundering without scrubbing (כיסכוס) is not considered laundering at all, resolving a contradiction regarding soft items like pillows and covers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rava's principle applies to soft items like pillows and covers, citing a mishnah that requires pouring water on a leather item until it is absorbed.
Rava resolves the contradiction by establishing that any laundering without scrubbing (כיסכוס) is not considered laundering at all.

items.text: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi's testimony about Rav's practice
items.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi's testimony about Rav's practice
items.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi testifies that he often saw Rav rinsing his shoes in water, indicating that rinsing is permitted but full laundering is not, and this is explained according to the opinions of soft or hard materials.

sub.text: Supporting baraita from Rav Chiyya bar Ashi
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from Rav Chiyya bar Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi testifies that he often saw Rav merely swish his shoes in water, indicating that swishing is permitted but laundering is not.
The Gemara resolves that Rav's practice aligns with Rava's principle: for soft shoes it follows the majority view, for hard shoes it follows the minority view.

items.text: Application to garments and Rava's broader principle
items.text_en: Application to garments and Rava's broader principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the same applies to garments, but distinguishes that a garment's soaking is its laundering. Rava's consistent view is illustrated: throwing a scarf or flax into water incurs liability, but for flax it is because it becomes soggy, unlike grains which have moisture or reeds which form a paste.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the same principle applies to a garment, but answers that a garment's soaking is its laundering.
Rava's consistent view is illustrated: throwing a scarf or flax into water incurs liability, but for flax it requires explanation.
Rava explains that flax becomes soggy, unlike grains which have moisture or reeds which form a paste.

items.text: Rava's retraction regarding laundering a shoe on Shabbat
items.text_en: Rava's retraction regarding laundering a shoe on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rava initially permitted laundering a shoe on Shabbat, but when Rav Pappa challenged him with Rav Chiyya bar Ashi's testimony, Rava publicly retracted, declaring his earlier statement a mistake and ruling that rinsing is permitted but laundering is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rava initially taught that it is permitted to launder a shoe on Shabbat.
Rav Pappa objects by citing Rav Chiyya bar Ashi's testimony that Rav only swished his shoes, not laundered them.
Rava retracts his earlier ruling, publicly declaring that swishing is permitted but laundering is forbidden.

items.text: Source for laundering in a sacred place and related laws
items.text_en: Source for laundering in a sacred place and related laws
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from verses that laundering must be done in a sacred place, breaking an earthenware vessel, and rinsing and scrubbing a copper vessel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source for the requirement that laundering of a sin-offering garment must be done in a holy place.
The baraita cites verses: 'תְּכַבֵּס בְּמָקוֹם קָדֹשׁ' for laundering, 'יִשָּׁבֵר' for breaking an earthenware vessel, and 'וּמֹרַק וְשֻׁטַּף' for rinsing a copper vessel.

items.text: Discussion of additional stringencies of the sin-offering
items.text_en: Discussion of additional stringencies of the sin-offering
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the sin-offering has stringencies not found in other offerings. The Gemara questions if there are more, such as blood entering the inner sanctum, atonement for kareit, and four placements of blood. It concludes that the Mishnah lists only one of several possible stringencies.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the sin-offering has a stringency not found in other offerings.
The Gemara asks whether there are additional stringencies, noting that the sin-offering's blood enters the inner sanctum.
The Gemara answers that this applies only to external sin-offerings, following Rabbi Akiva who rules that blood entering the Sanctuary invalidates the offering.
The Gemara further asks about the sin-offering's atonement for kareit (extirpation), noting that this applies only to the sin-offering for hearing a public oath.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah lists only one of several possible stringencies, as the requirement of four blood placements follows Rabbi Yishmael's view, and other features like the horn, finger, and tip are also possible stringencies.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of vessels that left the courtyard
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of vessels that left the courtyard
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details the procedures for garments, earthenware, and copper vessels that left the courtyard or became impure outside: they must be brought back and processed in a sacred place, with tearing, puncturing, or cutting as needed.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah lists the procedures for garments, earthenware vessels, and copper vessels that left the Temple courtyard or became impure outside.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding tearing the garment
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding tearing the garment
items.desc_en: Ravina challenges the Mishnah's requirement to tear a garment that became impure, arguing that tearing renders it no longer a garment. The Gemara answers that one must leave a remnant the size of a ma'aporet, and Rav Huna adds that if such a remnant is left, it remains a connected entity.

sub.desc_en: Ravina challenges the Mishnah's requirement to tear the garment that became impure, arguing that tearing it renders it no longer a garment (בגד), contradicting the Torah's requirement.
The Gemara answers that one must leave a remnant the size of a ma'aporet (an apron-like remnant), so the garment retains its status.
Rav Huna adds that if such a remnant is left, the torn garment remains a connected entity (חיבור), supporting the Gemara's resolution.

items.text: Gemara's ruling on the source
items.text_en: Gemara's ruling on the source
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the previous ruling is rabbinic in origin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara declares that the previous ruling is of rabbinic origin (מִדְּרַבָּנַן).

items.text: Clarification on clay and copper vessels
items.text_en: Clarification on clay and copper vessels
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a clay vessel that left the Temple is still considered a vessel if it has a small hole at its root, and a copper vessel that is patched is still considered a vessel because it is lined with solder.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a clay vessel that left the Temple can still be considered a vessel, since it is no longer in the Temple.
The Gemara answers that the vessel is still considered a vessel because it has a small hole at its root, which does not disqualify it.
The Gemara questions how a copper vessel that is patched can still be considered a vessel.
The Gemara answers that the copper vessel is still considered a vessel because it is lined with solder, which seals the patch.

items.text: Reish Lakish's statement on a defiled garment
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's statement on a defiled garment
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish teaches that a priestly garment that became impure can be inserted into a patch smaller than three by three fingerbreadths and laundered, based on the verse 'it shall not be torn'.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish rules that a priestly garment (מעיל) that became impure can be inserted into a patch smaller than three by three fingerbreadths and laundered, citing the verse 'it shall not be torn' (לא יקרע).

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahavah's objection
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah raises an objection from a baraita that thick and soft materials are not subject to the three-by-three fingerbreadth rule.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah objects by citing a baraita that thick and soft materials are not subject to the three-by-three fingerbreadth rule.

items.text: Gemara's answer: significance due to the parent garment
items.text_en: Gemara's answer: significance due to the parent garment
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the patch is considered significant because of its connection to the parent garment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the patch is considered significant because of its connection to the parent garment.

items.text: Further objection: requirement of seven ingredients
items.text_en: Further objection: requirement of seven ingredients
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another objection: the laundering requires seven ingredients, as stated by Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha, and a baraita teaches that urine is not brought into the Temple.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that laundering requires seven ingredients, citing Rav Nachman's statement and a baraita that urine is not brought into the Temple.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the contradiction regarding the seven sprinklings
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the contradiction regarding the seven sprinklings
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction about how the seven sprinklings can be performed together, suggesting that the blood is absorbed with spittle, as Reish Lakish stated that tasteless spittle must accompany each sprinkling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if one tries to absorb the seven sprinklings with all seven spices together, the mishnah rules that doing so is invalid.
The Gemara raises an alternative: if one absorbs them with a single spice, the mishnah requires stirring three times for each sprinkling, which is impossible.
The Gemara resolves that the blood is absorbed with tasteless spittle, citing Reish Lakish's statement that tasteless spittle must accompany each sprinkling.

items.text: Mishnah: Vessels requiring merikah and shetiḥah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Vessels requiring merikah and shetiḥah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any vessel used for cooking sacrifices, whether by boiling in it or pouring hot contents into it, requires rinsing and scouring. Rabbi Shimon exempts קדשים קלים (lesser holy offerings).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that any vessel used for cooking sacrifices, whether by boiling in it or pouring hot contents into it, requires rinsing and scouring.
Rabbi Shimon exempts קדשים קלים (lesser holy offerings) from the requirement of rinsing and scouring.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of pouring hot contents from the verse
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of pouring hot contents from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraitha that derives the requirement for pouring hot contents from the verse 'וַאֲשֶׁר תְּבֻשַּׁל בּוֹ יִשָּׁבֵר' (and in which it was boiled it shall be broken).

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from the verse 'אֲשֶׁר תְּבֻשַּׁל בּוֹ' (in which it was boiled) that pouring hot contents into a vessel also requires מריקה (rinsing) and שטיפה (scouring).

items.text: Rami bar Chama's query: Suspending a vessel in the oven's air
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's query: Suspending a vessel in the oven's air
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether suspending a vessel in the oven's air (without direct contact) requires merikah and shetiḥah, focusing on whether the Torah is concerned with cooking without absorption. The Gemara clarifies that absorption without cooking is not in question, only cooking without absorption.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether suspending a vessel in the oven's air (without direct contact) requires merikah and shetiḥah, questioning if the Torah is concerned with cooking without absorption.
Rava attempts to answer by citing the Mishnah that includes both cooking in the vessel and pouring hot contents into it.
The Gemara clarifies that absorption without cooking is not in question; only cooking without absorption remains unresolved.

items.text: Rava's proof from the metal oven of the Temple
items.text_en: Rava's proof from the metal oven of the Temple
items.desc_en: Rava brings a proof from Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha that the Temple oven was made of metal, implying that cooking without absorption is a concern; otherwise, a clay oven would suffice. The Gemara explains that due to the leftover meal-offerings baked in the oven, which involve both cooking and absorption, a metal oven is used.

sub.desc_en: Rava brings a proof from Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha that the Temple oven was made of metal, implying that cooking without absorption is a concern; otherwise, a clay oven would suffice, but due to leftover meal-offerings involving both cooking and absorption, a metal oven is used.

items.text: Rabbah bar Ahilai's ruling and its refutation
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Ahilai's ruling and its refutation
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Ahilai forbade bread baked in an oven that had been smeared with fat, even with salt, lest one eat it with condiment. The Gemara refutes this with a baraitha that permits bread from an oven smeared with fat after heating it, concluding that Rabbah bar Ahilai's ruling is refuted.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Ahilai forbade bread baked in an oven smeared with fat, even with salt, lest one eat it with a condiment (כותחא).
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that permits bread from an oven smeared with fat after heating the oven, contradicting Rabbah bar Ahilai's blanket prohibition.
The Gemara declares that Rabbah bar Ahilai's ruling is conclusively refuted (תיוּבְתָּא).

items.text: Ravina's question and resolution regarding Rav's ruling on Pesach pots
items.text_en: Ravina's question and resolution regarding Rav's ruling on Pesach pots
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi why Rav said that Pesach pots should be broken, given the refutation of Rabbah bar Ahilai. Rav Ashi answers that Rav's ruling applies to metal pots, or alternatively to a clay oven heated from inside, but since heating from inside would break the oven, the practice is to heat from outside, rendering the oven forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi why Rav ruled that Pesach pots should be broken, given that Rabbah bar Ahilai's position was refuted.
Rav Ashi answers that Rav's ruling applies specifically to metal pots.
Rav Ashi alternatively explains that Rav's ruling applies to a clay oven heated from inside, unlike the practice of heating from outside.
The Gemara objects that one could heat the oven from inside, but notes that this would break the oven.
The Gemara concludes that since the oven is heated from outside, it is forbidden to use it for Pesach.

items.text: Question about Temple pots
items.text_en: Question about Temple pots
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah requires earthenware pots used in the Temple to be broken, rather than being returned to the kiln for reuse. Rabbi Zeira answers that kilns are not made in Jerusalem.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why earthenware Temple pots must be broken rather than returned to the kiln for reuse.
Rabbi Zeira answers that kilns are not made in Jerusalem, so the pots cannot be refired.

items.text: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that ashes are not disposed of in the Temple courtyard, but then recalls the teaching of Shemayah of Kalnevo that broken earthenware is absorbed in place.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that one does not make ash-heaps (אשפתות) in the Temple courtyard (עזרה), questioning how broken earthenware can be disposed of there.

sub.text: Abaye's resolution via Shemayah of Kalnevo
sub.text_en: Abaye's resolution via Shemayah of Kalnevo
sub.desc_en: Abaye recalls the teaching of Shemayah of Kalnevo that broken earthenware vessels are absorbed in their place (נבלעין במקומן), resolving the disposal concern.

items.text: The Temple oven must be metal
items.text_en: The Temple oven must be metal
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Temple oven was made of metal rather than earthenware, since it is heated from within. It answers that because the Two Loaves and the Showbread are baked and sanctified in the oven, it becomes a service vessel, and service vessels are not made of earthenware.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Temple oven was made of metal rather than earthenware, given that it is heated from within.
The Gemara answers that because the Two Loaves and the Showbread are baked and sanctified in the oven, it becomes a service vessel (כלי שרת), and service vessels are not made of earthenware.

items.text: Opening statement: Even Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda only said wood, not earthenware
items.text_en: Opening statement: Even Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda only said wood, not earthenware
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that even Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, who permits using a vessel that absorbed flavor, only permits wood vessels, not earthenware, which absorb more.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that even Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, who permits using a vessel that absorbed flavor, only permits wood vessels, not earthenware, which absorb more.

items.text: Story of Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda and Rami bar Chama
items.text_en: Story of Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda and Rami bar Chama
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama confronts Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda for leaving him to study with Rav Sheshet, and Rav Yitzchak explains that Rami bar Chama answers from logic while Rav Sheshet answers from a Mishnah, which is more authoritative.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama confronts Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda for leaving him to study with Rav Sheshet, accusing him of arrogance.
Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda explains that Rami bar Chama answers from logic which can be refuted by a Mishnah, while Rav Sheshet answers directly from a Mishnah, which is more authoritative.

items.text: Question about cooking in part of a vessel and the answer from a kal vachomer
items.text_en: Question about cooking in part of a vessel and the answer from a kal vachomer
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda whether a vessel that cooked in part requires rinsing and scouring. He answers it does not, based on a kal vachomer from a garment: just as a garment only requires washing where the blood is, so too a vessel only requires rinsing where the cooking occurred.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda whether a vessel that cooked in part requires rinsing and scouring or not.
Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda answers that it does not require rinsing and scouring, based on a comparison to the law of sprinkling (הזאה).
Rami bar Chama objects that this ruling is not taught in a baraita.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda's kal vachomer
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda's kal vachomer
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda supports his answer with a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from a garment: just as a garment only requires washing where the blood is, so too a vessel only requires rinsing where the cooking occurred.

items.text: Objection and resolution from a Tosefta and a verse
items.text_en: Objection and resolution from a Tosefta and a verse
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama objects that cooking causes bubbling unlike blood, and cites a Tosefta that says if one cooked in part of a vessel, the entire vessel requires rinsing and scouring. Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda concedes and explains the verse 'And if it was cooked in a copper vessel' includes even partial cooking.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama objects that the analogy to a garment fails because blood does not bubble and spread like cooking does.
Rami bar Chama cites a Tosefta that explicitly states that if one cooked in part of a vessel, the entire vessel requires rinsing and scouring, contradicting Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda's position.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda's concession and explanation
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda's concession and explanation
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Yehuda concedes the Tosefta and explains the verse 'And if it was cooked in a copper vessel' includes even partial cooking, thus requiring full vessel treatment.

items.text: Tannaic dispute: which sacrifices require rinsing and scouring
items.text_en: Tannaic dispute: which sacrifices require rinsing and scouring
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tosefta where Rabbi Yehuda derives from the verse that all sacrifices require rinsing and scouring, excluding terumah, while Rabbi Shimon limits it to most holy sacrifices. The Gemara explains their reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by deriving from the verse that the law of rinsing and scouring applies to all sacrifices, not only the sin offering, using the phrase 'קֹדֶשׁ קָדָשִׁים הִיא' (it is most sacred).

Rabbi Yehuda states that one might include תרומה (priestly portion), but the verse excludes it with 'אוֹתָהּ' (of it), implying that all other sacrifices, including קדשים קלים (offerings of lesser sanctity), require rinsing and scouring.
Rabbi Shimon limits rinsing and scouring to קדשי קדשים (offerings of the most sacred order), excluding קדשים קלים (offerings of lesser sanctity), based on the phrase 'קֹדֶשׁ קָדָשִׁים' (most sacred).

The Gemara asks for the reasoning of Rabbi Yehuda and explains that since the verse needed to exclude תרומה (priestly portion) with 'אוֹתָהּ' (of it), it implies that קדשים קלים (offerings of lesser sanctity) are included in the requirement.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon interprets 'אוֹתָהּ' (of it) differently, as referring to a disqualified sin offering, as previously stated in the chapter.

items.text: Question about terumah and three answers distinguishing its laws
items.text_en: Question about terumah and three answers distinguishing its laws
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether terumah really does not require rinsing and scouring, citing a baraita that a pot used for meat and milk requires rinsing. Abaye, Rava, and Rabbah bar Ulla each answer that the baraita refers to a different leniency: only the place of cooking, allowance of wine or diluted wine, or hot water.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the exclusion of תרומה (priestly portion) from scouring and rinsing by citing a baraita that a pot used for meat and milk requires purging, and similarly a pot used for תרומה requires purging when cooking חולין (non-sacred food).
אביי (Abaye) answers that the exclusion of תרומה applies only to the rule that cooking in part of a vessel requires scouring the entire vessel; for תרומה, only the place of cooking needs treatment.

רבא (Rava) answers that the exclusion of תרומה applies to the requirement that scouring and rinsing be done only with water, not wine or diluted wine; for תרומה, even wine or diluted wine may be used.
רבה בר עולא (Rabbah bar Ulla) answers that the exclusion of תרומה applies to the requirement that scouring and rinsing be done with cold water; for תרומה, even hot water suffices.

The Gemara objects that this works only for the opinion that both scouring and rinsing are with cold water; but for the opinion that scouring is with hot water and rinsing with cold, the exclusion of תרומה applies only to the additional rinsing.

items.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Tarfon and the Sages on cooking during a festival
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Tarfon and the Sages on cooking during a festival
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Tarfon allows cooking in a vessel from the beginning of the festival throughout, while the Sages limit it to the time of eating. It also defines rinsing and scouring as like a cup, and says they are done with cold water.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Tarfon's lenient position that one may cook in a vessel from the start of the festival throughout, and the Sages' restrictive position limiting cooking to the time of eating, then defines rinsing and scouring as like a cup and done with cold water.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a spit and a grill used for sacrifices must be purged with hot water.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a spit and a grill used for sacrifices must be purged by scalding in hot water.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on Rabbi Tarfon's view
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on Rabbi Tarfon's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Tarfon's reasoning from a verse, then raises an objection about piggul and notar on the festival, and resolves it by citing Rabbi Nathan and Rav Nachman's principle that each day purges for the next.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural basis of Rabbi Tarfon's view.
Rabbi Tarfon cites the verse 'וּפָנִיתָ בַבֹּקֶר' (Deut 16:7) to show that all festival offerings are treated as one morning, allowing a single purging.
Rav Achadvoi bar Ami objects: if all days are one morning, how can piggul (פיגול) and notar (נותר) apply on the festival?
A baraita of Rabbi Nathan rejects the objection, stating that Rabbi Tarfon's ruling applies only to this specific case (the spit and grill).

sub.text: Rav Nachman's resolution in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's resolution in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman resolves the issue by stating that each day's purging (גיעול) serves for the next day, so piggul and notar still apply.

items.text: The Sages' opinion and the source for merikah u-shtifah
items.text_en: The Sages' opinion and the source for merikah u-shtifah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Sages' view that one waits until the time of eating, then performs merikah and shtifah. Rabbi Yochanan cites a verse to derive this timing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the mishna means by 'until the time of eating'.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains that one waits until the time of eating and then performs scouring and rinsing.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source for this timing.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Abba Yosei ben Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Abba Yosei ben Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan derives from the juxtaposition of verses that one waits until the time of eating and then performs scouring and rinsing.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi and the Sages on merikah and shtifah
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi and the Sages on merikah and shtifah
items.desc_en: The Tosefta records a dispute: Rabbi holds both are done with cold water, the Sages say merikah with hot and shtifah with cold. The Gemara explains their reasoning from the verse and the word order.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that scouring is like the scouring of a cup and rinsing is like the rinsing of a cup.
The baraita records Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's position that both scouring and rinsing are performed with cold water.
The baraita records the Sages' position that scouring is with hot water and rinsing with cold water.
The Gemara asks for the reasoning of the Sages.
The Gemara explains that the Sages analogize to purging vessels from gentiles, and Rabbi responds that he is discussing scouring and rinsing after purging, not the purging itself.
The Sages counter that the verse's wording 'וּמֹרַק וְשֻׁטַּף' implies two different methods: scouring with hot and rinsing with cold.
Rabbi explains that the verse uses two different verbs to teach that scouring and rinsing are two distinct actions, not that they require different temperatures.

items.text: Mishnah on mixtures of offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah on mixtures of offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one cooked different categories of offerings together, the lighter ones follow the stricter ones in terms of eating and purification, and only the place of absorption is prohibited when solids touch.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one cooked different categories of offerings together, the lighter ones follow the stricter ones in terms of eating and purification, and the vessels do not require scouring and rinsing, nor do they disqualify through contact.
The Mishnah adds that when a fit wafer touches an unfit wafer, only the place of absorption is forbidden, not the entire item.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's cases
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the Mishnah's meaning, questions why both cases are needed, and resolves with Abaye and Rava's explanations, concluding that both are necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means, clarifying that if there is a taste component, the lighter sacrifices are eaten like the stricter ones and require rinsing and washing, but if not, they do not.
The Gemara objects: even if the most holy sacrifices do not require rinsing and washing, the lighter sacrifices should require them.
Abaye explains that the Mishnah's statement 'do not require' refers only to the most holy sacrifices, but lighter sacrifices do require rinsing and washing.
Rava answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that lighter sacrifices do not require rinsing and washing.
The Gemara asks: according to Rava, the Mishnah's listing of both cases is understandable, but according to Abaye, why are both cases needed?

The Gemara resolves that both cases are necessary: one case teaches that non-sacred food nullifies sacrifices, and the other teaches that sacrifices nullify other sacrifices, and each alone would not imply the other.

items.text: Baraita on the verse 'all that touches'
items.text_en: Baraita on the verse 'all that touches'
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the verse 'all that touches' implies only when absorption occurs, not mere contact.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites the verse 'all that touches' and deduces that it applies only when absorption occurs, not mere contact.

items.text: Laws of absorption and impurity
items.text_en: Laws of absorption and impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the verse 'until it is absorbed in its flesh' (עַד שֶׁיִּבָּלַע בִּבְשָׂרָהּ), teaching that only the part that touched the impurity is invalid, not the whole piece. It also specifies that absorption applies to flesh, not to sinews, bones, horns, or hooves.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'עַד שֶׁיִּבָּלַע בִּבְשָׂרָהּ' (until it is absorbed in its flesh) as the basis for the law.
The Gemara asks: if impurity touched part of a piece, might the whole piece be invalid?
The Gemara answers: the verse says 'יִגַּע' (it touches) — only the part that touched is invalid.
The Gemara resolves: one cuts away the place that absorbed the impurity.
The Tanna Kamma teaches that the absorption applies only to flesh (בשר), not to sinews, bones, horns, or hooves.

items.text: The principle of 'יִקְדָּשׁ' – becoming like the absorbed item
items.text_en: The principle of 'יִקְדָּשׁ' – becoming like the absorbed item
items.desc_en: The verse 'יִקְדָּשׁ' teaches that the absorbed item becomes like the meat: if the meat is invalid, the absorbed item is invalid; if it is valid, it is eaten with the stringencies of the meat.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states the principle that the absorbed item becomes like the meat: if the meat is invalid, the absorbed item is invalid; if it is valid, it is eaten with the stringencies of the meat.

items.text: Positive commandment does not override a negative commandment in the Temple
items.text_en: Positive commandment does not override a negative commandment in the Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the positive commandment of 'יִקְדָּשׁ' does not override the negative commandment of breaking bones. Rava answers that a positive commandment does not override a negative commandment in the Temple, citing the verse 'וְעֶצֶם לֹא תִשְׁבְּרוּ בוֹ'. Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya extends this to all bones, with or without marrow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the positive commandment of 'יִקְדָּשׁ' does not override the negative commandment of breaking bones.
Rava answers that a positive commandment does not override a negative commandment in the Temple.
The Gemara cites the verse 'וְעֶצֶם לֹא תִשְׁבְּרוּ בוֹ' as support for Rava's principle.
Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya extends the prohibition to all bones, with or without marrow.
The Gemara again asks why the positive commandment does not override the negative commandment.
The Gemara resolves that a positive commandment does not override a negative commandment in the Temple.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that 'יִקְדָּשׁ' is itself a positive commandment, and a positive commandment does not override a negative commandment combined with a positive commandment (לא תעשה ועשה).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that 'יִקְדָּשׁ' is a positive commandment, and a positive commandment does not override a negative commandment combined with a positive commandment (לא תעשה ועשה).

items.text: Deriving laws for all sacrifices from the sin-offering
items.text_en: Deriving laws for all sacrifices from the sin-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that other sacrifices are also sanctified through absorption. Shmuel cites Rabbi Eliezer, who derives from the verse 'זֹאת הַתּוֹרָה לָעֹלָה וְלַמִּנְחָה וְלַחַטָּאת וְלָאָשָׁם וְלַמִּלּוּאִים וּלְזֶבַח הַשְּׁלָמִים' that all sacrifices share common laws.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that other sacrifices are also sanctified through absorption, having found this law for the sin-offering.
Shmuel cites Rabbi Eliezer, who derives from the verse 'זֹאת הַתּוֹרָה לָעֹלָה וְלַמִּנְחָה וְלַחַטָּאת וְלָאָשָׁם וְלַמִּלּוּאִים וּלְזֶבַח הַשְּׁלָמִים' that all sacrifices share common laws.

items.text: Deriving the requirement of a knife from the burnt-offering
items.text_en: Deriving the requirement of a knife from the burnt-offering
items.desc_en: From the word 'לָעֹלָה' the Gemara derives that just as the burnt-offering requires a vessel (a knife), so do all sacrifices. It questions whether a basin is meant, but concludes it is a knife, citing Abraham's use of a knife for the binding of Isaac.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the word 'לָעֹלָה' that just as the burnt-offering requires a vessel, so do all sacrifices.
The Gemara questions what vessel is meant, suggesting a basin but noting that communal peace-offerings also use basins.
The Gemara concludes that the vessel is a knife, citing Abraham's use of a knife for the binding of Isaac as proof that the burnt-offering requires a knife.

items.text: Deriving the rule of male priests eating from the meal-offering
items.text_en: Deriving the rule of male priests eating from the meal-offering
items.desc_en: From the word 'מִנְחָה' the Gemara derives that just as the meal-offering is eaten only by male priests, so are all sacrifices. It clarifies that for sin-offerings and guilt-offerings this is explicit, and for communal peace-offerings it is derived from a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the word 'מִנְחָה' (meal-offering) that just as the meal-offering is eaten only by male priests, so are all sacrifices.
The Gemara objects that for sin-offerings and guilt-offerings the rule is already explicit in the verse.
The Gemara answers that for communal peace-offerings the rule is derived from a verse, 'בְּקֹדֶשׁ הַקֳּדָשִׁים תֹּאכְלֶנּוּ כׇּל זָכָר יֹאכַל אֹתוֹ'.

items.text: Conclusion: a dispute among Tannaim
items.text_en: Conclusion: a dispute among Tannaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the derivation from the meal-offering is a matter of dispute among Tannaim (תַּנָּאֵי הִיא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the preceding derivation is a matter of dispute among Tannaim (תַּנָּאֵי הִיא).

items.text: Derivations from chatat, asham, miluim, and shelamim
items.text_en: Derivations from chatat, asham, miluim, and shelamim
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents four derivations using the word 'chatat' to teach that all sacrifices become sanctified through absorption (balu'a), that fetal sacs are not sanctified in an asham, that surplus of miluim is burned and living animals are not subject to surplus, and that shelamim can become piggul and cause piggul.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that there are different derivations from various verses.
From the word 'חטאת' (sin-offering), the Gemara derives that all sacrifices become sanctified through absorption (בלוע).

From the word 'אשם' (guilt-offering), the Gemara derives that fetal sacs are not sanctified in an asham, based on the principle that offspring of sacrifices are sanctified only in their own state and one derives the possible from the impossible.
From the word 'מלואים' (inauguration offerings), the Gemara derives that surplus of miluim is burned and living animals are not subject to surplus.
From the word 'שלמים' (peace-offerings), the Gemara derives that all sacrifices can cause piggul and become piggul.

items.text: Addition of minchah and necessity of both verses
items.text_en: Addition of minchah and necessity of both verses
items.desc_en: A baraita in the name of Rabbi Akiva adds a derivation from minchah for sanctification through absorption. The Gemara explains that both minchah and chatat are necessary: minchah because it is soft and absorbs well, chatat because it is cold, so each teaches what the other might not.

sub.text: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: A baraita in the name of Rabbi Akiva adds a derivation from minchah (meal-offering) that all offerings are sanctified through absorption, just as minchah is.
The Gemara explains that both minchah and chatat (sin-offering) are necessary: minchah because it is soft and absorbs well, and chatat because it is cold, so each teaches what the other might not.

items.text: Derivation from chatat for chullin, daytime, and right hand
items.text_en: Derivation from chatat for chullin, daytime, and right hand
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from chatat that all sacrifices must come from chullin (non-sacred property), be offered by day, and with the right hand. The source for chullin is from Rav Chisda citing a verse about Aaron's bull. The daytime law is derived from 'b'yom tzavoto' (taken as given). The right hand is derived from Resh Lakish's principle that wherever 'etzba' and 'kehuna' are mentioned, it is the right hand; alternatively, it follows Rabbi Shimon's view that 'etzba' does not require kehuna but kehuna requires 'etzba'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by deriving from the chatat (sin-offering) that all sacrifices must come from chullin (non-sacred property), be offered by day, and with the right hand.
The Gemara asks the source for the chullin requirement and cites Rav Chisda's answer from the verse about Aaron's bull.
Rav Chisda derives the chullin requirement from the verse 'and Aaron shall offer the bull of the sin-offering which is his' — from his own property, not from public or tithe property.
The Gemara states that the daytime requirement is derived from the phrase 'b'yom tzavoto' (on the day of His command), taken as given.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Resh Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Resh Lakish
sub.desc_en: The right-hand requirement is derived from Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Resh Lakish's principle that wherever 'etzba' (finger) and 'kehuna' (priesthood) are mentioned, it is the right hand.
Alternatively, the Gemara follows Rabbi Shimon's view that 'etzba' does not require kehuna (priesthood), but kehuna requires 'etzba'.

items.text: Derivation from asham for bones and Rava's certainty
items.text_en: Derivation from asham for bones and Rava's certainty
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from asham that the bones of all sacrifices are permitted (for benefit). Rava states that this is obvious to him, implying the derivation is straightforward.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the term 'אשם' (guilt-offering) that the bones of all sacrifices are permitted for benefit, just as the bones of an אשם are permitted.
Rava states that this derivation is obvious to him, indicating that the conclusion is straightforward and requires no further proof.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that blood of a sin-offering placed below the blood line and blood of a burnt-offering placed above require laundering.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that blood of a sin-offering placed below the blood line and blood of a burnt-offering placed above require laundering.

items.text: Rava's query and resolution
items.text_en: Rava's query and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava asks about the case where blood of a burnt-offering is below and blood of a sin-offering is above: does it require laundering because of contact or because of absorption? He later resolves that it does not require laundering.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks: if blood of a burnt-offering is placed below the line and blood of a sin-offering above, what is the law — does the garment require laundering?
Rava considers two possibilities: the laundering requirement is due to contact with the garment (which occurred) or due to absorption into the fabric (which did not occur).
Rava resolves the question: such garments do not require laundering.

items.text: Rava's query about blood and congealed fat
items.text_en: Rava's query about blood and congealed fat
items.desc_en: Rava states that blood on one's garment is a barrier unless he is a butcher, and congealed fat is a barrier unless he is a seller of congealed fat. He then asks about a mixture of both on the garment: if he is a butcher, the congealed fat is problematic; if a seller, the blood is problematic. The Gemara clarifies the case is when he does both, and questions whether he is particular about two substances but not one, or even about two. The matter stands unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that blood on one's garment is a barrier unless he is a butcher, and congealed fat is a barrier unless he is a seller of congealed fat.
Rava asks about a mixture of blood and congealed fat on the garment.
The Gemara clarifies that the case is when he does both butchering and selling congealed fat.
The Gemara questions whether he is particular about two substances but not one, or even about two.
The matter stands unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The standard closing formula for the chapter is stated.

sub.desc_en: The gemara marks the end of the chapter with the formula 'הדרן עלך דם חטאת' (we return to you, chapter 'Blood of a Sin-Offering').

items.text: Mishnah: Who may partake of sacrifices
items.text_en: Mishnah: Who may partake of sacrifices
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those who may not partake of sacrificial meat: a טְבוּל יוֹם, a מְחוּסַּר כִּיפּוּרִים, and an אוֹנֵן. It then states that blemished priests may partake but not offer sacrifices. Finally, it derives from a verse that one who is impure at the time of blood sprinkling does not receive a portion of the meat, even if pure at the time of burning the fats.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a טְבוּל יוֹם (one who immersed but awaits sunset) and a מְחוּסַּר כִּיפּוּרִים (one lacking atonement) do not receive portions of sacred meat to eat in the evening.
The Mishnah adds that an אוֹנֵן (one in acute mourning) may not touch, offer, or receive a portion of sacred meat to eat in the evening.
The Mishnah states that blemished priests, whether with temporary or permanent blemishes, receive portions and eat, but do not offer sacrifices.
The Mishnah rules that anyone unfit for service does not receive a portion of the meat, and anyone who has no portion in the meat has no portion in the hides.

The Mishnah derives from the verse 'הַמַּקְרִיב אֶת דַּם הַשְּׁלָמִים... לוֹ תִהְיֶה' that even one impure at the time of blood sprinkling but pure at the burning of fats does not receive a portion of the meat.

items.text: Derivation from the verse
items.text_en: Derivation from the verse
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish derives from the verse 'the priest who sprinkles it shall eat it' that only a priest who can sprinkle may eat, implying one who cannot sprinkle cannot eat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where are these matters (that a priest who cannot sprinkle does not eat) derived?
Reish Lakish derives from the verse 'the priest who sprinkles it shall eat it' that only a priest who can sprinkle may eat, implying one who cannot sprinkle cannot eat.

items.text: Refinement: 'fit to sprinkle' vs. 'fit to eat'
items.text_en: Refinement: 'fit to sprinkle' vs. 'fit to eat'
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the entire watch eats without sprinkling, so the verse must mean 'fit to sprinkle' shares, not that only the sprinkler eats. It then reinterprets 'yochalennah' as 'yechalkennah' (he shall divide it), so one fit to sprinkle receives a share, one unfit does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the entire watch eats without sprinkling, so the verse must mean 'fit to sprinkle' shares, not that only the sprinkler eats.
The Gemara reinterprets 'יֹאכְלֶנָּה' as 'יְחַלְּקֶנָּה' (he shall divide it), so one fit to sprinkle receives a share, one unfit does not.

items.text: Blemished priest included by 'all males'
items.text_en: Blemished priest included by 'all males'
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that a blemished priest, though unfit to sprinkle, receives a share, because the verse 'all males among the priests' includes him. It rejects including a tevul yom (one who immersed that day) because he is not yet fit to eat that night.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a blemished priest, who is unfit for sprinkling, nevertheless receives a share, contradicting the principle that only those fit for sprinkling receive a share.
The Gemara answers that the Torah itself included a blemished priest through the verse 'all males among the priests'.
The Gemara counters that perhaps the verse should include a טבול יום (one who immersed that day) instead of a blemished priest.
The Gemara resolves that a blemished priest is more fitting to include because he is currently fit to eat, whereas a טבול יום is not yet fit to eat that night.

items.text: Rav Yosef's alternative derivation
