items.text_en: Rav Yosef's alternative derivation
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef argues that if the verse meant 'divide', it should have said 'yechalkennah'; instead, 'yochalennah' teaches that one fit to eat receives a share, one unfit does not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef argues that the verse's unusual wording 'יֹאכְלֶנָּה' instead of 'יְחַלְּקֶנָּה' teaches that only one fit to eat receives a share, while one unfit does not.

items.text: Reish Lakish's query: blemished and defiled priest
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's query: blemished and defiled priest
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks whether a blemished priest who is also defiled receives a share. Rabbah resolves from the rule that a High Priest who is an onen may offer but does not eat or receive a share, proving that fitness to eat is required.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks whether a blemished priest who is also defiled receives a share, considering the competing principles of the Torah's inclusion of a blemished priest versus the requirement of fitness to eat.

Rabbah resolves the query by citing the rule that a High Priest who is an onen (mourner before burial) may offer but does not eat or receive a share, proving that fitness to eat is required for receiving a share.

items.text: Rav Oshaya's query: defiled priest in communal offerings
items.text_en: Rav Oshaya's query: defiled priest in communal offerings
items.desc_en: Rav Oshaya asks whether a defiled priest who sprinkles communal offerings receives a share. Ravina resolves from the same onen rule that fitness to eat is required.

sub.desc_en: Rav Oshaya asks whether a defiled priest who sprinkles communal offerings receives a share, posing two alternatives: the verse 'the one who sprinkles' includes him, or only one fit to eat shares.
Ravina resolves from the case of the High Priest as an onen (mourner before burial) who offers but does not eat or share, proving that fitness to eat is required for receiving a share.

items.text: Onen touching sacred food and the need for immersion
items.text_en: Onen touching sacred food and the need for immersion
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states an onen may touch but not offer; the Gemara questions this, citing that an onen needs immersion for sacred food. Rabbi Ami resolves that one who immersed is permitted, but Rabba bar Rav Huna notes that anenut returns after immersion. The Gemara distinguishes between cases of diverting attention from corpse impurity vs. from sheretz impurity, and Rabbi Yirmeya introduces the concept of guarding against what defiles vs. what disqualifies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that an onen may touch sacred food, citing a baraita that an onen and one lacking atonement require immersion for sacred food.
Rabbi Ami in the name of Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction: one case is where the onen immersed, the other where he did not.
The Gemara objects that even if he immersed, his anenut (mourning status) returns upon him, citing Rabba bar Rav Huna's statement.
The Gemara distinguishes between one who diverted his attention from the corpse impurity and one who did not.

sub.text: Supporting baraita via Rabbi Yostai bar Rabbi Matun citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita via Rabbi Yostai bar Rabbi Matun citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yostai bar Rabbi Matun in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that one who diverted his attention requires sprinkling on the third and seventh days.
The Gemara further distinguishes between diverting attention from corpse impurity (requiring sprinkling) and from sheretz impurity.
The Gemara objects that one impure from a sheretz is a full-fledged impure person requiring sunset for terumah as well, so the distinction seems irrelevant.
Rabbi Yirmeya explains that the distinction is between guarding against what defiles (requiring immersion) and guarding against what disqualifies (not requiring immersion).
The Gemara objects that there is no such thing as partial guarding, and cites a baraita about a basket on one's head to illustrate the point.

items.text: Opening discussion: the case of the basket and the scoop
items.text_en: Opening discussion: the case of the basket and the scoop
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with a case where a basket and a scoop are together, and the owner says his intention was only for the basket. The basket is pure and the scoop impure. The Gemara asks why the scoop does not contaminate the basket, and Rava answers that he guarded it from something that makes it impure but not from something that disqualifies it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where a basket contains a scoop, and the owner declares his intention is only for the basket, resulting in the basket being pure and the scoop impure.
The Gemara asks why the impure scoop does not contaminate the basket or its contents.
Rava answers that the owner guarded the basket from something that makes it impure but not from something that disqualifies it.

items.text: Rabbi Abba bar Memel cites Rabbi Yochanan on third-degree terumah
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel cites Rabbi Yochanan on third-degree terumah
items.desc_en: The matter reached Rabbi Abba bar Memel, who said they should have heard the statement of Rabbi Yochanan quoting Rabbi: one who eats third-degree terumah is forbidden to eat but permitted to touch. This shows that the rabbis instituted a higher degree for eating but not for touching.

sub.desc_en: The matter reached Rabbi Abba bar Memel, who asked whether they had heard Rabbi Yochanan's statement in the name of Rabbi: one who eats third-degree terumah is forbidden to eat but permitted to touch.
The gemara concludes that the rabbis instituted a higher degree of stringency for eating but not for touching.

items.text: Clarification: the onen does not divide but eats when invited
items.text_en: Clarification: the onen does not divide but eats when invited
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the onen does not divide the offering but if invited, he eats. This is a brief note about the onen's status.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the onen does not divide the offering but if invited, he eats.

items.text: Contradiction about the onen eating Passover and other sacrifices
items.text_en: Contradiction about the onen eating Passover and other sacrifices
items.desc_en: A contradiction is raised: an onen immerses and eats his Passover in the evening, but not other sacrifices. Rav Yirmeya from Difti resolves: here it refers to Passover, there to the rest of the year. On Passover, since he eats the Passover, he also eats other sacrifices; during the rest of the year, since he is not eligible, he does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: an onen immerses and eats his Passover sacrifice in the evening, but not other sacrifices.

Rav Yirmeya from Difti resolves: here it refers to Passover, there to the rest of the year; on Passover, since he eats the Passover, he also eats other sacrifices, but during the rest of the year he does not.

items.text: Rav Asi's resolution and the tannaitic dispute on nighttime onen status
items.text_en: Rav Asi's resolution and the tannaitic dispute on nighttime onen status
items.desc_en: Rav Asi resolves differently: one case is where the relative died on the 14th and was buried on the 14th; the other where he died on the 13th and was buried on the 14th, because the day of burial does not take the night rabbinically. The Gemara then asks which tanna holds that nighttime onen status is rabbinic, and answers it is Rabbi Shimon, citing a baraita.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between two cases: one where the relative died and was buried on the 14th (the onen status is biblical), and one where he died on the 13th and was buried on the 14th (the onen status is only rabbinic because the day of burial does not take the night rabbinically).
The Gemara asks which tanna holds that nighttime onen status is rabbinic, and answers that it is Rabbi Shimon.

A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda holds that nighttime onen status is biblical, while Rabbi Shimon holds it is only rabbinic, as evidenced by the ruling that an onen immerses and eats his Passover offering in the evening but not other sacred foods.

items.text: Challenges to Rabbi Shimon's view and the baraita on offerings an onen cannot bring
items.text_en: Challenges to Rabbi Shimon's view and the baraita on offerings an onen cannot bring
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges whether Rabbi Shimon really holds nighttime onen status is rabbinic, citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon says an onen does not send his offerings, and questions if that includes Passover. It then brings another baraita where Rabbi Shimon derives from the verse that an onen brings only when he is complete (shalem), and lists all offerings excluded, including the Passover.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Shimon really holds that nighttime onen status is rabbinic, citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon says an onen does not send his offerings, and asks if that includes Passover; the Gemara answers that it excludes Passover.

A baraita is cited where Rabbi Shimon derives from the verse that an onen brings offerings only when he is complete (shalem), and includes the thanks offering because it is consumed in joy like a peace offering.
The baraita continues, including the burnt offering, firstborn, tithe, Passover, sin offering, and guilt offering in the list of offerings an onen cannot bring, each derived from the verse.

The baraita concludes by including bird offerings, meal offerings, wine, wood, and frankincense, teaching that all offerings are brought only when the person is complete (shalem), not when he is an onen.

items.text: Discussion of the Passover in the baraita and Rav Sheshet's explanation
items.text_en: Discussion of the Passover in the baraita and Rav Sheshet's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita explicitly includes Passover. Rav Chisda says: Passover when he takes it. Rav Sheshet says: what Passover? The peace-offerings of Passover. The Gemara questions that this is the same as peace-offerings, and explains that the baraita teaches peace-offerings that come because of Passover and peace-offerings that come on their own, to prevent the assumption that those from Passover are like the Passover itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita explicitly includes the Passover offering.
Rav Chisda says: The mention of Passover is incidental, as if he takes it.
Rav Sheshet says: The term 'Passover' in the baraita refers to the peace-offerings of Passover.
The Gemara objects: If so, that is the same as peace-offerings, which were already mentioned.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita teaches both peace-offerings that come on account of Passover and those that come on their own, to prevent the assumption that those from Passover are like the Passover itself.

items.text: Rav Mari begins a statement
items.text_en: Rav Mari begins a statement
items.desc_en: Rav Mari begins to speak, but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mari begins to speak, but the text cuts off without completing his statement.

items.text: First resolution: distinction between day of death and day of burial
items.text_en: First resolution: distinction between day of death and day of burial
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing two cases: one where the relative died and was buried on the 14th (the day of death is biblical), and one where he died on the 13th and was buried on the 14th (the day of burial is rabbinic, and its night is only rabbinically binding).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a death and burial on the 14th (biblical onenut) and a death on the 13th with burial on the 14th (rabbinic onenut).

items.text: Rav Ashi's objection to the first resolution
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection to the first resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi challenges Rav Mari: the baraita of Rabbi Shimon discusses an onen who immerses and eats his Passover offering, which involves biblical onen status (day of death), but the resolution introduced a rabbinic day of burial. This is inconsistent.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's objection to Rav Mari
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection to Rav Mari
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects that the baraita of Rabbi Shimon, which discusses an onen who immerses and eats his Passover offering, deals with biblical onen status (day of death), whereas the previous resolution introduced a rabbinic day of burial, making the two inconsistent.

items.text: Abaye's resolution: before or after midday
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution: before or after midday
items.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing whether the death occurred before or after midday on the 14th. Before midday, the person was not yet fit for the Passover offering, so onen status applies; after midday, he was fit, so onen status does not apply.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing whether the death occurred before or after midday on the 14th: before midday, the person was not yet fit for the Passover offering, so אוננות (onen status) applies; after midday, he was fit, so אוננות does not apply.

items.text: Proof from the baraita of Yosef HaKohen
items.text_en: Proof from the baraita of Yosef HaKohen
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about Yosef HaKohen, whose wife died on Passover eve, and he was forced to become impure for a mitzvah corpse. This is contrasted with another baraita that says one who is on his way to slaughter his Passover offering should not become impure for his sister. The Gemara infers that the distinction is before or after midday.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for a proof that the distinction between before and after midday applies to the laws of אונן (mourner before burial).

The Gemara cites a baraita about Yosef HaKohen whose wife died on Passover eve, and he was forced to become impure for a mitzvah corpse, establishing that impurity for a mitzvah corpse overrides the priest's prohibition.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from another baraita that says one who is on his way to slaughter his Passover offering should not become impure for his sister.
The baraita resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between impurity for one's sister (forbidden) and impurity for a mitzvah corpse (permitted).
The Gemara infers from the two baraitot that the distinction is based on whether the death occurred before or after midday.

items.text: Rejection: perhaps the dispute is between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Rejection: perhaps the dispute is between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, suggesting that the two baraitot might both refer to after midday but reflect a dispute between Rabbi Yishmael (who says impurity for a mitzvah corpse is optional) and Rabbi Akiva (who says it is obligatory).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, suggesting that both baraitot might refer to after midday but reflect a dispute between Rabbi Yishmael (who says impurity for a mitzvah corpse is optional) and Rabbi Akiva (who says it is obligatory).

items.text: Final rejection: the baraita is from Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Final rejection: the baraita is from Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the rejection is untenable because the beginning of that baraita is explicitly taught by Rabbi Akiva, who holds that impurity for a mitzvah corpse is obligatory. Thus the distinction must be before or after midday.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous explanation, stating that it cannot enter one's mind because the beginning of that baraita is taught by Rabbi Akiva.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Akiva explains that 'nefesh' refers to relatives and 'met' refers to non-relatives.
The baraita continues, teaching that a nazirite may not become impure for his father but may become impure for a met mitzvah.
The baraita teaches that even a priest who is a nazirite may not become impure for his mother but may become impure for a met mitzvah.
The baraita teaches that even a High Priest who is a nazirite may not become impure for his brother but may become impure for a met mitzvah.

The baraita concludes with the case of a nazirite going to slaughter his Paschal offering or circumcise his son, teaching that he may not become impure for his sister but may become impure for a met mitzvah.

items.text: Rava's resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Rava's resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the two conflicting rulings refer to different times: one before the paschal lamb was slaughtered and its blood sprinkled for the onen, the other after.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between before and after the paschal lamb was slaughtered and its blood sprinkled for the onen.

items.text: Objection and Ravina's citation of Rabbah bar Rav Huna
items.text_en: Objection and Ravina's citation of Rabbah bar Rav Huna
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Masna objects that after slaughter and sprinkling, the matter is already done. Ravina counters that eating the paschal lamb is indispensable, citing Rabbah bar Rav Huna.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Masna objects to Rava's distinction: after slaughter and sprinkling, the matter is already done, so why would the timing matter?
Ravina counters that eating the paschal lamb is indispensable (מעכבא), citing a ruling of Rabbah bar Rav Huna.
Rav Adda bar Masna dismisses Ravina's citation, telling him to listen to what his master (Rava) says.

items.text: The baraita about day of hearing and day of burial
items.text_en: The baraita about day of hearing and day of burial
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita that compares the day of hearing news of a death to the day of burial for mourning, and for eating the paschal lamb to the day of gathering bones. It concludes that both allow one to immerse and eat sacrifices in the evening.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita that equates the day of hearing news of a death with the day of burial for mourning, and for eating the paschal lamb with the day of gathering bones, concluding that both allow one to immerse and eat sacrifices in the evening.

items.text: Contradiction within the baraita
items.text_en: Contradiction within the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction: the baraita first implies that on the day of burial one may not eat even in the evening, but then says both allow eating in the evening.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the baraita: it first implies that on the day of burial one may not eat even in the evening, but then concludes that both cases allow eating in the evening.

items.text: Rav Chisda's answer: Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's answer: Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda answers that the baraita reflects a dispute between Tannaim.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda answers that the contradiction in the baraita reflects a dispute between Tannaim.

items.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's resolution and inference
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's resolution and inference
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between cases near sunset and after sunset. The Gemara infers from this that eating the paschal lamb is indispensable.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between cases near sunset and after sunset.
The Gemara objects that after sunset, the paschal lamb has already been eaten, so the distinction is meaningless.
The Gemara infers from Rabbah bar Rav Huna's statement that eating the paschal lamb is indispensable (מעכבא).

items.text: Rav Ashi's interpretation and rejection
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's interpretation and rejection
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the baraita means both the day of hearing and the day of gathering bones allow eating in the evening. The Gemara rejects this as fabricated, since the baraita uses 'this and that' implying two distinct cases.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the baraita's phrase 'one this and one that' means both the day of hearing and the day of gathering bones allow one to immerse and eat sacred food in the evening.

The Gemara objects that Rav Ashi's interpretation is fabricated, because the baraita should have used the phrase 'this and that' (זֶה וָזֶה) if it meant both cases, but it uses 'one this and one that' (אֶחָד זֶה וְאֶחָד זֶה), implying two distinct cases.

items.text: Analysis of the Tannaitic dispute about onen status
items.text_en: Analysis of the Tannaitic dispute about onen status
items.desc_en: The Gemara explores the Tannaitic dispute regarding how long one is an onen, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer says all day and Rabbi says until burial. It discusses whether the day of death or burial includes the night, and concludes that Rabbi holds night-time onen status is rabbinic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Tannaitic source underlies the dispute, and introduces a baraita.
The Gemara questions whether the baraita deals with the day of death, noting that even the Sages agree that the night of the day of death is only rabbinically prohibited.
The Gemara further questions Rabbi's statement that onen status lasts until burial, asking whether anyone disputes that the end of onen status is as bitter as the day of death.
Rav Sheishet answers that the baraita deals with the day of burial, not the day of death.

Rav Yosef objects, citing the baraita that one who hears news of a death or gathers bones immerses and eats sacred food in the evening, implying that on the day of burial one may not eat even in the evening, and proposes a revised version of the baraita.

Rabbi Yirmeya objects that Rav Yosef's version is inconsistent with a baraita where Rabbi holds onen status lasts as long as the body is unburied, even up to ten days, and the Sages limit it to that day alone.

The Gemara resolves by proposing a corrected version: the first Tanna says onen status lasts the entire day without its night, and Rabbi says it lasts until burial, and if buried, the night is included.
Rava infers from Rabbi's statement that the night of the day of burial is rabbinic, implying that the night of the day of death is Torah-level.
The Gemara objects, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda holds that night-time onen status is Torah-level, but Rabbi explicitly says it is only rabbinic.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi's position is that night-time onen status is always rabbinic.

items.text: Opening statement: Sages strengthened their words more than Torah
items.text_en: Opening statement: Sages strengthened their words more than Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a general principle that the Sages made their enactments stronger than Torah laws.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a general principle that the Sages made their enactments stronger than Torah laws.

items.text: Baraita: Three phrases in the verses
items.text_en: Baraita: Three phrases in the verses
items.desc_en: A baraita explains three biblical phrases: 'for so I was commanded' refers to eating in aninut, 'as I commanded' refers to the time of the act, and 'as the Lord commanded' indicates Moses spoke not from himself.

sub.desc_en: A baraita explains three biblical phrases: 'כי כן צויתי' (for so I was commanded) refers to eating in aninut, 'כאשר צויתי' (as I commanded) refers to the time of the act, and 'כאשר צוה ה׳' (as the Lord commanded) indicates Moses spoke not from himself.

items.text: Contradiction raised from another baraita
items.text_en: Contradiction raised from another baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: another baraita says the sin-offering was burned because of aninut, citing the word 'like these'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from another baraita that states the sin-offering was burned because of aninut (mourning), citing the word 'like these'.

items.text: Shmuel resolves: Rabbi Yehuda vs. Rabbi Nechemya
items.text_en: Shmuel resolves: Rabbi Yehuda vs. Rabbi Nechemya
items.desc_en: Shmuel resolves the contradiction by attributing the two baraitot to different Tannaim: one to Rabbi Nechemya (aninut) and one to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon (tumah). The latter bring proofs against the aninut explanation.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel resolves the contradiction by attributing the two baraitot to different Tannaim: one to Rabbi Nechemya (aninut) and one to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon (tumah).
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Nechemya says the sin-offering was burned due to aninut (mourning), while Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon say it was burned due to tumah (impurity).

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon's objection
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon's objection
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon argue that the sin-offering was burned due to impurity, bringing three proofs against the aninut explanation: all three sons should have burned it, it could have been eaten in the evening, and Pinchas was with them.

items.text: Rava's alternative resolution: temporal vs. eternal sanctity
items.text_en: Rava's alternative resolution: temporal vs. eternal sanctity
items.desc_en: Rava says both baraitot are Rabbi Nechemya, but one refers to offerings of the time (the Tabernacle) and the other to offerings for generations.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by asserting that both baraitot align with Rabbi Nechemya, but one deals with offerings of the time (the Tabernacle) and the other with offerings for generations.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Nechemya and the Sages would each reconcile the contradictory verses about the sin offering.

items.text: Rabbi Nechemya's interpretation of the verses
items.text_en: Rabbi Nechemya's interpretation of the verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains how Rabbi Nechemya interprets the verses: Moses asked Aaron if the blood entered the inner sanctum, if it left its boundary, or if they offered it in aninut. Aaron responded that he offered it, and Moses concluded they should eat it in aninut. Moses then questioned whether this applied only to temporal offerings, as a kal vachomer from maaser would forbid it for eternal offerings. Moses admitted he forgot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Nechemya's interpretation: Moses asked Aaron if the blood entered the inner sanctum or left its boundary, and Aaron answered that it remained in the sacred area.
Moses asked if the offering was disqualified by aninut (acute mourning), but Aaron responded that he, the High Priest, offered it, and Moses concluded they should eat it in aninut.
Aaron objected that Moses' command might apply only to temporal offerings (קדשי שעה), not to eternal ones.
Aaron supported his objection with a kal vachomer (a fortiori inference) from maaser (tithe): if an acute mourner is forbidden from eating maaser, all the more so from קדשי דורות (eternal offerings).
Moses immediately conceded, admitting he had heard the halakha but forgotten it.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon's interpretation of the verses
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon's interpretation of the verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains how Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon interpret the verses: Moses asked about the blood entering the inner sanctum, leaving its boundary, or aninut. Aaron responded that they offered it (implying aninut would disqualify), but he himself offered it. Moses then asked about tumah, and Aaron denied any disrespect. Moses concluded they should eat it in aninut, but questioned whether this applied only at night, as a kal vachomer from maaser would forbid it during the day. Moses admitted he forgot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon reconcile the verses about the sin-offering.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon's answer
sub.desc_en: They explain that Moses first asked whether the blood entered the inner sanctum or left its boundary, and Aaron answered that neither occurred.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon's answer (continued)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon's answer (continued)
sub.desc_en: Moses then asked about aninut and tumah; Aaron denied both, asserting he would never disrespect sacred offerings.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon's answer (continued)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon's answer (continued)
sub.desc_en: Moses concluded that since the blood was not brought inside and the offering remained in the sacred place, they should eat it in a state of aninut.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon's answer (continued)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon's answer (continued)
sub.desc_en: Moses questioned whether the permission applied only at night, as a kal vachomer from maaser would forbid it during the day.

items.text: Opening statement about Moses' response
items.text_en: Opening statement about Moses' response
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Moses was not ashamed to say 'I did not hear' but rather 'I heard and forgot'.

items.text: Question about delaying and eating at night
items.text_en: Question about delaying and eating at night
items.desc_en: A question is raised: should they have delayed and eaten it at night? The impurity came through duress.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbis and Rabbi Nechemiah on 'today'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbis and Rabbi Nechemiah on 'today'
items.desc_en: The Gemara contrasts the views of the Rabbis and Rabbi Nechemiah regarding the word 'today' in the verse. For the Rabbis, it is straightforward; for Rabbi Nechemiah, it means the obligation of the day. Similarly, 'behold today' is explained differently by each side.

items.text: Explanation of the three sin-offerings
items.text_en: Explanation of the three sin-offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the three sin-offerings mentioned: the goat of Nachshon, the sin-offering of the eighth day, and the goat of Rosh Chodesh. It clarifies that only one was burned, and Moses' double inquiry identified which one.

items.text: Rabbi Nechemiah's reasoning and the night of mourning
items.text_en: Rabbi Nechemiah's reasoning and the night of mourning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Nechemiah holds that mourning does not disqualify temporary sanctified items, and that night-time mourning is biblical.

items.text: Pinchas' priesthood and the alternative explanation
items.text_en: Pinchas' priesthood and the alternative explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the objection that Pinchas was with them, and Rav Ashi explains that Pinchas only became a priest after killing Zimri. The Gemara then addresses counter-arguments from verses.

items.text: Rav's statement that Moses was a High Priest
items.text_en: Rav's statement that Moses was a High Priest
items.desc_en: Rav states that Moses was a High Priest and shared in the sacrifices, citing a verse. An objection is raised about Pinchas, and the Gemara answers that Moses was preoccupied with the Divine Presence.

items.text: Discussion on whether Moses could eat sacrifices
items.text_en: Discussion on whether Moses could eat sacrifices
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about the priest eating from holy offerings and questions whether Moses was included. Rav Sheishet explains that it refers to a non-priest at a bamah. Another objection about Miriam's isolation is raised.

items.text: Challenge: Moses as a priest and the laws of negaim
items.text_en: Challenge: Moses as a priest and the laws of negaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the idea that Moses served as a priest, noting that a non-priest (zar) cannot view negaim (skin afflictions), and Aaron, as a relative, also could not. It concludes that God Himself honored Miriam by declaring He would act as priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Moses could have been a priest, since a non-priest cannot inspect negaim (skin afflictions), and Aaron as a relative also could not; it concludes that God Himself acted as priest for Miriam.
The Gemara objects that the baraita explicitly states Moses was a non-priest, contradicting the idea that he served as a priest.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's distinction
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's distinction
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that the laws of negaim are different because the Torah explicitly mentions Aaron and his sons in the passage, implying that only they, not Moses, are authorized.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that the laws of נגעים (leprous marks) are different because the Torah explicitly mentions Aaron and his sons in the passage, implying that only they, not Moses, are authorized.

items.text: Challenge from Elisheva's joys
items.text_en: Challenge from Elisheva's joys
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing five joys of Elisheva, including that her brother-in-law (yavam) was king. It questions whether this implies the king was not a high priest, and resolves that the text means 'also a king'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing Elisheva's five joys, including that her brother-in-law (יָבָם) was a king, and challenges: this implies the king was not a high priest, contradicting the earlier claim.
The Gemara resolves the challenge by reinterpreting the baraita: it does not exclude the high priesthood from the king, but rather adds that he was also a king.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on Moses' priesthood
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on Moses' priesthood
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute about whether Moses was ever a priest. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says the anger at Moses left no mark, implying he was not demoted. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says it did leave a mark, as God said 'Aaron the Levite'—indicating Moses was demoted to Levite. The Sages say Moses was only a priest during the seven days of consecration. Another opinion holds that priesthood never ceased from Moses' descendants.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a tannaitic dispute regarding the anger at Moses, with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha stating that this anger left no mark.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai argues that the anger did leave a mark, interpreting the verse 'הלא אהרן אחיך הלוי' (Is there not Aaron your brother the Levite) as a demotion of Moses from priest to Levite.
The Sages state that Moses was only a priest during the seven days of consecration, and some say the priesthood ceased only from his descendants, citing verses from Chronicles and Psalms.
The Gemara asks why the second verse was needed, and explains that it counters the possibility that the first verse only applies to future generations.

items.text: Discussion on anger and respect for kings
items.text_en: Discussion on anger and respect for kings
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether every instance of anger in the Torah leaves a mark, citing Moses' anger at Pharaoh. Resh Lakish says Moses struck Pharaoh. A contradiction is raised about Resh Lakish's view on Pharaoh, and Rabbi Yannai and Rabbi Yochanan offer proofs that one must show respect to kings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa's claim that every anger in the Torah leaves a mark, citing Moses' anger at Pharaoh where no action is recorded.
Resh Lakish answers that Moses did act — he slapped Pharaoh and left.
The Gemara objects that Resh Lakish elsewhere said Pharaoh is a king and one should be amiable, contradicting the claim that Moses slapped him.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by reversing the attributions: Resh Lakish actually said Pharaoh is wicked and one should be insolent.
Rabbi Yannai provides a proof from Moses' speech that one must always fear the kingship, as Moses did not address Pharaoh directly.
Rabbi Yochanan cites Elijah running before Ahab as another proof that one must show respect to a king.

items.text: Moses' request for kingship and its implications
items.text_en: Moses' request for kingship and its implications
items.desc_en: Ulla says Moses sought kingship but was denied, as 'halom' (here) refers to kingship. Rava cites Rabbi Yishmael that Elisheva's yavam was king, meaning for him and his descendants. The Gemara questions whether 'halom' always implies perpetuity, citing Saul. Two answers are given: Saul's case involved Ish-bosheth, or Saul was unworthy. Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Chanina explains that greatness is granted to a person and his descendants forever, but if he becomes haughty, God humbles him.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that Moses sought kingship but was denied, interpreting 'הלום' (here) as a reference to kingship based on a verse.
Rava objects by citing Rabbi Yishmael's statement that Elisheva's yavam was king, and explains that this refers to him and his descendants, implying perpetuity.
The Gemara questions whether 'הלום' always implies perpetuity, citing the case of Saul where the term appears but his kingship did not continue to his descendants.
The first answer suggests that Saul's case is different because he had a son, Ish-bosheth, who succeeded him, or alternatively, Saul himself was unworthy of lasting kingship.
Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Chanina resolves that greatness is granted to a person and his descendants forever, but if he becomes haughty, God humbles him.

items.text: Inclusion of blemished priests in the division of sacrifices
items.text_en: Inclusion of blemished priests in the division of sacrifices
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'all males' that blemished priests are included in the division of sacrificial meat. Three baraitot are cited, each adding a further inclusion: blemished priests, those blemished from the start, and those with temporary blemishes. Rav Sheshet suggests reversing the order, but Rav Ashi says no reversal is needed, as each derivation is necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that blemished priests are included in the division of sacrifices.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source for including blemished priests.
The first baraita derives from 'all males' that blemished priests are included for division (not eating).
The second baraita adds that 'all males' includes a priest who was originally unblemished and then became blemished.
The third baraita adds that 'all males' includes a priest with a temporary blemish.
Rav Sheshet suggests reversing the order of the baraitot, implying the derivations are redundant.
Rav Ashi explains that no reversal is needed, as each derivation is necessary to counter a possible exclusion.

items.text: Gemara's initial explanation of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's initial explanation of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's statement that one who is not fit to eat does not receive a portion, drawing an analogy from a tamei person who cannot eat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's rule is derived by analogy from a טמא (ritually impure person), who cannot eat, to one who is not fit to eat.

items.text: Challenges to the Mishnah's rule
items.text_en: Challenges to the Mishnah's rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah by pointing out that a ba'al mum is unfit for service yet receives a portion, and a tamei person in communal offerings is fit for service but does not receive a portion. The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah refers to fitness for eating, but then notes that a minor is fit to eat yet does not receive a portion, concluding that the Mishnah does not address that case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's rule by citing counterexamples: a ba'al mum (blemished priest) is unfit for service yet receives a portion, and a tamei (impure) person in communal offerings is fit for service yet does not receive a portion.
The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's phrase 'fit' refers to fitness for eating (אכילה), not fitness for service.
The Gemara objects that a minor (קטן) is fit to eat yet does not receive a portion, and concludes that the Mishnah does not address that case.

items.text: Resolution of the challenges
items.text_en: Resolution of the challenges
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the challenges by stating that the Mishnah's rule stands as originally explained, and that the cases of tamei and ba'al mum are not included in the Mishnah's statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the challenges by reaffirming the Mishnah's original explanation and stating that the cases of a tamei (ritually impure) priest and a ba'al mum (blemished) priest are not included in the Mishnah's rule.

items.text: Abba Shaul's opinion on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Abba Shaul's opinion on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling that a priest who is tamei at the time of blood sprinkling but pure at the time of burning the fats does not receive a portion, while one pure at sprinkling but tamei at burning does receive a portion, contradicts Abba Shaul, who requires purity from sprinkling until burning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the Mishnah's ruling: a priest who is טמא (ritually impure) at the time of blood sprinkling but pure at the time of burning the fats does not receive a portion, while one pure at sprinkling but טמא at burning does receive a portion.

The Gemara notes that the Mishnah contradicts Abba Shaul, who requires purity from the time of sprinkling until the burning of the fats, citing the verse 'המקריב את דם השלמים ואת החלב' (who offers the blood of the peace offerings and the fat).

items.text: Rav Ashi's question about impurity in between
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's question about impurity in between
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks what the law is if the priest became impure between the sprinkling and the burning: does he need to be pure at both times, or continuously from sprinkling to burning? The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks whether impurity between the sprinkling and the burning invalidates the priest's portion, and the question remains unresolved (teiku).

items.text: Rava's narrative about Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon and a tevul yom
items.text_en: Rava's narrative about Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon and a tevul yom
items.desc_en: Rava recounts a story he learned from Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, where a tevul yom (one who immersed but awaits sunset) argues with Rabbi Elazar about receiving portions from various sacrifices. Rabbi Elazar refutes each request with a kal vachomer argument, and the tevul yom responds with a counter-argument, until Rabbi Elazar cites a verse to support his position.

sub.desc_en: Rava introduces a halachic ruling he learned from Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who adjudicated it in the bathroom, and sets the scene: a tevul yom (one who immersed but awaits sunset) asks for a portion of a minchah (meal offering) to eat.
The tevul yom requests a portion from the minchah (meal offering) to eat.

Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon refutes the request with a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument: since the tevul yom is excluded from the chatat (sin offering) of Israel, he should certainly be excluded from the minchah (meal offering).

The tevul yom counters with a parallel קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument: since his exclusion from the chatat (sin offering) is balanced by the priest's equal exclusion, the same logic should apply to the minchah (meal offering).
Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon cites a verse (Leviticus 7:9) to resolve the dispute: only the priest who offers the minchah (meal offering) may eat it, so the tevul yom must first offer it.
The tevul yom now requests a portion from the chatat (sin offering) of Israel.

Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon refutes with another קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument: since the tevul yom was excluded from the minchah (meal offering), he should certainly be excluded from the chatat (sin offering).

The tevul yom counters again with a parallel קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument: the exclusion from the minchah (meal offering) is balanced by the priest's equal exclusion, so the same should apply to the chatat (sin offering).
Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon cites a verse (Leviticus 6:19) to resolve: only the priest who performs the purification (offers the chatat) may eat it, so the tevul yom must first offer it.
The tevul yom requests a portion from the breast and thigh (חזה ושוק) of the shelamim (peace offering).

Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon refutes with a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument: since the tevul yom was excluded from the chatat (sin offering), he should certainly be excluded from the breast and thigh (חזה ושוק) of the shelamim (peace offering).

The tevul yom counters: the exclusion from the chatat (sin offering) is because the priest's power is weakened regarding his wives and slaves, but regarding the breast and thigh (חזה ושוק), the priest's power is strengthened, so the analogy fails.

Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon cites a verse (Leviticus 7:14) to resolve: only the priest who sprinkles the blood of the shelamim (peace offering) may eat the breast and thigh (חזה ושוק), so the tevul yom must first sprinkle the blood.

items.text: Conclusion of the tevul yom's departure
items.text_en: Conclusion of the tevul yom's departure
items.desc_en: The tevul yom leaves, carrying his leniencies and stringencies on his head, with an onen on his right and a mechusar kapparah on his left.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the tevul yom departs with his leniencies and stringencies, flanked by an onen and a mechusar kapparah.

items.text: Rav Achai's challenge and resolution about the narrative
items.text_en: Rav Achai's challenge and resolution about the narrative
items.desc_en: Rav Achai questions why the tevul yom did not ask for a firstborn animal, and the Gemara explains the counter-argument. Another challenge is raised about the appropriateness of discussing Torah in the bathroom, which is resolved by noting that it was under duress.

sub.desc_en: Rav Achai challenges why the tevul yom did not simply ask for a firstborn animal (בכור) to eat.

The Gemara explains that the priest could have responded with a kal vachomer argument: if he excluded the tevul yom from the chatat where the priest's power is weaker, then from the bekhor where the priest's power is stronger, he certainly excludes him.

The tevul yom could have countered that just as the priest's power is weakened in the chatat case, so too the tevul yom's power is weakened; but in the bekhor case, the priest's power is strengthened, so the tevul yom's power should also be strengthened.
The Gemara cites the verse 'את דמם תזרוק... ובשרם יהיה לך' (their blood you shall sprinkle... and their flesh shall be yours) as the scriptural basis for the priest's claim: come, sprinkle and eat.

Another challenge is raised: the verse does not say 'their flesh shall be for the priest who sprinkles' but rather 'their flesh shall be yours' — implying it is for any priest, not specifically the one who performed the service.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution about the bathroom context
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution about the bathroom context
sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the priest could discuss Torah in the bathroom, citing Rabba bar bar Chana quoting Rabbi Yochanan that one may only think Torah anywhere except a bathhouse or bathroom, and resolves that the case of duress (אונס) is different.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the altar did not acquire the meat of an offering, the priests do not acquire its hide, citing the verse "Olat Ish" (the burnt-offering of a man). It then lists exceptions: a burnt-offering slaughtered not for its sake, where the hide goes to the priests; and the general rule that hides of lesser holy offerings go to the owners, while hides of most holy offerings go to the priests. A kal vachomer argument is presented but rejected because the altar itself has no hide.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that if the altar did not acquire the meat, the priests do not acquire the hide, citing the verse 'עֹלַת אִישׁ' (the burnt-offering of a man).

The Mishnah lists an exception: a burnt-offering slaughtered not for its sake, though not accepted for the owner, its hide goes to the priests; and both male and female burnt-offerings' hides go to the priests.
The Mishnah states the general rule: hides of lesser holy offerings go to the owners, hides of most holy offerings go to the priests.

sub.text: Mishnah's kal vachomer and its rejection
sub.text_en: Mishnah's kal vachomer and its rejection
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a kal vachomer argument that most holy offerings should grant hides to the priests, but rejects it because the altar itself has no hide to serve as a counterexample.

items.text: Baraita on the verse
items.text_en: Baraita on the verse
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: "Olat Ish" excludes a burnt-offering from Temple funds (Rabbi Yehuda) or a ger's burnt-offering (Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda).

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: the verse 'עֹלַת אִישׁ' (burnt-offering of a man) excludes a burnt-offering from Temple funds (Rabbi Yehuda) or a ger's burnt-offering (Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda).

items.text: Explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.text_en: Explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef explains that "Olat hekdesh" refers to a burnt-offering brought from leftover funds (mosrot). The Gemara questions this based on a dispute about whether leftover funds go to communal or individual offerings, and resolves it by citing Rava's interpretation of the verse "haOlah" as the first burnt-offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'except for a burnt-offering of consecration' means in Rabbi Yehuda's statement.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef explains that it refers to a burnt-offering brought from leftover funds (mosrot).
The Gemara objects that this explanation works only for the view that leftover funds go to communal offerings, but what about the view that they go to individual offerings?
Rava resolves the objection by interpreting the verse 'haOlah' as the first burnt-offering, so the same applies here.

items.text: Rabbi Ayvu's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Ayvu's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ayvu in the name of Rabbi Yannai says the verse excludes one who designates a burnt-offering for Temple maintenance (bedek habayit). The Gemara notes that even according to the view that such consecration does not take effect biblically, it does take effect regarding the hide.

sub.text: Rabbi Ayvu in the name of Rabbi Yannai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ayvu in the name of Rabbi Yannai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ayvu citing Rabbi Yannai explains that the verse 'עולת איש' excludes one who designates a burnt-offering for Temple maintenance (בדק הבית).

The Gemara clarifies that even according to the view that consecration for Temple maintenance does not take effect biblically, this applies only to the meat, but the hide is still subject to the priests' rights.

items.text: Rav Nachman's statement and challenge
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's statement and challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha also says the verse excludes a burnt-offering from leftover funds. Rav Hamnuna challenges him, noting that Rabbi Yehuda retracted this view in a baraita where he says such an offering's hide does not go to priests. Rabbi Nechemya (or Rabbi Shimon) objects that this nullifies the midrash of Yehoyada the Kohen, which teaches that the hide of such offerings goes to priests.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha states that the verse 'עֹלַת אִישׁ' excludes a burnt-offering brought from leftover funds (מוֹתָרוֹת) from the rule that priests receive the hide.

sub.text: Rav Hamnuna's challenge to Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's challenge to Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna challenges Rav Nachman, asking if his view aligns with Rabbi Yehuda, and notes that Rabbi Yehuda retracted this position in a baraita where he ruled that the hide of such an offering does not go to priests.
Rabbi Nechemya (or some say Rabbi Shimon) objects that this ruling would nullify the midrash of Yehoyada the Kohen, which teaches that the hide of such offerings goes to priests.

items.text: Resolution: the baraita refers to one who consecrates his property
items.text_en: Resolution: the baraita refers to one who consecrates his property
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman responds that he interprets the baraita as referring to one who consecrates his property, following Rabbi Yehoshua's view. In that case, the animals themselves become burnt-offerings, but the hide is still consecrated for Temple maintenance. Even Rabbi Yehoshua, who allows splitting the consecration, agrees that the hide is not given to priests.

sub.text: Rav Hamnuna's question to Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's question to Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna asks Rav Nachman how he interprets the baraita that excludes the hide from priests for an עולה (burnt-offering) brought from leftover funds.
Rav Nachman responds that he interprets the baraita as referring to one who consecrates his property.

sub.text: Supporting citation of Rabbi Yehoshua's view
sub.text_en: Supporting citation of Rabbi Yehoshua's view
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites the Mishnah where Rabbi Yehoshua rules that males consecrated for the Temple are themselves offered as עולות (burnt-offerings), unlike Rabbi Eliezer who requires selling them.
The Gemara explains that even Rabbi Yehoshua, who allows splitting the consecration, agrees that the hide is not given to priests but remains consecrated for Temple maintenance.

items.text: Explanation of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.text_en: Explanation of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda says the verse excludes a ger's burnt-offering. Rav Simai bar Chilka asks Ravina: is a ger not a man? Ravina answers: it excludes a ger who died without heirs.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda states that the verse 'עֹלַת אִישׁ' excludes a ger's burnt-offering.

sub.text: Rav Simai bar Chilka's question to Ravina
sub.text_en: Rav Simai bar Chilka's question to Ravina
sub.desc_en: Rav Simai bar Chilka asks Ravina: is a ger not considered an 'איש' (man)?
Ravina answers: the verse excludes a ger who died without heirs, whose offering has no owner.

items.text: Another baraita on the verse
items.text_en: Another baraita on the verse
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that "Olat Ish" includes only a man's burnt-offering, but the verse "Or haOlah" (the hide of the burnt-offering) includes gerim, women, and slaves. The verse "Olat Ish" then teaches that it excludes a burnt-offering slaughtered outside its time or place, so the priests do not get its hide. One might think to include one slaughtered not for its sake, since it does not count for the owner, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that the verse 'עֹלַת אִישׁ' (a man's burnt-offering) limits the hide to a man's offering, but the verse 'עוֹר הָעֹלָה' (the hide of the burnt-offering) includes gerim, women, and slaves.

The baraita then explains that the verse 'עֹלַת אִישׁ' teaches that only a burnt-offering that 'עָלְתָה לְאִישׁ' (counts for the owner) gives the priests the hide, excluding one slaughtered outside its time or place.
The baraita raises a possibility: one might think to include a burnt-offering slaughtered not for its sake, since it does not count for the owner, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Derivation of priests' right to the hide of kodshei kodashim
items.text_en: Derivation of priests' right to the hide of kodshei kodashim
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'עור העולה' that priests acquire the hide of the olah, and extends this to all kodshei kodashim via the phrase 'אשר הקריב', excluding kodashim kalim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether priests are not entitled to the hide of the olah, and answers with a verse.
The Tanna Kamma derives from the verse 'עור העולה' that the hide of the olah is given to priests, and extends this to all kodshei kodashim via the phrase 'אשר הקריב', excluding kodashim kalim.

items.text: Rabbi Yishmael's kal vachomer argument
items.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's kal vachomer argument
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael argues from a kal vachomer: if priests acquire the hide of the olah even though they do not eat its meat, they certainly acquire the hide of kodshei kodashim whose meat they eat. The Gemara counters with a piyus from the mizbe'ach, but Rabbi Yishmael's logic prevails because priests already have partial rights.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael opens with a kal vachomer argument: if priests acquire the hide of the olah even though they do not eat its meat, they certainly acquire the hide of kodshei kodashim whose meat they eat.
The Gemara objects with a piyus from the mizbe'ach: the altar acquires the meat but not the hide, disproving the kal vachomer.
The Gemara resolves: the priests, who already have partial rights (they acquire the hide of the olah), are unlike the altar which has no partial rights, so the kal vachomer stands.

items.text: Rabbi's alternative derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi's alternative derivation
items.desc_en: Rabbi (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) states that the verse was only needed for the hide of the olah itself, since elsewhere the hide follows the meat.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) states that the verse was only needed for the hide of the olah itself, since elsewhere the hide follows the meat.

items.text: Mishnah: general rule for hides of sacrifices
items.text_en: Mishnah: general rule for hides of sacrifices
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the disposition of hides for different categories: parim hanisrafim and se'irim hanisrafim are burned with their hides; chatat, asham, and tzibbur shelamim are given to the priest; kodashim kalim to the owner. For the olah, the verse 'והפשיט את העולה' might imply priests do not get the hide, but the verse 'עור העולה אשר הקריב' teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the disposition of hides for different categories of sacrifices: parim hanisrafim and se'irim hanisrafim are burned with their hides; chatat, asham, and tzibbur shelamim are given to the priest; kodashim kalim to the owner.
For the olah, the verse 'והפשיט את העולה' might imply priests do not get the hide, but the verse 'עור העולה אשר הקריב' teaches otherwise.

items.text: Exclusion of invalid priests from the hide
items.text_en: Exclusion of invalid priests from the hide
items.desc_en: The verse 'לו יהיה' excludes a tevul yom, mechusar kippurim, and onen from acquiring the hide, even though one might think they could get the hide since it is not for eating.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma derives from the verse 'לו יהיה' that a tevul yom, mechusar kippurim, and onen are excluded from acquiring the hide of an olah.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the derivations
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the derivations
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Tanna Kamma needed a verse if the kal vachomer suffices, and explains that the Torah wrote a verse for something that could be derived logically. It then discusses how Rabbi Yishmael uses the phrase 'אשר הקריב' to exclude invalid priests, and explains that Rabbi Yishmael follows his own view that 'לו יהיה' in the olah is compared to 'לו יהיה' in the asham to permit the bones, and that this comparison is mufneh (free for derivation).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Tanna Kamma needed a verse if the kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) would have sufficed, and answers that the Torah wrote a verse for something that could be derived logically.

The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yishmael does with the phrase 'אשר הקריב' (which he offered), and answers that it excludes a טבול יום (one who immersed that day), a מחוסר כיפורים (one lacking atonement), and an אונן (a mourner before burial).

The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yishmael does not derive the exclusion from 'לו יהיה' (it shall be his), and explains that Rabbi Yishmael follows his own view that 'לו יהיה' in the olah is compared to 'לו יהיה' in the asham to permit the bones.
The Gemara resolves that the comparison is mufneh (free for derivation), because otherwise one could refute it, and the extra word 'יהיה' (it shall be) indicates it is a superfluous verse.

items.text: Mishnah: effect of disqualification before or after flaying
items.text_en: Mishnah: effect of disqualification before or after flaying
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a disqualification occurs before flaying, the hide does not go to the priests; after flaying, it does. Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim testifies he never saw a hide sent to the burning place. Rabbi Akiva deduces that if a firstborn is found tereifah after flaying, the priests may use the hide. The Sages disagree, saying 'we have not seen' is no proof, and the hide must be burned.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: if disqualification occurs before flaying, the hides do not go to the priests; after flaying, they do.
Rabbi Chanina Segan HaKohanim testifies that he never saw a hide sent to the burning place.
Rabbi Akiva deduces from Rabbi Chanina's testimony that if a firstborn is found tereifah after flaying, the priests may use the hide.
The Sages reject Rabbi Akiva's deduction, arguing that 'we have not seen' is no proof, and the hide must be burned.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah's first clause as following Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who holds that blood does not effect atonement on the hide independently. The second clause follows Rabbi, who holds it does. Abaye resolves the contradiction by saying the entire Mishnah is Rabbi, but he concedes that flaying before blood application does not give the hide. Rava says the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, and 'before flaying' means before flaying for the sake of the hide.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the Mishnah's principle: if the altar did not acquire the meat, the priests do not acquire the hide, even if flayed before blood application.
The Gemara asks whose opinion this first clause follows.
The Gemara identifies the first clause as following Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who holds that blood does not effect atonement (רצוי) on the hide independently.
The Gemara examines the second clause of the Mishnah, which says that after flaying the hides belong to the priests.
The Gemara identifies the second clause as following Rabbi, who holds that blood does effect atonement on the hide independently.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah would then be inconsistent, with the first clause following Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon and the second clause following Rabbi.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by saying the entire Mishnah is Rabbi, but Rabbi concedes that flaying before blood application does not give the hide to the priests.
Rava resolves the contradiction by saying the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, and 'before flaying' means before flaying for the sake of the hide.

items.text: Clarification of the dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Clarification of the dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the positions of Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon regarding whether the blood effects atonement for the hide independently, and whether the hide is considered like the flesh when a disqualification occurs before or after sprinkling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is meant by 'other than flaying' — whether it refers to before or after the hide becomes fit for flaying.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: Rabbi holds that blood effects atonement for the hide independently, and when a disqualification occurs either before or after sprinkling, the hide is like the flesh. Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon holds that blood does not effect atonement for the hide independently; if a disqualification occurs before sprinkling, the hide is like the flesh, but after sprinkling, the flesh has been accepted for a moment, so he may flay it and the hide goes to the priests.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the dispute is between Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon, and cites Rabbi's position that the blood effects atonement for the hide independently, and when a disqualification occurs before or after sprinkling, the hide is treated like the flesh.

Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon states that the blood does not effect atonement for the hide independently, and after sprinkling the flesh is accepted for a moment, so one may flay it and the hide goes to the priests.

The baraita states Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon's position: blood does not effect atonement for the hide independently; if disqualification occurs before sprinkling the hide is like the flesh, but after sprinkling the flesh was accepted for a moment, so he may flay it and the hide goes to the priests.

items.text: Connection to the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.text_en: Connection to the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon may align with the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding the verse 'And you shall make your burnt offerings, the flesh and the blood.' Rabbi Yehoshua says that without blood there is no flesh, and without flesh there is no blood. Rabbi Eliezer says that blood is valid even without flesh, as it says 'And the blood of your sacrifices shall be poured out.' The verse 'flesh and blood' teaches that just as blood is applied by sprinkling, so too flesh is applied by sprinkling, implying a space between the ramp and the altar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute is between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, citing Rabbi Yehoshua's position that without blood there is no flesh and without flesh there is no blood.

Rabbi Eliezer holds that blood is valid even without flesh, citing the verse 'וְדַם זְבָחֶיךָ יִשָּׁפֵךְ', and explains that the verse 'וְעָשִׂיתָ עֹלֹתֶיךָ הַבָּשָׂר וְהַדָּם' teaches that just as blood requires sprinkling, so too flesh requires sprinkling, implying a gap between the ramp and the altar.

items.text: Analysis of the alignment of opinions
items.text_en: Analysis of the alignment of opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the one who says the hide is accepted (Rabbi) follows Rabbi Eliezer, and the one who says it is not accepted (Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon) follows Rabbi Yehoshua. However, the Gemara refines this: according to Rabbi Eliezer, everyone agrees; the dispute is only according to Rabbi Yehoshua. The one who says not accepted follows Rabbi Yehoshua. The one who says accepted argues that Rabbi Yehoshua only said his ruling there regarding flesh, where there is no loss to the priests, but regarding the hide, where there is a loss to the priests, even Rabbi Yehoshua concedes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the one who says the hide is accepted follows Rabbi Eliezer, and the one who says it is not accepted follows Rabbi Yehoshua.
The Gemara refines: according to Rabbi Eliezer, everyone agrees; the dispute is only according to Rabbi Yehoshua.
The one who says not accepted follows Rabbi Yehoshua.

The one who says accepted argues that Rabbi Yehoshua only said his ruling there regarding flesh, where there is no loss to the priests, but regarding the hide, where there is a loss to the priests, even Rabbi Yehoshua concedes.

items.text: Support from a Mishnah about post-facto acceptance
items.text_en: Support from a Mishnah about post-facto acceptance
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah: If the flesh became impure or disqualified or left the courtyard, Rabbi Eliezer says one may sprinkle, Rabbi Yehoshua says one may not sprinkle. But Rabbi Yehoshua concedes that if one did sprinkle, it is accepted. This supports the idea that Rabbi Yehoshua may concede in cases of loss.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua dispute regarding a case that already happened, and Rabbi Yehoshua concedes that if one sprinkled, it was accepted.

items.text: Discussion of Rabbi Chanina's statement about the hide of a blemished firstborn
items.text_en: Discussion of Rabbi Chanina's statement about the hide of a blemished firstborn
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Chanina's statement that the hide of a blemished firstborn is given to the priests only after flaying, citing exceptions like bulls and goats burned outside, and cases before flaying and before sprinkling. The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Chanina refers to a case after flaying and after sprinkling. It then addresses Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon's view that blood does not effect atonement for the hide, and suggests that Rabbi Chanina follows Rabbi, or even that Rabbi concedes that flaying cannot precede sprinkling. Finally, it discusses the case of a tereifah found in the intestines, concluding that it effects atonement, as supported by Rabbi Akiva's statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Chanina's statement that he never saw a hide go out to burning, citing the case of bulls and goats that are burned with their hides.
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Chanina was not referring to hides burned in fulfillment of the mitzva, but only to those burned due to disqualification.
The Gemara objects that there is a case of disqualification before flaying and before sprinkling, where the hide is burned.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Chanina was referring specifically to a hide that has been flayed (stripped from the flesh).
The Gemara objects that according to Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon, there is a case after flaying but before sprinkling where the hide is burned.

The Gemara answers that Rabbi Chanina holds like Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi), who says blood effects acceptance for the hide; alternatively, even according to Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi concedes that flaying cannot precede sprinkling.
The Gemara objects that there is a case of an animal found to be a tereifah in its intestines after flaying and sprinkling.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Chanina holds that a tereifah found in the intestines still effects atonement, and cites Rabbi Akiva's statement as support.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Akiva's statement adds, and answers that it teaches the halakha applies even in the outlying areas (outside the Temple).

items.text: Halachic conclusion and Mishnah about burned offerings
items.text_en: Halachic conclusion and Mishnah about burned offerings
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: The halacha follows Rabbi Akiva, but only when an expert permitted it. The halacha is like the Sages: the flesh is buried and the hide is burned. The Mishnah then discusses bulls and goats burned outside: when burned properly, they are burned in the ash pit and defile garments; when not burned properly, they are burned in the Temple and do not defile garments.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: רבי חייא בר אבא (Rabbi Chiya bar Abba) reports in the name of רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) that the הלכה (binding law) follows רבי עקיבא (Rabbi Akiva), but only when a מומחה (expert) permitted the firstborn; otherwise, the hide is not permitted.
The Stam rules that the final הלכה (binding law) is like the חכמים (Sages): the flesh is buried and the hide is burned.

The משנה (Mishnah) introduces the rules for bulls and goats that are burned: when burned כמצותן (in accordance with their mitzva), they are burned in the ash pit and defile garments; when not burned properly, they are burned in the Temple and do not defile garments.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the process of carrying the red heifer on poles, and the laws of impurity for the carriers depending on whether the first or last carriers have left the Temple courtyard. Rabbi Shimon adds that they are not impure until the fire has consumed most of the heifer.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the law of impurity for carriers of the red heifer on poles, with Rabbi Shimon adding that impurity begins only when the fire has consumed most of the heifer.

items.text: Gemara's question on 'Birah'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on 'Birah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'Birah' means in the Mishnah. Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says it is a specific place on the Temple Mount called 'Birah', while Resh Lakish says the entire Temple is called 'Birah', citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'Birah' means in the Mishnah.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says 'Birah' is a specific place on the Temple Mount called 'Birah'.
Resh Lakish says the entire Temple is called 'Birah', citing the verse 'וְאֶל הַבִּירָה אֲשֶׁר הֲכִינוֹתִי' (and to the palace which I have prepared).

items.text: Three ash-pits (בתי הדשנים)
items.text_en: Three ash-pits (בתי הדשנים)
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha states there are three ash-pits: one in the courtyard for burning disqualified holy of holies and other offerings, one on the Temple Mount for offerings disqualified after sprinkling, and one outside the three camps. Levi's baraita adds that the first ash-pit also includes offerings disqualified after sprinkling, and the second is for those disqualified during their exit.

sub.text: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha states there are three ash-pits, and describes the first: a great ash-pit in the courtyard for burning disqualified holy of holies, sacrificial portions of lesser sanctity, and bulls/goats that are burned that were disqualified before blood sprinkling.

sub.text: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha (continued)
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha (continued)
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman continues: the second ash-pit is on the Temple Mount for bulls/goats disqualified after sprinkling, and the third is for those burned in accordance with their mitzva outside the three camps.

Levi's baraita presents a different version: the first ash-pit includes offerings disqualified both before and after sprinkling, and the second is for those disqualified during their exit from the courtyard.

items.text: Does linah disqualify burnt-offerings?
items.text_en: Does linah disqualify burnt-offerings?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeyah asks whether linah (overnight stay) disqualifies the flesh of the red heifer and other burnt-offerings. Rava says this was asked by Abaye and resolved from a baraita: just as improper intent does not disqualify, so too linah does not. The Gemara then challenges this with a baraita that seems to say linah does disqualify, but resolves it by distinguishing between the flesh and the sacrificial parts.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeyah raises a dilemma: does לִינָה (being left overnight) disqualify the flesh of bulls and goats that are burned, or is it ineffective since they are not fit for consumption?
Rava says that Abaye had asked this and he resolved it from a baraita: just as improper intent does not disqualify, so too לִינָה does not disqualify.
The Gemara objects: perhaps only improper intent does not disqualify, but לִינָה does disqualify.
The Gemara cites a baraita that states that after slaughter, these offerings become susceptible to disqualification by לִינָה, implying it refers to the flesh.
The Gemara answers: no, it refers to לִינָה of the sacrificial portions, not the flesh.
The Gemara objects: the latter clause mentions flesh, so the first clause must also refer to flesh; the answer retorts that the cases are not comparable.

The Gemara cites Levi's baraita about disqualification upon emerging, but rejects that it refers to לִינָה, explaining it means disqualification by טומאה (ritual impurity) or by leaving the courtyard.

items.text: Does yetzi'ah disqualify burnt-offerings?
items.text_en: Does yetzi'ah disqualify burnt-offerings?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks whether yetzi'ah (exit) disqualifies the red heifer and other burnt-offerings. Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Abba explains the question is according to the opinion that it has not yet reached its time to exit. The Gemara attempts to resolve this from Levi's baraita, but concludes it refers to impurity and linah, not yetzi'ah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks whether yetzi'ah (exit) disqualifies the red heifer and other burnt-offerings.
Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Abba explains that the question is according to the opinion that it has not yet reached its time to exit.
The Gemara articulates the doubt: whether the rule applies only to meat that has no obligation to exit, or also to these that must exit.
The Gemara attempts to resolve the question from Levi's baraita, but concludes it refers to impurity and linah, not yetzi'ah.

items.text: Partial exit of a limb
items.text_en: Partial exit of a limb
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks about a case where most of the animal's body has exited but only a minority of a limb, or half of it with most of a limb. The Gemara clarifies that the question is about the latter case, where the minority of the limb follows the majority of the limb, not the majority of the animal.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks about the status of a limb when most of the animal's body has exited but only a minority of a limb, or half of it with most of a limb, questioning whether the minority of the limb follows the majority of the limb or the majority of the animal.
The Gemara clarifies that the question is about the latter case, where the minority of the limb follows the majority of the limb, not the majority of the animal.

items.text: Unresolved questions on majority of limbs vs. animal
items.text_en: Unresolved questions on majority of limbs vs. animal
items.desc_en: Two unresolved queries (teiku) are posed: first, regarding an animal whose limbs exited the courtyard—do we follow the majority of limbs or the animal? Second, a similar question with five people carrying an animal—three exit, two remain—do we follow the majority of people or the animal?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara poses an unresolved query: for an animal whose limbs exited the courtyard, do we follow the majority of limbs or the animal itself?
The Gemara leaves the first query unresolved (תיקו).
Rabbah bar Rav Huna presents a parallel version of the query: with five people carrying an animal, three exit and two remain—do we follow the majority of people or the animal?
The Gemara leaves this second query also unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's query on returning sacrificial animals
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's query on returning sacrificial animals
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks whether bulls and goats that were taken out for burning and then returned become impure (since they exited) or remain pure.
