Rabbi Abba bar Memel brings a baraita showing that the first carriers who exit the courtyard become impure, but the last ones do not until they exit, implying that exiting alone does not automatically impart impurity. Ravina objects that the verse requires 'after he comes to the camp,' which is not fulfilled. The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Elazar's query applies when the animals are carried on poles (b'kulsei), not directly.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks whether bulls and goats that were taken out for burning and then returned become impure (since they exited) or remain pure (since they returned).

Rabbi Abba bar Memel brings a baraita showing that the first carriers who exit the courtyard become impure, but the last ones do not until they exit, implying that exiting alone does not automatically impart impurity.
Ravina objects that the verse requires 'after he comes to the camp,' which is not fulfilled, so the baraita does not prove the point.
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Elazar's query applies when the animals are carried on poles (בְּבָקוּלְסֵי), not directly, so the baraita's case is different.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on impurity of sacrificial animals
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on impurity of sacrificial animals
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi Meir holds that bulls, the red heifer, and the scapegoat render food and drink impure but not garments, while the Sages distinguish—the scapegoat, being alive, does not render food and drink impure. The Gemara questions the Sages' source, noting that if they accept Rabbi Yishmael's derivation (that only items with no potential for severe impurity require preparation), they should include the scapegoat; if not, how do they derive the impurity of bulls and heifer? Rav Dimi reports that in the West they say these require preparation for impurity from another source.

sub.desc_en: A baraita records the dispute: Rabbi Meir holds that bulls, the red heifer, and the scapegoat render food and drink impure, while the Sages distinguish the scapegoat as alive and thus not rendering food and drink impure.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir's position aligns with the school of Rabbi Yishmael, which derives that only items without potential for severe impurity require preparation (הכשר).
The Gemara objects: if the Sages accept Rabbi Yishmael's derivation, they should include the scapegoat; if not, how do they derive the impurity of bulls and the heifer?
Rav Dimi reports that in the West they say these items require preparation for impurity from another source, resolving the Sages' position.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's query on impurity inside vs. outside
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's query on impurity inside vs. outside
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks whether bulls and goats that are burned render food and drink impure inside the courtyard as they do outside—is lacking exit like lacking an action, or not? He then resolves it: lacking exit is like lacking an action, so they do not render impurity inside.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks whether bulls and goats that are burned render food and drink impure inside the courtyard as they do outside—is lacking exit like lacking an action, or not?
After raising the dilemma, Rabbi Elazar resolves it: lacking exit is like lacking an action, so they do not render impurity inside.

items.text: Query on impurity of a pure bird carcass
items.text_en: Query on impurity of a pure bird carcass
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Shmuel asks Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba: according to Rabbi Meir, does a pure bird carcass render impurity in the size of an olive-bulk? The query is narrowed: if the carcass is on the ground or in the mouth, it is clear; the question is when held in the hand—is lacking proximity like lacking an action, or not? The Gemara then records that he resolved it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Shmuel (רבי אבא בר שמואל) asks Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba (רבי חייא בר אבא): according to Rabbi Meir (רבי מאיר), does a pure bird carcass (נבלת עוף טהור) render impurity in the size of an olive-bulk (כזית)?

The Gemara narrows the query: if the carcass is on the ground or in the mouth, it is clear; the question is when held in the hand—is lacking proximity (מחוסר קריבה) like lacking an action (מחוסר מעשה) or not?
The Gemara records that after raising the dilemma, Rabbi Abba bar Shmuel resolved it.

items.text: Opening statement: מחוסר קריבה vs. מחוסר מעשה
items.text_en: Opening statement: מחוסר קריבה vs. מחוסר מעשה
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a bird offering lacking the act of bringing it near (מחוסר קריבה) is not considered lacking an action (מחוסר מעשה). This sets up the discussion about the status of such an offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that a bird offering lacking the act of bringing it near (מחוסר קריבה) is not considered lacking an action (מחוסר מעשה).

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding the Mishnah of neveilah of a kosher bird
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding the Mishnah of neveilah of a kosher bird
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the opening statement with a baraita about thirteen rules of a kosher bird carcass, asking if it follows Rabbi Meir. After attempts to attribute it to the Rabbis, the Gemara concludes that the first and last clauses are Rabbi Meir, while the middle clause is the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah by citing a baraita listing thirteen rules of a kosher bird carcass, asking if the rule requiring intent (מחשבה) without prior wetting (הכשר) follows Rabbi Meir's position.
An anonymous voice answers that the baraita follows the Rabbis (רבנן), not Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara objects that the first clause of the baraita (requiring intent) is known to be Rabbi Meir's view, so the entire baraita must be his.
The anonymous voice rejects the objection, arguing that the baraita is not a single unified statement but each clause stands on its own (each as it is).
The Gemara objects further that the last clause (slaughter or pinching purifies a tereifah bird) is also Rabbi Meir's view, so the baraita seems to mix Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis inconsistently.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita is composite: the first and last clauses follow Rabbi Meir, while the middle clause follows the Rabbis.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's question to Rabbi Zeira about first and second degrees
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's question to Rabbi Zeira about first and second degrees
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna asks Rabbi Zeira whether, according to Rabbi Meir, a kosher bird carcass is counted as a first and second degree of impurity. Rabbi Zeira answers that wherever it imparts impurity to a person through contact, it is counted; otherwise, it is not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna asks Rabbi Zeira whether, according to Rabbi Meir, a kosher bird carcass (נִבְלַת עוֹף טָהוֹר) is counted as a first and second degree of impurity.
Rabbi Zeira answers that wherever the carcass imparts impurity to a person through contact, it is counted as first and second; otherwise, it is not.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry about חיבורי אוכלין על ידי משקין
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry about חיבורי אוכלין על ידי משקין
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Ammi bar Chiyya (or Rabbi Avin bar Kahana) whether the principle of חיבורי אוכלין על ידי משקין (connection of foods through liquids) applies to counting first and second degrees. The answer is the same: if it imparts impurity to a person, it is counted; otherwise, not.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Ammi bar Chiyya (or Rabbi Avin bar Kahana) whether the principle of חיבורי אוכלין על ידי משקין (connection of foods through liquids) applies to counting first and second degrees of impurity.
Rabbi Ammi bar Chiyya answers that the same principle applies: if it imparts impurity to a person, degrees are counted; otherwise, not.

items.text: Derivation of three camps for the bull and goat offerings
items.text_en: Derivation of three camps for the bull and goat offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the source for the rule that the bull and goat offerings are taken outside three camps, using a series of verses. It concludes with Rabbi Shimon's view, citing Rabbi Eliezer's gezerah shavah linking the phrase 'outside the camp' to the Yom Kippur service.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the rule that the bull and goat offerings are taken outside three camps.
The baraita cites a verbal analogy: just as the Yom Kippur service requires three camps, so too here, once the offering leaves one camp it defiles garments.
The Gemara asks for the source of the three-camp rule itself.
The baraita derives the second camp from the redundant verse 'outside the camp' in the bull of the congregation.
The baraita derives the third camp from the redundant verse 'outside the camp' in the context of the ash removal.

Rabbi Shimon explains that the verse is used for Rabbi Eliezer's גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) linking the phrase 'outside the camp' here to the Yom Kippur service, establishing three camps to the east of Jerusalem.

items.text: Location for burning disqualified sacrifices
items.text_en: Location for burning disqualified sacrifices
items.desc_en: The Gemara first addresses the Rabbis' view on where to burn such sacrifices, citing a baraita that places it north of Jerusalem. Rava identifies the disputant of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili as Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, but Abaye suggests they may only argue about the requirement for the place to be sloped.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that, according to the Rabbis, disqualified sacrifices are burned east of Jerusalem, analogous to the burning of the bull and goat.
The Gemara asks: according to the Rabbis, where exactly are these sacrifices burned?
A baraita is cited: the place of burning is north of Jerusalem, outside the three camps; Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says they are burned at the ash pit.
Rava identifies the disputant of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili as Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, based on a baraita about the ash pit.
Abaye objects that perhaps the dispute is only about whether the place must be sloped, not about the location of burning.

items.text: Who burns and when garments become impure
items.text_en: Who burns and when garments become impure
items.desc_en: A baraita defines who is considered the 'burner' that imparts impurity to garments, excluding the one who kindles the fire or arranges the wood. It then limits impurity to the time of burning, not after ashes form, with Rabbi Shimon adding that once the flesh is melted, it no longer imparts impurity. Rava explains the difference between the Sages and Rabbi Shimon concerns a case where the flesh is charred.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines who is considered the 'burner' that imparts impurity to garments, excluding the one who kindles the fire or arranges the wood, and specifying that the burner is the one who assists at the time of burning.
The baraita limits impurity to the time of burning, not after ashes form, with Rabbi Shimon adding that once the flesh is melted, it no longer imparts impurity.
Rava explains that the difference between the Sages and Rabbi Shimon concerns a case where the flesh is charred (but not yet melted).

items.text: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The standard closing formula for a chapter, 'Hadran alach Tevul Yom', is stated.

sub.desc_en: The standard closing formula for the chapter, 'Hadran alach Tevul Yom', is recited.

items.text: Mishnah: Liability for slaughter and offering outside
items.text_en: Mishnah: Liability for slaughter and offering outside
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who slaughters and offers up outside is liable for both. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili exempts one who slaughters inside and offers outside, or slaughters outside and offers outside, because he offered a disqualified item. The Sages respond that even in the first case, once taken out it is disqualified. Similarly, a tamei person who eats either tamei or tahor kodashim is liable, but Rabbi Yosei HaGelili exempts one who eats tamei kodashim, and the Sages respond that even tahor becomes tamei upon contact.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that one who slaughters and offers up outside is liable for both.
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili exempts one who slaughters inside and offers outside, or slaughters outside and offers outside, because he offered a disqualified item.
The Sages object that even in the first case, once taken out it is disqualified.
The Mishnah states that a tamei person who eats either tamei or tahor kodashim is liable, but Rabbi Yosei HaGelili exempts one who eats tamei kodashim.
The Sages object that even tahor becomes tamei upon contact.
The Mishnah concludes that a tahor person who eats tamei kodashim is exempt, because liability is only for bodily impurity.

items.text: Gemara: Scriptural sources for liability
items.text_en: Gemara: Scriptural sources for liability
items.desc_en: The Gemara finds sources for the prohibition and punishment for offering up outside. For slaughter, it derives the punishment from the same verse but seeks the prohibition, finding it in 'וְלֹא יִזְבְּחוּ עוֹד'. However, this verse is needed for Rabbi Elazar's teaching about idolatry. Rabbah resolves this by reading the verse as two separate phrases. Yet it is still needed for another baraita about sacrifices during the period of forbidden high places.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for offering up (העלאה) outside, both a punishment and a prohibition are explicitly written in the Torah, citing the verse 'הִשָּׁמֶר לְךָ פֶּן תַּעֲלֶה עוֹלוֹתֶיךָ' and the principle of Rabbi Avin in the name of Rabbi Elazar that 'הִשָּׁמֶר', 'פֶּן', and 'אַל' indicate a negative commandment.

The Gemara asks: for slaughter (שחיטה) outside, the punishment is derived from the same verse, but from where do we derive the prohibition? It answers that the verse 'וְלֹא יִזְבְּחוּ עוֹד' provides the prohibition.

The Gemara objects that this verse is needed for Rabbi Elazar's teaching that one who slaughters an animal to the idol Mercury (מרקוליס) is liable, by applying the verse to an atypical manner of worship.

Rabbah resolves the difficulty by reading the verse as two separate phrases: 'וְלֹא יִזְבְּחוּ' (they shall not slaughter) for the prohibition of slaughter outside, and 'וְלֹא עוֹד' (no longer) for Rabbi Elazar's teaching about idolatry.
The Gemara objects further that the verse is still needed for a baraita discussing sacrifices consecrated and offered during the period when high places (במות) were forbidden.

items.text: Initial derivation of warning from verses
items.text_en: Initial derivation of warning from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to derive a warning (אזהרה) for sacrificing outside the Tabernacle from the verse 'הִשָּׁמֶר לְךָ פֶּן תַּעֲלֶה עֹלֹתֶיךָ', but this is rejected because it applies only to animals sanctified during a permitted time. The verses then provide a positive commandment and a prohibition, but the possibility of karet is excluded by another verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the punishment (כרת) is stated in the verse about the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, and attempts to derive a warning (אזהרה) from the verse 'הִשָּׁמֶר לְךָ פֶּן תַּעֲלֶה עֹלֹתֶיךָ' (take heed lest you offer your burnt offerings).

The Gemara rejects this derivation, explaining that the warning applies only to animals sanctified during a permitted time of high places (במות) and offered during a forbidden time, as the verse 'עַל פְּנֵי הַשָּׂדֶה' treats it as if offered in the open field.
The Gemara cites the verse 'וֶהֱבִיאֻם לַה׳' as a positive commandment, and asks for the negative commandment, answering with 'וְלֹא יִזְבְּחוּ עוֹד' (they shall no longer slaughter).
The Gemara considers whether the punishment of כרת (karet) applies, but excludes it by citing the verse 'חֻקַּת עוֹלָם תִּהְיֶה זֹּאת לָהֶם' — this law applies to them and no other.

items.text: Rabbi Avin's kal vachomer
items.text_en: Rabbi Avin's kal vachomer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin proposes a kal vachomer: if in a place where there is no punishment (like the wilderness) there is a warning, then in a place where there is punishment (the Land of Israel) there should certainly be a warning.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avin proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if in a place where there is no punishment (the wilderness) there is a warning, then in a place where there is punishment (the Land of Israel) there should certainly be a warning.

items.text: Ravina's challenge and Rava's refutation
items.text_en: Ravina's challenge and Rava's refutation
items.desc_en: Ravina challenges Rabbi Avin's kal vachomer by suggesting a parallel: if the same logic were applied to chelev, it would render the explicit prohibition unnecessary. Rava responds by showing that each proposed parallel (neveilah, sheratzim, orlah, etc.) has a unique stringency that breaks the kal vachomer.

sub.desc_en: Ravina challenges Rabbi Avin's kal vachomer by proposing a parallel: if the same logic were applied to chelev, it would render the explicit prohibition unnecessary.
Rava responds that the parallel from neveilah fails because neveilah has the unique stringency of conveying טומאה (ritual impurity).
Rava shows that the parallel from unclean sheratzim fails because they convey impurity even in a minute quantity.
Rava shows that the parallel from clean sheratzim fails because their prohibition applies even in a minute quantity.
Rava shows that the parallel from orlah and mixed vineyard fails because they are forbidden even for benefit (הנאה).
Rava shows that the parallel from the Sabbatical year fails because its sanctity attaches to its monetary value.
Rava concludes that the parallel from terumah fails because it was never permitted in principle, and the same applies to all the cited cases.

items.text: Rava's alternative kal vachomer and Rav Ashi's refutation
items.text_en: Rava's alternative kal vachomer and Rav Ashi's refutation
items.desc_en: Rava proposes a kal vachomer from the law of notar (leftover sacrifice) to derive a warning for Pesach and milah. Rav Ashi reports that Rav Kahana refuted this, because notar has no remedy, whereas Pesach can be rectified.

sub.desc_en: Rava proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from the law of notar (leftover sacrifice) to derive a warning for Pesach and milah, since notar has no punishment yet is warned, while Pesach and milah have punishment.

sub.text: Rav Kahana's objection via Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana's objection via Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that Rav Kahana refuted Rava's kal vachomer, because notar has no remedy (תקנה), whereas Pesach can be rectified.

items.text: Conclusion: Warnings cannot be derived through kal vachomer
items.text_en: Conclusion: Warnings cannot be derived through kal vachomer
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the principle that warnings cannot be derived through logical inference (אין מזהרין מן הדין), even according to those who hold that punishments can be derived. Instead, it relies on Rabbi Yochanan's gezerah shavah of 'havayah-havayah', which teaches that just as in the wilderness punishment only came after a warning, so too in the Land of Israel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks rhetorically whether warnings can be derived through logical inference (קל וחומר), implying they cannot.
The Gemara states that even according to the opinion that punishments can be derived through logical inference, warnings cannot be derived that way.

The Gemara resolves the issue by citing Rabbi Yochanan's גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'הבאה-הבאה', teaching that just as in the wilderness punishment only came after a warning, so too in the Land of Israel.

items.text: Rava's derivation via Rabbi Yonah's analogy
items.text_en: Rava's derivation via Rabbi Yonah's analogy
items.desc_en: Rava cites Rabbi Yonah's principle that a warning must precede punishment, derived from a verbal analogy between 'there' in the context of the sin-offering and 'there' in the context of forbidden sacrifices outside.

sub.desc_en: Rava derives the requirement of a warning before punishment from Rabbi Yonah's verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between 'שם' (there) in the sin-offering context and 'שם' in the context of forbidden outside sacrifices.

items.text: Source for inner offerings burned outside
items.text_en: Source for inner offerings burned outside
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that inner offerings burned outside are liable. Rav Kahana cites the verse 'And to them you shall speak' to include adjacent matters, but Rava objects that the verse says 'And to them' (ואליהם) not 'And upon them' (ועליהם). The Gemara resolves with the school of Rabbi Yishmael's interpretation that the verse serves to interweave the sections.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we found the source for inner offerings burned outside; from where do we derive liability for outer offerings burned outside?
Rav Kahana answers that the verse 'ואליהם תאמר' (and to them you shall speak) includes adjacent matters.
Rava objects: the verse says 'ואליהם' (and to them), not 'ועליהם' (and upon them), so it cannot mean 'upon adjacent matters'.
The Gemara resolves with the school of Rabbi Yishmael's interpretation that the verse 'ואליהם תאמר' serves to interweave the sections.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's analogy and Rav Bibi's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's analogy and Rav Bibi's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan derives liability for outer offerings burned outside via a verbal analogy of 'bringing'. Rav Bibi objects based on a mishnah listing 36 kareit punishments, noting that 'the one who brings up' and 'the one who brings up' would be two separate categories, making the count 37, which is a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan derives liability for outer offerings burned outside via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the word 'הבאה' (bringing) used in both contexts.

Rav Bibi objects based on the mishnah listing 36 kareit punishments, arguing that if Rabbi Yochanan's analogy were correct, the count would be 37 because 'המעלה' (the one who brings up) would appear twice, which is a difficulty.

items.text: Source for liability for sprinkling blood outside
items.text_en: Source for liability for sprinkling blood outside
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that one who sprinkles even part of the blood outside is liable. It cites a baraita where Rabbi Yishmael derives it from 'blood it shall be considered' and Rabbi Akiva from 'or sacrifices'. The Gemara then explains how each sage interprets the other's verse: Rabbi Yishmael uses 'or sacrifices' for division, while Rabbi Akiva derives division from 'he shall not bring it'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that one who sprinkles part of the blood outside is liable.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yishmael derives liability from 'דם יחשב' (blood it shall be considered) and Rabbi Akiva from 'או זבח' (or sacrifices).
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yishmael does with the verse 'או זבח' (or sacrifices).
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yishmael uses it for division (to separate liability for different types of offerings).
The Gemara asks from where Rabbi Akiva derives the principle of division.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Akiva derives division from the verse 'לא יביאנו' (he shall not bring it).
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yishmael uses 'לא יביאנו' to teach that one is liable only for a complete offering, not a deficient one.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva derives the rule about completeness from the verse 'לעשות אותו' (to make it).

items.text: Liability for incomplete offerings
items.text_en: Liability for incomplete offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the dispute regarding offerings that are missing parts: Rabbi Yishmael exempts one who offers an incomplete inner or outer offering outside, while Rabbi Akiva holds one liable for an incomplete inner offering outside.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yishmael's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yishmael's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yishmael derives two exemptions from the repetition of 'אותו' (it): one for incomplete inner offerings offered outside, and one for incomplete outer offerings offered outside.

A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yishmael explicitly states that one might think one is liable for an incomplete inner offering offered outside, but the verse 'לעשות אותו' (to sacrifice it) teaches that one is liable only for a complete offering, not an incomplete one.

sub.text: Gemara's statement of Rabbi Akiva's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's statement of Rabbi Akiva's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Akiva, who has already expounded both mentions of 'אותו' (it), holds that one is liable for an incomplete inner offering offered outside.

items.text: Derivation for slaughtering a bird outside
items.text_en: Derivation for slaughtering a bird outside
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains how Rabbi Akiva uses the verse 'blood it shall be considered' to include slaughtering a bird, while Rabbi Yishmael derives it from 'or who slaughters'. A baraita clarifies that 'or who slaughters' includes a bird but excludes pinching (melikah), using the phrase 'this is the thing'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Akiva does with the verse 'דם יחשב' (blood it shall be considered), and answers that he uses it to include liability for slaughtering a bird outside.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yishmael derives the liability for slaughtering a bird from the verse 'או אשר ישחט' (or who slaughters).
Rabbi Akiva explains that the verse 'או אשר ישחט' (or who slaughters) is needed to teach that one is liable only for slaughtering, not for pinching (melikah).
The Gemara states that Rabbi Yishmael derives the exclusion of pinching from the phrase 'זה הדבר' (this is the thing).
A baraita is cited: the verse 'אשר ישחט' (who slaughters) only includes an animal; to include a bird, the verse adds 'או אשר ישחט' (or who slaughters).
The baraita raises a possible objection: one might think pinching (melikah) should also be liable via a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument, since it is the valid method inside.
The baraita resolves the objection by citing the verse 'זה הדבר' (this is the thing), which limits liability to slaughtering alone, excluding pinching.
Rabbi Akiva explains that the phrase 'זה הדבר' (this is the thing) is needed for a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) with the passage on vows.

items.text: Exemption for kemitzah and receiving blood outside
items.text_en: Exemption for kemitzah and receiving blood outside
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that one who performs kemitzah (taking a handful) or receives blood outside is exempt. It considers deriving liability from slaughtering (which is invalid for Passover if not for eaters) or from sprinkling (for which a non-priest is liable with death), but these analogies are rejected.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that one who performs kemitzah (taking a handful) or receives blood outside is exempt, and from where would liability be derived.
The Gemara proposes deriving liability from slaughtering, which is invalid for Passover if not for eaters.
The Gemara alternatively proposes deriving liability from sprinkling, for which a non-priest is liable with death.

items.text: Gemara's attempt to derive liability from other cases
items.text_en: Gemara's attempt to derive liability from other cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to derive the liability for offering outside from other cases like sprinkling and slaughtering, but concludes that a specific verse is needed because the derivation fails.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes deriving liability for offering outside from other cases (sprinkling, slaughtering, offering up), listing their unique stringencies.
The Gemara concludes that a specific verse is necessary because the derivation from other cases fails.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Abbahu and Abaye on liability counts
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Abbahu and Abaye on liability counts
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abbahu and Abaye debate the number of liability counts for performing multiple actions (slaughtering, sprinkling, offering) outside, based on the views of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abbahu states that for slaughtering and sprinkling outside, according to Rabbi Yishmael one is liable for one count, and according to Rabbi Akiva for two counts.
Abaye objects that even according to Rabbi Akiva one is liable for only one count, because the verse 'שם תעשה' (there you shall do) treats all actions as one service.
Rabbi Abbahu responds that for sprinkling and offering up, according to Rabbi Yishmael one is liable for two counts, and according to Rabbi Akiva for only one.
Abaye objects that even according to Rabbi Akiva one is liable for two counts, because the verse distinguishes between 'שם תעלה' (there you shall offer up) and 'שם תעשה' (there you shall do).
The gemara concludes that for slaughtering, sprinkling, and offering up, according to all opinions one is liable for two counts.

items.text: Baraita on the definition of 'camp' for liability
items.text_en: Baraita on the definition of 'camp' for liability
items.desc_en: A baraita clarifies that liability for slaughtering outside applies only to a place not fit for any sacrifice, excluding the south of the Temple courtyard which is fit for lighter sacrifices.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by questioning whether slaughtering an עולה (burnt offering) in the south of the Temple courtyard would incur liability, and answers with a verse excluding it.
The baraita asks whether the term 'camp' includes the Levite camp, and answers with a verse derivation.
The baraita again questions whether slaughtering an עולה in the south is liable, and answers with a different verse.
The baraita concludes that the south is excluded because, unlike the outside, it is fit for slaughtering lighter sacrifices (קדשים קלים).

items.text: Dispute between Ulla and Rava about the roof of the Sanctuary
items.text_en: Dispute between Ulla and Rava about the roof of the Sanctuary
items.desc_en: Ulla holds that slaughtering on the roof of the Sanctuary incurs liability, while Rava argues that the verse 'at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting' excludes the roof.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that one who slaughters on the roof of the Sanctuary is liable, because the roof is not fit for any sacrifice.
Rava objects: if the roof is included, why does the verse need 'אֶל פֶּתַח אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד' (at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting)? It must come to exclude the roof.
The Gemara counters: according to Rava, if the roof is excluded, why does the verse need 'בַּמַּחֲנֶה' and 'מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה'? They must come to include the roof.
Rav Mari resolves: the verses come to include a case where the entire animal is inside and its neck is outside.

items.text: Rav Mari's resolution and Gemara's clarification
items.text_en: Rav Mari's resolution and Gemara's clarification
items.desc_en: Rav Mari suggests the verse includes a case where the animal's body is inside and its neck outside, but the Gemara clarifies it refers to the body outside and neck inside.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mari proposes that the verse includes a case where the animal's entire body is inside the sanctuary and its neck is outside.
The Gemara objects that this case is obvious, since the neck is outside and the slaughter occurs outside, so no special verse is needed.
The Gemara corrects Rav Mari's proposal: the verse actually includes the reverse case where the body is outside and the neck is inside.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish on offering in the present era
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish on offering in the present era
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish argue whether offering outside the Temple is liable today, based on whether the original sanctity sanctified for the future. The Gemara connects this to a Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan holds one who offers outside in the present era is liable, while Resh Lakish holds he is exempt.
The Gemara explains the rationale: Rabbi Yochanan holds the original sanctity sanctified both for its time and for the future, while Resh Lakish holds it sanctified only for its time.

The Gemara suggests that the dispute parallels a Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehoshua holds that the original sanctity sanctified for the future.
The Gemara infers from Rabbi Yehoshua's statement that Rabbi Eliezer must hold that the original sanctity did not sanctify for the future.
Ravina rejects the inference, suggesting that both Tannaim may agree that the sanctity sanctified for the future, and Rabbi Eliezer's curtains were merely for modesty.

items.text: Dispute on offering less than an olive's bulk with a bone completing it
items.text_en: Dispute on offering less than an olive's bulk with a bone completing it
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish argue whether offering less than an olive's bulk of meat, with a bone completing the olive's bulk, incurs liability, based on whether bone attachments are considered like the meat itself.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan holds one is liable for offering less than an olive's bulk of meat with a bone completing it, while Resh Lakish holds one is exempt.
The gemara explains the reasoning: Rabbi Yochanan considers bone attachments (חיבורי עולין) like the offering itself, while Resh Lakish does not.
Rava raises a question about a related case, which is cut off at the end of the daf.

items.text: The question of salt completing a kezayit
items.text_en: The question of salt completing a kezayit
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about a dove's head that lacks a kezayit of flesh, and salt completes it to a kezayit. Rava from Parzikya asks Rav Ashi whether this is the same dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding bone completing a kezayit. The Gemara explores whether each would apply their reasoning here, concluding with teiku.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about a dove's head that lacks a kezayit of flesh, and salt completes it to a kezayit.

sub.text: Rava from Parzikya to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rava from Parzikya to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rava from Parzikya asks Rav Ashi whether this is the same dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding bone completing a kezayit.

The Gemara explores whether each would apply their reasoning here, considering Rabbi Yochanan's distinction of bone being from the same category as flesh versus salt not being from the dove's category, and Reish Lakish's distinction of the obligation to bring up the bone versus salt.
The Gemara concludes with teiku (the question stands unresolved).

items.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's statement
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's statement
items.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's opinion, which is the basis for the subsequent debate.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Yose HaGelili's opinion (abbreviated).

items.text: Replies of Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Replies of Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon each offer a response to Rabbi Yosi HaGlili's position. Rabbi argues that slaughtering inside and offering outside had a time of fitness, unlike slaughtering and offering outside. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon argues that inside, the sanctity accepts it, but outside it does not.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi responds to Rabbi Yosi HaGlili by arguing that slaughtering inside and offering outside had a time of fitness, unlike slaughtering and offering outside.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's reply
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's reply
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon responds to Rabbi Yosi HaGlili by arguing that inside, the sanctity accepts it, but outside it does not.

items.text: Difference between the two replies
items.text_en: Difference between the two replies
items.desc_en: Ze'eiri and Rabbah explain the practical difference between the two replies: Ze'eiri says it is a case of slaughter at night, while Rabbah says it is a case of receiving the blood in a non-sacred vessel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between the two replies of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yose HaGelili.
Ze'eiri answers that the difference is a case of slaughter at night, which is invalid for sacrifice but the blood is still received in a sacred vessel.
Rabbah answers that the difference is a case of receiving the blood in a non-sacred vessel, which is valid for slaughter but invalid for offering.

items.text: Debate about impurity: body vs. flesh
items.text_en: Debate about impurity: body vs. flesh
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the case of a impure person who ate sacred meat. Rava explains that all agree if body impurity preceded flesh impurity, one is liable. The dispute is when flesh impurity preceded body impurity: the Rabbis apply the principle of migo, while Rabbi Yosi HaGlili does not. Rav Ashi questions whether body impurity is indeed more severe, suggesting flesh impurity might be because it has no purification in a mikveh.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that the Rabbis' objection to Rabbi Yosi HaGlili is well-founded.
Rava explains that when body impurity precedes flesh impurity, all agree one is liable because body impurity carries the penalty of כרת (excision).
Rava specifies that the dispute is only when flesh impurity preceded body impurity.
Rava explains that the Rabbis apply the principle of מיגו (since the flesh impurity could have been more severe, it is treated as if it were), while Rabbi Yosi HaGlili rejects this principle.

sub.text: Gemara's objection to Rabbi Yosi HaGlili
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to Rabbi Yosi HaGlili
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: even without מיגו, let the more severe body impurity take effect upon the flesh impurity.
Rav Ashi challenges the assumption that body impurity is more severe, suggesting flesh impurity might be more severe because it has no purification in a mikveh.

items.text: Mishnah: Stringencies of slaughter and offering
items.text_en: Mishnah: Stringencies of slaughter and offering
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists stringencies: slaughtering for a commoner is liable, but offering for a commoner is exempt; two people holding a knife are exempt, but two holding a limb are liable; offering multiple times incurs liability for each according to Rabbi Shimon, but only once according to Rabbi Yosi; one is not liable until bringing to the top of the altar, but Rabbi Shimon says even on a rock or stone.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that there are stringencies in slaughter (שחיטה) and in offering (העלאה) relative to each other, and gives the first example: slaughtering for a commoner (הדיוט) is חייב (liable), but offering for a commoner is פטור (exempt).
The Mishnah gives the second example: two people holding a knife and slaughtering are פטורים (exempt), but two holding a limb and offering it are חייבים (liable).

sub.text: Mishnah citing Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yosi
sub.text_en: Mishnah citing Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yosi
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: if one offers multiple times, Rabbi Shimon holds he is חייב (liable) for each offering, while Rabbi Yosi holds he is only חייב once.
The Mishnah concludes with another dispute: the first opinion holds one is not חייב until bringing to the top of the altar, but Rabbi Shimon says even if one offers on a rock or stone, he is חייב.

items.text: Gemara: Deriving the exemptions from verses
items.text_en: Gemara: Deriving the exemptions from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why offering for a commoner is exempt, citing the verse 'to God'. It then addresses why slaughter for a commoner is liable, using the verse 'ish ish' to include two people. The Gemara further explains that the word 'hahu' excludes two people in slaughter, but then questions why the same word doesn't exclude two in offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why offering for a commoner is exempt, given that the verse 'to God' appears in both offering and slaughter contexts.
The Gemara answers that the word 'איש איש' (each man) in the slaughter context includes two people, but the same word in the offering context is needed to teach liability for two who offer together.
The Gemara objects that the same logic should apply to slaughter, but the verse 'ההוא' (that one) excludes two people from liability in slaughter.
The Gemara questions why the same word 'ההוא' does not also exclude two people in the offering context.

items.text: Deriving exemptions from 'ההוא' and the purpose of 'לה׳'
items.text_en: Deriving exemptions from 'ההוא' and the purpose of 'לה׳'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse needs to exclude an unintentional, coerced, or misled person, and notes that two instances of 'ההוא' are written. It then asks what 'לה׳' comes to teach, answering that it excludes the scapegoat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse needs to exclude an unintentional, coerced, or misled person, and notes that two instances of 'ההוא' are written.
The Gemara answers that two instances of 'ההוא' are written, and 'לה׳' comes to exclude the scapegoat.

items.text: Introduction of the Mishnah clause
items.text_en: Introduction of the Mishnah clause
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that there is a stringency in offering (compared to slaughtering) regarding liability for multiple acts.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces the principle that offering (העלאה) has a stringency regarding liability for multiple acts.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yosei on 'איש איש'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yosei on 'איש איש'
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that 'איש איש' implies that two people holding a limb and offering it are liable, contrary to a logical deduction from slaughter. Rabbi Shimon holds this, while Rabbi Yosei argues that 'ההוא' indicates one person, not two, and 'איש איש' is just the Torah's normal speech.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by asking what 'איש איש' (each man) comes to teach, and answers that two people who hold a limb and offer it are liable, despite a logical deduction from slaughter.
The baraita presents a logical deduction: just as two people holding a knife for slaughter are exempt, so too two people offering a limb should be exempt, but the verse 'איש איש' overrides this.
Rabbi Shimon holds that 'איש איש' teaches that two people are liable when offering a limb together.
Rabbi Yosei argues that 'ההוא' (that man) indicates one person, not two, and 'איש איש' is merely the Torah's normal speech pattern.

items.text: Reconciling the views of Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Reconciling the views of Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon uses 'ההוא' to exclude unintentional acts, while Rabbi Yosei derives this from 'הוא'-'ההוא'. Rabbi Shimon does not expound 'הוא'-'ההוא'. Rabbi Yosei argues that since one 'איש איש' is normal speech, the other is too, and derives liability for slaughtering for a common person from 'דם יחשב לאיש ההוא דם שפך'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon uses the word 'ההוא' to exclude unintentional, forced, and mistaken acts.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei derives the exclusion of unintentional acts from the juxtaposition of 'הוא' and 'ההוא'.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Shimon does not expound the principle of 'הוא'-'ההוא'.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei argues that since one instance of 'איש איש' is normal speech, the other is also normal speech.
The Gemara asks: from where does Rabbi Yosei derive that one who slaughters for a common person is liable?
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yosei derives liability from the verse 'דם יחשב לאיש ההוא דם שפך' — even one who slaughters for a common person.

items.text: Mishnah clause on repeated offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah clause on repeated offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one offered and then offered again, he is liable for each act.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one offered and then offered again, he is liable for each act.

items.text: Dispute between Resh Lakish, Rabbi Yochanan, and Ulla on liability for multiple limbs
items.text_en: Dispute between Resh Lakish, Rabbi Yochanan, and Ulla on liability for multiple limbs
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish says the dispute is about four or five limbs, where one opinion holds liability only for a complete animal, the other for each limb. Rabbi Yochanan says the dispute is about a single limb, regarding offerings that were missing parts. Ulla offers two versions: either all agree on liability for missing inner offerings, or all agree on exemption for missing outer offerings.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that the dispute in the mishna concerns four or five limbs: one opinion holds liability only for a complete animal, the other for each limb, but all agree that for one limb one is liable only once.
Rabbi Yochanan says the dispute is about a single limb regarding offerings that were missing parts, but all agree that for four or five limbs one is liable for each.
Ulla (first version) says all agree on liability for missing inner offerings, and the dispute is only about missing outer offerings.
Ulla (second version) says all agree on exemption for missing outer offerings, and the dispute is only about missing inner offerings.

items.text: Support for Ulla's first version from Avuh deShmuel
items.text_en: Support for Ulla's first version from Avuh deShmuel
items.desc_en: Avuh deShmuel says that we return popped-out limbs to the altar only according to the opinion that is not Rabbi Yosei, which aligns with Ulla's first version.

sub.desc_en: Avuh deShmuel states that we return popped-out limbs to the altar only according to the opinion that is not Rabbi Yosei, which supports Ulla's first version.

items.text: Deriving the opinions of Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon from biblical verses
items.text_en: Deriving the opinions of Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon from biblical verses
items.desc_en: Rav Huna explains Rabbi Yosei's reason from Noah's altar, and Rabbi Yochanan explains Rabbi Shimon's reason from Manoach's offering. The Gemara rebuts each by saying the other verse is just for height or a temporary ruling. An alternative explanation is given for Rabbi Shimon based on a baraita about a bamah lacking an altar.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna explains Rabbi Yosei's reason by citing the verse about Noah building an altar to God.
Rabbi Yochanan explains Rabbi Shimon's reason by citing the verse about Manoach offering on a rock.
The Gemara objects that the verse about Noah could also support Rabbi Shimon, but dismisses it as merely teaching about height.
The Gemara objects that the verse about Manoach could also support Rabbi Yosei, but dismisses it as a temporary ruling.
The Gemara offers an alternative explanation for Rabbi Shimon based on a baraita that distinguishes between a bamah lacking an altar and a stone or rock.
The Gemara clarifies that the baraita means during the period when bamot were forbidden, offering on a stone or rock makes one liable.

items.text: Inquiry about the requirements for a bamah
items.text_en: Inquiry about the requirements for a bamah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina asks whether the horn, ramp, base, and square are required for a bamah. Rabbi Yirmeya answers that they are required for a large bamah but not for a small one.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's question
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's question
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina asks whether the horn, ramp, base, and square are required for a bamah.
Rabbi Yirmeya answers by citing a baraita that these elements are required for a large bamah but not for a small one.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one is liable for offering either fit or disqualified sacrifices outside the Temple, provided their disqualification occurred in the sanctuary. It also specifies that offering an olive's bulk of the burnt-offering or its sacrificial parts outside incurs liability.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who offers either fit or disqualified sacrifices outside the Temple is liable, provided their disqualification occurred in the sanctuary.
The Mishnah adds that one who offers an olive's bulk of the burnt-offering or its sacrificial parts outside is liable.

items.text: Derivation of liability for various sacrifices from verses
items.text_en: Derivation of liability for various sacrifices from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse "who offers a burnt-offering or sacrifice" that not only the burnt-offering but also the sacrificial parts of other offerings are included. It further expands to include the handful, frankincense, incense, meal-offerings, and libations, and then extends liability to disqualified sacrifices through additional verses.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'אֲשֶׁר יַעֲלֶה עֹלָה אוֹ זָבַח' (who offers a burnt-offering or sacrifice) and derives that the term 'עֹלָה' (burnt-offering) alone would limit liability, but the word 'זֶבַח' (sacrifice) includes the sacrificial portions of guilt-offerings, sin-offerings, most sacred offerings, and lesser sanctity offerings.

The baraita further derives from the phrase 'וְאֶל פֶּתַח אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד לֹא יְבִיאֶנּוּ' (and to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting he shall not bring it) that any item fit to be brought to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting—such as the handful, frankincense, incense, meal-offerings of priests and the anointed priest, and libations of three log of wine or water—incurs liability when offered outside.
The baraita asks: from where do we include disqualified sacrifices whose disqualification occurred in sanctity?

The baraita lists examples of disqualified offerings: those left overnight, taken outside, impure, slaughtered with improper intent, collected or sprinkled by unfit persons, blood placed in the wrong location, or Paschal and sin offerings offered not for their own sake.

The baraita answers that the verse 'לֹא יְבִיאֶנּוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת' (he shall not bring it to make) teaches that any item which is acceptable at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting—even if disqualified—incurs liability when offered outside.

items.text: Combining burnt-offering and its parts for the olive's bulk
items.text_en: Combining burnt-offering and its parts for the olive's bulk
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's statement about the burnt-offering implies that only the burnt-offering and its sacrificial parts combine, but not peace-offerings and their parts. It then cites a baraita that explicitly states that the burnt-offering and its parts combine to form the olive's bulk for liability when offered outside, and also for piggul, leftover, and impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that only the burnt-offering and its sacrificial parts combine for the olive's bulk, but not peace-offerings and their parts.
A baraita is cited that explicitly states the burnt-offering and its sacrificial parts combine for the olive's bulk for liability when offered outside, and also for piggul, leftover, and impurity.

items.text: Contradiction regarding combination for piggul and leftover
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding combination for piggul and leftover
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: while the baraita says only the burnt-offering and its parts combine for piggul and leftover, a Mishnah states that all piggul items combine and all leftover items combine. The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between piggul itself and the thought of piggul, and between leftover that remains after the blood is sprinkled and leftover that remains before. It attributes this distinction to Rabbi Yehoshua.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita's rule about combination for piggul and leftover applies only to the burnt-offering and its parts, given that a Mishnah states all piggul items combine and all leftover items combine.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah says all piggul items combine and all leftover items combine, contradicting the baraita's limitation.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction regarding piggul by distinguishing between piggul itself (the status) and the thought of piggul (מחשבת פיגול).
The Gemara resolves the contradiction regarding leftover by distinguishing between leftover that remains after the blood is sprinkled and leftover that remains before.
The Gemara attributes this distinction to Rabbi Yehoshua, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehoshua states that all sacrifices that have a olive-sized portion of meat remaining combine.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Laws of offering blood and portions outside
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Laws of offering blood and portions outside
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one has a kezayit of fat, he may sprinkle the blood; but if he has half a kezayit of meat and half of fat, he does not sprinkle. For an olah, even half and half is sprinkled because it is entirely burnt. For a meal-offering, even if it is entirely intact, he does not sprinkle.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that one who has a kezayit of fat may sprinkle the blood, but half a kezayit of meat and half of fat does not permit sprinkling.

items.text: Gemara's clarification on the meal-offering
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification on the meal-offering
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the meal-offering referred to in the Mishnah is the meal-offering of libations that accompanies a sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what meal-offering (מנחה) is doing in the Mishnah's context of blood offerings.
Rav Pappa answers that the meal-offering is the meal-offering of libations (מנחת נסכים) that accompanies the sacrifice.

items.text: Mishnah: Liability for offering parts outside
items.text_en: Mishnah: Liability for offering parts outside
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items (kemitzah, levonah, ketoret, etc.) for which offering a kezayit outside incurs liability. Rabbi Eliezer exempts until the entire item is offered. If one offered inside and left a kezayit to offer outside, he is liable. If the item was missing any amount and offered outside, he is exempt. Offering sacred parts or limbs outside incurs liability.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items (kemitzah, levonah, ketoret, etc.) for which offering a kezayit outside incurs liability.
Rabbi Eliezer exempts until the entire item is offered outside.
If one offered inside and left a kezayit to offer outside, he is liable.
If the item was missing any amount and offered outside, he is exempt.
Offering sacred parts or limbs outside incurs liability.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying 'patoor' in the baraita
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying 'patoor' in the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: one who offers a kezayit outside is liable; one who offers half a peras inside is patoor. Initially thought to mean patoor for a zar (non-priest), but that is problematic because offering is a valid act. Rabbi Zeira quotes Rav Chisda quoting Rav Yirmeya bar Abba quoting Rav: patoor means the community is exempt (from bringing a sin-offering).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: one who offers a kezayit outside is liable; one who offers half a peras inside is patoor.
The Gemara initially assumes patoor means the non-priest (zar) is exempt, but objects: offering is a valid act.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira quoting Rav Chisda quoting Rav Yirmeya bar Abba quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira quoting Rav Chisda quoting Rav Yirmeya bar Abba quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira transmits a tradition from Rav: patoor means the community is exempt from bringing a sin-offering.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's difficulty and resolution regarding Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's difficulty and resolution regarding Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira questions Rav's statement, noting that even Rabbi Eliezer would agree in this case, since Rabbi Eliezer's exemption is based on the act not being considered 'offering'. Rabba resolves: the dispute is about inner offering (in the Heichal), where all agree; the dispute is about inner offering (in the Kodesh Kodashim), where one holds 'meloh kofnav' is precise and the other holds it is not.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira raises a difficulty: Rav's statement that even Rabbi Eliezer would agree here is problematic, because Rabbi Eliezer's exemption is based on the act not being considered 'offering' (הקטרה).
Rabba answers: regarding the inner offering (הקטרה) in the Heichal (היכל), all agree it is considered an offering.

Rabba explains: the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages is specifically about the inner offering (הקטרה) in the Kodesh Kodashim (קודש קודשים), where one holds that 'מלא חפניו' (his handful) is precise and the other holds it is not.

items.text: Abaye's objection and alternative resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and alternative resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye objects: the verse 'chukah' is written regarding inner offering. He reinterprets: all agree about inner offering; the dispute is about outer offering, where one derives from 'inner' to 'outer' and the other does not.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the verse 'חוקה' (a statute) is written specifically regarding the inner offering, not the outer.
Abaye reinterprets: all agree regarding the inner offering; the dispute is about the outer offering, where one derives from 'inner' to 'outer' and the other does not.
Abaye concludes: the dispute is about the outer offering, with one sage deriving the law of inner from outer and the other not.

items.text: Rava's objection and final resolution
items.text_en: Rava's objection and final resolution
items.desc_en: Rava objects: if the Rabbis do not derive outer from outer, how can they derive inner from outer? He cites a baraita that one is not liable for less than a kezayit of kemitzah or less than three log of wine/water, even though they contain many olive-bulk measures, showing they do not derive outer from outer. Rava concludes: the case is where they fixed two half-peras measures.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects: if the Rabbis do not derive outer from outer (חוץ מחוץ), how can they derive inner from outer (פנים מחוץ)?

Rava cites a baraita that one is not liable for less than a kezayit of kemitzah or less than three log of wine/water, even though they contain many olive-bulk measures, showing the Rabbis do not derive outer from outer (חוץ מחוץ).
Rava concludes: the case is where they fixed two half-peras measures (שני חצאי פרס), resolving the objection.

items.text: Dispute about the significance of vessel designation
items.text_en: Dispute about the significance of vessel designation
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between two opinions: one holds that designating a vessel for a specific sacrifice is significant, while the other holds it is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: one opinion holds that designating a vessel for a specific sacrifice is significant (מִילְּתָא), while the other holds it is not (לָאו מִילְּתָא).

items.text: Rava's ruling on partial offerings outside
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on partial offerings outside
items.desc_en: Rava explains that according to the opinion that vessel designation is insignificant, if one designated six animals for a bull but offered four outside, he is liable because they are fit for a ram; similarly for a ram and a lamb. However, if the offering is missing any amount, he is exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that according to the opinion that vessel designation is insignificant, if one designated six animals for a bull but offered four outside, he is liable because they are fit for a ram; similarly for a ram and a lamb.
Rava concludes that if the offering is missing any amount, one is exempt when offering it outside.

items.text: Rav Ashi's derivation of libation from burning
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's derivation of libation from burning
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that libation is not derived from burning, even when both are performed outside; only burning is derived from burning, even when one is outside and one inside.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asserts that the rabbis do not derive the laws of libation (ניסוך) from those of burning (הקטרה), even when both are performed outside the Temple; rather, they derive burning from burning even when one is outside and one inside.

items.text: Inquiry about deficiency outside
items.text_en: Inquiry about deficiency outside
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether a deficiency that occurs outside the Temple is considered a valid deficiency, or whether once the offering has left, it is already invalid regardless of deficiency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether a deficiency that occurs outside the Temple is considered a valid deficiency, or whether once the offering has left, it is already invalid regardless of deficiency.

items.text: Abaye's proof from Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Abaye's proof from Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: Abaye attempts to prove from Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that he exempts until all are offered, implying deficiency outside is not considered. Rabba bar Rav Chanan challenges him, and Abaye clarifies that he heard from Rav that the Sages only disagree with Rabbi Eliezer when the offering is intact, but agree in a case of deficiency, and that deficiency was inside.

sub.desc_en: Abaye proposes to prove the issue from Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that he exempts until all are offered.
Rabba bar Rav Chanan challenges Abaye, questioning whether he can simply deduce from Rabbi Eliezer's ruling.
Abaye clarifies that he heard explicitly from Rav that the Sages only disagree with Rabbi Eliezer when the offering is intact, but agree in a case of deficiency, and that deficiency was inside.

items.text: Another attempted proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Another attempted proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove from the Mishnah that all offerings that are deficient and offered outside are exempt, suggesting deficiency outside is considered, but deflects that the deficiency occurred inside.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah that all offerings that are deficient and then offered outside are exempt, implying that deficiency outside is considered.
The Gemara deflects the proof by clarifying that the deficiency occurred inside, not outside, so the case does not address the question of deficiency outside.

items.text: Discussion on interposition in offering
items.text_en: Discussion on interposition in offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why one who offers sacred items outside is liable despite an interposition. Shmuel says it is when he turned them over; Rabbi Yochanan says even without turning, following Rabbi Shimon who holds one is liable even if offering on a rock; Rav says that like items do not interpose.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why one who offers sacred items outside is liable, given that there is an interposition (חציצה) between the offering and the altar.
Shmuel answers that the case is when he turned the items over, so the interposition is removed.
Rabbi Yochanan says that even without turning, one is liable, following Rabbi Shimon who holds that one is liable even if he offered on a rock.
Rav answers that like items (מין במינו) do not constitute an interposition.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on meal-offering without removal of handful
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on meal-offering without removal of handful
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a meal-offering was offered outside without its handful removed, one is exempt; but if the handful was removed and returned, one is liable. The Gemara questions why the remnants do not nullify the handful, and Rabbi Zeira answers that burning is stated for both, and just as the handful does not nullify its fellow, so too the remnants do not nullify the handful.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a meal-offering was offered outside without its handful removed, one is exempt; but if the handful was removed and returned, one is liable.
The Gemara questions why the remnants (שיריים) do not nullify the handful (קומץ) when they are mixed together.
Rabbi Zeira answers that burning (הקטרה) is stated for both the handful and the remnants, and just as the handful does not nullify its fellow, so too the remnants do not nullify the handful.

items.text: Mishnah on handful and frankincense, and two bowls of frankincense
items.text_en: Mishnah on handful and frankincense, and two bowls of frankincense
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one offered the handful or frankincense outside, he is liable; Rabbi Eliezer exempts until he offers the second. Similarly for two bowls of frankincense. If one is offered inside and one outside, he is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: one who offers the handful or frankincense outside is liable, but Rabbi Eliezer exempts until he offers the second.
The Mishnah adds that if one is offered inside and one outside, he is liable.
The Mishnah states the parallel rule for two bowls of frankincense: one who offers one outside is liable, but Rabbi Eliezer exempts until he offers the second.
The Mishnah adds that if one bowl is offered inside and one outside, he is liable.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's inquiry about the handful permitting the remnants
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's inquiry about the handful permitting the remnants
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha asks whether the handful permits its counterpart in the remnants, or merely weakens the prohibition. The Gemara analyzes this according to different Tannaic opinions: Rabbi Meir, the Rabbis, and Rabbi Eliezer, concluding with a teiku.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha raises a dilemma: does the handful permit its counterpart in the remnants, or does it merely weaken the prohibition?
The Gemara considers the dilemma according to Rabbi Meir, who holds that one can render piggul with half a permitter, so the handful would entirely permit its counterpart.
The Gemara considers the dilemma according to the Rabbis, who hold that one cannot render piggul with half a permitter, so the handful would neither permit nor weaken the prohibition.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that the dilemma was raised according to Rabbi Eliezer, since he holds like the Rabbis that one cannot render piggul with half a permitter.
The Gemara concludes that the dilemma was raised according to the Rabbis of the mishna, who hold one is liable for sacrificing only the handful, and asks whether it permits or weakens.
The Gemara concludes that the dilemma stands unresolved (teiku).

items.text: Beginning of next Mishnah
items.text_en: Beginning of next Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins discussing one who sprinkles part of the blood outside.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah begins discussing one who sprinkles part of the blood outside.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Elazar holds that one who pours the water of the Sukkot festival outside is liable, while Rabbi Nechemya holds that one who offers the remnants of blood outside is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a dispute: the Tanna Kamma holds one liable for offering outside, Rabbi Elazar adds one who pours the water of the Sukkot festival outside is liable, and Rabbi Nechemya adds one who offers the remnants of blood outside is liable.

items.text: Rava's qualification and the baraita
items.text_en: Rava's qualification and the baraita
items.desc_en: Rava states that Rabbi Elazar concedes regarding blood libations. A baraita is cited where Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon say that one begins from where one left off, implying a principle about the order of libations.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that Rabbi Elazar concedes regarding blood libations (that offering them outside is liable).
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon say that one begins from where one left off, implying a principle about the order of libations.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of Rabbi Elazar's view
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation of Rabbi Elazar's view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains in the name of Rabbi Menachem Yodfa'ah that Rabbi Elazar follows Rabbi Akiva's view that water libation is a Torah commandment, based on the verse 'and its libations' referring to two libations: water and wine.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Menachem Yodfa'ah explains that Rabbi Elazar follows the view of his teacher Rabbi Akiva, who derives the water libation (ניסוך המים) as a Torah obligation from the verse 'וּנְסָכֶיהָ' (and its libations).

items.text: Resh Lakish's objection
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's objection
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish objects to Rabbi Yochanan: if water libation is like wine libation, why does Rabbi Elazar specify three logs and only on the festival? The Gemara notes that Rabbi Elazar explicitly says 'water of the festival' and 'on the festival'.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish objects to Rabbi Yochanan: if the water libation is like the wine libation, then it should require three לוגים (log) and apply all year, but Rabbi Elazar specifies 'מי החג' (water of the festival) and 'בחג' (on the festival).

items.text: Resolution via Rabbi Asi's tradition
items.text_en: Resolution via Rabbi Asi's tradition
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by citing Rabbi Asi's tradition from Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Nechunya of the Valley of Beit Chortan: the ten saplings, the willow, and the water libation are a halakha from Moses at Sinai, establishing the water libation as a distinct law.

sub.desc_en: The gemara resolves the objection by citing Rabbi Asi's tradition from Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Nechunya: the ten saplings, the willow, and the water libation are a הלכה למשה מסיני (law from Moses at Sinai), thus not derived by analogy.

items.text: Baraita on the liability and the dispute
items.text_en: Baraita on the liability and the dispute
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one who pours three logs of water on the festival outside is liable, and Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon says he is liable only if he filled them for the sake of the festival. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that they disagree about whether there is a fixed measure for water libation.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that one who pours three logs of water on the festival outside is liable, and Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon adds that he is liable only if he filled them for the sake of the festival.
The gemara asks what is the practical difference between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that they disagree about whether there is a fixed measure (שיעור) for water libation.

items.text: Rav Pappa's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa offers a different explanation of the dispute, though the text breaks off, indicating the Gemara will continue with his view.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa begins to speak, but the text cuts off without completing his statement.

items.text: Dispute about libations in the wilderness
items.text_en: Dispute about libations in the wilderness
items.desc_en: Ravina and Rabina argue whether the dispute among earlier authorities concerns whether libations were offered in the wilderness or whether it is about deriving the water libation from the wine libation.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens by stating that the dispute among earlier authorities is about whether libations were offered in the wilderness.
Ravina explains that the dispute is actually about whether the water libation is derived from the wine libation by a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy).

items.text: Liability for pouring libations outside
items.text_en: Liability for pouring libations outside
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one who pours three logs of wine outside is liable, with Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon adding that it must have been sanctified in a vessel. Rav Adda bar Rav Yitzchak and Rava bar Rabbah debate what distinguishes their positions: whether it concerns the rounding of measures or whether libations were offered on a private altar.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that one who pours three logs of wine outside is liable, and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon adds that it must have been sanctified in a vessel.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Rav Yitzchak's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Rav Yitzchak's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Rav Yitzchak answers that the difference lies in the rounding of measures (whether partial logs combine).
Rava bar Rabbah answers that the difference concerns whether libations were offered on a private altar (במה).

items.text: Dispute about libations on a private altar
items.text_en: Dispute about libations on a private altar
items.desc_en: The Gemara connects the previous dispute to a Tannaitic debate about whether a private altar requires libations. Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva argue over the interpretation of the verse 'When you come'—whether it refers to the great altar or a small altar, leading to conclusions about whether libations were offered in the wilderness.

items.text: Rabbi Nechemya on leftover blood offered outside
items.text_en: Rabbi Nechemya on leftover blood offered outside
items.desc_en: Rabbi Nechemya holds that one who offers leftover blood outside is liable. Rabbi Yochanan explains this follows the view that leftovers are indispensable. An objection is raised from a debate with Rabbi Akiva, who argues that leftovers are merely a remnant of a mitzvah, and the Gemara concludes this is a refutation.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Nechemya states his position: one who offers leftover blood outside is liable (חייב).
Rabbi Yochanan explains that Rabbi Nechemya's view follows the position that leftovers (שיריים) are indispensable (מעכבין) for atonement.

An objection is raised from a baraita where Rabbi Akiva argues that leftovers are merely a remnant of a mitzvah (שירי מצוה) and not indispensable, and Rabbi Nechemya's attempted proof from limbs and fats is rejected.

The Gemara concludes that if Rabbi Nechemya truly held leftovers are indispensable (מעכבין), he should have answered Rabbi Akiva with that claim; since he did not, the objection stands as a refutation (תיוּבְתָּא) of Rabbi Yochanan's explanation.

items.text: Resolution: distinction between inner and outer leftovers
items.text_en: Resolution: distinction between inner and outer leftovers
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between inner leftovers (which are indispensable) and outer leftovers (which are not). Rabbi Akiva misunderstood Rabbi Nechemya as referring to outer leftovers, but Rabbi Nechemya was speaking to Rabbi Akiva according to his own reasoning.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah resolves that the dispute is about inner leftovers (שיריים הפנימיים), which are indispensable, while outer leftovers (שיריים החיצוניים) are not; Rabbi Nechemya's statement refers to inner leftovers, but the baraita that challenged him refers to outer leftovers.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva did not understand Rabbi Nechemya's intent and mistakenly thought he referred to outer leftovers, while Rabbi Nechemya was actually speaking according to Rabbi Akiva's own reasoning.

items.text: Mishnah: Melikah and slaughter of birds
items.text_en: Mishnah: Melikah and slaughter of birds
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who performs melikah on a bird inside and then offers it outside is liable, but if done outside and offered outside, he is exempt. One who slaughters a bird inside and offers it outside is exempt.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the Tanna Kamma's ruling that one who slaughters outside and offers up outside is liable, while one who slaughters inside and offers outside is exempt, and vice versa. Rabbi Shimon adds that any act for which one is liable outside is also liable when performed inside and offered outside, except for slaughtering inside and offering outside.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma rules that one who slaughters outside and offers up outside is liable, while one who slaughters inside and offers outside is exempt, and vice versa.
Rabbi Shimon adds that any act for which one is liable outside is also liable when performed inside and offered outside, except for slaughtering inside and offering outside.

items.text: Gemara's textual correction
items.text_en: Gemara's textual correction
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the Mishnah's phrase 'דֶּרֶךְ הֶכְשֵׁירוֹ' (way of its fitness), arguing it should be 'חִיּוּבוֹ' (its liability), and suggests a textual emendation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the Mishnah's phrase 'דֶּרֶךְ הֶכְשֵׁירוֹ' (way of its fitness), arguing it should be 'חִיּוּבוֹ' (its liability).
The Gemara resolves the objection by suggesting the Mishnah should be read as 'חִיּוּבוֹ' (its liability) instead of 'הֶכְשֵׁירוֹ'.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Shimon's position
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Shimon's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to determine which part of the Mishnah Rabbi Shimon's statement refers to. It considers and rejects possibilities that he is commenting on the first clause or the second clause, because his wording does not match the expected formulation. The Gemara concludes that his statement cannot be reconciled with the Mishnah as it stands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which part of the Mishnah Rabbi Shimon's statement refers to.

The Gemara considers the possibility that Rabbi Shimon refers to the first clause, but rejects it because his wording 'all that one is liable for outside' should have been 'all that one is liable for inside'.
The Gemara considers an alternative reading of the first clause, but rejects it because Rabbi Shimon's wording should have been 'all that one is not liable for outside'.
The Gemara considers the possibility that Rabbi Shimon refers to the second clause, but rejects it because his wording should have been 'all that one is not liable for'.
The Gemara considers an alternative reading of the second clause, but rejects it because the Mishnah already explicitly excludes the case of slaughtering inside and offering outside.

items.text: Ze'iri's resolution: nocturnal slaughter
items.text_en: Ze'iri's resolution: nocturnal slaughter
items.desc_en: Ze'iri explains that the dispute concerns slaughtering an animal at night. The Tanna Kamma holds that slaughtering inside at night and offering outside is exempt, while slaughtering outside at night and offering outside is liable. Rabbi Shimon equates the two cases, saying that if one is liable for the outside act, one is liable for the analogous inside act, except for slaughtering a bird inside and offering outside.
