sub.desc_en: Ze'iri resolves the dispute by explaining that the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Shimon disagree about slaughtering an animal at night, with the Tanna Kamma distinguishing between inside and outside slaughter, while Rabbi Shimon equates them except for slaughtering a bird inside and offering outside.
Ze'iri cites Rabbi Shimon's position that liability for an outside act extends to a similar inside act, except for slaughtering a bird inside and offering outside.

items.text: Rava's resolution: reception in a non-sacred vessel
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: reception in a non-sacred vessel
items.desc_en: Rava offers an alternative explanation: the dispute is about receiving blood in a non-sacred vessel. The Tanna Kamma exempts one who receives inside in a non-sacred vessel and offers outside, but holds liable one who receives outside in a non-sacred vessel and offers outside. Rabbi Shimon again equates the cases, with the same exception for slaughtering a bird inside and offering outside.

sub.desc_en: Rava introduces the dispute as being about receiving blood in a non-sacred vessel (כלי חול), explaining that the Tanna Kamma exempts one who receives inside in such a vessel and offers outside, but holds liable one who receives outside and offers outside.
Rabbi Shimon equates the cases, holding one liable for offering outside what would be liable outside, with the exception of slaughtering a bird inside and offering outside.

items.text: Baraita of Avuha deShmuel bar Rav Yitzchak
items.text_en: Baraita of Avuha deShmuel bar Rav Yitzchak
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that presents a different version of the dispute: regarding melikah of a bird, the Tanna Kamma holds that one who performs melikah inside and offers outside is liable, while one who performs melikah outside and offers outside is exempt. Rabbi Shimon holds the latter liable, and his statement is interpreted as referring to this case.

sub.text: Stam (citing baraita of Avuha deShmuel bar Rav Yitzchak)
sub.text_en: Stam (citing baraita of Avuha deShmuel bar Rav Yitzchak)
sub.desc_en: The gemara cites a baraita from Avuha deShmuel bar Rav Yitzchak that presents a different version of the dispute: regarding melikah of a bird, the Tanna Kamma holds that one who performs melikah inside and offers outside is liable, while one who performs melikah outside and offers outside is exempt; Rabbi Shimon holds the latter liable, and his statement is interpreted as referring to this case.

items.text: Mishnah on blood reception in multiple cups
items.text_en: Mishnah on blood reception in multiple cups
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a sin-offering whose blood was received in one cup and then applied partly outside and partly inside, or in two cups with various combinations of inside and outside application. It also draws an analogy to a case where a sin-offering was lost and replaced, and both are then slaughtered.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for a sin-offering whose blood was received in one cup and then applied partly outside and partly inside: the one who applies is liable, because all the blood was fit for inside application.

The Mishnah presents the case of two cups: both inside exempts, both outside makes liable, one inside and one outside exempts, but one outside first and then one inside makes the one who applied the outside cup liable while the inside cup atones.
The Mishnah draws an analogy to a case where a sin-offering was lost and replaced, and both are then slaughtered: the same pattern of liability and exemption applies.
The Mishnah concludes with a general principle: just as the blood of a sin-offering exempts its own flesh from being offered outside, so too it exempts the flesh of its companion.

items.text: Gemara's initial question and identification of the Tanna
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and identification of the Tanna
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that offering blood inside then outside is liable, noting that leftover blood (שיירי הדם) is involved. It identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Nechemya, who holds that offering leftover blood outside is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that offering blood inside then outside is liable, noting that leftover blood (שיירי הדם) is involved.
The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Nechemya, who holds that offering leftover blood outside is liable.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah's seifa and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah's seifa and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the seifa of the Mishnah (two cups of blood, one inside one outside) rules exempt, contradicting Rabbi Nechemya's view. It resolves that the seifa follows the Tanna Kamma of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who holds that one cup renders its fellow cup rejected (דחוי).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah's first clause follows Rabbi Nechemya, the seifa (two cups of blood, one inside one outside) rules exempt, contradicting Rabbi Nechemya's view that leftover blood offered outside is liable.
The Gemara resolves that the seifa follows the Tanna Kamma of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who holds that one cup renders its fellow cup rejected (דחוי).

items.text: Analogy to a lost sin-offering and identification of the Tanna
items.text_en: Analogy to a lost sin-offering and identification of the Tanna
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the need for the analogy of a lost sin-offering. It identifies the analogy as following Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who holds that a sin-offering lost at the time of designation dies. The Gemara explains that the analogy teaches that if one designates two sin-offerings for backup, one is inherently an olah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an analogy: one who designates a sin-offering that was lost, then designates another in its place, and then the first is found.
The Gemara questions why the analogy is needed, implying the Tanna's identity is already known.
The Gemara identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who holds that a sin-offering lost at the time of designation dies.
The Gemara explains the analogy: only when the first was lost does the second serve as a sin-offering; if one designated two sin-offerings for backup, one is inherently an olah.

items.text: Support from Rav Huna's ruling and objection
items.text_en: Support from Rav Huna's ruling and objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara supports the principle with Rav Huna's ruling that a guilt-offering sent to pasture and slaughtered without specification is valid as an olah. An objection is raised that a sin-offering is female, unlike a guilt-offering or olah. Rav Chiya from Yostinya answers that the case involves a he-goat of a leader (שעיר נשיא), which is male.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rav Huna's ruling
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rav Huna's ruling
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Huna's ruling that a guilt-offering sent to pasture and slaughtered without specification is valid as an olah.
The Gemara objects that a sin-offering is female, unlike a guilt-offering or olah which are male.
Rav Chiya from Yostinya answers that the case involves a he-goat of a leader (שעיר נשיא), which is male.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous chapter with the standard formula 'הדרן עלך' (we return to you).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous chapter with the standard formula 'הדרן עלך' (we return to you).

items.text: New Mishnah: Parah Adumah and scapegoat offered outside
items.text_en: New Mishnah: Parah Adumah and scapegoat offered outside
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a Parah Adumah burned outside its pit or a scapegoat offered outside is exempt, based on the verse 'and to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting he did not bring it' – anything not fit to enter the Tent of Meeting is not liable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a Parah Adumah burned outside its pit or a scapegoat offered outside is exempt from liability.
The Mishnah cites the verse 'and to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting he did not bring it' to derive that anything not fit to enter the Tent of Meeting is not liable.

items.text: Mishnah: List of disqualified animals offered outside
items.text_en: Mishnah: List of disqualified animals offered outside
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists animals (e.g., a rove'a, a tereifah) that are exempt when offered outside, based on the verse 'before the Mishkan of Hashem' – anything not fit to come before the Mishkan is not liable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists animals disqualified from being offered (e.g., a rove'a, a tereifah) and states that offering them outside the Mishkan is exempt from liability.
The Mishnah cites the verse 'before the Mishkan of Hashem' to derive that anything unfit to enter the Mishkan is exempt from liability when offered outside.

items.text: Mishnah: Blemished animals
items.text_en: Mishnah: Blemished animals
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins discussing blemished animals, both permanent and temporary, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah begins listing blemished animals, both permanent and temporary, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Mishnah: Liability for offering blemished animals and birds at the wrong age outside
items.text_en: Mishnah: Liability for offering blemished animals and birds at the wrong age outside
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute between the first Tanna and Rabbi Shimon regarding blemished animals and birds offered outside. The first Tanna exempts all, while Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between permanent and temporary blemishes, and between turtledoves before their time and pigeons after their time, imposing a negative commandment for some.

sub.desc_en: The first Tanna states that one who offers blemished animals outside the Temple is exempt from punishment.
Rabbi Shimon distinguishes: permanent blemishes exempt, temporary blemishes incur a negative commandment.
The first Tanna adds that turtledoves before their time and pigeons after their time offered outside are exempt.
Rabbi Shimon rules: pigeons after their time are exempt, but turtledoves before their time incur a negative commandment.
The first Tanna states that offering 'it and its offspring' or a מחוסר זמן (time-deficient animal) outside is exempt.
Rabbi Shimon rules that a מחוסר זמן (time-deficient animal) incurs a negative commandment but not כרת (excision), because it would become fit later.
The Sages object: anything that does not carry כרת (excision) also does not carry a negative commandment.

items.text: Mishnah: Definition of מחוסר זמן in the owner
items.text_en: Mishnah: Definition of מחוסר זמן in the owner
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines מחוסר זמן (time-deficient) as applying both to the animal itself and to its owner. It specifies that a zav, zavah, yoledet, and metzora who offer their sin-offering or guilt-offering outside are exempt, but their burnt-offerings and peace-offerings outside incur liability.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the category of מחוסר זמן (time-deficient) applies both to the animal itself and to its owner.

The Mishnah elaborates on the definition of מחוסר זמן in the owner, listing the zav, zavah, yoledet, and metzora, and specifying that their sin-offerings and guilt-offerings offered outside are exempt, while their burnt-offerings and peace-offerings incur liability.

items.text: Mishnah: Actions exempt from liability outside
items.text_en: Mishnah: Actions exempt from liability outside
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists various items and actions that are exempt when performed outside the Temple, including offering certain sacrificial parts, performing preparatory rites like pouring, kneading, and waving, and arranging the showbread. It concludes that these actions do not incur liability for priesthood, impurity, or other disqualifications.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the sacrificial items that are exempt from liability when offered outside the Temple, including flesh of certain sin-offerings, guilt-offerings, most holy offerings, lesser holy offerings, and leftover grain offerings.
The Mishnah lists preparatory rites performed outside the Temple that are exempt from liability, such as pouring, kneading, waving, and arranging the showbread.
The Mishnah concludes that these actions do not incur liability for priesthood, impurity, lack of priestly garments, or unwashed hands and feet.

items.text: Mishnah: Historical periods of bamot and their rules
items.text_en: Mishnah: Historical periods of bamot and their rules
items.desc_en: The Mishnah outlines the history of bamot (high places) from before the Tabernacle was established until the arrival in Jerusalem. It describes when bamot were permitted or prohibited, and where different categories of sacrifices were eaten during each period: Gilgal, Shiloh, Nov and Gibeon, and finally Jerusalem.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by describing the first period: before the Tabernacle was established, bamot were permitted and service was by firstborns; after the Tabernacle was erected, bamot were forbidden and service was by priests, with קדשי קדשים eaten inside the curtains and קלים anywhere in the camp; then at Gilgal, bamot were permitted again, with קדשי קדשים inside the curtains and קלים everywhere.

The Mishnah continues with the period of Shiloh: bamot were forbidden, the structure was a stone house with curtains above, called 'מנוחה' (rest), and קדשי קדשים were eaten inside the curtains while קלים and מעשר שני were eaten anywhere within sight.
The Mishnah describes the period of Nov and Gibeon: bamot were permitted, קדשי קדשים were eaten inside the curtains, and קלים were eaten in all cities of Israel.

The Mishnah concludes with the final period of Jerusalem: bamot were forbidden permanently, called 'נחלה' (inheritance), and קדשי קדשים were eaten inside the curtains while קלים and מעשר שני were eaten within the wall.

items.text: Mishnah: Liability for offering consecrated animals at the wrong time
items.text_en: Mishnah: Liability for offering consecrated animals at the wrong time
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses cases where animals were consecrated and offered during different periods of bamot permission. If both consecration and offering occur during a prohibited period outside, one is liable for karet. If consecrated during a permitted period but offered during a prohibited period, there is no karet. If consecrated during a prohibited period but offered during a permitted period, there is no negative commandment.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the first case: if both consecration and offering occur during a prohibited period of private altars (במות), one is liable for a positive commandment, a negative commandment, and karet.
The Mishnah states the second case: if consecrated during a permitted period but offered during a prohibited period, one is liable for a positive and negative commandment but exempt from karet.
The Mishnah states the third case: if consecrated during a prohibited period but offered during a permitted period, one is liable only for a positive commandment, with no negative commandment.

items.text: Mishnah: Sacrifices offered in the Tabernacle vs. bamah, and differences between individual and communal bamot
items.text_en: Mishnah: Sacrifices offered in the Tabernacle vs. bamah, and differences between individual and communal bamot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah specifies which sacrifices are offered in the Tabernacle: those consecrated for the Tabernacle, communal sacrifices, while individual sacrifices may be offered on a bamah. It then lists the differences between an individual's bamah and a communal bamah, beginning with semikhah and slaughtering in the north.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing which sacrifices are offered in the Tabernacle: those consecrated for the Tabernacle and communal sacrifices, while individual sacrifices are offered on a bamah; individual sacrifices consecrated for the Tabernacle must be offered there, and if offered on a bamah one is exempt.
The Mishnah asks what distinguishes an individual's bamah from a communal bamah, and begins listing the differences, starting with semikhah and slaughtering in the north.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Differences between bamah and Mishkan
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Differences between bamah and Mishkan
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items that apply to the Mishkan but not to a bamah, including the requirement of 'outside the gate' (חוץ מגיתה). It then states that the laws of time, leftover, and impurity are common to both.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items unique to the Mishkan versus a bamah, and states that the laws of time, leftover, and impurity are common to both.

items.text: Gemara's question and first answer: Defining 'outside the gate'
items.text_en: Gemara's question and first answer: Defining 'outside the gate'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'outside the gate' (חוץ מגיתה) means. Reish Lakish says it means outside a place that has been checked for graves. Rabbi Yochanan objects that all of Eretz Yisrael is checked, and instead explains it refers to slaughtering inside the wall of Jerusalem.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'outside the gate' (חוץ מגיתה) means in the Mishnah.
Reish Lakish explains that 'outside the gate' means outside a place that has been checked for graves.
Rabbi Yochanan objects that all of Eretz Yisrael is already checked for graves, so Reish Lakish's explanation is insufficient.
Rabbi Yochanan instead explains that 'outside the gate' refers to slaughtering inside the wall of Jerusalem.

items.text: Alternative answer: Slaughtering not opposite the entrance
items.text_en: Alternative answer: Slaughtering not opposite the entrance
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the case is slaughtering outside the wall but not opposite the entrance. It cites Rav Adda bar Ahavah's teaching that slaughtering not opposite the entrance is invalid, based on a hekesh to sprinkling. It then notes a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on this point.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah cites a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) that slaughter must be opposite the entrance, like the sprinkling.
Rav Adda bar Ahavah teaches that slaughtering not opposite the entrance is invalid, based on a hekesh (verbal analogy) to sprinkling.
The Gemara anticipates an objection that the hekesh might not apply, and counters by citing a dispute on the matter.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish's dispute
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish's dispute
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan holds slaughtering not opposite the entrance is invalid, citing the hekesh; Reish Lakish holds it is valid, citing the verse 'אֶל מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה וְשָׁחַט' (outside the camp he shall slaughter).

items.text: Dispute about burning not opposite the entrance
items.text_en: Dispute about burning not opposite the entrance
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a parallel dispute regarding burning the red heifer not opposite the entrance: Rabbi Yochanan says it is invalid, deriving from a hekesh to sprinkling; Rabbi Oshaya says it is valid, based on the verse 'על פרשה ישרוף' meaning it should be burned where it dies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara records a parallel dispute about burning the red heifer not opposite the entrance, with Rabbi Yochanan invalidating and Rabbi Oshaya validating.
Rabbi Yochanan derives the invalidity from a hekesh (verbal analogy) between burning and sprinkling, linking the verse 'וְשָׂרַף' to 'וְהִזָּה'.
Rabbi Oshaya derives validity from the verse 'עַל פִּרְשָׁהּ יִשְׂרֹף', interpreting that the red heifer should be burned where it dies, regardless of orientation to the entrance.

items.text: Clarification: The Mishnah's case is inside the wall
items.text_en: Clarification: The Mishnah's case is inside the wall
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's case is not about outside the wall, but even inside the wall, where one might think it is valid because it is closer, the Mishnah teaches it is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's case is not merely outside the wall, but even inside the wall, teaching that proximity does not validate.

items.text: Dispute about the Flood in Eretz Yisrael
items.text_en: Dispute about the Flood in Eretz Yisrael
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish: Rabbi Yochanan holds that the Flood did not descend on Eretz Yisrael, so it is 'checked'; Reish Lakish holds it did. Both derive their views from the verse 'ארץ לא מטוהרה היא לא גושמה ביום זעם'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: On what do Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish disagree regarding the Flood in Eretz Yisrael?
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that both derive their positions from the same verse: 'ארץ לא מטוהרה היא לא גושמה ביום זעם'.
The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Yochanan reads the verse rhetorically (the Flood did not descend on Eretz Yisrael), while Reish Lakish reads it literally (the Flood did descend).

items.text: Challenges and resolutions regarding graves in Jerusalem
items.text_en: Challenges and resolutions regarding graves in Jerusalem
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan with a baraita about courtyards built on hollow space to avoid grave of the deep. Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish with a story about bones found in the Chamber of the Wood, which Rabbi Yehoshua dismissed by asking where the dead of the Flood are. The Gemara resolves that the bones were removed.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan with a baraita describing courtyards in Jerusalem built on hollow space over a grave of the deep (קבר התהום), implying that the land was not entirely free of grave impurity.
The baraita details the elaborate procedure for drawing water for the red heifer, showing that the courtyards were built with hollow space to avoid any grave impurity.

sub.text: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's explanation
sub.text_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's explanation
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua explains that the stringency of using hollow space was a special מעלה (extra precaution) for the red heifer, not a general rule about Jerusalem's purity.

Rabbi Yochanan counters with a story about bones found in the Chamber of the Wood, where Rabbi Yehoshua dismissed the concern by rhetorically asking where the dead of the Flood and of Nebuchadnezzar are, implying that bones can be removed.

The Gemara resolves the challenge by arguing that just as the bones of Nebuchadnezzar's victims existed but were removed, so too the bones in the Chamber of the Wood existed but were removed, reconciling the baraita with Rabbi Yochanan's position.

items.text: Gemara's objection to Reish Lakish's position
items.text_en: Gemara's objection to Reish Lakish's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the flood did not reach the land of Israel, the people there would not have died, but the verse says all on dry land died. It distinguishes between those who died from the flood and those who died from the heat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even if the flood did not reach Jerusalem, it must have reached the rest of the land of Israel, otherwise the people there would not have died.

items.text: Alternative version: Reish Lakish's challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Alternative version: Reish Lakish's challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that Reish Lakish challenged Rabbi Yochanan from the verse about the deaths of the flood generation and Nebuchadnezzar's men, implying they all died in the same way.

sub.text: Reish Lakish's question to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish's question to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan: if the flood did not reach Israel, where did the people of Israel die? Does the verse not imply they were among the flood victims?
The Gemara resolves that each case is distinct: the flood victims died by water, the people of Israel died by the heat.

items.text: Proof from the verse 'from all on dry land they died'
items.text_en: Proof from the verse 'from all on dry land they died'
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish cites the verse that all on dry land died, arguing that if the flood did not reach Israel, why did they die? He answers that they died from the heat, as per Rav Chisda's teaching that they sinned with heat and were punished with heat.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish cites the verse that all on dry land died, challenging Rabbi Yochanan: if the flood did not reach Israel, why did those in Israel die?
Reish Lakish answers that they died from the heat, citing Rav Chisda's teaching that they sinned with heat and were punished with heat.

items.text: Alternative version: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge to Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Alternative version: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge to Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: In another version, Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish from the same verse, arguing that if the flood did reach Israel, why does the verse say 'dry land'? He explains that it refers to land that was originally dry, and cites Rav Chisda that fish were not punished.

sub.desc_en: In an alternative version, Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish from the verse 'מכל אשר בחרבה מתו' (from all that was on dry land they died), arguing that if the flood reached Israel, why does the verse say 'dry land'? He explains it refers to land that was originally dry.

The gemara supports Rabbi Yochanan's explanation by citing Rav Chisda that in the generation of the flood, no decree was issued against fish in the sea, as the verse says 'מכל אשר בחרבה מתו' (from all that was on dry land they died) — not fish in the sea.

items.text: The re'em (unicorn) and the flood
items.text_en: The re'em (unicorn) and the flood
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses how the re'em survived the flood if it was too large for the ark. Rabbi Yannai says they brought only its young, but Rabbi Yochanan says they brought its head, and Reish Lakish says they tied its horns to the ark. The Gemara resolves the contradiction about the hot water by saying a miracle occurred that the water cooled around the ark.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the view that the flood did not reach the land of Israel, the re'em could have stood there, but according to the view that it did, where did the re'em stand?
Rabbi Yannai answers that they brought only its young into the ark.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from Rabba bar bar Chana
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from Rabba bar bar Chana
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabba bar bar Chana saw a one-day-old re'em calf as large as Mount Tabor, so even its young would be too large for the ark.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that they brought only its head into the ark, and when challenged about the size, he clarifies they brought only the tip of its nose.

sub.text: Gemara's clarification about Rabbi Yochanan's view
sub.text_en: Gemara's clarification about Rabbi Yochanan's view
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan himself holds the flood did not reach Israel, so his answer was only according to Reish Lakish's view.
Reish Lakish answers that they tied the re'em's horns to the ark.
The Gemara objects that Rav Chisda said the flood waters were boiling hot, so the re'em would have been scalded.
The Gemara resolves that a miracle occurred: the water cooled around the sides of the ark, protecting the re'em.

items.text: The names 'Metzulah' and 'Shinar'
items.text_en: The names 'Metzulah' and 'Shinar'
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan explain the names of places where the flood victims ended up, and Rabbi Abahu explains that Shinar shakes out its wealthy, but the Gemara notes that wealth did not last three generations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that even according to Reish Lakish, who holds the flood came to Israel, the dead were concentrated in the place called Metzulah, which he explains as the place where all flood victims were 'drowned' (נִצְטַלְּלוּ).
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the name 'Shinar' (שִׁנְעָר) indicates that all flood victims were 'shaken out' (נִנְעֲרוּ) there.
The Gemara objects that it is impossible that some of the dead did not stick to the land, implying that the names Metzulah and Shinar are not fully consistent.
Rabbi Abahu explains that the name 'Shinar' means it 'shakes out' (מְנַעֶרֶת) its wealthy inhabitants, referring to the loss of wealth.
The Gemara objects that we see wealthy people still exist in Shinar, contradicting the claim that it shakes out its wealthy.
The Gemara resolves that the wealth does not last for three generations, so the shaking out is a delayed effect.

items.text: Eating the dust of Babylon
items.text_en: Eating the dust of Babylon
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami says that eating the dust of Babylon is like eating the flesh of one's ancestors, and a baraisa supports this, with some saying it is like eating vermin.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami says that eating the dust of Babylon is like eating the flesh of one's ancestors, and a baraita supports this, with an alternative opinion comparing it to eating vermin.
A baraisa is cited that supports Rabbi Ami's statement verbatim.
Some say alternatively that eating the dust of Babylon is like eating vermin and creeping things.

items.text: The scapegoat and other excluded offerings
items.text_en: The scapegoat and other excluded offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the scapegoat (שעיר המשתלח) and other offerings that are excluded from the requirement to bring to the Tent of Meeting, resolving contradictions about the timing of the exclusion relative to the lottery and confession.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the scapegoat (שעיר המשתלח) as an offering excluded from the requirement to bring to the Tent of Meeting.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: the verse 'קרבן' might include even consecrated property for Temple maintenance (קדשי בדק הבית), which are called 'קרבן' in the verse.
The baraita resolves: the verse 'ואל פתח אהל מועד לא הביאו' limits the exclusion to offerings fit for the Tent of Meeting, excluding קדשי בדק הבית which are unfit.

The Gemara objects: if the criterion is fitness for the Tent of Meeting, the scapegoat (שעיר המשתלח) is fit and should be included; the baraita counters with the verse 'לה׳' to exclude the scapegoat, which is not exclusively dedicated to God.
The Gemara initially resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between before and after the lottery (הגרלה), but then objects that after the lottery there is still the confession (וידוי).
Rav Mani resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between before and after the confession (וידוי).
The Mishnah lists the animal that mounts and the animal that is mounted (הרובע והנרבע) as excluded offerings.
The Gemara questions why these animals need separate mention, as they could be derived from the general exclusion of 'פתח אהל מועד'.

items.text: Initial question about rove'a and nirba
items.text_en: Initial question about rove'a and nirba
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by noting that rove'a (an animal that copulated with a human) and nirba (an animal that was copulated with) can be consecrated before the transgression, so they are valid for the altar if consecrated earlier.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that rove'a (an animal that copulated with a human) and nirba (an animal that was copulated with) can be consecrated before the transgression, so they are valid for the altar if consecrated earlier.

items.text: Problem with mukshe and ne'evad and solution via Rabbi Yossi HaGlili
items.text_en: Problem with mukshe and ne'evad and solution via Rabbi Yossi HaGlili
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: mukshe (an animal worshipped) and ne'evad (an animal used for worship) cannot be forbidden by a person if they are not his property. The solution is that these apply to קדשים קלים (lesser sanctities) according to Rabbi Yossi HaGlili, who holds that such animals are the owner's property. A baraita supports this view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: mukshe (an animal worshipped) and ne'evad (an animal used for worship) cannot be forbidden by a person if they are not his property.
The Gemara answers that the case involves קדשים קלים (lesser sanctities) according to Rabbi Yossi HaGlili, who holds that such animals are the owner's property.
A baraita is cited, deriving from the verse 'וּמָעֲלָה מַעַל בַּה׳' that קדשים קלים are the owner's property, according to Rabbi Yossi HaGlili.

The Gemara concludes: rove'a and nirva (bestiality cases) are forbidden due to the prohibition of ערוה (illicit relations), while mukshe and ne'evad are forbidden due to עבודה זרה (idolatry), specifically in the context of קדשים קלים.

items.text: Etnan, mechir, kil'ayim, yotze dofen apply to offspring of consecrated animals
items.text_en: Etnan, mechir, kil'ayim, yotze dofen apply to offspring of consecrated animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that etnan (hire of a harlot), mechir (price of a dog), kil'ayim (diverse kinds), and yotze dofen (an animal born by caesarean section) are invalid when they are offspring of consecrated animals, because such offspring are sanctified from their moment of formation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that etnan (hire of a harlot), mechir (price of a dog), kil'ayim (diverse kinds), and yotze dofen (an animal born by caesarean section) are invalid when they are offspring of consecrated animals, because such offspring are sanctified from their moment of formation.

items.text: Need for multiple cases: ba'alei mumim, torin, and oto v'et b'no
items.text_en: Need for multiple cases: ba'alei mumim, torin, and oto v'et b'no
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah lists ba'alei mumim (blemished animals), torin (doves), and oto v'et b'no (the animal and its offspring) separately: each case teaches a unique point about Rabbi Shimon's opinion that they are not offered, and the repetition is necessary to avoid assuming agreement in other cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's list of ba'alei mumim (blemished animals), torin (doves), and oto v'et b'no (the animal and its offspring) as the subject of analysis.

The Gemara asks why the Mishnah lists all three cases, explaining that if only ba'alei mumim were listed, one might think the Rabbis only disagree there because the animals are repulsive, but would agree with Rabbi Shimon regarding torin (doves) which are not repulsive.

The Gemara explains that if only torin were listed, one might think Rabbi Shimon only disagrees there because they were never fit and then rejected, but would agree with the Rabbis regarding ba'alei mumim which were fit and then rejected.

The Gemara concludes that all three cases are necessary: even if ba'alei mumim and torin were listed, one might think the Rabbis agree with Rabbi Shimon regarding oto v'et b'no because its disqualification comes from an external source, so the Mishnah lists all three to preclude that assumption.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's scriptural derivation from Deuteronomy
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's scriptural derivation from Deuteronomy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon explains his reasoning: Moses told Israel that when they enter the land, they may only offer voluntary offerings (ישרות), not obligatory ones (חובות). This is derived from the verse 'לֹא תַעֲשׂוּן כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר אֲנַחְנוּ עוֹשִׂים פֹּה הַיּוֹם', even though Gilgal was a time of missing the Tabernacle (מחוסר זמן).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is Rabbi Shimon's reasoning for his position?

Rabbi Ila'a in the name of Reish Lakish explains that Moses told Israel: when you enter the land, you may only offer voluntary offerings (ישרות), not obligatory ones (חובות), derived from the verse 'לֹא תַעֲשׂוּן כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר אֲנַחְנוּ עוֹשִׂים פֹּה הַיּוֹם'.
The Gemara notes that Gilgal, compared to Shiloh, was a time of missing the Tabernacle (מחוסר זמן), yet Moses still commanded 'לֹא תַעֲשׂוּן' (do not do), supporting Rabbi Shimon's derivation.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira: if that is the case (that the prohibition applies even at Gilgal), then what follows? The daf ends with this question, implying further discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira: if so, what follows?

items.text: Gemara's question on lashes and Rabbi Zeira's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's question on lashes and Rabbi Zeira's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why one should not also receive lashes for violating the positive commandment, citing Rabbi Zeira's principle that the text transformed it into a positive commandment. It then notes that this applies only to the Rabbis, but for Rabbi Shimon it is different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why one should not also receive lashes, citing Rabbi Zeira's principle that the text transformed the prohibition into a positive commandment.
The Gemara answers that this applies only to the Rabbis, but for Rabbi Shimon it is different.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explanation of Gilgal's status
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explanation of Gilgal's status
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the interior of Gilgal relative to Shiloh is considered like the exterior, providing a geographical distinction.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that the interior of Gilgal relative to Shiloh is considered like the exterior, resolving the geographical distinction.

items.text: Rabba's explanation of Rabbi Shimon's reasoning and the debate on Pesach
items.text_en: Rabba's explanation of Rabbi Shimon's reasoning and the debate on Pesach
items.desc_en: Rabba cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon derives from the verse 'You may not sacrifice the Pesach' that one who offers a Pesach on a private bamah during the prohibition of bamot violates a negative commandment. The Gemara questions whether this applies after midday (when one would be liable for karet) or before, and concludes it refers to after midday during a time when bamot are permitted, with the prohibition being specific to that person while others are permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rabba introduces a baraita where Rabbi Shimon derives from the verse 'You may not sacrifice the Pesach' that one who offers a Pesach on a private bamah during the prohibition of bamot violates a negative commandment.
The baraita clarifies that the prohibition applies only when all Israel enters through one gate (i.e., the central sanctuary), not during a time when private bamot are permitted.
The Gemara questions the timing: if after midday, one would also be liable for karet, so it must be before midday.
The Gemara answers that it is indeed after midday, but during a time when private bamot are permitted, so karet does not apply.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the prohibition is specific to that person (who is forbidden to offer on a private bamah) while others are permitted.

items.text: Question about the Mishnah's list and Ze'iri's addition of a metzora
items.text_en: Question about the Mishnah's list and Ze'iri's addition of a metzora
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists 'those liable for ashamot' when they are not valid on a bamah, and Ze'iri answers that one should teach 'a metzora' together with them, implying the list includes those whose offerings are brought on a bamah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists 'those liable for ashamot' (guilt offerings) when such offerings are not valid on a private bamah.
Ze'iri answers that one should teach 'a metzora' (leper) together with them, implying the list includes those whose offerings are brought on a bamah.

items.text: Question about 'their olot and shelamim' and Rav Sheshet's addition of a nazirite
items.text_en: Question about 'their olot and shelamim' and Rav Sheshet's addition of a nazirite
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah mentions 'their olot and shelamim' when these are peace offerings, and Rav Sheshet answers that one should teach 'a nazirite' instead. It notes that Ze'iri's addition was established by the Tannaim, but Rav Sheshet's was not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah mentions 'their olot and shelamim' when these are peace offerings, which are not brought by a nazirite.
Rav Sheshet answers that one should teach 'a nazirite' instead of 'their olot and shelamim' in the Mishnah.
The Gemara notes that Ze'iri's addition was established by the Tannaim, but Rav Sheshet's was not, explaining why the Mishnah retains Ze'iri's version.

items.text: Rabbi Chilkiyah's distinction and Rav Huna's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Chilkiyah's distinction and Rav Huna's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chilkiyah bar Rav Tovi says the Mishnah's exemption applies only when the offering is for its own sake, but if not for its own sake, one is liable because it is fit for that purpose inside. The Gemara objects that if so, even for its own sake one should be liable since it is fit for not for its own sake inside, but the Gemara answers that it requires an act of designation. Rav Huna then strongly objects: is there anything that is not valid for its own sake but valid not for its own sake?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chilkiyah bar Rav Tovi distinguishes the Mishnah's exemption: it applies only when the offering is slaughtered for its own sake (לשמו), but if slaughtered not for its own sake (שלא לשמו), one is liable because the offering is fit for that purpose inside the Tabernacle.
The Gemara objects: if the criterion is fitness for that purpose inside, then even slaughter for its own sake should also be liable, since it is fit for not-for-its-own-sake inside.
The Gemara answers that slaughter for its own sake requires an act of designation (עקירה) to redirect the offering, so it is not automatically fit for not-for-its-own-sake.
Rav Huna strongly objects: is there any case where an offering is not valid for its own sake (לשמו) but is valid not for its own sake (שלא לשמו)?

items.text: Gemara's initial challenge to Rav Huna
items.text_en: Gemara's initial challenge to Rav Huna
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Huna's view by citing the case of a Pesach sacrifice offered during the rest of the year, which is invalid for its own sake but valid not for its own sake, implying a similar rule for asham.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Huna's position by citing the case of a Pesach sacrifice offered during the rest of the year, which is a sheep of the flock that is invalid for its own sake but valid not for its own sake.

items.text: First baraita and its analysis
items.text_en: First baraita and its analysis
items.desc_en: A baraita excludes asham from the rule of mechusar zeman, but the Gemara analyzes whether it refers to lishmo or shelo lishmo, concluding it follows Rabbi Eliezer who compares asham to chatat, and the baraita mentions the secondary case while the primary is implied.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that a baraita supports the position by asking whether one might exclude a mechusar zeman olah and asham nazir and asham metzora.
The baraita cites the verse 'שׁוֹר' 'כֶּשֶׂב' 'עֵז' to include all cases, but excludes chatat, implying asham is included.
The Gemara asks what case the baraita discusses, concluding it must be shelo lizman (not in its proper time), because if it were in its proper time, chatat would also be excluded.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita deals with lishmo or shelo lishmo, and concludes it must be shelo lishmo, but then suggests it could be in its proper time and shelo lishmo.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer, who compares asham to chatat via a verbal analogy.
The Gemara explains that the baraita mentions the secondary case (asham) while the primary case (chatat) is implied by the same rule.

items.text: Second baraita and its analysis
items.text_en: Second baraita and its analysis
items.desc_en: Another baraita excludes asham from liability for mechusar zeman, and the Gemara again determines it deals with shelo lishmo and follows Rabbi Eliezer, this time stating the primary case and all the more so the secondary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that excludes asham from liability for being offered while מחוסר זמן (lacking proper time), stating the rule includes olah and chatat but leaves out asham.
The Gemara asks what case the baraita addresses — if offered לִשְׁמוֹ (for its own sake), asham would also be exempt; therefore it must involve shelo lishmo (not for its own sake).

The Gemara establishes that the baraita deals with shelo lishmo and follows Rabbi Eliezer, who equates asham and chatat; the Tanna taught the primary case (עיקר) and all the more so the secondary (טפל).

items.text: Third baraita and resolution of contradictions
items.text_en: Third baraita and resolution of contradictions
items.desc_en: A baraita from the school of Rabbi Levi excludes asham nazir and asham metzora, but Rav Dimi and Rav Ashi resolve contradictions between this baraita and Levi's teaching by distinguishing between lishmo and shelo lishmo.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita from the school of Rabbi Levi that excludes asham nazir and asham metzora from liability, but notes that the derivation is unknown.
Ravina explains that the derivation is from the verses 'שור' (ox), 'כשב' (sheep), and 'עז' (goat), which include all cases, and the Gemara notes that this is the same as the earlier question.

Rav Nachman points out a contradiction between the baraita of Rabbi Levi's school and Levi's own teaching, which states that asham nazir and asham metzora slaughtered שלא לשמו (not for their own sake) are valid but do not fulfill the owners' obligation.
Levi's teaching adds that if these offerings are slaughtered when they are מחוסר זמן (lacking time) in their owners or are two years old, they are invalid.
Rav Dimi resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the case where the offering is slaughtered לשמו (for its own sake) and where it is slaughtered שלא לשמו (not for its own sake).
Rav Ashi similarly resolves a contradiction between a Mishnah and a baraita by distinguishing between לשמו (for its own sake) and שלא לשמו (not for its own sake).

items.text: Conclusion: defense of Rav Huna
items.text_en: Conclusion: defense of Rav Huna
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests this is a refutation of Rav Huna, but Rav Huna responds that the case involves setting aside two ashamot for surety, where one is actually an olah from the outset.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether this constitutes a refutation of Rav Huna's position.
Rav Huna responds that the case involves setting aside two ashamot for surety, where one is actually an olah from the outset.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on a guilt-offering designated for pasture
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on a guilt-offering designated for pasture
items.desc_en: Rav Huna cites Rav that if a guilt-offering was set aside for pasture (because the owner was already atoned) and then slaughtered without specifying its purpose, it is valid as a burnt-offering. This introduces the principle that certain animals can be repurposed for a different sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna cites Rav that a guilt-offering designated for pasture and slaughtered without specification is valid as a burnt-offering.

items.text: Tannaitic derivation of exemption for certain offerings and actions
items.text_en: Tannaitic derivation of exemption for certain offerings and actions
items.desc_en: The Tannaim derive from the verse 'עוֹלָה' that only items fit for the altar are subject to the prohibition of offering outside. They then extend this to actions that are not the completion of the service, such as pouring, mixing, and salting, based on the phrase 'אֲשֶׁר יַעֲלֶה עוֹלָה אוֹ זָבַח'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by listing various offerings (e.g., sin-offering flesh, guilt-offering flesh, etc.) and asks: from where is it derived that one who offers them outside is exempt?
The baraita answers: the verse says 'עוֹלָה' (burnt-offering) — just as a burnt-offering is fit for the altar, so only items fit for the altar are subject to the prohibition.
The baraita asks: from where is it derived that one who performs preparatory actions (pouring, mixing, salting, etc.) outside is exempt?

The baraita answers: the verse says 'אֲשֶׁר יַעֲלֶה עוֹלָה אוֹ זָבַח' — just as offering up is the completion of the service, so only actions that are the completion of the service are subject to the prohibition.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Ketina's reading and Rabbi Asi's comment
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Ketina's reading and Rabbi Asi's comment
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Ketina reads the verse about the young men of Israel, and Rabbi Asi comments that they brought offerings and then ceased. This sets up a discussion about the period before the Tabernacle was erected.

sub.text: Narrative: Rav Huna bar Rav Kattina before Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Narrative: Rav Huna bar Rav Kattina before Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Kattina sits before Rav Chisda and reads a verse; Rav Chisda cites Rabbi Assi that the young men brought offerings and ceased.
Rabbi Asi comments that the young men brought offerings and then ceased, indicating a limited period of sacrificial activity before the Tabernacle was erected.

items.text: Baraita on offerings before the Tabernacle and the dispute about flaying and cutting
items.text_en: Baraita on offerings before the Tabernacle and the dispute about flaying and cutting
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to challenge a statement from the baraita but is answered by Rav Adda bar Ahavah that the burnt-offering in the wilderness did not require flaying and cutting. The baraita itself lists the rules for the period before the Tabernacle: altars were permitted, firstborns served, and all animals were fit for offering, but the burnt-offering did require flaying and cutting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially sought to challenge a statement from the Mishnah, but then heard Rav Adda bar Ahavah's teaching.
Rav Adda bar Ahavah states that the burnt-offering brought by Israel in the wilderness did not require flaying and cutting, and the Gemara then cites a baraita that agrees with all points.

The baraita lists the rules before the Tabernacle was established: altars were permitted, service by firstborns, all animals fit for offering, and the burnt-offering required flaying and cutting; gentiles today are permitted to do likewise.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha and Rabbi on the verse 'וְגַם הַכֹּהֲנִים'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha and Rabbi on the verse 'וְגַם הַכֹּהֲנִים'
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha interprets the verse as referring to the separation of the firstborns, while Rabbi interprets it as referring to the separation of Nadav and Avihu. The Gemara explains the scriptural basis for each view and then recounts a narrative about Aaron's silence and the lesson of accepting divine judgment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Tannaic dispute regarding the interpretation of the verse 'וְגַם הַכֹּהֲנִים הַנִּגָּשִׁים אֶל ה׳ יִתְקַדָּשׁוּ', with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha and Rabbi offering different explanations.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi's interpretation (separation of Nadav and Avihu) is supported by the verse 'הוּא אֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר ה׳ לֵאמֹר בִּקְרֹבַי אֶקָּדֵשׁ'.

sub.text: Gemara's question for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's view
sub.text_en: Gemara's question for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's view
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's interpretation (separation of firstborns) is hinted in the verse.
The Gemara answers that the hint is in the verse 'וְנֹעַדְתִּי שָׁמָּה לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְנִקְדַּשׁ בִּכְבֹדִי', read as 'בִּכְבוּדַי' (my honored ones), referring to the firstborns.
The Gemara recounts that God told Moses about the sanctification through the death of Aaron's sons, and when Aaron understood they were honored, he was silent and received reward.

sub.text: Supporting verses from David and Solomon
sub.text_en: Supporting verses from David and Solomon
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses from David ('דּוֹם לַה׳ וְהִתְחוֹלֵל לוֹ') and Solomon ('עֵת לַחֲשׁוֹת וְעֵת לְדַבֵּר') to reinforce the lesson of silent acceptance of divine judgment.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan explains the verse 'נוֹרָא אֱלֹהִים מִמִּקְדָּשֶׁךָ' as referring to God being feared and exalted when He executes judgment on His holy ones.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction regarding the burnt-offering and the source for all animals being fit
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction regarding the burnt-offering and the source for all animals being fit
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction about the burnt-offering by attributing the views to different Tannaim: Rabbi Yishmael says general principles were given at Sinai and details in the Tent of Meeting, while Rabbi Akiva says both were given at Sinai and repeated elsewhere. Finally, Rav Huna derives from Noah's altar that all clean animals, including wild beasts, are fit for sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction regarding the burnt-offering (עולה) from the earlier baraita.
The Gemara resolves that the contradiction stems from a dispute between Tannaim.
Rabbi Yishmael states that general principles were given at Sinai and details in the Tent of Meeting.
Rabbi Akiva holds that both general principles and details were given at Sinai, repeated in the Tent of Meeting, and restated in the plains of Moab.
The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that all animals are fit for sacrifice?
Rav Huna derives from Noah's altar that all clean animals, including wild beasts (חיה), are included in the category of בהמה (domesticated animals) for sacrifice.

items.text: Opening statement on valid animals for Noahide offerings
items.text_en: Opening statement on valid animals for Noahide offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both males and females, and both unblemished and blemished animals are valid for Noahide offerings, based on the comparison of animals to birds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that both males and females, and both unblemished and blemished animals are valid for Noahide offerings, citing Mar's teaching that the requirement of תמות וזכרות (unblemished and male) applies only to animals, not birds, and that animals are compared to birds.

items.text: Exclusion of missing limbs and the source for Noahides
items.text_en: Exclusion of missing limbs and the source for Noahides
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar derives from the verse 'וּמִכׇּל הָחַי מִכׇּל בָּשָׂר' that an animal missing a limb is forbidden for Noahides. The Gemara questions whether this excludes a tereifah, and resolves that a tereifah is derived from 'לְחַיּוֹת זֶרַע'. It further discusses the possibility that Noah himself was a tereifah and concludes that the verse 'אִתָּךְ' indicates animals similar to Noah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah's phrase 'תְּמִימִין וּבַעֲלֵי מוּמִין' (unblemished and blemished) excludes a missing limb (מחוסר אבר), which is forbidden for Noahides.
Rabbi Elazar derives from the verse 'וּמִכׇּל הָחַי מִכׇּל בָּשָׂר' (from every living thing, from all flesh) that an animal whose limbs are alive (i.e., not missing) is required for Noahides.

The Gemara questions whether the verse excludes a טריפה (animal with a fatal condition) instead of a missing limb, and answers that a טריפה is derived from the verse 'לְחַיּוֹת זֶרַע' (to bring forth seed).
The Gemara objects that the derivation from 'לְחַיּוֹת זֶרַע' works only for the opinion that a טריפה cannot give birth, but for the opinion that it can give birth, what can be said?
The Gemara answers that the verse 'אִתָּךְ' (with you) teaches that only animals similar to Noah (i.e., whole and healthy) are permitted.
The Gemara questions whether Noah himself might have been a טריפה, and answers that the verse calls him 'תָּמִים' (whole) and 'צַדִּיק' (righteous).

The Gemara objects that 'תָּמִים' might refer to his ways and 'צַדִּיק' to his deeds, not his physical state, and answers that if Noah were a טריפה, God would not have told him to bring only animals like himself.

The Gemara questions why the verse 'לְחַיּוֹת זֶרַע' is needed if the exclusion of a טריפה is already derived from 'אִתָּךְ', and answers that 'אִתָּךְ' might only exclude the old and sterile, so 'לְחַיּוֹת זֶרַע' teaches that a טריפה is also excluded.

items.text: Identification of pure animals for the ark
items.text_en: Identification of pure animals for the ark
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains how Noah knew which animals were pure (fit for sacrifice) and which were impure. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan says they were those that had not sinned. Rav Chisda says they were identified by whether the ark accepted them. Rabbi Avahu derives from the verse 'וְהַבָּאִים זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה' that they came of their own accord.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Noah could distinguish pure from impure animals before the Torah was given.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan answers that the pure animals were those that had not sinned (i.e., had not engaged in bestiality).
The Gemara asks how Noah could know which animals had sinned.
Rav Chisda answers that Noah passed the animals before the ark; those the ark accepted were pure, and those it rejected were impure.
Rabbi Avahu derives from the verse 'וְהַבָּאִים זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה' that the animals came of their own accord, implying the ark's acceptance was a sign.

items.text: Debate on whether Noahides offered peace-offerings
items.text_en: Debate on whether Noahides offered peace-offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially states that all offered burnt-offerings, but a verse mentions peace-offerings. It then presents a dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina: one says Noahides offered peace-offerings, the other says they did not. Each brings a prooftext, and the Gemara reconciles the verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that according to the earlier statement, all Noahides offered burnt-offerings (עולות) but not peace-offerings (שלמים).
The Gemara questions this, citing the verse that says Noah offered peace-offerings (שלמים) after the flood.
The Gemara revises the statement to say that all offered both burnt-offerings and peace-offerings.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that explicitly says Noahides offered only burnt-offerings, not peace-offerings.
The Gemara identifies the baraita as following the opinion that Noahides did not offer peace-offerings, and introduces a dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina.
The Gemara states the two positions: one says Noahides offered peace-offerings, the other says they did not.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar's or Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's proof (first opinion)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's or Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's proof (first opinion)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the proof for the opinion that Noahides offered peace-offerings: from the verse about Hevel's offering, which describes a sacrifice whose fat is offered but not the whole animal, which is characteristic of peace-offerings.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar's or Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's proof (second opinion)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's or Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's proof (second opinion)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the proof for the opinion that Noahides did not offer peace-offerings: from the verse 'עורי צפון ובואי תימן' (Awake, north wind, and come, south wind), which refers to the nation whose deeds are in the north (Israel) and the nation whose deeds are in both north and south (Noahides).
The Gemara rejects the first proof by reinterpreting 'ומחלביהן' (from their fat) as referring to the choicest parts of the animals, not specifically to peace-offerings.
The Gemara rejects the second proof by stating that the verse 'עורי צפון' refers to the ingathering of the exiles, not to Noahide offerings.

items.text: Proof from Moses and Jethro regarding peace-offerings
items.text_en: Proof from Moses and Jethro regarding peace-offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings verses from Moses and Jethro to argue that Noahides offered peace-offerings. It distinguishes between before and after the giving of the Torah. A dispute between the sons of Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi about when Jethro arrived is cited, with the opinion that if Jethro came before the Torah, it proves Noahides offered peace-offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the claim that Noahides only offered עולות (burnt-offerings) by citing the verse where Moses mentions both זבחים (slaughtered offerings) and עולות, and resolves that זבחים here refers to eating, not sacrificing.
The Gemara further questions by citing Jethro's offering of both עולה and זבחים, and answers that this occurred after the giving of the Torah, not before.

The Gemara objects that this resolution works only for the opinion that Jethro arrived after the Torah, but for the opinion that he arrived before, it proves that Noahides offered שלמים (peace-offerings).

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on what Jethro heard
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on what Jethro heard
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a baraita with three opinions on what Jethro heard that led him to convert: Rabbi Yehoshua says the war with Amalek, Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i says the giving of the Torah, and Rabbi Eliezer says the splitting of the Red Sea. The section ends with a question about the difference in phrasing between two verses.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the dispute over what Jethro heard that led him to convert.
Rabbi Yehoshua says Jethro heard about the war with Amalek, citing the adjacent verse.
Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i says Jethro heard about the giving of the Torah, which caused the nations to tremble.

sub.text: Narrative of Bilaam and the kings
sub.text_en: Narrative of Bilaam and the kings
sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts how the kings consulted Bilaam about the noise, and he explained it was the Torah being given to Israel.
Rabbi Eliezer says Jethro heard about the splitting of the Red Sea, citing the reaction of the Canaanite kings and Rahab.
The Gemara asks why the verse about the Canaanite kings uses different phrasing than the verse about Rahab.

items.text: Rahab's background and conversion
items.text_en: Rahab's background and conversion
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains how Rahab knew that the Egyptians were impotent, citing that every prince had relations with her. It then recounts her age at the Exodus and her conversion after 50 years, saying 'May I be forgiven for the sake of the rope, the window, and the flax.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that even impotence did not occur among the Egyptians, and explains that Rahab knew this because every prince had relations with her.

The Gemara recounts that Rahab was ten at the Exodus, prostituted herself for forty years in the wilderness, and converted after fifty years, saying 'May I be forgiven for the sake of the rope, the window, and the flax.'

items.text: Gentiles and bamot: permission and assistance
items.text_en: Gentiles and bamot: permission and assistance
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'Speak to the children of Israel' that only Israelites are commanded regarding slaughter outside the Temple, but gentiles are not. Therefore, each gentile may build a private altar and offer whatever they wish. Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha in the name of Rav Asi prohibits assisting them, but Rabbah permits teaching them. The story of Ifra Hormiz, mother of King Shapur, who sent a korban to Rava, illustrates how to offer it properly.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that gentiles are currently permitted to offer sacrifices on private altars, and the Gemara derives this from the verse 'Speak to the children of Israel,' which excludes gentiles from the prohibition of slaughter outside the Temple.
The Gemara concludes that each gentile may build a private altar and offer whatever they wish.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha in the name of Rav Asi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha in the name of Rav Asi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha in the name of Rav Asi prohibits assisting gentiles or acting as their agents in offering sacrifices.
Rabbah permits teaching gentiles how to offer sacrifices properly, distinguishing instruction from active assistance.

sub.text: Story of Ifra Hormiz and Rava
sub.text_en: Story of Ifra Hormiz and Rava
sub.desc_en: The story of Ifra Hormiz, mother of King Shapur, who sent a korban to Rava, illustrates how Rava instructed Rav Safra and Rav Acha bar Huna to offer it using new wood and fire from a new stone, all for the sake of Heaven.

items.text: Abaye's question: Rava's ruling follows Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua
items.text_en: Abaye's question: Rava's ruling follows Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua
items.desc_en: Abaye questions Rava's ruling, suggesting it aligns with Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua, who requires new wood for the altar. However, Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua concedes regarding a bamah (private altar).

sub.desc_en: Abaye questions Rava's ruling, suggesting it aligns with Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua, who requires new wood for the altar.
Abaye objects that Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua concedes regarding a bamah (private altar), so Rava's ruling cannot be based on him.

items.text: David's purchase of the threshing floor: resolving the contradiction
items.text_en: David's purchase of the threshing floor: resolving the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses the apparent contradiction between two verses: one says David paid 600 shekels of gold, the other says 50 shekels of silver. Various resolutions are offered: the 50 was collected from each tribe (totaling 600), or the 50 was for the cattle and wood while 600 was for the entire site. Rava explains that the wood was new, as per the earlier story. The discussion includes the meaning of 'morigim' (threshing sledges).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that presents a contradiction between two verses about David's payment for the threshing floor.
The anonymous first resolution explains that the 50 shekels were collected from each tribe, totaling 600 shekels.

sub.text: Rabbi's answer in the name of Abba Yosei ben Dostai
sub.text_en: Rabbi's answer in the name of Abba Yosei ben Dostai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi, citing Abba Yosei ben Dostai, resolves the contradiction by saying the 50 shekels were for the cattle, wood, and altar site, while the 600 were for the entire Temple site.
Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua offers the same resolution as Rabbi, citing the verse where Araunah offers the threshing sledges (מוֹרִיגִּים) for wood.
Rava adds that the wood mentioned was new, consistent with the earlier story about using new wood for the altar.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the word 'מוֹרִיגִּים' (threshing sledges).
Ulla explains that 'מוֹרִיגִּים' means a 'מִטָּה שֶׁל טוּרְבֵּל' (a bed of turbel, a type of sledge).
Abaye clarifies that 'מִטָּה שֶׁל טוּרְבֵּל' is a 'עִיזָּא דְּקֻרְקְסָא' (a goat-like sledge with teeth), citing a verse from Isaiah.
Rava teaches his son by raising the same contradiction and giving the same resolution of collecting 50 from each tribe.
The Gemara objects that the contradiction remains because one verse mentions silver and the other gold.
The Gemara resolves the objection by explaining that the 50 shekels of silver were collected from each tribe, totaling the weight of 600 shekels of gold.

items.text: Kodashim kalim: eaten in all places of the camp of Israel
items.text_en: Kodashim kalim: eaten in all places of the camp of Israel
items.desc_en: Rav Huna explains that קדשים קלים are eaten in all places of Israel, but not in the actual camp. Rav Nachman objects, citing that there were camps in the desert corresponding to Jerusalem. The Gemara clarifies that the phrase means 'in every place of the camp of Israel,' and this teaches that they are not invalidated by being taken outside the camp, as the verse 'And the Tent of Meeting journeyed' indicates its sanctity even when moving.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that קדשים קלים (lesser holy offerings) are eaten in all places of the camp of Israel.
Rav Huna explains that the phrase means 'in all places of Israel,' but not in the actual camp.
Rav Nachman objects by citing a baraita that there were camps in the desert corresponding to Jerusalem, implying that 'camp of Israel' is a defined place.
The Gemara resolves the objection by reinterpreting the Mishnah to mean 'in every place of the camp of Israel,' teaching that the offerings are not invalidated by being taken outside the camp.
The Gemara cites the verse 'וְנָסַע אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד' (And the Tent of Meeting journeyed) to prove that the sanctity of the camp remains even when it moves.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: an additional camp and the camps of Shiloh
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: an additional camp and the camps of Shiloh
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai states there was an additional camp (the חיל or עזרת נשים) for which no penalty was incurred. In Shiloh, there were only two camps. Rabbah suggests that the missing camp was the camp of the Levites.

sub.text: Baraita citation: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Baraita citation: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai states that there was an additional camp (the חיל or עזרת נשים) for which no penalty was incurred, and that in Shiloh there were only two camps.
The Gemara asks which of the two camps was missing in Shiloh.
Rabbah suggests that the missing camp was the camp of the Levites (מחנה לויה), reasoning that if it were otherwise, a difficulty would arise.

items.text: Gemara's question on the number of camps
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the number of camps
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how zavim and those impure from a corpse can be sent outside one camp when the Torah says 'do not defile their camps', implying multiple camps. It suggests that each impurity requires its own camp.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how zavim and those impure from a corpse can be sent outside one camp when the Torah says 'do not defile their camps' (plural), implying each impurity requires its own camp.

items.text: Rava's objection
items.text_en: Rava's objection
items.desc_en: Rava objects: if so, zavim and lepers would be sent to the same place, but the Torah says 'he shall dwell alone'—no other impure person with him. This refutes the previous suggestion.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects: if so, zavim and lepers would be sent to the same place, contradicting the Torah's command 'he shall dwell alone' (בדד ישב) that no other impure person may stay with a leper.

items.text: Resolution: three camps, but only two for refuge
items.text_en: Resolution: three camps, but only two for refuge
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that there were indeed three camps in the wilderness, but the statement 'only two camps' refers to cities of refuge. It then asks whether the Levite camp in the wilderness served as a refuge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that there were indeed three camps, and the statement 'there were only two camps' refers to the cities of refuge (קליטה), implying that in the wilderness the Levite camp served as a refuge.
The Gemara asks whether the Levite camp in the wilderness served as a refuge.

items.text: Proof that the Levite camp in the wilderness was a refuge
items.text_en: Proof that the Levite camp in the wilderness was a refuge
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that the verse 'I will appoint you a place' teaches that they exiled to the wilderness, specifically to the Levite camp. It then derives that a Levite who kills goes from his district to another, and his own district does not absorb him, based on a verse from Rav Acha bar Rav Ika.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that the verse 'וְשַׂמְתִּי לְךָ מָקוֹם' (I will appoint you a place) teaches that manslaughter exiles to the wilderness, specifically to the Levite camp.
The baraita rules that a Levite who kills goes from his district to another, and his own district absorbs him.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's proof
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's proof
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika cites the verse 'כִּי בְעִיר מִקְלָטוֹ יֵשֵׁב' (for in his city of refuge he shall dwell) to prove that a Levite's own district absorbs him.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on sacrifices at Gilgal
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on sacrifices at Gilgal
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute: Rabbi Meir says that all vowed and freewill offerings were brought at the bamah (high place) in Gilgal, including meal-offerings and nazirite offerings. The Sages say only burnt-offerings and peace-offerings were brought by individuals.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis taught: when they came to Gilgal, every vowed or freewill offering was brought on a private altar (במה), but not obligatory offerings; this is the view of Rabbi Meir.
The Sages say: an individual only brought burnt offerings (עולות) and peace offerings (שלמים) on the private altar.
The Sages disagree, stating that individuals only brought burnt-offerings and peace-offerings at the bamah (high place).

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion on Gilgal
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion on Gilgal
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda says that whatever the community and individual offered in the Tabernacle in the wilderness was offered in the Tabernacle at Gilgal, but the difference is that private bamot were permitted at Gilgal. On his private bamah, one only offered burnt-offerings and peace-offerings.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda says: whatever the community and individual offered in the Tabernacle in the wilderness, they offered in the Tabernacle at Gilgal; the difference is that private altars were permitted at Gilgal, but one could only offer burnt offerings and peace offerings on his rooftop altar.
Rabbi Yehuda asks what distinguishes the Tabernacle in the wilderness from the Tabernacle at Gilgal.
Rabbi Yehuda answers that at Gilgal private bamot were permitted, unlike in the wilderness.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that on one's private bamah one only offered burnt-offerings and peace-offerings.

items.text: Sages and Rabbi Shimon's opinions
items.text_en: Sages and Rabbi Shimon's opinions
items.desc_en: The Sages say that only what the community offered in the wilderness Tabernacle was offered at Gilgal, and individuals only brought burnt-offerings and peace-offerings. Rabbi Shimon adds that the community only brought Passover offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Sages say: whatever the community offered in the Tabernacle in the wilderness, they offered in the Tabernacle at Gilgal; but here and there an individual only offered burnt offerings and peace offerings.
Rabbi Shimon says: even the community only offered Passover offerings (פסחים) at Gilgal.

items.text: Opening statement of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening statement of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that obligatory offerings that have a fixed time may not be brought on a private bamah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that obligatory offerings with a fixed time may not be brought on a private bamah.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Meir's reasoning and the Rabbis' response
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Meir's reasoning and the Rabbis' response
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Meir's reason from the verse 'Do not do as we do here today' – that in the Land of Israel, only voluntary offerings (like meal-offerings and Nazirite offerings) are brought, not obligatory ones. The Rabbis counter that meal-offerings are not brought on a bamah, and Nazirite offerings are obligatory.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind Rabbi Meir's position.

sub.text: Gemara's answer citing Rabbi Meir's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer citing Rabbi Meir's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir derives from the verse 'לֹא תַעֲשׂוּן' (Do not do as we do here today) that in the Land of Israel, only voluntary offerings (ישרות) like meal-offerings and Nazirite offerings are brought, not obligatory ones.
The Rabbis counter that meal-offerings are not brought on a private bamah, and Nazirite offerings are obligatory, not voluntary.

items.text: Shmuel's first statement on the scope of the dispute
items.text_en: Shmuel's first statement on the scope of the dispute
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis is only regarding sin-offerings and guilt-offerings, but regarding burnt-offerings and peace-offerings, all agree they are voluntary and may be brought.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis is limited to sin-offerings (חטאת) and guilt-offerings (אשם), but regarding burnt-offerings (עולה) and peace-offerings (שלמים), all agree they are voluntary (ישרות) and may be brought.

items.text: Rabbah's objection to Shmuel's first statement
items.text_en: Rabbah's objection to Shmuel's first statement
items.desc_en: Rabbah raises an objection from a baraita about the breast, thigh, and bread of a thanksgiving-offering that are practiced on a large bamah but not a small one, and notes that the foreleg is omitted. If the dispute is about burnt-offerings and peace-offerings, the baraita aligns with the Rabbis; but if it is about sin-offerings and guilt-offerings, the baraita is difficult to explain.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah cites a baraita listing the breast, thigh, and bread of a thanksgiving-offering as practices on a large bamah but not a small one, noting that the foreleg is omitted.

Rabbah argues that if the dispute is about burnt-offerings and peace-offerings, the baraita aligns with the Rabbis, but if it is about sin-offerings and guilt-offerings, the baraita is difficult to explain.

items.text: Shmuel's revised statement
items.text_en: Shmuel's revised statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that if Shmuel's statement was said, it was said in the reverse: the dispute is about burnt-offerings and peace-offerings, but regarding sin-offerings and guilt-offerings, all agree they are obligatory and not brought.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by stating that Shmuel's statement was actually said in the reverse: the dispute is about burnt-offerings and peace-offerings, but regarding sin-offerings and guilt-offerings, all agree they are obligatory and not brought.

items.text: Explanation of the Rabbis' reasoning
items.text_en: Explanation of the Rabbis' reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Rabbis' reason from the verse 'Each man does what is right in his eyes' – an individual may only bring voluntary offerings, but the community may even bring obligatory offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the Rabbis' position from the Mishnah regarding what may be brought on a private altar (במה קטנה).
The Gemara asks for the scriptural basis of the Rabbis' ruling.
