The Gemara cites the verse 'אִישׁ הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו יַעֲשֶׂה' (Each man does what is right in his eyes) to derive that an individual may only bring voluntary offerings (ישרות), but the community may even bring obligatory offerings (חובות).

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's view on chovot at the great bamah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's view on chovot at the great bamah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda argues that the verse 'the upright in his eyes' applies only to the small bamah, but at the great bamah even chovot may be brought. The Gemara questions the word 'ish' which seems to limit offerings to voluntary ones, and answers that 'ish' comes to include a non-priest (zar), not to exclude chovot. The Gemara then notes that the zar's inclusion is already derived from another verse, but the teaching is needed to avoid requiring firstborn consecration.

items.text: Identifying the dispute between the first Tanna and the Sages
items.text_en: Identifying the dispute between the first Tanna and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Sages seem identical to the first Tanna (Tanna Kamma). Rav Pappa explains that the difference between them is whether libations (nesachim) were brought in the wilderness.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's reasoning and Rabbi Yochanan's teaching
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's reasoning and Rabbi Yochanan's teaching
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Shimon's view that only chovot similar to the Pesach offering were brought at the great bamah, based on the verse about the Pesach in Gilgal. The other opinion (the Rabbis) uses the verse for Rabbi Yochanan's teaching that an uncircumcised person can receive sprinkling (haza'ah).

items.text: The Tanna's statement about the great and small bamah
items.text_en: The Tanna's statement about the great and small bamah
items.desc_en: A Tanna taught before Rav Adda bar Ahavah that the only difference between the great bamah and the small bamah is regarding Pesach and chovot with a fixed time. Rav Adda questioned: for an individual, where do we find chovot with a fixed time? The Tanna suggested interpreting the statement as referring to an obligatory olah (which has a voluntary counterpart), since an individual's chatat has no fixed time. The Gemara then considers a minchat chovah, but the Tanna holds that there is no minchah on a bamah.

items.text: The nature of the Shiloh sanctuary
items.text_en: The nature of the Shiloh sanctuary
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the description of Shiloh as having no roof but stones below and curtains above, and being called 'menuchah' (rest). Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan cites verses that indicate Shiloh was a temporary structure, not a permanent building.

items.text: Source for eating kodshei kodashim outside the sanctuary
items.text_en: Source for eating kodshei kodashim outside the sanctuary
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the rule that kodshei kodashim (most holy sacrifices) could be eaten anywhere one sees (i.e., within the camp). Rabbi Oshaya derives from a verse that one may not offer burnt offerings everywhere but may eat everywhere. The Gemara questions whether the verse might permit slaughtering everywhere, but Rabbi Yannai and Rabbi Avdimi bar Chassa cite other verses to clarify that the permission is for eating, not slaughtering.

items.text: Interpretations of the name 'Shiloh' and the blessing of Joseph
items.text_en: Interpretations of the name 'Shiloh' and the blessing of Joseph
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with two interpretations of the verse 'וְלוֹ תַּאֲנַת שִׁילֹה' and the blessing 'בֵּן פֹּרָת יוֹסֵף'. Rabbi Avahu and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina each explain that the eye that refrained from benefiting from what was not its own will be rewarded by eating to its fill or among the hated ones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by interpreting the verse 'וְלוֹ תַּאֲנַת שִׁילֹה' as a place where every viewer sighs over the loss of its sacred offerings.
Rabbi Avahu explains that the eye that refrained from benefiting from what was not its own will be rewarded by eating to its fill.
Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina offers an alternative interpretation: the eye that refrained from benefiting from what was not its own will be rewarded by eating among the hated ones.

items.text: Definition of 'seeing' the Tabernacle and unresolved questions
items.text_en: Definition of 'seeing' the Tabernacle and unresolved questions
items.desc_en: A Tanna states that 'seeing' means seeing the entire Tabernacle, not just a part that interrupts. Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim explains this to Rabbi Elazar with an example like the synagogue of Maon. Rav Pappa argues it means seeing part of it. Rav Pappa and Rabbi Yirmeya raise unresolved questions about cases where one sees while standing but not while sitting, or from above a stream but not within it.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna states that 'seeing' the Tabernacle means seeing the entire structure, not just a part that interrupts between the viewer and the Tabernacle.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim's explanation to Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim's explanation to Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim explains to Rabbi Elazar that the Tanna's statement is analogous to the synagogue of Maon, where one must see the entire building.
Rav Pappa argues that 'seeing' means seeing only part of the Tabernacle, not the entire structure.
Rav Pappa raises an unresolved question: if one sees the Tabernacle while standing but not while sitting, does that count as 'seeing'?
Rabbi Yirmeya raises another unresolved question: if one sees the Tabernacle from above a stream but not from within it, does that count as 'seeing'?
The gemara concludes that both questions remain unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rabbi's statement on the three places of the Shechinah
items.text_en: Rabbi's statement on the three places of the Shechinah
items.desc_en: Rabbi states that the Shechinah rested on Israel in three places: Shiloh, Nov and Givon, and the eternal Temple, and all were in the portion of Benjamin, as derived from the verse 'חֹפֵף עָלָיו כׇּל הַיּוֹם'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports in the name of Rabbi that the Divine Presence rested on Israel in three places—Shiloh, Nov and Givon, and the eternal Temple—and all were in the portion of Benjamin.

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding the Shechinah in Benjamin's portion
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding the Shechinah in Benjamin's portion
items.desc_en: Abaye reports a challenge from Kaylil: if the Shechinah was only in Benjamin's portion, why does the verse say God forsook Shiloh and rejected the tent of Joseph? Rav Adda suggests the Shechinah was in Benjamin but the Sanhedrin was in Joseph's portion, similar to the Temple where the Shechinah was in Benjamin and the Sanhedrin in Judah. The Gemara resolves that a strip of land extended from Joseph's portion into Benjamin's, as taught by Rabbi Chama bar Chanina, and this is the meaning of 'תַּאֲנַת שִׁילֹה'.

sub.desc_en: Abaye reports Kaylil's challenge: if the Shechinah was only in Benjamin's portion, why does the verse say God forsook Shiloh and rejected the tent of Joseph?
Rav Adda answers that the Shechinah was in Benjamin's portion while the Sanhedrin was in Joseph's portion, analogous to the Temple where the Shechinah was in Benjamin and the Sanhedrin in Judah.
The Gemara objects that in the Temple the portions of Benjamin and Judah were adjacent, but Joseph's portion was far from Benjamin's.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution via Rabbi Chama bar Chanina
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution via Rabbi Chama bar Chanina
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that a strip of land extended from Joseph's portion into Benjamin's, as taught by Rabbi Chama bar Chanina, and this is the meaning of 'תַּאֲנַת שִׁילֹה'.

items.text: Tannaitic interpretations of 'חֹפֵף עָלָיו'
items.text_en: Tannaitic interpretations of 'חֹפֵף עָלָיו'
items.desc_en: A Tanna interprets the verse as referring to the First Temple, Second Temple, and the days of the Messiah. Rabbi offers an alternative interpretation: this world, the days of the Messiah, and the World to Come.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma interprets the verse 'חֹפֵף עָלָיו' as referring to the First Temple, 'כָּל הַיּוֹם' to the Second Temple, and 'וּבֵין כְּתֵפָיו שָׁכֵן' to the days of the Messiah.
Rabbi offers an alternative interpretation: 'חוֹפֵף עָלָיו' refers to this world, 'כָּל הַיּוֹם' to the days of the Messiah, and 'וּבֵין כְּתֵפָיו שָׁכֵן' to the World to Come.

items.text: Chronology of the Tabernacle periods
items.text_en: Chronology of the Tabernacle periods
items.desc_en: The Gemara calculates the years of the Tabernacle in the wilderness (39 years), Gilgal (14 years), Nov and Givon (57 years), and Shiloh (369 years). It derives these from verses: the wilderness period from the year of the spies, Gilgal from Caleb's age, Nov and Givon from the time of the ark in Kiryat Ye'arim and the reigns of Samuel, Saul, and David.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the total years of the Tabernacle in each period: wilderness (39 years), Gilgal (14 years), Nov and Givon (57 years), and Shiloh (369 years).
The Gemara derives the 39 wilderness years from Mar's statement that the first year Moses built the Tabernacle and the second year it was erected and the spies were sent.
The Gemara derives the 14 years of Gilgal from Caleb's statement that he was 40 when sent as a spy and 85 when he spoke, indicating 7 years of conquest.
The Gemara calculates that Caleb was 78 when crossing the Jordan, and his statement at 85 confirms 7 years of conquest.
The Gemara offers a first answer: the 7 years of division are derived from the parallel of 7 years of conquest.
The Gemara offers a second answer: the 14 years are derived from the verse 'after the city was smitten' (Joshua 14:10), which implies 14 years of conquest and division.

sub.text: Gemara's question for Nov and Givon
sub.text_en: Gemara's question for Nov and Givon
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the 57 years of Nov and Givon.
The Gemara cites the verse about mentioning the ark and the baraita that Shiloh was destroyed when Eli died, then Nov when Samuel died, leading to Givon.
The Gemara cites the verse that the ark was in Kiryat Ye'arim for 20 years, which is part of the calculation for Nov and Givon.
The Gemara breaks down the 20 years into 10 years of Samuel's sole reign, 1 year of Samuel and Saul, 2 years of Saul, and 7 years of David, totaling 57 years for Nov and Givon.

items.text: Calculation of years for Shiloh
items.text_en: Calculation of years for Shiloh
items.desc_en: The Gemara calculates the years of David's reign and Shlomo's building to determine that Shiloh's duration was 369 years.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara calculates the years of David's reign and Shlomo's building to determine that Shiloh's duration was 369 years.

items.text: Source for the distinction between Shiloh and Jerusalem
items.text_en: Source for the distinction between Shiloh and Jerusalem
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that interprets 'rest' as Shiloh and 'inheritance' as Jerusalem, explaining that the verse separates them to permit offerings between the two periods.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive the distinction between Nov and Givon and the periods of Shiloh and Jerusalem?
The baraita interprets 'rest' as Shiloh and 'inheritance' as Jerusalem, explaining that the verse separates them to permit offerings between the two periods.

items.text: Question about ma'aser sheni and answer according to Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Question about ma'aser sheni and answer according to Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks why ma'aser sheni is not listed among offerings permitted in Nov and Givon. Rabbi Yochanan answers that ma'aser sheni is derived from the Ark via a verbal analogy, and since the Ark was absent, ma'aser sheni was not brought. When challenged about Pesach and kodashim, he explains the mishna follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that only fixed-time offerings were brought, and ma'aser behemah (linked to ma'aser sheni) is not fixed-time.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan why ma'aser sheni (second tithe) is not listed among the offerings permitted in Nov and Givon.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that ma'aser sheni is derived from the Ark via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of 'שם' (there), and since the Ark was absent in Nov and Givon, ma'aser sheni was not brought.
The Gemara objects that if the verbal analogy from the Ark applies, then Pesach and kodashim (sacrifices) should also be excluded, yet they are listed in the mishna.

Rabbi Yochanan resolves that the mishna follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that only fixed-time offerings were brought in Nov and Givon; ma'aser behemah (animal tithe) is not fixed-time, and ma'aser sheni is linked to it by analogy.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's view on ma'aser in Nov and Givon
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's view on ma'aser in Nov and Givon
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that according to Rabbi Yehuda, ma'aser sheni and ma'aser behemah were eaten in Nov and Givon. Rav Adda bar Masna confirms this, and Rav Yosef's teaching about three 'birot' is reconciled by saying it refers to eating ma'aser sheni according to Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that according to Rabbi Yehuda, ma'aser sheni and ma'aser behemah were offered in Nov and Givon, and affirms this.
Rav Adda bar Masna states that ma'aser sheni and ma'aser behemah were eaten in Nov and Givon according to Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara objects that ma'aser requires a 'בירה' (central sanctuary), which Nov and Givon were not.
The Gemara cites Rav Yosef's teaching that there are only three 'בירות' (sanctuaries): Shiloh, Nov and Givon, and the eternal Temple, implying Nov and Givon were not valid for ma'aser.
Rav Yosef himself explains that his teaching about three 'בירות' refers to eating ma'aser sheni, and only according to Rabbi Yehuda's view.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on 'rest' and 'inheritance'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on 'rest' and 'inheritance'
items.desc_en: A baraita presents Rabbi Yehuda identifying 'rest' as Shiloh and 'inheritance' as Jerusalem, while Rabbi Shimon reverses them, citing supporting verses.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the verse and identifies 'rest' (מנוחה) as Shiloh and 'inheritance' (נחלה) as Jerusalem.
Rabbi Yehuda cites two supporting verses that depict Jerusalem as a problematic 'inheritance' (נחלה).
Rabbi Shimon reverses the identification: 'rest' (מנוחה) is Jerusalem and 'inheritance' (נחלה) is Shiloh, citing verses that describe Jerusalem as God's chosen 'resting place' (מנוחה).

items.text: Resolution of the verse order according to Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Resolution of the verse order according to Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse says 'rest' before 'inheritance' if Rabbi Shimon reverses them. It answers that the verse means: not only have you not reached the rest (Jerusalem), but even the inheritance (Shiloh) you have not reached.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the verse order 'rest' before 'inheritance' fits Rabbi Shimon's identification of 'rest' as Jerusalem and 'inheritance' as Shiloh, since the verse should then say 'inheritance' first.
The Gemara resolves that the verse means: not only have you not reached the rest (Jerusalem), but even the inheritance (Shiloh) you have not reached.

items.text: Alternative opinions: both refer to Shiloh or both to Jerusalem
items.text_en: Alternative opinions: both refer to Shiloh or both to Jerusalem
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael says both terms refer to Shiloh, while Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says both refer to Jerusalem. The Gemara begins to analyze these views.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael states that both terms 'מנוחה' and 'נחלה' refer to Shiloh.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai states that both terms refer to Jerusalem.

items.text: Analysis of "Menuchah" and "Nachalah" regarding Shiloh and Jerusalem
items.text_en: Analysis of "Menuchah" and "Nachalah" regarding Shiloh and Jerusalem
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the interpretation of the verse "el ha-menuchah ve-el ha-nachalah" for those who identify both terms with either Shiloh or Jerusalem, and resolves the difficulty by explaining the distinct meanings of "menuchah" (rest from conquest or rest of the Ark) and "nachalah" (division of inheritances or eternal inheritance). It also addresses the case of Manoach's offering as a hora'at sha'ah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: for the opinion that both terms refer to the same place (Shiloh or Jerusalem), the verse should have said 'menuchah nachalah' as a single phrase, not 'el ha-menuchah ve-el ha-nachalah'.
The Gemara answers that for the opinion identifying both with Shiloh, 'menuchah' refers to rest from conquest and 'nachalah' refers to the division of inheritances there, as per Joshua's allotment.
The Gemara answers that for the opinion identifying both with Jerusalem, 'nachalah' means eternal inheritance and 'menuchah' refers to the rest of the Ark, as per the verse 'when the Ark rested'.
The Gemara supports the Jerusalem opinion by noting that Manoach's offering on a private altar (במה) was permitted, consistent with the view that private altars were allowed during the Shiloh period.
The Gemara answers that for the Shiloh opinion, which forbids private altars, Manoach's offering was a hora'at sha'ah (a temporary exceptional ruling).

items.text: Support for Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's view
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's view
items.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael rules like Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who says both terms refer to Jerusalem, with a mnemonic about the men drawing each other.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael rules like Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, that both 'מנוחה' and 'נחלה' refer to Jerusalem, with a mnemonic about the men drawing each other.

items.text: Rav Kahana's statement on liability for offering outside and its refutation
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's statement on liability for offering outside and its refutation
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana asserts that the Mishnah's leniency (no karet) applies only to slaughter, but for offering (ha'ala'ah) one is liable to karet. Rabbah objects based on the verse's wording, and a baraitha of Rabbi Shimon's four categories of sacrifices regarding bamot is brought as a refutation, concluding that Rav Kahana is refuted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana asserts that the Mishnah's leniency (no karet) applies only to slaughter, but for offering (העלאה) one is liable to karet.

The Gemara asks for Rav Kahana's reasoning, and he cites the verse 'ואלהם תאמר' (to them you shall say) to argue that the prohibition applies to those who are 'adjacent' (i.e., offering after slaughter).
Rabbah objects: the verse does not read 'ועליהם' (and upon them) but 'אלהם' (to them), and we read it as 'אליהם' (to them), not supporting Rav Kahana's derivation.

A baraita of Rabbi Shimon's four categories of sacrifices regarding bamot is cited, showing that in cases where slaughter and offering occur during a forbidden period, karet applies only when both acts are done in the forbidden period, contradicting Rav Kahana's distinction.
The Gemara concludes that Rav Kahana is refuted (תיוּבתא).

items.text: Scriptural sources for practices that apply only in the Temple
items.text_en: Scriptural sources for practices that apply only in the Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists various practices (semichah, slaughter in the north, blood applications, tenufah, hagashah, priestly service, garments, vessels, re'ach nicho'ach, mechitzah, hand-washing) and cites the verses that limit them to the Temple (before Hashem).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the verse for semichah (laying of hands), showing it is limited to the Temple.
The Gemara cites verses for slaughter in the north (צפון) and blood applications around the altar, both requiring the Temple.
The Gemara cites verses for tenufah (wave offering) and hagashah (bringing near), both tied to the Temple.
Rabbi Yehuda states that there is no meal-offering (מנחה) at a private altar (במה), and Rav Sheishet deduces that the same applies to bird-offerings.
The Gemara cites the verse 'זבחים' (sacrifices) to exclude meal-offerings and bird-offerings from private altars.
The Gemara cites verses for priestly service (כהן) and sacred garments (בגדי שרת), both limited to the Temple.
The Gemara cites verses for sacred vessels (כלי שרת) and the pleasing aroma (ריח ניחוח), both tied to the Temple.
The Gemara cites verses for the blood partition (מחיצה בדמים) and hand-washing (ריחוץ ידים), both limited to the Temple.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's distinction between large and small bamot regarding mechitzah
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's distinction between large and small bamot regarding mechitzah
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama states that the Mishnah's rule (no mechitzah) applies only to sacrifices of a small bamah offered on a small bamah, but if offered on a large bamah, mechitzah applies. Rabbah challenges this with a baraitha about chazeh vashok and terumat lachmei todah, and an alternative version of Rami's statement is presented, with a supporting statement from Rabbi Elazar.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama distinguishes that the Mishnah's rule (no mechitzah) applies only to sacrifices of a small bamah offered on a small bamah, but if offered on a large bamah, mechitzah applies.
Rabbah challenges Rami bar Chama with a baraitha about chazeh vashok and terumat lachmei todah, which are practiced on a large bamah but not on a small bamah, implying the opposite distinction.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rami bar Chama's statement
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rami bar Chama's statement
sub.desc_en: An alternative version presents Rami bar Chama's statement reversed: the Mishnah's rule applies only to sacrifices of a large bamah offered on a large bamah, but for small bamah sacrifices even on a large bamah, there is no mechitzah.

sub.text: Supporting baraitha for the alternative version
sub.text_en: Supporting baraitha for the alternative version
sub.desc_en: The gemara suggests that the baraitha about chazeh vashok and terumat lachmei todah supports the alternative version, as it distinguishes between large and small bamot in the opposite direction.

Rabbi Elazar states that an individual's bamah olah brought inside the Temple precincts is absorbed by the partitions for all purposes, supporting the idea that large bamah status can override small bamah rules.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry about an individual bamah olah brought inside
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry about an individual bamah olah brought inside
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira raises a question about the status of an olah from an individual bamah that was brought inside the Temple, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira raises a question about the status of an olah from an individual bamah that was brought inside the Temple, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Question about entering and exiting the inner sanctum
items.text_en: Question about entering and exiting the inner sanctum
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if an object was brought inside the inner sanctum and then taken out, does it retain the sanctity of the inner area? It suggests this may be the same dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef regarding whether an animal slaughtered in the wrong place may be brought back up to the altar. The Gemara then analyzes whether each opinion would apply here, concluding with teiku.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether an object brought into the inner sanctum and then taken out retains the sanctity of the inner area, or whether exiting nullifies it.

The Gemara suggests this question may be identical to the dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef about whether kodshei kodashim (most holy offerings) slaughtered in the south may be brought back up if they ascended.
The Gemara cites the dispute: Rabbah says they may not ascend, Rav Yosef says they may ascend.

The Gemara analyzes whether each opinion applies here: perhaps Rabbah's leniency only applies to the altar which sanctifies what is fit for it, but a partition (מחיצה) sanctifies even what is unfit; thus the question remains open for Rabbah.
The Gemara alternatively considers that even Rav Yosef might distinguish here because these are two separate locations, leaving the question unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rabbi Yannai's question about limbs of a private altar burnt offering
items.text_en: Rabbi Yannai's question about limbs of a private altar burnt offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai asks a similar question: if limbs of a burnt offering from a private altar went up onto the altar and then came down, what is the law? He specifies that the question applies only if fire had already taken hold of them. The Gemara leaves this unresolved with teiku.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai raises a question about limbs of a private-bamah olah that ascended the altar and then descended, specifically when fire had taken hold, and the Gemara leaves it unresolved (תיקו).
The Gemara leaves the question unresolved with תיקו (teiku).

items.text: Dispute about night slaughter on a private altar
items.text_en: Dispute about night slaughter on a private altar
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute whether slaughter at night on a private altar is valid. They argue based on verses from the story of Saul, where one interprets the verses as referring to non-sacred meat and the other as distinguishing between the great altar and private altars.

sub.desc_en: It was stated: Rav and Shmuel dispute whether nighttime slaughter at a private bamah is valid, and they argue based on Rabbi Elazar's teaching.
Rabbi Elazar juxtaposes two verses: one about a great stone and another about Saul telling the people to slaughter at night, showing a contradiction.
One master (Rav) resolves the contradiction: one verse refers to non-sacred animals, the other to sacred offerings.
The other master (Shmuel) resolves the contradiction: one verse refers to offerings of the great bamah (Mishkan), the other to offerings of a private bamah.

items.text: Dispute about flaying and cutting up a private altar burnt offering
items.text_en: Dispute about flaying and cutting up a private altar burnt offering
items.desc_en: Rav and Rabbi Yochanan dispute whether a burnt offering on a private altar requires flaying and cutting up. They base their views on Rabbi Yose HaGelili's statement about the wilderness offerings, with one holding that these requirements apply only to the great altar and the other that they apply to both great and small altars.

sub.desc_en: It was stated: Rav and Rabbi Yochanan dispute whether a private-bamah olah requires flaying and dismemberment, and they argue based on Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili states that the olah offered in the wilderness did not require flaying and dismemberment, as this practice only began from the Tent of Meeting onward.
One master (Rav) holds that from the Tent of Meeting onward, there is no difference between great and small bamot — both require flaying and dismemberment.
The other master (Rabbi Yochanan) holds that flaying and dismemberment apply only to the great bamah, not to a private bamah.

items.text: Baraita listing differences and similarities between great and small altars
items.text_en: Baraita listing differences and similarities between great and small altars
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Yochanan's view, listing items unique to the great altar (horn, ramp, base, square, laver, breast and thigh) and items common to both (slaughter, flaying and cutting up, blood permitting and causing piggul, blemishes, and time). The Gemara then derives that the laws of leftover (notar) and piggul apply to private altars as well, using a logical comparison.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists items unique to the great altar (horn, ramp, base, square, laver, breast and thigh).
The baraita lists items common to both altars: slaughter, flaying, cutting up, blood permitting and causing piggul, blemishes, and time.
The baraita concludes that leftover (notar), time, and impurity are treated equally on both altars.
The baraita derives that the law of time (זמן) applies to the small altar by analogy from piggul: just as piggul disqualifies on a private altar, so too leftover (לן) disqualifies.

The Gemara raises an alternative analogy: leftover (לן) could be compared to 'outside' (יוצא), which is valid on a private altar, but then rejects this by noting a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from birds.

items.text: Kal vachomer from bird offerings
items.text_en: Kal vachomer from bird offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer: if bird offerings, which are not invalidated by a blemish, are invalidated by time, then offerings of a small bamah, which are invalidated by a blemish, should certainly be invalidated by time.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if bird offerings, which are not invalidated by a blemish, are invalidated by time, then offerings of a small bamah (private altar), which are invalidated by a blemish, should certainly be invalidated by time.

sub.text: Gemara's objection to the kal vachomer
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to the kal vachomer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: what is true of bird offerings is that a non-priest (זר) is not qualified to offer them, but in a small bamah a non-priest is qualified; therefore the kal vachomer is refuted — time should not invalidate there.

The Gemara resolves the objection by citing the verse 'וְזֹאת תּוֹרַת זֶבַח הַשְּׁלָמִים' (and this is the law of the peace-offering), which teaches that the time restriction of a small bamah is equated to that of a large bamah (the Tabernacle).

items.text: Refutation and scriptural answer
items.text_en: Refutation and scriptural answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara refutes the kal vachomer by noting that bird offerings have a stricter element (a non-priest is invalid for them), which does not apply to a small bamah. It then cites a verse to establish that the time limit applies to a small bamah as it does to the large bamah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara refutes the kal vachomer by pointing out that bird offerings have a stricter element (a non-priest is invalid for them), which does not apply to a small bamah.
The Gemara cites a verse to establish that the time limit applies to a small bamah as it does to the large bamah.
